The music has introduced me to a genre I've been hooked on eversince I first heard the soundtrack, making me look for more artists similar to the holy grail provided in the game.
I won't review the story, but I need to bring out how the game is paced. One hit kills for you and the enemy. If you die, you don't see it coming, it doesn't waste time with multiple menus and loading the save again- you just press R and get back into the action. This is a game about the adrenaline, you can't have boring words and options keeping you from the seconds of action you often have on a life. Lives? There is no game over here, you keep creating alternative realities until you get it right. Four thousand or a million deaths doesn't even mean a game over anymore- just the R button, which kicks you back into the action.
Let's say you're taking your driving test, you ♥♥♥♥ up on something small and have to wait a week before being able to take it again. Now imagine if you could just press a button and run it again instantly? The hormones are off the scale!
I recommend this game from the bottom of my heart.

Middle-earth: Shadow of War is the sequel to the popular wide open sandbox, action RPG videogame Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor by Monolith productions. Taking place in the famous fantasy setting envisioned by J. R. R. Tolkien (albeit in an alternate timeline), this sequel continues the story of Talion, a Gondorian ranger living on the borders of Mordor who has been killed by Sauron's forces and is now bound to the wraith of Celebrimbor, the elven smith who created the Ring of Powers and was betrayed by the Dark Lord himself. In Shadow of War the duo create a New Ring in order to arness unspeakable powers and defeat Sauron, the Witch-King of Angmar, the Ringwraiths and their hordes of uruks once and for all.
As a sequel to a very successfull game, Shadow of War manages to improve on many elements of the original Shadow of Mordor while also adding some very interesting and entertaining features. On top of tweaks to general gameplay (including stealth, combat, abilities) and a much more unique and contestualized presentation for the side quests, this sequel offers the following major additions:
1) Instead of a single, huge game's world map divided into two very similar zones, Shadow of War features a big region's map you can navigate and check available quests on and several sub-regions where the actual gameplay takes place. Said sub-regions are bigh enough on their own and offer very different environments. The transiction between the various areas you can acess is incredibly well-done and makes moving around incredibly easy.
2) There's now a gear system available for Talion: high-ranked uruks have always a chance to drop a particular piece of gear you can equip to boost your defense as well as gain new passive abilities by either wearing all the parts of a given set or complete specific challenges. You can equip a sword, a bow, a dagger, a cape, an armor and a rune for the New Ring and all the pieces come in different qualities (depending on the uruk who dropped them). You can also randomly find gems you can socket into your gear: these gives benefits like increased damage, health or experience/loot and they can be combined into superior gems with better effects.
3) Each region of the world features a fortress you can capture with your army. You can either go on the offense, taking on the enemy warchiefs protecting it with their own men and defenses, culminating in a climatic battle with the resident, powerful enemy overlord, or defend a fortress you already attacked from an invading enemy horde and its captains. Said sieges revolve around taking a hold of a fortress' control points and guide your followers to victory. All in all, they are a nice change of pace in the gameplay and feels appriopriately epic.
The nemesis system, the main selling point of Shadow of Mordor, also makes a come back in Shadow of War, and it has been greatly expanded: not only you can meet even more diverse and unique uruks (who now can also come in epic and legendary qualities), but you are now given far more options in dealing with them, especially when it comes to branded orcs, who can now be banished from your army, be revived in a pinch or summoned as loyal bodyguards. That said, a lot of features from the new system are completely based on a player's bad luck and are totally outside of your control, which can get annoying after a while (especially when it comes to betrayals, where a branded orc will leave your army for no reason at all).
Shadow of War also features more fullfilling boss fights than the original game, althought many of them are about defeating incredibly powerful, premade uruk captains or facing the same kind of unique enemy over and over again, only with a different skin and slightly different attacks.
This sequel also contains an in-game shops which allows you to buy RNG loot boxes (either with the in-game currency you can farm in-game or with real money) containing a random set of powerful equipment or uruk captains, ready to be used. Althought said addition was totally uncalled for and doesn't have much of a place in a single player game, it is completely possible to finish the whole game without having to buy something from the shop ever.
That said, it does make level grinding a lot easier, and it doesn't help that the final leg of the game, the fourth act (dubbed Shadow Wars), is basically a huge playable epilogue with no new story nor gameplay where the player is pretty much forced into an extensive level grinding in order to overcome high-level fortress scenarios and unlock the true ending of the game. As anyone could figure out, this last act is arguably one of the weakest part of the entire game and a pain to see through the very end.
The main story of Shadow of War is a fair improvement over the plot of the first game, with a more interesting plot, new and unique characters who interact between themselves in beliveable ways and an ending which really sticks to the main themes of Tolkien's narrative. That said, this time around the writers decided to follow the books' lore far less closely, to the point that several plot elements and how some characters were adapted for the game will appear with very little sense to whoever read Tolkien's novels: the "rule of cool" over a faithful adaptation is therefore in full effect here.
While I'd had preferred this sequel to end in a more satisfying manner (gameplay-wise) and there were a pletora of other small and big things to be further improved by the developers, Middle-earth: Shadow of War still remains a very strong follow-up to a very good game and manages to be a very entertaining experience for most of the ride

The appeal of life is strange relies on the charisma of the town it created: characters, setting, art style and dialogue all melt pretty nicely to create something that is clearly a work of fiction, but
real; it's high school drama, weird town mysteries and a touch of sci fi. But personally it's a divisive game.
The "Twin Peaks" appeal of this game is what ultimately draws the player in, the sci fi aspect brings an interesting gameplay mechanic but doesn't have a consistent logic, feels complimentary to the story, not part of it. The emotional attachment is entirely dependant on the player's relationship to Chloe, but the circumstances sorrounding the character are more effective at making you feel sorry for her rather than making her likeable.
Ultimately the game aknowledges all of your choices, but still offers two possible outcomes in the end.
In short, Life is Strange wasn't the masterpiece I expected, under deeper analysis it has many flaws for a very minimal gameplay experience,
it's a unique experience that can be an emotionally rewarding ride for those who enjoy the game without questioning it too much.

If you're looking for a hidden gem, then the UFO Aftermath, Aftershock and Afterlight games are certainly that in my opinion, Please don't let low hours on steam reflect my review as I had all of these as new games on CD.
They have flaws for sure, yet there is something about these games that when I saw them on steam I bought them again (Old disks are long gone now) There used to be a good comunity of and most likely these mods can still be found online.
You can set the games up to be real time with three speed settings, fully turn based or a combination of both, choosing for example to pause the game when an enemy is sighted (A range of other options) but allowing play to run while fighting.
You get a squad of soldiers to train up, each of the three games does this slightly differently, They also do bases slightly different with Afterlight giving you only one base.
You also choose which research to focus on, what weapons and equipment to build, There is not an extensive list of these thigns and often the research is tied into the story, i.e you research a certain thing and the plot advances.
The missions while they can get repetative towards the end, can be delegated to "civilian" forces, local militias etc allowing your squad of soldiers to focus on the ones you think are important.
These games don't cost a lot now and I felt were worth the money when they came out.

Firstly,
This game is fantastic, I was a huge fan of Mafia 2 and I must have played it 4-5 times until Mafia 3 came out.
All this FPS drama aside, I'm running a 980ti and the frames hold steady on high at 30, maybe I'm lucky but the game is smooth as butter and I've had the pleasure of live streaming it at 720p while I did so.....so perhaps everyone else is just having a rough go of it?
Immersion- The immersion of this game is fantastic, if not as fantastic as Mafia II, the original soundtracks, the absolutely dominantly realistic (If set for Simulation) car handling and the absolutely 'abhorrent' racism, shines light on the character, the game and the feel of the century.
Combat/Gore/Fights- Needless to say, if you dominated Mafia II, don't even waste your time setting this game on "Normal" difficulty, crank it straight up to Hard or higher, otherwise you're gonna breeze through it. The headshot gore is phenominal, the brain matter, the blood pooling etc, brings realism to it all and makes you wanna do it AGAIN and AGAIN. The animations of the AI when you shoot them, weather it be via the leg, the arm, the chest, is extremely well responded and realistic weather it be a shot to the leg causing them to limp around, or a chest shot putting the guy on the ground crying for his mommy before you cap him again in his miserable face.
I could go all day about the things I love about this game.
CONS: (Not going to address things such as FPS or Outfits, which are already being worked on in patches. However, needless to say...should have been in the release from the start, but respect 2K's decision in focusing on the stuff that mattered first and foremost and the game is great without them for the time being.)
-The story is phenominal, but keep in mind there is A LOT more 'side content' in Mafia III than there was in Mafia II (if there was any) which leads you randomly tangenting yourself from the main story, which isn't necessarily a con. But I felt that a lot of the side stuff, didn't quite tie to the main stuff?
-Police are wonky? I've done some pretty horrendous stuff infront of officers and they don't always seem to respond, let alone that the "Witness" system is too easily devoided. A lady spots you murder someone, you run her down and knock her out cold infront of dozens of other civilians and no one seems to give a damn.....police encounter avoided?
Also keep in mind, that police no longer seem to drop AMMO, so if you're looking to have a long term gun fight with the cops......don't. You will eventually die, getting swarmed by 30 cops and having no ammo, even though you gunned down 15+ dudes with pistols all of which would use the same ammo as your own?
-Bugs (My run in's with these are minor, also I hardly care because it's a release and i've come to accept they always have them.) AI Stuck in the walls, Can't get into some vehicles, Cops not responsive.
-Also on a side note, from my personal experience, the "Racket" missions that take place AFTER you've taken and assigned a district, such as "Weed Smuggling" are relatively not well detailed and don't do a good job explaining, just how you go do them. So make sure you listen closely to them when they talk about you "extending" their business, also check your Assets, in the menu. If you click the Asset it will show you the Racket missions available, even though they aren't on the map?

Update 25.03.15
Positive:
+ Terrain deformation
+ Tire pressure simulation
+ Realistic water behaviour
+ Driving physics in general
+ Maps are pretty big, and full of challenging terrain
+ You can mow down trees ^_^
+ Multiplayer
+ Vehicles of all sizes, ranging from the small UAZ (Jeep) to the monstrous 8x8 Maz.
+ Winching is fun and very useful. You can attach it to both other vehicles and trees.
+ Attaching a crane to your truck, to pick up lumber, move rocks out of the way and sometimes to help push the truck up.
+ The game is very well optimized.
+ Trucks take damage, and consume fuel. You can install a utility addon for mobile repairs, or a fuel cistern for re-fueling in the field.
+ Patch released on 27/10 -14 added wheel support.
+ Patch released on 27/10 -14 added analogue controller input.
+ Patch implemented individual saves for all maps. Big plus in my book.
Negative:
- The camera could be much better. With the tallest addons it can be a real challenge to see ahead.
- Maps could be more varied. It's mostly the same mix of grass, trees, mud and water.
- The only official objective is to haul lumber. More variety would be welcome.
- Lack of proper manual shifting.
- Draw distance should be customizable.
With all that said... As a VIP backer on the kickstarter campaign, and having had access to the beta since May 9, I can safely recommend this game to anyone with an interest in off-roading. If you've tried the tech demo, you know what to expect. Just think bigger; more trucks, more functionality and much bigger maps. All in all, even in beta, this is perhaps the most fun I have had in a realistic off-road game so far. Try the tech demo first; if you like it - there's a safe bet that you will enjoy the full game.
The devs seem committed to continuing to improve the game after launch, both with free updates and dlc packs later on.

Let me start this off by saying I personally love this game but I still wouldn't recommend it at full price.
The game is great and the they've done almost a complete remake of the UI and the skill tree this go around. Some of the new abilities as well as how some of the mechanics work is a tad hard to grasp at first, but once you get into the swing of things it becomes second nature almost. The story has moments where thing really take off and you want to see where and how thing play out and other times you really just want to skip this damned cutscene because it's so drab and boring. Like some other RPGs there are going to be main story quests that are more of a chore and tedious rather than fun, but for me, the gameplay makes up for it. It's just as, if not more, satisfying in this game to cut someone in half or decapitate them this go around.
The strongest aspect of this game is obviously the Nemises system and forging your army of Uruks and Ologs. And damn is it fun. The fact that you get to take over strongholds and make them your own and you're able to put one of your own stronger orcs in charge is cool as hell. The grind to get your army up to par for storming the strong hold can be a bit of time consumer, but it's all worth it when you're sitting at the fortress gates with the orcs you've honed and trained for those few hours and you finally take down the overlord of that area.
And the fact that every fight is different keeps you on your toes constantly. While I was completing some side quests, two orcs that defied death came back as legendaries to come and kill me at the same time. Mind you I was already facing ANOTHER legendy orc already. The battle was long and difficult but I'd be lying if I said I didn't feel like a champion when I came out on top of that epic fight.
Gear drops like pinata candy in this one so dont bother trying to stock up on anything, even if you may like the item, there's almost an 80% chance that you're going to get something that does what your current gear already does, but better.
The scenery is just as breath taking as it was in the last game. Old fortresses taken over by time and nature, baren landscapes due to over foraging from orc tribes, great vistas from high vantage points. All of these are back in this new game and look just as good, if not better.
My biggest personal gripe is like I said, the tedious story missions and cutscenes that you can't skip or speed through. Such as following a certain character to a point on the map. They wont reveal the point on the map and force you to follow this person, who walks slower than old ladies at the damn super market. And there are A LOT of missions like that.
Now let me get back to the reason why i don't recommend this game at full price. Other than the new UI, the upgraded nemises system, and the better graphics, there's really not much that's different about this game compared to SOM. That's not exactly a bad thing. I mean "if it ain't broke don't fix it", right? But with that being said, it doesn't really feel like a step up from the last game, it really just seems like you're playing SOM that has some new DLCs and patch updates. If that doesn't bother you and you really want to buy this game now, by all means go ahead. But if you can wait until it drops down to at least 30 bucks, then I'd recommend you do that.
All in all 7/10, would fist uruks again.

Stephen King once wrote that “Nightmares exist outside of logic, and there’s little fun to be had in explanations; they’re antithetical to the poetry of fear.”
Alan Wake, a survival horror game developed by Remedy Entertainment and published by Microsoft Game Studios. You are Alan Wake a best selling thriller novelist trapped in a horror story he wrote which has to come to life and has taken his wife. The game is heavily inspired by thriller which draws concepts from the T.V show Twin Peaks and draws inspiration from the works of Stephen King!
As Alan Wake you must battle through the night to fight the Taken, a darkness that takes over living things and brings life to inanimate objects while trying to find yourself and your wife, which the darkness has taken. Gameplay is in third person and the primary weapon used in the game is light (Flashlight, Flares, flareguns, environmental lighting, flashbangs) as well as guns.  Fighting through lush green national parks and into the town of Bright Falls, Washington the atmosphere psychologically engulfs you, waking up from this nightmare is not an option!
Pros:
-The use of light as a weapon
-A great story, short but sweet will really leave you with a "Wow, amazing!"
-The atmosphere although intense is also distrubing and horrifying
-Narration really makes it easy to understand whats really going on.
-Truly is a great looking game, feels like you're really in a national park XD
-Highly replayabe, played through about 4 times
-Combat mechanics make you feel like your are constantly in danger
-Stephen king, Stephen king, Stephen king, Stephen king!
Cons:
-Weak ending
-The game was a little short but there are DLC as well as American Nightmare.
-Facial animations could've been done better
-The recaps at the end of each chapter aren't necessary, it does feel like its trying to be a T.V show
But all in all a solid and rich game full of awesome, 10 foxes out 10 foxes, put de lime in de coconut!

If I'm being honest, this wouldn't exactly be a game I would otherwise have chosen to play. I'm more into games which have a grander scale. But, after being recommended it, I bought it and decided to give it a try. ... My God, it was so worth it. I can only name a single major flaw in this game (beyond my personal biases) which is that ultimately your choices culminate in naught; you choose one path or another and that is how it ends. Other than that, 'Life is Strange' has an interesting plot, compelling characters who in their own ways have their own developments (even your main tormentor in later episodes...assuming you're patient with her of course, shows herself to be a decent person at heart), an absolutely amazing soundtrack (the outro of Episode 2 with it for example is masterful), and a lot of emotional weight. I'm not a sentimental person but this game had me bawling my eyes out several times (y'all know which moments I'm talking about).
If you want a primarily linear experience which focuses on character development, exemplary story-telling and a ride on an emotional rollercoaster, take a chance on 'Life is Strange,' I hope you enjoy it just as much as I have.

Don't bother. If you want X-Com style gameplay, go get the original X-Coms, the new XCOMs, Xenonauts, Rebelstar: Tactical Command (okay, that last one is for Game Boy Advance, but still. Get it), or check out others.
This game has some serious problems with its difficulty, and I've only been playing on Medium. Early on, it's way too easy. Gather your guys in one blob, roll them around the map, and concentrate fire on one enemy at a time.
Later, the aliens start using explosives. Or fire. Or bees (not kidding). They will kill you in two, three hits tops. All of you. You will die. Think the aliens used grenades too much in X-Com? Buddy, those guys got NOTHING on the AOE-spamming aliens here.
Tactical movement does not help. This only separates your guys, and makes it easier for them to die, alone, cold, and abandoned in an increasingly horror-filled world. You will not get any weapons that help you: the biggest, best guns still require you fire in Gettysburg-style vollleys, and half of those require you set them down, bolt them to the ground, and unfold them into a delicate origami flower of insufficent firepower.
I will confess, without embarassment or shame, that I activated cheats to get through this game, just to finish the storyline. It is dull and without any characterisation. I've found more intriguing things on the nutrition facts panel of my cereal boxes.
None of your men matter. You will not get attached. You will not feel pride in hard-fought victory. You will not feel sorrow at their tragic loss. You will be numb to the grind. You will feed man after woman after man into the beast of battle, never to see nor remember their faces. You will only be haunted by the memory their AGGRAVATINGLY BAD VOICE ACTING.
This was a junkies' fix, trying to rekindle the feeling of the original X-Com: UFO Defense (Enemy Unknown in Europe). It was not worth my time. In fact, ranting about it here was the most enjoyment I'd gotten out of revisiting this old game.
Put this one back in the closet, and let nostalgia drive you back to the originals.

Alright, so I've now played through the game. There are bugs, to be sure, I experienced graphics glitches and annoying crash-to-desktop interruptions ever so often, at the end of a mission.
That said; playing through the game is possible and mostly tolerable.
It's an open world game like so many before it. And I don't mind - that is exactly what I wanted from this game. But here's the thing:
The missions. They're almost all the same. "Go there, and blow some stuff up", "Go there and kill that guy and his bodyguards". Over and over and over again.
The game forces you to drive everywhere (no skip or taxi option) - so you spend about half your time just driving from A to B with nothing to do in between. And here's the problem; unlike games like GTA for instance, this game doesn't really offer much (anything) in way of extra content or mini games or exploration points. Nothing. You're driving through the city streets or rural countryside, and nothing there inspires you to stop and explore. Nothing.
And if the game added a skip-travel feature, you end up with just jumping from location to location, shooting up the same 4-5 types of enemies and beating down the same type of boss. Don't think for a minute btw, that this is a "boss fight". You just press a button and watch the dialogue.
There's just not enough game here. That's my opinion. Not for this sort of price tag.

Update 25.03.15
Positive:
+ Terrain deformation
+ Tire pressure simulation
+ Realistic water behaviour
+ Driving physics in general
+ Maps are pretty big, and full of challenging terrain
+ You can mow down trees ^_^
+ Multiplayer
+ Vehicles of all sizes, ranging from the small UAZ (Jeep) to the monstrous 8x8 Maz.
+ Winching is fun and very useful. You can attach it to both other vehicles and trees.
+ Attaching a crane to your truck, to pick up lumber, move rocks out of the way and sometimes to help push the truck up.
+ The game is very well optimized.
+ Trucks take damage, and consume fuel. You can install a utility addon for mobile repairs, or a fuel cistern for re-fueling in the field.
+ Patch released on 27/10 -14 added wheel support.
+ Patch released on 27/10 -14 added analogue controller input.
+ Patch implemented individual saves for all maps. Big plus in my book.
Negative:
- The camera could be much better. With the tallest addons it can be a real challenge to see ahead.
- Maps could be more varied. It's mostly the same mix of grass, trees, mud and water.
- The only official objective is to haul lumber. More variety would be welcome.
- Lack of proper manual shifting.
- Draw distance should be customizable.
With all that said... As a VIP backer on the kickstarter campaign, and having had access to the beta since May 9, I can safely recommend this game to anyone with an interest in off-roading. If you've tried the tech demo, you know what to expect. Just think bigger; more trucks, more functionality and much bigger maps. All in all, even in beta, this is perhaps the most fun I have had in a realistic off-road game so far. Try the tech demo first; if you like it - there's a safe bet that you will enjoy the full game.
The devs seem committed to continuing to improve the game after launch, both with free updates and dlc packs later on.

Ufo Aftershock is pretty much similar to XCom (UFO Defense for the geoscape and real time Apocalypse for the battlescape) with the difference that the aliens already destroyed humanity and it's up to you to conquer Earth back and eventually save it from a devouring biomass.
It is simple and fast paced. There is no economy so your choices are mostly about what you need the most and a good positioning of your military bases.
The tactical layer offer various missions for your squads. A big plus for this game is that you do not need to kill all the enemies, some missions can be finished in two minutes if you know what you are doing. Plus, if you can skip missions by delegating them.
You can equip your soldiers in various ways with grenades, rocket launchers, sniper rifles, shotguns and even slow but powerful collapsible railguns. All these weapons are good for their roles and you'll need to properly use them to win.
The only big downside of this game is the weird difficuly curve. First it is really easy, but at a certain step of the story, the enemy gets suddenly really powerful. This gives the false feeling that the game is first too easy then impossible. Truth is that you only need to use all the tools you collected in the later half and, with a proper strategy, you can still win.
So it's a good game that you should play if you are a fan of tactical games.

*sigh* Another day, another crushing disappointment.
So look, the combat is uninspired and boring. Now, it isn't bad because the options are limited, it's bad because it's design is so shallow abd the tactical options are so very few. Fundamentally combat boils down to two options: Click on target to attack or run away, not exactly deep or engaging stuff.
The story is reasonably good, at least from what i've seen, but the dialogue therein emits the overwhemingly pungent aroma of particularly strong cheese.
Graphically the game doesn't look too much of an improvement over fallout 2, indeed the low poly character models are just all kinds of wrong in a game being released in this day and age. Some might give Wasteland a pass for being an old school game, i'm not one of them, whilst I agree that graphics aren't everything, when you're trying to create a game like this, atmosphere and immersion are fundamental, having my eyeballed flicked every few minutes by those low res, low poly models and the peculiar animations does not lend well to the mise en scene when it comes to creating a convincing narrative. The graphical fidelity is something that struck me almost straight away and remains the elephant in the room the entire time, it's incredibly jarring and blows away immersion from the outset, the lack of atmosphere in the game is truly disappointing considering it's a game that would have benefitted exponentially from some sense of environmental depth of scene. The other aspect of this is that the animations are so poor. The way people hurry about is deeply unnatural, and indeed combat animations are every bit as unconvincing. This all adds to the game's lack of depth and continually smashes any sense of immersion to pieces.
There's a whole raft of smaller things that bug me too, for instance, the lack of a day/night cycle, which even the original Baldur's Gate had, which could have added a much needed layer of depth to that chronically boring combat - creatures that only come out at night, reduced visibility, the need for different tactics at different times of night. That's just one example of the smaller things, and before anyone dons their majestic white armour and starts foaming at the mouth, consider this: The investment level was huge so far as crpg games go, so why exactly does the gameplay feel so shallow? You cannot honestly tell me it all went into the sparce voice acting or the fmv sequences, and it's abundantly clear that it didn't go into the engine, so what gives? Where did the money go?
Still, all told, by far my biggest gripe is how low rent the game looks and plays.
Fargo set out to make an old school game, and whilst he has achieved that, unfortunately, I suspect in literally doing so, he has failed to take full advantage of modern technology and game design techniques. Like so many dinosaurs of the industry, it seems he too has failed to adapt, just because you're making your vision does not mean that you should shun the good that has come from the advances in both technology and the games industry at large. What irks most is that this was a game with a £3m development budget, for a crpg it should have been absolutely jawdropping with an investment like that. That, above all else, is what makes Wasteland singularly disappointing, and also raises some rather pointed questions about just where the hell that £3m went, because it sure as♥♥♥♥♥♥doesn't look or feel like it went into the game itself in any truly meaningful way.
Larian came out of left field with an absolute stunner of a game this year with Divinity, maybe i've just been spoilt by it and can't look at Wasteland in the same light when you hold the two side by side, but to be honest, when you look at what Larian achieved with a budget a fraction of the size of Wasteland, I can't help but feel that Briand Fargo, for all his good intentions, was taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥when he released Wasteland into the wild. Divinity is now far and away the market leader in the crpg market, and not because of a huge budget, because the guys and girls at Larian had the kind of vision and sense to use what they have available to them to the absolute best of their ability. I can't help but feel that not only was development time on Wasteland squandered, but also kneecapped by Fargo's single minded determination to make something 'old school'.
the tl;dr boils down to this: if you're a fan of Wasteland 1 or the original Fallout games, and can look past a distinctly shoddy game engine, then you might find something to like here. Otherwise, wait for a very significant sale, or just take a pass altogether and play Divinity or Xcom instead, both are vastly superior alternatives that do what they do a good deal better than Wasteland ever can, or I suspect, ever will.

I'm playing on Normal difficulty and have about 6 hours in. The game starts out really promising, but then throws a bunch of missions at you at one time. When you get to the second big mission of the game, the enemies are extremely powerful and your band of mercenaries will not stand a chance.
GOOD Things:
The tactical combat is nice. There are a variety of weapons and it is critical to manage your squad's inventory.
Resource Scarcity makes gameplay feel exciting and changes how you approach conflict. The world seems interesting and you won't feel bored reading through all the text.
BAD Things:
This game is difficult. This comes from someone who loves Dark Souls. Whereas another game could be difficult and fair, this one does not seem fair in the least. Oh, your squad member can shoot once per turn? Awesome. Here is a pack of enemies that can empty their magazines into you. Or, here are some people carrying machetes who can cross the whole of the wasteland and smack you in the face in the same turn you may get a chance to unjam your weapon.
Seriously, this is infuriating. Let me shoot this pistol with a 3 percent chance to jam. 3 percent is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. You can set your watch to that thing jamming. No kidding, the game is incredibly unfair. I am a huge fan of the old school fallout games as well. I've played Ghosts and Goblins on the NES. I've seen unfair games, and this is such.
WHO will enjoy this?
Sadists. Masochists. People who love playing CIV on unfair difficulties. People who like pulling triggers and having their guns jam while criminals beat you in the face with spiked 2 by fours.

*Disclaimer: I played Lego MARVEL Super Heroes prior to playing this game. I have all the DLC (as of 23/05/17) for both Lego Marvel games*
++TLDR: This is not 'Lego MARVEL Super Heroes 2', but there's heaps of fun once you get past the (often frustrating) Story Mode. 'Go to Space' is where most of that fun is accessed.++
This is Lego MARVEL's Avengers - the Lego game of the first 2 movies (DLC adds more content from other movies and TV series).
PROS:
-Improved Graphics
-New (Different) Characters
-New Team Up fighting abilities
-Has all the key locations and scenes of the movies
-Has the voice acting from the movies
-Has borrowed resources from Lego MARVEL Super Heroes game
-Lego have added in their own extra stuff into cut scenes to enhance hilarity (those poor Lego Chickens and Pigs!)
-The last half of Story Mode is decent
-Freeplay after finishing Story Mode and visiting all the hubs is heaps of fun
-MARVEL's Agents of Shield content for the Daisy fans!
CONS:
-The gameplay in the first half of Story Mode is frustrating:
Higher than expected unfair deaths for a lego game
Cut scenes, level skips, and hint items get in the way of lego stud grinding
Extended QTEs stop you from defending yourself.
-Using the voices from the movies' audio track was a great idea, however could have done with running through an audio equilizer to help make it match the characters on screen. Mostly it's ok, sometimes characters near you sound like they have a cold and are driving through a far away tunnel.
-Everytime the game is loaded it connects to the MARVEL lego server to promote Games/DLC you already have
-Captain America must be Old Man Steve Rogers as somehow he is worse in 1 on 1 fighting than any other story mode character. Maybe it's the speed of his fighting animation or glitchy 'block mode' but I would recommend fighting random npcs with any other character.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
It is a good game but let down by the first half of the Story Mode. I wouldn't recommend buying this game INSTEAD of Lego MARVEL Super Heroes, but if you already have that game and are looking for more - there is plenty of fun... if you persevere.

Shadow of the Comet is a Lovecraftian point and click (PnC) adventure game with a decent storyline and a few interesting characters.  It takes place over three days and nights, and the protagonist progressively unravels a mystery about a cursed town and eventually finds himself in a position to save the world from a terrible fate.
The game came out in 1993, which means a couple things: the graphics are obviously extremely dated, but more importantly, the market audience was more patient and forgiving of obtusity.  Obtuse PnC games were the norm.  I have fond memories of the Goblins and King's Quest games, to name a few similar examples, and I don't know that I beat a single one of them as a kid.  It wasn't that my interest trailed off, it was simply that I got completely stuck, and I didn't have internet access to find help guides.  That didn't bother me 20+ years ago, but it does now.  I don't mind having to take notes and make maps and such - I actually think that's part of the charm of these games - and I enjoy solving the (sometimes weak) riddles as well.  I do not, however, appreciate having to rely on walkthroughs despite those efforts.
My only other complaint about the game is based on the emulation (DOSBox).  I frequently ran into issues where the number of times I hit a key wasn't registering properly, and so I would accidentally skip several lines of dialogue or find it impossible to navigate the inventory.  I can't knock the game itself for that, though.
Recommended for PnC fans who are used to this sort of obtusity, or for Lovecraft fans that don't mind using walkthroughs occasionally.

This game is alright. It's someone else's re-imaganing of the original XCOM games. The game is real time, but it can be paused whenever you want. There is a global map screen where you select missions, though they appear at random. UFO interception is purely RNG. You can have a dogfight end with all of your jets intact when they have no upgrades, and the same UFO can wipe out your squadron with full upgrades.
In battles, your squad is limited to a maximum of 7. Soldiers gain generic XP for kills/KOs, and you can then choose which attribute to level up at the end of the mission if they get enough XP.
There is no economy to speak of. Good for those just wanting to get into this type of game, but maybe a turn off to those who want micro-management. This game is certainly more macro-management on the globe screen, with micro-management for your soldiers (don't forget to pack extra ammo!).
The aliens late game can be brutal. I get the feeling I'm doing something wrong or using the wrong weapons, but they can drop my soldiers in 2 hits even with the best armour. I'm using some of the strongest rifles in the game and it takes 10 hits to put them down.
I'd give it a 6/10. Not a masterpiece, but enjoyable enough. I should also note, that this game does not fully support the Steam overlay. You can still access it, but key presses are still registered in game. So typing in chat leads to a load of key presses in game.

Call of Ctuhlhu : Shadow of the Comet is one of the first generation point-and-click adventure games and was released in 1993 and I have to say, back in the day this games was way eerie and had (and still has) a fantastic truly lovecraftian atmosphere.
Coming back today, you can clearly tell it is dated and there was not really put a lot of effort into improving it even slightly so you  can actually play it without making your eyes hurt.
The voice acting is okay, does never go as low as RE, but is also not really Oscar material. The music and sound is actually pretty good, IMHO.
The point-and-click elements and riddles range from easy to mind-bending, and for all of you who are just starting out with point-and-click games, there is NO HELP option, nope, none whatsoever. So besides from using a walkthrough online,you're on your own. Good Luck doing it on your own.
Also this game is a game where you can die. Yep, this time your choices do matter, cause if you enter the wrong doors, or ask the wrong question to the wrong person, you just might end up very dead. So I strongly advise you to save often.
The overall atmosphere is what makes this game shine, even by today standards. It's somehow truly eerie and unsettling sometimes. The townsfolk are all somewhat off and you never quite know if they are helping you or if they are going to kill you the next chance they get.
Controls are not very comfy, quite frankly I've seen way better in the last years, and if they would have put a little more work into it , honestly, I would be more than willing to shell out $15 or so for a truly remastered, maybe even HD version, for this old gem of a game. Heck I'd even pay $20. That's how good it is.
Definitely a must buy for veteran point-and-click gamers with a penchant for a gripping lovecraftian setting and storyline, others beware the dated graphics and the tough riddles.

First of all, this game was made for those that are familiar with the works of H.P. Lovecraft, so if you have not read his work, you may want to before purchasing. It will give you a greater understanding of the themes and key players in the game.
First lets cover the many positives. This game is genuinely creepy, from beginning to end. The pixelated art is beautiful, if you appreciate pixelated art. I would have done so many screenshots, but sadly with DOSBox I was unable to. The town of Innsmouth is charming, yet you can definitely sense the sinister presence that surrounds and invades the town. The people themselves are also not quite right. It's fun trying to discern who is there to help, or bring about your demise.  The soundtrack is very creepy, letting you know that you are about to enter a world of nightmare. The sound effects are also great. There are times when you are walking through a forest, and you can hear the animals, which can create either a very pleasant or sinister effect, depending on when you go. There is an instance when you have to visit a cemetary, and there is no soundtrack. The sounds of what you would expect to hear in a cemetary at night is all you need to set the mood. The voice acting, for the most part is pretty good, with just a hint of cheese. You can either read the dialogue, listen to the spoken dialogue, or use both. If you use both, expect lag. The written text stays much longer than what the actors say. You can right click if you want to skip the awkward pauses. This really is the only technical hiccup, and I find it forgivable, since there are other modes available.
Now the puzzles. They range from everywhere to pretty easy, to having to use your head, to receiving no help at all, and just figuring it out by trial and error. Don't worry, there is not a lot of the latter. Save often, since there a million ways to die. The game takes place over a span of three days. The first day lays the groundwork for the mystery and the horror that you will encounter. The second day is the most stressful, yet it is very rewarding once completed. The third is...well that would be telling.
Now I must cover the things that separates this from every point-and-click I've played to date. First, instead of using your mouse and clicking where you want Mr. Parker to go, the mouse is in the shape of an arrow, and you move him by choosing which direction you want him to go. Once you get the hang of it (it shouldn't take long), it's easy to maneuver. Next, and this is the awesome thing, is that if you are within eyesight of something you can pick up, a dotted line appears, directing your gaze to an object. NO PIXEL HUNTING! It's great because you find things you didn't know you needed, and when you get to the part of the game when you need said item, you have it! However, you still have to open cabinets and search places, but once you see it, you'll know immediately if you can pick it up. Why don't other point-and-click games do that?
I could talk quite a bit more about this game. The look, the sounds, the soundtrack, the game mechanics, are just great for the time it was made. You also have a journal to keep notes that can help you on your way. The cut scenes and animations are creepy, disturbing, and well done. Lovecraft would be pleased.

Garry's Mod is a sandbox game that can waste a short amount of one's time with the construction props and tools it provides. It gives numerous NPCs, and every Half-Life 2 weapon to use as well as many, many props. It allows for scene-making and maybe a few hours killed. Does this sound appealing? Probably not. Then why, do you ask, is this recommended?
Garry's Mod is not good because of Face Punch studios working on the game, Garry's Mod is an amazing game because of the community workshop for the game. The people in the workshop have added tons of content to play with in this game, and without it, Garry's Mod would be something to pass up. The workshop creators, however, give Garry's Mod a great charm that no other game shares with it. If you ever wanted something to play with friends (for fun, not serious play), the Garry's Mod workshop will often hold what you want. Want to roleplay as Shrek characters in a space ship? Done. Want to play a ton of (terrible) horror maps with friends? Done. Want to summon a rainbow space death laser upon London? Done. The possibilies the workshop creates is rather amazing.
The base game itself is not worth the cost in my personal opinion, but the access to the Garry's Mod workshop is. Garry's Mod is a great game not because of the creators, but the players. This is one of the few games that shows what a great (and weird) game is that Valve could learn from in TF2's regard. The only thing keeping Garry's Mod incredibly popular are the many people creating more content for it out of their love for the game.
- It's a fantastic sandbox game but without much to do in it. The community, however, solves the lack of things to do. There ends up being many more things to do than just building due to the community, which is incredible.
- I still have yet to see a community that does as much as this one for their game. No, the community isn't the friendliest in the world, but they do all share a great love for this game that keeps them making more content and coming back to it.
- The game can and will be intense on any computer due to poor optimization. Thankfully the performance isn't too bad on tanky computers, but it will be noticeably bad on anything that tends to overheat (like my old computer).
- There is so much content to use with the community workshop, and the base game with all Valve games mounted has plenty of props to work with, too. The amount of gamemodes, maps, props, playermodels, vehicles, NPCs, and more is amazing. Once you get bored of something in Garry's Mod, you can quite literally move onto the next addon and enjoy what it has to offer.
As my last note for anyone getting into Garry's Mod with no Valve Games, there are YouTube tutorials to get all of the Valve textures that are not included in the base game for free.

6/10
The Good: This is atmospheric third person action game with a poor man's Stephen King plot. After Alan Wake's wife is taken by darkness, he has to fight it to win back his woman. One of the main weapons against darkness, shock, is light. So everything that is attacking you in this game has to be weakened first with your trusty flashlight, and finished off by a small array of weapons such as shotguns and flashbangs. This makes the game semi "tactical". The story is somewhat entertaining. The graphics are nice to behold, and the music is atmospheric, though forgettable.
The Bad: The biggest downfall of Alan Wake is the repetitive and shallow combat. There is barely any variation in mobs and mechanics, from beginning to end. Weaken them with light, finish them off. Rinse and repeat until game is over. There is no skill slope as in other games, where combat gets gradually more complex. I was hoping for more novel fighting scenes such as the one on the Anderson farm.While the story picks up towards the end of the game, I never much cared for its characters, and it is riddled with writing cliches and plot holes.
Vedict: A fun, albeit flawed game. The topic matter of dreams and creativity could have been exploited for a much more interesting and surreal experience. I wouldn't pay more than 5 bucks for it, so get it on sale.

I just finished playing Act I of Broken Age. I'm not a big adventure game fan, but this was a lot of fun—great art and amazing voice acting! As far as adventure games go, the puzzles are super–easy, but I don't think anybody was looking for a return of obtuse, old–school puzzles and pixel hunting. But the story is actually quite interesting, and some of the dialog has gotten me to laugh out loud (not something that happens frequently, so it's a high mark of praise, in my book).
But the experience of playing through this was particularly significant to me because it is the first game that I ever backed through the crowdfunding platform Kickstarter. At the time (almost two years ago), I don't think any video game projects had even broken $200K in pledges, so when Tim Schafer and Double Fine Productions set a funding goal of $400K ($300K to make an adventure game, and another $100K for 2 Player Productions to create an ongoing documentary of the development process), but then went on to reach over $3.3M in total pledges…
Including my $15. So it is with both a sense of pride and satisfaction that I can say, "I helped bring this about".

One of the reasons I like these games is that they manage to be both kiddified (lotsa humor, relatively easy, player death is only a minor money penalty, almost no character is fully dead) and yet complex (lots of stuff to collect even after the story mode is done!).
The other big reason is an attention to detail, especially in a licensed property like this.  There's plenty of room to approximate film and story locations to a remarkable, if somewhat simplified degree.  References and easter eggs abound in the hub quests.  Characters who give you quests have a few words to say, yet drop some reference that honors some aspect or variant or story.
Also, try to spend time with most of the characters you collect for a while.  Every playable character gets a couple idle animations that accurately hints at some aspect to that character.  And there's a great variety in hand-to-hand fighting styles, with most well-chosen for the hero.  Armor-less Tony Stark throws a punch first, while Doctor Strange will rear back for a roundhouse kick.
The main story consists of the first two Avengers movies, (Avengers and Avengers: Age of Ultron), but also gives you levels pertaining to Captain America: Winter Soldier, Iron Man 3 and Thor: The Dark World.  (That's all the movies sandwiched between the Avengers movies, minus Guardians of the Galaxy.)  There's also a flashback to the key event that set up Winter Soldier.
Available DLC includes a Captain Marvel story, a Masters of Evil story, a Classic Black Panther story. a Doctor Strange story (based on the 2015 All-New All-Different redesign), plus Agents of SHIELD (based on the back half of Season Two, regarding Skye's true identity), and one based on the Ant-Man movie.
Also, in the main game, Agent Carter gets a lengthy quest series, with a neat trick to flash back to the 1940's.  (But, oof, the filter used makes some things hard to see.)
DLC levels are in the same style as the "intermission" levels between the Avengers movies, with cutscenes rendered as LEGO-fied comics and voiceovers.
Game FIRST throws you into the assault on the wintery HYDRA base (to retrieve Loki's staff) that kicks off Age of Ultron.  Only then does it take you to the start of the first Avengers movie, with a SHIELD base evacuation because of experiments with the Tesseract which leads to Loki's arrival.
The reasons for this narrative choice quickly become apparent.  First, that sequence has the Avengers as a team, allowing the player to immediately sample the core six:  Black Widow, Hawkeye, Cap, Thor, Iron Man and Hulk.  Thus, the player does not have to wade through the team-assembly phase of the first movie before playing as their favorite Avenger, at least in this core six.
Second, certain events in Avengers turn one or other member of that core six against you for part of the movie.
Spoilers:
So, while this intro is unexpected (all other Lego movie adaptations put you in the first sequence from the first movie at the start),  it makes sense here.  You see the core characters and their abilities in the game right away, if only a taste.
Usual zero scripted tutorial.  As with the previous Marvel Superheroes game, hints and explanations pop up from Maria Hill or Phil Coulson when you hit a floating Avengers logo.  Relevant button for action pops up.  Hints in the form of the portrait of a character that has the ability you need also appear.
As with other movie adaptations since LoTR, cut scenes are animated with dialogue lifted from the movies, if tweaked for humor and kiddification.
Example:  Phil Coulson's
is a plot point that galvanizes the motley crew into a heroic team, and is therefore far, far too important to dodge completely.  It's handled quite deftly, and preserves the drama of the moment.
There are also some comments during gameplay that have been pulled from the movie dialogue, which means that sometimes the audio is a little weak because they were speaking softly.  Characters employed for quests and DLC often have vocalizations and comments done directly by their voice actors and are much clearer.  Fortunately, there's a subtitle option.
Plus, several actors from the movies and other projects have contributed additional voice content.  Clark Gregg as Phil Coulson is as game as he was in the other Marvel Superheroes game.
Game engine might have improved.  The only slight stuttering of video on my machine (better than recommended specs) came when turning while flying high up in Manhattan.  It feels like there's a better allocation of resources.  There seems to be more compartmentalization within the sections of levels.
Audio controls, howevver, have weakened.  Just on/off for the (loud!) music yet volume control for sound effects?
That first game had an integrated story, but efforts to squeeze in all those heroes gave some short shrift and only a handful of uses.  Here, there's a core team to concentrate on.
No Spidey, X-Men or Fantastic Four, not even as collectible characters or DLC.  Heck, the Baxter Building and Oscorp are not represented in the skyline this time around.  Strictly MCU stuff now.  But that just leaves much more room for many other obscure heroes.
Minikit rewards here are neat:  LEGO-fied versions of some notable comic cover related to the events in the level.  The Avengers as a group and in their individual titles are represented.
This game gives you nifty, if annoyingly slo-mo power moves and combo moves.
Unfortunately, there's no world map.  Level selection is accomplished through launching a Quinjet and roaming around the Earth.  The Avengers are a globe-trotting team!
That sets up several hub worlds, of which Manhattan is the largest.  With Marvel Superheroes, only Manhattan and the Helicarrier were hubs.  Both hubs return in this game, with their layouts largely unchanged. But, as a Manhattan pedestrian comments, they've also changed it up a lot.  Far fewer rooftop agility courses this round!
The lack of a world map is a PAIN when it comes to navigating Manhattan.  Oh, the ghost stud trail when heading to a new story mode level is its usual helpful hint, but trying to find a specific area of the island (so you can pick up your favorite character or vehicle early) is difficult without even a partial minimap and a constant arrow pointing North.  And you cannot set a target location to trigger a pathfinding trail.
Instead, all the Gold Bricks and race locations and mission/quest NPCs are dots on a radar screen.  What they stand for do not show up on radar until you are very close.  However, there are little red and green arrows on top of the nearby icons that tell you if it is higher or lower than you, and the indicators granted by Red Bricks point very closely to their actual location.
Fortunately, Marvel's version of Manhattan sticks to the basic geography of its RL counterpart, and the game captions broad areas. Once you get to Free Play or must transition to a new story mode level with Iron Man or another flying character, navigation becomes far easier.
Sadly, for the first time in several games in the Lego series, after 100% completion, there's apparently no smashy-smashy bonus level in which you need to collect a million studs.  Instead, Avengers Tower's penthouse suite gets slowly decorated as you finish some of the hub quests.  Better for the partial completions.
All in all, it's the usual LEGO fun, this time in the Marvel movie/TV universe!

'Broken Age' is a delightful, whimsical and funny adventure game from LucasArts alumnus, Tim Schafer. It features some of the most beautifully animated and visually unique graphics in adventure games I have seen to date. The puzzles are not particularly challenging, but creative enough to keep you entertained. This is particularly so for Act 1, and it's unfortunate that Act 2 fails to realize the game's full potential.
The game was released in two parts, sadly almost a year apart. Act 1 features one of the more creative stories in PC adventure games. It is full of surprises and intrigue as we do not quite know how our two playable protagonists' storylines relate to each other -- if at all! The similarities and differences between the protagonists, in their upbringing and relationships with those around them, told through parallel gameplay make the introductions to these characters all the more enjoyable. Act 1 plays like a game about adolesence, rebellion, empowerment and curiosity that ends with a great cliffhanger, making you yearning for more of this "something (thematically) different".
Now, in the time that it took for Double Fine Productions to churn out Act 2, one would expect them to produce something worthy to follow the (doubly?) fine first chapter. Sadly, no. Unlike Act 1, Act 2 feels like an average classic adventure game, in which you solve a long series of isolated puzzles to achieve a single objective -- and you get to do it for two characters! This may be more acceptable if it weren't for us visiting the same locations and interacting with the same characters again. Plus, the protagonists do not seem to be at a disadvantage despite being in wholly unfamiliar settings relative to their prior experience. Such wasted opportunities for adding a new layer of challenge to the gameplay!
Act 2 does bring a few new twists. While these twists are interesting, they fail to enlighten or completely surprise me. In fact, these twists confuse me more, making me ask questions that I surprisingly find the characters not asking throughout Act 2. If questions are asked, they are asked by the wrong protagonist, as if the protagonists share a psychic connection through the player. The inconsistency in characterization and storytelling perspective make the gaming experience slightly jarring.
Perhaps Act 2 will be more enjoyable if 'Broken Age' were not released in two parts. If so, perhaps the wonder, magic and intrigue of Act 1 would have spilled over to the second act, and I would not have felt the "been-there-done-that" effect as greatly. (Hmm, maybe that's why Tim Schafer recommended replaying Act 1 before playing Act 2?) Despite my criticism of Act 2, 'Broken Age' as a whole is a good game. It is one of the better adventure games out there; it is easy to pick up and enjoy, and I recommend this feel-good game. As long as you keep your expectations in check, you are unlikely to be disappointed by it.

So I thought I'd buy this game as it was crazy cheap, so I wouldn't lose much anyways in case it sucked. Turns out it kinda does, but it's still fun. The game is incredibly trashy, but that's not really a valid point to criticise as that kind of comes with the "Dinosaur FPS" genre. It's so trashy, it even has bullet time. (You can create lobbies without it though, but why would you?)
Basic Gameplay Elements
====================
Basically, it's a wave-based co-operative horde mode against various types of dinosaurs. Waves are not all of the same type though, some are simple survival, others require you to capture an objective. (You will be rewarded with vehicles for doing so)
During the wave, you'll collect credits for killing dinosaurs, and killing them in rapid succession gives you a multiplier, so getting good streaks is actually important to earn money for upgrades and weapons. Upgrades appear to be interesting for the most part, there are some boring "do twice as much damage" upgrades, which I don't think should be there.
Inbetween waves, you're able to purchase upgrades at your base. The time between rounds is pretty short though (one minute), and the buildings are not always placed in a way that allows you to purchase weapons and upgrades during that short interval. You have a teleporter to beam you back to the base, at least, but in some maps, the base is pretty spread out. Furthermore, some dinosaurs seem to spawn inbetween waves.
Apart from smaller, easier to kill dinos, big ones will occasionally spawn, and as long as those live, more smaller ones will spawn. However, the game tells you when it does so, and also informs you about the health of the big dinosaurs, which makes things a bit easier.
There are three classes in the game, and two of them seem to be completely useless because the first one has a jetpack. The jetpack is pretty useful to avoid getting eaten by Dinosaurs, and is more of a lifesaver than any medic gun ever will be.
Teamplay is not all that important. Having someone repair the generator before it goes offline is nice but barely an issue most of the time. If you manage to die, you'll go into a borderlands-style last-stand, where you can revive yourself by killing an enemy. Teammates can revive you aswell, either by holding down E for a while or healing you with a medic gun.
Criticisms
========
There are things in the game that are legitimately crappy, which do affect the enjoyment. Guns feel ♥♥♥♥♥♥, mostly because recoil is unbiased and pretty much random, but also due to bad sound assets and cheap animations. The latter two are probably due to budget constraints, but the former is not really excusable. Vehicle guns have such a huge cone of fire that they're pretty useless altogether. Most guns seem to not be hitscan, however, which is a good thing, as it adds some much needed depth to the gunplay.
Furthermore, the game has plenty of glitches. While the Dinosaur AI is not completely braindead at times and tries to make it hard for you to hit them, they occasionally get stuck, or just run at you in a straight line while you're running backwards, making it easy for you to shoot them. Physics seem to bug out at times (buggy physics seem to be a common trope in dinosaur games, remember Trespasser?), but not in a way that really affects gameplay. It's mostly limited to corpses breakdancing on the ground.
Graphics seem good for a budget title, that is until you take a closer look at the textures, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ animations. That is, if you can even see those over the ridiculous amounts of bloom and occasional motion blur. I'm sure those can be toggled off, however, but that means you'll see more of the low-res textures and weird animations.
Dinosaur animations seem to suffer from the same quality issues, and they♥♥♥♥♥♥♥out a bit when you sit on a cliff that they can't reach. Speaking of cliffs that they can't reach: This is where the jetpack really comes in handy, because it allows you to escape from anything that isn't a pterodactyle, or doesn't have a ranged attack.
The netcode seems to have some issues aswell. Other players rubberband around almost always, as there seems to be almost no movement prediction for players. Unless you are the host, the game will be extremely laggy, and not much fun to play.
Conquest gamemode appears to be a more boring Survival gamemode, so I have no clue what that is all about.
The microtransactions don't seem to interfere with the game and appear to just be cosmetic, but I still think they shouldn't be in the game at all.

+Real-time pausable element provides an interesting twist to the usual turn-based X-COM formula.
+Geoscape is aesthetically appealing and directly reflects how well you're performing in the war against the enemy.
+It has a plot. With twists.

There are many things wrong with this game.
1. This game has tiers, like in Robocraft, so you aren't supposed to be put with people who will annihilate you in one shot. However, I was put in a match with one of the top 10 players on the enemy team. They one-shotted me, and later, two others, on my team. To put this into context, destroying an enemy robot in this game can take over 10 seconds of non-stop fire.
2. As I mentioned before, this game has tiers. But you can only 'tier-up' when you upgrade your robot's parts. However, the only thing upgrading parts does is give them more health, except weapons, which get more damage as well as more health. This means, in higher tiers, your robot will have more health and do more damage. This also means every other robot will have more health and do more damage. What's the point? Am I missing something?
3. There is no progression in this game. Yes, you can upgrade your robot, but as I said, the whole 'upgrading' system is linear and useless.
4. There are very few people playing it. Getting into a match doesn't usually take any more than about 30 seconds, but being put into matches with, quite often, the same people, who are quite often, using the same robot each time, can get repetitive, especially when they use over-powered weapons.
5. You will occasionally get a box as a reward after completing a match. You can open these boxes with credits, the in-game currency, with a success rate as low as 0.25%, upto 5%. Failed attempts will not destroy the box, only the tools. You can alternatively pay real money in exchange for 'sparks', which you can use to open the box first time. This wouldn't be a problem if it weren't for the fact that these crates can give unique robot parts. That's right, people who pay real money get an advantage over those who don't.
Personally, I have enjoyed this game so far, but I simply cannot recommend it to anyone.

At present, Guns And Robots is more than a bit of an unbalanced mess. The game divides up robots you create into weight classes and 'Tier' ranks, in an attempt to make sure that any robot you design will never face down a robot considered to be 'more powerful' or in a higher 'weightclass'. Unfortunately this system is extremely broken and is constantly getting exploited by experienced players so they can game the system and earn fast coin.
The basic issue is that right now.. since robots are so highly customizable, every individual part needs to be invidually 'scored' based upon its power curve and over all effectiveness. Two Dragonov (Spelling?) Sniper Rifles, while considered Heavy Weapons, can actually be bolted onto a light weight robot chassis and have only minimal impact on your over all speed. This allows for high speed, high maneuverability designs that still pack a heck of a damage _punch_. This problem compounds even further when you move up from a 2-Weapon Robot Frame to a 4-Weapon Robot Frame. 4 Sniper Rifles, or 4 Hailfire Rocket Launchers basically allow you to faceroll over most of the competition, yet still somehow keep your robot ranked in the "Tier 1" ("Lightweight") groupings.
If you want a 'build your own robot' game with a ranking system that WORKS, go try "RoboCraft". "Guns And Robots", at present, is an unbearable mess.

I just completed the game. Holy crap was that fun!! This game is like crack!

(I didn't do this until late in the game unfortunately, keeping your medic in the center of your group helps ALOT when YOU'RE being blitzkrieged.)
BE SURE TO QUICK SAVE AT THE START OF EVERY BATTLE, NOT DURRING!! You'll see why soon enough.

You have the delegate, you have to plan, you have to crunch numbers, you have to take humiliating losses here and there, you have to give 100% But, somehow, you always JUST BARELY have what you need to get the job done. Ballance. MASTERFUL ballance.
So, in summary, if you're a bargain hunter and/or a supporter of indi games (I'm a hardcore one, myself ` La Résistance indépendant!!!) but try to get quality when you can - this is a game for you. Well, if you dig strategy games that is. This isn't so much of a veg out genere. Don't wait for it to go on sale either. It's only $7 last I looked. After 2 months of little to no activity from the developers (wooo, 2 patches) and not listening to their community, I no longer recommend this game. 6/10
The Good: This is atmospheric third person action game with a poor man's Stephen King plot. After Alan Wake's wife is taken by darkness, he has to fight it to win back his woman. One of the main weapons against darkness, shock, is light. So everything that is attacking you in this game has to be weakened first with your trusty flashlight, and finished off by a small array of weapons such as shotguns and flashbangs. This makes the game semi "tactical". The story is somewhat entertaining. The graphics are nice to behold, and the music is atmospheric, though forgettable.
The Bad: The biggest downfall of Alan Wake is the repetitive and shallow combat. There is barely any variation in mobs and mechanics, from beginning to end. Weaken them with light, finish them off. Rinse and repeat until game is over. There is no skill slope as in other games, where combat gets gradually more complex. I was hoping for more novel fighting scenes such as the one on the Anderson farm.While the story picks up towards the end of the game, I never much cared for its characters, and it is riddled with writing cliches and plot holes.
Vedict: A fun, albeit flawed game. The topic matter of dreams and creativity could have been exploited for a much more interesting and surreal experience. I wouldn't pay more than 5 bucks for it, so get it on sale.

Unknown Battle is my favourite game, as a long time fan of the series and a fan of Nikolai Patrakov's titles, I feel like it's my duty as a player to give my honest opinion on Unknown Battle. That being said, I'll try to be as unbiased as possible because it'll be real easy for me to dive right into this and just say "The game's amazing."
First off, the story. Nikolai Patrakov's releases in general recieve a lot of flack for lackluster and uninspired storywriting. I can safely say this has been true for the most part in a lot of Patrakov's titles. This is not to say the story is "bad" per se, but rather the way it's been presented hasn't been the most, clear, or thorough. Whilst a lot of people also have this view on Unknown Battle, I can say this is not the case. Unknown Battle's storytelling whilst not perfect, is a vast improvement on Patrakov's previous titles. It feels concrete, thought out and the individual characters which are part of the story feel real, with realistic emotions, decisions and outlooks. Whilst on the contrary in Bloodbath Kavkaz for example, some character's felt like they were simply there as scenery and held no real association with the story. In Unknown Battle it feels like every character has something interesting to say with their own stories to tell.
Gameplay:
I'm going to use Bloodbath Kavkaz as a reference point here because there's a lot to be said on how Unknown Battle differs from it. The gameplay, in my opinion is Uknown Battle's finest feature is has to offer. If we go back in time 7 years to release of Kavkaz and compare the two in terms of gunplay for example, we'll have two completely opposing scenes, so vastly different that it's staggering to imagine the games were made by the same company. Kavkaz, whilst I hold the game dear to my heart, had some of the worst gunplay imaginable. It was clunky, mouse sensitivity was an issue, there were no iron sights and VATS was almost needed just to do anything. Now fast forward to Unknown Battle and we have a robust, very up-to-date and all around fun combat system. There are dozens of options to choose from, combat wise, a very detailed and intricate weapon modding system and to top it off, the aiming is smooth and VATS is no longer a necessity, but rather, an option. Kavkaz also didn't have the vast majority of features that Unknown Battle does today. One obvious big difference is the addition of base building, something Kavkaz never had. The base building is not perfect and there are recommendations everyone could make to improve it but regardless, it is still very fun, intuitive and an absolute blast to build your first settlement and look upon it thinking "I did that."
Without rambling too much, or ruining some of the game's features for those that haven't played it yet, or are wondering whether they should get it I'll move on to one last controversial topic before I round this off.
Speech/Dialogue options.
In previous games, speech was vastly different to how it is now. For those who don't know or haven't played other titles, your protagonist wasn't voiced, but there were a lot more detailed speech options and usually delineated what you wanted to say accurately. However in Unknown Battle many have argued that the new speech system doesn't hold up the same standard it did before in other games. The speech options are vague at times and often don't portray what you want to fully say; This take's away from the RPG element of the game as a whole and whilst this is not game breaking or ruining in any sense, it is my only minor complaint about the game that could be tweaked.
To top this review off, I'm going to say what I've wanted to say throughout this entire wall of text. Unknown Battle is fantastic. Simple as that. If you're a big as fan as me, then you'll agree with me when I say this game was worth the wait and then some. Unknown Battle, to me, feels like home and gives me this inexplicable sensation whenever I play it. The same feeling I had playing Kavkaz all those years ago, wandering through the wastes and being absolutely dazzled by the vastness of everything and the immersion it gave me. I have no doubt in my mind that given the success of Uknown Battle, Patrakov will continue to make games for years to come. But there will never be another game like this. There will never be another Unknown Battle game that lives up to the hype, and wonder that Unknown Battle has lived up to.
