This is the first game in a very long time that's held my interest for as long as it has. I've thoroughly enjoyed what I’ve played of the game so far and it's also a shining example of what a Kickstarter project can evolve into and become.
Of what I’ve played of the game so far it's well polished, it runs smoothly and everything more or less just works the way it should. The gameplay overall is good, transitioning from exploration to battle and back is smooth and the battles themselves are rewarding if you plan out the battle beforehand.
The map and exploration of the wasteland in itself is an interesting experience that allows you to freely explore where you want (depending on where though you may need rad suits and extra supplies). Finding new locations as you travel is also a nice touch and in my experience at least, aren’t just distractions but can be fun and rewarding as well. Each area looks and feels different although there are things common to most of them (it is a wasteland after all) but aside from one particular destination that has earned my disdain by the end of the time I time spent there, most places are pretty interesting and are intriguing enough that I wanted to explore. When exploring and in engagements make sure to move your directional camera by holding down your mouse wheel button and moving to mouse around to give you a better view of objects/people/baddies.
the combat is solid, choosing where and how you want to begin an engagement (location, location, location) can help you if done right and planning out a battle properly can mean the difference between losing no health or very little health/using very little ammo or potentially dying and wasting ammo and even exhausting your medical supplies. Obviously, having good weapons and items are hugely important in engagements and making sure your weapons are up to scratch but also weighing up damage/ap used/potential to jam so as to equip the most suitable weapon could mean the difference between a fight going well or poorly. Having a team that's proficient in the use of different weapons is crucial as you'll need to use a variety of weapons and weaponry to overcome foes of whatever shape and form that they may come and baddies just in general. After each battle remembering to reload (and unjamming) your weapons will help you be prepared for the next engagement, you don't want to be caught with your pants down. Unfortunately in this case, fighting wars with duct tape will ultimately make you very dead and therefore it is not very smart. Preparation is everything. protip: high explosives are your friend when used wisely.
Abilities in the game are extensive but nothing less than what you would expect from a game of the genre. There are a wide range of abilities and attributes and having a diverse team that possess a variety of abilities is critical for succeeding in the vast and testing wasteland. Every ability has its purpose and doesn't go wasted although lock picking/safe cracking/hacking/detection and communication truly are core abilities in my opinion that, in my current play through, I’ve used extensively and it seem as though any waste lander simply can't go without.
Staying on top of your inventory is also hugely important and as mundane a task as it is to sift through your inventory and decide what is junk and what you should keep and which team member is best suited to carrying which items and ammo and balancing out each pack to make sure no one in your party is being hindered by gear, it really helps to sort that stuff out before continuing on your journey. The last thing you want is to run out of ammo specific to a party member’s weapon and be too far from other teammates to acquire more.  As at the end of most victorious battles you will generally collect a lot of junk, scrap, weapons, ammo and supplies and so keeping inventory will help you in the long run.
NPC's you meet whilst travelling often have side quests for you or requests and should you fulfil either you'll earn their gratitude and maybe some nice items too. You may come across some that wish to join your party and travel with you. Choosing your companions is integral to the party's survival as a whole as the right companions will make your travels easier.
The dialogue in the game is extensive and depending on your actions and abilities, conversations can go in different ways. While I think a bit more voice dialogue would have been nice in certain conversations, the point generally gets across. The constant radio activity from both ranger citadel and sources unknown helps fill the otherwise empty airwaves when travelling across the map and leaves you wondering sometimes as to what you'll find out there.
My conclusion of wasteland 2 thus far is this: it's a game that's well made and executed, I haven't had any issues graphically although I have experienced a gameplay bug here and there but nothing terrible. The people are interesting, the animals are interesting/disturbing (dem goats...hoo boy), environments reflect the state and general mood of different areas and foes come in all shapes and sizes. I’ve had a blast playing the game so far. TLDR: Basically I would definitely recommend this game.

Alan Wake is masterfully written mystery horror thriller with great narrative, excellent level design, memorable supporting characters and a combat system that starts out excellent but turns into a chore near the end. If you love a good mystery story and don’t mind that it uses the age-old light versus dark theme, then Alan Wake is certainly a game you should play.
Alan Wake is a little bit like playing a video game version of Stephen King’s early novels; after all it’s a supernatural psychological mystery thriller set in a small US town in the middle of nowhere. (Though instead of Maine it’s situated in a heavily forested area somewhere in the state of Washington.) Therefore the main focus of the game is on the story and the narrative, which complement each other in such levels that is very rarely seen in a video game.
As a game, Alan Wake is a mixture of survival horror (the Alone in the Dark kind, not the Resident Evil type) and third-person shooter. The early parts of the game focus mainly on the mystery and the narrative, all enemies are only there to keep up the suspense. Sadly it eventually turns into straight-up arena combat against waves and waves of enemies. And the combat mechanic is really working against these scenarios, turning the last part of the game into a series of trial-and-error fights.
The game also has way too many collectibles– almost four hundred, counting the ones in the DLCs– and only two type of them serve any real purpose: the hidden chests, which give you some additional gear; and the manuscript pages, that will eventually tell the story of Alan’s missing week, and shed some more light on the mystery.
If you can get past of the combat system, that turns the game into a nightmare in late levels, and focus on the story only, Alan Wake will be one of the best thrillers you have ever played, on par with the most well-known movies in that genre. Good enough to play it more than one time, which is a rare thing on story-focused mystery games. Just don’t try and get all achievements, unless you have a very large amount of patience…

Voi is a lovely little monochromatic puzzler based on overlapping shapes to make a specific pattern.  Unlike other shape-fitting games, this game uses the "XOR" principle whereby overlapping a piece over another piece produces a white gap.
You have a small number of squares, diamonds and triangles placed in the middle of the screen, and you have to use the limited space, aligning them using the grid of dots to make the pattern shown on the right.
The puzzles are all relatively straightforward.  one or two require a bit of cunning, but for the most part they can be solved in less than 60 seconds.  Some of them in less than 30.
The music is just ambient chillout music, and the sounds are soft chimes, so you're not jarred from your relaxed gameplay.  The only two colours are black and white, but that's just perfect for what is really a very simple, flowy, fun little game, which doesn't get in your way while you're puzzling it out.  It just has exactly what you need.
I think die-hard puzzlers who prefer the Times Crossword will find this a little simple for their tastes, unless they just want to relax with a cup of tea for an hour or so.   Those who don't really like puzzlers, or who find other games (like Lyne, Knights) look a little hardcore, this is perfect.
One of the unexpected pleasures of this game was accidentelly creating really pretty (but wrong) patterns as the solution to some puzzles.  Sometimes, those pretty patterns would reappear later as solutions.  Another unintented amusement was when the shapes can come together to make the solution's 90-degree rotation, and then spending 2x as long trying to make it the right way.
Yes, it could do with a little more interaction (A "well done, thanks for playing" at the end would be nice, or a "quit" button?), also a sandbox mode, or the ability to make some cool shapes and upload them to user challenges would be fun...  But for the price, I can't complain.    Get it on sale, or as part of a bundle, and leave it for a lazy afternoon where you just want to put your feet up for an hour and while away some time.

I remember playing the original Wasteland on my dads computer 13 years ago and I was clueless as to how the game operated and I spent no more than 2 minutes with it and never went back to it until last year.
I played through Wasteland and found myself pleasantly suprised by the depth the game had and how enjoyable and how much I got attached to my custom made rangers.
So now we have finally come to Wasteland 2 a game which has been patiently waited for by fans of the series for over 25 years (You give Half Life fans a run for their money) and it's return is glorious.
The story of Wasteland 2 is as follows, You and your group of rangers(All of which you can personally customize) are tasked with regulating the hostile wastes of Arizona and later Los Angeles from raiders, mutants, robots, cyborgs and more.
One aspect of Wasteland 2 is choice, like most games that have cropped up recently Wasteland 2 is no acception to choice based gameplay.
One of the first choices you make is decieding whether to save the town of highpool from raiders or saving an agricultural facility from mutants.
It was great to see that this choice had a lasting effect, as I choose the AG Center first, Highpool was destroyed and taken over by raiders as a result.
The gameplay is similar to the original Wasteland but thanks to the advancement of technology we now have gameplay which will be more remeniscent of the games which Wasteland inspired allah Fallout with it's turn based gameplay and chance based combat, this means you have action points which are used in combat and anything from movement, attacking, healing and reviving all take up points.
This means you have to be strategic and choose your actions carefully so 2AP for crouching, 3 for moving into position and 3 to take a shot.
Weapons all have different AP usage rifles typically use 7AP and using pistols and fists takes up 3AP.
Now onto the graphics.
Wasteland 2 uses the unity engine and it does a pretty good job of capturing the look and feel of the post apocolaypse with run down buildings, sandy plains and nature taking back the enviroment with green plantlife and vine covered roads and buildings.
It's been a long time coming and it does not disappoint in the slightest.
If you are a fan of the original Wasteland, Fallout or stories set in the post apocolaypse Wasteland 2 is one that will kick you to the ground, stick your head into an irradiated toilet and keep you invested until the bitter end.

Overall, I am pretty happy with this game. I would say that the graphics took a step back from Shadow of Mordor, but I expect that maybe some microupdates are forthcoming to enhance that. The high resolution texture pack really didn't make that much difference and the 4k cinematic pack apparently caused so many problems for players that I stayed away from it. One of the biggest things that contributes to my satisfaction is that it still is so well rendored that I don't get the raging headaches and dizziness that I usually get from just about every stinking FPS game on the market
The fight mechanics have changed slightly, and the talent tree has changed exponentially - but essentially, the transition from Shadow of Mordor is seamless. I noticed players are already crying about the fight mechanics not being radically different but I am glad it is not. If you are playing from PC like I am, I DO recommend spending the time to remap the mouse and keys to your comfort because in many instances hitting the wrong key will lose the fight and then its really hard not to put a fist through the monitor. Believe me, this game will bring out a guy's aggressive side if you have any testosterone whatsoever in your body.
The game definately has a grindy feel. This is probably because when the Shadow of Mordor version first came out, many players whined that the game was too quickly won. This game will make it absolutely necessary to play it like you were meant to. Prepare to sink some good hours into this game - be thorough in completing mind controlling all orc leaders before you siege the keeps or you will suffer immensely.
I recommend getting Grog barrel poisoning at range early on - some Orc leaders are hella tough and poison works wonders.
Also, the difficulty ramps up exponentially by Act 4 because the Orc captians can all be resistant to mind control - depending on how the game rolls that dice. I spent an effing long time reducing them in level only to find out that the iron will effect does not go away. It's better, if they have it, to kill that leader and hope the replacement doesn't have iron will.
The biggest annoyance I have encountered is that the steam achieves do not all work. I have destroyed every monument in the game, and yet do not have the VANDEL achievement. I also have completed requirements for FORGER, AVENGED, and BETTER LUCK NEXT TIME several times over and didn't get credit for those either so expect this.
Also, never forget that Orcs can't be trusted. Some will betray you. Expect it. It's no hard feelings, only business.  If an orc breaks your heart, let him know you love him, and then bury him in a cement floor somewhere. More than once, if necessary.
Another thing implimented into the game is an online store and loot boxes. If you hand over actual money for these things you need to have your head examined. I completed the game without going beyond the in-game currency just fine. Loot boxes are for petulent people who are too lazy to play the game.
Overall, the game is excellent. The storyline is great if you are not a pinhead too stuck on demanding that the game follows LOTR lore. The enemies are bigger and the thrill of winning a stronghold siege is awesome. Some of the conversations the Orcs hold are amusing and BRUZ's personality makes him a cool orc IMO.

So I thought I'd buy this game as it was crazy cheap, so I wouldn't lose much anyways in case it sucked. Turns out it kinda does, but it's still fun. The game is incredibly trashy, but that's not really a valid point to criticise as that kind of comes with the "Dinosaur FPS" genre. It's so trashy, it even has bullet time. (You can create lobbies without it though, but why would you?)
Basic Gameplay Elements
====================
Basically, it's a wave-based co-operative horde mode against various types of dinosaurs. Waves are not all of the same type though, some are simple survival, others require you to capture an objective. (You will be rewarded with vehicles for doing so)
During the wave, you'll collect credits for killing dinosaurs, and killing them in rapid succession gives you a multiplier, so getting good streaks is actually important to earn money for upgrades and weapons. Upgrades appear to be interesting for the most part, there are some boring "do twice as much damage" upgrades, which I don't think should be there.
Inbetween waves, you're able to purchase upgrades at your base. The time between rounds is pretty short though (one minute), and the buildings are not always placed in a way that allows you to purchase weapons and upgrades during that short interval. You have a teleporter to beam you back to the base, at least, but in some maps, the base is pretty spread out. Furthermore, some dinosaurs seem to spawn inbetween waves.
Apart from smaller, easier to kill dinos, big ones will occasionally spawn, and as long as those live, more smaller ones will spawn. However, the game tells you when it does so, and also informs you about the health of the big dinosaurs, which makes things a bit easier.
There are three classes in the game, and two of them seem to be completely useless because the first one has a jetpack. The jetpack is pretty useful to avoid getting eaten by Dinosaurs, and is more of a lifesaver than any medic gun ever will be.
Teamplay is not all that important. Having someone repair the generator before it goes offline is nice but barely an issue most of the time. If you manage to die, you'll go into a borderlands-style last-stand, where you can revive yourself by killing an enemy. Teammates can revive you aswell, either by holding down E for a while or healing you with a medic gun.
Criticisms
========
There are things in the game that are legitimately crappy, which do affect the enjoyment. Guns feel ♥♥♥♥♥♥, mostly because recoil is unbiased and pretty much random, but also due to bad sound assets and cheap animations. The latter two are probably due to budget constraints, but the former is not really excusable. Vehicle guns have such a huge cone of fire that they're pretty useless altogether. Most guns seem to not be hitscan, however, which is a good thing, as it adds some much needed depth to the gunplay.
Furthermore, the game has plenty of glitches. While the Dinosaur AI is not completely braindead at times and tries to make it hard for you to hit them, they occasionally get stuck, or just run at you in a straight line while you're running backwards, making it easy for you to shoot them. Physics seem to bug out at times (buggy physics seem to be a common trope in dinosaur games, remember Trespasser?), but not in a way that really affects gameplay. It's mostly limited to corpses breakdancing on the ground.
Graphics seem good for a budget title, that is until you take a closer look at the textures, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ animations. That is, if you can even see those over the ridiculous amounts of bloom and occasional motion blur. I'm sure those can be toggled off, however, but that means you'll see more of the low-res textures and weird animations.
Dinosaur animations seem to suffer from the same quality issues, and they♥♥♥♥♥♥♥out a bit when you sit on a cliff that they can't reach. Speaking of cliffs that they can't reach: This is where the jetpack really comes in handy, because it allows you to escape from anything that isn't a pterodactyle, or doesn't have a ranged attack.
The netcode seems to have some issues aswell. Other players rubberband around almost always, as there seems to be almost no movement prediction for players. Unless you are the host, the game will be extremely laggy, and not much fun to play.
Conquest gamemode appears to be a more boring Survival gamemode, so I have no clue what that is all about.
The microtransactions don't seem to interfere with the game and appear to just be cosmetic, but I still think they shouldn't be in the game at all.
Conclusion
========
Definitely worth the price during the sale. If you've been waiting for a game that lets you hunt T-Rexes with a bow while flying around with a jetpack, then this is your game. I'm not sure if it's worth the full price though. Most likely not. And the bad netcode ultimately kills it.

TL;DR If you liked Mordor, buy this, and when you get to Act IV, look up the "true ending" on youtube unless you really, really like the siege battles.
This game is getting a ton of hate, with people saying that they're forcing you to buy loot boxes. That is a complete lie. The fourth act is terrible, but buying loot boxes won't make it any less terrible.
The only reason it's terrible is that because the game tells you at the end of the third act that the "final quest" will irreversibly change the world, you go hunt down all the side stuff, and do all the side quests. This means that in the fourth act, you have NOTHING TO DO except siege after siege after siege, which tires the game out quite a bit.
You get way more than enough gear, orcs, and experience just by playing the game like you would any other RPG. Do the side stuff, that's literally all they ask of you to make sure that you're powerful enough for the endgame. And as any RPG fan would know, there's plenty of great games out there with terrible, boring grinds at the end, even without having loot boxes even be an option.
I enjoyed all my time training my followers, going through epic battles, finding all the collectables, powering up Talion and Celebrimbor, the combat is just as fast, fluid, and cinematic as it was in the first game, along with having many improvements, like how now Celebrimbor has a skill in the talent tree where he will still counter orcs who attack you as you try to do a ground finisher on someone.
The only time I wasn't having fun was when I had to do battle after battle after battle in Act IV, with nothing to really split up the action. It wasn't difficult, it wasn't that I didn't have good enough gear or strong enough orcs, so loot boxes wouldn't have fixed the problem.
So to anyone who loved Mordor, pick up this game, you'll be doing yourself a favor. Just look up the "true ending" on youtube instead of forcing yourself through the Act IV. Save those siege battles for a week from now, when you're thinking "Man, I really feel like slaughtering some Orcs about now." and pace yourself.

HOWEVER... I cannot think of a game that is more random.  Virtually every aspect of this game has some aspect of RNG to it.  Enemy type, level size, enemy actions (sometimes they just stand there and let you kill them, sometimes they will make your 2nd level a bulet hell), what upgrades/mutations you get, what weapons you get, what ammo you get.  And there's more.
If you want a consistent game, stay away.  Hell, if you want a BIT of RNG in your game, stay away.  I cannot play this anymore as all the random generation and other RNG elements have worn me down.  Sometimes the game is challenging and fun, other times you will die because the game hates you.  Sometimes you can get good enough to compensate for the RNG, but sometimes the game just ends your run.
If you can stand that level of RNG, I whole-heartedly recommend this game.  If you can't stomache RNG, don't even consider this game, no matter what.

This game is fun for a little while, once you get past the awful voice acting, boring gray color scheme, and terrible controls.
My favorite part of the game is the "delegate" option, which lets you delegate some missions you don't want to do to the local armed forces. Consider it a "skip this mission" button. The game would be enjoyable, but then things suddenly go horribly, horribly wrong...
That little while ends when the game starts throwing aliens with mega green armor at you. On top of that, the aliens get rocket launchers, yellow death beams which drop you faster than you can say "Well, time to reload a save," psi guns that incapacitate or possess your troops even if they have heroic willpower and psi-helmets, and these blue alien grenade launchers which do rapid-fire, mega-splash damage and can wipe out your entire squad in four shots.
All the enemies in this game are somewhat creative but almost all are colored the same, dull, dusty gray. There's an enemy in  the game that looks like a giant larva which zaps your troops with a physically harmless purple beam which has a good chance of stunning them for an incredibly long time. Just one of these creatures can stunlock your entire squad permanently because they're also rapid fire, then you have to reload a save.
I tried save-scumming my way through this game on easy mode, and I couldn't do it. I tried waiting in a corner and luring the enemies to get killed when they round the corner, and it still was insanely difficult. I had elite troops with high stats in all fields, with the best equipment I could get, and I still wound up reloading saves constantly, and still not being able to beat the campeign. The difficulty curve of this game is so strong, sudden, steep, and unforgivingly hard that it breaks the game into a near-unplayable state. My guess is that the developers decided to make the game more challenging not by adding new situations and tactics but by just making all the enemies stronger.
In a nutshell, this game is just so ridiculously hard that it's not worth buying.

I hate point-and-click adventure games. I'm that gamer. I like my adventure games to be of the Assassin's Creed variety, and I like my clicking games to be pure puzzlers. So to play a game that has neither the sheer volume of puzzles that puzzlers have and does not boast the freedom which sandbox adventure games boast and actually like it is incredible. Genuinely, I'm in awe. It took a lot of friends quite a bit of convincing to get me to buy this game, and being the non point-and-click adventure type of person I am, I rushed through it. Still, the dialogue was charming, the characters were interesting, the art was beautiful, and the storyline was magnificent.
The end of Act I left me practically drooling for Act II. It also didn't hurt that Wil Wheaton was in the game as a hipster lumberjack. Normally inanimate objects have more personality in this game than the entire CoD franchise and their dog. This game is... everything that is right with small game development and a testament to the greatness that is Double Fine. Play this game, friends. Even if you, like me, do not think you would like it. I guarantee you will. Unless you don't have a soul, in which case, you don't deserve this game anyway.

I can't recommend this game strongly enough. It's just good. I'm not even that good at it, but I find myself coming back to it more and more.
First off, the art style. It's beautiful, with what I want to say is a bit of an arcade feel? The character designs, from players to enemies to bosses to... vans and radioactive chairs? just looks good. Not overly complex, not too simple. A nice balance. There's other visual effects such as sccreen shake to make you almost feel the explosions and guns firing.
Next, the soundtrack. Gorgeous. Post-apocalyptic. The game makes nice use of its own leitmotif, in a similar vein to how Undertale uses its own, though the soundtracks have a much different feel to them for sure. Ambience is used to excellent effect, with the best example probably being the Crystal Caves. Those spidery scamper sounds will send shivers up your spine. Annoying alliteration aside, all the other audio is also amazing. Sound effects are great. You swing a melee weapon and it sounds, as one Nuclear Throne YouTuber would put it: crunchy. You shoot a Revolver and it really sounds and even feels like you're shooting a gun.
Finally, gameplay. An excellently paced rogue-like top-down bullet-hell shooter. Areas follow an interesting floor pattern of 3,1,3,1 and so on. Areas with 3 floors hold a boss at the end, while areas with one serve as a vastly different transition area, with darker lighting to boot. The leveling system involves collecting "rads" which function like EXP, though they disappear if you don't collect them in time. With enough rads, you can mutate, granting buffs like revenge damage, extra ammo storage, reduced enemy health, and even... bolts that somehow seek out enemies? Speaking of bolts, there are several weapon types, each with their own ammo class and sub-types, such as Bolts/Seekers/Splinters, Shells/Slugs, Bullets/Bouncers, and others. I don't know exactly how many weapons are in the game, but there are plenty, and finding the ones that work best for you is part of the fun. There are also plenty of secrets in the game as well... try taking a Screwdriver to the gold car in 3-1 some time.
There are also some great mods for the game. The two that stand out the most are Ultra Mod and Together. Ultra adds seeral new weapons, areas, characters, enemies, and bosses. Probably about double of everything. Unfortunately, it was started before the Throne was actually added, so that feature is missing, but it's still an excellent mod. Together is fully based around the current version and through some miracle adds online support to a game that currently has none, as well as altering some of the mechanics introduced for the Local Co-op already included in the game. In fact, I'd recommend getting this mod off the bat, since it's literally just Nuclear Throne... Together.
Seriously. It's just a good freakin game. Buy it. Support the devs in their quest to work on the PS3 port, which they've unfortunately been struggling with since it's literally the first Game Maker game ported to the system, which leads to all sorts of problems that aren't necessarily the Vlambeer devs' faults. Help them bring this amazing game to a wider audience.

Really nice game that filled the gaping hole left after the various X-com failures after TFTD. Now, of course, we have a new "true" X-com game, but this little gem is still worth playing I think. It's not really turn-based like the older games (rather it uses a hybrid system with pausing) and it lacks some stuff in the micromanaging departement (like the ability to have and equip multiple ships to take care of multiple missions, etc) but it's still a bunch of fun.
Like others have mentioned, it runs at a 4:3 resolution (1024x768) which means it stretches on most modern monitors. I was able to make my monitor not stretch it using the monitor's own menus. Great success! Now I can play fullscreen without stretching!
Another little trick: Not sure if it's been documented, but I find scrolling in battle using Alt+Shift+mouse movement much easier and quicker than using the arrow keys. I just hate that "camera inertia" of the arrow keys and the slowness of using the screen borders. So Alt+Shift works for me.

This game is a worthy successfor to the original x-com, and is one of the high-water marks for the genre. It takes all of the core ideas of the original x-com (many of which were sadly cut from Enemy Unknown) and adds a lot of meat to them. The "geopshere" world map phase of the game is particularly excellent. The aliens have a plan, and it's up to you to not only figure out what it is, but how to stop it.
One of the greatest improvements is that the game is "pause and play." You can pause the game at any time (and the game will automatically pause when certain events occur, like spotting an enemy), and issue orders to your squad. Every action has a timer associated with it to tell you how long it will take to complete, rather than having action points and a "you go, I go" turn-based system. Things make a lot more sense as a result, and you can plan tactics without enemies taking their turn to run across gaps or cross the map without you being able to do anything about it since it's not your turn.
It also lets you have multiple soldiers moving at the same time, and group-select and move orders, which means that the squad sizes and maps can be *far* larger without the game slowing to a crawl as you move an entire team one at a time down a hallway or street.
The one thing I really miss that was in the original xcom which is missing from UFO: Aftermath is the environmental destruction and the interesting tactical options it provided. Also, this game was significantly superior to its own sequels.

As the team expands, so does the technology based, from simple kevlar sytle armour to power suits. From earth based weapons to the use of alien ones or just weilding miniguns! Bewarned that this is a game best played cautiously as combat is now quick and easy, and there can be a learning curve when facing various new aliens.
The game follows a story line unlike its predecessors where the objective was getting to the enemy base. The story is basic, but there. The aliens are not your typical sectoid look with a large variety of some quite difficult species to bring down.
A great new feature is the training of soldiers, though there is no determined way of controlling how stats increase, you can now train soldiers in certain specialities which align to their favoured skill. This adds another form of creating a more specialised and team with a personal touch.

This is your classic Post Apocalyptic non linear adventure.  You form a band of party members and decide how each person should contribute to the squad based on their skills and attributes.  Exploration is realtime and allows you to setup combat before it starts if you can detect them soon enough.  Once combat begins its all sequenced based on who has the strongest combat attributes and flows this way until all of the enemy combatants are eliminated.
Once of the strongest characteristics of this game and its predessor the originial Wasteland were the choices you could make good and bad that can leave you with consequences later you hadn't even considered.   I think in this way it gives alot of replay value as you consider things like what if I had done it this way or that.
Just like in many of these types of games your quick save quick load and saving often are a necessity.  In many cases though your put on the spot to make a decision at a point you hadn't realized until later so you either replay that zone or accept the results as is.  In many ways this comes back to a player's style and for example you have to make a hard choice early on if you want to save one place or another and the place you don't save is completely different as a result.
This game has evolved considerably since the original beta, the graphics are crisp, the map navigation is incredible (how many times in these style games do parties get stuck because the obstacle navigation waspoorly done)  The gameplay is quite long and well written, the variations of choices and party make up is incredible.  This is not a game for the weak, your fallout experience will not prepare you even in the slighest.
What I recommend for all new players is head out and run through the first couple of towns to get used to the gameplay.  If you feel like you didn't prepare your team well enough go ahead and restart based on this learning.  On the positive side though even if your team isn't the best in the beginning it doesn't have to be.  You'll have plenty of time to clean them up as you continue and you always have the opportunity to return to former zones to finish up things.

In my opinion, this game is pretty fun, but there are some things that kinda make it difficult to enjoy.
One thing I don't like is how they lock a majority of the characters and the only way to unlock them is by playing about 15 or more games to get enough money to unlock them. This is annoying to me because the starting heroes you start off with don't include a healer, so a lot of the time, I join a game where my team can't sustain themselves very well.
Another thing I don't like is hero balance. A lot of the maps make it hard to use some one like Kinessa to her full potential as a sniper, so I would end up using her rifle more so than the sniper because of the close range and lack of points to cover as a sniper. On top of this, some heroes are just out right better than others. Evie has a weapon that does 930 damage, has the ability to fly in any direction she wants for 2 seconds, has Mei's cryofreeze that makes her immune to damage and self-heals for 3 seconds and also marks and slows any enemies nearby. Marked enemies take 30% more damage from her basic attack, dealing ~1209 damage. And her last ability lets her teleport and increase her damage by another 20%. Meanwhile, Kinessa deals 1300 damage per fully charged up shot, and about 1800 damage per fully charged headshot. To fully charge a sniper shot, you have to wait about 2 seconds, then to maximize damage, you're trying to land a headshot on a target constantly moving in close quarters combat, which means missing a lot of your scoped shots. Her abilities is being able to switch between sniper and carbine, laying 2 mines that slow enemies and deals a pitiful 4 damage per .2 seconds (~12 damage per second, squishies have 2000 hp) and gives your carbine 30% more damage (Doesn't apply to sniper), and a teleporter that you have to place, then get automatically teleported to it after a time.
So Evie can deal 1860 damage per second, with poetential to deal 2790 damage per second, compared to Kinessa's 650 per second, poetential 900 per second, or 1000 damage per second, poetential ~1300 damage per second with her carbine. Not to mention, Evie has way better mobility and self healing, and her basic attack is basically a rocket projectile.
While it is fun to mess with heroes in an AI match, in a PvP match, there's just only 3 or 4 heroes to use to even stand a chance against the other team, if you even have them unlocked yet. Just making all heroes availble from the start would make the game a lot better, or at least, reliable healers as part of the starter set.
Also, note that my opinions will change as I play more, but this is what I think so far.

Tactical turn based combat, a cover system, optimal fire range's on all the weapons that you will have to consider, crouch and head shot options, overwatch mode, weapons that can jam and need to be reloaded mid battle, all of which will cost you action points to utilize in combat. You also have a skill system for outside of combat that include things such as toaster repair (think the wasteland version of treasure chests), perception (land mines, trap/alarms on objects), lock pick and safe crack, computer repair, mechanical engineering and much more. All of your skills you will be finding yourself using quite often in your travels to do many things such as get the core out of a plastic man to performing surgery (a skill) on a kid who had his leg blown off from a land mine or fixing various broke down machines you come across for the people of the wastes to make their lives easier. There are so many places for you to use your skills that they never feel like a useless point dump when your weapon skills are high enough. With a story set in a post apocalyptic wasteland where life is cruel and unfair and just a bit radioactive (maybe more if you're not careful) that's what kind of game this is. The variety of people you meet along the way and places you will journey is just amazing, there were a few times where I found myself laughing out loud at something stupid I came across from some junkie's camp or in wonder at the place I had just discovered filled with robotic junk and run down machinery. It really was a joy to explore in this game I have to say. Many of the characters have some real personality to them that you will remember long after you move on which really makes it feel more personal when the NPC's you meet aren't soulless bunches of code and pixels you know? Often there were times where I found it had a very elder scrolls quality to it where you just look around you and go wow I can explore ALL OF THIS which, if you ask me, is just a fantastic thing to feel in a game.

Never have I felt so conflicted about a game as Shadow of War. The gameplay is excellent, except for a few small annoyances and gamebreaking bugs. I enjoy playing the game quite a bit. But it's just... Not right.
The main problem with the gameplay is that it's clunky. The movement isn't great- it's better than assassin's creed, but still just doesn't feel particularly smooth. When things get crunched together- near Olog-Hai, near the feet of a Graug, in victory points during sieges, things just don't flow right. Enemies seem to fade out of visibility, prompts don't seem to work well, controls become unresponsive, and the combat just doesn't work well. For a game based around these huge battles, this is a pretty big issue.
I have a lot of other gripes about small things, polish, poor design decisions, and glitches, but I could spend hours writing ten thousand words about that- and I don't want to. But the other big issue is the microtransactions.
The whole microtransaction issue is just obscene. The game is very poorly paced, the second act blows by with little challenge but the third act has this long grind that strongly encourages you to use microtransactions to alleviate that. We've all paid $60 or more for this game, it's just not right that we're expected to pay more money to fix the pacing of the game. We shouldn't need to fix the pacing in the first place, and we shouldn't have to pay extra money to do so. It's not like these microtransactions are discreet, either, every menu is littered with advertisements for them. You have to go through the store to get your rewards from multiplayer. It's just a constant reminder of how little respect WB Games has for us, how greedy they are that they're willing to make us pay full price for a product knowing it's designed to make us pay even more money.
This game is really dissapointing. Not in that I'm dissapointed with my purchases, but in that it could have been so much more but the execution was bungled- seems to be the case with almost every AAA title these days. As much as I enjoy this game, I can't justify reccomending it.

It's about time I gave my opinion on FSX:SE.
I never owned the boxed edition of FSX, however, I had a friend of mine who did, and he reccomended that I get FSX. I got it about a year ago when it was on sale for $5.00. When my friend found out, he was as excited as I was.
Simply put, it was the best $5 I ever spent. I love FSX:SE. As this was my first full fledge flight simulator, I didn't need all the bells and whistles of newer flight sims such as X-Plane. I just enjoyed flying planes. I really learned a lot playing this game, as it taught me the basics of aircraft flight. I started off on small Cessnas and Pipers but gradually worked my way up to larger Boeings. The default aircraft are good but not perfect. If you are just beginning, you won't be able to tell the difference, but if you are an experienced flight simmer/actual pilot, you will see some things missing. However, if you get bored with the default aircraft, you can always download more planes for free at
.
The multiplayer is very fun. The Steam multiplayer works well and I enjoy flying formations and airline hops with other players online. As a member of the FSX Competition Center, I can participate in landing competitions online. However, I do have a few complaints about multiplayer. The first is that the microphone communication is TERRIBLE - it's almost impossible to make out anything anyone says. It is for this reason that most servers use TeamSpeak to communicate. I personally prefer using the chat box. My other issue is that you can't use the direct connect feature - which prevents FSX:SE from playing online multiplayer with FSX Boxed. This was something dissapointing I found out when I tried playing with my friend - luckily, he recently purchased FSX:SE himself, so now we can do multiplayer! My last problem isn't with the multiplayer itself, but with the people. Many people on the SE multiplayer are less experienced than people who played the boxed edition. So if you want the most realistic ATC multiplayer possible, you may want to get VATSIM (which works great with FSX:SE BTW).
The graphics are nothing special, considering this game is over 10 years old. But I can ignore poor graphics if the gameplay is good, which the gameplay in FSX is OUTSTANDINGLY FUN!!! However, if you want improved graphics, they have addons for that.
The most notable thing about FSX:SE is how WELL it runs on my PC. My laptop is far from a gaming powerhouse, and it even struggles to run some of the most basic games at times. However, at times, I am getting maximum framerates on FSX:SE at high settings! FSX:SE is the most playable game on my PC by far, so if your PC is weak, don't worry, it will likely handle FSX:SE fine. Also, I'm running Windows 7.
In the end, FSX:SE is a great flight simulator. It has excited me for hours and taught me a lot about aviation in the process. It may have even inspired me to eventually get a real pilot's liscence! If you are a beginner or expert in flight simming, and you want an excellent flight simulator that will grow with you, then FSX:SE is the game for you. I give it a 9.5/10.
Tip: Be sure to pick up the game when it is on sale, as the price sometimes drops as low as $5.00!

During the boring hours of work, do you ever wish you could do something else? To still be paid for playing rather than working? NSFW - Not a Simulator For Working explores this concept.
You play as a Stefan, a new employee working at NSF&W. The first week on the job is to see how you would do if you were hired. But it doesn't go exactly as planned as you become bored very quickly, and NSF&W can't have a bored employee. Despite disliking your new job, Stefan must find a way to stay happy which manifest as naughty videos. Can you last the whole week without getting caught?
NSFW has a pretty standard gameplay. Make sure you're Fun Scale doesn't run out while also making sure no one sees you watching the videos. You can hear the foot steps of your coworkers a few seconds before they come through the door, giving you some time to click off of the videos. You have an option of making some small talk, cut them off if they start the conversation, or let them walk by. Just watch your fun scale and make sure your coworkers are out of site.
However, it gets more difficult as you continue playing. The job and the videos have different modes, which act as minigames. With each upgrade, the minigames become more interactive, and in turn louder. The moans activated when you earn hearts. This can easily take your attention away if you're not careful. While it doesn't seem significant to do the minigames for the jobs, it does in the simulator mode. Whether your actually doing your job or not, the minigames can quickly take your mind off of the objective. The minigames serve as a way to earn currency, one for getting jobs (which shows after the campaign) and one to get more videos. Checks also become more frequent and hidden. This gives more depth as you can hear the coworkers, but you can't hear the check unless it's too late. Other conditions are added, such as no talking day, to add to the difficulty as you try to not get fired.
The coworkers, while pegged to be annoying, do have some depth. Each character talks, acts, and work in a different area in NSF&W. You have options to befriend them, which gives you more about their background and more videos, having specific interactions that increase your reputation. In any other situation, these characters would be interesting to interact with. However, most of them snitch on you. If NSF&W wasn't so forgiving, how would you get money for videos?
NSFW uses sound as it's main advantage and disadvantage. You can hear coworkers coming with footsteps or the squeaking of wheels but the moans from the videos almost drowns out everything. If you don't listen closely, the day will end quickly. Despite this, the sound is balanced in a way that you can still hear the signs of your coworkers coming under the moans.
NSFW has a pizelated style throughout the gameplay. The office, workers, and the videos each stand out by themselves, with the minigames only including coins or hearts to distinguish them from everything else. The coworkers have a simple walking and reactions animations that draw attention as they walk past. This is different from the various job animations that completes in junks instead of bits at a time. While the videos include eye catching color and different animations from the rest. This truely succeeds in making work boring and watching naughty videos fun.
NSFW runs pretty well. The only lag that might show would be in the minigames, but it quickly goes away.
The Campaign might seem like that is all to the game, along with if you search up gameplay, but that is untrue. Once you survive the 7 days another mode appears. This allows players to get all of the videos, while having the player buy the programs needed to do various jobs. This is endless, as long as you are determined to play it can deliver. Steam achievements encourages more gameplay which can easily be achieved in this mode. Once all videos are collected, another mode is unlocked to view all of the videos.
+ Artwork
+ Various emails are entertaining
+ Balancing of working and watching videos
+ Added difficulty in forms of conditions and hidden checks
- Some of the minigames might not be enjoyable
- Can be tiresome after reading all the emails and trying to get all achievements
NSFW - Not a Simulator For Working as all about balance. Would you work more or play more? Listen closely between moans for coworkers and watch the time. Make friends with your coworkers while you are still working at NSF&W and unlock secret videos with them as the star. All-in-all NSFW- Not a Simulator For Working is a good game to play during the weekend. This will certainly keep your fun scale up.

If you played and enjoyed the original Fallout 1 and 2, or if you played the original Wasteland (I haven't), you will love this game.
Even if you haven't played any of those, Wasteland 2 is still a great game. It's a fairly hardcore isometric party based RPG with turn-based combat. There are many different skills to choose from, but it never felt like there were too many. Each one is useful, and you really won't regret putting points into any of them. Also, you get to start with a party of 4, and you can custom build each character including their appearance and background history. I named all of mine after friends, making their attributes in ways that they might actually be if they were in the wasteland.
Combat is turn-based, and feels a little like X-COM. The rest of the exploration is real time, and you travel the world via a map, where you can have random encounters. Be careful, if you one character has to fire through a tile a friendly character is standing on, there is a chance for friendly fire!
Overall, the game is a lot of fun, and after 20 hours, I'm really enjoying it. The developer clearly has a sense of humor, and there are tons of cultural references in the game, and even on the main menu. Check it out, you won't be disappointed.

VOI is a nice, minimalistic puzzle where you overlap puzzle pieces (which invert in color when overlapped) to try to match a determined shape.  It's a simple idea and it does it pretty well.
That said, it does have a couple
:

I'm currently writing this review through gritted teeth and clenched fists and I'm trying hard to stay objective and clear headed.  Firstly I'm list the positive things.
The atmosphere of this game is excellent and it truly feels like a real post apocalyptic world.  Immersed in this environment are numerous choices you must make that really do affect different outcomes.  Many games offer multiple conversation lines that lead to the same answer regardless of what you choose (giving the illusion of a more broad conversation) but in this game there was clearly a lot of thought put into the writing.  The replay value of this game is definitely immense.  I've read different reviews on different sites, and some of the weaknesses others have mentioned about this game, I actually see as strengths.  As an old-school gamer and a big fan of deep RPGs, I'm not looking to have things served to me on a plate.  So having to rotate my camera around, to see chests behind trees or whatnot, isn't a hinderance but actually adds to my gaming experience.
Also with the large number of skills and their gradual progression, it makes possible something else I really enjoy in video games; which is revisiting old places with higher skills to make new discoveries.  That's why I always have one character with high perception skills.  Some have complained that combat in this game is repetitive.  I don't agree, I enjoy dividing my party and placing snipers at high points and using high AP characters to lead enemies into ambushes.  That's just one of the many tactics I use during combat.
I could go on and on about the positives.  Now here's the negative:
I can't play it for more than an hour without a crash.  The game is extremely unstable.  I've tried every workaround mentioned by inXile staff and not a single one has worked.  I did have the Early Access version (which had the same crash problem) but I uninstalled it before I installed the released version.  Nothing works.  Now I'm just waiting for a patch that will fix these crashes before I can play again because it's really ruining the experience.
Another annoyance is the right-click move button.  I need to click an area a few times before the party will actually move there.
Other than that, the game is great and I highly recommend it.  I only wish these crashes would stop.

TL;DR If you liked Mordor, buy this, and when you get to Act IV, look up the "true ending" on youtube unless you really, really like the siege battles.
This game is getting a ton of hate, with people saying that they're forcing you to buy loot boxes. That is a complete lie. The fourth act is terrible, but buying loot boxes won't make it any less terrible.
The only reason it's terrible is that because the game tells you at the end of the third act that the "final quest" will irreversibly change the world, you go hunt down all the side stuff, and do all the side quests. This means that in the fourth act, you have NOTHING TO DO except siege after siege after siege, which tires the game out quite a bit.
You get way more than enough gear, orcs, and experience just by playing the game like you would any other RPG. Do the side stuff, that's literally all they ask of you to make sure that you're powerful enough for the endgame. And as any RPG fan would know, there's plenty of great games out there with terrible, boring grinds at the end, even without having loot boxes even be an option.
I enjoyed all my time training my followers, going through epic battles, finding all the collectables, powering up Talion and Celebrimbor, the combat is just as fast, fluid, and cinematic as it was in the first game, along with having many improvements, like how now Celebrimbor has a skill in the talent tree where he will still counter orcs who attack you as you try to do a ground finisher on someone.

So to anyone who loved Mordor, pick up this game, you'll be doing yourself a favor. Just look up the "true ending" on youtube instead of forcing yourself through the Act IV. Save those siege battles for a week from now, when you're thinking "Man, I really feel like slaughtering some Orcs about now." and pace yourself.

For those that don't know what Hotline Miami is, it's a game that was originally made using Gamemaker.  Eventually it was picked up by Devolver Digital and tweaked a little bit for mass publication.   The gameplay consists of having to kill everyone in a series of rooms inside a building to move onto the next segment or level, but the catch is that everyone dies in one hit, eve you.  The game requires a lot of precision timing and fast reaction time with lots of twitchy gameplay, all from a top down perspective.  The game is highly skill based and once you start getting good at it you feel great.  I don't want to spoil the story but it's very interesting and offbeat, it really fits the tone of the game.
Be wary that although the game has colorful pixel art it is extremely and satisfyingly gory.  It's really satisfying to see a streak of brains and blood across the room after bashing an enemy's head in.  The sound effects and upbeat high energy soundtrack also really help the kills feel more satisfying in this game.
In conclusion, I highly recommend you play this game right now! It's worth the full price and more than worth the usual sale price of $2.49 due to it's replayability, especially when trying to A+ all the levels.  It's truly a game that is better experienced than read about and is also a testament to how one can still make a great game no matter what engine and tools they're limited to.  Seriously, buy it and play it.

A rogue like top down shooter.
+ Interesting design
+ Good balance between linear sections and auto generated levels
+ Huge variety of weapons, enemies and abilites
+ Many hidden maps, power ups and easter eggs
+ Has a wiki
- Graphics could have higher resolution
- Often unfair (e.g., cramped space full of enemies)
- Locked at 30 fps
Recommended if you like hard rouge-like top down shooters with lots of hidden features and variety.
The objective of this game is simple: kill every enemy in each map. Once all enemies are killed you are teletransported to the next level. The maps, weapons and enemies positions and types are always generated but the theme of each level is fixed. Each 3-4 levels you must defeat a boss.
There are 6 classes of weapons: bullet, shell, bolt, explosive, energy and melee. You start off with a revolver and other weapons can be obtained through chests or by killing enemies but only two weapons can be carried at the same time. The chances of getting more powerful guns depends on the level; higher levels mean better weapons. Each class has a large set of weapons. The ammo is shared ammong weapons of a class.
Each character has one or two special abilities. For example, cristal can shield itself from bullets and robot can eat weapons to get ammo or HP. When you level up (by getting rads) and finish the current level you also mutate. Each mutation gives you permanent special abilities, such as, better accuracy or a chance of getting HP with each enemy kill. One mutation can be chosen from a set of 4 to 6 mutations.
There a lot of enemies in this game, each with its own specialty. Most enemies have an interesting design, while others are a little bland. Either way the particularities of each enemy make the game well balanced and interesting. With each level the enemies get a lot more difficult so you have to be prepared with much better weapons. The bosses have easy to recognize patterns, so they're not too hard. Same for the minions. Problem is that you do not have much HP or ammo in this game and neither are drops frequent so you have to hit and not get hit during the entire game. It is not an easy game.
Overall this is a very interesting game and I totally recommended it but it does have some problems. The game generator is often very unfair. It is not uncommon for the level to have you start in a small space sorrounded by enemies. The other issue is that the game is locked at 30 fps. You do get used to the 30fps but this game would benefit a lot from at least 60fps.
There are also easter eggs and many hidden zones and power ups. They're not easy to find but if finding things is too much trouble for you there is a wiki on this game. Personally I hate having to search for something. It's always a good sign when there's a wiki about a game; that must mean the game is good. Last but not least do not quit on this game just because you're losing a lot. You will eventually get decent weapons and with those win the game.

Nuclear throne makes the curious design decision to put a large amount of content (around 30% or so) at a skill level that is outside what most players are capable of accomplishing under normal circumstances.
This game is very, very hard, and unlike hard but inherently progressable games like Dark Souls or Risk of Rain, there is not really anything you can do to get around it - you can't grind or progress your way to victory. At some point, it's likely you'll "cap out" your skill level, or get to a point where only hundreds of hours of practice will improve your chances.
This capping out point might even be before you "finish the game", proper - reaching the Throne is something several of my friends gave up on after 40+ hours of gameplay. "Looping" the game is even further out of reach, far beyond anything I was ever able to achieve even as a long time player of difficult shoot-em-ups - you'll notice that many, if not most, of the players discussing loop gameplay on the forums have 100 to 200+ hours of gameplay.
This is where content comes in. 5 out of the game's 9 bosses are loop-only. One (and arguably three) of the game's characters are so difficult that they are effectively not practical for most players. Many of the bonus stages are late in the game and require a great deal of skill and luck to unlock. And for many players, runs will end far before they even reach the majority of the stages and enemies in the game. This is a lot of content that if you're not an extremely skilled or dedicated player, you will not (and unlike other similar games, may *never*) get value from.
I think it should be obvious from the other reviews that the game's gameplay is pretty on point. There's of course elements of irritation regarding random spawns and powerful enemies, which are also covered better by other reviews. But ultimately, I cannot recommend this game to most players, because a huge proportion of its content is not actually intended for most players. Even if you're able to get decently far, as I did, the sheer amount of content that feels permanently out of your reach can leave a bad taste in your mouth.
There's so much that cannot be accessed by a player who is not prepared to sink hundreds of hours into the attempt, and if you're not confident that that's something you'll be willing or able to do, you should be cautious before buying Nuclear Throne.

Nuclear Throne is a game that highly excels in every regard applicable except for gameplay.
You'll be pulled in because of its great graphics, soundtrack, characters, lore, style and desire to explore, but once you start playing you'll slowly start to resent the game.
I guess I'll start off by saying that the only real progress you make is through collecting crowns (think of them as mutators) and starting weapons. Although you'll want to dedicate runs to getting better starting weapons (Gold Weapons), you'll find that collecting crowns isn't as desirable. The majority of the crowns have risks that do not outweigh the rewards, leaving them to be largly ignored. Unlike other titles such as Spelunky or Risk of Rain, Nuclear Throne does not have a checkpoint system. Every run you do will start from 1-1 and will end either when you inevitably die or beat a certain boss. There is no practice mode, so if you want to familiarize yourself with a certain world, you'll have to start from 1-1 and hope that you even reach it.
I say hope because Nuclear Throne is essentially a dice roll of a game. The game is random to a fault. Levels are procedurally generated and have you spawn at random points. Sometimes you'll spawn in a safe area, and other times you'll spawn completely surrounded by enemies and with nowhere to take cover. You finish levels by killing all the enemies and walking into a portal that randomly spawns somewhere in the map, usually somewhere near the last enemy's corpse. Many times you'll find yourself screwed over by portal spawns because they'll block paths, explode nearby cars, or spawn at your feet, ending the level before you're ready to leave.
Weapons can be dropped from enemies or can spawn from red chests you'll find in every level. Enemy drops are completely random and weapon drops will provide weapons depending on what level you're in. In 1-1, you'll start off with a small pool of weapons you can get, and with each passing level, more weapon tiers will be available. This would be completely acceptable if (1) the weapons were balanced and (2) if your chance for a weapon was weighted properly. Currently, weapons are balanced in a way that by the time you reach the Nuclear Throne, weapons that use bullets or shells are mostly useless, and having a melee weapon is almost mandatory.
Mutations are offered to you after you collect enough rads to level up. You are randomly given 4 mutation choices and are expected to take 1. I'd say there are around 15-20 general mutations, not including Ultra mutations (character specific), and you're only allowed to hold onto 8-9, depending on the circumstance.
Most of the game is about making as good a build as you can with what you're given, which is to be expected from a rogue-like, but what ends up happening in Nuclear Throne is that after a certain point, you aren't given nearly enough compared to what you need (usually starts post-loop). The levels will keep on getting harder and harder, but your capabilities will stagnate. You'll get your 9 mutations and your 2 weapons and that's it. With weapons becoming so useless, you'll essentially be praying that the game will provide you with two of only a handful of weapons that can handle the mess of enemies that the game lops onto the level, and that you'll have the correct mutations at the time to carry you through the run (spoilers: you'll always feel like you're missing a mutation). In Risk of Rain, you can collect power-ups until you're practically a God, and the threats will scale up to you. In Nuclear Throne, the threat will keep on growing without you.
Every run will end in death and start you again from the very beginning, and a lot of the times, the game is so random that you'll feel like the game cheated you. Spawned you in the middle of a room full of enemies. Didn't provide you with any viable mutations/weapons until it was too late. Portal spawns without warning, blowing up a nearby car and killing you in the process. Off-screen enemy comes at you before you can even react. There's even an enemy in the game that instantly kills you upon contact, and can also instantaneously teleport to your proximity. This game is so full of questionable design decisions that calling Nuclear Throne "difficult" just doesn't even begin to describe it. Nuclear Throne is straight up unfair. After a while, you'll find yourself getting too frustrated way too often to be able to say that Nuclear Throne is a 'fun' game. There's only so many times where you can get cheated out of a solid run before you decide that you've had enough. The game is too random and unbalanced for its own good, and that is why I honestly cannot recommend it to anyone.

Look, I'll cut to the chase.  Is the game fun?  Yes.  But, is the game buggy AS HELL?  Extremely, like all LEGO games are, and I'm sick of it.  The only reason Traveller Tales keeps releasing these games in this state is because we all let it pass, and we really, REALLY shouldn't.  I might give it a pass if it was something that they patched out the first few days, but they don't do it.  They never do it.  They release a patch or maybe two in order to correct specific stuff, but the kind of errors that all of these games have had since the beginning are still there in every game.
Here's a bit of a rundown of the kind of stuff that makes the game unplayable:
- Characters will get stuck in the scenery and won't let you progress, forcing a restart.
- Stuff that should spawn at given points in a stage fails to spawn, forcing a restart.
- Activating certain stuff with a certain character in Free Play mode instead of doing it the way it's done in Story mode will make the scene get stuck, unable to advance, forcing a restart.
- In this particular game, literally every time I want to start playing, I can't just load a save.  No, I have to first start the game's story mode normally without using a save file and once I can move the characters THEN I can load the save.  Otherwise, the game crashes.  EVERY. SINGLE. TIME.
I've played LEGO games on PC, PS2, PS3, PS4 and 3DS.  All of them have these kinds of problems.  And they will keep having them because people will ignore them even though we shouldn't.  As much as I like LEGO games, this is the last time I buy one until they start caring about their customers.

In my opinion, this game is pretty fun, but there are some things that kinda make it difficult to enjoy.
One thing I don't like is how they lock a majority of the characters and the only way to unlock them is by playing about 15 or more games to get enough money to unlock them. This is annoying to me because the starting heroes you start off with don't include a healer, so a lot of the time, I join a game where my team can't sustain themselves very well.
Another thing I don't like is hero balance. A lot of the maps make it hard to use some one like Kinessa to her full potential as a sniper, so I would end up using her rifle more so than the sniper because of the close range and lack of points to cover as a sniper. On top of this, some heroes are just out right better than others. Evie has a weapon that does 930 damage, has the ability to fly in any direction she wants for 2 seconds, has Mei's cryofreeze that makes her immune to damage and self-heals for 3 seconds and also marks and slows any enemies nearby. Marked enemies take 30% more damage from her basic attack, dealing ~1209 damage. And her last ability lets her teleport and increase her damage by another 20%. Meanwhile, Kinessa deals 1300 damage per fully charged up shot, and about 1800 damage per fully charged headshot. To fully charge a sniper shot, you have to wait about 2 seconds, then to maximize damage, you're trying to land a headshot on a target constantly moving in close quarters combat, which means missing a lot of your scoped shots. Her abilities is being able to switch between sniper and carbine, laying 2 mines that slow enemies and deals a pitiful 4 damage per .2 seconds (~12 damage per second, squishies have 2000 hp) and gives your carbine 30% more damage (Doesn't apply to sniper), and a teleporter that you have to place, then get automatically teleported to it after a time.
So Evie can deal 1860 damage per second, with poetential to deal 2790 damage per second, compared to Kinessa's 650 per second, poetential 900 per second, or 1000 damage per second, poetential ~1300 damage per second with her carbine. Not to mention, Evie has way better mobility and self healing, and her basic attack is basically a rocket projectile.
While it is fun to mess with heroes in an AI match, in a PvP match, there's just only 3 or 4 heroes to use to even stand a chance against the other team, if you even have them unlocked yet. Just making all heroes availble from the start would make the game a lot better, or at least, reliable healers as part of the starter set.
Also, note that my opinions will change as I play more, but this is what I think so far.

Broken Age makes me excited for adventure games again.
Intuitive puzzles, clever and funny dialogue, and all brought to life with incredible graphics which make the game look more like a living cartoon than a game, Broken Age is easily one of the best modern adventure games out there.
You play the game alternating between two lead characters, each with his and her own unique situation from which they're anxious to escape. I won't spoil anything here - I'll just say that both characters have an interesting story, and you won't be bored with either or them. Control is simple adventure game stuff, so if you've ever played a point-and-click game (or even if you haven't) you won't have any difficulty here.
My only complaint so far is that when you get a game series off to such a good start, the wait between episodes is going to be tough. What's here now though is worth your time and money, and I highly recommend it.

Let me start off with I do own, and have played a
of Overwatch.
Paladins is much more fun and rewarding, IMO, then Overwatch in some key ways which I will go into below.
1:
Your shooting, sneakiness, and other abilities are much more important and play the major role in deciding which team will win an engagement. I think a lot of folks feel like I do, in that the Ultimates in Overwatch are TOO game defining and match decisive. Paladins' Ultimate abilities are a lot more in line with the rest of a characters abilities, and will give you a good boost, but won't Team Kill the other side with a single action.
2: Paladins rewards intelligent play and alternative play styles
as much as Killer Aim and Flick Shot Mastery. Being a skilled harrasser/flanker can have a real effect on the opposing team, beyond just sending them to Respawn. Disorientation, Traps, and Misdirection are all here.
3: Head shots and hit-box issues are no where near the problems they are in OW. Many heroes have some version of Healing, Stealth, Movement, or Area Denial. Used with guile they are fun and totally solid ways to help your team win.
4: The Card System and Buy ups during games. These allow for some very different play styles and strategies, even from the same hero from game to game. It adds a lot of depth, mystery, and unpredictability to games..... ie.... FUN!
- Truly Free to Play, and no Pay to Win. Most skins are decent, Overwatch has better graphics and skins/models.... But Paladins is pleasant on the eyes and a lot less loot box frustration to get what you want.
- Intelligence and Tactics on much more equal footing with Shooting skill.
- Card system is a lot of fun, and allows for some big differences in play styles within a hero.
- A lack of really unique and fun skins..... but this is something easily added into the game in the future. Much better to have a solid game now!
- No In-Game voice chat. Makes team talk more tricky..... but it also keeps folks from raging abuse on each other.
- Chat box is inaccessbile as soon as game ends.... no way to tell your team Awesome Work, or ask about teaming up or adding friends. (You can try to add them blind from social screen, but its nicer to ask first.) Again, this also prevents a lot player abuse when your team loses, so another almost Pro, Con.
EDIT: 11/6/17
The game has changed a lot since launch. Hi-Rez isn't taking cheaters to task, and they are pretty rampant, for a competitive game that is not cool.
They release new characters unbalanced, and without thought to how they will disrupt play. Change can be good, but in this case its chaos and Flavor of the Month on crack.
Starting to really feel like its morphing into a pure money grab, as they realize they aren't getting a significant share of Overwatches player base, those they get they are targetting for $$.
It was fun at first, and the idea of rewarding skilled play over Ultimate stacking was right on, they have lost their way. So I have to change my vote to a Thumbs Down. GLHF all.

If you loved "Fallout 1" and "Fallout 2" as well as "The Fall - Last Days of Gaya" you will absolutely love Wasteland 2.  Party based RPGs have been missing for a LONG time, those in a post-apocalytic setting for even longer. Wasteland 2 brings this forgotten genre back to live with thrilling tactical combat, great story telling and that sense of humor that made the orignal Fallouts so great in the first place.
I am not sure how far in the story I am now but after doing the first set of major places (4 of them visited) I can also say that they really stuck through with their promises that choices in this game would matter. Both local and immidiatly as well as on the grand scheme of things to come. And I love the game for it.

A game of contradictions really. At first, wandering through dark & creepy forests armed only with a flashlight and a six-shooter is really atmospheric. Many a time I panicked at the sight of a shadow, thinking it was a creeper, only to find as I drew closer it was a mere road sign. Sadly, this feeling is soon replaced by boredom. Oh, another forest. Same as the last forest. Ho-hum, A few times the game ventures into alternate settings; the town, a garden with a maze, a rock concert on a farm (possibly the finest set-piece in the game) but you soon return to the forest.
Collectibles are scattered about the areas, including the manuscript pages which attempt flesh out the games story. Reading these isn't integrated into the gameplay, you're expected to head into a a menu to plough through the prose. Why even make a game if you're going to deliver your story as a book? Other story elements are better integrated into the game. Well, we get cutscenes. The real gems are theTV & radio shows scattered through the game, which do an excellent job of fleshing out the setting. Most of them seemed to be on the route you have to take through the levels, so it's definitely worth checking them out.
As for the creepers themselves, the very act of shooting at them seems kinda wrong at first due to not knowing what they are. Are these just normal townsfolk who are possessed? Is it OK to just gun them down if they don't know what they are doing? Luckily these ethical considerations soon beome irrelevant as their true nature is revealed. I won't go into further details because I don't want to spoil the game.
Another flaw the game has is its inventory system. Many a time you'll be fully tooled up with all the guns and equipment you need to fight off waves of bad guys, only to find that everything is gone after a cutscene with no explanation. There are times when the game shows how you lost your equipment, but other times its as if Alan decides to just leave it behind, It just feels like a cheap way to increase the games difficulty.
There's the core of a good game here, but so much of it just feels like padding

In almost all accounts, Alan Wake is passable at best. The only redeeming quality that grants my recommendation is the overall theme of the game.
