Officially licensed games are typically not all that impressive due to publishers making a profit on the name alone if not the substance of the game. Shadow of Mordor was a surprisingly good game in that regard. It was released an underdog and turned out to incorporate some interesting new ideas in its nemesis system, some nice tidbits from Tolkien's legendarium to find, and some nice sound design. It provided me 40ish hours of decent entertainment until I grew bored of the grind towards the end. I still haven't finished the game. There just wasn't enough meat on that bone to keep me playing past the 40 hour mark.
When I first saw it previewed, Shadow of War really interested me in terms of its overarching metagame. But sadly there really isn't much new here despite the efforts at evolving the original game. There's a new system in which you're fighting a literal war between orc armies, but it's so bogged down by an abysmal UI and a grindfest of new orcs constantly flowing into areas that it really doesn't do anything to add fulfilling gameplay on top of the foundations set by the first game. There's a neat system of storming enemy forts but there's so much dry, boring legwork to do ahead of this that it feels like a grind almost immediately despite a lot of it being new to this game. You're supposed to be able to manage your own loyal orcs into attacking others and doing certain more subtle treacherous acts, but it's so difficult to keep track of what your orcs and your enemies traits are that the whole thing is just an obtuse cluster♥♥♥♥ and I ended up just saying screw it and killing the enemy orcs myself, which became tedious after a dozen or so hours. This is in large part due to the bad UI, but also because the core gameplay mechanics here just aren't all that much fun after you've done them 20 or 30 times -- Especially to thsoe of us who've done this stuff in the first game. And this is a game that expects you to repeat them many, many more times than that.
There are some new areas this time around to differentiate the game from the same brown, crappy areas that permeated the first game outside of Nurnen. Minas Ithil, initially, was amazing! It was so cool seeing a city that I'd read about in Tolkiens works come to life. Sadly, there just isn't much substance to the areas outside of the initial feeling of, "hey, this is different!" One of my favorite things to do in open world games such as the Assassin's Creed series or Witcher 3 is to wander the open world, immersing myself in its environments, its denizens, and their daily lives while I collect all of the things listed on the map. The collectibles in this game don't do very much for you at all, and the world itself is unfortunately pretty bare, without much depth past orcs taking dumps in bushes or walking around aimlessly from point A to point B. Sure, there's a human, Gondorian city in the beginning. But beyond the visuals being different, ie. marble buildings and streets instead of muddy ground and wood huts, there isn't anything actually setting it apart from the Mordor areas of the first game. There don't seem to be any civilians, anywhere (where'd they all go? Minas Tirith?), and the soldiers that are present are either fighting, standing around, or behind the gate lying there injured. And that's just a very small portion of the map -- 80% of it is just a ton of orcs running around doing the same orc things they were doing in the first game. It doesn't feel like a real, lived-in space; it feels like a gamey arena in which you're supposed to fight orcs. This game suffers from what old open world games used to suffer from back when they all copying the GTA3 -- It's got a vast, wide open space peppered with absolutely nothing interesting aside from lots of bad guys to fight and some collectibles that, while they give you some interesting tidbits of information, do very little to make you want to chase them down otherwise.
A lot of this is hurt by the fact that the combat and stealth are almost wholly unchanged from the first game. If you loved the gameplay of Shadow of Mordor, you'll like this one. I was always lukewarm on the combat and stealth of the first game and was disappointed not to see it evolved upon in this game.
The story is laughably bad in most cases and forgettable in others. Most of the characters are cliche and there are some plot holes present that make me think any time spent in the writing room here was likely spent trying to finagle Tolkien's legendarium into justifying some of the odd writing moves here. For example, why did Shelob even want the "new ring" (ridiculous in its own right but whatever)? She had it for like a quarter of the game and didn't do a single thing with it but sit in her cave, presumably staring at the wall? Another character has been fighting orcs his entire life and knows the treachery they're capable of, yet still tries to make a deal with them that you can see going wrong from a hundred miles away. The entire thing is ridiculous and the prerendered cutscenes suck you right out of the moment anyway.
They've added some loot and some RPG elements to this one, which was very interesting to me in previews, but they're incredibly basic and don't even really warrant mentioning. The equipment is all very generic looking and the stats make the barest modicum of a difference. There are class tiers of equipment now, and the only stuff different enough to notice is the top tier stuff, but obtaining a full set of legendary gear requires so much grinding that it isn't even worth it. Perhaps if the top tier stuff was interesting in some way it might warrant the grinding in the way that a game like Diablo, Destiny, or Borderlands does, but this stuff doesn't. And all of the lower and middle tiers are not notably different. Sure, the middle tier stuff has some unique perks, but none of them make any real impact on the gameplay.
The loot system seems only to have served to make the balance of this game skew heavily towards grindiness. You've got to accomplish the same tedious stuff over and over but the loot perks and abilities give you very disappointing rewards for doing so. And what you're doing to gain experience and loot is not only uninteresting, but requires you to repeat the same activities so frequently. You can spend 4 hours grinding experience by taking out or recruiting enemy orcs, but they'll be replaced again by fresh orcs once time passes and you'll have to spend another 4 hours doing the same stuff over again with the new guys that have just come in, all while these activities and the setting get old and tiresome, while rewarding you with loot that you never see making an actual difference in gameplay. It loses its fun factor very quickly and this continues ad nauseam throughout the entire game.
It's really the pacing that's a problem here. Some of this stuff is fun initially, but not for the amount of repetitions that you're required to do to progress into conquering an area. Something else aside from this core gameplay loop of kill/recruit, then take fortresses needs to be present to drive you forward -- Whether it's an enticing plot, interesting characters with good dialogue, loot or new abilities that greatly increases your player character's power, a well-crafted game world you can lose yourself in, SOMETHING! And there's nothing here that does that. It's the same repetitive, dry task of killing/recruiting/ambushing orcs that leads to chasing loot that has no impact, upgrading your abilities not far past what they were in the first game, or progressing an unengaging story.
I didn't even notice the much-maligned microtransactions but I can't help wondering if they ruined the balance, because this is just not a fun game to play after a few hours. If you loved Shadow of Mordor, then sure, give this a shot. But after putting 40 hours into the first game I found that I grew tired of this one way before that.
This game has a good chance of making you lose track of time.

This is a true, proper PC game through and through. It performs amazingly well. The game controls just as well on Keyboard & Mouse as on controller. The game is highly optimized, performing great on a variety of PCs. There is an in-game preset that varies from Very Low to Very High, as well as multiple settings. The game can even be customized with shortcut commands for various effects to be turned off or to be run on special resolutions. The game on max settings looks mighty better than its console equivalents. There are better textures, better shadows, the light shafts generated by different light sources are active at all times, compared to only story sections at night in the console version and there is the draw distance is higher. Plus the framerate is unlocked of course. The game also knows to use FXAA, and AA, between 4 to 8, or 16 (forgot if its 8 or 16). There is even a FoV (field of view) slider. It also knows how to properly use 2-4 cores (maybe more ?).
Alan Wake is great. It's a product of love and care, with attention to detail. The main thing going for it is its story. If you are one of those people who play games for their story, you owe it to yourself to play Alan Wake. It's exactly one of those games which you cannot stop playing because you want to see what happens next. Of course, you wouldn't be so engaged if the game wasn't dripping with atmosphere. You actually don't need me telling you this. Just look at the screenshots from Steam. Also, the voice acting? Some of the best in business. The main character, Alan Wake is one the better voiced characters ever made. Especially as he narrates his own adventure from 2 different perspective in the game.
From a gameplay perspective, it is engaging and dynamic. You actually uses a flashlight to either kill enemies or make them weak enough to be killed. The combat is frenetic. You are always surrounded, enemies don't wait up on you like say, Assassin's Creed and you constantly need to be dodging, checking your surroundings and monitoring how much ammo and battery life your flashlight has left.
I finished the main campaign in about 18-19 hours on Hard and then I played another 2 pieces of DLC for another 2 hours. The game is not hard. Just don't go guns blazing and be a good shot. There is one section in the 3rd act that may prove a bit difficult because you are sort of helpless, but besides that, I recommend starting on Hard for a proper experience.
Not that many bad things I have to say about this game. Actually all of these might not even bother most of you.
• I experienced one or two crashes and maybe 2 bugs. So the game is not 100% technically perfect. Maybe 95%.
• Consider this as you will, but this games has no ... bosses, not really anyway.
• While the games is great as a whole and has some surprising elements that happen from time to time, it lacks some especially WOW element. There are maybe 3 set pieces, but they're not quite "WOAH DUDE".

The game has 7 different types of collectibles.
• 3 are just for the sake of it (I didn't do them).
• another one are basically stashes of ammunition, indicated in the game like the stashes in Half-Life 2.
• another one are Radios. These are actually quite fun because they provide backstory on the game and fuel the universe's lore.
• second to last are TVs, which can be powered on and Alan can watch an episode of TV show closely resembling Twin Peaks. They are short, 1-4 minutes in length but are quite interesting indeed.
• the last ones, and most important, are Manuscript Pages.
The replayability is decent. The game has 4 difficulty levels and the last one is unlocked after finishing the game once. In Nightmare difficulty (fitting name for the game's theme) there are Pages to collect that further expand the background of the story. The game is quite long as I said so maybe you won't want to replay right away.
Now, the STEAM achievements, for the people that care. The game has a lot of achievements for a singleplayer game and a surprising number of achievements for its included 2 DLCs. Most of these are story moments, but there are quite a few that needed a conscious effort. Actually most of the achievements for the DLCs need a conscious effort. And there are of course 16  achievements for finding every collectible in the game, main + DLCs.

Although the early main quest and tutorial was horrible (hey devs, stop making us follow people that move more slowly than us, this is the thing I'd least like to be doing in your open world sandbox) ultimatly the later quests, side quests and conquest mechanics were enjoyable and I liked the direction the game took for the most part.
The post game shadow wars became tedious and although I stuck it out I'd suggest to anyone that they should play as long as they find it engaging then look up the true ending on youtube. I liked the ending but the true ending could be derived from the actual ending, and was not worth the extra 4 hours I spent doing tedious grind after I'd grown bored of doing the same defence mission over and over.
You never need to engage with lootboxes, but you can feel the entire game warp around them trying to sell you lootboxes, and I think anyone who really hates the idea of single player loot boxes more than they like playing a good game (not being sarcastic, I was only a smidgeon off not buying the game myself) should not buy this game as the practices shown and the way it affects gameplay (and in one case story) is disgusting.
At the end of the day, of the 36 hours I played this game, I really, really enjoyed 30 of them. This game is much better than the first in almost every way. The first game I got bored entering the second act at about 11 hours but until the shadow wars post game I never felt like stopping. People have said the shadow wars are made grindy to make you buy orcs but I don't feel that buying orcs would make it any better, and for the purposes of that section legendary orcs don't feel any better than epic orcs, and you can get away with running mostly normal orcs.
Its a bit easier to see the cogs turning with the nemisis system this time but multiple times in the playthrough an orc coming back in one way or another elicited something close to real emotion from me and in one case I really didn't expect what happened with an orc I dubbed spider bro (because he f***ing loved spiders).
Overall, this is a 7/10 game that should have been a 9/10 game, I still reccomend it but its hard to look past poor quest design (especially early) and the way you can feel the whole game creak as it warps around the horrible lootboxes - it doesn't matter if you don't buy them, you're still affected by them existing and I hate to think how much dev time was wasted on them.

There should be a somewhat recommend option, because that's how I'd sum the game up. It could be the best flight simulator out there, but it isn't and I'll get into the why it's good, and why it's bad with 4 points:
1st point: It's highly convenient. Microsoft set it up with simplicity in mind, it works well with both old and new joysticks, aircraft are set up to fly as soon as the game has loaded without any random surprises & it's highly modifiable with semi-competent knowhow required. If you're after complexity to rival the real world you can set that up too.
2nd point: The whole world is in the simulator, and is practically complete. Fly from seattle to Sydney with a stop off in Honolulu & you can see iconic buildings, entire downtown districts surrounded by their suburbs and dynamic weather if chosen to give you a near perfect realistic experience. The detail the microsoft team put in with the default game is unrivalled.
3rd point: The support online is huge. Add mods to update the games graphics to todays next-gen standards, or add to your library of flyable aircraft with hundreds, if not thousands of additional aircraft.
4th point: The age of the game is getting up there. Released in 2006, the last support for the game was in around 2007-08 before microsoft discontinued the series after disbanding the dev team. Dovetail games, the new publishers have been denied access by microsoft to modernise the internal code to utulise todays hardware. What this means for you is if your pc is newer than 2009, regardless of your pc's graphics power you will have performance issues. Stuttering, low framerate will be a plague unless you can tweak your system and the game's external code to fix performance, and these tweaks are different for each computer, requiring a high level of competency in knowing what you're doig. This is the biggest letdown & you can blame microsoft for that.
The other option is X plane 10, but that's not perfect either unfortunately. Watch that space though, the game developers are still highly active...

Broken Age is a very cute and enjoyable game, which takes the best from the olden days of the point-and-click genre, and merges it with modern gaming.
First of all, I was impressed about the sheer simplicity and quality of the game. Everything seemed polished and "done". Somethings were different from other PoC games, but very much in a good way. There is very little GUI. Long forgotten are the "push/pull/talk to/give to/open/close" options the inventory box, that always took up half the screen. In this game, you only have a context-specifix cursor, and a small inventory panel, which slides up from the bottom of the screen, and thus takes up zero screen real estate during gameplay.
Secondly – and this is the games strong point – it excells with it's setting and storytelling. All through, the player is immersed in a fun, but also somewhat upsetting story. The writing is sublime, and the voice acting is quite possibly the bes from any game ever, with stars such as Jack Black, Elijah Wood and Wil Wheaton on the team.
Another special thing about Broken Age, is the fact that there are actually two (seemingly) completelly separate storylines. You control two different characters, with very different situations, and you may change between them at will. Their storylines will intertwine later on in the game.
Some people complain that the game is too easy. There may be a little truth to that argument, but not enough to disregard the game. Personally I felt the game was moderatelly easy – not hard enough to be completelly stuck, but never patronizingly easy either. Most of the time, however, I knew exactly what to do.
To be completelly honest, and I want to be honest with you now, seeing we're best friends and all, I don't think the magic of the LucasArts-era of PoC gaming was ever about the mind-boggingly hard puzzles. It was about telling a story. And that goal has been perfectly achieved with this game.

NSFW is a game where you play short sessions in your 'working week'. Every day you start by reading email and accepting a task, sometimes from multiple choices, then stare at a screen of your work. Every so often co-workers pass by, heralded by their footsteps.
Just like real work, doing this gradually drains your soul and leads to death... err game over.
Instead of working, you can right-click at any time to change the work screen into something more fun. These can be non-interactive small films you can watch, or small mini-games. You can right-click to go back to work at any time and should do so as soon as you hear footsteps, because ALL your co-workers will snitch on you, leading to you being fired (game over).
The longetivity of this game is in unlocking all the various mini-games and small movies, which you pay for with your working day salary. As days go by the company starts to notice someone is abusing the system and it becomes more and more difficult to keep your actions hidden, as special checks may occur at given times, etc.
Recommended if you like a little naughty humour.

They attempted to market this one as a "psychological action thriller", but make no mistake...this is a HORROR game, and one of the highest calibre at that.  Not the "scariest" of its kind, perhaps, but that aside this is absolutely top-notch in every conceivable department - story, gameplay, graphics, sound - you name it.
It even has that rarest of horror game features...ally A.I. which actually WORKS!  No "babysitting" an annoying NPC who stands in your way three-quarters of the time, or hovers idiotically between you and the enemy you're attempting to kill...these ones fight competently alongside you, without "carrying" you to the point where you can just stand back and let them do all the dirty work.
This game also manages to be quite "long" without overstaying its welcome; another rare feat, at least in my estimation.  It's so good, in fact, that it's even worth the full thirty - count 'em, thirty - dollars still being standardly asked on Steam, but really...we all just wait for the sales on anything which isn't brand spanking new and/or under ten dollars anyway, don't we?  I do, but then again, I am a bit of a cheapskate.
Expect a review of the sequel soon, kids...
Verdict: 10/10.

Dear Cantina:
Brace yourself for a long review. There's a tl;dr at the end.
Before I recieved this game from a friend, I was telling nearly everyone I knew how awesome this game looked. The trailer where Fen and the bleeding man are outside made the game look like there was going to be this big world to explore, and that the characters would have meaningful deaths that could actually hit the player kind of hard.
I read the reviews when the game came out, of course; I was thinking, "Hah! Haters. I'll bet they're all wrong!"
Well... a lot of them ARE haters. But even more of them had a good point to make.
This game, while still only in Act 1, is anywhere from 30 minutes to 1.3 hours long. No longer.
I've played longer flash games, and those are free!
More about the trailer: I felt like it was lying to me after I played the actual game.
There's no open world; not to mention, most of it was completely pointless and did nothing but waste the player's time. The outdoor areas had literally nothing to do. When you make a game, your goal is to entertain. When a player feels like the game is boring or is wasting their time, they will quickly lose interest, especially if it's right at the start.
The characters are ALL lifeless. No personality, no interactions, nothing. I'm not going to tell you that fixing this is easy, but there are some easy changes you could make. Something as simple as having people pet Fen when clicked on goes a long way. Hell, based on the person's personality, they could push him away; they could talk to him; they could do all sorts of things.
A codex would have been great. I had to take a picture with my phone of a poster in someone's room, instead of being able to take notes in-game. The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask had an incredible notebook that showed the schedule of every person in the town, allowing players to use the time system to their advantage and anticipate where people are at what times. This is essential for a time-based game, and lets a player know that they can do things like access a computer while someone is away.
Another problem was the puzzles. There are so few of them, and most of them are REALLY obscure. One example was as follows:
*SPOILERS*
How was I supposed to figure out that I was supposed to click on a poster in someone's room to get the code in the cafe? Clicking on any other poster does absolutely nothing, and Fen can't even leave the vent to get close enough to read it!
*END SPOILERS*
The aesthetic: The visuals were appealing at first glance, but over time, I got bored of the lack of character in each room... which is important, seeing as how few rooms there are. Take a look at the game Fez. The developer put together each area with great love and care, so that no two platforms looked alike. This makes a game look amazing, and adds a metric sh*t ton of depth. A Point/Click game heavily relies on the visual appeal, and this game sadly lacked quite a bit of that. EXAMPLE: Some of the bedrooms look literally identical. Copied and pasted.
Another thing about the visuals: The animations went by way too fast. A kill took only a split second, and wasn't satisfying in the least. And this is just a personal gripe... but don't censor swearing in a game like this. And change the font to something more sinister than comic sans! Jeez! Realism, man!
The sound almost wasn't even there. A horror game always, ALWAYS needs sound. I'm serious! Play a game like Amnesia or Spooky's Jumpscare Mansion, and you'll see what I mean. Without sounds, those games wouldn't even be that scary. Sure, they look spooky, but half the fun in being scared is the build-up(ambient sounds, if you will) or the jarring noise. This game didn't even have sound effects for kills. Dead silence. It really took away from the experience.
Put these two together, and you get anti-immersion: the feeling of being distant from what's happening in the game.
Kills also had to be executed perfectly and in ONLY the intended way. If I'm the monster, I want strategy. I want to kill my victims how I want to kill them. Hell, the game description highlights strategy! Where was the strategy? Did you mean the puzzles? That's just a logic puzzle. Strategy implies freedom of choice; or, more importantly, tactics. I wanted to do the thing where you isolate your victim, pop out of a vent, grab them, and splatter them back through the vent. Then, the humans who are left would investigate this, and you would immediately arouse suspicion being in the vents, and they could catch you if you're in them. THIS is strategy. All you have so far is puzzles, and very few of them at that. Never once did I see anyone in the lounge, or wandering the halls.
Another lie: The vents.
Holy mother of god, this was disappointing. I spent about 10 minutes trying to figure out how the vents worked, only to learn that I couldn't use them at all! And I never could! At night, Fen can roam the vents around his room. Why, then, were there inaccessible vents all throughout the Outpost? They're misleading! Also, I wanted to see the rooms I had cleared. I wanted to see how the humans reacted to what I had done, peering in through the vents.
The game also needs WAY more interactivity. The whole game had only a few things to interact with, and all of them were for puzzles. At least say, "The door is locked." over impassible doors. And why did the locked doors look identical to the unlocked ones? I had to go door to door, clicking all over until I found out which ones led somewhere. It was confusing and tedious, to say the least. And when you can't access something yet, like a keyboard, say "You can't get to the keyboard right now." to at least let the player know they can mess with it later. Paired with the aforementioned notebook, this could be great. It's the little things like this that add character to the game. More examples: "It's your bed. Wait (x) hours?"; "You can hear voices through the door."; "You can hear frantic voices through the wall."; "You didn't find anything worth taking on the corpse."; "The vent won't open from here."; "Quit without saving?".
Last one, I promise. This game is VERY hard to figure out at first for all the wrong reasons. It's due to a lack of conveyance. The game never tells you what to do, ever. Thanatos says to make some trouble, so you're supposed to mess with people, right?
WRONG. You're supposed to STAY OUT OF TROUBLE. Kill people WITHOUT being noticed. Wreak havoc SILENTLY.
The game also gives the player zero feedback! I mixed some chemicals, but it did nothing. What now? I clicked 'drug coffee', and it did nothing. Sure, the guy was standing right there, but I thought I had actually drugged it, since my red bar went down. Turns out, nothing had happened and the game hadn't alerted me of this.
The inventory was also confusing. There are 2 items to find in the game TOTAL, and unlike most Point'n'Click games, you can't pick them up and try them with different things. You can't even mouse over them for info! And, when you use one, it stays in your inventory, with the exception of one puzzle.
tl;dr:
Great concept, but it needs lots of work. Consider hiring a friend to work with you; being an indie developer is tough work, especially if you plan on making more games in the future.
Suggestions:
-Add feedback: "The door is locked", etc.
-Add the ability to strategize, such as killing from vents as advertised, or killing in any way the player wants, rather than just adding death as the end result of solving puzzles
-Make every area look unique
-Make every area significant; useless areas waste time and patience of both the developer and the player!
-Give the humans personalities
-Add pause menu
-Add codex/schedules
-Add what the trailer/description says you can do! Don't lie!
Thanks for reading. Hope I could help; I want to see this game become something incredible. Looking forward to future updates!

This is one of the most embarrassingly bad games ever created. First of all, the Twin Peaks / adventure game thing is a dupe: for a game about a writer, this has no plot.
It's divided into days and nights. The days last about fifteen minutes in game-time. Here is one day's plot: Alan arrives at a caravan park. He follows the owner across the park, listening to his dreary waffle. There's a cut scene, then it's night again. Here's another day's "adventure": Alan wakes up in a loony bin. The doc lets him out and Alan follows him across the building, listening to his dreary waffle. Then it's night again. You get the idea.
Each night seems to last an eternity. Alan walks through repetitive woods and lumber yards shooting the same three enemies. The batteries in his torch last about ten seconds, so Ever Ready's product placement was somewhat ill-conceived. That's it.
Other than the game being terrible, there are a few other flaws. Alan has trouble walking, or climbing, or jumping. His legs often disagree with his body and he regularly falls down stairs or trips over his own feet. He can only carry about three bullets. The voice acting is unbearable. He's also an abysmal writer who needs to learn the meaning of "show don't tell". Every time something vaguely interesting happens, the game tears away your view and Alan tells you about what you're being forced to watch. The game should just cut to the chase and not bother giving you control at all, as it never seems to amount to much.
Alan Wake is a terrible writer and a terrible bore and a completely excruciating game. It would be more fun to control his wife who died in the first ten minutes.

Having heard so many good things about this game, I was certainly hopeful going in.  However, despite doing a decent job as a thriller/horror experience, the almost unbelievably tedious and clunky combat mechanics had me calling it quits after just a few chapters.  Combat isn't even that hard per say, but its semi-broken targeting system, awkward movement and dodging, and its extreme repetition in terms of enemies and tactics required really drags everything down into frustrating tedium.
I think this game would have actually been a lot better with little to no traditional combat, and instead focusing its action sequences on more of a fearful avoidance of baddies and environmental dangers (e.g., the Amnesia games).  That would have allowed it to spend more time on conveying a compelling and harrowing tale through more of the things it pulls off well: frightful tension and suspense, fearful dreamscapes and flashbacks, and gradually unravelling the mysteries of whatever dark forces are terrorizing Alan, his wife, and the inhabitants of the formerly cozy backwater.
The mysterious darkness and its seeming relation to Alan's own writing was an interesting concept that I would have otherwise wanted to see taken to its logical conclusion, but it was also really hard to empathize and become invested in Alan as a character since, to be frank, he is consistently painted as a self-absorbed jerk.  In general, if you're willing to suffer through the terribad combat elements, this game is probably worth your time; but if not, then you might want to look elsewhere for something that gets story AND combat right.

Tough, painful, and worthy of ragequitting. And no, I'm not talking about the game being difficult.
I'm talking about:
A skill system which is broken
Attributes which mean nothing
clunky game mechanics
the AI taking multiple turns in a row with unlimited SP and near 100% hit rate
statistics shattering weapon jams and misses
utterly no roleplaying experience
a tactical game where you only need one tactic
and the list goes on.
In fact here's one example, you have an assault rifle, there's no one around you, your enemy is in the "sweet spot" as in not too close, not too far. Your gauge shows that you have a 70% chance to hit. and you miss. not just once, but 5 times in a row. or more. As I posted on another person's review in a comment: "I really think the devs need to go back to hs and take some statistics, cause the odds of missing so many shots in a row when it's 70% or more "to hit"... is beyond stupid. Think about it, a 3 in 7 chance to miss five times in a row is 3 in 16,807 (or a 0.01% chance of happening). But it happens so frequently it's more like the reverse 70% chance to miss. But then again, even the odds of missing 5 times in a row would still be 7 in 243 (or a 2.88% chance of happening).. which is still absurd. And yet the game does this for most people I've heard talking about it."
This is a common experience. and it just keeps going. enemies almost always hit, have twice the range of your snipers (from even the beginning missions), your guns jam at least once a battle (when each gun's jam rate is 5% or less), and so on.
I just about rage quit the other night because the immersion in the story is so awful it just breaks you out of the game by destroying the suspension of disbelief. You get "badass" rangers telling you that they are the team that goes in and kills other rangers, and get told stories of other rangers making tough choices and coming out on top. Then you try and do anything contrary to the story and you're done. You do one thing wrong and an entire town aggros against you. And no there's no charisma stat that calms people down, no speechcraft skill which says "slow down compadre," no kill the leader and stop the aggro, it's just one bugged out exchange where you might as well reboot to your last save (if you're lucky enough to not trust the game to make backup saves from time to time) or you kill the entire town/area and (as some have said) you cannot complete the game. I personally don't have any experience with that, as I'm only 20 something hours in, but come-on, this is ridiculous.
It's not about a complex storyline or making a game that's tough, it's sloppy game design mixed with poor story writing. And it's bad programming, on numerous occasions I've experienced a plethora of bugs including one where the camera won't pan, but for some reason I can move the sun in the sky (yeah, no joke). And the stuff that is programmed "right" is just poor. There is no choice in the game other than linear save town A and you have problems with town B for the game, or save town B and have problems with town A down the line. Then there's the AI and battles, at first it's new and fun and interesting. Then it's just a poorly designed squad tactics game where the enemies do the same thing every time and so do you. I really only employed one strategy in 20+ hours of gameplay. set up 2 short range fighters, set up 2 assault rifle fighters and 1 sniper and the rest of the game is a cake walk. It's not fun, it's repetitive.
Another problem is the "fans" who jump on any topic you make or post and immediately say it's your fault the game is bad, or that you're not reading all the text, or that you are doing combat wrong, or... blah blah blah, but the game is as I've stated above, one-dimensional, clunky, broken and worthy of ragequitting. This last bit about the fans can't be the dev's fault, but the hype about this being the game everyone wanted Fallout 3 to be, is like gasoline on a fire, it just burns hotter and less controlled. If you take an objective look at the game, you'll see the same stuff that I and many others have pointed out. At least with the story stuff I'm willing to agree to disagree, as I can see how if you don't think about the story or complete failure on the roleplaying aspect of the game then you've got yourself a repetitive one-tactic game where you make choices like a train choosing which railroad track to take, sure you can take the long way around, but the end result is the same, you're still stuck on the tracks.
I really really really wanted to like this and I just can't. Maybe I'll give it another try down the road, but I've got a sour taste in my mouth right now.

Lets get this out of the way first: Doing time travel right is pretty hard but hats off to the devs for doing their best. Another thing: I don't know why this game is labeled as "SJW propaganda". I never got that vibe once while playing. Is it because Chloe has a blue hair? Do people not realize "punk" has been a thing decades before the melodrama of 2011? Hell I didn't even get the gay vibe that everyone says the game forces. There was the one option to kiss Chloe, that's about it. No ♥♥♥♥ing idea where bigoted people get the idea the game is pushing a "gay agenda".
I knew a little about the ending of the game before I played it. You had to choose between the town and Chloe, and that's it. I thought to myself, "Wow that's an easy choice", but as I came to finally understand Chloe I thought about how unfair it was.
I went with the sacrifice Chloe option, which was to my surprise the majority of what others chose as well. Chloe is a very tragic character. I felt myself not liking her to start with but as the game progressed I started to understand why she acts out the way she does. Now I sympathize heavily with her character. She had a tragic childhood with her father dying and her best friend stepping out of her life, and right when she finds someone to finally open up to they're taken from her in the worst way possible. Life is never fair to her, and the ending I chose is a conitnuation of that.
The final choice wasn't a matter of picking between what was right and wrong for me, I was going to save the Bay no matter what, but rather coming to the realization of how much I cared about Chloe and how ♥♥♥♥ed up it was that there was no happy ending no matter what ending you chose. It helped that Chloe herself leaned heavily towards saving the town. The fact that she was ready to give everything she had left to save the place that took everything from her really speaks about her true character. In the end I felt really in touch with Max, because her thoughts and emotions summed up and mirrored mine. I just have to say that ending cutscene was brilliant, and I'm not ashamed to say I cried.
Lastly, I have to mention the music. This game is probably the best example I can think of when it comes to the music lending weight and emotion to a video game. It plays such a part that it wouldn't be anywhere near the same game without it.

Officially licensed games are typically not all that impressive due to publishers making a profit on the name alone if not the substance of the game. Shadow of Mordor was a surprisingly good game in that regard. It was released an underdog and turned out to incorporate some interesting new ideas in its nemesis system, some nice tidbits from Tolkien's legendarium to find, and some nice sound design. It provided me 40ish hours of decent entertainment until I grew bored of the grind towards the end. I still haven't finished the game. There just wasn't enough meat on that bone to keep me playing past the 40 hour mark.
When I first saw it previewed, Shadow of War really interested me in terms of its overarching metagame. But sadly there really isn't much new here despite the efforts at evolving the original game. There's a new system in which you're fighting a literal war between orc armies, but it's so bogged down by an abysmal UI and a grindfest of new orcs constantly flowing into areas that it really doesn't do anything to add fulfilling gameplay on top of the foundations set by the first game. There's a neat system of storming enemy forts but there's so much dry, boring legwork to do ahead of this that it feels like a grind almost immediately despite a lot of it being new to this game. You're supposed to be able to manage your own loyal orcs into attacking others and doing certain more subtle treacherous acts, but it's so difficult to keep track of what your orcs and your enemies traits are that the whole thing is just an obtuse cluster♥♥♥♥ and I ended up just saying screw it and killing the enemy orcs myself, which became tedious after a dozen or so hours. This is in large part due to the bad UI, but also because the core gameplay mechanics here just aren't all that much fun after you've done them 20 or 30 times -- Especially to thsoe of us who've done this stuff in the first game. And this is a game that expects you to repeat them many, many more times than that.
There are some new areas this time around to differentiate the game from the same brown, crappy areas that permeated the first game outside of Nurnen. Minas Ithil, initially, was amazing! It was so cool seeing a city that I'd read about in Tolkiens works come to life. Sadly, there just isn't much substance to the areas outside of the initial feeling of, "hey, this is different!" One of my favorite things to do in open world games such as the Assassin's Creed series or Witcher 3 is to wander the open world, immersing myself in its environments, its denizens, and their daily lives while I collect all of the things listed on the map. The collectibles in this game don't do very much for you at all, and the world itself is unfortunately pretty bare, without much depth past orcs taking dumps in bushes or walking around aimlessly from point A to point B. Sure, there's a human, Gondorian city in the beginning. But beyond the visuals being different, ie. marble buildings and streets instead of muddy ground and wood huts, there isn't anything actually setting it apart from the Mordor areas of the first game. There don't seem to be any civilians, anywhere (where'd they all go? Minas Tirith?), and the soldiers that are present are either fighting, standing around, or behind the gate lying there injured. And that's just a very small portion of the map -- 80% of it is just a ton of orcs running around doing the same orc things they were doing in the first game. It doesn't feel like a real, lived-in space; it feels like a gamey arena in which you're supposed to fight orcs. This game suffers from what old open world games used to suffer from back when they all copying the GTA3 -- It's got a vast, wide open space peppered with absolutely nothing interesting aside from lots of bad guys to fight and some collectibles that, while they give you some interesting tidbits of information, do very little to make you want to chase them down otherwise.
A lot of this is hurt by the fact that the combat and stealth are almost wholly unchanged from the first game. If you loved the gameplay of Shadow of Mordor, you'll like this one. I was always lukewarm on the combat and stealth of the first game and was disappointed not to see it evolved upon in this game.
The story is laughably bad in most cases and forgettable in others. Most of the characters are cliche and there are some plot holes present that make me think any time spent in the writing room here was likely spent trying to finagle Tolkien's legendarium into justifying some of the odd writing moves here. For example, why did Shelob even want the "new ring" (ridiculous in its own right but whatever)? She had it for like a quarter of the game and didn't do a single thing with it but sit in her cave, presumably staring at the wall? Another character has been fighting orcs his entire life and knows the treachery they're capable of, yet still tries to make a deal with them that you can see going wrong from a hundred miles away. The entire thing is ridiculous and the prerendered cutscenes suck you right out of the moment anyway.
They've added some loot and some RPG elements to this one, which was very interesting to me in previews, but they're incredibly basic and don't even really warrant mentioning. The equipment is all very generic looking and the stats make the barest modicum of a difference. There are class tiers of equipment now, and the only stuff different enough to notice is the top tier stuff, but obtaining a full set of legendary gear requires so much grinding that it isn't even worth it. Perhaps if the top tier stuff was interesting in some way it might warrant the grinding in the way that a game like Diablo, Destiny, or Borderlands does, but this stuff doesn't. And all of the lower and middle tiers are not notably different. Sure, the middle tier stuff has some unique perks, but none of them make any real impact on the gameplay.
The loot system seems only to have served to make the balance of this game skew heavily towards grindiness. You've got to accomplish the same tedious stuff over and over but the loot perks and abilities give you very disappointing rewards for doing so. And what you're doing to gain experience and loot is not only uninteresting, but requires you to repeat the same activities so frequently. You can spend 4 hours grinding experience by taking out or recruiting enemy orcs, but they'll be replaced again by fresh orcs once time passes and you'll have to spend another 4 hours doing the same stuff over again with the new guys that have just come in, all while these activities and the setting get old and tiresome, while rewarding you with loot that you never see making an actual difference in gameplay. It loses its fun factor very quickly and this continues ad nauseam throughout the entire game.
It's really the pacing that's a problem here. Some of this stuff is fun initially, but not for the amount of repetitions that you're required to do to progress into conquering an area. Something else aside from this core gameplay loop of kill/recruit, then take fortresses needs to be present to drive you forward -- Whether it's an enticing plot, interesting characters with good dialogue, loot or new abilities that greatly increases your player character's power, a well-crafted game world you can lose yourself in, SOMETHING! And there's nothing here that does that. It's the same repetitive, dry task of killing/recruiting/ambushing orcs that leads to chasing loot that has no impact, upgrading your abilities not far past what they were in the first game, or progressing an unengaging story.
I didn't even notice the much-maligned microtransactions but I can't help wondering if they ruined the balance, because this is just not a fun game to play after a few hours. If you loved Shadow of Mordor, then sure, give this a shot. But after putting 40 hours into the first game I found that I grew tired of this one way before that.

Black tangrams that overlap to create white space.
Pretty straightforward in concept. Arrange the provided shapes in such a way that your result matches the target shape. Your workspace includes a dotted grid so you can have a sense of scale.
Some minor visual gripes:
Neither of these is game-breaking, as they don't prevent correct solutions from registering, and there's sort of a snap-to-grid function at a very fine scale.
Larger gripe: The game doesn't let you know that you've solved the final puzzle (although it does properly award the achievement). Even with a correct solution, there is no congratulation, no roll-credits, no jump menu back to beginning. It just stays on puzzle 66 and you think you got something wrong. I retried 3 or 4 times before I realized I had already been given the achievement.
I tore through this game in a sitting, and if you're a fan of this type of geometric puzzle, you'll probably tear through it quickly as well. I hope that this game will either see the addition of more puzzles or a more substantial sequel.

Oooh, Guns and Robots... It is such a shame how unpopular you are. Sure, you are not the greatest game out there, suffering a number of issues both big and small... But deep down there is a fun game here.
Alas, what holds G&R back so hard is it's balancing and small, unsocial community. With any game that allows you to build your own weapon, there are bound to be dirty players who exploit this fact and abuse it to create frustrating builds that take the fun out of the game and either force you to build your own cheap build, or just attempt to tough it out and try your best to beat them (And if you have skills, chances are you will at the very least do a considerable amount of damage to their bot).
As for the community, there is hardly anyone left... On average, there is probably around 150-100 players daily, if you are lucky.. Often this means fighting the same people over and over (said people probably being the cheap builds that frustrate you so), meaning it gets dull seeing the same robot over and over, nothing new and creative coming your way, and even worse for noobs to the game who get put together with level 80 vets. Even moreso, the community is very quiet for the most part, not much chattering going on between players, which further makes the game feel empty.
Does this mean the game isn't worth playing? Hell naw, when I first started playing, I really enjoyed it. It is fun making your own personal robot that suits your playstyle, mixing and matching parts and painting them all up to make a fancy killing machine that people will easily remember and adore/fear, and when you join a guild, it is fun working together to gather enough money to help invest in the guild to purchase buffs that give you a slight edge against your rivals. That, and the fact that this is the most generous F2P game I played in a long time, where all the things you can buy with real money don't have serious impact in the game, keeping it fun for everyone.
If you do plan on playing this, though, I suggest you bring some friends... It is much more fun when you have a crew you can rely on instead of having to go solo and risk having to be paired up with bots... yeah...

Broken Age is the game that essentially started the kickstarter craze.  They wanted $400,000 to make their game idea a reality.  What they got was over $3,300,000.  With their new budget they started making a 'larger' and 'better' game.  Double Fine then went way beyond budget and had to break the game into two parts.  The backers, such as myself get both parts (once completed) while anyone who buys act 1 is simply funding act 2.  As of this review they have made enough money to make the second act.  This review is about part 1.
Broken Age is about 2 hours long.  It is an old school point and click adventure game where you play as two characters in very different worlds.  The humor in the game is what you would expect from Tim S. and Double Fine.  The game is very creative and beautiful.  The game runs smoothly and I didn't experience any bugs.  The puzzles in the game are laughably easy though.  Aestheticly and humorously entertaining the gameplay itself is just to simple.
I would recommend this game for it's imaginitive design and it's humor.  I have to not recommend this game though, knowing the whole story of development, because it is just to short and to easy to feel anything more than a simple flash game someone could hammer out in a few weeks and toss up on newgrounds for free.  I feel that I did get what was promised, a game and a movie of how it is being developed.  When you weigh the time of development and the money spent on it, compared with what the final product became, I have to say that you should buy this game as cheaply as possible.  I hope Double Fine learns to manage their money better from here on out.  If you are looking for a unique set piece and story that is short and has simple gameplay mechanics that you don't have to put much mental thought into then this game is just perfect for you...for the next two hours.
Update:
Act 2 is finally finished and just as simple and short as act 1. The game even has an achievement for beating it in under one hour. Gee, thanks Tim.

Lego Marvel's Avengers is a fun game to play. If you are a fan of Lego games and/or Marvel properties, I would pick it up. There are a few issues and things that I experienced. One being that when you get to the game menu and it says connecting to the game servers, if it is unable to connect to the games servers, good luck playing the game. You'll select a svae file and then load the save and then go to a blank screen where nothing will happen and you'll have to restart your PC and try again. For me, I have had to restart at least 3 times before the game will work. Then, while it's loading the save, the game will close window and go back to desktop even though the game will still be running. Occassionally the game will close and return to desktop randomly. Also if you pause the game for a bit and come back, the gameplay will go i and  out of freezing and running normally. The game itself is fun but can be a bit boring after a while. The story takes you through the two Avengers movies with levels that speedily give you an overall idea of what happened in Iron Man 3, Captain America: The Winter Soldier and Thor: The Dark World. They use a fair amount of lines from the movies to immerse you but ulitmately could have used more, though I am sure there are copyright issues and other tings trying to get A-list actors to voice a Lego game or someone who could mimic their voices. I do appreciate the time spent to give each Iron Man armor some kind of animation. Basically as I read in another review, the story feel "phoned in" and there was not much effort put into it. The way to get red bricks to unlock extras is that when you play a level in free play, The Collector will appear in a segment of the level and ask you to do something for him. Aside from the okay story, there are DLC levels from Captain Marvel, All New, All Different Doctor Strange, Black Panther, Ant-Man and Marvel's Agents of Shield and Masters of Evil and the DLC missions also include new characters. There are additional character packs from Spider-Man, The Thunderbolts, Captain America: Civil War and The Avengers Adventure Pack. So if you finish those there is more to do. There are 8 hub areas to explore and collect Gold Bricks, Character Tokens and Vehicle Tokens. The areas are Asgard, Barton's Farm, Malibu, Shield Base, Manhattan, Sokovia, South Africa and Washington D.C.Character Tokens can also be found in levels as well as the Gold Bricks. In the hub areas, you obtain Character Toekns by helping various characters do odd and often stupid tasks like finding cats. You find Vehicle Tokens by doing races in hub areas. Overall, this games is fun but can get boring and the story could have had more effort put into it.

This is one of the most embarrassingly bad games ever created. First of all, the Twin Peaks / adventure game thing is a dupe: for a game about a writer, this has no plot.
It's divided into days and nights. The days last about fifteen minutes in game-time. Here is one day's plot: Alan arrives at a caravan park. He follows the owner across the park, listening to his dreary waffle. There's a cut scene, then it's night again. Here's another day's "adventure": Alan wakes up in a loony bin. The doc lets him out and Alan follows him across the building, listening to his dreary waffle. Then it's night again. You get the idea.
Each night seems to last an eternity. Alan walks through repetitive woods and lumber yards shooting the same three enemies. The batteries in his torch last about ten seconds, so Ever Ready's product placement was somewhat ill-conceived. That's it.
Other than the game being terrible, there are a few other flaws. Alan has trouble walking, or climbing, or jumping. His legs often disagree with his body and he regularly falls down stairs or trips over his own feet. He can only carry about three bullets. The voice acting is unbearable. He's also an abysmal writer who needs to learn the meaning of "show don't tell". Every time something vaguely interesting happens, the game tears away your view and Alan tells you about what you're being forced to watch. The game should just cut to the chase and not bother giving you control at all, as it never seems to amount to much.
Alan Wake is a terrible writer and a terrible bore and a completely excruciating game. It would be more fun to control his wife who died in the first ten minutes.
1/10.

Having heard so many good things about this game, I was certainly hopeful going in.  However, despite doing a decent job as a thriller/horror experience, the almost unbelievably tedious and clunky combat mechanics had me calling it quits after just a few chapters.  Combat isn't even that hard per say, but its semi-broken targeting system, awkward movement and dodging, and its extreme repetition in terms of enemies and tactics required really drags everything down into frustrating tedium.
I think this game would have actually been a lot better with little to no traditional combat, and instead focusing its action sequences on more of a fearful avoidance of baddies and environmental dangers (e.g., the Amnesia games).  That would have allowed it to spend more time on conveying a compelling and harrowing tale through more of the things it pulls off well: frightful tension and suspense, fearful dreamscapes and flashbacks, and gradually unravelling the mysteries of whatever dark forces are terrorizing Alan, his wife, and the inhabitants of the formerly cozy backwater.
The mysterious darkness and its seeming relation to Alan's own writing was an interesting concept that I would have otherwise wanted to see taken to its logical conclusion, but it was also really hard to empathize and become invested in Alan as a character since, to be frank, he is consistently painted as a self-absorbed jerk.  In general, if you're willing to suffer through the terribad combat elements, this game is probably worth your time; but if not, then you might want to look elsewhere for something that gets story AND combat right.

VOI, short game, scarcity of mechanics, bound to be a short review. This would be an example of a Zen-like game. It's minimalistic, has a simple rule-set, two positives equals a negative, two blacks make a white, etc, but quite quickly you realize there is a nice interplay of reason and intuition.
It is this interaction of vague logic with intuitive or trial and error game-play that makes the game not entirely Zen, but instead at times quite frustrating. It's not like other similar experiences that are minimalistic and rely heavily on sound and simple mechanics to create some type of relaxing situations. It does not retain its tranquility in a consistent way. Not that it's a bad thing, but it goes from intuitive and pleasant to logically dizzying swiftly, and without consistency.
I'd say the vast majority of the puzzles are very simple, they are solved within a 30-second span of time. Then we have more complex ones, that I for no good reason understand the complexity of. Usually you can count how many square dots the new form you are creating is confined to, and you can at times reduce the possible positions of the forms you have available quite a bit, “this particular shape can only be created by having this piece here”. So you start to build up this logic for how to approach the puzzle, but it all breaks apart as soon as you run into a wall, after having tried these methods. At least that was the case for me.
Perhaps my thinking with shapes is not as sharp as it should be, or could be, and I suppose that is where the difficulty of this game sometimes come from; not knowing how to create one set of shapes with a different set of shapes. It is so deceptively simple that it's infuriating to not be able to pinpoint a method or thought-process to deal with these puzzles. The puzzles that were solved within 30-seconds were so intuitive that it felt brilliant, I solved it before I could acknowledge “Yes, that's how you do it!”. And many times I redid the puzzles after having thought “What was it I actually did here?”.
The puzzles are always solved in a sequence, and after you apply the method of looking at how the shapes interact with each other and within what confines they need to exist, solutions come about almost automatically. This adds to the idea of a calm and relaxing experience, every solution is coupled with a pretty sound and a clear sense of progression and accomplishment which reinforces this feeling. But then you have the ones where you get stuck. I probably had one or two of them that I was stuck on for at least 20 minutes each one. Each time I thought to myself that I had hit the difficulty curve, but after every such difficult puzzle, the subsequent puzzle was solved in a matter of seconds. If this was intentional, it's a very nice aspect, and relieves a lot of that frustration. The worst thing in a game is to hit a wall, after which you hit an even bigger wall – it becomes somewhat demoralizing, unless you like that kind of thing, a “challenge”. While it is possible this difficulty curve was a matter of chance, a lapse in logic or luck not at all to do with the puzzles themselves or any intentional difficulty spike from the developer, My experience became ameliorated as a result of the fortunate difficulty-flux.
I believe, despite its simplicity and lacking visuals, that it holds up as a game. The audibles are constituted by a general droning of soft meditative tones, which further adds to the relaxation factor, despite being a distinct loop. Looping drones usually add to what I consider to be relaxing, but I imagine that's far from a universal opinion. The audio could similarly be called minimalistic, and if minimalism isn't you thing, then obviously this game isn't either, more than for its (to my knowledge) novel game mechanic. It's a nice holistic experience, every aspect fits together well and makes for an interesting exploration of a simple game-mechanic based in a logical rule and geometrical shapes. If you are in the mood for an at times relaxing, at times challenging, puzzle-game, this is cheap and short enough to not really serve as a risk by any means. I imagine it is also more pleasant if you, instead of forcing yourself to try to figure out a puzzle, leave it and come back to it later, maybe even another day. That seems to reset your mindset a bit, and gives recourse to the intuitive solutions, and eliminates the greater feelings of frustration. Have fun, or not.

Being a big fan of
as well as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, I was incredibly eager to pick up
. Although it has faults,
provides the same amount of fun as its predecessor.
Unlike
which told its own original story,
is based off of the films in the MCU, specifically
and
(though there are a few levels based on other films, such as
and
). The gameplay is identical to
and other TT Lego games, in that you go through levels while fighting enemies and solving lego-themed puzzles. Like every other Lego game, you can have a friend drop in or drop out via co-op.
One thing that made
so great was its giant New York hub, where you could do missions or just fly around for fun.
not only has the New York hub, but also has seven other "mini" hubs such as Washington D.C. and Asgard. This allows for more freedom and more fun in completing side missions.
Being based on the MCU, there are no X-Men, Fantastic Four, or Spider-Man characters (aside from a few Spider-Man variants in a free DLC). This doesn't bother me too much since the game mainly deals with the MCU, but I have to ask... WHERE ARE THE GUARDIANS OF THE GALAXY!?!? There are a few characters from the film that are in this game (Nebula, Collector, Ronin) but the main heroes (Star-Lord, Gamora, Drax, Rocket, and Groot) are mysteriously absent, which is odd since they were in the previous game. Although many iconic characters from
like Venom and Deadpool may be absent,
makes up for it by adding a ton of new characters that are not as well-known. Despite these characters not being popular as say Doctor Doom, they are still a blast to play as. The amount of characters and variations more than makes up for missing some popular characters.
This game is not without its problems though. For one thing, the NPCs in this game are some of the most obnoxious I've ever heard in a game. You can't go 5 minutes in the Manhattan hub without hearing an old lady speak in a cringey voice, or someone say the same line about Iron Man fanfiction over and over again. The worst is when you're trying to solve a puzzle while someone is being mugged/attacked, in which case they'll constantly yell "IT'S MINE, HELP" every 3 seconds. Also some of the character variations are questionable: did we really need Steve Rogers (gym) and Stever Rogers (boxing gloves)? Another problem I have is that the camera often stares at an object for about 5 seconds just to make sure you know what to do, in case it wasn't obvious.
These issues are mainly nitpicks that don't deter with my overall enjoyment of the game. I'd recommend this to people who enjoyed
since it is very similar and just as enjoyable.

This game is amazing. The story-telling is super emotional, well-thought out, gripping, suspenseful, etc. I can't even really call any TV shows or movies I've watched in a long time that were this good from start to end. There are times where I just couldn't stop crying - some of the scenes and events in the story really affected me. I feel wiser for having played through the game, and I feel like I've experienced something that I can take with me long after my episode 5 end credits.
All of the characters - major and minor - are believable, unique and complex, like real people. I really connected with all of the characters in some way, and if I didn't, I still felt something else for them. They were all very well developed. I really connected with Chloe especially - I knew someone sort of like her in my long past that meant a lot to me too, and I'm female and gay, so lots to relate.
The sound track fits the game perfectly. The voice acting is incredible. The colours and attention to even the smallest details and consistency is truly amazing. The story has so much suspense, with lots of twists and turns that will keep you guessing for quite awhile, and everything makes sense when the answers are finally revealed. The themes of friendship and love are the most powerful I've ever seen done in pretty much any media.
I can't really call this a game though - if you buy thinking you want a challenge or to experience a permanent failure - like jumping into a pit in a Mario game or losing all of your health in a shooter - then this game isn't for you (and if that's you, that's cool, but that also doesn't mean the game should get a 0). It's really an interactive story, that really connects with you on a personal level - something movies and comics simply can't do.
In terms of mechanics within the game, I think the only criticism is the long wait times for rewinding large sections of the game, but that's honestly a minor blemish on an other perfect experience.
I will treasure this game forever, and you will to. Play it.

So far this is an excellent game!   I know everyone is going on about the 30 FPS lock but really...I've seen worse with newer games.   And give them time and they'll get it patched up to go 60+ FPS.
The story is what is making this game.   Being an older gamer a lot of this feels real for the time and the era.   Driving around the city feels like you are actually there.   There are details everywhere that you can go, 'Hey, I know where that is!' and help with the immersion of the game.   It is so easy to slip into this game and just live the story.
I will say that the arrows, door markers, and such are kinda annoying and I wish there was a way to turn them off to help stop the little breaks in the immersion of the game.   I also wish that the keybindings were a bit more flexible.   I'd love to bind a few things to the extra buttons on my mouse but the game isn't having it.   Hopefully these will be within the next couple of patches.
Overall, I LOVE this game so far.    If you want something with a good story and an excellent way of telling the story, this is your game.   No game is perfect out of the box.   Even with testers there are things that are missed or need improvement but I have faith that this one will be ranked up there just as high as the previous Mafia games and hopefully there will be more in the future.

Outpost 13 the only way it can be described as a short but sweet game. the intro begins with a man in the snow and a dog, where after a few seconds the dog turns into a horrible monster, this looks to be a really nice touch to John Capenters "The Thing" with a few minor changes. Instead of playing the heros that escape the horrible nightmare that lives in outpost 13, the player is the monster, with a very clear objective... Kill everyone, the "Evil personality" that follows the player around helps out with giving hints to push the player to the right path of destruction. These hints arn't exactly clear and can turn the game from short and sweet to really long and confusing, the game mechanic that is used is a locked path of what the player will take. Hovering the mouse over all the objects in the rooms that are available give to clues of what needs to be done next, some of these are unclear and can lead the player astray. The timed events are clear of how to proceed but aren't very clear on what order that everything needs to be done in. These events are very forgiving allowing the player to make a number of mistake before having to wait for the time window and starting again. The best way to proceed through this short game is to pay extra attention to what is being said, and the objects/ Notes in the enviroment and that will explain the best of the plan of what the player needs to do. Outpost 13 is one of those games where once the "Ball" starts rolling, everything falls into place like a giant jigsaw puzzle. Great storyline, great art work and a awesome perspective from the "Evil" side of things.
Personally Outpost 13 is a great puzzle game once everything comes together. The game should have been longer personally but I haven't played act 2 yet and look forward to doing so. 8 / 10 in my review and thank you all so much for reading.

I love the LEGO games, and love Marvel. The game is mostly playable and enjoyable.
But I agree with other revivewers. The voiceover clips are a problem.
The voiceovers in the previous game, LEGO Marvel Super Heroes, were all recorded specifically for the game, using some of the same voice actors from some of the popular Avengers cartoons.
The voiceovers in LEGO Marvel's Avengers are a mishmash from movie clips (some badly edited) and specifically-recorded voiceovers.
The voices of Agent Coulson and Maria Hill are authentic, provided by Clark Gregg and Cobie Smulders. Meanwhile, among authentic clips and voiceovers, all of Gwennyth Paltrow's applicable movie dialogue as Pepper Potts uses another actor.
Also the sonic quality of the specific voiceovers doesn't match that of the poorly-lifted movie clips. The clips that are from the movies do not feel related to the game. At every occasion, they only disconnect the player from the game experience.
Personally, I blame Warner Brothers. In case people failed to notice the game credits, this installment involved WB who are Marvel's biggest "competition" in the superhero movie genre. It would be unfortunate if WB took a lazy and slapdash approach to the game in order to weaken the Marvel brand.
I would also like to note that the story within the game jumps between various Marvel movies and TV shows, and game-original content, without regard to their chronological order... making it somewhat difficult to follow.
I played the game for a while but the dialogue drove me crazy. I'm a professional theatrical Sound Designer and this is shotty design, especially for such high-profile brand recognition.
I'm glad I got the game on sale instead of paying full price. But if I had it to do over I would have tried another title instead.
I'm sorry, LEGO and Marvel. Go back to the old formula... and leave Warner Brothers out of it.

Note: This review is a work in progress, this review will be updated when the update for Act 2 comes out.
This game was reviewed using a code sent by the developer.
Outpost 13 struck me as a very interesting concept for a game. You can choose from three different characters: Graham, Fen and Dr. Meow Meow Jones. The game's description say's Fen is the main character, but in the end there's no difference.

The story is something straight out of late 80's or early 90's Sci-Fi flick. You play as the crews dog. The story takes place on an ice planet. You find out there's something special about you and the team wants to conduct experiments, but you can't let that happen. So it's up to you to kill the entire crew as a mysterious being guides you and helps you to escape the Outpost.
When I started playing, I found it hard to find my footing as the game doesn't really hold your hand and it's up to you to figure out how to kill everyone.
You have a day and night cycle so you can spy on the crew to figure out they're weaknesses, so you can use that against them.
The outpost itself is rather small. You have a sneak peek at the outside of the outpost, but there is literally nothing you can do outside.
The puzzles range from head scratching, to rather simple. The only puzzle that gave me trouble was the chemistry puzzle, but I figured it out rather quickly.
The art style and the soundtrack really help build mood and it feels like you are stranded.
Act 1 took me 1 hour to finish. After the one playthrough there is next to no replay value. Act 2 is coming out this winter so I hope it expands on the games length.
I didn't run into any issues while playing the game. It ran perfectly from start to finish. I didn't encounter any bugs whatsoever, but I'm aware that some other people have, but I hope the dev fixes it.
Overall Outpost 13 just barely gets a positive rating. The idea is fantastic and has tons of potential, but Act 1 is too short and not worth the full price. I will highly suggest getting the game once Act 2 is out, but for now only buy if you don't mind paying for Act 1.
Final Rating:
6/10 - Wait for Act 2, before buying

If I was to sum up the experience, probably the best way would be in one word: disappointing.
Don't get me wrong, the premise is great, reminiscent of The Thing in more ways than one and packaged in a point and click format. You even get to wander around the base with a day night cycle. Basically the premise is great. Of course its the execution that's the problem.
There's no real point for the sandboxy style nature because the game doesn't utilize it in any meaningful way. Yes you can wander from room to room but what does that matter when you need to get an item from one room to solve the puzzle in another, it's like the game is telling us the challenges are self-contained (you get a room cleared message when finishing a puzzle in a location) but at the same time some rooms need to be cleared before others. There's no real point in allowing the player to mess with a later puzzle when you won't yet hand them the item needed to solve it.
The linearity of the puzzles is in contrast to what the game appears to be, at first glance it looks like a more sandboxy experience, but as you wander you'll notice that practically nothing changes as time passes until the night where you're limited to spying on sleeping crewmates and trying to discern important puzzle hints from the setup of their personal belongings, so you can figure out how to kill them.
The killing itself seems to lack any sort of logic as well, you go through the trouble of timing your actions so you can drug a person when it's already established that you're a monster that can tear a grown man apart just like that and could easily clear the room by brute force. Hell, the intro has you do just that! Yet here you are elaborately solving a puzzle about mixing chemicals just so you can knock out a person, so that you can then transform and tear apart their remaining colleague by brute force. Why  you couldn't just kill them both and save yourself the trouble of the puzzle is beyond me. Perhaps even give the player a multitude of ways to clear a room, wouldn't that be more fun to make them want to figure out the sneaky way to do it, rather than force them?
But even this is pointless when a gamebreaking bug impedes your progress. I got stuck on a puzzle due to being unable to click a console, I didn't realize it was interactable due to the game refusing to let me click it, thus missed out on the puzzle solution. Only after several attempts at doing the same thing did I randomly notice the caffeteria console can be clicked on while randomly mousing over it the 5th time.
There's other bugs too, map showing wrong location occasionally, the main character not being kicked out sometimes when the 'attention' meter depletes and so on. Rooms are annoyingly empty for a point and click game, with very little to examine and interact with and some are even seemingly completely pointless. It's not even a very long game, perhaps I missed something but it seems I reaced the ending in less than 2 hours including getting stuck on multiple puzzles.
For what it's worth the game is a great idea, has nicely stylized graphic look and I enjoyed the soundtrack as well. But it fails on poor execution and it's not like the idea itself is worth the money when there's even free games that took this premise and did it better.
Not recommended in its current state.

Great idea, really muddled execution. Game is very slow, mistakes are punished harshly, and a lot of stuff is very confusing.
For instance there's a potion puzzle with a "red x1 purple x1" marker right above it. Surely that's the solution, right? Well no, you actually have to wait until night time, sneak into the right bedroom and follow the exact instructions on a poster to solve that puzzle. And if you spend too many attempts trying to figure it out on your own you get killed.
The game's structure is rather suspect as well--there's a sort of hub and you have to walk super slowly between areas, and there's only a tiny few areas that are actually interactive. You spend as much time finding things to do as you do in puzzle rooms, and having to wait for time changes gets old fast.
When you actually solve a puzzle it's pretty nice, you actually feel like an evil monster succeeding in defeating the foolhardy crew of an action movie. But it might take you 10 minutes of fiddling to cause that 5 second death (and after the actual death scene, little seems to actually happen--no one has reacted to the set of 8 deaths I've caused so far).
I hope long-term this turns into a recommendation because the idea is great, but at the moment there's more to enjoy in the concept and intro than the actual game.
Best thing I can say is the game is being patched very frequently and the dev has been responsive to certain specific problems. They've already fixed some major problems (the map and timeshifting by saving are huge)
