Fantastic story where's always a mystery: Alan Wake is writer who for vacations goes to a little town called Bright Falls, which resemble Twin Peaks, with his wife Alice. After moving to theirs house, they start an argue and Alan walks out of it. After some time he hear screams. He run into the house to check what happened, then he finds his wife in the lake, he jumps after her and he... wake up in the car. Yeah, the rest is mystery and it's revealing itself during story playthrough. What makes the mystery more mysterious is that we're finding manuscript pages in which a little glipse into the future is written. Graphics is beautiful with fantastic landscapes. Fighting with enemies is interesting and unique too, we can't just shoot them, no, the light is our strongest ally. First is needed to light the enemies until theirs "darkness shield" is off, then we can shoot. It's not a shooter game so there isn't too much of a weapon choice, couple of rifles, revolver, flash granades and flares. Too bad that there's no puzzles at all, most of them look like: go from A point to B point, but still game is fantastic. The last what I want to write about is game soundtrack. Alan Wake has fantastic OST! I can even say that OST from this game will be in my Top 3 OST's from games. :)

It's an okay game I guess. Graphics are above average and the gameplay is interesting but like just about any other Tom Clancy game it has an air of childishness about it. What it actually is is a very dumbed down RTS game designed to function well on the consoles, which is the real reason there is a voice command system. Beware though, more than a tiny bit of ambient noise can make it malfunction. The good thing is that using the voice command is optional. Most likely on the PC you won't want/need to use it.
So anyway, you can actually finish this game in as little as 3 turns but you can drag it out longer than that and you can play or replay as a different country but what you'll find is that no matter what country you play or what strategy you use the game is always the same. There are some annoyances like the WMD option that you get if you are losing the game but the thing is that once you use it then the other side gets the option too and there's really not much you can do but resign yourself to losing a lot of units. About the only remedies to this is to always attack on two fronts, never jumble up your forces in a small area, and don't try to overwhelm the enemy with sheer numbers. Keep plenty on reserve.
It's cool to be able to upgrade your weapons and armor and the upgrades do work very well, they aren't just for show. You can even change the camo patterns. This feature is, in my opinion, about the best the game has to offer. Enemy AI will at times pull some good tricks out of it's hat but for the most part it's a simple, go through the motions and you're done type of game. Typical of Tom Clancy games in that even on the hardest settings they are never very hard to complete, mostly I think because they were made for kids.
I guess as long as you don't go into this thing expecting large-scale,epic battles that require alot of planning and strategy then you'll be satisfied. World in Conflict this game most definitely is not. To the casual RTS gamer that doesn't have alot of patience for strategic planning and tactical supremacy I would recommend this game but hardcore strategists and armchair generals will probably be highly disappointed. That's not to say that their is no need for strategy or tactics because there is but the game is very light on the amount of them that are required to be successful and there is always, always a workaround for bad decision making.

Perhaps if I play this game long enough, I will stop wishing it was Time Pilot.
I wish it were Time Pilot.
It's a top-down shooter - endless planes to shoot, challenge set by a deliberately limited screen size. Missions to complete. Stars to earn, feeling of progression. Lots of power ups (some of which are not good). Lots of planes to unlock (some of which are not good).
I feel like the developer didn't spend enough time playing the game to realise - unlocking a faster plane is not such a good thing when you have a limited screen and bullets that are too weak to shoot down an enemy quickly. And that some of the power-ups act as a hindrance.
The "move a mouse pointer with a joystick to navigate menus" system is really not great. It breaks flow at the end of every game.
I know it is not generally helpful to describe a work in terms of the things it is not, but I so dearly wish this game were Time Pilot. But retaining this game's mission and unlockables structure, which I like because it keeps the game fresh.
All in all, it's a very reasonable game for its price. For that, I give it an overall thumbs-up. But it's not brilliant.

The world that's been built here is void of life and dead: which is critical for a game of the Point and Click genre, and even more so for a horror based one. The game lacks impact: you don't get connected to characters that you kill, and those deaths are barely passable with a lack of sound design and frankly nothing behind it other then the echo of the lifeless chambers of Outpost 13. The game is an implementation mess without even a pause menu (which is actually necessary for this game considering the time based implementation of it. In the end, I can't even given a recommendation for Act 2 and the potential future: Outpost 13 swings for the fences, but falls over its own attempted swing and puts its face into the dirt.

From the moment I laid eyes on Outpost 13 I was intrigued by the idea of playing the monster. Preying upon the poor unaware denizens of the outpost in the guise of an adorable pooch named Fen. The idea of seeing how this story would be presented and unfold intrigued me even more. Upon completion of Act 1 though I realized that Outpost 13 is an incomplete tale with many mechanical elements that need definition. At heart, the game is a point and click adventure game but most of the elements such as stealth and puzzles are far from complex and to be honest I beat the game within 40 minutes time. While game length isn't always a requirement when it comes to Indie Games, the experience of the game itself left me wanting more. What Outpost 13 does have going for it is the atmosphere. The game feels creepy, and the pixel art is fantastic! The music is well done and the intro sets the tone for what is to be a mind screw. Sadly, after the intro everything shifted and I wanted more of what I saw in the intro. The dialogue is mostly from the internal evil voice inside Fen and characters for the most part disregard your presence unless you do something "suspicious" such as telekineticly poisoning a drink or tampering with computer systems. These actions seem strange to me as Fen for the most part is still a dog with no opposable thumbs. Also as you begin slaughtering the denizens of the Outpost, they have literally no reaction other then continuing their work. The game has great possibility and is a fun and interesting idea that until fully completed is hard to make a judgement call on. I wanted more from this game but that isn't a bad thing. I wanted more story, more puzzles, and the chance to terrify the inhabitants of the Station. Only Act 2 will tell if I get what I am looking for or be left a sad puppy.

This is a great premise, great foundation - but as it is now, it's essentially a prototype of itself.
Almost everything is trial and error - sometimes costly trial and error, as the clock is constantly going and there's no guidance or direction whatsoever. While this is okay in some games, in this one it's frustrating at best. The counter-intuitive solutions to some puzzles (all found on accident) had me scratching my head, and more often than not, they could be solved by simply doing the same thing again and getting a different result.
I was left in the dark about certain game mechanics, which goes back to the constant trial and error bit. Learning the controls consists of reading over a pop-up window that comes up before the game starts, and its stance on controller support is utterly silent (will a 360 controller work with this? If so, how? etc).
There is no pausing, which makes it harder to take in the environment.
Dialogue is strictly represented on an eyesore of a black ticker with a tacky comic sans-ish font. The cursor is a clashy lime green reticle that makes it feel like you're in some kind of debug mode (an eyeball or something may be more immersive).
The excellent soundtrack is ruined by this strange "tapping" sound that never stops. I don't know if it's a sound effect or part of the music, but whatever it is, it's absolutely madness inducing.
(EDIT: This is a random glitch where if you go outside into the snow and then go back inside, the game sometimes thinks you're moving even when you aren't, and it reads all surfaces as snow, therefore a never-ending tap-tap-tap...)
Animations are stiff and jerky, and the humans move rapidly and suddenly, giving you very little chance to react in some situations (along those same lines, you move VERY slowly).
There is a nasty glitch where some doors/exits cannot be used or don't trigger when you click them, and exiting to the menu to fix it ends your current session entirely.
I haven't actually managed to kill a single person (I...think that's what you're supposed to be doing?...) yet. I got to a place in a science lab where I was told to mix some chemicals - but when I thought I had it and hit 'MIX', a random soldier spawned in the room, I burst into flames, and the screen just cut to 'Thank you for playing...'
Um, what? I don't even...
THAT BEING SAID:
This thing has extreme potential, and what does work and what is clearly explained has a meticulous quality. There's nothing else quite like it. I see great things in its future.
In its current state, this would be perfect as a mobile/tablet game, but as a Steam title, it needs a couple liters of polish. I'm definitely going to keep poking it with a metaphorical stick until something...happens. Will keep an eye on it and adjust my recommendation accordingly.
***UPDATE***
I finally found out how to actually cause deaths, and cleared almost all of Act 1 within 15 minutes. It turns out, interactive parts of each room are tiny, extremely obscure spots that you'll just have to find on your own. Clicking them only triggers the desired effect half the time.
Some solutions you're going to have to Google to find, or just get really really lucky.
On the actual deaths...
Wow, what a disappointment. They look great, but the problem is that they play out in fast-forward, with rapid and awkward animations that cause the whole sequence to last maybe a second. There's absolutely no sound and it feels completely uninspired. All that guesswork and searching, only to be rewarded with what feels like an alpha stage test animation.
The humans don't feel human at all. They're just stiff, mindless scenery that fly across rooms once in a while. The rooms themselves seem bare. Maybe a flickering light or mold/stains would add to the whole atmosphere.
As it stands, with a $10 price tag the game needs to be at least twelve times the size it is, with /way/ more involved death sequences, sounds etc.

This has to be one of the best (if not actually the best) games that I've played so far in my entire life. Still, it has some negatives, for instance that the "freedom of choice" is basically a well-made illusion and many of your choices may not even matter later on.
I also experienced some weird sound bugs during the gameplay, like that sometimes (every 5 - 10 minutes) in the middle of a dialog there was approx. 50ms sound cut, or generally the first and the last cutscenes from every episode were a lot louder than the actual game itself, even when I tried to tweak the volume in the options. (Well, after all it doesn't have to mean much, since it can also be a problem on my side tbh.)
On the bright side, the game includes a top notch soundtrack which totally fits the atmosphere, and the story's just AMAZING! (There are some minor plot holes and ofc. little things that I personally would change about it, but hey, nothing can be perfect) General theme of the game suits it well - you're playing as an 18 year old wannabe artist girl capable of altering the course time, but dealing with her teenage problems. From the perspective of an 18 year old guy, I have to admit that I cringed during a few scenes, but since I'm in the same age as the main protagonist, I found myself in the story pretty easily and understood it mainly due to my teenage experience.

That also might be one of the game's positive/negative, since it has it's target group. If I were 25+, I'm sure it wouldn't entertain me as much since clearly there's the casual teenage drama motive there. On the other hand, If I were younger (for ex. 10), I probably wouldn't understand the struggle that the main characters are going through during their teenage-early adult years.
TL;DR; If you're 15 - 20 y/o, this game's DEFINITELY for you. But even else, it's a masterpiece worth buying and playing.

Gah, this game; developed by Ubisoft just as they started their downward spiral.
This is EndWar, an RTS released on consoles back in '08 for the Xbox 360 and PS3, that means its a rather streamlined game considering the demographic the consoles were aimed at.
It's a simple storyline. it's 2020 and the world is in an oil crisis, the petrol plant in Rozenburg is attacked by a group known as the "Forgotten Army" which is comprised of people from failed Balkan, African and South American nationales. As a result, the Big Three, America, The European Federation and Russia all prepare for a war against the group, not knowing that Russia itself was behind the debacle.
Russian troops disguised as Forgotten Army forces raid a European military base, infecting the mainframe computer and causing a space laser to fire on an American space shuttle, effectively causing a Third World War.
The game is as simple as it gets; point, click and watch the action. It's an RTS in the sense that an overcooked piece of steak is still edible, it's a real time strategy game and the ingredients are all there. But EndWar just doesn't hold a candle to the likes of Command and Conquer 3 or even Supreme Commander, both of which were released on the same console at an earlier date than this.
The strategy is also as simple as it gets. Rock, paper, scissors gameplay means that versatility is out of the window. Wanna use your tank to destroy that engineer? Better make sure he's out of cover or else you're toasted.
Another quirk I have is the way combat actually appears, they all just stand there, whittling away at each other until only one is left...and then that one vehicle or squad, whom you would think would make a last stand, becomes a disabled lump of metal or just five people standing around waiting for an evac chopper.
Don't even bother with this...it's just a simple RTS that tried to hide behind amazing trailers and interviews.
A mediocre game at best, a terrible example of hype at worst.

Sigh, what a complete letdown, they completely half-arsed the game.  I was a $100 backer on kickerstarter and the short of it, this game sucks.  Bugs are one thing, and there are plenty of those here which is quite disappointing.  But the real problem is that the game itself does not even look remotely close to a $3,000,000+ game.  What the did they spend that on, because it sure was not the cheapo Unity3d engine (looks just as bad as Shadowrun did with Unity3d, which just makes me mad).  The miserably bad live action intro (really?  I mean really???) maybe?  I'm guessing they pocketed it.
I am looking at this game from the perspective of having played every single major isometric in the history of gaming, period.
If you were letdown by Shadowrun (which I was in a BIG way), be prepared to be let down again, just as hard.
The Bad:
- Really bad, very primitive interface, does not seem to avail itself of any modern interface concepts.  Want a chat log?  forget about it, best write stuff down *manually* or just have photographic memory.  Quest tracker?  Forget about it, it is kind of there but is missing critical quest details, especially if you save and come back the next day you are left wondering what the heck is going on.  Moving items between people is painful.  In game help system is terrible, it is arbritrary not reviewable, fire once and then disappear forever which seems to be the basis for the entire game design.  Want to rotate your camera?  Be prepared to be fustrated by the terrible pausing mechanism (camera "hitches" on the cardinal directions) which prevents smooth rotation.  Limited options all around, the interface options you want are probably not going to be there.  Awkward, clunky, primitive, not a $3,000,000 interface!
- 3d characters looks cartoony, again the same problem with Shadowrun and I will just straight up blame Unity3d and the laziness of not just doing it yourself.  In a game like this, a "serious" game, a $3,000,000 game, the last thing I think you would want is any kind of cartoon look and they blew that.
- Very limited skill selection and character customization.  You load it up and you are like, huh, looks like quite a few skills there, especially in character creation (if the rest of the game had that level of customization, the game may have been worth a damn).  Then you realize it's mostly gun skills with a few tacked on skills like lockpicking and then the lol "hacking" skill that all work EXACTLY THE SAME WAY.  Click, watch an icon change color a few seconds, soon you will be bored.  And then a few hours later in the game you will be depressed by the limited amount of customization available once you start the game and next thing you know you are leveling up "submachine guns" to get 5% better chance to hit.  Joy, so fun.
- Inventory / loot - terrible.  Just terrible.  You walk around mostly picking up Junk, literally called Junk.  Oh sure they spent some time putting description on the Junk, which you can one-click sell to vendors.  Whoop De Frickin Do.
- The world map.  SIgh.  Why, why not just take some time to make it *cool*.  But no, it is half arsed like the rest of this game, you get to watch a spinning sheriffs star icon move across a static map.  Sometimes you find an "oasis" where absolutely nothing happens except to fill your water bottle, fabulous.  Some random encounters, with no plot attachment, no story, just random meaningless garbage.
- The bugs.  I love watching NPC's run around with empty text bubbles over their head.  Right in the beginning of the game.  Right where even the most primitive QA process would have caught it.  QA.  That's an interesting word, one they obviously did not bother googling even, certainly did not spend any money on it.
- I'm depressed, not because the game was super awesome, dark, apocalyptic and really drew you into the setting of the game and left you with the post apocaplytic feeling you have been craving for years after dumping money into this kickstarter project.  No just the opposite, it was so bad it draws you *out* of the game as you are appalled by the low quality that $3,000,000 can produce.  Well done there Inxile, a good notch on your belt. I usually love LEGO games. I've been playing LEGO games since LEGO's first video game outing, LEGO Island. And I've loved most of them. But this? Traveller's Tales, what have you done?
On the surface, you'd imagine LEGO Marvel's Avengers to adapt the Marvel Cinematic Universe in a way that other LEGO games do: they poke fun at their source material using charming plastic toys to underscore dramatic moments. Not so in this game. It's mostly downgraded to unfunny gags with "LOL SO RANDUMB" humor and awkward bits of dialogue that go nowhere.
A LOT of the dialogue is lifted directly from the films... and not in a good way. It's as if Traveller's Tales hasn't gotten access to the pre-movie-score dialogue and is forced to try and filter out the music in the backgrounds of quotes, because every time the characters say something, it's quite muffled and sounds bad. Not only that, but it's extremely out of place with the extra dialogue that was recorded for the game, which is quite clear and without noise. It comes across not as an official Marvel media product, but as a mod for another game that's been haphazardly smashed into it.
Another problem is that the game takes a heavy hand in trying to introduce the tutorials to the player, by forcing them to seek out Avengers logos which tell you how to progress, rather than letting the player gradually introduce themselves to the game's mechanics and gameplay.
LEGO Marvel Super Heroes also includes a full cast of characters, including the X-Men and Fantastic Four. This game, being an adaptation of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, doesn't - but that wouldn't normally bother me if the presentation of the game wasn't so bad.
The game is held back by the game's self-imposed voice-over restrictions and ham-fisted, childlike gameplay and sense of humor. You might argue that this itself is a children's game, and I'd agree, but other LEGO games have been appropriate for all ages without being too easy or too hard.
If you have young children, they'll probably enjoy this. If you're looking for a good LEGO game, look elsewhere.

I have barely scratched the surface of Wasteland 2, but numerous people have been asking my opinion so I figured I would post a "first impressions" review.
I came to Wasteland 2 as a Fallout 1/2 fan. The kickstarter was the first time I had heard of Wasteland so I didn't know what to expect. All I knew was that it was a combat heavy turn-based strategy game set in a nuclear wasteland. Based on the fact that "Toaster Repair" is a useful skill made me it assume it had a healthy dose of snark as well.
When I started the game I found out it was both what I expected and entirely different. The interface was more or less exactly what I had expected. The descriptive text and conversations were a lot more detailed than anticipated, but still lived up to expectations. [WARNING: This game has swearing.]
The fact that the interface was as expected made it seem easy to jump right in and start exploring. Wow, was I wrong. The content and difficulty were another beast.
From what I've seen thus far the overall tone is best described as “Dark Attitude”. The rangers aren't lights in darkness, they are flawed individuals who find themselves in the roles of peacekeepers. Its not a game where you get thanked for helping, its one in which those you help will gripe about it taking too long to get there and generally be jerks. Fellow Fallout fans should be prepared for a very different tone.
Contrary to what I expected it was not easy to jump in. I had chosen a party of pregenned characters, thinking they were relatively balanced, and was proven very wrong. This became very obvious in the Ag Center and led to me restarting. Chance to hit was low, ammo usage was high, and eventually I was running around punching everything with characters spec’ed for ranged combat. If you don’t explore everywhere and carefully manage your ammo, you are in for a hard time. Don’t forget your shovel, safe-cracker, and toaster repair expert!
Despite, or perhaps because of, the difficulty, I find myself continually thinking about the game and wondering what is next. If you like turn based combat and don’t mind having to work for victory it is worth getting. Just don’t go in expecting a Fallout clone because its an entirely different game.

VOI is a visual puzzle game which features three simple premises:
1. Black shapes occupy positive space, while the white background/shapes occupy negative space. (black = 1, white = 0)
2. When black shapes overlap each other, the overlapping part becomes white negative space. (1 - 1 = 0)*
3. When a black shape overlaps within a white shape, the overlapping part remains as a black positive space. (1 - 0 = 1)
Though simplistic they may sound, these premises can produce a variety of brain teasers. Each level requires the player to arrange a set of shapes so that it matches the given picture. The earlier tutorial levels are straightforward, but soon you'll probably find your own eyes playing tricks on your mind, especially when it's hard to tell where you need to overlap the shapes exactly.
On the other hand, the level navigation needs work since there is no proper "menu" for the players to jump into a specific level. Aside from that, I highly recommend this game if you're intrigued by visual and spatial puzzles.

In the 1980s, when I was young, there was a great game released for the Commodore 64 called "Aztec Challenge." That game was filled with all kinds of challenging puzzles, dodging spears, avoiding traps, all while running through each subsequently harder level.  “Aztec Challenge” was impossibly challenging, and the game would start over at the beginning every time you chose poorly or weren’t fast enough with your reflexes.  As frustrating as that was, I could never get enough of the game – always trying to outdo my previous attempt.  This game feels like the spiritual successor to “Aztec Challenge” in many ways, especially if someone mixed a round of “Mortal Combat” (the original arcade version, mind you, not the latest watered-down stuff) between levels of trap navigation.  You might ask, "Will I die"? Oh, yes, you most certainly will.  Will that stop you from picking up the controller and trying for another round? It shouldn’t.  “Arena” pulls you in with its challenge – and that makes it a masterpiece as far as I am concerned.  The visuals are stunning, the soundtrack is a thrill, and the gameplay will keep you challenged.  Even if I never make it to the end, I am having fun trying to outdo my previous record – and that is what great 80s-style gameplay is really all about. So I tip my hat to the creators of “Arena: An Age of Barbarian Story” because they have made something that allows me to recapture the gaming experience of my youth.

I have never been more disappointed in a triple A game in my entire life.
I first played Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor a year or two after it's release and loved it, I 100% my first save and played the game a second time when I had no internet for a few weeks.  So back in February when I saw the reveal trailer for Shadow of War I was ecstatic.
After 7 gruelling months the game came out, and I wish I never dropped the gold edition pre-order all those months ago.
1. Combat and Movement.
The combat in this game is hit and miss.
For the most part the combat hasn't changed from Shadow of Mordor, but only had more skills and mechanics put on top of what was already there.  The combat feels satisfying with all the executions, new skills like Bird of Prey where you can use your bow in mid-air and the increased amount of enemies present at one time making fights seem more cinematic and therefor more enjoyable to be apart of.
However, the combat can take away just as much as it gives.  Targeting a specific enemy in a large scale fight can be a chore, you will find yourself constantly hitting the wrong enemy, even your allies.
A similar issue is dominating/healing.   If you want to dominate a broken captain, or heal a fallen ally you best make sure no other Uruk in between you two.  I found it to be a lucky draw whether I could target the Uruk I wanted to in a fight.  and those small mistakes led to some of my highest level captains bleeding out.
Fighting captains becomes dull after the 2nd act of the game.  After a while you've seen everything the nemesis system has to offer and you can defeat a captain no matter his level or traits.  Just vault over him, flurry attack him, ground execute and then execute him again with the might you've built of from the first three steps, rinse and repeat until he adapts, breaks or dies.
Going back to a positive note, the movement in this game is outstanding.
Controlling your character is silky smooth outside of combat, you go where you want to go.  Nothing clunky, no ifs or buts.  Along with this the regions in this game are much larger than the regions in Shadow of Mordor, and with this our mobility skill tree has expanded too.  Monolith has really struck a sweet spot in finding the balance in traversing the world.  Not too slow, but not too fast either.
2. Loot Boxes and Online Play
I gotta cut this part out of the review to make space for the rest of it, long story short.  Online play is underwhelming and loots boxes weren't that tempting to buy.  I have not spent a penny on this game after buying it (coming from a guy who spent £1000 on dota)
3. Fortresses
After completing the final act, I never want to see another fortress again.
You start to take fortresses at the beginning of the second act, when the game fully opens up to the player.
When I assaulted my first fortress I was excited, but after conquering my last fortress I was bored with it.
If you watch the 'Official Middle-earth: Shadow of War™ Gameplay Walkthrough' on YouTube.  You'll see a very cinematic assault, full of action, nemesis system triggers and a very exciting time for the player.  What we got was a very boring, uneventful experience for all 4 fortresses where you climb the walls, capture the 4 points, kill the overlord and... that's it.  I had ONE nemesis system trigger and that was when my assigned bodyguard saved me from death.  I'm pretty sure that would happen at chance in or out of a siege.  So I can barely count it.
Reminds me of the Ubisoft downgrades a little.
The worst part of this for me was that the fortresses was one of biggest if not the biggest marketing points for the game. And it turned out to be one of the worst parts of the game in my opinion.
4. The Story
Good God the story was dreadful.
I really, really wanted to enjoy the story, and at some parts it was good.  But, the final act ruined not only the story, but the entire game.
The game's story has strong points, but overall it's weak and uninteresting.  You will see some extremely good revelations about the main characters
But as good as these parts of the story were.  They were utterly ruined by the 4th act of the game.
The game techinally ends with the 3rd act.  By completing the 4th act you reveal the 'true ending'.
The ending is excellent, but what it took to achieve it was anything but excellent.
What stands between you and the true ending is a tedious, microtransaction driven, morally bankrupt grind that will last nearly 10 hours.  You'll need to defend over 10+ sieges scaling is difficulty.  This may not seem too bad, but believe me it becomes a chore to play the game, when a game becomes a chore it is NOT FUN.  The game asks you to defend all 4 fortresses from attackers, then asks you to do it again, then again, and again for the FOURTH TIME (maybe more, I honestly lost count).  The war chiefs leading the fights were normally higher level than you, higher level than your own captains and the only way you could speed this painful process up with to give money to the game.  That's right, you needed to buy loot chests to speed this up.
Whoever thought this would be a good idea is the slimiest person on Earth.  I am willing to wager this game would've been a game that would be remembered for years if they replaced act 4 with an actual story and cut out microtransactions.
The Side Stories
Shadow of War has numerous stories, all given to you at different times.  You'll find yourself working with Carnan, the Gondorians from Minis Ithil, Bruz and Ratbag from act 2 and Eltariel.  All the side story missions follow the same formula.
Objective 1: Meet with side story character
Objective 2: Do a generic task that you've done before,
Objective 3: If you have not killed a captain in objective 2 you'll kill one now
Mission complete!
Yeah, nothing special
TL:DR Great game mechanically, Story is dreadful, 4th act destroys all desire for replayability and ruins an otherwise amazing game.

Alan Wake is a third person adventure game which gradually leads you into a nightmare world. The storyline, sound track and style of graphics reminded me a lot of the subtle atmosphere of the game Heavy Rain. Because of this I recommend this game. There is a hefty price tag on this game. I bought it in the summer sale 2014 and I would highly recommend you to buy it when its on a similar offer only. If you do buy it for the full price it will dramatically change the way you feel about the game.
The graphics are very detailed even on its lowest setting. There is a nice combination of generated graphics and video. The lighting in the game is exceptional. Light is what this game is all about and used in many ways as a gaming mechanic. Light is used for creating safe havens, reading messages and when using the touch to aid in taking down enemies.
The storyline is written well and the transition to normal life into the nightmare world of Alan Wake works nicely. As you go deeper into the story the game gradually gets more and more surreal until you get to the point where you are unsure what is real and what is a nightmare.
The combat system in the game can be a little awkward at first using your touch and gun on multiple enemies. But with a little practice the combat system does get easier however the game does not. The controls itself does feel a little unresponsive at times during combat, but that just might be me being a bad loser. Generally the controls are good throughout the game. Combat can make the game a little repetitive at times but the world in which you inhabit does not.  The nightmare world of Alan Wake gets more interesting as you go on.

First a disclosure on my bias: Yes, I was a backer; Yes, I'm an old school gamer; This isn't a full review, more like a first impression; I played the game on Ranger difficult (Hard)
After 34 hours of play time I've decided to write this review regarding my experience and how I take the game.
The first thing you'll notice is how overall high quality this game is for the Unity engine. The voice acting is good and helps with player immersion, but don't discount the reams of quality dialogue and in-game descriptions; it's seriously like reading a book.
Character creation is varied, but playing on hard with loopy character builds is going to bog you down fast, especially on harder difficulties. On "Ranger" difficulty there has really been no let up, each fight needs careful planing and maybe a bit of luck to get through. My team wiped about 3 times before I got a handle on weapon ranges and enemy toughness.
Now, on the downside you may encounter a few bugs on the way. The most common for me were cursor problems, sometimes dragging and dropping things (mostly trophy equipment) and the odd disappearing cursors. Usually opening and closing a menu fixes the cursor, but other times the game needed to be restarted. This really didn't slow me down though and it was usually encountered during heavy inventory managment either during loot sorting or trading.
The final thing I want to say is that the scope of this game is massive. Probably bigger than Icewind Dale 2 and maybe on par with Baldur's Gate 2. I'm 34 hrs in and I'm pretty sure there is another 34 at least left.

Most people know about Starcraft, and to a lesser extent the Command and Conquer series. If you were to ask a crowd about End War, almost everyone (if not everyone) would be wondering what you are talking about. It’s certainly not popular, mainly because the age of RTS games has come to an end.
The unique part of this game is the fact you primarily control units though use of your voice with a microphone. This may seem like a drag, which it was some of the time, but as you got used to it, you could logically think things though. Unlike “pro” players who attempt to boost their actions per a minute by clicking randomly/excessively, using your voice gives not only a much more even experience for all, but also a much more clear and concise one.
The campaign was quite simple, but had an interesting twist as all of Tom Clancy’s games (with the exception of Rainbow Six Siege). With 6 unit types it can certainly feel like rock paper scissors but that just means that unit placement is much more important. If you played command and conquer games, units garrisoned in structures will feel natural in this game.
In many ways, the game plays like Risk, but is much more than that. After playing the game, I am honestly surprised that this game isn’t heard of as much as the other popular RTS titles. Then again, when was the last time people played a true RTS game?

Overall it's a good game that's worth 10 euro to relive the 80s aesthetic and stories! The amount of glitches also seems to be far lower than the original, which still has a couple that made me have to restart the level (basically I got killed and after respawning the edges of the screen remained in combat, but with no enemy in sight, meaning I was stuck). But I can understand playtesting and QA being a tricky thing with almost no team and doing it all on your own.
That kind of thing, though, never happened with this game. Arena has much better and fluid combat than in the original Age of Barbarian, with one exception being that I miss space being used as the jump command. Having to press forward + forward and then up is trickier than pressing space at the end. Also wondering why weapons didn't stay bloody in the original, while in arena they always stay clean? I'd prefer them to get bloodied and stay such, perhaps even blood splatter on your characters a bit when they do a dismemberment - but that's a minor graphical suggestion really.
In conclusion, I'd definitely suggest anyone who has a sweet tooth for 80s cheesy, ultra-gory, juvenile and stereotype-laden barbarism, but hasn't yet played the original Age of Barbarian, to get this instead and play it first. It's much shorter, a lot faster paced without all of the original's exploration segments, that still have their nostalgic charm, but I can understand would likely frustrate a modern gamer with how odd they are sometimes (they annoyed me sometimes too). In this game, you don't get that - just the fights and the minigames and several ways the quick and dirty story can end based on whom you choose and what you do.
Now comes my personal suggestion for the obvious followup in this series, if anyone other than the developer feels like reading it...
For AoB Revenge, I'd suggest the following - ultimately, an epic adventure is definitely what I'd prefer, like in the original (as Mako says in Conan: "Let me tell you of the days of high adventure!"), but by all means do not feel like that means you have to have all the standard RPG things in it because of that! Such as items, that barely do much (hello glowing light stone) or whose purpose is hard to discern (I still have no idea what picking up the tankards or eggs actually did in the original). Don't feel like you have to have levels or better weapons either for that matter! I'd much more prefer the option to have Arena's 6 different characters, each with their own spin on the adventure of revenge and instead unlock their special character moves purely based on which area you have unlocked (area-specific enemies having the appropriate moves to counter yours too of course).
No doubt that would take much longer to write, draw up and implement, but I'd much more prefer seeing Mombata villain his way through a story, then compare that to Sion's journey being more mercenary, Xula continuing to be the great Amazon mom she is, Ayla being the vision-following crazy girl she is or Sheyna continuing her sass and justice than have each of them level up with generic-looking, but slightly better weapons. To me, the characters and their utter cheesyness going through the story ARE the reward, not any kind of loot or better weapons or, heavens forbid, actual armor! Just seeing Rahaan's simple reaction at the end of Arena being entirely unique to him, and nobody else, made me laugh out loud.
So in summation, I wish the developer the best of luck! The art is brilliant, the juvenile, dirty and brutal humor is great and honestly, I wouldn't even bother getting better voiceovers or watching out for typos. It's all part of the charm for me. Just try to focus on iterating on what you find works well and making it better with each new release and I have no doubt I shall see and purchase many more of your nostalgic tales of high adventure. :)

This has to be one of the best (if not actually the best) games that I've played so far in my entire life. Still, it has some negatives, for instance that the "freedom of choice" is basically a well-made illusion and many of your choices may not even matter later on.
I also experienced some weird sound bugs during the gameplay, like that sometimes (every 5 - 10 minutes) in the middle of a dialog there was approx. 50ms sound cut, or generally the first and the last cutscenes from every episode were a lot louder than the actual game itself, even when I tried to tweak the volume in the options. (Well, after all it doesn't have to mean much, since it can also be a problem on my side tbh.)
On the bright side, the game includes a top notch soundtrack which totally fits the atmosphere, and the story's just AMAZING! (There are some minor plot holes and ofc. little things that I personally would change about it, but hey, nothing can be perfect) General theme of the game suits it well - you're playing as an 18 year old wannabe artist girl capable of altering the course time, but dealing with her teenage problems. From the perspective of an 18 year old guy, I have to admit that I cringed during a few scenes, but since I'm in the same age as the main protagonist, I found myself in the story pretty easily and understood it mainly due to my teenage experience.

That also might be one of the game's positive/negative, since it has it's target group. If I were 25+, I'm sure it wouldn't entertain me as much since clearly there's the casual teenage drama motive there. On the other hand, If I were younger (for ex. 10), I probably wouldn't understand the struggle that the main characters are going through during their teenage-early adult years.
TL;DR; If you're 15 - 20 y/o, this game's DEFINITELY for you. But even else, it's a masterpiece worth buying and playing.

ORION: Dino Horde is not unplayable, but that's never a great mark to shoot for. It is Killing Floor minus gun design,  gun play, and gun satisfaction. What it does have is poorly animated dinosaurs spawning out of thin air anywhere they please; a mile away, in direct LOS, or LITERALLY on you.
With that in mind why did I play hours of this game?
1) I like Killing Floor
2) I LOVE DINOSAURS!!!!!!
3) it cost my $1 (Put your "play for free weekend to try it first" pitchforks away, I did)
Response:
1) It uses the same mechanics as KF mostly OK....mostly OK....Its The TAB Cola for KF clones
2) Seriously, they don't make DINO games any more! I love Primal Carnage, like Dino D Day a bit, hated this, and already have Jurassic Park so that's IT for Steam. I got DINO FEVER!!
3) I played for about 3 or 4 hours before buying the game. I can't say I'll be back on again, but if I spend 3+ hours playing their game that at its fundamental core is more or less functioning, then I'm not going to be the guy that doesn't give them A dollar. No....'90's Arcade Me' died long ago....never go back...
Final thoughts:
Do I recommend this game? NO
-Over all game play is bland, the dinos look like they are missing several key frames of animation, gun models are weird and lack power when fired, over all sound effects are sub-par, and everything just feels like another game but less.
Could you still find some satisfaction in playing? SURE!
-I certainly  did...more or less...probably less...but I can't say I didn't, just like I cant say that anyone else has been specifically waiting for Killing Floor with dinosaurs. The game does work, the dinos do look good when not moving, there are several modes to play and the developer has made several MAJOR patches since release brining it, in my opinion, away from BAD and closer to MEDIOCRE.
Watch a gameplay video, you'll see all the bad it has to offer along with anything it has to offer you in return. For me it was dinos, for you it could be jet packs or teamwork or who knows what (only you, that was the whole point I was trying to make....geeze...)

Pretty dang solid game.  I was not disappointed.  If you like the other Lego hero games you will enjoy this one as well.  It was nice getting to play through the cinematic universe with the added flavor and humor Traveler's Tales puts into their games.
The stories were engaging despite having seen them all in movie form already and their as always is plenty of replay value in the game itself.  They have many hubs now and have largely kept the hub from the previous marvel game intact as well.  This game makes for a good free roam time spender for that reason.
The cast is vast and fun but I do think they limited the powers a bit more than they should have.  Many of the cast are also the same character in different outfits.  In some cases like Tony Stark these outfits are great because they change the character abilities.  Others though are only cosmetic but still fun.  That said the alternate costumes do not feel like they are taking away character slots from other heroes that could have been included.  The cast feels VERY thorough...I was hard pressed to find characters from the movies that they missed including.
There were a couple things I wish they had done though.  Understandably this is a cinematic universe game with focus on the movies...but I would have liked to see the marvel mainstays like the Fantastic Four and X-men still playable...even in non-movie form.  This would have made the cast massive and I understand they have license issues to deal with but I missed some of the characters from the first game nonetheless.  I also think they could have made the problem solving aspect a little funner.  This was the first Lego game where both I and my young niece started to find them repetitive as opposed to fun and entertaining.
Overall though I still recommend this game but I would wait for a Steam sale and get it then.

Alan Wake id undoubtedly a triple-A game and there's no questioning in it being a GOOD GAME. After playing for several hours and not completing it, there's one thing I need to point out: the. story. is. killer.
In all due seriousness, however, Alan Wake is a writer to have found himself in a messy situation when Mr. Wake and his wife just wanted to go relaxing outside of the city. His wife goes missing and he needs to figure stuff out. It all gets way more complicated than that, and it makes you scratch your head at times. Overall, the story makes you feel; that's what makes a good story!
And the environment certainly adds to it. Whoever designed the levels need to be glorified. They did a stellar work designing/creating levels that makes you fear the night (literally fear it) and adore the day. During the daytime, you're found in a 1960-style small town that really makes you just want to grab a chair, sit down and relax. It's so calm and beautiful. But then comes the night, and Alan needs to fight for his life and so do you.
Speaking of fighting for his life, you get extraordinarily limited attempting to do that very task. There's a ridiculous limit on the ammunition you can carry (despite ammunition being found everywhere, it does run out quickly) that makes it incredibly difficult to get out of a hairy situation. For example, if you get stuck and there's no ammo around & you meet a ton of enemies, well, tough luck.. your best bet is to run away from them.. in other words, no combat action. CHEAP AND UNACCEPTABLE ♥♥♥♥ING "SOLUTION". But, usually you do have ammo if you use your equipment very conservatively.. no fun doing that, however.
Story is fantastic, gameplay is great and the environment & the atmosphere are out of this world.. astonishing, really! And the game is so well done that it's essentially bug-free! Awesome! If there's a game that gives you a great bang for the buck, Alan Wake is certainly on that list. I thoroughly enjoy this.

I enjoyed Star Wars the Complete Saga, even with the really bad Movies Episodes I-III, I loved Indiana Jones II, found Marvels Super Heroes really good. I hated Lord Of The Rings for the unnessecary big map and huge amount of damn side missions. Most of them I couldn't even find. I dislike the Batman I and II Games, they were just boring unfortunately. For me the Lego Series was weak after some of those Games, had a little Peak wirh Super Heroes and Jurassic World, but Marvels Avengers was finally really awesome.
After the Games started to have real voice actors, I think the games lost their charm. Especially with the german localization I played with. And the worst thing was, that now the persons who gave you tips or directions were constantly talking. Talking and talking and talking and... you get the idea. I just stood there for some seconds, or was destroying things and this person yelled at me to do whatever I had to do. Argh.
But that wasnt the case with Marvels Avengers. They clearly learned from the previous games. The map was big enough to provide free space but not too big. The dialogues were good and no one was talking annoyingly troughout the missions. The mission design was generally good. More variety and more characters to play with. Why they only give you 6 people in free mode, and you have to switch the whole time instead of giving you 10 characters with all the skills you may need in the level, like they did with Star Wars, is a miracle to me. You have a World Map with the missions and locations displayed and this gives the opportunity to make proper DLC content. The stories in the DLC were good enough to be enjoyed in my opinion. The collectables were a waste, because to have 100% you don't need the ones from the DLC. It's good in one way, but why offer them anyway?
For me the game was especially great when I could play the Hulk and do the only thing I want to do as Hulk:
HULK SMASH!
You play basically the Story from the two Movies. I am a huge fan of Avengers, so i really enjoyed those episodes and missions. I even liked the characters I normally dislike (looking at you, Captain America).
So yeah, most things on this game were good. I payed 10 dollars and this is a really good price for the game. Even for 20 or maybe 30 dollars it has enough value.
One thing I found to be shameful is that objects in the Manhattan location popped in when I came near them. That was a lot better in Super Heroes.
Anyway, i definetly recommend that game, especially for kids. And Adults can like this game as well ;)

I personally purchased this game. I reviewed it for my 99 Cent Gaming series.
My expectations for low-budget SHMUPs took a nose dive (ha...plane humor) as I started review games for my series due to the tendency to put in the minimal amount of content. Thankfully, Coldwild Games avoids this with some pretty fun progression systems, multiple unlocks, and different modes.
Coming into this game with low expectations allowed me to breath a sigh of relief just from the character select screen and mode select screen alone. Frequent Flyer has 10 different ships with their own stats that can be unlocked throughout the course of the game, and 4 different modes which include Mission, Infinite, Organized (waves of a single ship attack you, one type at a time), and Time Attack. All these modes feature the roster of 10 enemies who themselves have different stats, tons of pick ups ranging from ammo refills, health, upgrades and MISSILES! As I said, it avoids having a lack of content.
Ships are locked behind a STAR collection wall which you earn from beating missions and picking them up during game play. There's also tasks you can complete that lets you earn them, which for me was the icing on the cake for Frequent Flyer. They stuff a lot of different activities for players to do that it's hard not to keep playing trying to unlock everything, earn all of the achievements, and start brushing up your skills for the leader board.
There were a few issues I had however. First was the inclusion of tweeting out your score to earn more stars. I felt that this was not necessary for a game that already had a lot of ways to do so. It gave me a mobile free2play feeling that just didn't sit well with me. That said it's not forced upon the player and you can choose to ignore it. I get wanted to tweet out something both for bragging rights and to show support, but this way is just not for me.
Secondly was using tank controls. Now this is less of a game issue and more of my personal preference, but having controller support left me wanting more of a dual-stick control scheme. I don't know if this can be added by the devs but I personally would love it.
Outside of those two things, and some aesthetic overlaps, I didn't find anything wrong with what I played and was overjoyed to see a developer attempt to stack their game with some fun options at such a low price. I have more to say in my video below, but was Frequent Flyer worth the 99 cents I paid for it: ABSOLUTELY.   They even mentioned that even though the game is complete, they are open to feedback and suggestions. Give this game a go to support this type of game, and let the developer know what you'd like to see in this fun little SHMUP.

Oh the nostalgia!  Fallout 2 remains, to me, the standard for post-apocalyptic turn-based RPG's.   Wasteland 2 is an amazing return to the genre.  Gone is the hand holding that today's games give you.  Instead...you are thrown into the mix to learn for yourself.  The quicksave is your best friend as almost every move and decision you make can impact the future of your party...and the wasteland, itself.  Chose your team and skills carefully, or perish in the toxic tundra.  There's no regenerating health.  There's limited ammo.  Your party members can die and you will mourn their loss and the loss of their skills until you can find help in some random town.
Also there's a return to fun and quirk.  As you travel the wastes you'll run into characters and scenarios that will make you laugh (like the screaming goat)...and others that will make your blood boil (camp full of forced prostitution).  Sometimes you'll open a random crate in the desert praying for some .38 ammo...only to find a broken Rubix Cube or Teddy Ruxpin (Seriously).
This is the game that's been missing for quite a long time.

One thing leads to another and the defense system attacks on accident an American space station. Thus begins world war three.
Over all, this is one of my very favourite games of all time. The graphics are incredible for its age, the AI is [GENERALLY] pretty smart about combat tactics, and battles change and evolve based on the player's actions. Being an older game, it is rather lacking in a few parts, and some of the maps are pretty much Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V 'ed, but for the most part, no one tactic (like my NEEDS MOAR TANKS! Tank bum rush tactic) will work in every battle. There is all sorts of upgrades, and some of them even change the models of the units.
My overall rating for this RTS is about 8.75 out of ten, I just wish Ubisoft kept upgrading it to this day.

Also, the factional warfare multiplayer part of the game is long long dead. I think you might still be able to play with a friend but I was turned off before I could attempt it.

They're also the only other thing aside from Artillery and WMD strikes that keep this game from being completely rock paper scissors style combat (Tanks --kill--> LAV's --kill--> Helicopters --kill--> Tanks)
With all this said. I loved this game on console, the voice commands are very responsive and the game is legitimitaly challenging. However for PC, I can't reccomend this game.
If they made a legit Endwar 2, kept the voice commands but made it a bit more classic rts camera style with more unique units. This game would be legendary.

Probably one of the best games this year, and one of the best hack and slash beat em up titles of all time. Builds off and improves pretty much everything from the last title, and adds new experiences and challenges that make the game refreshing yet challenging on even Normal difficulty.
In terms of lore, the ending you get for completing Act 3 ties up the games storyline together nicely, and the epilogue "true ending" you get for completeing Act 4 ties the game together into The Lord of the Rings original trilogy movies and book.
In terms of gameplay, nothings really changed except that you're more powerful in terms of amount of abilities you have, except you have less of a chance to use and abuse them like in the last game. Things like using consume on all enemies in a single fight are gone, since consume uses Might now, which is the same meter you use to perform executions and the  like.
Overall, a solid 9.5/10. I just wish the game was longer, only took me around 20 hours to complete the main game up to Act 3, and it will probably take me a bit longer to complete Act 4 Shadow Wars, where I am at Stage 6 and at 26 hours so far.
PS: The microtransactions in the game are a joke. They're in there to get money from the whales since they know they'll buy the stuff. You really don't need to buy the crates; you get powerful gear for free for completing Act 3 and Starting Act 4, and you can get another powerful gear set by completing Ithilden Poem doors. The only way I could justify buying crates is if you're low on Orc Captains and Warchiefs and need some leveled minions for the Shadow Wars.

Currently I have 40 slots in my inventory and to unlock the next 5 slots, it will cost me $4+.  Even parts you have equipped on robots count towards inventory so this gets filled up very quickly.

You would think the game had enough money sink?  No.  When you win matches you have a chance to get crates.  To stand a chance to open these crates you will have to use sparks otherwise the picklocking tool has 0.1% ~ 5% chance depending on crate level.  I have no problem with this in games but when you add in the other two money sinks then this makes the game have a bad f2p model.
Stay away from this game unless the developer gets their head out of the gutter.  Too many money sink.  With the inventory limit it literally forces you to use sparks to progress.  Yes you do get sparks in-game but no where near enough to make the game enjoyable on being free.  I have no problem spending cash on a f2p game but there are too many money sink that are not really optional.

Generally a good game and an enormous improvement on the last game. Only downside to the game itself are of course the microtransactions, but the game is perfectly enjoyable without spending a penny more than 60 dollars, euros, whatever it costs in your country.
PROS:
+++ Extremely on point with the lore
+++ Nemesis system is vastly improved and I love the addition of new classes and having more control over your followers
++ The combat is much improved on since the last game anbd flows more easily thanks to new abilities
++ I love everything in act I through act III, though there are some flaws of course (see CONS)
+ The return of some old fellas in an actually non-forced way (something not a lot of games do)
+ To expand on the previous point, some uruk captains are named after foes of the previous games and reflect that or are based on opponents of LOTR movies. I found a captain who was dubbed "the tower" and greatly resembled him even though he really was just a captain as well as another captain "of the white hand" who couldn't stop mentioning Saruman
CONS:
--- The entirety of act ♥♥♥♥ing IV, I mean I do love defending my fortresses but 10 ♥♥♥♥ing waves of an increasing amount of sieges? That's just a needless grind and it's so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ that I (a hardcore fan) have lost interest in continueing the story, that's right, I don't even want to progress, that's how tedious act IV is and the only way to make it less tedious is the microtransactions but NOT gonna do that. At least it's not a quick time event anymore to my knowledge.
-- The AI is sometimes frustratingly dumb. I lost a few legendary or really powerfull rare captains in the arena because they couldn't stop fighting some Olog followers while the enemy captain had their way with them. This can just make an entire half hour of work and an amazing looking captain go to waste.
- Why the bloody hell does every single quest need to have a part in every ♥♥♥♥ing region, for real. It almost becomes fast travel simulator. Luckily the loading times are extremely low so not really a big issue, more of an annoyance.
- Minor point: Why is Talion in the beginning such a useless♥♥♥♥♥♥ He was ultra powerful at the end of SOM so why did he lose all his skills and become so weak and powerless?
Nota Bene: Everyone complains about the microtransactions and while I agree that these are extremely stupid in a singleplayer game, I applaud them for making the transactions completely optional and not ever truly necessary. You can perfectly finish the game without spending a single extra penny, even though act IV becomes a pain in the rear end.
All in all: Great game, really an improvement on the last one. If they ever decide to make another one: DO NOT do the disaster that is act IV! I don't know if they're even be one because I still haven't finished it.

Insanely, ridiculously hard twitch shooter type game. But the impeccable, outstanding art design, music, sound design, and overall polish make it very addicting to keep trying.
My main criticism of the game is that so much of it is really trial and error, (e.g. there's no way to tell that X enemy will do Y thing that will kill you until you actually get killed by it and have to restart your run from the beginning). Once you have a good idea of the enemy behaviors it gradually becomes more doable.
However, the RNG is the main issue with the game, because if you get a badly generated level, your run will easily go south. Some of the things that can kill you through no fault of your own: getting a bunch of sucide bombing enemies charging at you RIGHT when you spawn, spawning in a crossfire of bullets/snipers, getting a poorly designed level to fight the boss in. The abilities and weapons you get are also 100% random, so you could be stuck with poor abilities AND weapons which will make the later levels far harder.
It is definitely a flawed game but when it works right it's very fun. I had more fun with it playing Co-op because it's a little more forgiving of stupid deaths.

Alan Wake is a refreshing break from the standard set of computer-games, whilst there is an element of shooting it has been done in a way that means this doesn't feel central to the game and second to the story.  I think of this piece as more of an interactive-story than a game in the traditional sense.  This does mean there is a fair bit of hanging-about during cut-scenes but each are critical to bringing the whole thing together.
The episodic format is an interesting approach but probably not entirely necessary, the frequent auto-saving means that you can pick up and put down the game as and when.
The genre is definitely of the horror-thriller ilk, it isn't a gory blood-fest but instead plays on visual and audio queues to get the heart going and your palms to sweat-up.  I would highly recommend playing this in small installments as to avoid the inevitable game-centered-dreams that follow a marathon session.  I am not a fan of horror, or being scared, and this game just about stayed in what was acceptable.
As with any game, once you start to learn the patterns of the designers and the engine things get a little less jumpy and a bit more mothodical.  There is a lull of repeatidness in the mid-area of the game, where you're going through cut-scene/walk in a dark area/kill some folk, this does clear though as more puzzles are introduced and more options for dispatching your enemies are presented.  The game keeps you challenged by removing your weapons at pretty much every opportunity, you are always starting off with the basics, and whilst this is frustraiting to the ammo-horder that I am, it is quite nice to know that you can feel confident running down to zero towards the end of each section.
I picked this up a sale and it was worth every penny, whilst the graphics are beginning to date in areas it's still full of plenty environmental eye-candy and georgeous lighting.  A lot of detail has been put in by the developers and at no point does this ever feel like a rushed job or a money spin.  This was a carefully crafted bit of creative development.
Would I recommend you play it?  Yes.  Will I play it again?  No.  How many hours did it consume?  A leasurely twelve.

I can generally recommend Alan Wake. While I find myself annoyed by many heavily scripted, linear games, this game does it better as there is some intrigue with the plot and the gameplay doesn't try to be complex. It plays somewhat like a third person shooter, but you are certainly not a military hero or athelete, so you must nearly dodge attacks and maintain stamina when running.
The dodging does feel a bit iffy at times, as I've pressed the dodge command during combat and I am still hit - you are  still hit if an attack hits you during the animation, unlike other games where just dodging may give your a temporary invincibility/lack of collision. Combat mostly involves weakening the "Taken" enemies with flashlights, stationary light sources, Flares, and flashbangs, and then finishing them off with a gun shot or vehicular take down. You can "strengthen" your flashlight at the cost of battery power - a skilled player can avoid using that ability in most of combat to preserve batteries (which honestly, isn't that necessary in normal difficulty). Combat can be avoided all together if you run away from combat to the next street lamp save point.
The episodes do feel a bit lengthy, especially episode 3, but there are only main episodes total (not including specials and Nightmare mode replay, which gives you more collectible Manuscript pages to pick up) and most episodes take 1-1.5 hrs to complete. The collecting of coffee thermoses makes no sense and feels like a feature that was supposed to be fuller, but reduced. (I've read that you would loose your save game in beta versions if you didn't get the thermoses). I originally thought this was a game wouldn't like for the story emphasis, but midway through the game, I became interested in what was happening. The story is about one of Alan's writings coming to reality for him and at one instance, he references Stephen King as an inspiration for his work. I haven't read any Stephen King, but that may give you an idea of what is happening.
I enjoyed my experience, and intend on finishing the special missions and the spin-off which I think is more action oriented. Because I'm focused on clearing my backlog, I'm not concerned with achievements or Nightmare mode manuscript pages, though, if I wasn't I'd play Nightmare mode and probably get most of the achievements.

War. War never changes. Wasteland 2 is such a spiritual successor to old Fallout games that I almost expected Ron Perlman to deliver those iconic lines during the opening video. Now, let’s not forget that the original Fallout was inspired by the first Wasteland game. And now, in turn, a Wasteland game is inspired by the first 2 Fallout games – and as such, should be a treat for all those Nuke Cola loving, bottlecap collecting vault-dwellers out there.
It’s been more than 2 years since Wasteland 2 campaign on Kickstarter was successfully funded – and after more than a few delays, a full version is finally available – but is it polished? Well, yes and no. While the reports of bugs are everywhere on the interwebs, in my 10+ hours of playing I encountered only one game-restarting bug when my party just refused to move from the spot. A quick restart solved the problem, but such bugs should not happen in a game that was delayed for so long and live tested with the huge community of early access players.
I won’t spoil the story so far, but the main premise is this – after the politicians “pushed the button”, the survivors of the nuclear wasteland are living in small interconnected communities, looked after by “Desert Rangers”, a self-made police of the apocalypse. You are one of them.
The choices you make in the game will affect the story, just like in any good RPG. For instance, near the beginning of the game, while you are patrolling the desert you get 2 distress calls at the same time – one from a farm where mutated plants and animals started wreaking havok, and one from a town being attacked by raiders. You can’t save both – I helped the town attacked by raiders, and when I managed to got to the other town, it was completely destroyed and overrun with mutant zombie plant people. Yup, enemies in Wasteland 2 are awesome.
Anyway, my choosing to ignore the first one while helping the other had a consequence – mutated plants were now spreading across the wasteland, so now you encountered zombie plant hordes on the map, solving additional quests that included ridding the affected villages of them and treating the water supply with the serum to stop them from spreading further.
This is definitely a game that just has to be played more than once – and I love that.
One more thing I loved about Wasteland 2 is the sense of “yikes, I’m getting the hell out of here and coming back later with better weapons” feeling – the dangers in Wasteland are real – and some of them will require you to run with your tail between your legs.
That’s all I’m willing to write without spoiling details of the game further. Except for this one little spoiler: there’s a skill in the skill tree called “Toaster Repair”. Yes, there’s an entire skill dedicated to repairing toasters. Of course I invested points in it! :)
In short, if you loved Fallout 1 and 2, you will LOVE Wasteland 2. If that was not your cup of radioactive tea, look elsewhere, because turn-based combat and slow but steady exploring is not for everyone.

I'm amazed that reviews for Wasteladn 2 are so mixed. There's nothing about this game that should discourage people from playing it. It's 100% in the spirit of the games that came before, be they the ancient artifact that is Wasteland, or the more direct analogue, Fallout. In fact, it immediately reminded me of the storytelling style of Fallout with the more capable squad-based skills and combat of the Fallout Tactics "experiment". Take the stengths of both, layer on the lore of the classic Wasteland. then run it through an extended Early Access period to ensure it delivers on its promises, and you have Wasteland 2.
I will say, this game is unforgiving. If you miss a sidequest opportunity the first time through an area, Wasteland does. not. care. That NPC could easily be gone the next time you visit... or worse. Whole zones play out differently based on how quickly you answer the call. Neglect a skill that was essential to solving a problem the way you want to, and you might have to admit defeat (or just do it the hard way.) Have a lot of regrets? Good, says WL2. That's life in the Wasteland. I'm impressed so far, and it all feels well done. Truly a game with an old soul, that learned a few lessons in the intervening years. Recommended without reservations.

I really wish instead of a yes or a no we could choose "Eeeeehhh" when it comes to whether to recommend a game, because that's basically how I feel about Wasteland 2. While the story is interesting and the character creation is deep, the combat is basically broken. Your party members will miss most of their attacks regardless of what their to-hit-chance is, and I literally just spent two and a half rounds watching every single character I had miss every single attack over and over, and each of them had a percentage chance to hit their enemy higher than seventy. This isn't unusual, and the frustrating thing is your enemies typically have no such issues, and always have greater AP than you do, so when you're frequently facing off against multiple enemies, you're basically just watching your party take piles of damage. It got so bad that at a certain quest location, I had to leave the area to purchase more supplies because my party had no way of healing itself, and the NPC who was with us called us cowards and left the group, and now I have no way to complete the current questline without going and grinding up levels so I can sink points into the required skills she had to pass obstacles.
It's not about challenge, it's about a lack of balance in the to-hit numbers generator. When my characters can succeed every single time cracking a safe or defusing a bomb with less than a 30% chance to do so, but they can't hit something standing right in front of them three times in a row with a 76% chance to land a blow, there's something broken. Similarly, though this is more an issue in the player's favour, early Raider loot is sort of ridiculous. If you wander around outside the Ranger HQ and grind levels there, after one level you should have no difficulty slaughtering the raiders that pop up as random encounters with ease. Not only do they give a solid chunk of EXP each time you win, but they drop PILES of expensive healing items and ammunition, sometimes multiple stacks of them, and everything else they drop can be sold for a ton of cash. The machetes, for instance, go for $42, and while not every Raider will have one, they still drop frequently enough that you can simply farm them for cash and equipment until you have stacks and stacks of healing items and armor and ammunition.
The other complaint I'd offer is that the setting and world doesn't feel very apocalypse-y. Yeah, it's all sand-blasted, but water seems to be plentiful, people are growing food, and the atmosphere fails to give a sense of tension and danger. This is largely due to the fact that travel simply happens on a map, and the random encounters take place in the exact same little mini areas each time (down to the placement of objects), so the world seems very small and empty rather than giving you an idea of scope and the consequences of the end of the world. It feels less like an RPG and more like a linear turn-based strategy game... there's no real reason to explore the world map, and there's nothing to do unless you continue the main quest, which you don't really get any input in. In all honesty, I likely would have been a lot less harsh on this game as a whole if the accuracy issue hadn't soured me towards it, and if that were patched I'd recommend it a lot more. It has the potential to be a rock-solid, challenging, deep strategy game, but as it stands, it feels like it needs more tweaking under the hood.

Yes, the art is great, the soundtrack is great, the story is great, but the actual gameplay itself wasn't very fun at all. This feels like it should have been a movie and not a videogame. You are almost always locked into one path. It didn't feel like an adventure at all- there's no real danger. Also it's very short. I definitely can't reccommend it until Act 2 comes out.
1) The game doesn't explain itself. Especially in the Vella story, I got through all the puzzles by clicking on things in my inventory randomly. Also, at one point in the Vella story you come to a puzzle that can only be solved by an object from much earlier in the game that, at the time, you didn't actually need to have. I ended up having to go all the way back for it. Then there's also the part with the snake that blocks the path. There's no way to get past the snake. It's basically an invisible wall. But I didn't realize this, so I spent a good amount of time trying to get past the snake because I thought that that was how I was meant to progress.
2) Yes, I get that there will be a second part, but even with all the wandering pointlessly and clicking randomly that I did, I still beat the game (both storylines) in 5 hours. Again, half of that time was spent wandering around between the beach and the woods. I beat the game the same day that I bought it.
3) Maybe this game isn't supposed to work this way, but there's no way to lose the game. When you finally confront Mog Chothra at the end of Vella's story, you can stand on the beach as long as you want, and even when Mog Chothra finally grabs you, you just dangle in front of its closed mouth for a minute until Vella frees herself automatically or you do something. There is absolutely no pressure on you to do anything. Take your time.

This has to be one of the best (if not actually the best) games that I've played so far in my entire life. Still, it has some negatives, for instance that the "freedom of choice" is basically a well-made illusion and many of your choices may not even matter later on.
I also experienced some weird sound bugs during the gameplay, like that sometimes (every 5 - 10 minutes) in the middle of a dialog there was approx. 50ms sound cut, or generally the first and the last cutscenes from every episode were a lot louder than the actual game itself, even when I tried to tweak the volume in the options. (Well, after all it doesn't have to mean much, since it can also be a problem on my side tbh.)
On the bright side, the game includes a top notch soundtrack which totally fits the atmosphere, and the story's just AMAZING! (There are some minor plot holes and ofc. little things that I personally would change about it, but hey, nothing can be perfect) General theme of the game suits it well - you're playing as an 18 year old wannabe artist girl capable of altering the course time, but dealing with her teenage problems. From the perspective of an 18 year old guy, I have to admit that I cringed during a few scenes, but since I'm in the same age as the main protagonist, I found myself in the story pretty easily and understood it mainly due to my teenage experience.

That also might be one of the game's positive/negative, since it has it's target group. If I were 25+, I'm sure it wouldn't entertain me as much since clearly there's the casual teenage drama motive there. On the other hand, If I were younger (for ex. 10), I probably wouldn't understand the struggle that the main characters are going through during their teenage-early adult years.
TL;DR; If you're 15 - 20 y/o, this game's DEFINITELY for you. But even else, it's a masterpiece worth buying and playing.
