Short review: Life is Strange is one of the greatest stories I've ever experienced. It has touched me in a way no other game has before. A more accurate title for this game is "Life is emotionally taxing". If you're not afraid of a little crying here and there, and you're looking for a good story-based game, you have to play this. It is better than Telltale games. Avoid spoilers and PLAY THIS GAME, especially if your name is Jeff. Keep reading for long review.
Pros:
+ Not your typical 'coming-of-age' story. Fairly original and keeps you hooked.
+ Gets you emotionally invested, throws plenty of curveballs, and punches you right in the feels.
+ Characters are colourful, diverse, and surprisingly memorable.
+ Absolutely amazing soundtrack, both original track and licensed music that is utilized superbly.
+ Your choices have more impact than is visible in things like Telltale games. The writing is able to refer to earlier choices and keep reminding you / guilting you about your previous decisions. Also can affect story/gameplay significantly.
+ Game rewards you for exploring and interactions - not just in optional photos/achievements, but also in information and story bits that can be important if you realize their importance.
+ Rewinding time is both a story and a gameplay feature that is utilized extremely well, especially for this game genre.
+ No quick time events or time limits, thank goodness!
+ Becomes apparent why this game won multiple awards for best soundtrack, voice performance, and original story/narrative as you play the game.
+ Many corny lines that will either make you laugh, or cringe hard, although apparently this is realistic dialogue in some teenage groups.
+ Helped me deal with issues related to my own mental health, and also inspired me to play music again.
Cons:
- Last episode feels a bit rushed compared to all the other episodes (noticeable lip sync or audio bugs can occur).
- As with most adventure games, the budget is not nearly as high as some other games, so if you pay too much attention to specific details, you may get thrown off (lip syncing, motion capture/animations, etc.)
- Many corny lines that will either make you laugh, or cringe hard, although apparently this is realistic dialogue in some teenage groups.
Long review:
Similar to Telltale games, LiS is pretty much a point and click adventure game (I recommend using a controller). The game is heavily narrative based, revolving around decisions you make in dialogue sequences. The 'gameplay', aside from dialogue choices, includes moving around in limited areas to interact with objects and people, as well as some light puzzle solving, before moving on to the next scene. You're not here for a challenge or adrenaline-inducing gameplay - you're here for the story. One thing I am thankful for is that unlike Telltale games, there are NO quick time events! This is actually a really good thing because QTEs often were more annoying than fun.
So what's the deal? Why does everyone keep saying stuff like 'made me cry', 'life-changing' and other glowing reviews? LiS revolves around Max Caulfield, a teenage girl transitioning into adult life. You quickly learn she moved away from her hometown of Arcadia Bay, Oregon, for 5 years, then moved back after successfully getting into a prestigious art school for photography classes. Like in her own words, "in the end it's still high school, which sucks". Her life then changes forever when an event happens that inexplicably triggers her ability to rewind time. The game starts off as a sort of teenage girl high school simulator, but quickly becomes something much more...It becomes one of the greatest stories I've ever experienced.
To say anymore would be spoilers, and trust me, you want to go into this game with as little spoilers as possible. The characters are well developed, easing you in from episode 1 and exploring their personalities and quirks alongside you as the player throughout the journey. What is interesting is that many characters offer more than their first impression gives you, if you're willing to learn more. The game smartly rewards exploration and interaction, and not just in direct optional achievements kind of way. You can learn additional story bits and information that can prove to be important, if you realize their importance on your own. And it's not just gameplay either - exploring things like your continously updating journal and text messages in the secondary pause menu offers a lot of rich insight and backstory you may not get otherwise.
The time rewind mechanic is actually quite a genius idea for a genre like this - it not only features heavily in the story, but is also a great gameplay mechanic. Throughout the game you'll be able to hold down a button to rewind time up to a certain point, undoing certain previous actions (like dialogue choices or a moved object, for example). The most obvious use of this is changing dialogue options, especially when it comes to important decisions. The game is filled with minor and major decision branches, and having the ability to rewind allows you to make a choice, undo it, and then immediately see how a character reacts if you choose the other option. Ever wanted to see what all the dialogue options are with an NPC, but they keep ending the conversation? Rewind and talk to them again with different options! This conveniently also allows you to experience more without having to reload a game save over and over.
However, rewinding is limited, so once you move on to the next scene, you can't undo your actions. This means you'll often be able to see the immediate consequences of your decisions (ex. a character's reaction right there), but in the end you will have to pick one of the options and live with whatever future consequences happen from it for the rest of the game. Apart from that, it's used cleverly in some light puzzle solving elements and optional interactions. Be warned that time rewind should not be relied on as a crutch...this plays heavily in the story and cleverly can screw with you if you go in with the wrong mentality.
LiS is a narrative based game, and it has a very solid story. Part of the emotional response from players is due to the fact that the story tackles a lot of heavy themes - and a lot of it is stuff people don't really want to talk about. Depression and bullying are some examples, but there's way more in there that again, I won't spoil. It also does a really good job of just capturing what it means to be human. As of result, it is VERY relatable - maybe you've personally never experienced what these characters have, but it is very easy to empathize with everyone's problems. As of result, many topics can hit 'hard at home', and overall the game sticks in your mind long after completion.
I played this game at a point in my life where I wasn't exactly the happiest. After some research wondering why this game is so meaningful to me, it turns out that A LOT of young people, especially young males, don't really know how to deal with mental health issues. We don't go to professionals - it just is. But finding ways to reflect and deal with your issues through other means (in this case a media - a video game) is often much more effective than the old-school ways of being expected to go to a professional. 'Life-changing' isn't an exaggeration - it's true for me at least.
The soundtrack is, simply put, amazing. The original score is absolutely fitting and memorable, but there are also plenty of licensed music that are used fantastically in every scene they were utilized for. They are so well utilized it becomes part of your memory of various scenes, and has inspired me to pick up my instruments again.
Thank you, Life is Strange, for an unforgettable experience. The prequel just came out days ago at the time of writing, but I recommend playing this first before any spin offs. One of the best stories I've experienced. Hella cool.

TL;DR You should play LEGO Marvel Super Heroes instead. I enjoyed this game as a (forgiving) Marvel nut, but I would not recommend it to the average consumer.
When LEGO Marvel's Avengers was first announced I got very excited. LEGO Marvel Super Heroes was by far my favorite LEGO game, and I've always been a huge MCU (Marvel Cinematic Universe) nerd. So when I heard a new LEGO game was being developed based specifically on the MCU and the Avengers movies, I was ecstatic. However, when I finally got my hands on the game, I was... rather disappointed.
The story mode is a pain to get through. While the first game had a fun and entertaining story, this game retold the Avengers films
. They used audio clips from the actual films, and created cutscenes around them that just... didn’t work. Throughout the actual gameplay, depending on who you played as, you got to hear a mixture of badly-implemented audio lines from the films, and newly-recorded lines for the game. The game would've been much better if they'd just recorded new audio for
of the characters, even if it meant recasting most of the characters who appeared in the films.
To the game's credit, six actors from the films reprised their roles and recorded new audio for the game, and they were all fantastic. Clark Gregg (Phil Coulson) and Cobie Smulders (Maria Hill) were the largest contributors, but you also got to experience a fair number of Free Play side quests from Hayley Atwell as Peggy Carter and Ashley Johnson as Waitress Beth. Additionally, Ming-Na Wen narrated the Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. DLC level as Melinda May, and Michael Peña narrated the Ant-Man DLC level as Luis. Hearing them all reprise their roles was an amazing treat.
Now, let's talk about what made the game worth playing for me: Free Play. That's always the best part of any LEGO game. However, you need to play through the
story mode to get to most of the Free Play features (and if you don't poke around menus too much you might not even realize how to get to Free Play at all before completing the story mode). And playing through the story mode is
. The fact that you basically need to beat the entire campaign before you can really start having fun is why I don't recommend this game to the average consumer.
Free Play itself is a blast. As a major MCU nut I really appreciated a lot of the characters they included in the game just so that major fans would notice. The day I unlocked Lorelei I was overjoyed.
I was so happy. I also loved the inclusion of the MCU lineup of the Defenders, although I'm pretty sure whoever wrote and directed Jewel's dialogue clearly never read Alias or watched Jessica Jones. That was about the farthest you could possibly get from any version of Jessica's personality.
Playing through levels and being able to switch between awesome characters at will has always been a major draw for Lego games. In recent years they’ve implemented overworld hubs as well, which is one of my favorite parts of the games. However, in this game you don't
get to explore Manhattan like you did in LEGO Marvel Super Heroes; you also get to explore seven other smaller hubs, including locations like Asgard and Tony Stark's estate at Malibu. Exploring them to find all of the secrets and unlockables is a
.
That's something that's very interesting about the game: The inconsistency of quality. Some parts of development, such as the art department responsible for creating the environments in the game, completely outdid themselves in creating amazing and beautiful levels and hubs to play through. You can also tell a lot of work was put into the fight animation, as a lot of it is really cool. But sometimes you’re required to watch through an entire automated battle while mashing whatever button is on the screen, and this is especially tedious when you're in Free Play and just wish the story elements would
.
Yes, some parts of the game, such as the environments, were impeccably well-made; but on the other hand, the game is a complete mess. Sometimes activating panels just doesn't work. Sometimes your map says you can collect something that's already been collected. Sometimes a vehicle will fall off a level in a way so that it never spawns on stable ground again unless you restart the level. Sometimes you can meet the requirements of an achievement, but it won't unlock because you exited a level the wrong way, and you might need to create a whole new save file to try and get it again. This game needed a much bigger QA team, far more than any other LEGO game has before it.
The hub side-quests are inconsistent as well. Sometimes a lot of work was clearly put into them. Others were just weird and sloppy. It really is strange how often this game flip-flops from fantastic to downright annoying. This can be said for some of the in-level puzzles as well.
Speaking of which, DLC. I'm not going to rage here about how the Season Pass doesn't include all of the DLC that it should, but...
. The DLC levels themselves are fun, and I love the additional characters that come with them. However, that fact that we're given all of the characters from a DLC pack right off the bat is just sad. The best part of having so many playable characters in these games is the journey it takes to unlock them. Having all of the characters from a DLC pack available before you even play the level makes the whole experience… kind of lackluster.
However, I do briefly want to talk about how happy I am that they included an Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. level pack. To have a LEGO game based on the MCU and not at least include a sizeable slew of S.H.I.E.L.D. characters would have been terrible missed opportunity. My only complaint with the DLC is that Skye's in-game character is named as her (spoilery) real name, when the level takes place at the end of S.H.I.E.L.D. Season 2, when she still went by the name Skye. For how much detail they attend to, I felt it a shame that they forwent it for marketing purposes.
As a huge Marvel and MCU fan, the experience was worth it to me. Playing through the game in Free Play with a huge cast of Marvel characters both from the films and the comics is, frankly, a total blast. But in order to unlock most of that experience, you first need to play through a tedious and poorly-made story mode, that I would say makes the game not worth it to the average consumer. If you truly want to enjoy yourself with a beautiful marriage of everything that’s good about Marvel and LEGOs, I highly recommend you check out LEGO Marvel Super Heroes instead.

text:
++ Charming characters and amusing dialog, as expected from any Double Fine production
+ Competent voice acting
+ Not-bad story.  Not great, but good
- Tumblr nose.  In fact, the only likeable thing about this game's art style are the backgrounds
-- Extremely short;  Act 1 only took 4 hours to complete, and word has it there's
going to be an Act 2 after this.  Unless Double Fine really digs in and amps up the elements of what makes the adventure game genre great in the forthcoming Act 2, I wouldn't recommend this game.
--- The most significant negative:  No challenge at all;  this adventure game has the easiest "puzzles" I've encountered in any point-and-click to date.  I'm not saying it should be Sierra-level difficult, but it's not unfair to expect a few good head-scratchers once in a while.  Alas, there were none.
Verdict:  Not Schafer's best.  I know he can direct and produce a better game than this.  Play Psychonauts and Grim Fandango instead.
P.S.:  If Act 2's development makes a 180 degree turn and ends up being awesome by not repeating Act 1's more egregious mistakes, I will happily eat my shoe and give credit where it's due.

Tom Clancy's Endwar presents unique addition to the RTS genre, breaking new ground with many concepts yet unprecedented at the time of its release. Featuring unique, relatively balanced gameplay, a fairly competent AI, exceptional graphics, RPG-style combat unit upgrading system, and a voice command interface, the game presents an attractive addition to an RTS enthusiast's library.
The game is set in the near future, in which the Middle East's oil market has long since collapsed due to nuclear fallout, causing worldwide increase in oil prices - and thus a worlwide state of panic. Russia, having taken advantage of the Middle East's collapse, is quickly becoming the world leader in oil production. The United States and European Union are rushing to complete superweapons capable of rendering nuclear weapons obsolete, while Russia initiates the largest martial buildup since the Cold War. Tension is quickly building up. The world as we know it is falling into chaos. The stage is set. 'Let the end begin.'
Tom Clancy's EndWar was a fresh, entertaining game when it was released, and still retains its charm even today. The game is well worth the $10, and has a good deal of replay value. If you're looking for decent RTS featuring a fresh perspective and gameplay, this game is certainly worth looking into.

Absolutely great!  As someone who recently went back and picked up Fallout 2 only to realise it was a LOT better in my memory, than in my 2014 spec PC reality - Wasteland 2 is exactly what I needed. OK so sure, I hear what some reviewers are saying - as far as tactical combat goes, this is not XCOM. Nothing is. But the game has all the elements I used to love in the original Fallout series; gritty humour, no imposed moral code, diverse skill system, crafting and more. This Review is Spoiler Free (Storywise)
After a week of playing this game (60 hours gathered so far) I have to say: this is one of the best games I've played so far.
Very Short Overview:
Story: 5/5 (Definitly a big improvement. The Story fits pretty good into Lotr lore - everything is just a bit ... exxagerated. You know, Gimli and Legolas killing 40-60 Orcs in one  battle, pretty good  Warriors. This dude here, your protagonist, killing hundreds of orcs, fighting all kinds of big♥♥♥♥♥♥in Mordor ... it makes sense, its entertaining. Its jsut a liiiiiittle bit over the Top :D)
Gameplay: 5/5 (awesome fighting system, good stealth system, nice leveling up ... Just a pretty amazing game)
Graphics: 4/5 (pretty good, especially considering that most enemy characters are randomly generated)
But lets talk about the negativ things first:
- The Microtransaction-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. So many People are flaming about this, understandable. I dont like it either, but I have to say: YOU. CAN. IGNORE. IT. You dont have to spent a single Dollar after buying this game. Everything you get through those, you can get through playing ingame too. Its that simple. Its annoying af, true, its a bad sign that even a Single Player game gets those, true, and we should be upset about it. It just hurts my soul to see such a fantastic game suffer under such a greed, so many people miss this game because of that.
- Sometimes your Character prioritizes things wrong. Most common example: 1) you want to EXECUTE someone (instakill that you have to earn by comboing 10-15 hits), but since there are more then 1 targets somewhat around you, you accidently kill the wrong one. Annoying. 2) If you want to suck someones Energy out you also get the wrong one accidently. Which makes you easy to hit by your wanted target, possibly a Boss. Annoying as hell.
- This triggers me the most: sometimes when I'm about to get killed, one of my "Friends" comes to save me. This is supposed to be an awesome "wow, cool! Thanks buddy!" scene. IT IS NEVER FOR ME. 1/4 of all my Enemies are people I'd say: hey, I want to have them on my Team later on. And ever single god damn time one of my Savior shows up to KILL OF my future plans in front of me. This is so triggering.
Now lets talk about the Positiv Things:
You feel like an absolut badass slaughtering Orcs left and right. I'll recommend you play it on the hardest difficulty (you can always switch if you feel like it). After like 5 to 10 Hours into the game (depending on how fast you follow the story) you get the Ability to control Enemies, Dominating them. You start building an Army, attacking Castles, promoting some of your Orcs to the new Leaders. Saurons Army might tries to take the Castle back, so you have a defending Gamemode too. You can attack other players castle, and fight their Orcs too. This is very intriguing, it makes you build a nasty or funny combination of Orcs on your defensive Side. You learn to tame Beasts like Caragors (Wolflike Beasts), Graugs (Giants) and Dragons, you can ride and control all of them. You will fight a Balrog & Nazguls (Ring wraiths).
One other thing is really like: You can make two Orcs fight each other in an Arena, Gladiator Style. Or how I like to see it: Pokemon for Adults. Gotta catch'em all, then let them fight each other. Between 30 Seconds up to 3 Minutes Fight, you just sit and watch them unleash their Attacks, making bets about who wins.
Your Character is pretty overpowered. He has to be, since you run in alone against dozens or hundreds of Enemies. You can do really badass things, and use some Tactics to overcome Problems. Its not that difficult though most of the time. The main reasons to die are:
1) You overextended a lot and got caught off guard
2) a nasty combination of difficult to handle abilities are in front of you, surprising you.
3) 1+2 together.
You can probably finish the Story of the Game in about 20-30 Hours if you rush through it. If you enjoy all the side quests, do everything you can and grind up your character, it takes about 70-100 Hours.
I will replay the game for sure to make a different playstile.

Microsoft Flight Simulator has been and still remains the gold standard of flight simulation. This version has, remarkably, been around since 2006, but has worn amazingly well. While it gets stiff competition nowadays from Prepar3D and X-Plane in particular, it can still more than hold its own.
For the purposes of this review, I am only going to concentrate on the default, "out-of-the-box" scenery and aircraft - in other words, what you first get when you buy this game. As is the case with P3D and X-Plane, there are numerous add-ons that can enhance the game enormously, but I think the fairest way to review a game like this is focus on what it comes with initially.
One thing I really love about Microsoft Flight Simulator X (hereinafter: FSX) is the extent to which it teaches you about the basics of flying. Quite aside from tutorial missions, there is a section called the "Learning Center" which has an incredible wealth of information. There are detailed instructions about how to fly each of the default aircraft, for instance. Then too there is a tab in the "Learning Center" called "Lessons". This will give you highly detailed "ground school" articles by professional flight instructor Rod Machado, along with practical lessons guided by Rod. You will learn the fundamentals of taking off, landing, turning, stalls, VOR/DME/ADF navigation, ILS landings and so much more besides. You can also do checkrides and, if you pass them, get a certificate that will go into your "Pilot Rewards" (an unnecessary but fun component of FSX).
"Boring," you may say. "I want to fly, not study!" Well, there's nothing stopping you from flying straight away if you want. (Indeed, I did.) But take it from me, repeatedly crashing because you have no clue about how to land a plane, or much of a clue about any aspect of flying, is not a lot of fun. Yes, it may take a bit of time to go through Rod Machado's lessons and study some of the other articles in the Learning Center, but it will enhance your experience of the sim enormously in the long run. And it is immensely satisfying when you apply what you have learned and begin to master new skills. FSX can, if you are willing to make the effort, train you in a way that its rival X-Plane will not. (I don't know about Prepar3D, so can't comment on how helpful or otherwise it is to flying and flight simming novices.)
There are two main ways you can play FSX. The first is "Free Flight". With this mode, you can select an airport and simply take off from it to go wherever. Or you can file a proper flight plan and fly from one airport to the next. If you change your mind mid-flight, just open up the appropriate menu and file another flight plan. You get pretty much the whole world - including Antarctica - to fly in. You also get plenty of noteworthy landmarks to see.
The other main playing mode is Missions. There is a great variety of different missions you can do, with difficulty levels ranging from "Beginner" to "Expert". Some of the missions seem a bit mis-classified though. Several of the "Beginner" lessons require some pretty advanced piloting skills, although you don't have to know about navigation or ATC interaction to fly them. In that sense, they are "Beginner" difficulty, but they're otherwise really hard. Other missions are more straightforward though. The missions are a good way to get acquainted with the different kinds of aircraft that FSX has to offer and see what types you like best (I discovered for instance that I really enjoy GA planes and airliners, but can take or leave helicopters and gliders aren't my scene at all). They are also a good way to challenge yourself in a variety of interesting situations. And if the default missions aren't to your liking or just aren't enough for you, there is no shortage of mission packs on offer (such as "Cargo Crew", "Arctic Rescue" and "Dangerous Approaches" available here on Steam). You get rewards for passing missions (nothing that special, just a "sticker" in your Pilot Records, but still, quite good fun).
Actually, there is also a third mode: Multiplayer. However, I have never used that, so can't comment on how good or otherwise it is. All I will say is that it doubtless adds another dimension if you want to use it.
Planning a flight couldn't get much easier in FSX. This process is very intuitive and easy to learn. I especially love the Navigation Log that is generated, and which you can refer to on your "Kneeboard" (press Shift + F10 for that) during a flight. Interacting with ATC is also very straightforward. The ATC window can be used to auto-tune your "comms" radio, although you can also quite easily tune radios manually if you want to do things more like a real pilot. Aircraft come with both 3D virtual cockpits and 2D panels. When you're in 2D mode, you can make mini-panels pop up (press Shift + 1, 2, 3 etc.) that give you access to things like the radio stack, throttle quadrant and overhead panel. Very handy, and saves a lot of fumbling around trying to find where things are.
As seriously awesome as this game is however, it is not without its faults. The "out-of-the-box" scenery of instance is pretty blah. Cities - especially less well-known ones - are not very accurately rendered, and the textures are decidedly average. Topography is one area where X-Plane 10 beats FSX hands-down. However, there are plenty of add-ons to improve the scenery (I especially recommend Orbx's FTX products), and at least FSX gives you buildings at airports, which certainly can't be said for X-Plane in a lot of cases! In flight dynamics too, FSX can be a bit ho-hum, especially when it comes to helicopters. Taxiing can also be rather fiddly. The "Pilot Records" section is a bit of a mess. It would be nice if some real airlines were represented rather than just generic ones (although it's quite easy to add new liveries). And because FSX is so old, it is only capable of running in 32-bit mode, which means that it tends to struggle with more sophisticated add-ons.
That said, there is a vast amount of add-ons out there, and you can do a tremendous amount to FSX without breaking it. But the more advanced computers become and the more sophisticated add-ons get, the more FSX will struggle in the future. For now though, it still works very well and there are so many great ways to enhance it. Steam alone offers a lot of great add-ons, but there are more to discover at places like The FlightSim Store or Just Flight. No shortage of freeware to be found either (check the AVSIM Library for instance).
Another thing I sometimes struggle with is visibility. However, a neat trick I have discovered is to open a "mini-window" while in 2D panel mode and set this "mini-window" to Outside Spot view. This way, I can keep an eye on my instruments while being able to see easily to taxi or land. Best of both worlds!
All in all, I recommend Microsoft Flight Simulator X very highly indeed. If you are new to flight simming and flying generally, as I was when I bought this game a little over a year ago, this game, with its Learning Center, will teach you a tremendous amount. It gives you a far better grounding in the basics of flying than X-Plane, which is really designed for people who already have a reasonable amount of experience. (Again, I don't know how novice-friendly or otherwise Prepar3D is.) And once you have grasped the fundamentals of flying, there is no end of fun to be had and discoveries to make. Be warned though that it is quite addictive once you master it (also the case with real flying, so I've heard), and while the basic game is very cheap (certainly a better deal initially than X-Plane or Prepar3D), your wallet can still suffer as you chase after add-ons to further fuel your virtual flying addiction. You may or may not be in love with flying (virtually or otherwise) now, but once you have played FSX, you will be!

I just completed this game (both endings) in 44 hours total and completed 50% of the achievements.
So the short story of this review is that I really enjoyed this game, and if you enjoyed the first one, you'll enjoy this one.
I think the most important thing to note is that I did all of the above without paying gold for a single loot box or spending money on the loot boxes, which means they are optional in that sense. They may/may not speed up your progress, and I will readily admit that the Shadow Wars portion of the game took me several days on its own. For that reward you get a cut scene, and some really nice credit tributes. If anything, I'd recommend getting the free gold and buying one of the XP boost packs. That is the only way I'd say you'd guarantee solid progress quicker.
I'm recommending it, with the understanding going into it that the 4th Act is pretty long, but you'll know if you want to complete it or not by your time in Acts 2 & 3. If not - no worries, you're not missing out on anything you can't see on YouTube. I personally completed it just to see how long it would take, and from my understanding the upcoming DLC will make it "infinite" which I can tell you I have no interest in.
Replace value is probably nil for me. I'm not interested in online fort taking/holding forever. I've got other games to play. The campaign will keep you busy for 30+ hours at least, and you will find the Nemesis system and orcs as fun and memorable as ever. If you played the first game, there are even some surprises in store relating to returning characters (some based on your save data!)
Make an informed choice. Buy it, or don't. But I will say don't spend money on the loot boxes. They are unnecessary.

First off, to address the issue of loot boxes so many have issues with.
You can COMPLETELY ignore the store and pay no extra money.  Silver boxes can be bought in game with the silver coins you earn while playing.  Vendetta boxes can be earned by completing Online Vendetta missions.  Only the gold boxes require you spend real money to buy gold coins to purchase them.
As for the game itself.   TLDR version:  If you liked SoM, you'll like SoW too.
Anyone familiar with Shadow of Mordor will feel right at home.  Combat and movement are what you expected from the first game.  There is more to progression, as you don't just equip runes to you weapon anymore.  You will get new weapons, each of which can be of varying quality.  Each has a gem slot that can have a colored gem (also of varying quality) to give each weapon an additional ability.  Weapons you don't want/need can be destroyed to quickly earn you silver coins used to buy silver loot boxes or upgrade gear.
Skill points are used to buy abilities or to enhance an already purchased ability.  You gain skill points from leveling up or from completing other activities.   You do NOT gain XP from killing regular Orcs anymore.  Only by completing quests, challenges or killing Orc Captains earn you XP.
Stealth is still rather forgiving like in the first game.  There are upgraded cloaks you can acquire which increase your stealth, making it harder for Orcs to detect you or slower for them to react to noticing you.
Unlike Shadow of Mordor, Orcs are more varied now.  It's not just they have more strengths & weaknesses.  Some orcs will ambush you, others will return after you "killed" them.  The Captains personalities are much more varied now too.
Side note....
I would strongly recommend NOT downloading the free 4k Cinematic Pack or the Hi-Res Texture Pack.  The former can make your cutscenes jittery with poor audio.  The latter just takes up 10gb of space for a slight upgrade in video quality.  The game looks fine as is, gameplay or cutscene wise.
Overall it's a good sequel with much more to do, none of which seems "grindy".  I'm not at endgame so I cannot comment on complaints of the grindy endgame.

Pros:
1. Gameplay surprisingly felt enganging; the concept of the "Taken" and their immunisation to bullets discourages the player have a "trigger happy" experience compared to other well-established 3rd person shooters. Instead, the player could choose to run away (not viable in harder difficulties) or use their flashlight to expose enemies prior to shooting them. This mechanism causes tension to the player as it fits beautifully to the atmosphere to the game.
2. The atmopshere; there's a misconception on a claim that this game is a survival horror. I would imagine for the targetted audience (teens to adults), with myself included, won't/ don't find the genre fitting to horror. A psychological thriller-themed 3rd person shooter is more like it, and boy, it plays the theme of light and darkness well.
- Bear in mind that the game is a PC port from the Xbox 360 version, and ultimately, the PC version is absurdly better in almost every aspect of quality (mouse acceleration was locked on, but I believe it's been patched)
Cons:
1. I can't recommend the story and characters to be engaging; I personally enjoyed it, despite the overusage of tropes in the story that quickly became cliché. The characters themselves drive the plot, but they lack development throughout the game. An exception would be the reason why the protagonist cares for his significant other early in the game. Otherwise, I was more interested in "what would happen next" rather than caring for the characters.

Mountain is a neat little time-sink where you watch a chunk of rock slowly turn and grow while constantly making telltale games-style choices, like at what point the best time would be to blow it up.
In all seriousness, I don't get this game. I can appreciate a good art game like Dear Esther and Gone Home but at least there you had some level of agency. In this game you have gimmicks instead, such as raining frogs and raining hearts. I generated a new mountain several times and failed to see much of a difference between them.
It feels more like an artistic statement than an artistic game, and while I don't mind artistic statements I'm not sure I like being charged so that somebody else can make one. If I just wanted to stare at something moving and growing I have a really nice hourglass that I got as a gift (I mean REALLY nice!) and I feel like I'd get just as much enjoyment watching that. In fact I just confirmed it. It moves at more than 20 frames per second, has better sound effects, and if a celestial body comes crashing down it won't look like someone attached a translucent red glass texture to a very low polygon sphere.
So I can't recommend this artistic statement. It has some charm but that alone isn't enough. If you want to see my first impressions of this game, check out my video below. I do indie game first impressions every so often.

DISCLAIMER: No spoilers but, at the time of writing, the second act has yet to be released.
The logic puzzles in the game are cunningly simple; each time I solved one I felt rewarded. At one odd moment I found myself wishing, for whatever sadistic reason, that there were more of the moments where you simply could not find what you needed next (aka nearly any moment of the original "Monkey Island" game). I was not denied my wish, of course, but the moment was fleeting, and the reward afterward made up for any animosity I had felt. By the end the game succeeded in training my thought patterns so that solutions came easily and I was able to bask in my smug superiority, the true goal of any gamer.
The visuals are gorgeous, but don't expect the sweeping vistas of games like "Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" or "Castlevania: Lords of Shadows". Instead, each scene is exquisitely crafted. The hand painting provides a lush and vibrant world. The animations have a crafted quality that does nothing but add to the art. I will not voice my only complaint, since it may cause people to notice it constantly and ruin things, but know that it was minor to the point of disappearing after the first few minutes.
The voice acting is superb. There is little else to be said, it is simply superb. My favorite is the ship's "Mom"; Jennifer Hale does an exceptional job. The characters and their dialog do not disappoint.
Then there is the story. Play the entire game! The story is fantastic. Every assumption I made was wrong. I eagerly await the second act, and I would gladly pay for more games of this caliber.
So my recommendation:
If you enjoy point and click adventures then you will only be disappointed that the second act is not yet here.

It is March 10, 2014. I have played four hours of Broken Age. It was four of the most enchanting, beautifully-designed hours I've ever spent. It was four hours of rich detail, adorable storytelling, and classic adventure game mechanics well-aged and pressed though the welcome filter of sensible logic. Then it cut off at the halfway point, and now I know how men feel at strip clubs when the lights go up and the bouncers close in.
I mean, I'm not saying don't buy this. It's absolutely fantastic. It's exactly what I hoped, but never thought it could be. It was precisely what I wanted to see out of that Kickstarter campaign, out of Double Fine, out of all the luminous talent responsible for this treasure. It has a ship made of yarn, valley girl cultists, a jetpack that is actually a large tin of whipped cream, and Pendleton Ward. It's also halfway done, and will cut you off at an infuriating point so, y'now, be forewarned.
If I actually remember I wrote this review a year from now, maybe I'll edit it up. But, so it is. So it is.
Edit, October 9, 2015: It's done. The second half declines somewhat in quality, due mostly to an exceedingly irritating puzzle that they make you do over and over again. The message gets a bit muddled, and the thing I loved most from the first half - exploring these beautiful, ridiculous landscapes, poking them and stealing their things - is necessarily curtailed. The game, as a whole, is still worth it - but keep a pencil and paper around. Trust me.

It should be warned that this game is not your usual have-a-fun kind of game.
I'm a Chinese Indonesian who lived in Jakarta during this dark age period. It's interesting to see the perspective of outsiders in depicting May 1998 riots.
The story of "Mayjasmine episode 01 - where is God?" is quite good but I think it's a little exaggerated. From the historical point-of-view, the tragedy occurred because of global monetary crisis. Some higher-ups in Indonesia used this opportunity to end the regime of Soeharto (~30 years as an oppressive leader). To put it short, they tried to manipulate some minority extremists (especially from lower end economy) and used Chinese ethnics as a scapegoat. The number of casualties are around thousand people, including native Indonesian who were trapped in fire during this chaos.
After played throughout the game, it seems that the creators try to generalize that almost all Chinese in Indonesian are killed and all sectors in Jakarta are filled with extremists. Personally, I've studied in a public university with 60% of native Indonesian and I need to say that this game was entirely about history, so don't try to judge any side as good or bad during playing this game.
The music is quite good, except for several parts where sound effects seem a bit off. For example, the sound effect overshadows the actual conversation, since it keeps playing in the background when you try to continue the conversation.
The graphics (and lolis) are excellent, that's why you are here right now, reading through these reviews and try to decide whether you want to buy this game or not.
The translations are off in some scenes. Overall, it still quite good except for some grammatical errors.
The game is quite short, around 8 hours or so. If you want to learn more about May 1998 riots, go ahead. If you "love" to see dying people or a masochist, go ahead too. If you just want to grab the lolis, well, you're coming to wrong neighborhood.

First of all, the topic about May Tragedy is one of the Dark History in Indonesia that happened in 1998.
It's a racial discrimination incidents so expect this game to be racist, discriminate, horror, & gore.
There is riots and the main targets of the violence were ethnic Chinese.
I'm Chinese Indonesian and I'm still at the age of those two lolis you saw in the picture. To this day I can still feel the traumatic feeling of that tragedy.

When I saw the game on Steam Greenlight, I voted NO! because I felt this dark history is far better explained by my fellow Indonesian. But It turn out to be wrong, just by playing this game I can see how Taiwanese see this event occured although I didn't know there is a racial issue happened against Chinese and Taiwanese.
For the introduction part, the game did introduce you with various Indonesia culture especially foods. And yeah that's also the social & political situation back in 1998.
For the tragedy part, the game really did depict Chinese Indonesian POV. Thought it should be rated R18+ cause the scene is gore.
NB: People really died IRL (especially women), you can search for the NSFW images via google.
Some points for improvement:
- The game did have poor english translations but I have no problem at all (I know Chinese [中文]).
- There is no ending credit/image. If you reach a bad ending, the game will just send you back to title screen.
If you come for the fun and lolis, I suggest that you stay away from this game.
But if you come to learn history or into dystopia, you can pick this game up.

Ok, so I'm 20 hours in (according to Steam), and I've owned the game for less than 2 days. Was Wasteland 2 worth it for me? I'd say so. I like complex, difficult games. Should YOU buy it? I'm not so sure. I'd give the game a 8/10 so far, but I can't recommend it to everyone. I'll breifly give you some points of reference to understand the game, and then I'll go over some more detailed points to explain why I feel the game rates an 8. Also, I did not judge the game on it's graphics. If that's what's important to you there's a massive line-up of AAA titles out there right now that will blow up your computer. W2 is not one of them.
If you like XCOM Enemy Uknown/Within, then you should understand how combat works, yet the combat in W2 is much slower than in XCOM. This is, in large part, due to the depth of W2's combat system. I'll go over some of those points in a minute, but suffice to say that most of the important parts of combat are never explained, or poorly explained. The are intuitive, and they make sense, but the learning curve is far steeper than XCOM, for sure.
As far as the story goes, well, the story of XCOM is told in your own head and in the moment to moment action (especially after you've played the game for hundreds of cumilitive hours), while in W2 the majority of the story is told in conversations. It's actually very similar to KOTOR or Fallout 3 in that the combat takes less than half of your playtime. Maybe even less. Unless you skip all the conversations in W2, which I imagine many players will. I fear, however, that the game loses much of its charm and drive if you don't pay attention to the written dialogue. I just think that most players aren't playing a video game to read massive amounts of text, even thought the writing is done rather well and I personally enjoy it. But then I enjoy reading and writing in my spare time, which is not representative of the average gamer.
I imagine the replayability to be very high, however, since after 20 hours I'm already regretting my character builds and wishing I'd done things differently. But I'm still in the bottom quarter of the world map, and barely past level 10 with my main charaters. Even with up to seven people in your party you can't possibly have all the necessary skills for every given situation, which is both cool and frustrating.
For example, your first companion, Deth, is a complete badass, and quite overpowered, and 20 hours in she is still in my party. She was essential at the beginning, yet she made one of my 4 custom charaters basically obselete. I diversified later, but unlike in XCOM, you can't switch out one of your 4 primary soldiers until one of them dies. I even purposely killed my melee warior because in the end I found him useless. Down the line you can flesh out your team somewhat using the 3 additional party slots, but it bums me out that their stories are more fleshed out than the 4 custom charaters I spent an hour making.
The game truly does throw you in the deep end make you figure things out on your own. For example, does the Demolitions skill make you more proficient with exlosives? No. Apparently anyone can use explosives fairly well without training. What the demolitions skill allows you to do is disarm explosive traps. Not seeing the traps that keep on exploding in your face, even in the early game? Well, that's because you need to level up your perception skill. "But I made sure my Awarenes skill is at Max!" you may say. Tough luck, you should have invested that in intelligence so you'd have more skill points after each level to upgrade your Perception skill. Which is a passive ability, byt the way, but you NEED TO TURN IT ON. According to Wasteland 2 and every dictionary ever Perception and Awareness mean very different things. But in the context of most video games some may think they are interchangable or at least related. In W2 they're not. This game doesn't hold your hand.
This symbiosis or abilities does play out in fun and intersting ways, however. A simple example is when you break a safe while trying to crack it, you can repair it with the mechanical repair skill and try to crack it again. If you detect a boobytrapped door you can Percieve the mine, use the Demolition skill to disarm the explosive trap, then try to pick the lock, fail and set off an alarm, then use another skill to deactivate the alarm, while simultaneously smashing the broken door in with brute force. Moments like that are cool, though really only present in the more scripted story missions.
Also, believe it or not, in the middle of combat you can see all the information you need about your currently equiped weapon just by hovering your mouse over certain areas to generate tooltips. It wasn't until 10 hours in that i finally found out that's where you find out your weapon's optimum range - float your mouse over the bar with mini arrows just aove the gun portrait. I could also have checked the weapon in my inventory, but who has the time for all that?
Also, armor is poorly explained, so I'll explain it to you. Armor does not lessen damage taken in the traditional may like add HP or subtract from incoming damage. What it does is lessen the damage from weapons with lower armor penetration. A badass looking weapon may suck against everyone but the most basic of enemies if it has low armor penetration. That expensive new assault rifle doesn't look like much of an upgrade? Guess again, if it penetrates even ONE MORE armor layer. Seriously.
I'll give you a hypothetical example. Lets say you have 2 characters weilding hypothetical pistols that both do 20-25 base damage. One of the pistols has 1 armor penetration while the other has 5. Now let's say a wolf with 1 armor ran at your two characters, and both your charaters shoots it. Both guns would do 20-30 damage. Now a human comes along, but he has 3 armor. This time the two guns do 5-8 and 20-30 damage. Huge difference, right? Now if you send that team against an enemy with 5 armor one of your soldiers will still be doing a solid 20-30 damage, but the second will be doing 1 damage every time. I barely won a few tough fights because I didn't grasp this for a long while.
Honestly, I feel like I can write a guide about this game, and I'm sure there are guides out there. Yet I'd say that less than half of the people who may have tried to read this review have reached this far. In my opinion those poeple shouldn't buy the game. If you didn't have the patience to read this review, then the odds are you will not have the patience for the game. If you have completed this review, and I haven't turned you off from playing it, then follow my lead and buy it. It's pretty good. I like XCOM better, but in some ways the two games are like apples and oranges. Good thing I like both.

I heartily recommend EndWar. Its twist compared to other RTS games is that you can use voice commands to order your troops or off-battlefield assets, and it suprisingly works incredibly well. However, don't push aside that mouse and keyboard yet as your voice commands are mostly simple commands. Move point A-Z, this unit attack that hostile, bomb this target, etc. Finer movements like better positioning or finding cover cannot be done with voice commands alone. Like I said before the combat mechanics make the game seem like a complicated rock-paper-scissors game, which it is in the prologue campaign, which you should still go through to learn all the commands or simple strategies to the game, but once you finish that campaign the game opens up into a much more complex RTS. Not WarGame levels of depth, but it is manageable for newer players. If there is one issue I find with the game is it's camera system. Your overhead camera  is always locked in on one unit and its immediate vicinity, which must be on purpose as there is a binoculars button that lets you zoom in on farther off objects that you can't see very well, because your cmaera is locked on your own unit. The way around this is by using your command vehicle unit which also allows you to use a birds eye view of the entire battlefield. However, even with this view you miss out on the action, and it doesn;t account for varying terrain height which can block line of sight. But overall I'm absolutely loving this game.

Almost a quarter of a century ago. I remember a game called "Buck Rogers: Countdown to Doomsday." I was around 10 at the time and one of the few in my circle of friends to have a PC. We didn't have the internet back then. The game's anti-piracy measure was to include a paperback book with the game, from which you would have to lookup words at a specific page and line on start-up.
I was probably too young for the game at the time. I didn't make it far before my characters would start dying off due to venomous stings from the early creatures you encountered. That said, the game still left an impression on me to the kinds of experiences games can deliver.
Flash-forward to today. I have never played Wasteland. I have played Diablo 1-3, Fallout 3 & New Vegas, Dragonage Origins, and various other RPG games and games with RPG elements (350+ hours in Borderlands 2, come to mind).
This game takes me back to that time trying to play Buck Rogers. I've grown older, but that means I've also gained the experiences that would help me appreciate this game for what it is.
This game is NOT Fallout 3, or New Vegas. Yes, some of the New Vegas guys were involved. This is because they _love_ RPGs, and not just 3D games with RPG elements. Think closer in genre to Fallout 1&2, but not the same style of story.
If you are new to RPG games, try something else first. In fact, try a few others first. If you make this your first RPG like I did for Buck Rogers, you'll get lost, frustrated, and give up after the first couple missions. Go play Diablo 2 first (not 3, don't get me started about 3).
If you are experienced in RPG and RPG style games and are looking for an "advanced" experience. This is a game for you.

Plays more like an action game than survival horror in my opinion. On 'Normal' difficulty ammunition was far from scarce, it was not particularly difficult to dodge enemy attacks (this is done with a single timed button press), more powerful weapons frequently appear and if you are conservative with the ammunition for these then the more challenging encounters will be completed with ease. The camera angle changes to alert you of any enemies that attempt to flank you, so you are rarely surprised. All enemies up to the portion of the game I've completed (over half way) carry only melee weaponry, so combat situations *never* feel particularly dangerous when you are sufficiently well equipped.
Disappointing if you're seeking a survival horror experience, although may be a completely different experience on the hardest difficulty - you need to complete the game once to access this.
Aside: The dialogue is cringeworthy at times and the protagonist isn't particularly likeable.

If you enjoy the Silent Hill games, you will definitely enjoy Alan Wake. I am merely making the Silent Hill reference to show you what a great story-driven and carefully crafted game Alan Wake is. It is certainly not a Silent Hill clone and is very unique.
Clever story, fun combat, and some very tense moments. The atmosphere and story work together perfectly. I couldn't wait to see what was going to happen next, and some parts of the game will really get your heart pumping. I won't spoil anything. I'll just say some of the scenes get really intense. There are a few puzzles thrown into the mix, but they are pretty basic and easy. The story and fun combat is where this game shines.
I will admit that some parts of the game were really hard for me, even on easy mode, but you can get through them with a little learning (learn to find the hidden item caches, look for alternate paths, run instead of fight, etc). I don't fault the game for this because it made me think of alternate solutions and made it feel really satisfying when I finally beat a part of the game that was giving me problems. Don't worry about it too much though. Checkpoints are encountered often so you won't have to replay much if you die.
Picked it up for $5 during a sale, but would have no problem paying the full price. You can easily tell within moments of playing that the creators were passionate about making a great game. It's an awesome game worth playing for people who enjoy adventure/action horror games.

At first I thought this game was going to be fun.  Building robots and marching them into battle.  Sounds good right?
In two days I leveled past 20.  I estimate I was doing above average.
However, in that time I started to notice wildly mismatched games happening.  I started to notice wildly OP weapons -- I'm talking weapons that could literally one or two shot me when in quad configuration -- and I was running a fully geared and very slow (as a result) heavy build with 5 levels of armor throughout, etc.  It seemed like that should have meant something.
Well, it doesn't.
There are severe imbalances throughout Guns and Robots and it's a Pay2Win game along the same lines that World of Tanks is.  It might not be SEVERE pay2win, but it's still there, just like WoT.  It's a damn shame.
This model of game is also designed to create addiction.
So, I uninstalled it.
Your experience will vary, but I cannot recommend this game.  I typically end up locking such games or uninstalling them, and in this case, since the balance is nowhere near as good as WoT, and because the game itself has a paltry inventory space that's basically begging you to pay money to field more than one robot, the variety isn't even close to WoT, where you can field a half-dozen tanks easily without feeling anyone pinching your wallet, etc.: Guns and Robots earned an uninstall.
I'm just tired of this sort of game design.  It's all shiny, candy-coated and looks good on the outside, but once you start chewing on it, it leaves a bad taste in your mouth.

Well, I've read it through. What can I say? It's quite controversial.
On the one hand it's a gasp of fresh air after all this generic staff like "Any VN about school\lolis"
This VN rises some serious topics and gives you a lot of different perspectives throughout the stories
and that I should say leaves you deep in thought once you've read it all. I don't remember reading a VN
that was be so serious and deep about it, in the majority of them, they would male an elephant out of a moss
or would just be forcing drama on us with a happy ending, of course. Unfortunately, in the real world not all the
problems have solutions. The closest VN about the atmosphere (closer to the end) is the Swan Song, I thing.
And it has similar drawbacks, I'm afraid. I'm not familiar with the events that happened in 1998 in Indonesia but, I believe, the authors went too far with the display violence.
I would also like to say a thing about the components of the game.
Graphics.
Authors did a good job drawing audience's attention with loli pics. The topic of the VN (national identity disputes in some far east country) simply can't be appealing for the grand majority of people here, so it did its job.
I'm a bit disappointed though about disproportionate sprite sizes of the kids here. When a 8 yo girl looks bigger than her dad it's... bizzare. Then there are no proper event CGs, they are all made in chibi style, I have nothing against chibi
but its such an obvious manifestation of artist's laziness... I just can't keep quiet about it.
Overall the art is good. But I hope it will be better in the sequel.
Music
Can'y say much about it. It's nice to listen to, but not memorable. There could be more compositions if you ask me.
Voices
Well, after japanese VNs've set a high degree of quality, you can't help but notice fake in emotions. It is especially obvious when someone's angry. They sound too reserved , if you don't know what they are talking about you would think it's just a slight dissatisfaction. But what really grinds my gears is the maid's voice actress... if it's a person of course and not a robot. I've never heard such an unnatural voice acting before. It's like they were short on staff (chinese, haha) and summoned a nearby cleaner to read some lines from the script... I was desperately searching for the option to turn it off in the game but failed;(
Translation
A lot of other reviews are spanking the VN for it's bad quality. I can't disagree, though it didn't pose a big problem for myself. I wouldn't even say it's bad in translation, rather in editing and proofreading. The language (except in some places, which are not many) is failry simple to understand and thus easy to read. It's a plus in my opinion, I hate VNs which are overloaded with heavy grammatical structures. And one more thing - I don't know about the degree of swear words in the original chinese but these kids could take on verbally any delinquent in the most run down, gangsta turf.
Overall
I guess it is either you read it through or drop it after ten minutes or so, the topic just isn't for everyone, not that it makes it less interesting though.
I recommend everyone try it, and I'm looking forward to the sequel, the VN breaks at the most interesting part.
Thanks for attention, everyone!
P.S. Sorry for my english, it's been ages since I wrote something in it.

Ignoring the discrepancies in grammar, it's a visual novel that tells a story of the May 1998 riots of Indonesia.
Based on history, it allows us to have a greater understanding of what the people at that time had been forced to experience. It talks about the discrimination and racism between Chinese, Taiwanese and Indonesians.
An interesting quirk is that there are various quotes cited from pieces of literature with the intent of being meaningful and encouraging you to think.
If you think you can at least take some newfound knowledge or understanding from this visual novel, then it's worth it. Otherwise, don't bother.

If you get this game for free, really cheap, or get gifted it by a friend then it's probably worth playing, but as it stands I would not reccomend paying full price for it.
-There are many spelling and grammatical errors with the translation, I often find myself having a hard time understanding what's being said.
-The game is very short, it only took me about 4 hours including a lot of time spent messing around and accidentally leaving the game idle.
-It comes off very preachy and pretentious about the message it's trying to convey. Of course I'm an ignorant American, so the culture is pretty much lost on me, but most of the characters seem overly racist just to shove the "don't be racist" message down your throat.
- The characters' relationships either aren't explored much or just don't make any sense, I honestly don't know why the main character is friends with Zi-Jin, that's not to say that they shouldn't be friends, but their friendship/history just isn't explained very well. Maybe it's just me
-Some scenes tend to drag on for quite a while unnecessarily, mainly the first cafeteria scene comes to mind.
-The sound effects are always either bland or unfitting, and the ambience tends to abruplty stop and then loop, of course this isn't a big complaint, just thought I would mention it.
The game has good artwork, the voice acting sounds great, and while the majority of the game was mainly boring, it wasn't too bad and I've definitely played a lot worse.
Bottom line, if you want it for the history/satire aspect of the game, go for it, I'm sure you know a lot more than me. But don't get suckered in by the cute lolis and somewhat misleading trailer.

Okay, I'm going to give the Developers a "forgive and forget" once they release the patch/update that fixes the FPS bottlenecking. Despite that, I'm going to address this game from my experiences alone, being 12 hours in.
Main aspect here is mostly story. Most games sometimes tend to irritate or bore me during cutscene segments, however the  angle of certain scenes in cutscenes and the voice acting is executed perfectly. While watching these cutscenes my eyes where firmly fixated on the scene as I let the story unwind. Speaking of which, I expected this game to have a real gritty dark depressing revenge story, something that I'd expect out of games like Grand Theft Auto: The Lost And Damned or Max Payne 3, however the game manages to sneak humor in ever-so-perfectly at the right times. And I don't think I've ever laughed that hard when seeing that certain cutscene. If you've laughed at it in your current playthrough you may be in, or you've just started and laughed at a certain cutscene, then I assure you we both had the same reaction.
2k and the developers almost dun goofed as I thought when they released their trailers they where giving too much information away about your accociates, Cassandra, Burke and Vito. Playing the game though, their characters pretty much unravelled much, much more. I'm kind of glad the trailers where actually being light on information and not giving too much away. To me, it's not a major spoiler about what happens in the end, because from the very get-go. You know what you're probably going to expect at the end. It's the journey and progression in the story that I didn't want bumped, and I'm fairly glad the trailers didn't spoil it.
That being said though, this game did have a few dissapointing features here and there, mostly no quicksave feature (if there was one, I wasn't aware of it) and some of the requests to take down rackets of rival mobs and gangs are kind of follow this formula of; "RUN IN, SHOOT, KILL OR SPARE THE TARGET FOR CASH NOW OR CASH LATER", but the redeeming feature of killing him everytime and hearing the Protagonist Lincon say something badass like "Go with god Motherfu'" makes the grind almost worth it.
Also, the game world is great I guess. Feels alive, and the radio having songs from bands like the Rolling Stones, Johnny Cash and stuff is pretty cool too.
I guess this was worth taking the risk for a preorder anyway so, yeah it wasn't bad, do I reccomend this game? Probably once the update patch comes out to stop the bottlenecking of the FPS, sure! But if you really can put aside that (Which is hard, I understand) and really just want a story-rich experience? Go for it.

Gonna try to make this review a little shorter than my usual. If you've played one LEGO game, you've (nearly) played them all.
==========
Once again we get another great LEGO title! This time, TT Games gave the Avengers the LEGO treatment. To put it simply, yes: this game is worth buying. If you love LEGO games, you will love LEGO Avengers.
==========
LEGO games don't really change much between titles. Break stuff, get studs, spend studs on characters and other unlockables. Solve puzzles, find secrets, cash them in. This game puts you in the shoes of the Avengers, and follows along the story of not only the Avengers films, but also Captain America, Thor, and Iron Man. You will be playing through levels based scenes from each of these films.
One downside, I found, is that this title is a bit more difficult to progress though. Usually you are able to figure out what to do to progress the story on each stage very quickly in a LEGO game, but this one seems more difficult. I found myself looking up guides on the Internet to progress many times. It's annoying, to say the least, but it's something I felt I had to mention.
==========
Not much has changed in LEGO graphics, but overall it looks very nice. It might be a bit more colorful than usual, but everything retains the same look and feel as previous LEGO titles. That's not necessarily a bad thing, though. Sticking to a familiar formula works for some, and it definitely works for these LEGO games.
==========
Ever since one of the older LEGO titles (can't recall which), all titles since have had voice acting. Usually ripped straight from the source material. LEGO Avengers is no different. It sounds like they did a better job doing it this time though. The soundtrack works really well for the game, especially in the epic battles you WILL face.
==========
I ran into no issues while playing this game. No lag, stuttering, or FPS issues. PC Specs are on my profile if you are curious. Playing with a controller is highly recommended, but keyboard can work pretty well if you don't have any other options and get used to it.
==========
If you are looking for a relaxing, casual title based on one of the more popular comic book superhero teams, look no further. LEGO Avengers scratches the LEGO itch and the superhero itch very well. There's plenty to do, and plenty to collect. You can't go wrong with this title. It's great for relaxing after a hard day at work, or a rough day at school.

Great game, but comes with a catch!
I've had a lot of fun and challenging experiences fighting the AI (though at sometimes it is extremely predictable). You have a large amount of customization and tactical options for your army, not to mention the ability to command your troops through voice commands!
There is however a major downside: EA has pulled the plug on the 'Theater of War' (the entire Online/Multiplayer component) and rendered a large chunk of the game inert. Unless you take to the Bungle jungle or Hamachi Haven there is no way to even play online with your friends or others. And even then, you will never be able to participate in an all-out World War III conflict as you were able to in the past. You will be doomed to roundabout skirmish games.
This has also damaged the community severely. There are still a few lost souls that roam the forums looking for fresh meat but their numbers are ever dwindling.
In the end, is this game really worth buying if a major component 'doesn't work?' Well, that's up to you! The game itself is great and you can still play the entire war out in single player, alone. Hell, you could even try to revive the game base and create a regular group on Hamachi. But honestly, wait for a sale if you are still unsure. If you can grab it for 5 bucks you will not be disappointed!

I kind of felt as if this game was just a copy of LEGO Marvel Superheroes at first. But after playing it for a while, this game turned out to be even better. I'm not saying Superheroes was a bad game, but it had some bugs and flaws that Avengers really improved on (we can all agree that the flying mechanics are garbage, right?). The hub world's mostly the same area (New York), but with the addition of smaller hubs such as Barton's Farm, Asgard and the S.H.I.E.L.D base, it's a lot more fun and diverse, with side missions and puzzles a lot more organised. They also have less repetitive phrases (Because if I heard "Ugh, watch it buddy!" one more freakin' time I would've turned green and smashed my computer) They've also got a new system which has crimes take place that you can stop, like robberies and mugging. Really, Avengers is just Superheroes again but with more polished gameplay.
The only real downside to Avengers is that, since it's following the MCU, there's much less diversity in the characters. This means there are no Spider-Man, Fantastic 4 and X-Men characters to be found (except Spidey himself and a few alternate costumes such as Civil War and Iron Spider, but that's in a DLC). This is a shame because I loved playing with more characters. Though the new Ms Marvel character pretty much plays the same as Mr. Fantastic did.
The helicarrier is also different, with the collector taking Deadpool's place as the red brick distributor. Also, the custom character maker has been greatly improved, with easier selection and more characters to use parts from. If you've unlocked the minifig, you can use its parts. The X-Mansion has been replaced with the Avengers Facility, and the lighting is different, set in the evening/morning as the sun is a little lower.
All in all, Lego Marvel's Avengers is an awesome game.

The title of the game is "The Walking Dead"..
but it actually should be called "Life Lessons & Choices: The Game"
When you hear 'The Walking Dead', you expect mindless zombie killing, guns, shooting, survivors... whatever.
This is simply not true, in this game, those are more like side elements and actions than actual main focus points.
It WILL surprise you, and it'll hit you on a personal level in the real world.
This game teaches you perspectives, consequences, loyalty, morality, individualism, aswell as respect for others and what you do with that. It will also make you think about the negatives and limits of every single one of those words i just said.
This game will teach you more about yourself than any petty personality test will give you...
What happens if you are in THIS situation? What happens when THAT wasn't true?
Your own choice will surprise you, and maybe, you might even regret it when you're not satisfied with the end result.... An end result you can do nothing about, other than sit there and live with it afterwards in regret. Wishing you could have done more, wishing the characters you loved would just fall in line and be all OK in the end.
Afterwards, you approach choices with more and more care and knowledge.. but in the end.. you will just end up regretting more.
Buy this game (After you've played the first Season, of course). It goes on sale big time due to it's age, but remember you're not just buying it for entertainment...
You're buying it for the experience.

Let's see, I got this game for sale and honestly, I think that would be the best time to get it. It's like getting the game for full price and all free DLC. But this is a review, so let's review it.
Pros- The gameplay is great, with a whole slew of new characters never seen before in LEGO, including some never seen by myself (You learn something new every day.) Some characters get additional powers, such as Hawkeye, who can now melt gold lego, as well as some new powers, such as super speed (It's about time, too.) Also, Manhattan is no longer the only hub, though it remains the largest. You now can visit the Barton farm, the South Africa shipyard, a segment of Washington DC, a downsized Asgard, the SHIELD base, and a portion of Novi Grad, Sokovia. Original voice acting by Clark Gregg, Cobie Smulders, and Hayley Atwell add additional depth to the game, though it is occasionally cringeworthy. Nolan North returns, though not as Deadpool. He voices the Damage Control guy, which is obvious, and Agent Williams, which is less so. Combat is improved, with team-up moves, though unique ones only for Avengers characters, and one-on-one duels are common and quite fun. The character creator is vastly improved, with non-glitched no hair/helmet options, and the ability to change piece colors (though it seems to be broken on mine.)
Cons- The story is based directly off of the movies, causing the now old problem of terrible sounding dialogue. The levels fail to impress, specifically the Captain America level, which doesn't remind me of the movie at all (also, for some reason, they had to re-record Bucky's lines, making him sound twelve.) Maria Hill is constantly stating the obvious, and Agent Williams does most of the talking when he's working with other Avengers, humorously making it seem like they're intentionally ignoring him. People complain about how the flying is awful, but to be precise, it's the transition from still to moving that makes it hard to control. If you take your hand off the accelerator, you stop completely, and when you put it back on, you snap forward. Some jokes, that should have been left out, such as the "Party Trick" joke by Bruce Banner, feel even more out-of-context than if you had just gone with the film's interpretation. Also, What's with the sheer amount of chickens?!?
Personal quips- They just can't get Captain America's levels right. If they can make new designs for Iron Man, Why not Cap? They use the Avengers film outfit without the helmet when the cutscene shows A:AoU Cap with the helmet? Why? Also for some reason they switched the Empire State Building with the Chrysler Building. Not a complaint, just an observation. For some reason, the torso pieces in the character creator won't take other colors, and I cannot for the life of me find out how to make Lola fly.
TL:DR- Gameplay is far better than the story, and I recommend, but wait to go on sale.

The Political Machine 2016 is a very simple campaign simulator. Based around the 2016 election, you can play as one of about 20 or so candidates on either the Democratic or Republican side, which affects your candidate’s statistics.
The game is very simple – really, almost board-game like. On each turn, you have a certain amount of “stamina”, which affects how many actions you can take. Going to another state takes one stamina; creating an ad or raising money takes three; giving a speech or building a new campaign headquarters takes four.
Your goal is to win the presidency, and to that end, you can buy ads (either local or big TV ads that affect the whole country) about a particular issue to promote your stance on it or attack your enemy’s stance on it; each state has three issues it primarily cares about, and trying to boost or lower these can help or hurt you. You can also give speeches which seem to have a similar effect, increasing your local popularity as well as showing your stance off to the country.
The headquarters have various effects, mostly seeming to give you some sort of passive boost in the area; you can upgrade them to increase the size of these boosts, as well as their primary effects (giving you money, giving you points that allow you to buy endorsements, and giving you points that allow you to buy campaign operatives, independent units that are similar to buildings, but which can be moved around, and give you some sort of boost in whatever state they’re located in).
While all of this sounds like there’s a fair bit of complexity to it, in reality the game is actually extremely simple; basically, you build some headquarters at the start to maximize their value, building them up as high as possible because that gives you a larger boost to the stats without costing too much stamina, as well as their larger local influences, and then you run around building HQs and ads to try and shore up support, with your visits doing much the same. Every game seems to play out almost identically, with no real crises seeming to appear, or anything really compelling you to react. The game just feels like it is very simple, encourages a very unidimensional pandering strategy, and just fails to engage. Despite the bobble-headed figures, the game isn’t very humorous, and a lot of it is very vague, possibly to avoid offending anyone, but also just making it much less interesting.
The first round let me see all the game had to offer, and after that point, I was left wondering why I should bother playing the game any further. This isn’t really worth your time; it is a very ephemeral experience, and feels like it lacks any real depth or character.
