I'm gonna start off with saying that this game had so much potential. Lincoln Clay is an absolute badass, and his voice actor suits his hard-boiled personality perfectly. The problem is that this game is plagued with so many issues that it makes it hard to enjoy the creative story and environment.
Let's start off with pros and then proceed to talk about the cons:
Pros:
-As previously stated, this game has a lot of potential to be game of the year. The main character, story, and setting are all top notch, but the execution is awful.
-Even though game runs with 30FPS cap, the 30 FPS was smooth for me. It's definitely playable and wasn't as distracting as I thought it would be since I'm used to playing games in 144 Hertz.
- Story is interesting, I'm enjoying what I'm seeing so far. The characters are nicely designed and voice acted, and most importantly are believable.
-Gameplay is solid. Not necessarily addicting or perfect, but solid.  Most guns feel good to shoot, and Melee works well most of the time.
-Sadly the positive aspects of this game are few and far between, but one last thing I want to mention I enjoy is animations and cutscenes. The cutscenes are well acted and look graphically superb to the game. The animations are very brutal and feel good to execute.
Cons:
-Awful 21:9 support. I'm playign this game on an Acer Predator X34, and the image is definitely sub par to other 21:9 games I've played this year.
-Graphics make the game look like an HD PS2 game. It was obviously not properly supported on PC to allow player with powerful hardware to take advantage of it. It feels like a lazy console port, with absolutely no benefit of playing on PC other than the promise of a future patch for 60 FPS and unlimited frame rates. Character model faces are muddy and unclear, textures are muddy, field of view is awful, anti-aliasing has no advanced options like SSAO, MSAA, or even FXAA, just low, medium, high, textures don't even have a settign to control, meaning you're stuck with what look like console textures on a game by a huge Publisher in 2016. Overall graphic options and presentation are absolutely abysmal.
-No keyboard key remapping, meaning I had to use controller since KB&M controls were wonky.
-Visual glitches such as green waves covering Lincoln's face in scenes with dark shadows.
-Game crashing to desktop issue that occured for me twice in one hour, unacceptable.
Conclusion:
Had the potential to be a stellar release, but dropped the ball big time. Rushed PC port with awful visuals, unnacceptable CTD issues, and no 60FPS support at launch.
4/10 - Absolutely below average, and sadly not one of the better games of this year.

This game is a good game but it has quite a few problems. Like crashes. But that not a reason to not play it. It is a really fun game.

Combat: Works well, in most fights it allows for real tactical decisions to be made, however the huge number of melee enemies in the game is very annoying as they turn combat into a messy slugfest. Against stuff with opposable thumbs and guns, enjoyable. Against mutated bugs, pretty dull.
Writing: Both the writing and voice acting have been fantastic so far, no real complaints here. High evel of fidelity throughout, voice acting is consistent, the keywords system is very interesting and actually rewards you for paying attention.
Graphics: Not to my taste, but they work well. Everything that needs to stand out does, I very very rarely get confused by the terrain, everything seems to have been designed and laid out well. Animation quality is higher than I expected, your rangers do move pretty naturally and seem alive.
Sound: Fantastic, atmospheric music is great, SFX are all good, no complaints here.
Gameplay: All skills/items are easy to use and not at all fiddly, which is a common problem with these kinds of games. Switching between party members and ordering them around seperately works well. There's a lot of stuff you need to do outside of combat, and it just all works, once you get into the flow of it it becomes second nature.
Overall, 8/10. Would've been a 9/10 if not for the slight problems with combat, which really is the highlight of this game. The difference between a great fight and an overwhelming failure can be slight and not always so obvious. I find that game logic trtumps actual logic in too many places which can leave you frustrated. With future patches to balance combat I would recommend this game to anybody.

While I did enjoy the game, there is one big elephant in the room.
ACT IV: The Shadow Wars is a gauntlet of grinding. In ACT IV, you must defend fortresses you've already taken, over and over and over. This is not optional; the true ending is locked behind this.
Just for anyone who wants exact numbers it breaks down like this. There are 10 stages in Act IV.  In stages 1-3 you defend one of your bases per stage, in stages 4-7 you are tasked with defending two bases per stage, and in stages 8-10 you have to defend three bases per stage. This means you have to defend the same bases you played in the main game TWENTY additional times.
This design would be easier to stomach if not for the fact that many of the encounters see the attacking forces about 5-10 levels higher than any of your own army. The first 4 stages are the worst, requiring the longest grind. You will eventually get to a comfortable level but since every stage increases the challenge, you are constantly having to continue grinding to level up your orcs to catch up. This doesn’t consider that sometimes they die, sometimes they turn on you, and few of them are ever epic or legendary, unlike the orcs attacking you.
This unreasonably long mode all ties into the loot boxes, which give you epic and legendary high-level orcs for real money and no time sink. In my opinion, the developer hid the true ending behind a 10 hour grind fest just to entice you to spend more money. You can either spend an inordinate amount of time leveling up your armies over and over again or you can spend 20 bucks and get as many high-level orcs as you need to breeze through Act IV.
If this mode was optional and not tied to the main story then I wouldn’t be as annoyed by it but this design is a direct result of the micro-transactions. There is no variety to ACT IV, no cutscenes, no side missions, just defending the same 4 bases an absurd amount of times (TWENTY). This is not how a single player game should be structured. These game design decisions should not be acceptable in a $60 release.

Wow! The game has grown up and is pretty much everything one could hope it could turn out to be. I'd say the vanilla game is almost certainly in the 8.75/10 ballpark but quite probably in the 9/10 ballpark. With mods, that can easily go up to 10/10.

But if what you read in other reviews about the nature of the gameplay, and/or what you see in videos looks appealing, let me tell you, it is a FANTASTIC game. The community is wonderful, and the quality and variety of mods available are also top-notch.

At the time of writing, I've only clocked 1.2 hours into the game, but I feel I've seen enough to give a general review of it.
TL;DR Version:
This game could be fun amongst a small group of friends over multiplayer, Multiplayer in general is a bit edgy. On top of that, this game was obviously never developed with singleplayer in mind, and as such, the difficulty doesn't scale properly. If you were planning to play solo, I recommend finding another game. Overall: This game has a long ways to go to be worth $15, so for now, I will be giving it a negative review.
For starters, let me just say, while this game isn't nearly as bad as everyone is running around saying it is, it most certainly isn't a very good game either... There are still a lot of things that are broken, missing or just straight up edgy. On the flipside, there are a lot of things that I also enjoyed within the game. Instead of trying to explain in an incoherent way, let me simply throw together a pros and cons list.
Pros:
The game is well optimized! Runs flawlessly on my XFX R7970HD Ghz Edition GPU at full settings with minimal strain.
On top of that, most of the graphics/textures are actually fairly nice looking to boot.
The environment is well designed, with mostly, fairly nice textures and meshes.
Guns seem original and feel accurate when properly aimed.
Animations, for the most part, appear to be fairly smooth.
The wave based gameplay is reminiscent of games such as Killing Floor or Call of Duty: Zombies, and make for a fun time.
The gear upgrading after each wave screams Killing Floor. Alongside that, the upgrades have had a surprising amount of thought put into them.
The game supports a gamepad as well as rebindable keys for they Mouse + Keyboard and the gamepad.
Cons:
A LOT of models in this game look very generic and as a result, I find myself nicknaming them as such. For example, the 2 seat + minigun vehicle in the game might as well be a Warthog from the Halo Franchise. Additionally, the the primary flying vehicle found in the game bares a striking resemblance to the Reaver from Planetside 2. The playermodels are NOT exempt from this either, as most of them look like a mixture between clone troopers, Halo Spartans, and GoW Gear Troopers.
The guns, while I mentioned them feeling accurate, lack the feeling of power. This is a result of poorly replicated Recoil, and bad sound assets. The only weapons I've noticed having a good feel to them are both miniguns and the bow.
The AI is also absolutely terrible at times. I've found myself sitting on a rock picking off dinos that can't seem to decide if they want to kill me or destroy my generator.
I did say that most of the animations seem smooth, but the ones that aren't fluid are cringeworthy examples of janky, jittery movement in terms of player and dino animations. If you stand still and watch a Velociraptor attack you, you might die of laughter faster than by the deadly fangs the beast posesses.
The vehicle controls are a bit wonky in my own humble opinion. Quick to accelerate and slow to brake. Not to mention that the steering bindings are on the left and right strafe keys (A and D) as well as the Mouse's left and right axis. I often find myself getting confused and steering into my comrades. I haven't tried this game with a controller and I wouldn't doubt it if they translated over a little better.

While it's fun to mess around for a bit, the game does have its fair share of issues.
The pros:
- the novelty of it all

The cons;
- create a character doesn't give you enough points to even have an inherent belief on pretty much any issue, I'm not talking about campaigning or anything - it's pretty much impossible to have beliefs that mirror your own unless you only know or care about like 3 political issues out of the 25+ they give you

UPDATED: I wrote my original review of this game back in 2014 when it was called Orion: Dino Horde. It was a complete mess, not even worth the 0,9$ I paid (see the bottom). But suddenly, it had a lot of positive reviews, a name change and a new trailer acknowledging how bad the original game was and promising years of hard work improving the game. So I decided to give it another chance and after 10 minutes, I concluded that not much had actually changed, after an hour, I decided to update my review by re-describing all my original criticisms that still applied: The game has hardly improved. The game it self doesn't crash as often any more, but the connection is very unstable and have already disconnected me 5 times (doesn't happen in any other game). There is a few nice new graphic details like a very beautiful looking rain and your vizer getting frost marks, but they clearly have used their time on that instead of fixing the basic faults. The graphic still have faults like you can stand halfway through dead dinosaurs and the colours are a complete mess more than half the time. The aim is the worst I've seen in a modern shooter and you can just as well forget anything about smoothness or accuracy. The dinosaurs can still end up standing in mid air if they try to charge you while you're on top of a building and cause you damage even though they are clearly several meters from hitting you in the graphic. Even if we ignore all those basic flaws, the game is boring. In less than 10 minutes, I had already both the best weapons and most of the bonuses, bosst-ups and augments and killed all different types of big dinosaurs. After that, it's just repetition. Back in 2014 they claimed "Don't trust the metacritic score", now they say "We have made the worst game ever into a great game". Don't trust them, it's still not worth a single dollar and I don't think it ever will be.

My first night playing the final version of this game I found myself up past 3am. This hasn't happened since the Mass Effect series and Skyrim.
The theme of Wasteland 2 is consequence. This is very much the same as Wasteland 1, but more pronounced. Everything you do has consequences, not just the little things like missing a target on the battlefield or epic things like the survival of mankind; though, those are certainly there. Your choices decides what individuals, factions, and settlements survive. Who you help affects who will help you in turn and even make new enemies. Despite the natural technical limitations of any scripted game, inXile has managed to deliver a game that provides a near a living, breathing world as I've ever seen. Even if that world is a radioactive wasteland rasping out what could be its last breath at any moment.
There is a certain level of complexity to the game, but the character system (attributes, skills, equipment, and combat) is simple enough that you can grasp them quickly. The reason for this complexity quickly becomes apparent as you find you can use different skills to try to get around the same obstacles, offering you multiple approaches to the same problem.
This freedom cascades in all things: how you build characters, how you approach encounters, the soluitons you choose, and the direction you take. Where there is a certain amount of gating (e.g. you must have these rad suits to safely proceed), you are free to explore, ignoring missions and quests as you like. This exploration can be quite rewarding as you find shrines and caches, but it can also get you in trouble as you face enemies more powerful than you. Again, consequences. Enemies don't "level" with you; so if someone's too tough, just come back later.
There's still some bugs, sure, especially once you leave the desert for overgrown marsh of LA, but none of them are game breaking and I'm sure they will get shaken out.

First off, I am giving this an up vote, despite the fact that if there was a neutral option, I'd be going there. Would I really recommend this game? No, but I enjoy VNs, and I've really enjoyed some of the makers other offerings. I consider this as much an investment in keeping the company making enjoyable VNs as anything. It would be great if Steam would implement a neutral option for people to review a game without negatively affecting a company. Anyway...
Really short (less than an hour), kinetic visual novel by the folks at Invert Mouse. There is also a mini-game that's sort of like a boring hide and seek, that is skippable (fortunately). The story itself is about the abduction of three people from the mainland by an "alien" spaceship/submarine, and the interations of two of those characters with the "aliens" after the device that is used to return them to land malfunctions. The story is, well... ok. It has some nice messages, but it's hard to get very attached to characters in one hour. A little preachy with as much mention of God/faith in so short a read. The music was... ok. The art was probably the VNs best asset, but wasn't anything to write home about. Voice acting was pretty bland for a couple characters, but was good for others. It was fully voice acted. Inexpensive, so even if you're disappointed, you aren't gut punched by the price.
So, in short. Buy it if you are a lover of VNs and have run out of other titles, or if you are just looking for a way to support the Mice. If you go in not expecting all that much, you might end up pleasantly suprised. Definately check out some of the other Mouse offerings if you are in search of good VNs, and haven't read them all already.

The narrative of this game is certainly the real core of the experience, while not being a very horror-like story barring a few jump-scares here and there, the game still has a deliciously atmospheric tale about the forces behind creativity, light, and darkness. The plot pacing occasionally makes the story feel less stronger than it could be, but it certainly didn't prevent me from wanting to see it through to the end, even it does sort of just stop.
The gameplay is what really took away from this game for me. The crux of most of the game is going down familiar cabin-y/wood environments and mowing down wave after wave of enemies that aren't challenging or intimidating. I couldn't for the life of me get the dodging mechanic to work on a consistent basis, and Alan himself runs out of breath when he's sprinting faster than me on a treadmill. This meant the only way to proceed through the environment was shooting. Endless shooting. Mind-numblingy tedious shooting. In most action games, the shooting is broken up by a large weapon and combat variety or different kinds of gameplay brought into the mix, such as platforming or puzzle solving. The weapon variety is non-existant, you've got a gun, a shotgun, a rifle, grenades and that's about it. And the puzzles are normally so simple that you'd rather go back to just shooting things. You'll come across many obstacles too and the jumping button just doesn't handle any of them rather well.
TL;DR Engrossing Narrative, Poor and Tedious Game Mechanics.

It wasn't until I was playing the Thor: The Dark World level in this game (Lost in the Aether) that I realized exactly the metaphor for this game. It is the Thor: The Dark World of the LEGO series.
Okay, so maybe you looked at the first one of the two, and thought, "eh, worth a shot", but chances are you walked out impressed. Very impressed. You wanted more, and reasonably so; it was quite high-quality! For the most part, you sated yourself on other works that were released under the same banner, but not focusing on the same cast, so when you hear they're returning to one of the ones you loved the most, you're estatic. Finally, there's more of it!
Except when it actually happens, it's... okay. I mean, it's not terrible. But it serves absolutely no purpose but to let your eyes glaze over and your brain shut off for a solid few hours. You could call it a comedy, but you laugh exactly twice. All of the characters you came to expect after all the entries in between are just gone for no good reason besides because they said so. And for the first time, while these have been wildly successful so far, you start to finally think, "you know what, maybe we're stretching it a bit. I think we can stop soon." And it hurts all the more, because the first one was freakin' awesome, but this just sorta exists. It's a time-waster. Nothing less and, sadly, nothing more, a phoned-in sequel cashing in on the name and making the bare minimum of extra effort to be "new". It's one of those things you can't recommend not because it's terrible, but because it just... sorta is. It just exists You can live without it.
(Also, you hire voice actors for a reason. The audio quality from the film clips is rather low-quality and not delivered nearly as well as the lines, well, voiced by voice actors. At least there's a lot of recognizable VAs, but they should be front-and-center as well, instead of leaving the main characters mostly mute or blurting random sentences out-of-context. Feels like a MUGEN mod. This game holds the dubious honor of being the first LEGO adaptation title I've played to crash mid-level.)

I love the Marvel Cinematic Universe and the LEGO Games so this was a must buy for me :)
Pros:
- It's got good graphics (Well for a LEGO Game of course, this obviously won't be the next Crysis).
- The music is awesome (Then again, most of it is from the movies :D).
- The huge selection of characters (And that's without the DLC included).
- The big open HUB worlds you can visit and explore (This is where you get most of your golden bricks and characters/vehicles after beating the main missions).
- Free Play mode lets you go back and visit the levels as any characters you want (I love playing The Sentry cause he's basically unkillable :P).
- The addition of Stan Lee in the game (The guy's a freaking god :D).
- The quests for The Collector were a nice touch and really expands on his character (Since you didn't see him much in the MCU).
- The Red Bricks return once more and can make the game alot more fun (Using the Stud modifier helps getting the rest of the characters without having to revisit all the levels again for more Studs).
Cons:
- Some sections in the game can be really fricking annoying due to a time limit (Example: In the level "Ultron Undone", you're on a time limit for Scarlet Witch to charge up her powers. Normally, it's not an issue BUT when you get to the third section of Part C (Before the QTE with Ultron), its makes you so angry on Free Play mode cause you're trying to get all the collectables but it forces you into the cutscene, meaning you have to restart the sequence again just for another shot).
- There's inconsistent audio throughout the game (For example, sometimes when Captain America talks during a take-down, he sounds super quiet).
Overall: This game is a must have if you're a fan of either Marvel or Lego (Or even both if you're like me :D).

Key reasons:
The matchmaking itself is pitiful at best, you can have teams set up in such a way where all the experienced (sometimes even veterans) players are on one team, and all the new people are on the other. So it seems it does not balance player levels, only robot tiers. Sadly it is very difficult to find any decent games with anything above a T2 robo (it goes up to 10). At T3 I am lucky to be able to to score a 2v2 match, which often ends up including T4 bots (on the opposing team), with just the T3 going vs the T4.
You cannot choose what game mode you want to play, and yet there are daily missions that ask for very specific things such as "win x amount of team deathmatch/bomb squad/capture the battery games" and countless other daily missions that require you to be the one to fulfill the objective of such matches, which is exceedingly difficult, because not only are you unable to choose your game mode, but far more often than not, players treat every match (regardless of game mode) more like it is team deathmatch.
Inventory is also constricting enough to strongly encourage using some $$ to expand it, though you can get most if not all things from simply playing the game ... the time it would take to achieve such things will really have you question if its worth it, especially with the quality of the game as it is now.
There is apparently also a problem with people using auto-target and wallhack cheats, I have been in games where not even 5 seconds in, I would be getting shot by an enemy using railguns (in the suburbia map) across 5 walls, not being in line of sight, and not even firing in my direction (evident by bullet trails into the sky in another direction).
Lastly, it seems there is no real support for the community, as there have been countless times when i have seen the chat being absolutely flooded with spam (with no apparent chat bans or otherwise), and throughout the weeks I have been playing it I have not seen any key updates to solve any of the major problems of the game. In fact, a report button seems non-existent! So with that I feel we can probably assume the game developers arent that interested in really keeping the game in a good shape it should be.

While I did enjoy the game, there is one big elephant in the room.
ACT IV: The Shadow Wars is a gauntlet of grinding. In ACT IV, you must defend fortresses you've already taken, over and over and over. This is not optional; the true ending is locked behind this.
Just for anyone who wants exact numbers it breaks down like this. There are 10 stages in Act IV.  In stages 1-3 you defend one of your bases per stage, in stages 4-7 you are tasked with defending two bases per stage, and in stages 8-10 you have to defend three bases per stage. This means you have to defend the same bases you played in the main game TWENTY additional times.
This design would be easier to stomach if not for the fact that many of the encounters see the attacking forces about 5-10 levels higher than any of your own army. The first 4 stages are the worst, requiring the longest grind. You will eventually get to a comfortable level but since every stage increases the challenge, you are constantly having to continue grinding to level up your orcs to catch up. This doesn’t consider that sometimes they die, sometimes they turn on you, and few of them are ever epic or legendary, unlike the orcs attacking you.
This unreasonably long mode all ties into the loot boxes, which give you epic and legendary high-level orcs for real money and no time sink. In my opinion, the developer hid the true ending behind a 10 hour grind fest just to entice you to spend more money. You can either spend an inordinate amount of time leveling up your armies over and over again or you can spend 20 bucks and get as many high-level orcs as you need to breeze through Act IV.
If this mode was optional and not tied to the main story then I wouldn’t be as annoyed by it but this design is a direct result of the micro-transactions. There is no variety to ACT IV, no cutscenes, no side missions, just defending the same 4 bases an absurd amount of times (TWENTY). This is not how a single player game should be structured. These game design decisions should not be acceptable in a $60 release.

So.
Where do I start?
Tom Clancy's EndWar is a real-time strategy/real-time tactics game, unfortunately neglected by its developers, released in 2008 and featuring a World War 3 where your decisions decide the course of the war. It involves three factions - the USA, the European Federation (A unified EU) and the Russian Federation (Which has again expanded into Eastern Europe. Including, to nobody's big surprise, Sevastopol). The interesting thing about EndWar is that it is not like other RTS or RTTs - you do not decide where each army strikes, or what to research, or even if you want to make nice with China so it invades Russia - you are a mere colonel in a special operations branch of your faction's army, and the only control you have over the world is where
deploy. Whether you win or lose the battle as a result of said deployment changes whether your faction grows or shrinks. Other world events, such as typhoons or the U.S.S. George Bush being sunk by your nation's WMD and airstrikes are communicated through the world map's news service.
The campaign is split into two parts - a Prelude to War, in which the game explains the backstory and the game mechanics, as well as how and why World War III erupted and to give you a feel for each faction, and the Third World War itself. The AI is competent depending on difficulty level (On normal, for example, it is fairly competent, while on the hardest difficulty it is very competent), and the graphics are good for a game released in 2008.
All-in-all, I would very much recommend this game to everyone. Unfortunately, the Theatre of War servers (WW3 multiplayer) have been shut down and as a result players are restricted to games with friends or offline games. There are groups that still play EndWar matches, however I am not sure exactly of their URLs - they are, however, active on the Community Hub.

This game is everything I wanted it to be when taking my complaints from the first game into account. But it's certainly not perfect. The best way I can describe it is that the games story is pretty mediocre but MY personal stories make this one of my favorite AAA games this year. Everything involving the Nemesis System is so well done. I ran into dozens of memorable orcs that created dozens of unique personal stories i'll recount to friends and people on Reddit. The Orcs are so unique and memorable that when they would pop back up whether it was to betray me or that they cheated death I instantly remembered them.
As for the gameplay, it's more fun to play then the previous title but it has its problems. For example, certain abilities you had from the start of the first game are locked behind an extensive skill tree, meaning it'll take at least a few hours of game time before you get to a place where you'll have all the abilities you're used to. Also the sub skills are great for varrying your playstyle but for me personally, I didn't like being limited to 1 of the 3 sub skills at a time. With so many skills it was hard to keep track of which sub skills I had active and it turned intp busy work switching up my abilities all the time.
My biggest complaint though is the Shadow Wars, the final act of the game. It's basically a long series of base defense missions, which are super fun and one of the main reasons to purchase the game. But I just didn't like how long the shadow wars dragged on for to get the true ending. I never spent a dime on the loot boxes (a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ practice but not neccesary to complete the game) so the grind was certainly present and it started to weigh on me after the 10 or so hours I spent on the Act 4 portion of the game.
Overall I loved my time spent with this game and I can understand why people are cautious to play it given the whole loot boxes fiasco. But i'd say pick it up on a sale at the least. Super fun game if not flawed in some areas.

Certainly not the best in genre, but pretty entertaining nonetheless. Not a bad price at $10, although I would still wait to buy it on sale. $10 is worth it IMO....but still pushing it. I tend to have a higher tolerance for mediocre games than most, so others will probably only want to spend $5, at the most.
The story isn't real fantastic...or really even there at all after the short prolouge. You do get news casts after every mission for the first 20 turns or so....but they don't really add anything at all to the experience. Most of it doesn't even pertain to what you are doing in any way. (a major disaster in America, for instance, won't actually affect any missions you do in that same exact area) The parts that DO pertain to what you are actually doing....still don't affect the missions at all whatsoever. Basically just mentioning how well/poorly you're doing in the war. Not really sure why they even added this in the game, especially considering they eventually stop appearing.
The gameplay itself is where the game really shines (albeit, not very brightly. Especially not when compared to other games in the same genre). At the start of the main campaign, you choose to play as one of the three world powers (Russia, USA, or Europe) and then select a battalion to control (each with differing bonuses and unit preferences). Each mission consists of you deploying units and then using them to either capture uplinks, destroy "critical buildings", or destroy all hostile forces. Uplink missions can also be completed if you destroy all the hostiles, which ends up happening more often than capturing enough uplinks (especially towards the end of the game and/or when playing defense). After each success (or failure), you'll gain CR (credits) that can then be used to upgrade your troops for future battles. Units that survive the battle (even if they're defeated but successfully evacuate) will also gain ranks, which is mostly used to access the upgrades you purchase for that specific unit type.
There's not a lot of resource collecting in this game. The only "resources" you have are CP (command points) with only two ways to collect them. The first is the capture/upgrade uplinks, and the other method....is just to wait until they recharge by themselves. CP is used for deploying troops, and also for using your supports. Supports include Air Support (bombing), Electronic Warfare (disables enemy vehicles) and Force Recon (deploys troops on the battlefield that can't actually be controlled, but can still be useful for defending).
During most (not all) missions, you'll also gain a 4th support after the mission enters "defcon" phase (towards the end). The support is a WMD, and you can use it without spending any CP whatsoever! The bad news? You can only use it once before a long recharge time, which typically takes longer than finishing the mission. Another bad thing (or good, depending on the situation) is that the losing side gets dibs on using theirs first (although there are rare occasions when they actually won't). Another thing to keep in mind when using this WMD....is that you can hit your own troops with it as well.
When it comes to missions, the game is very open-ended. There will usually be 3 or more missions to choose from, and it's entirely up to the player which mission is undertaken that turn. Often after completing a mission, your country will win/lose OTHER missions as well. This can result in one mission's victory turning into 3 or 4 new territories! It can also result in gaining one territory in exchange for losing another....
While the voice commands are a great idea on paper, in practice they are absolutely HORRIBLE. The system is waaaaaaay too finicky to be of any use if you can't talk 100% perfectly in the way the game wants you to. You're better off just sticking to using the keyboard and mouse for everything.
Overall the game is a pretty enjoyable experience, but nowhere near the best option. I would really only recommend buying it if you're looking for a cheap RTS and don't mind the outdated graphics (the game is from 2009, after all. Wasn't really top-of-the-line back then, either). If you've got money to burn....spend it on the latest Sid Meier or Age of Empires game instead.

If you're looking for a relaxing, entertaining story experience, Broken Age delivers. The charming art and entertaining story more than make up for any shortcomings in the simple and familiar adventure game puzzles of Act 1. There's not much in the way of challenge here, but that's not really a problem. Fans of classic adventure games will likely find the things they enjoyed most well represented here -- great atmosphere, great art, great writing, and a whole lot of charm. This game takes its time, and the more impatient players out there might not stick with it to the end, but if you're the type that explores every branch of every dialogue tree or rubs every inventory item against everything in the game world just to hear the responses, this might be for you.
Playing through at a leisurely pace, all of Act 1 took about 3 hours and 45 minutes to complete. I don't see much replay value, except maybe to appreciate some of the more clever story elements that might have been missed the first time around.
Overall, I really enjoyed it. There were some dry bits, particularly during Shay's scenes, but the high points certainly make up for them. I can't wait for Act 2.

This game is not Fallout or even Fallout tactics. It is horrible game that might be okay for 1980, but not for 2014.
-Horrible skill system
Yeah, it is. Artifically bloated skill list in order to put some artifical replayablility in the game. If character with sniper rifle skill 10 will take assault rifle (it's like sniper rifle, but without a scope) - he won't hit anything and vice versa. Stupid? Indeed.
Social skills - pretty much the same. Instead of one skill responsible for speech, we have 3. And those skills aren't alternatives to each other in order to bring diversity in gameplay - different situations will require different skills. Why? Of course to enforce you to replay the game again and again. Let me remind you how it was in Fallouts: one skill that gave you different choices and those choices affected the result. When they wanted diversity - they were adding other skill/perk check in play. And don't even get me started on trade skills - it is all the same. We've got separate skill for cracking safes and we've got separate skill for picking locks. Why? Oh, see above.
We also got WTF skills like 'brute force'. While it will be used once or twice in game - it is still separate skill. Why devs couldn't make strength check instead of it? Well, cause we need 'diversity'. Oh, and you can't recover mines you disarm and use them later. Cause, well, this isn't Fallout, it's much much worse game.
And stealth skills in game about SpecOPs unit? Never heard of them.
And this isn't even deep analysis of how horrible skill system is - I can go on and on about every skill. And perks/traits like in any proper RPG these days? Nope, they don't exist
-Horrible level design
Yup. Your ranger team can't climb on the roofs or hide in the trenches, unless designers intended you to do so. They convinently put the boxes in the battleield so you could use them as intended. Awesome. Levels feel like they are copypasted. Night/Day cycle? Nay.
-Horrible (N)PCs
In Fallout 2 a lot of named NPCs followed schedule. Shops opening and clothing, NPCs eating and drinking and so on. That was 1998. In 2014 Wasteland 2 we have static NPCs that stand or patrol all day and do nothing. Not acceptable for the game that position itself as RPG. Even more - your rangers in unit never talk to each other or in any other way express their personality. Even followers don't express themselves as personalities. You can't talk to them at all.
-Horrible gameplay
But maybe all other problems is redeemed by awesome gameplay and plot? Nope. Plot is all the same - save the world, blah, blah, blah. But it gets worse. We've got long checklists instead of proper reputation system. For example. We got 2 tribes that are going to war. In normal RPG we help each of the tribes, build the reputation and then convince them to stop fighting and bring the peace.
What we have in WL2? We have chief of the tribe with checklist: "You disarmed bomb - check, saved us from raiders - check, saved child from the lake - check, found drug dealer - check, but you gave my dog beef instead of chicken and therefore the war won't end". This gameplay design is crap.
Oh, and don't forget the forced choice between settlements to save. You can't call reinforcements, you can't split your group, you have to make choice and then the game will make sure that you feel guilty about the choice you made, even if it was forced.
Conclusion: don't buy it and don't believe those who compares it to Fallout 2. It's much much worse. If you don't believe me - watch letslpays on youtube - they will confirm everything I said.
P.S. I didn't mention outdated game graphics, because I don't think that graphics is what determines how good or bad game is.

I am a fan of Guns and Robots, I will admit at first I was skeptical about G'n'R but after I found out what parts I was best with, I wil admit I started having a lot of fun. There is a huge amount of part combinations, but I will admit many of them are nearly useless. It is important to try lots of parts and see what you are best with, otherwise you may be in for a tough time.
I like that there is no pay to win in game, everything can be unlockied in game, and to make matters better I have never had to grind for anything, I actually have too much currency! How often does that happen in a free to play shooter? There are also a good amount of cosmetics and paints to decorate your many many robot parts with, and there are a decent amount of maps and game modes as well. You probably won't get bored  fast.
Overall I recommend this game to anyone looking for a good free to play shooter, lots of customizations, lots of weapons, and  a good mixture of game modes and maps. and best of all no pay to win!

LOADS of weapons, and you can use up to 4 of them in any combination you want on your robot. If you use 4 you will be slow, so most of the times you will be using 2 of them, but its okay since the balance is needed. Every part (chassis, body, head, weapons and , yes, HATS) has around 10 different models on shop with different status so you can make the perfect robot for your style. Its like Team fortress, loadout and robocraft combined.
The downside is that it is new so it still have some problems like having only a few maps and some balance problems (there was a specific very overpowered wepon but it got nerfed yesterday, but still some are clearly stronger than others). But at least every weapon cost basically the same and it is not pay-to-win since you can earn all the currency just playing. The only 'pay to win' thing here (too expensive to buy just playing it normally) are cosmetic things, like hats and painting. All in All, it gives loads of fun but need new maps. Would recommend for sure.

The idea is amazing, but the end result is very average.
If the designers comitted truly to the voice command idea, it could have been a very sweet game. Instead you are left struggling with both keyboard, mouse, and voice. Why use voice when you can just click? It seems to me for this idea to work, you have to either be able to do everything by voice or there would be no point.
1) You can't take cover using voice, you have to click
2) You can't control the camera using voice, not even with something as simple as "camera left left left", so you have to keep your hand on the mouse if only to rotate the view
3) To move something or attack something, you have to know the number of the unit. What if you have 4 helicopters on the field and you want to attack a tank with the closest one? you can't, because you can't see the number of units on the map. So you have to keep guessing or switching between units looking for the right one. A better solution would be to have a bigger map, with numbers clearly shown above the unit icons.
4) In time sensitive situations where you have to react quick, it is a real mess to attack the enemies because once again, it can be difficult to know the number of the unit you want to attack. Enemy tanks flanking on the left? Your helicopters are ready, but even if the tanks are on your screen often their number won't be displayed (it seems to depend on distance or visibility) so you can't efficiently react, and since you can't even send your units to a location by voice you'r back to right clicking.
5) Mission command actually talks to you as you play, and if you are issuing commands at the same time you won't hear what is being said.
So to make it short, even if the available voice commands work well, voice recognition is reliable, the game relies too much on keyboard / mouse for the "voice commanding" thing to really fly. But i can see how if they make aonther game in the series and address all these issues, this concept of "hands free strategy" could be really fun.

All in all I'd say it's a worthy sequel!

I like this game a lot and I'm going to return to it many times, but I have various issues with it that somewhat spoiled the experience. The coolest thing, though, is a unique artstyle (often introducing some gore elements) that brings to mind expensive full-colored comic books. Multitude of choices and fast, user-friendly interface make the replayability a great feature.
The greatest issue of the Swordbreaker is its trial-and-error gameplay. Some decisions you make during this choose-your-own-story game are significant and cleaver and will represent various resoults or playstyles you want to make, but very often it's just the case of "oh, so this choice kills me instantly for no reason. I need to remember to select the second one instead".
The best (worst?) example of this is the scene during which you enter a suspicious room with obvious dark magic in it. You can either take a look into the wardrobe, or go to sleep. What will you do? Well, if you're going the bed, the game will continue. But if you choose the wardrobe, RIP! An invisible enemy cuts your throat. Not the best piece of writing, huh?
Also, the music sucks. I played in a silent mode, but I think you can just play some cool fantasy music on YouTube to fill the musical void.
Sometimes the English translation from Russian struggles and for some reason the voice actor that narrates video-cutscenes got a different script than the subtitles suggest, what should be an easy to fix issue, but well. I also don't understand why can't you just modify the game's volume instead of turning off and on the sound... But only parts of the sound. This makes no sense to me.
Nevertheless, a great purchase and a great example that game books can function quite well in a video game format.

Swordbreaker is an interactive fiction adventure visual novel both developed and published by DuCats Games Studio. As chance would have it, a down on his luck battle-hardened adventurer receives an old scroll from a dying man just as he manages to take his last breath. Furthermore, the scroll actually turns out to be an old map with a clearly marked location. With no other prospects on the horizon, the hero known as the Swordbreaker sets out on a perilous journey across dangerous territory until said map leads him to an apparently abandoned old castle. What awaits our hero on the other side of the door? Could it be glorious adventure and untold treasures or terrifying horrors and certain doom? How the story of the Swordbreaker unfolds is entirely up to you in this clever non-linear story!
The great thing about this visual novel is that it plays much like the old "choose-your-own-adventure" books from back in the day. For anyone not familiar with these books, it was a series that literally let you choose your own path as you read the story. For example, your character comes to the end of a long dark corridor with two doors exiting. Do you choose "Door #1-go to page 12" or "Door #2-go to page 20"? The fantastic thing about these books was that any choice could lead to the continuation of your adventure or a very gruesome death and the end of the story..."Whoops I'm dead let me quickly flip back to page such and such.". This V.N. does an excellent job of re-capturing that wonderful series but in videogame format. Much to my chagrin, I have an innate ability for making poor choices in life. This also seems to have translated to my gaming habits as well because most of the time I always made the absolute wrong choices in Swordbreaker although I must state that some of the options given to you in this particular story did seem rather illogical. I WISH that I could give you some examples because there are MANY but I don't want to spoil the story for you. With that said, Swordbreaker manages quite well to bring back a nostalgic storytelling method for this terrific adventure that you embark on.
Visually, Swordbreaker looks wonderful with a really nice artstyle that is, drum roll please, not anime or manga-inspired which is a breath of fresh air considering that most of the visual novels that I've read to date on Steam have been. The art is beautiful, has nice colors and shading as well. The U.I. for the novel is very simple and easy to follow. Sadly there are no ambient sound effects or any sound effects at all other than the soundtrack which isn't very memorable in my opinion. Also, I can't say for certain but some of the words and phrasing seemed odd and out of place so I'm assuming that English is not the writer or translator's first language maybe? In conclusion, while the visual presentation is very good sadly the aural quality of this V.N. leaves much to be desired.
This was a really great but short read and a little different from the typical visual novel experiences that I tend to have on Steam so that was quite refreshing. I enjoyed this story so much that I'm going to make it a point to keep my eye out for more V.N.'s like this one because I really miss the "choose-your-own-adventure" books. Sadly there are very few options for Swordbreaker other than selecting the language and turning the sound and music on and off. However, there are quite a number of Steam Achievements to hunt down and Steam Trading Cards to collect as well. Also the replayability is quite high as there are a number of outcomes and death sequences to discover as you take alternate paths and make different decisions throughout the castle walls. To summarize, even though it can be highly frustrating at times, Swordbreaker is RECOMMENDED to visual novel and choose-your-own adventure fans.

I don't normaly write reviews, but I felt that as a avid lego game player, if you are considering buying this, you should know what you are getting.  This is the shortest lego game to date, the base game is only 7 levels, with some minor side free roaming missions (nothing like the free roaming you get in the last Marvel game).  Compare this to the typical 15-24 level base game for most of the lego games, and it seems really really short.  In fact, I finished the base game in about 2 hours.  Then they have a huge amount of DLC that you can get with the season pass for another 10 dollars, which isnt too bad, but even with that, it currently adds 12 very short levels, which I ran thru in about an hour.  Of course, like all lego games, you will have the option of running back thru all the levels and picking up all the hidden stuff and unlocking all the characters and cheats, but even taking all those things (base game, DLC, extras) into account, this is by far the shortest lego game to date.
Now, was the game fun, yes it was, and it was pretty cool that they got all the voice cut scenes from the movies (everyone except pepper potts, what was up with that?)  Sometimes, it felt like the game matched the movies a little too much, but that is a minor thing.
Bottom line, you are currently paying full price ($40.00) plus another $10 for DLC, that still doesnt equal the amount of content from the last Marvel game.
Totally not saying you shouldn't buy it, but I just want to be fair, because I read several reviews just like this before buying it, and I have to say, honestly, I thought maybe people were just picking on the game, but now I know its totally true.
UPDATE:  THey have now released 2 DLC packs for Civil War, but neither are included in the Season Pass, which was supposed to include ALL DLC, showing once again that this game is much more of a money grab that all the previous lego games so for another 3 bucks you can have 9 new skins plus a new level.

Every gamers' fear is facing the "Meh" review. It's true, not everything is a life-changer, or worth the money, or worth the effort, but some games are. We all love the joy of that truly AAA game that we rush to play at every open chance and that we think about despite ourselves, but games can be taken slowly and pacifically too. This is where I would throw LEGO: Avengers. While not the best LEGO game (LEGO: Star Wars), or the worst (LEGO: Indiana Jones 2: The Adventure Continues), Avengers tries to be what it can with its astonishing limitations. Avengers steps up the fighting mechanic game while kicking down the puzzle solving game. It's....fine, but truth be told, I starting missing the puzzles halfway through. It tries to fight against the "It's just formula!" arguments by sacrificing some of the most enjoyable parts of a LEGO game. I like the expansions, and yeah, I'd say it's worth it, but my recommendation comes with a cautious yes. This is not a game you will likely replay. However, this is not a game you will rage-quit because it's terrible or annoying (LEGO: Indiana Jones 2: The Adventure Continues). In the end, yeah....it's fine. If you're looking to extend your LEGO library (me), then you might just like throwing some hours onto this.

Being a fan of everything related to super heroes and also of LEGO games, this one is just for people like me. Relive the events of both Avengers movies, plus some extra levels from almost all movies that led to them, in the classic LEGO way, full of hilarious twists in classic scenes to make them suitable for all ages. But as in all LEGO games (or at least the most recent ones), the fun only starts once you finish the main campaign (which has its flaws with level design, as with any LEGO game). You can free play as any character of the Marvel Cinematic Universe (except the Guardians of the Galaxy, which is a huge disappointment) in several HUBs related to the movies. You have tons of characters to unlock, tons of Stan Lees to save (and when you unlock him, there is a big surprise coming!) and tons of golden bricks to collect. There are also side quests all over these HUBs refering to several instances of the MCU, including Agents of SHIELD, Agent Carter, Daredevil, Jessica Jones and the upcoming Luke Cage and Iron Fist. Whatever the MCU has, this game has, except the Guardians as I previously stated. Also, Spiderman! And it's FREE!
Also, I've seen some reviews complaining about the lack of X-Men or Fantastic Four in this game (though Human Torch is present). This is not a game based on the Marvel universe, it's based on the Marvel Cinematic Universe. As in, the movies and the TV shows broadcasted since 2008. Keep that in mind.
All in all, I think this is the best LEGO game I've played, followed very closely by LEGO Batman 3. Take into account that I haven't played LEGO Marvel Superheroes yet, it's on my to do list.

While the emotional depth is turned down in this game compared to its predecessor, this entry into the series introduces new characters and gameplay features, combining Telltale's great storytelling with quicktime events and choices to make

The metacritic might reflect a previous version, but it isn't that far off.  Graphics are decent, flying around with a jetpack or the hoverbike is entertaining, but that's about where the good news dies off.
-Guns jerk around like the player is inside a paint mixer every time they pull the trigger.  Using anything but a pistol is a waste against all but the largest of targets, sheerly because the odds of you hitting them while spazzing out is increased.
-Tanks will get stuck or flip around if you get too close to anything.  Anything.  Even inside one, large mobs virtually one-shot you as they charge and gnash.  The slam move they perform seems to have a 200 yard radius. Flying a heli late in the game is more about shooting down other flying enemies chasing you than helping your team directly with rockets.
-Shooting lacks 'feeling' and there is a noticeable disconnect while firing.  The enemies don't react to it, so combining those issues you more-or-less spam fire and wait until you see an enemy flop to the ground like a water balloon and aim at the next one.
-Guns sometimes don't even animate.  You'll fire and see a flash but your avatar's hand doesn't jerk back, the gun remains frozen on screen.
-Barring fliers and spitters, enemies cannot react to players on a cliff or anything other than a flat plane.  Using a jetpack to reach something off the ground lets you fire at fish in a barrel as they pace around trying to find a way to reach you.
-To limit this, flying mobs sometimes grab a player and lift them into the air.  Shooting them drops you, which can easily be jetpack'd right back to where you were.  Better yet, slowly strafe a foot left and right to avoid being picked up by them in the first place.
-You can punt small enemies in the hoverbike, though speed doesn't seem to matter.  Flying at max speed usually drops them, lightly tapping them usually punts them up or away a huge distance.  My only guess is Aliens.
-Did I mention this has an in-game cash shop, too?  For only $50 you can get 75,000 coins to get skins, hats, and only the best priced bundles this side of Jurassic Park.
-When you log in right now, you are promptly reminded that not only can you get this masterpiece on sale, but they also have a Kickstarter campaign starting in just over a day from right NOW!  What are the odds of that?  What luck!
End result: Thumbs emphatically -down-.  If you like dinosaurs and cannot resist the urge, feel free to get it now while it is a dollar.  Heck, get the four-pack so if any of your friends in the future, even long-term future, decide to want to get this, trade it to them for a TF2 hat or something.  Spare them, anonymous review reader.

My feelings regarding
are rather ambivalent; take this rating as a thumbs in the middle leading down. I enjoyed much of the gameplay itself but it just turns into so much of a slog clearing one room after the next. There's little variation in methods, no introduction of new mechanics, the objective (killing everybody) is always the same, your rewards don't really add much to the way you handle a stage.... Overall, the drug-hazed murderous rampage get's old pretty darn fast.
Also, I realize I've played a lot of
so I could be accused of bloodbath burnout but
at least had
. And playable rewards that changed how you looked at a level. And the violence-enabling side characters were A LOT funnier. Anywho...
It's not like there's nothing to like. Enemies that
to only move in preset patterns display some rather dynamic behavior when provoked; just knowing the stage layout and having a plan does not ensure victory. Similarly, the game acknowledges that much of your deaths will come from unfair circumstances and won't unduly punish you for it. Save points are frequent and as often as you die, you never spend any time
; although it does feel at times like you're just save-scumming through random enemy patterns until you find the one that allows you to progress.
I think my biggest problem with
is that, in a way, there's only one button that does anything of value. Just left click (or right trigger) to punch, swing your weapon, shoot... There's no alternate attacks, no way to do environmental deaths (my favorite deaths!) and the closest thing to a physics engine would be manipulating the weird double-hinged doors into knocking out bad guys. The game is mostly about planning your method of approach but without any extras, it's pretty cut and dried. For a game based on prolific drug use, there's little thinking outside the box.
I might be missing the point entirely.
seems to be the game's main selling point, and
has atmosphere to spare within its retro packaging. You're a nameless, faceless, silent protagonist who only interacts with his environment through murder. A surreal "trippy" narrative downplays the constant violence in which you are immersed but reinforces the central theme of neon-hued nihilism. The experience succeeds in being offsetting in its brutality and made it difficult for me to play for any extended length of time. Overall, I recommend watching the game being played rather than playing the game personally.

While I liked Unhack, Bermuda has nothing from what made Bermuda good, while it's similarly short, ~ 1h.
Long story short: main character, friend and friend's girlfriend get abducted by "aliens", they teleport the girl home, and the guys want to get away + know more about the strangers.
The characters are basically archetypes, or if you don't want to phrase so lightly, clichés.
The friend, who can be told from first glance that he's a badboy type of a character - prison backstory, aggressive take on strangers, the usual.
The girl, who's friends with the main character from childhood, ended up with the bad guy because of the protagonist get them together, and who's obviously into him.
The main character who's calm, nice, and a well-mannered religious character- yes, no wonder people are always mentioning this - mentions God in every single dialogue he has. God may lead you, return to God, God can forgive then I can, God help us, God's mercy, etc. He basically doesn't have a personality, he does everything because that's the nice and good way to do it.
The captain of the ship, who's nice, sees wonder in the world, and trust the guys.
The bodyguard-like character, who's paranoid, aggressive yet follows captain's orders whom she idolizes
+ between acts you can talk to random people on the ship, who are saying stuff that's supposed to be funny and totally out of the story. They are playing games (khmUnhackkhm) on duty, there because of the tax benefits, and things like that - they take the quirky role.
Voice acting is kind of lifeless - it's understandable really well, but totally lacking any emotions or reflects to the happenings - main character tells us how the alarm triggers and they get surrounded just as calmly as he would be reading out the newspapers while having his breakfast.
The game's minigames are much less fun than they were in Unhack, and their implication are also not as deep as in Unhack was - in Bermuda, for example you sneak up to the control room - meaning you snak through 3 levels of guards in the minigame, then you're up in the control room, stuff happens. Meanwhile in Unhack the minigames were actual (un)hacking happening, you were getting information on your way, and not just padding instead of telling us " We barely got passed the guards, but we done it"
I can't recommend Bermuda to buy. The characters lack personality, the story is meh and characters are so void it's hard to care about them.  If you have the game, you can as well play it while you're idling it for hours for the cards (took me 8 hours to drop - game is 1h long...).
If you're intrested in a similarly short Visual novel, instead of Bermuda I can recommend Shen Gui which has really good atmosphere, or from Bermuda's creator : Unhack which is basically a story-driven series of a minigame, where the story being presented in a Visual Novel format.

Well, the pictures are fantastic, and the music is...erm...decent, if a tad "inappropriate" at times. But the writing is, let's be honest, downright juvenile on the whole. Which would normally be a fairly fatal thing for an interactive novel, if the quality (and sheer quantity) of the illustrations didn't make up for a good deal else.
The "story" itself also has its moments: at the very least, for every slightly naff idea, there's a half-decent one. So ♥♥♥♥ it, I kind of enjoyed it. There's certainly a huge variety of choices on offer, though the "three lives, ♥♥♥♥ you, start all over again" policy is a bit harsh considering how easy it is to die (and we're not always talking "logic" here, either...in the finest Fighting Fantasy tradition, trial-and-error is just as likely to get you kilt as it is to reward you generously).
When all is said and done, though, you really can't fault the price. For three bucks, you get a whole lot of interactive novel, a bucketload of bad humour, and an absolute slew of lovely images (which you can even choose to view by themselves, both within the game and in a separate gallery; there's a nifty map of all the areas as you explore them, too). The♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of Achievements are also a wise idea on the behalf of the devs, as they'll no doubt give many a player the motivation to replay the darned thing again and again, trying out every single option on offer just to see what happens (and what nifty pic accompanies said outcome).
Bottom line: don't go in expecting too much for your moolah, and chances are you won't be too disappointed.
Verdict: 7.5/10.

EndWar is a decent real time strategy with a groundbreaking voice control feature. Unfortunately it doesn't always work as promised, so occasionally you have to shout your commands a couple of times more than planned. Eventually you'll just go back to the way you usually give commands; by using menus. It was a good idea but it was too early to implement it just yet. The technology wasn't entirely ready for this kind of gameplay back then.
And yet despite this flaw I had a good time with it, because it does give you the idea that you're the commander in charge and there's an actual war going on. Now, there's not a lot of tactics involved when we're talking about the battles here, because the idea is based on the real life rock paper scissors game. So if you use the right unit against the other you'll most likely win (depending on the amount of units, of course). It's simple, but it works and it doesn't make the game tediously boring, like many other strategy games. It's by no means perfect, but it's definitely fun. Just avoid the voice control feature.

alright everyone, let me start with an important fact that a lot of people tend to forget, but i think is very pertinent to "mountain":
"pretentious"
adjective
1.
characterized by assumption of dignity or importance, especially when exaggerated or undeserved:
a pretentious, self-important waiter.
2.
making an exaggerated outward show; ostentatious.
now before i really begin i would like to debunk something people have been saying about mountain. people seem to find it difficult to categorize mountain, they compare it to a screen saver, they say it "pushes the boundaries of what you consider a game". this is donkey doo because the mountain is not the first of it's kind, it falls into a new genre called "idle-games". the most famous of the idle-games is cookie clicker. idle-games are games you play when you aren't playing games. they usually involve getting points, or some limited range of progression, and are something you come back to on and off during the day.
in mountain, you generate a mountain, you let it sit there, you do other things, a pleasant sound runs in the background, and you come back and -- oh my goodness! a pie has found a home on your mountain, and you are very amazed. you realize the keyboard plays different notes on a disembodied piano, and you might even be lucky to discover that playing different songs will do... things.
and also -- oh my GOSH! you can move the pie around! and you laugh and cheer and oh my good lord how this is fun!
mountain is getting a lot of press and i think it is kind of unfair to much better games of it's breed. there are a lot of idle-games that actually do challenge you to think about what you find fun, and what interests you in a game. i think click-hero is a good idle game, which has you fighting monsters and buying and leveling heroes to make your clicks more valuable. i think cookie-clicker is a testament to the genre, proving how addictive an extra integer can be.
mountain does not really do anything for me. if it didn't have objects in it to interact with, it would have nothing, which leads me to believe the creator put the objects in out of necessity. there is little to no progression, the game is poorly optimized, and it's just plain dull and has nothing to show for itself.
but, i'm sure, people will tell me how i "just don't get it". i get it.
let me tell you briefly how "mountain" could have been an interesting game:
as you play mountain, you notice a village of people have built a settlement on the side of you. they seem to be using the resources inside of you for industry, and to great benefit! their cities and town grow as you leave the game running in the background. the sound effects change from peaceful and serene, to a dull chug, a soft clicking of cogs, and eventually the great repetitive doom of heavy industry. The game makes an interesting point, being the mountain, you get no say or interaction in how the people progress. you just watch and observe the people as they grow in populace and in technology until their eventual demise, whether it be by destruction, or the graceful transition from existing, to ascending amongst the stars. either way, you, the mountain, remain, to watch the process happen again.
that would have been amazing. that would have made an ACTUAL statement.
so, mountain is a dollar. why don't i recommend it? if you want pleasant sounds, go to
if you want a good idle-game, try cookie-clicker. the beta has a lot of updated mechanics and it's really turning into something amazing. also it's free.
if you want a mountain... buy skyrim. it's a game, and debatably fun, plus you climb a mountain!
if you want objects, try katamari damacy. it's also a game.
save your dollar.

Bringing the FSX world to Steam, making the game playable for Windows 10 made it so I could finally upgrade from Windows 7. It has kept the same level of realism and compatibility with most after market add ons. I have not had any problems adding Blue Sky Scenery with helps the ground realism (in select areas) greatly, while also adding many vintage warbirds for truly exciting flying.
The added attraction of the multiplayer capability makes an interesting new dimension to flight, where you have to avoid other fliers that may maneuver irregularly. The only drawback to the multiplayer realm is that you get an interpreted display of other's aircraft unless you have the exact same plane installed, with precisely the same name on your system. With there being literally tens of thousands of add-on aircraft and helicopters out there it makes it a guarantee that many, perhaps MOST, will be flying something entirely other than what you see. If there was some way to have the game transmit the appearance of the plane you are flying so others see you as you are, this would add a level of realism that would have me in multiplayer every time I fly.
I truly enjoy the level of realism FSX has over older versions of Flight Simulator. I've been flying various versions for 27 years and having it available in Windows 10 means that I will still have many more years to enjoy this simulation.

Life is Strange features charming writing, well-rounded and multifaceted characters, and absolutely fantastic story arcs. Almost every major development was either a white-knight fantasy moment, or a tear-jerking punch in the gut. I readily admit to breaking down crying when I saw one scene in particular
.
One gripe is that the teenage angst which was central to the plot was a little hard to relate to/sit through at times; the same goes for the often meme-centric dialogue and "easter eggs". Having been a teenager recently, I feel like the story could have used a little more realistic input from a few of them. Another part that briefly lost me, and may have even devalued the ending
was
. However, that's not nearly enough to turn this review into anything other than a glowing one. A few moments made me laugh (albeit probably for the wrong reasons), but far more moments made me want to/actually tear up, and I find that a lot more compelling in a game.
Gameplay-wise, it's interesting, but sometimes it could get a little awkward controlling it with a mouse and keyboard (I'm not plugging in a controller for this). In particular, the rewinding mechanic often seemed to transpire at frustratingly variable rates, but I soon realized that it depended on whether you were rewinding through dialogue that's already happened or something going on in the environment. Basically, the main character's time-rewinding powers - while a clever mechanic which, combined with its adept weaving into the plot, kept this game from being an interactive soap opera - got pretty irritating at certain points. It should be noted, however, that this may have been intentional (or at least excusable), since
, so I'll overlook that one too!
Moreover, I cannot believe I put off playing this game until a year after I got it, since it has become my all-time favorite game in only the twelve hours I've played it so far (at time of writing). Get this game if you want to feel everything a person can feel, in a short period of time!

Ignore that MISLEADING metascore!  Good gravy, if they actually rated game as it is now it could at least score in the 80s.
Anyway, if you like dinosaurs and scifi shooters then you'll love this game.  It's like Killing Floor mixed with Tribes 2 and that awesome Jurassic Park arcade game from the 90s!  It's a real treat.  I do have to say though, it's not really innovative or anything, its more like a throwback to awesome scifi shooters like the original Halo or Tribes(complete with jetpack!!)
The worlds(servers) are pretty massive and it gives the game an openworld feel kind of like Far Cry(more like Far Cry Dragon Blood because of the dinosaurs!) and you get a large variety of vehicles to cover the distance.  The way the vehicle stations work reminds me of Tribes 2 along with augments, which are upgrades that can let you run faster or jump higher or give you various bonuses.
All the best scifi guns are included and, though some of the deisgns seem derivative, they all look pretty great and the handling/tracking and hit detection is really spot on.  You may want to play as the lighter/faster but less armed Assault class, or you might like the heavier and more explosive Support class, or even the stealthy Recon class.  It's not a huge variety of classes but they're all versatile so you really don't need more than these 3 classes just that basic archetype is more than enough to build a great character from.
If you've played Tribes then you recognize the outpost/repairing and engineering aspects the game includes and theneed to maintain outposts mso you can have weapons, vehicles and augments readily available for the waves of raptors and all other sorts of dinosaurs.  Limiting this game to 5 players(usually) per server makes it a super fantastic coop game.
Another great thing about this game is the leveling and money system, it works just like Killing Floor, as in the more you kill the more money you get and in between waves(yeah this is an enemy-wave based game) you can use it to buy upgrades or weapons, and vehicles to move from outpost to outpost.  You better hurry though because you can only buy between waves, which adds a nice bit of relief for the ends of a hard round and maybe some tension for what's to come next.
After I've played more I'll probrably update this post with more details but you should definitely give this game a try, it's on sale now for 99 cents and it usually only costs about 15 dollars, which is amazing considering the replay value this game has to offer.

Without a doubt. The most broken, frustrating, unsatisfying experience I have had in a LONG time.
Horribly clunky unresponsive, glitchy movement. Luck based pointless spamfest "fighting". Absolutely no story to speak of whatsoever.
All you do is go through an ambiguously stereotypically asian city filled with spikes, rolling barrels that spawn literally out of thin air, bullets that literally spawn out of thin air, and ambiguously stereotypically asian enemies. You beat them all up in exactly the same fashion, none of them act differently other than slightly different barebones animations, even the "bosses" are exactly the same as the mooks, except with more health and a unique sprite.
Once you beat the last "boss" the game cuts to a black screen with "...a good workout" or something like that, and then your booted to the title screen.
Also did I mention that there is NO way of saving progress in any way. You quit? You start over. Your PC died suddenly? You start over.
Many MANY times I have been killed because the game just did not read my inputs, or straight up did the wrong thing, resulting in my death, and sometimes the game just sends you flying upwards forever when you jump up a ledge (thankfully there is a reset checkpoint button), and the collision detection is extremely random, something that would normally kill me doesn't, and vice versa.
The last level (Level 5) is absolutely disgusting and highlights all of the game's problems I mentioned previously. As well as stupidly long rooms.
The soundtrack is decent at best. But writing this review after beating it, I don't remember any of it already.
Overall I can't recommend this to anyone wanting to actually have fun. AVOID.
