To start this review, I would like to introduce "Lorm the Legend" -- the plague that I created upon middle earth.
Chapter I - The Creation
The story and creation of Lorm begins shortly after I conquer the frosty stronghold of Seregost, in which doing so unlocks the pit challenges. Time passes and I start finishing up all that is left to do in Seregost and that beaming orange light circle on the map draws me in - I have to try my hand in a bit of Uruk fighting. As I prompt the challenge I am given the opportunity to select one of my brave and deadly warriors to undergo the task of murdering the challenging fighter. This is where my favourite and most loyal Uruk comes in -- Borgu Quick-Blades; A poisonous dark slayer who has been my bodyguard for as long as I can remember. The fighting begins and Borgu makes quick work of the first two challenges without me breaking as much as a sweat, little did I know this was just the beginning of the end for poor Borgu. Full of lust for blood I send Borgu into the pit once more against a foe I thought to be harmless - Lorm the Legend. I started the fight without checking what Lorm was capable of, boy was that a mistake. Lorm the Legend wasn't just legend by title: he was actually a legendary, not only that he was 20 levels higher than my prime captain Borgu. The fight begins and I start sweating bullets, will Borgu prevail despite being at such a disadvantage? Will Lorm have mercy and spare my poor captain? -- No. He did no such thing. He unsheaths his poisonous spear and metallic shield from his back and charges into battle with a stupid♥♥♥♥♥grin on his face. Borgu didn't stand a chance, as soon as he landed a single blow against Lorm it was over... Lorm grabbed him, threw him to the ground and beat him to death. To me this was an act of WAR. I could not sit there idly and let him escape having murdered my trusty Borgu. I proceed to charge into battle against Lorm with dominated Uruks by my side, full of rage and ready to fight. As I engage with Lorm and we clash weapons, he laughs and witters on about how he is the greatest Uruk who has ever lived - I thought he was joking... but what happened afterwards is nothing to laugh at. The fight continues and it's just Lorm and I left in the pit; I'm down to my last chance to get back up again and the battle looks to be nowhere near finishing. This mother trucker would not take damage from range and poison, to make it even worse he could not be executed and couldn't be frozen or vaulted. After numerous blows to each other, Lorm extended his long arm of the law and grabbed me by the throat. This is when I knew it was all over. Lorm throws me to ground and does a repeat of what happened to Borgu -- he mashed my face in with his bloodied fists. Lorm the Legend had won, he began to join the Uruk army of Seregost and had increased his level all the way to 49 which was 20 levels above my own. Time had passed after our duel in the pit and after much frustration and failed attempts to take him down I had well and truly had enough - it was time to leave.
Chapter II - The Destruction
There I am; playing my hand in the arena once more -- except this time it was in Nurnen. Since my duel with Lorm I had created a few decent Uruks from the pits and was trying to forge the ultimate warrior in an attempt to bring him down once and for all. Little did I know he was onto my plan like a tramp on a chips. I'm in southern Nurnen, chasing down a potential new recruit to the legion. BANG -- An Uruk has just ambushed me and thrown me to the side, It was Lorm. He had tracked me down from Seregost just to add even more insult to injury. He laughs as he begins to attack me once more; I knew this was my going to be my final encounter with the Legend known as Lorm or he was once more going to strike me down and continue to plague my army. I have learnt many knew things since our first encounter and I have learnt how to cheese move him, although that still didn't make him an easy opponent to beat as he could two shot me whenever he pleased. I proceed to call forth a Graug and my newly appointed Olog Beastmaster bodyguard known as Ur-Hakon the Faithful - and boy did he live up to his title. Ur-Hakon arrives with his pack of Carragor to help finally elimate the legend of Lorm. The battle starts and there is constant explosions and the sounds of beasts rattling through my headset. This was intense. All of Lorms loyal followers were quickly dealt with and he was all alone. Surrounded by a Graug, pack of Carragor and the mighty Ranger -- he knew he was about to be bested. Nothing is ever quite that easy with Lorm though, to add a final slap in the face he had downed Ur-Hakon in an attempt to kill another one of my most trusted captains. I couldn't let this happen again, flashbacks of Borgu were flashing right before my eyes, I could picture the exact moment his skull was crushed -- I was not going to let this happen again. I drew my legendary sword of vengeance from it's sheath and ran straight for Lorm; it was now or never. I start slashing him from side to side, lowering his health from slither to practically non-existant. It was at this moment I knew that one more hit and he will be gone forever, the plague of Lorm lifted from Mordor. Although, despite wanting to rip his head off where he stood I knew the defeat of Lorm couldn't come down to a slimy bash of the sword. One idea quickly sprung to mind before he took his last breath; Elven Rage. I proceed to beam up in a beautiful blue light, mashing the X button so hard that there would be nothing left of Lorm. The rage stops, the dust dissapears and everything comes to a holt. There he is, laying flat on the floor soaked in his own blood -- Lorm the Legend had be slain.

TL;DR: THIS GAME IS BAD, AND YOU SHOULD PROBABLY BUY IT.
If the game designers has made Swordbreaker as a movie, I suspect that it might have attained a very minor cult status in the vast pantheon of 80s-inspired shlock fantasy drivel. I don't mean that in the "hidden-gem" kind of way, I mean it in the "get drunk, munch on whatever's left in the back of the fridge, and fall asleep about two-thirds in" kind of way. It would have been a few tiers below a Krull or a Conan, but not fallen so far down into the muck as to be outright boring. The art screens, at the very least, deserved better than the plot and the design.
So, there's a few things you should know going in ...
Accept that your choices are nearly arbitrary, and that the most consistant logic to them is the audibly giggling writer screwing over his players. Accept that the story that could only really please a hyperactive six-year old boy who'd taken a testosterone shot to the face, and that it's been brought to you in quasi-adequete fan translation. Accept that you may never learn what, exactly, a Swordbreaker Attack is, or how our manly-man hero learned to perform one, or why it can work so well on creatures without swords or even opposable thumbs. Maybe it's in the all-Russian intro video? I don't want to go check.
Accept all that, and note that the game is only three bucks ... unless you want the totally worth is Delux Edition!!! (I'm joking, don't do that.) Buy it, and waste an hour or so getting lost in some really enjoyable absurdity. You'll soon learn to hate the death scene music that always plays half a second before the story text loads.

Wasn't sure what to expect going in to Alan Wake, but had trust in Remedy from their Max Payne days. I was in no way disappointed. The protagonist isn't an amazing action hero... There aren't any shady mob bosses or any globe trotting... Instead it's a claustrophobic, beautiful, tense, well paced adventure.
Everything takes place in a mountain range wherein Bright Falls, the town Alan Wake visits, is located. The graphics in the game are incredible for still being stuck on DX9, and the environments/draw distance are incredible. Characters are unique and at times genuinely funny, and there are some out of left field but welcome campy moments akin to twin peaks or donnie darko.
The storyline, for once, was the biggest draw of the game for me. It followed an almost Stephen King kind of pace, giving just enough airtime to the evil permeating the game, but never revealing it until the right moments... But even then not giving a full enough answer to make you lose interest in what will happen next.
Finally, the combat... I have never been more impressed with how light and darkness have been used as "weapons". It becomes integral and makes you think a little "out of the box" in terms of how to approach certain combat situations. 4 guys approaching, a bulldozer, and 2 heavier guys all coming at you at once? Throw a flashbang! If that confuses the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you... Yeah, this games combat is very unique, but once you get the hang of it you'll be poppin' flares and takin' names in no time.
Highly recommended, for something different, something unique and one of the few games that doesn't need a sequel.

Swordbreaker is not a VN; it's a CYOA with a broad but short decision tree. I came into it with no expectations of a deep or even interesting story, so I ended up enjoying it for what it is.
As I played it, I started thinking of it as a gory, text-based spin on Dragon's Lair, with modular situations in which you have simple life-or-death decisions, and the wrong choices can immediately lead to ridiculously over-the-top deaths.
I agree with other reviewers that it is tedious to scroll every time to read the entire description, and I really wish I could have used numbers on the keyboard to make choices. It is also a bit of a chore to replay paths by memorization to get farther along. And yes, the English translation is not terrific, but it has its little moments--and since this is not a story-driven game, I can forgive its lapses.
In the end, I liked the comic-style art and the zany, don't-take-it-seriously situations and antagonists. I also like how the castle map shows you the corresponding scenes when you hover over the icons, so you can get an idea of which paths you've taken and missed.
I found this game fun for a short time--nothing deep or even particularly satisfying, but enjoyable for a brief spin.

Swordbreaker is a very simple game, it is essentially a digital choose your own adventure novel. I was a fan of the style of books as a kid and even wrote some of my own for school assignemnts (guaranteed B at the very least for creativity) So I gave this one a try. The game opens witha very throwaway backstory and set up for the rest of the game. Essentially the hero hears about a castle with treasure and decides to go there. From there you are faced with a text box describing the current scene and buttons for each choice you can make at that point. You continue to make choices for the whole game. Inevitably you will make a wrong choice leading the hero's death. You have threee lives each one giving you a repeat from where you died. This is welcome as if it wasnt there you would have to play through the game a minimum of 324 times to see everything. The map acessible from the main menu makes it seem as if there are three paths you can take to the end but in reality the paths all criss cross multiple times. The map conveniently lets you see where choices you havent seen can be found, although it would be nice to access it in game.
As the game plays out and assuming you dont die a bunch right at the start you are given points based on what types of choices you make, heroic, murderous and cowardly. These ultimately effect which of the three true endings you can receive.
There is very little actual story telling going on. Essentially you enter one of various rooms deal with the trap, character or monster inside and move on. Pretty much every single room can kill you. From making the wrong move in a battle or choosing to nap or not nap. (Yes there is actually a room that will kill you for resting and another that will kill you for not resting.) Some of these are creative and rather amusing, like stubbing your toe while fighting a Kraken. Most however are just being impaled or eviscerated or poisoned or beheaded etc. This is one of my biggest issues with the game is that every ending except for the true endings and 2 of the game over endings involve you dying. With the setting there are plenty of mroe creative endings you could add in like getting stuck in a magic mirror, transformed into an animal or even turning into one of the mosnters. But no, every single one of them involves death. As a warning pretty much all the death scenes are pretty gruesome, this isnt intended for kids.
The creators did at least have some fun with the traps and monsters themselves. There are tons of classic fantasy tropes but a good deal of sillier things pop up as well including an alien a nuke and tons of pop-culture references. Thats all there really is. At a few points you can potentially gain some items or even people who will offer to aid you in battle. The issue there is that they can only be used in a single specific instance, not wherever you want.
I will give credit for the sheer amount of images, almost every single choice has an image to go with it even mundane things like starting a conversation or walking down a hall. There seem to be at least three artists because the style does change from image to image. This works fine most of the time except for one artist who has noticeably less kill than the others and it stands out. It isn't bad but it is different enough to catch your eye.
If you liked reading Choose Your Own Adventure novels as a kid where any choice can lead to your abrupt death than you may enjoy this game. However dont come in expecting any substantial plot or payoff. Its just a time waster at best.
Summary:
+Tons of art
+Takes liberties with setting
+Sponge Joe
~Multiple artists
~Morality system
-No real story
-All endings are violent deaths
-No reward for 100%
-I dont think he ever uses his swordbreaker to actually break a sword...

This game is absolutely superb!
Artfully balancing action-adventure with something a bit more cerebral, it provides an immersive, atmospheric landscape as well as keeping a neat balance between cutscene & gameplay, something that I have often witnessed failing to occur in other plot-driven games, wherein cutscenes detract from the actual gameplay itself.
The characters are flawed (This is a good thing!) and intriguing people; Alan himself making a refreshing change as a protagonist given his somewhat gruff, cantankerous and (Positively diva-ish at times) disagreeable nature; he is still very likeable. The plot is fantastic yet grounded at the same time, riddled with clever what-ifs and many-layered implications of what it means to write creatively and what it is to truly push the boundaries between imagination and reality in this process; as a writer, this especially appealed to me. The subtly of what is being suggested often allows for varying interpretation of the possible meaning and this is wonderful; it does NOT give you all the answers, it leaves room for your own analyses.
The gameplay itself is pretty damn epic as well. Action remains fast-paced and challenging without being too frustrating, supplies such as ammo or batteries are plentiful enough to stop you ever running the risk of being completely defenceless (Most of the time in any case) while remaining sparse enough to keep you considering what to preserve and when, and there is a varying degree of weaponry and enemy strength and speed to keep it interesting.
Additionally, while this may not be gameplay related, I could write a whole other review about how phenomenal that soundtrack is...
My one and only complaint might be that it remains yet another instance of white-male-protagonist-ing, however, that is not to say the protagonist is in any way a stereotype himself, or that this was an ill-balanced decision, I love this for what it is, my issue is more with the consistency of this pattern within the games industry than this game specifically.
Other than that, even the most glowing of reviews probably couldn't do this game justice, and really you ought to just see for yourself.

Microsoft Flight Simulator X: Steam Edition (FSX:SE or simply FSX is commonly abbreviated by players) is a simple multiplayer or singleplayer game which falls into the genre of Simulation games, specifically Flight Simulation (if it isn't obvious already). In this game, you fly a plane in real-world terrain and airport layouts with real-time simulation.
Pros:
-Almost never crashes (on my system, anyways. See my system specifications listed below.)
-Real-world terrain, making you feel like you're a pilot.
-(Mostly) functional cockpit, which allows you to turn off engines, taxi lights, etc. There is also autopilot (both IFR and VFR).
-In-flight radio communications with audio in singleplayer. You can contact air traffic control towers and includes human speech (not ugly robotic sounds).
-Multiplayer support. Allows you to interact with other FSX players and plan group flights (commonly called 'hops') between  airports.
-Affordable for low-end machines (though I wouldn't recommend it much). You can still play it on lower-end machines and laptops if you can handle lower quality.
-Crashed only on one instance (for me, at least). It's when I open a new window when FSX is simulating a flight. I solved this issue by going into windowed mode (Alt+Enter).
-Missions. To challenge yourself.
-Public and Private Multiplayer. There are public servers, which are listed in the multiplayer window. Some are public but require passwords. There are also private servers, which can be accessed by entering one's IP address so you can play with your friends and without strangers.
Cons:
-LOTS of keyboard shortcuts. You're gonna have to get used to them.
-Can be hard to fly on your first days of flight. In my first days, I forced the turning too much and ended up crashing a lot of times. However, with some patience, you can easily fly a plane.
-Low quality terrain (though solvable with paid DLC). The terrain and airport's terrain are quite poor in quality. Though there are DLCs to solve this, they require money.
My opinions: If my playtime hasn't predicted what I'm about to say, then... here are my opinions.
It's the perfect non-combat full flight simulator and certainly the best one. I love the customizability (if not just a biiit pricey) but either way it's pretty realistic (though I've never been a pilot, so take that with a grain of salt). Broken Age is a point-and-click adventure with an intriguing story and gorgeous visuals that you would swear popped right out of a children’s book. I’m a sucker for adventure and this delightful outing by Double Fine had me going from start to finish. Broken Age won’t blow you away with gameplay mechanics or mind-bending puzzles, but you will find great storytelling with fun and interesting characters.
The story follows a boy and a girl from different worlds, both of which are trying to escape what life has planned for each of them. Perhaps on some level it’s easy to relate to these two characters, as I’m sure many of us have probably felt trapped at some point in our lives. Maybe you tried to shake things up a bit and did the opposite of what’s expected of you from your friends or family. Discovering who you are and what you’re made of is all part of growing up. The same goes for our two protagonists Shay and Vella. They need to break free and in the process might learn a thing or two about themselves.
Broken Age is truly a delight to look at and there were times when I would just sit back and drink up the scenery. Vella lives in world that I can only describe as a fairytale land. She lives in a small village where its citizens offer her up to a giant, many-eyed monster, named Mog Chothra. Before you know it, Vella escapes certain death and begins her journey that takes her high into the clouds.
Shay’s world is much different than Vella’s and rather than exploring different regions, he is stuck on a spaceship with only a maternal computer to keep him company. Shay has been alone his entire life and has obviously outgrown the toys that were left for him. It’s time for Shay to explore new worlds and save others from enemy threats.
With any point-and-click adventure it’s up to the writing to keep the players engaged in the story. Gameplay isn’t really a factor here. Sure there are puzzles to solve and items to collect, but honestly they take the backseat in this journey. There were only a few occasions when I got stuck and couldn’t figure out what to do next. This wasn’t really a problem though, because players can switch between characters at any point to take a bit of a mental break. Furthermore, players have the option to skip cut-scenes and even walk faster to move things along.
There were times when I thought the dialogue options were a little on the dull side. This could be frustrating for some, especially if you’re not certain where to go and there’s always the possibility a character might have a clue or item to share with you. However, most items are easy to come by and fairly self-explanatory when solving puzzles. In most cases, you’ll simply click an item in your inventory and then click the object on your screen to complete the puzzle. However, on occasion, some items need to be combined in order to move forward.
I did find Vella’s story to be much more compelling than Shay’s, but that’s not to say I didn’t enjoy my time on his spaceship. Perhaps it was exploring the different settings in her world that kept me glued to my seat. With Shay, there were times I felt like I needed to just press on to get to the end of act one. In fact, some of the characters on the ship were just a little too childish for me. I’m sure if I was a kid playing this game I would love the little yarn guys, but they just didn’t do it for me. Their voices simply got on my nerves and I wanted to throw them out the nearest airlock.
Broken Age is perfect for those of you looking for a fun and sometimes dark point-and-click adventure. The game deals with some heavy themes like loneliness and sacrifice. Ultimately, it’s a coming of age tale that left me pleasantly surprised after nearly the four hours it took to complete. The puzzles range from easy to moderate difficulty and with the power of the internet at your fingertips, you can cheat your way to victory! I will admit to getting stuck once and couldn’t for the life of me figure out what to do next. Luckily for me, the Google knows…

Awesome game so far, first the bad points. Graphics could be better in places (and perhaps overall, there pretty rough in places such as the head models / textures in character customisation) and definitely show their 'asset store' origins here & there, (like many have said) a better way to sneak and setup your squad prior to battle (a formation system would be nice too since friendly fire is a possibility in this game) wouldn't go a miss and finally the lack of Steam Overlay at the moment so no favourite past-time for me of screenies (yet) :(
Aside from that the gameplay is very reminiscent to the also great Jagged Alliance 2 (reloading, crouching for better aim, squads with many varied specialities) and XCOM Enemy Unknown (as a more modern example especially with the 'Ambush' system which is that game's 'Overwatch' in this case and the levelling). I wasn't a big fan of Fallout 1 / 2 (Perhaps will have to try it on easy if there is a difficulty setting can't remember but I do remember getting destroyed on the first freaking enemies and having a timer which I never like) but did love 3 however this game does have the feel of those game's inspired by this game's original effort (albeit more gritty in tone although there is much humour to be found here).
Add in the plentiful looting and secrets (which are quite key to keep supplies nice at the moment) to find as well as the core rpg elements (story, skills, dialog, loads of locale etc) it's all there. So far I'm finding it far more flowing then the also awesome DOS (Divinity Original Sin) with a far easier to manage inventory system (with sort button, a distribution option which sends out evenly relevant items to each member of your squad such as all to vital ammo and 'set as junk' / 'sell all junk' buttons to quickly sort and sell the multiple items respectively in one go) and a better handling of complexity (although not as complex as DOS on the surface) which I think was DOS's shortcomings in comparison allowing far more time to actually 'play the game' and makes the moments of 'reading text' far less of an issue, so far, good times!
PS I'm playing on the lowest difficulty (I normally only ever play normal on 99% of my games) at the mo due to many saying / warning the difficulty is borderline too heavy, you can change difficulty mid game (there's no achievements at the moment anyway) but bear that in mind as it may colour your opinion on the game early & fast! (I still had to heal numerous times on 1/3 encounters with most of the already limited ammunition 'found', what-with you being pretty broke♥♥♥♥♥early game and all).

If you came here looking for a review, you have come to the wrong place, but if you want some very ♥♥♥♥ing good brownies, you have come to the right place. You're welcome for an actual recipe, not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ copy and paste pie recipe. Trust me nothing goes wrong with nutella.
INGREDIENTS:
1 c. unsalted butter
2 c. sugar
1/2 tsp. salt
1 c. flour
1 c. cocoa powder
4 eggs
1 (13-oz.) jar Nutella
5 Ferrero Rocher candies, unwrapped and crumbled
DIRECTIONS:
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F.
2. Melt butter in a medium-sized saucepan over medium heat. Add sugar, stirring until combined. 3. Remove from heat and add salt, flour, and cocoa powder, stirring to combine. Whisk in eggs, stirring just until the mixture is combined into a batter. Set aside.
4. Spray an 8"-x-8" pan with cooking spray. Pour half of the batter into the pan. Spoon or lightly drizzle most of the Nutella on top of the batter, forming an even layer over the brownie batter. 5. 5. Use a spoon or silicone spatula to cover the Nutella with the remaining brownie batter. (If you pour the batter straight on top of the Nutella, it will sink into the Nutella and combine into one marbled—yet delicious—mess.)
6. Bake until the top layer of brownies has browned and set, 28 to 30 minutes. It shouldn’t jiggle when you remove it from the oven. (The toothpick test doesn’t work here, since the toothpick will hit the Nutella layer, making the brownies seem uncooked.)
7. Let cool for 15 to 20 minutes, then top with a drizzle of Nutella and crumbled Ferrero Rocher chocolates. Cut into squares and serve.
Credits: ★ Billy

You know that game you saw at the arcade that had all of those flashy lights and drew you in the second you saw it?  Remember how you then went up to it and put your quarter into it, and then before you even knew it, you got a game over screen?  And then instead of walking away, you put another quarter in the game to give it figure out what even happened, only for you to just barely grasp the gameplay before you died again?  And then you dumped your entire wallet into the game and by the end of it all, the longest you lasted was 10 minutes?
Nuclear Throne is that arcade game.
It proclaims itself to be a roguelike, similar to Binding of Isaac.  In fact, a lot of people make comparisons between the two games, saying that they're similar.  To that I say, there's actually not very in much in common.  While they are both roguelikes and you need to get to go through a number of levels to reach the "end", as well as having the same movement scheme with the WASD keys, and having a variety of characters to play as, those are the only similarities they have.
One of the ways Nuclear Throne makes itself very different from Binding of Isaac is by making your primary means of attack with guns and melee weapons like wrenches and sledgehammers.  You use your curser to aim, and then you click whenever you want to hit/fire from your gun.  And as with real life guns, you need to reload and get more ammo after you've shot them all into your enemies' corpses.  The ammo is relatively easy to find, whether it's in chests or from drops after you kill enemies, but it's still a good idea to not unload all of your bullets at once, because some enemy will pop up when you need your bullets the most, and you WILL die.
Another thing about Nuclear Throne is that each level has no doors.  It's one solid room of different environments depending on where you are, meaning that your enemies will find out eventually if you don't hide behind some walls.  In order to progress to the next level you have to kill everyone on the current level, but levels are so small in general, it should take you not even 5 minutes to make a corpse out of everyone.
And finally, this game has a very arcade-like feel to it.  A single run can be done in 15 minutes, but just like all of those arcade games you might have tried to play, you will die.  You will die A LOT.  Enemies hit with a lot of power in this game, and if you're not quick, you'll get hit rather easily and blow up within 3 seconds.  Othertimes you'll get bombarded with ten enemies on the screen at once while you're also surrounded by tons of explosives.  Or even worse, you'll kill an enemy, and it'll explode, catching you in the blast and killing you that way.  The point is, you will shot full of holes all the time.  Success is not easily come by in this game.
And yet despite this, this game is extremely addicting.  The very short amount of time it takes you to get to the Nuclear Throne, along with the fast-paced action, makes it very easy to get sucked in for hours and hours.  That mentality of "just one more try..." will consume you.  Maybe you won't get drawn into it as much as the Binding of Isaac games due to less content, but the addiction factor is still there.
With that said, I can only reccomend this game to those who aren't afraid of a challenge.  You will die a lot, as I have reiterated many times in this review.  You will die because of stupid decisions, because you didn't move fast enough, or because the game decides it hates you and has hordes of rats storm you from both ends of a narrow hallway and sink their fangs into you.  This game does not care about you winning.  I'm pretty sure some of the Steam achievements make this apparent with how one of them requires you to sit upon the throne with a certain character when they're seconds away from death.
But if you don't mind that (and are perhaps a masochist), then by all means buy the game.  Just don't go expecting this to be Binding of Isaac, because you'll be in for quite a surprise then.

Nuclear Throne is a top-down roguelike shooter, and a relatively good one at that; you can drag the window size to fit any resolution you so desire. In terms of gameplay, you select a character, run around, shoot enemies, dodge bullets, pick up better guns, repeat. A tried and true formula that works very well with games of its genre.
I'm on the fence about this game, and if I could give it a "neutral" review, I would; since Steam only has "Recommended" vs "Not Recommended", I decided to lean towards the latter (therefore allowing all the rabid fanboys to downvote this without a second thought to help combat their own insecurities). Whatever helps you sleep at night, it doesn't change my review and what I have to say about the game.
The gameplay is all fine and good, but this game honestly feels more luck-based than skill-based. That's not to say this game is not skill-based; utilizing cover to avoid bullets, then shooting them at opportune moments is a key element of this game. I say the game is luck based because of primarily two things; the levelling system, and the procedural generation of each stage.
The levelling system is very straightforward; kill enemies, collect their exp drops, level up, select one of four randomly provided power ups at the end of the stage, continue. This is all fine and good, except for how (obviously) some power-ups are much better than others. Several times have I been starved for an ability that would prove most useful because the RNG failed to provide.
As for the procedural generated levels, several times have I had a somewhat decent run instantly taken away from me by spawning in the next level surrounded by enemies with absolutely no cover, obliterating me within seconds. Regardless of who you are and how long you've played these kinds of games, no amount of 'skill' can allow someone to pop into a brand new level and
avoid a slew of bullets coming from literally every direction while effectively fighting back. Sometimes the level spawns many enemies into a tight room with a 1-block entryway, making it almost impossible to clear it out without taking some form of damage. To add insult to injury in such scenarios, many enemies move very quickly and do collision damage. My use of the term 'procedural generation' is stretching it for this game; the only thing inherently procedural about it is the fact that there's never a part of the map that's inaccessible in some form.
Comparing other 'difficult' games (such as Spelunky, Hotline Miami, and Super Meat Boy), you die a lot, but each death in those games feels like it was your fault that you died, and you learn something from it that can be used to improve your next attempt. Nuclear Throne does not provide that. Each death feels cheap and the only thing you can really tell yourself in terms of improvement if you decide to try again is "get better". Have you ever asked a teacher for help, and they simply told you to "do better"? I have. He was subsequently fired. I've seen and played games that are hard for the right reasons; Nuclear Throne is hard for the wrong reasons.
Of course, all of what I said can be "expected of roguelikes", and "if you don't like that kind of game, don't play it". Roguelike fans call it art, I call it poor game design.
In conclusion, Nuclear Throne isn't a bad game by any means; it just has some glaring flaws that really take away from its long-term enjoyability. After all, only a masochist would enjoy repeatedly attempting something, only to result in failure with little to no sense of progress.

Sad to see so many players begin their review with, "its a great game, an improvement over the first game, BUT...microtransactions" and ultimately give it a thumbs down just based on that ideology.
These kinds of games have continued to get more and more complex and expensive to create...which is what we all want...yet, we, as a consumer base tend to act like we are entitled to paying the same price that was being paid for games 10 years ago. $59.
If there is not some way for a game developer to make more revenue, one of two things will happen...that game developer will need to be bought out by a bigger, more financially secure company that can front the MASSIVE costs for an eventual payout while paying people and keeping up a building and equipment necessary for making games...or they just go out of business. I am sure you can think of several examples of both of these things happening.
Listen, there is no alternative to those outcomes if we, as a consumer, refuse to pay any more than $59 for ALL games of ALL time. Perhaps game developers could just make games that fit the $59 budget we seem to insist they work with but I am sure we all can understand what those limitations will do to the games we look forward to playing eventually.
While we all operate in the mindset of playability and fun, they have to operate under the pressure of market potential, market projection, upfront costs and maintaining the development of a product that produces zero profit until it is complete. It is a huge gamble to the tune of 100s of millions of dollars with no guarantee they will sell enough to get into profit. Especially when a large portion of consumers, potentially interested in buying the product, tend to use their ability to review the product not based on the merits of the game itself but solely on any attempt made to increase revenue.
It is not pay to win here. The game is perfectly playable without paying a single cent over the original purchase price. Additional content, however, is available if you choose to purchase it.
I think the game is an improvement over the first and I enjoyed the first one very much so this game is made well and does exactly what I would reasonably expect it to do based on the price I paid...even more so.
A whole lot of elitist, entitled behavior in the gaming community that obviously has no idea what it takes to make a game we all want to play. If an alternative route towards increasing the capability for developers to recoup their expense doesn't make its way into the future of gaming in a way that we all can accept, there is no future for gaming. Its that simple.

You can probably complete all three ends in about one hour which may be exiciting in some extent, and the rest belongs to the achievements time (or boring rubbish time for this game), due to the inconvenient UI (your need to click on the text and scroll down EVERYTIME to see what the choices are, unless you can remember all of them/their numbers) and the inability to save/load (if you made a wrong choice, which of course happens a lot, you will have to start over from the beginning).
In summary, this game is a tiny dessert enjoyable for the first runs and its trading cards worth its price when discount. Not recommended for those who is looking for a fantasy visual novel with a good story.

Nuclear Throne is a rouge-like bullet hell shooter that's as fun to play as it is difficult. There's a lot of chaos that goes on during fights and it can get pretty hectic. Never has it felt more great to feel your controller rumble to the hits you place on enemies. You will die, a lot in this game. But that's what makes it so fun to play. You want to get better and reach new areas in hopes that you will reach the nuclear throne.
There are many characters to choose, each having their own strengths. Fish can roll, which makes for getting out of tight spots while Melting--the weakest of the bunch, can set off huge explosions. I personally love Fish due to his roll ability and Crystal--who can block attacks for a limited time. I do have to say that these unique abilites don't completely change the way you play with these characters, so it's a bit disappointing on that front.
Nuclear Throne's main hook is mutation. After exiting a level, you can choose a mutation (assuming you have enough Rads) which can range from having an extra life to faster reload times to reducing enemy HP. Even though these mutations aren't permanent you do feel a sense of progression as you fight your way from level to level.
From a visual standpoint, it looks pretty great, though many won't like that it's a locked 30fps game. My only gripe with this game is the lack of online play. Seriously, it's such a missed opportunity. I would love to play with people via online co-op.
Overall, I really like Nuclear Throne and really recommend the game. Enjoy the fustration. Enjoy the chaos. But more importantly, good luck reaching the Nuclear Throne!

Shadow of War is an immensely fun game. The dramatic, relatable storylines are a step above other mainstream games. The combat is insanely immersive. Each battle with an Orc Captain is wildly different. There are so many fine details at play during these battles, it would be rare to fight one Captain and be fully reminded of another. And new Captains seem to ambush you out of nowhere.
If you enjoyed Shadow of Mordor you will be in awe at all the cool stuff they've added for you to do. SoW has the best combat mechanics I've ever seen (especially melee), much improved and polished from it's predecessor. Sometimes I'll look at a zone on the map and think, "Hmm, it's kind of small," but then I'll get into the action and forget where I am. There's always a new angle with a different feel.
This game is massive and there's so much to accomplish and explore. Not to mention it's action packed all the way through. I don't want to get into detail about all the crazy things you can do because you can watch trailers and twitch, you know. But I will say:
If you've ever dreamed of flying around on a dragon and burning halpless groundies like Daenerys Targaryen, this game is for you.
That being said, there are two major complaints about this game and they have nothing to do with the gameplay experience. I will outline the chief complaint and explain why it is unfounded. I won't detail the "Forthog Orc-Slayer DLC controversy" because at the time of this writing WB has recognized their mistake, made the DLC free and sent a donation to the family.
1. Microtransactions:
The scope of this game is huge. The storylines, the battles, the dialog and all of the little things. Wow. Honestly, this game is worth way more than $60. I'm at 85 hours (on hard mode) and still loving it. 70 cents an hour for premium entertainment? That's one hell of a bargain.
Mainstream games have been selling for $60 for quite some time now. Set aside development costs. Let's think about inflation and growing player demands. Games have been getting better and better but the price has remained the same. There's only one way to keep that price where it is and that's microtransactions.
For those of you who haven't played this game, you can buy gold loot crates with cash and silver loot crates with in-game currency (free). Both types give you followers that you can position to your liking around the world or in one of the various forts you've conquered. You get slightly better rewards with gold crates, but they're the same type of rewards as in silver crates.
If you're a true bawss however, you can get followers by hunting them down and mind @#!%ing them into submission - in other words, by playing the game. And let me tell you, each encounter is going to be exciting, unique and worth your time and effort.
Of all the time I've spent on this game, not once have I felt the urge to purchase gold to buy loot crates for the simple reason that I'd rather play the game as much as possible. One important thing to note: it's not multiplayer, you don't have to buy these things because there's no one to get ahead of. Even still, you can complete online single player challenges to earn gold to buy gold loot crates.
____ In Closing ____
Middle-Earth: Shadow of War has seen a ton of bad press for all the wrong reasons. No one's out there bashing Blizzard games for their microtransactions in games such as Hearthstone or Overwatch. The loot crates in SoW don't help all that much and the game is not even multiplayer. Don't feed the frenzy and miss out on an amazing game experience. Because it is truly a badass game.

I've been holding off to write a review for this game for a while. I wanted to get a complete review out, and now, 33 hours later, I feel like I'm finally ready to write a complete review. So, here it is. My review for The Political Machine 2016. Let me just clarify that I did not play The Political Machine 2012.
Summary:
The Political Machine 2016 is an election simulator made by Stardock Entertainment. In this game, you can simulate the presidential election with a variety of candidates. If you play your cards right, you can come out on top with all 50 states, or, if you utterly fail, you can end up being humiliated by your political rival. Whether you win or lose is entirely up to you.
Candidates:
Some of the candidates included are candidates in the early stages of the 2016 Presidential election. This includes Chris Christie, Marco Rubio, Bernie Sanders, and Ted Cruz. This is only a small amount of the candidates. There are also memorable politicians such as Sarah Palin, Nancy Pelosi, Michelle Obama, and John Kerry. There are of course many more potential candidates than this, including some independents who barely agree with the party they are placed with(Gary Johnson is a Republican, and Michael Bloomberg is a Democrat). However, with the DLC, many more candidates are added, such as Jimmy Carter and Richard Nixon. I won't spoil the rest, since part of the fun is finding out who the other candidates are. There are a total of 6 candidates to beat(and unlock) for each party.
Game Mechanics:
Once you start your campaign towards the White House, there are many things to need to do. You can upgrade your Campaign Headquarters to bring in more cash rather than fundraising(trust me, you'll need to fundraise either way. Campaign Headquarters only bring in about $90,000, which is tiny compared to the costs of ads.). You can also build Outreach centers, which help you get endorsement points. Endorsements are very important, and can change the whole election for the better or for the worse. The last building you can build is a Consulting Office. These help give you points to hire operatives, which are crucial to the game. Operatives can give you a strategic advantage in certain states(such as keeping the rising democrat ratings in California when you have awareness maxed out), and can help you secure a victory.
The next mechanic in the game is ads. You can make Ground game ads, which are small ads promoting a certain view. They are extremely cheap, but very weak. If you want to get your views out there, you're gonna have to spend a lot more. This will let you place a TV ad, which can shift certain state demographics outside of the state you placed the ad in. TV ads are very useful, but very expensive. Use them wisely. The other extremely useful mechanic is the speech mechanic. Speeches can shift entire states, and allow you to turn that state towards your side, if your awareness is low. Be careful, however, since speeches in states with maxed out awareness can hurt you. The final crucial mechanic is fundraising. At some point in your campaign, you will lose money, in which case you will need to fundraise. In richer states, you can earn up to $450,000. This is a lot of money, when compared to the amount some less populated states will give you.
Playability:
This game is very fun. With the amount of variables such as Candidates and demographics, this will keep you very entertained. Also, with the campaign DLC, you could be spending a lot of time trying to get the really good characters. At some point, you will hit a wall, though. That is unfortunate about this game, since the first 10-20 hours are very fun(or even 30 hours in my case).
Errors:
While most of the time the game runs very smoothly, it does occasionally crash and freeze. I've seen many cases where I finish giving a speech, only to see the game run extremely slow, causing me to restart the game. And when the game restarts, it sets you back. It doesn't save where you left off, it set you back about 4 weeks. This is very annoying. Another issue is when a certain black box appears in the middle of the screen and breaks the game. Restart, setting the game back. This is by far the most annoying part of the game.
Final Verdict:
In the end, I'm very glad I bought this game. I feel like I got my money's worth. With all the candidates, and the possible creation of a custom candidate, this game is well worth the $9.99 price tag. The mechanics in the game are very smooth. While there are many glitches and crashes, and the game does hit a wall in terms of replayability, it was an overall fun experience. The Campaign DLC is worth it's price tag. In the end, I feel like this game was well worth the money I paid for it. With all factors considered, I'm going to give this game a final score of 84/100. I liked most of the game, however, I feel like Stardock could have done more to fix errors and put more things into the game. If they put those things in, this game is easily a 90/100. So, I leave you with that score and a lot to think about. If you are considering buying this game, understand that it may be not the most accurate, but it is certainly more fun than most political sims out there.

General Overview: This is a well done narrative driven game with some unique game play that reminds me of Dead Space, although the combat is a bit less intense.  Great mixture of action and story with excellent pasting.  Its occasional weak voice acting and outdated character models can be off-putting at times but in general the well written narrative makes those small this irrelevant.  Great Twin Peaks/David Lynch atmosphere with psychological horror that literally chilled my spine.  As a writer this game is ultimately appealing and greatly appreciated.  While there is little reason to replay other than to relive the story (which I for one will do in about a year or so) there are collectibles and achievements galore here.  Remedy did a great job with the game but a sequel would be difficult though not implausible  I would love for this to have a real follow up (American Nightmare is more like a DLC) but only if the quality of the narrative can be maintained.
TL;DNR: 9: A great psychological horror/survival game with a very strong narrative and unique game play.  For those who enjoy and value strong stories within their games and enjoy things by David Lynch (Twin Peaks, Blue Velvet...) then this is a must play.
Technology/engine: 8: Runs very smoothly and is well optimized for PC.
AI: 7: The AI is well developed but a bit predictable.
Graphics: 7: The graphics a decent although texture qualities are mix and the character models are dated.  The set pieces, however, are great - heavily detailed, great art style, and creates a depth of immersion and atmosphere that many games seem to ignore.
Sound: 10: The sound in this game is very well developed with lots of depth and variability in ambient sound and combat sounds are spot on.
Soundtrack: 9: Great soundtrack with well chosen episodic theme songs at the end of each of its 6 episodes and great music throughout that fits the action and the intensity of the moment and really adds to the games pacing as well as atmosphere.
Voice acting: 8:  Most of the voice acting is well done and convincing although there are moments where it fades into the acceptable range.  Never the less, its minor acting issues do not really detract from its story nor its immersion.
Crafting: N/A
Customization: N/A
Game play systems: 9:  The game play in Alan Wake is well developed and fun with a good mix of occasional splashes of reward exploration (at times the exploration for hidden caches of resources may not be a good choice and the intensity of that decision comes through very well), game relevant puzzles of sorts (more like just dangerous tasks really), wonderful use of light as a weapon, and all around just a fun game.
Controls: 10: This is a PC port done right.  The controls are excellent and can be rebound to any key.  The controls are simple and clean and are quickly picked up.
Story: 10: Very well written and very well executed.  A David Lynch style story that really pulls you in and makes you care about Bright Falls and its inhabitants as well as the Alan and his buddy Barry.  If you like David Lynch's work you owe it to yourself to play this game.
Multiplayer: N/A

I would give Alan Wake game a 6/10 overall.
You play as Alan Wake, a writer who becomes involved in a supernatural experience through which he must survive and find a way to destroy whatever is causing things to change. It is a combination of third-person action/shooter/adventure/horror/survival all in one game.
The game presents a well told story that spans a length of time that will keep you mostly interested throughout the length of the game. While some of the characters are interesting enough, some of them are pretty dull or cliche, making them pretty forgettable or downright irritating. Alan Wake himself isn't the most exciting charachter ever created as the main protagonist, but his role is well played out and realistic enough - a writer that is forced into a very unfamiliar and dangerous situation. It makes sense in that regard, which keeps it from being too over-the-top when mixed with the gameplay. The music and voice acting are good enough, though not mind blowing. Most of the characters are believable enough, and Wake himself does a fine job.
Gameplay largely revolves around using a 2-part combination of weapons to dispatch enemies. Alan Wake does a fantastic job with lighting effects, some of the best I have seen, even in an older game. Light is one of your main weapons that you use to strip an "outer defense barrier" of sorts; you then have a fairly basic set of weapons that you use to finish enemies off. Wake can perform dodge maneuvers that can help avoid attacks, which can create some very cinematic slow-mo sequences that look pretty good. Overall, the combat feels good, and when you successfully survive a tough wave or two of enemies, you feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥
Unfortunatley, the gameplay also has a few drawbacks. As good as the combat sequences can be at times, they can just as often be incredibly frustrating. For certain battles, it is as if the game expects you to fight, but for others it seems to expect you to know you are supposed to flee. This is fine and understandable within the realm of the world, but it makes it frustrating when there is no real way to tell which you are supposed to do. It is not very fun to run from all enemies as your character fatigues and you are attacked by bad guys you cannot see. This leads to you stumbling through the darkness time after time frantically lost with zero health and depleted ammo. At other times you are stocked with more ammo than you could ever hope to use. With unbalanced sequences, sometimes you are underpowered and sometimes an in-game God.
That being said, you do get the chance to fight with comrades later in the game, which works very well. They are helpful in killing enemies without doing all the work. It is too bad that, as with many other things, the second half of the game is much more interesting than the first. For the first half of the game you spend most of your time by yourself in dark forest after dark forest. While the vistas look very good, it can be a little dull and repetitive. I found it hard to come back to the game in the beginning especially.
In the end I recommend the game because it has some good parts, including a good story, interesting world/enemies, and gameplay that feels good when it works well. The downside to it though is that while it has good parts, most of them are offset or lessened by an equally strong negative aspect. I couldn't go through most of the game without encountering something that was designed poorly or executed in a weak way.
If you are able to get it cheap, as it usually goes on sale for only a few dollars on steam, I recommend playing it with knowing what you may run into that will frustrate you. Otherwise, play something else that has fewer flaws and stronger strengths.

I bought this game back in early access and I thought it was a cool idea.  It kept my attention for about 25 hours, enough for me to mess around with different ship configurations and get a couple things stranded in orbit.  I played the career mode back then and played without instructions, and had a very hard time understanding how to unlock new objects when I wasn't getting any more points from the missions I was doing.
I recently went back to play it and was not impressed with how overly-complicated everything was, how difficult it was to understand what I was supposed to do, and the walls of text during the tutorials.  Being bombarded with half-filling fuel tanks, center of mass and perfect placement of thrusters by the 4th tutorial made me not want to keep learning how to play the game properly (rather than just messing around and barely making any proress like before).
I think this game only appeals to a very niche market, and is the complete opposite of a casual, pick-up-and-play type of game.  If the controls and options were simplified and the design was more focused on seeing the breadth of content in the game, it would be much more enjoyable.  Considering I had already played before and the barrier for re-entry (no pun intended) was too high, I wasn't impressed with how the game has shaped up since Early Access.

Edit: Now that I've had some more time with the game, I'll give a more serious review. This is based on my experience after the first patch.
Pros:
- The story is fantastic and the characters are unique. The developers definitely met and exceeded my expectations in this area.
- The setting - I've always wanted to play an open-world game that allows me to explore New Orleans, and Mafia III has given me just that.
- Great animation and voice acting during cutscenes that make you genuinely care about this story's characters
- Several gameplay improvements over Mafia II, such as:
- You can now physically attack female civilians, instead of just pushing them (Hooray for equality!)
- You now have the ability to have a mobile weapons store delivered to you that allows you to buy all the guns you need, from pistols to automatic rifles to rocket launchers. You'll never have to drive across the map to stock up on specialized ammo again.
- Much better stealth gameplay
- A working rearview mirror when driving
- More I forgot, but will update this review if I remember them.
Cons:
- The game crashed a couple of times when I first began playing, but I believe the new patch fixed this issue (for me, at least).
- There is no animation that shows Lincoln honking the horn inside a car. You tap a button and sounds just magically come out of the car while Lincoln keeps both hands on the wheel (this didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game, just thought I'd point it out).
- The AI is pretty stupid. I remember one warehouse full of enemies I was able to clear out by hiding behind a door and stealth killing a gang member who came over to see what the noise was. Then I killed five of his friends in the same manner, because they each wanted to see what was behind the door that kept knifing criminals to death.
- Right now, my biggest issue with the game is the lack of dialogue for pedestrians. You'll often hear them repeating the same line over and over and over, even if you haven't left the area. I was playing one mission where I had to eliminate one of the crime bosses from a certain area of the city who was being guarded by several henchmen, so I decided to try and take a stealth approach. As I was sneaking around, trying to stealth kill them all one at a time, one enemy kept saying someting along the lines of "It's not right to keep a working man waiting." nonstop. I would have preferred him to just say it once and be done with it, but I had to listen to him repeat himself through the whole mission until I could sneak over and kill him quietly. It really discourages stealth approaches and urges players to go in guns blazing just to shut them up as quickly as possible. It also takes away a lot of the immersion in what otherwise feels like a dark, serious story.
Overall, it's a nice game so far. Although the gameplay is improved over its predecessor, it feels average compared to similar games that have come out recently. The story is definitely what makes the game stand out and I look forward to continuing the journey of Lincoln Clay. I'll try to update this review as I play more of the game, especially if more patches are released.

Update 10/8: The framerate has been officially unlocked and I'm getting 75-90 fps. The game is smooth as butter now.
I want to address the "Elephant in the Room" and admit the faults of the PC version. It has a 30 fps cap, and it suffers from similar issues as Quantum Break with blurry textures that appear upscaled. I have a decent pc with a GTX 1080 and a 1440p 144hz monitor. I was angry about the fps cap, but they are clearly working on a fix at the moment and I'd rather focus on the game itself, which ultimately will be what remains.
So far, the game has tremendous atmosphere. The story, which is traditionally a hallmark of the Mafia series, is on point. It will be subjective, but it hits close to home since I'm a veteran. I truly understand the difficulties adjusting when you get back home and falling back into the bad crowd. This goes beyond that, but we all have protagonists we gravitate toward whether they are right or wrong.
The story is gripping, and the style is cinematic. This is not a 30fps joke, but I really like the flashbacks and the attempt at character development. The racism is front and center, but it's accurate as a period piece. We live in a time where people are triggered by everything, so I commend the developers for showcasing the less dignified times of our history. I have family that still acts this way, and this really shows how deeply it is rooted in their minds based on their upbringing.
The music and sound are quite good, with many notable tracks. The radio stations in the car are littered with talk and advertisements. I always found this interesting in other open world driving type games.
Conclusion: The graphics in particular need some PC love. The models are quite good but the world is a bit lacking in places. This might just be an "open world" side-effect that won't be changed. I'm willing to accept it because the gameplay is good. The animations are exceptional. The lipsync is perfect in cutscenes and the combat animations are nuanced and fluid. This was unexpected, because I expected things to be a bit janky. Outside of the 30fps lock and the inconsistent textures, I've experienced some lighting issues while driving. It's not a deal breaker but it's worth mentioning. I wanted to write a review earlier than I would normally, because most have been negative. I completely agree with anyone being mad about the fps lock, but this isn't Arkham Knight. I've had no crashes and it runs at a consistent framerate. That being said, I'm looking forward to the patch that fixes some of these issues.

In real life, I'm a beginner pilot. To begin with, this game feels more like a "adjust your seat and field of view" simulator, than an actual flight simulator. I can't even comment on the simulation much, as I've only just got the game set up properly, although it seems very good from the 50+ hours I put up with the default view and flew around in the non steam version of this game.
When you first start the game, your field of view will be so far zoomed in you'll feel like a blinkered horse with its face smeared against the inside of the cockpit windscreen. If you want to look at your instruments (airspeed, altimeter, DI etc), you have to take your eyes completely off the horizon. VFR flight from the default view is damn near impossible.
To fix this, go to the game's settings, and note the key bindings for moving your eyepoint backwards (by default: Ctrl + Enter) and downwards (by default: SHIFT + Backspace). In your config files (Appdata\Roaming\Microsoft\FSX), open fsx.cfg in Notepad and set WideViewAspect to True (erase "False" and type "True". In the Cameras.cfg, under camera002, set InitialZoom to 0.3, so you have a bearable field of view (you can do this in-flight by holding the spacebar and scrolling the mouse wheel back).
Once you get in-flight, use the aforementioned eyepoint key bindings to move your view as you would like it, and if you hold the spacebar, you can use the mouse to move your view. When you let go of the spacebar, your view is locked there. Very handy IMO.
If you're hardcore and want all the options in-flight, an Xbox 360 controller doesn't really have enough buttons. You'll have enough bindings for your throttle, control surfaces, and I even set pitch and rudder trim, but if you want to mess with landing lights, carb heat, fuel mixtures, individual engine throttles etc, you'll need to mess with the keyboard bindings or invest in a proper flight joystick.
Sadly the game counts the keyboard's num pad buttons and the home, end, page up, page down, and arrow keys as the same thing, so you lose some key bindings there.
However once you've set everything up, this game is fantastic.

I really, really wish I could recommend this game... but I just can't.  The setting is great stuff, but virtually everything else is shoddy.  Skill balance is poor and you can completely do without many of them, stat balance is poor, combat is dull and uninteresting, the conversation system is pretty worthless, the custom character system doesn't really matter because you will never have situations that let you build personalities for anybody, navigating the big maps with no fast travel system is an enormous chore, skill checks like lockpicking eat up absurd amounts of time with the silly animation system from them (there is NO REASON they could not be instant checks instead of taking 15-30 seconds for every attempt) and you are CONSTANTLY using these checks, and considering that the game plain just doesn't look very good, it hogs an inexcusably-large amount of resources.  If any optimization at all was done, you wouldn't be able to tell; the minimum requirements for this game are ridiculous.
But by far the biggest failing of this game is that nearly everything seems designed to just waste more and more time.  Running speed is slow.  Skill checks are slow.  Traveling the world map is slow.  Trying to get to trade areas is slow.  Progressing the story is slow.  Even if you crank up the combat speed to maximum, you are going to get bogged down by the absurdly-high jamming rates on anything that shoots bullets, which just a plain terrible mechanic.  Even just maneuvering the dang CAMERA around is slow; it ratchets around to one of eight positions at an aggravatingly-slow speed you can't do anything about.
Basically, the game feels like it was designed with no regard for game design advances that have happened over the last couple of decades.  Not because it's "retro", but because of bad design.  Unless you simply MUST have another post-apocalyptic setting to play in, skip this game.  "Make everything tedious" seems to have been the one universal design objective here, and they succeeded, sadly enough.
If you must pick this up, wait for a sale.  This is not a purchase worth $40.
EDIT: Around 20 hours with this game now since it went to full release.  The issues do not get better, they just get worse.  Backtracking goes up enormously as the game continues, and the game starts throwing problems at you with literally zero explanation for how to solve them short of several hours of random searching.  Even on sale, this game won't be worth it until there's a fan patch to fix at least some of the severe shortcomings.
Save your money and buy Fallout 1 and 2.  If you already own them, save your time and play those instead of this.  At least the problems in those games are because they are ACTUALLY OLD instead of using "retro" as an excuse, but they're still a blast compared to this junky piece of work.

Life is Strange features charming writing, well-rounded and multifaceted characters, and absolutely fantastic story arcs. Almost every major development was either a white-knight fantasy moment, or a tear-jerking punch in the gut. I readily admit to breaking down crying when I saw one scene in particular
.
One gripe is that the teenage angst which was central to the plot was a little hard to relate to/sit through at times; the same goes for the often meme-centric dialogue and "easter eggs". Having been a teenager recently, I feel like the story could have used a little more realistic input from a few of them. Another part that briefly lost me, and may have even devalued the ending
was
. However, that's not nearly enough to turn this review into anything other than a glowing one. A few moments made me laugh (albeit probably for the wrong reasons), but far more moments made me want to/actually tear up, and I find that a lot more compelling in a game.
Gameplay-wise, it's interesting, but sometimes it could get a little awkward controlling it with a mouse and keyboard (I'm not plugging in a controller for this). In particular, the rewinding mechanic often seemed to transpire at frustratingly variable rates, but I soon realized that it depended on whether you were rewinding through dialogue that's already happened or something going on in the environment. Basically, the main character's time-rewinding powers - while a clever mechanic which, combined with its adept weaving into the plot, kept this game from being an interactive soap opera - got pretty irritating at certain points. It should be noted, however, that this may have been intentional (or at least excusable), since
, so I'll overlook that one too!
Moreover, I cannot believe I put off playing this game until a year after I got it, since it has become my all-time favorite game in only the twelve hours I've played it so far (at time of writing). Get this game if you want to feel everything a person can feel, in a short period of time!

You need to know this game inside and out to have a good run, and that may be seen as too much of a time investment for some, and the variety minimizes the deviation from run to run, making it a little more samey than other roguelikes.
In short, the skill celling is this genre's equivalent to Civ's, with a replay value that varies wildly from person to person. 7/10

- innovative game mechanics
- well written story
- great sense of humour
IT DOES NOT HAVE ANY.
You start as nameless adventurer, who enters some castle. With every passing scene of your journey through it, you will have to make decisions. Sadly, all you can choose is which door to pass, to slay or not to slay character you met, and to attack or dodge an attack.
THIS IS ALL THAT GAME HAS TO OFFER.

To start this review, I would like to introduce "Lorm the Legend" -- the plague that I created upon middle earth.
Chapter I - The Creation
The story and creation of Lorm begins shortly after I conquer the frosty stronghold of Seregost, in which doing so unlocks the pit challenges. Time passes and I start finishing up all that is left to do in Seregost and that beaming orange light circle on the map draws me in - I have to try my hand in a bit of Uruk fighting. As I prompt the challenge I am given the opportunity to select one of my brave and deadly warriors to undergo the task of murdering the challenging fighter. This is where my favourite and most loyal Uruk comes in -- Borgu Quick-Blades; A poisonous dark slayer who has been my bodyguard for as long as I can remember. The fighting begins and Borgu makes quick work of the first two challenges without me breaking as much as a sweat, little did I know this was just the beginning of the end for poor Borgu. Full of lust for blood I send Borgu into the pit once more against a foe I thought to be harmless - Lorm the Legend. I started the fight without checking what Lorm was capable of, boy was that a mistake. Lorm the Legend wasn't just legend by title: he was actually a legendary, not only that he was 20 levels higher than my prime captain Borgu. The fight begins and I start sweating bullets, will Borgu prevail despite being at such a disadvantage? Will Lorm have mercy and spare my poor captain? -- No. He did no such thing. He unsheaths his poisonous spear and metallic shield from his back and charges into battle with a stupid♥♥♥♥♥grin on his face. Borgu didn't stand a chance, as soon as he landed a single blow against Lorm it was over... Lorm grabbed him, threw him to the ground and beat him to death. To me this was an act of WAR. I could not sit there idly and let him escape having murdered my trusty Borgu. I proceed to charge into battle against Lorm with dominated Uruks by my side, full of rage and ready to fight. As I engage with Lorm and we clash weapons, he laughs and witters on about how he is the greatest Uruk who has ever lived - I thought he was joking... but what happened afterwards is nothing to laugh at. The fight continues and it's just Lorm and I left in the pit; I'm down to my last chance to get back up again and the battle looks to be nowhere near finishing. This mother trucker would not take damage from range and poison, to make it even worse he could not be executed and couldn't be frozen or vaulted. After numerous blows to each other, Lorm extended his long arm of the law and grabbed me by the throat. This is when I knew it was all over. Lorm throws me to ground and does a repeat of what happened to Borgu -- he mashed my face in with his bloodied fists. Lorm the Legend had won, he began to join the Uruk army of Seregost and had increased his level all the way to 49 which was 20 levels above my own. Time had passed after our duel in the pit and after much frustration and failed attempts to take him down I had well and truly had enough - it was time to leave.
Chapter II - The Destruction
There I am; playing my hand in the arena once more -- except this time it was in Nurnen. Since my duel with Lorm I had created a few decent Uruks from the pits and was trying to forge the ultimate warrior in an attempt to bring him down once and for all. Little did I know he was onto my plan like a tramp on a chips. I'm in southern Nurnen, chasing down a potential new recruit to the legion. BANG -- An Uruk has just ambushed me and thrown me to the side, It was Lorm. He had tracked me down from Seregost just to add even more insult to injury. He laughs as he begins to attack me once more; I knew this was my going to be my final encounter with the Legend known as Lorm or he was once more going to strike me down and continue to plague my army. I have learnt many knew things since our first encounter and I have learnt how to cheese move him, although that still didn't make him an easy opponent to beat as he could two shot me whenever he pleased. I proceed to call forth a Graug and my newly appointed Olog Beastmaster bodyguard known as Ur-Hakon the Faithful - and boy did he live up to his title. Ur-Hakon arrives with his pack of Carragor to help finally elimate the legend of Lorm. The battle starts and there is constant explosions and the sounds of beasts rattling through my headset. This was intense. All of Lorms loyal followers were quickly dealt with and he was all alone. Surrounded by a Graug, pack of Carragor and the mighty Ranger -- he knew he was about to be bested. Nothing is ever quite that easy with Lorm though, to add a final slap in the face he had downed Ur-Hakon in an attempt to kill another one of my most trusted captains. I couldn't let this happen again, flashbacks of Borgu were flashing right before my eyes, I could picture the exact moment his skull was crushed -- I was not going to let this happen again. I drew my legendary sword of vengeance from it's sheath and ran straight for Lorm; it was now or never. I start slashing him from side to side, lowering his health from slither to practically non-existant. It was at this moment I knew that one more hit and he will be gone forever, the plague of Lorm lifted from Mordor. Although, despite wanting to rip his head off where he stood I knew the defeat of Lorm couldn't come down to a slimy bash of the sword. One idea quickly sprung to mind before he took his last breath; Elven Rage. I proceed to beam up in a beautiful blue light, mashing the X button so hard that there would be nothing left of Lorm. The rage stops, the dust dissapears and everything comes to a holt. There he is, laying flat on the floor soaked in his own blood -- Lorm the Legend had be slain.
10/10

In Bermuda a group of friends gets suddendly abducted by seafaring humanoid aliens: after a few experiments the beam that'd have brought them back home and erased their memory malfunctions and they're left wondering whether they'd wait or try and escape the vessel.
The game is a short visual novel with a few simple stealth sections thrown in, it starts in a pretty light and funny way but isn't afraid to show violence and death in its final acts.
-the story is quite good and I appreciated the serious turn of events in the final acts
-fully voice acted, the actors themselves do a good job
-decent soundtrack
-optional conversations add to the story and flesh out characters
-the stealth sections mix up things a bit
-so-so graphics
-stealth sections are very easy
-quite many cliches thrown around
-very short at 1 hour long
I'm not a fun of visual novels but I appreciated the game as a whole: the story started in a pretty unoriginal way and some characters do feel as they're part of the usual visual novel fare but as things went along more mature themes started to emerge and certain individuals did show a pretty dark side with their actions. You'll also have to face 2D stealth sections where you hide from guards or distract them by turning off lights, entering bathrooms or activating alarms: they're quite short and easy but at least provide a change of pace from clicking through dialogue.
All things considered Bermuda wasn't a bad way to pass one hour, it's a decent novel at a reasonable price (even more so if on sale or, like me, it's from a bundle).
