Edit: Now that I've had some more time with the game, I'll give a more serious review. This is based on my experience after the first patch.
Pros:
- The story is fantastic and the characters are unique. The developers definitely met and exceeded my expectations in this area.
- The setting - I've always wanted to play an open-world game that allows me to explore New Orleans, and Mafia III has given me just that.
- Great animation and voice acting during cutscenes that make you genuinely care about this story's characters
- Several gameplay improvements over Mafia II, such as:
- You can now physically attack female civilians, instead of just pushing them (Hooray for equality!)
- You now have the ability to have a mobile weapons store delivered to you that allows you to buy all the guns you need, from pistols to automatic rifles to rocket launchers. You'll never have to drive across the map to stock up on specialized ammo again.
- Much better stealth gameplay
- A working rearview mirror when driving
- More I forgot, but will update this review if I remember them.
Cons:
- The game crashed a couple of times when I first began playing, but I believe the new patch fixed this issue (for me, at least).
- There is no animation that shows Lincoln honking the horn inside a car. You tap a button and sounds just magically come out of the car while Lincoln keeps both hands on the wheel (this didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game, just thought I'd point it out).
- The AI is pretty stupid. I remember one warehouse full of enemies I was able to clear out by hiding behind a door and stealth killing a gang member who came over to see what the noise was. Then I killed five of his friends in the same manner, because they each wanted to see what was behind the door that kept knifing criminals to death.
- Right now, my biggest issue with the game is the lack of dialogue for pedestrians. You'll often hear them repeating the same line over and over and over, even if you haven't left the area. I was playing one mission where I had to eliminate one of the crime bosses from a certain area of the city who was being guarded by several henchmen, so I decided to try and take a stealth approach. As I was sneaking around, trying to stealth kill them all one at a time, one enemy kept saying someting along the lines of "It's not right to keep a working man waiting." nonstop. I would have preferred him to just say it once and be done with it, but I had to listen to him repeat himself through the whole mission until I could sneak over and kill him quietly. It really discourages stealth approaches and urges players to go in guns blazing just to shut them up as quickly as possible. It also takes away a lot of the immersion in what otherwise feels like a dark, serious story.
Overall, it's a nice game so far. Although the gameplay is improved over its predecessor, it feels average compared to similar games that have come out recently. The story is definitely what makes the game stand out and I look forward to continuing the journey of Lincoln Clay. I'll try to update this review as I play more of the game, especially if more patches are released.

If you came here looking for a review, you have come to the wrong place, but if you want some very ♥♥♥♥ing good brownies, you have come to the right place. You're welcome for an actual recipe, not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ copy and paste pie recipe. Trust me nothing goes wrong with nutella.
INGREDIENTS:
1 c. unsalted butter
2 c. sugar
1/2 tsp. salt
1 c. flour
1 c. cocoa powder
4 eggs
1 (13-oz.) jar Nutella
5 Ferrero Rocher candies, unwrapped and crumbled
DIRECTIONS:
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F.
2. Melt butter in a medium-sized saucepan over medium heat. Add sugar, stirring until combined. 3. Remove from heat and add salt, flour, and cocoa powder, stirring to combine. Whisk in eggs, stirring just until the mixture is combined into a batter. Set aside.
4. Spray an 8"-x-8" pan with cooking spray. Pour half of the batter into the pan. Spoon or lightly drizzle most of the Nutella on top of the batter, forming an even layer over the brownie batter. 5. 5. Use a spoon or silicone spatula to cover the Nutella with the remaining brownie batter. (If you pour the batter straight on top of the Nutella, it will sink into the Nutella and combine into one marbled—yet delicious—mess.)
6. Bake until the top layer of brownies has browned and set, 28 to 30 minutes. It shouldn’t jiggle when you remove it from the oven. (The toothpick test doesn’t work here, since the toothpick will hit the Nutella layer, making the brownies seem uncooked.)
7. Let cool for 15 to 20 minutes, then top with a drizzle of Nutella and crumbled Ferrero Rocher chocolates. Cut into squares and serve.

Update 10/8: The framerate has been officially unlocked and I'm getting 75-90 fps. The game is smooth as butter now.
I want to address the "Elephant in the Room" and admit the faults of the PC version. It has a 30 fps cap, and it suffers from similar issues as Quantum Break with blurry textures that appear upscaled. I have a decent pc with a GTX 1080 and a 1440p 144hz monitor. I was angry about the fps cap, but they are clearly working on a fix at the moment and I'd rather focus on the game itself, which ultimately will be what remains.
So far, the game has tremendous atmosphere. The story, which is traditionally a hallmark of the Mafia series, is on point. It will be subjective, but it hits close to home since I'm a veteran. I truly understand the difficulties adjusting when you get back home and falling back into the bad crowd. This goes beyond that, but we all have protagonists we gravitate toward whether they are right or wrong.
The story is gripping, and the style is cinematic. This is not a 30fps joke, but I really like the flashbacks and the attempt at character development. The racism is front and center, but it's accurate as a period piece. We live in a time where people are triggered by everything, so I commend the developers for showcasing the less dignified times of our history. I have family that still acts this way, and this really shows how deeply it is rooted in their minds based on their upbringing.
The music and sound are quite good, with many notable tracks. The radio stations in the car are littered with talk and advertisements. I always found this interesting in other open world driving type games.
Conclusion: The graphics in particular need some PC love. The models are quite good but the world is a bit lacking in places. This might just be an "open world" side-effect that won't be changed. I'm willing to accept it because the gameplay is good. The animations are exceptional. The lipsync is perfect in cutscenes and the combat animations are nuanced and fluid. This was unexpected, because I expected things to be a bit janky. Outside of the 30fps lock and the inconsistent textures, I've experienced some lighting issues while driving. It's not a deal breaker but it's worth mentioning. I wanted to write a review earlier than I would normally, because most have been negative. I completely agree with anyone being mad about the fps lock, but this isn't Arkham Knight. I've had no crashes and it runs at a consistent framerate. That being said, I'm looking forward to the patch that fixes some of these issues.

Overwatch exists at an intersection between design and artistry, a crossroad at which pure tactile joy meets refined, intelligent design to create a rare spark of magic. As a 6v6 multiplayer, objective-based shooter, it finds accessibility not by lowering the skill ceiling, but by broadening the definition of skill. The person with deadshot aim is no more valuable than the person with the decision-making ability to know when a well-timed ability will turn an engagement, or the person with the map-sense to find the optimal locations to place sentry turrets. While it didn't exactly drown me in options, maps, and modes, it’s blessed with a multitude of tactical layers, and none of them ever came between me and my enjoyment of its intense, swirling teamfights, and thrilling overtime comebacks.
Overwatch does a great many things well, but above all else, its success is built on the backs of its many excellent characters. It’s fitting that the main menu is dominated by one of them at all times; their diverse appearances, origins, and personalities are all laid bare with every pose they strike. Reinhardt’s rocket hammer lands on his shoulder with a meaty clank that invokes a broadsword resting against a medieval knight’s plate armor, and Tracer’s jovial smile is just briefly interrupted by a rebellious bang that slides across her face, tempting her to blow it back into place before re-addressing the camera and blinking all over the place. There’s an intelligent gorilla scientist, a lithe, blue-skinned assassin, and a cybernetic, zen-practicing healer too. It speaks volumes that the one character that adheres to well-worn shooter tropes feels like the odd man out here. They’re all so different that you’d imagine them looking silly standing next to one another, but through careful, subtle visual cues baked into their equipment and attire, they manage to appear as if they share a common world, even if they all hail from different corners of it.
This diversity continues to bear out when you pick a hero and hit the battlefield with them. Though the 21 characters (all of whom are unlocked from the start) are roughly grouped into one of four “roles,” no two feel alike. The robotic, transforming Bastion and the anarchic, explosive-tossing Junkrat are both technically Defenders, but they couldn’t play any more differently from one another. The former looks for a cozy spot overlooking a key choke point and transforms into a minigun turret to run point defense; the latter plays an area-denial game by lobbing timed grenades over long distances, which then sit on the ground blinking angrily, as if to say “go somewhere else” to encroaching enemies before exploding. This strong sense of differentiation is important because it keeps team composition strategies from devolving into simple formulas. No, two Tanks, two Supports, and two Attackers is not the magic solution for a winning team. You have to look much deeper – and when you do, the true beauty of Overwatch’s gameplay shines through.

Lacking the charm, intelligence and writing of some of the better point-and-click games of the past decade, this seems to be a rather lackluster experience and one of the worse written games that came out of Tim Schafer’s production company.
The bad:
-A really lackluster story; and seeing how the story seems to be the game’s focus, this is saying a lot. A good setup for a story that starts out strong but turns out to be quite a mess in both character’s cases. Either lackluster or just completely stupid twists thrown in for good measure.
-Completely simple puzzle solution that most people probably won’t even want to think about. Use everything with everything wins the day here; and even then it is just way too easy to advance.
-Really bad, sometimes grotesque humor. Characters seem to try to be funny, but fail miserably most of the time. While some lines are worth a few chuckles, this does not come even close to some of the amazing writing and humor of other games of the genre like Sam and Max or the Monkey Island series.
-Short. Very short.
-Just really bland characters in general. Some of them can be entertaining, some of them even memorable, but most of the time you will just get thrown more and more characters onto your face without them having any sort of character development, interesting traits, stories, or anything else that would make them stand out.
The good:
-If you like how point-and-clicks work, this is a fairly clean UI that works well.
-Graphics are interesting, but obviously might not be for everyone’s taste. It has a unique art style though, and is visually interesting, so that should be noted.
-Voice acting is mostly really good.
-The atmosphere, especially at the beginning of the game, is really well presented. The game might make you feel uneasy, and even if it doesn’t, it presents its world very well at the start. Sadly, this somewhat falls off as the story progresses, and by the time you hit the end of Act 1, you will notice that the best part of the game was actually the beginning.
In general, it is a game that is hard to recommend to anyone. Horrifyingly short, quite silly mess of a story, uninteresting characters for the most part and just a lack of anything great besides the interesting art style and good voice acting make this a game that only die-hard fans of the genre or Tim Schafer’s games should check out. The rest might want to wait for a sale or just skip it completely.

Please stop comparing this game to Fallout 1 & 2.  Please stop saying things like it's "the true Fallout 3."
It's not.  It's not even close.  It lacks any and all of Fallout's whimsical charm, it forces you to create a squad at the beginning instead of striking out on a lonely, eerie struggle.
Moreover, the game feels like it's high on its own supply.  Overhyped, oversold, generally just not ideal for someone who wants an original Fallout experience.  There's a big difference between this super serious, staid setting and the wacky retro-future of Fallout.
Honestly, this is like a better verison of Fallout: Tactics at the end of the day.  I'm not saying this is a bad game, it's just extremely misleading to compare it to the original Fallout titles.  It is NOT like them.  No traits, no perks, no color or humor.  Not enough attribute and skill points at the beginning for an individual character, since you're supposed to make four.  There's no room for character development or finding your own identity.  The very first conversation, I'm pushed into saying "sir" constantly and being a military recruit.  Maybe I don't WANT to join the rangers.
Maybe I want to just run out into the wilderness or find a city hub and just make my own path - like I did in Fallout.
I realize everyone is different.  But part of the reason I loved Fallout was that my companions had their own minds and I didn't have to micromanage them constantly.  It ended up creating hilarious (and sometimes awful) situations in which my companions surprised me in combat.  Overall, it was more immersive (to me) because I was focused entirely on my own character, instead of mysteriously mind-controlling a group.
Overall, it's hard to say whether or not I recommend the game.  I know some people will love it.  But I can't get over the vast disappointment after I was lead to believe, from literally everyone, that this is like Fallout.  It's not.  Fallout, in my opinion, is way more fun.  Mechanically, aesthetically, and otherwise.
Just one woman's point of view.  Take it or leave it.

This was my first Tele-Episodic game and I will recommend it to people, even if you haven't tried these kind of games before.
I found the story captivating and emotionally fulfilling, though it had some minor flaws. The gameplay is for what the genre is decent.
Although I found that the game isn't particularly aimed at my demographic (Male in his twenties), I still think it was enjoyable. I definitely believe that the game is much more suitable for a teenager as I felt that it could've gained a lot if there was more mature dialogue scenes, violence and sex, not just for the sake of it but I really think the story would've benefited from it. It did tease those things a couple of times but that was it.
That being said, some of the immature decisions the characters make does fit them as they are after all teenagers so it didn't bother me too much in the end.I can still recommend it to everyone but especially if you're a teenager.
I'll keep this short since I do not want to spoil it for you.
This is the main ♥♥♥♥ing selling point of the game. The story is great, it will keep you on edge and make you buy all the episodes so you find out what happens. It
.Had it not had such an emotional story and a roller coster of a ride the game  would not be what it is.
The characters are for the most part great, I didn't really care for any of the main ones however. The ending is satisfying.
One of the problems I have with the story are that some of the 'side-plots' and decisions you make in the game around them really absolutely do not matter in the end. A lot of side story things that are displayed as in 'this will have an effect' later on really do not and in some cases you don't even ever see what your choice ended up changing so they're really filler material but this is a minor pet peeve as the main story is great and your choices do matter.
Many cases of illusion of choice as user HOTSPOT puts it.
The second problem is that the story is flawed and paradoxical in nature once you begin to think about it but I feel like you can easily get past that as that's a thing that a lot of fiction related to time travels suffers from, the point is that this is not detrimental to your enjoyment at all.
The gameplay is decent for what the game is.. as I mentioned this is my first Tele-Episodic game and the only experience I've had was watching a stream of the Walking Dead Gameplay and I really felt that these games are boring and are only story telling based on that. Well this game is a little bit different and it might surprise you, it did surprise me.
There's a really cool element in it where you could reverse time and go back to alter your choices (that's what the game is basically based upon). This is really cool and not only does it tie in with the story perfectly and it makes sense but it also drastically improves your gameplay experience as you're not forced to commit to a choice and you can alter game as you go on.Absolutely amazing feature that was integrated flawlessly and I can barely see myself playing another Episodic game without it.
That being said, one thing that was annoying with the time travel mechanic is that sometimes you couldn't time travel back and immediately alter a choice you made which was a bit random.
In the game at certain points it is exactly explained why you can't go back in time and immediately change what you said and it makes sense but other times you're just immediately presented with a cut scene and then you can't go back.. without a warning.. while at other times you still just made a decision that will impact the whole game but you can just go back and rewind. So this made up for a somewhat mixed experience because at some points I was led to believe that I could rewind back what I just did/said and I would simply go for the wildest answer even though it's not the one I want but I'd end up not being able to reverse it, while at other times I could actually do that..I think a optional warning when things could or not be reversed might of helped or just more consistency.
Other than that feature however ,there's no much really for you to do in the game. The gameplay is somewhat repetitive. The main things you do is go back in time, talk to people and explore.
There are 2 main distinct mini challenges in the game.
The first one is to focus on photos. This is a very bad implementation and was really tedious and did not add anything to the table, it didn't make sense either and it was quite buggy so I really disliked it.
The other mini game was basically solving a puzzles out of the clues you've collected in episode 4 and connecting the dots or for example entering keycodes/passwords etc. This I found fun.
I would've enjoyed seeing a bit of a more interactive gameplay even though it's an episodic game, the time travel scenarios kind of expand in episode 5 which I liked a lot.
The other flaw is that you can't skip cut scenes at all, unless you just watched that cut scene. If you want to replay the whole game you'll have to re-watch all the cut scenes.. this is really putting me off from replaying the whole game and really diving deep in to the whole story and you can't even let the cut scenes drag as if you alt-tab the game will auto pause and it wont resume until you focus on it again.
There were a few audio glitches/bugs in the game while I played it but nothing major.
Anitmation and graphics are ok.
Voice acting is ok for the most part but there are times that it's not so great and you can barely recognise that it's the same voice actor.. so kind of a mixed bag.
Music is sometimes annoying and I ended up severely lowering it as I progressed. I just didn't feel the need of yet another cheesy alt-j song while the animations and transitions were playing and I like alt-j and most of the music that was played in it.
Worth? Yea.. it's worth it for the 5 episodes.. You'll probably end up buying them after playing the first one. I didn't particularly like that you can buy the episodes separately or that it's sold episodically at all. I think the game should be represent it for what it is and not be split in episodes since there's no clousure until the very last episodes, the previous ones always end up on a cliff hanger (of course to sell the other ones more). The game would really be wasted if you don;t play it through.
I'll definitely play the new one as well.

The decision on whether or not to give this a Yes or a No was a hard one; let it be said plainly that I do not think this game is horrible, mainly that it could have been executed much better.
To begin with, it has a lot of grand assets; the art is charming and simple, the sounds are easy to listen to and do not detract from the situation, and as they so prize, the voice acting is very well done.
That's as far as the good goes for me, though; the writing isn't bad by any stretch of the word - not to the extent of bad literature prevalent nowadays, or the plothole-ridden stories common in Visual Novels - it simply isn't driving, and it's hard to see it as something coherent what with the Bonus Conversations pulling you away from the situation to random tidbits about each character. I understand that they wanted to give it to you bit by bit, but the snippets of actual story are rather small, and to have even those few lines included, off-topic and flavorful as they are for the characters, lessens one's understanding of the story and takes away from the impact of presentation. The content of the Bonus Conversations are really just bonus tidbits meant to develop the characters, apparently, and not any actual plot-related content, which would have been more helpful had they not ruined the image cultivated in the story itself.
The minigame they have in between snippets and Acts also seems to be a bit out of place; it's rather simplistic and not intrinsically bad, mind, but it's out of place. It's not a tedious hassle to go through it, and one can finish it without much effort - the problem is that you have to spend time out of the story and into some mechanic-laden minigame.
The analogy I would use for this game's problem is when you're trying to read a book but these small mundane things just keep making you look up and lose where you were in the story - even if you're pausing to answer simple questions or digesting small tidbits.
For its price, I might still venture to get it - but dont expect too much out of it. This is an okay work, but  below the quality I expected from it. Ultimately, my final verdict is that I wouldn't recommend this game; nonetheless, I offer a respectful nod to the developer for making the game.

First off it's a great game, I mean it when I say that- I just think these reviews need a Maybe button. So as it stands, I flipped a coin and it landed on tails, hence the big red thumb down.
I've been a big fan of Vlambeer's stuff- but with that said... Consider this game carefully, because this is about as close as you're going to get to a virtual treadmill. Like running on a treadmill, it's fast paced and adrenaline pumping, yet you can't seem to go anywhere- but unlike a normal treadmill, this one violently kicks you in the balls if you so much as drop your speed by .5% and makes you start all over again.
Nuclear Throne is all or nothing- you either beat the game, or you start back at square one. Go big or go home. The end result is a game that feels fast, visceral and exhilirating at first, but transforms into something that feels long and grindy the more you play it. Beating a boss loses a lot of the thrill once you've killed him for the 80th time- it becomes routine.
The procedurally generated maps and randomized perks help mitigate this somewhat- enough to keep you always on your toes, but not drastic enough for any meaningful difference between playthroughs.  You're ultimately still  going through the same motions each time you die. And that's my real problem with it. I like the difficulty and the gameplay, I just think the failstate could have been handled differently to keep the game fresh.
So is it bad? No, it's not at all bad. I'd even say it's great. I just think 50+ hours to beat a game once (according to many playes on the Nuclear Throne subreddit) that could theoretically be beaten in 40 minutes might be a bit of a stretch. But chances are I'll still keep playing it anyway, sore balls and all.

Finished the visual novel in one hour, around seven chapters long. There's no save function so my recommendation is to either finish this in one sitting or quit the game - to take a break or do something else - after one chapter finished.
Overall, I can appreciate the voice acting although frankly it's just below average. At least it's something that's often missed when people make VNs.
Gameplay involves some mini games each chapters Stealth B@stard-style. You need to travel undetected to some points mostly using WASD control. I found this to be breaking my pace on reading thru the VNs so three out of six mini games I had them skipped (there's a function to skip the mini games at the top right of the screen).
Character developments are bad. There are five major characters in this VN and only one evolves adequately. Even the main char I found him rambling too much about 'god' to the point I honestly think it's annoying. This char developments correlate directly with the storyline, which is very important for VN. I find it to be rushed also, maybe because of time constraint or whatever. Story is not what I expected it to be. Being a sci-fi, I would hope it contains more, but then the progression is abruptly halted and the game ends prematurely.
Did I say the game's performance is HORRIBLE as well? I have more than decent laptop to run any VNs, yet even on my dedicated graphic card this runs choppily. Bad optimization.
Overall the game is sub standard, but still enjoyable if you like VN genre. Had it been more expensive, I would have given this a big thumb down. Get this when it's on BIG sale or in a bundle.

Swordbreaker the game is a fun choose-your-own-adventure-book kind of game. The artwork is stellar, while accompanied with some pretty good music. If you like these kind of games I highly recommend it (especially for such a low price). But keep in mind that this game is very short, if you just want to reach the end.
You play as an adventurer who sets out on a quest for some kind of great treasure in an old castle. The game lets you make choices. Some of these choices count towards one of three "Paths": The coward, hero or killer. These will eventually lead to three different endings. The artwork sometimes gives you hints to what you need to do to survive a specific situation. For example, you come into a hallway with corpses on the ground. You get the choice to run through the hallway or to crawl. When you look at the artwork you see a gaps in the wall, suggesting that you need to crawl because the gaps might contain blades that come out when passing through the hallway.
The game doesn't have many flaws. One of them is that the intro is narated, but the subtitles don't correspond to the narration. Another is that some paths lead to the same room. Sometimes the dialogue suggest that you came from one of the two paths, while you actually came from the other and thus it doesn't correspond to your current playthrough. This happens for example while doing a task for the cook.
These are very minor flaws in a great game. I look forward to what DuCats has in store next. If you are new to this genre, but find hero of kendrickstone to big to be your first game in the genre, this will be right game for you. Or even if you just want something else than a fps or an open world game.

Bermuda follows the story of three humans at the beach, Edward, Paul and Joanna, who get kidnapped by strange creatures to be experimented on in their submarine. When I say strange creatures I of course mean cute girls with blue hair and fish bowls over their heads, of course, because we need to hit those anime tropes.
These kidnappings have been going on for decades (inspiring the title of the game), and the creatures want to find out all about 'surfacers' and their strange ways before wiping their memories of the kidnapping and sending them on their way. At the last step of this process something goes wrong. As Joanna is transported back to the surface the teleportation beam unexpectedly breaks, leaving Edward and Paul stuck on the submarine.
Although it was kind of annoying to see the only human girls unceremoniously shoved out of (the majority of) the story it was a nice setup. Over the course of 6 chapters Edward and Paul await their fate, and explore the ship in a very rudimentary stealth game. Don't go expecting something like
here, even though this is also a 2D stealth game where you primarily use your environment to solve situations. 'Missions', as the game calls them, are short, <2 minutes short, and there is only one of them in each chapter. I'd complain about that more, but they honestly felt kind of tacked on and lazy so I didn't mind that they weren't a larger element of the game.
Taking all that into account this game would be teetering between a positive and negative recommendation about now.
There is one point that pushed my opinion a long way though, and not in the good direction.
The game's protagonist, Edward, is obnoxiously religious.
This could have been handled as a narrative element, teaching these weird alien abductors what God is or something. I'd probably still not have liked it then, but the way it is now it's just... sort of... there.
This isn't a minor character trait either. Flashbacks of Edward giving Joanna a crucifix, of how he met her at Church, constantly spouting that his faith is being tested or that he prays things will work out.
It's weird, and it utterly spoils all goodwill I had for this game.
Don't get this game unless you think you can handle the wonky religious angle it crammed into it.

Monolith has created a sequel that is better than it's predecessor in almost every way. Better story, better gameplay, better world, better side missions, etc. The story in Shadow of Mordor lacked the attraction and I couldn't care about it, whereas in Shadow of War, the story was much more entertaining and interesting, to say the least. However, there was a lot of re-used animations from SoM, so in ways, you can feel as if playing SoM is almost exactly like playing SoW. Also, only one sub-upgrade per time. And several minor bugs
What about the controversial "loot boxes" and "microtransactions". Yes, they exist. No, you don't need them, especially microtransactions.
You get loot boxes in SoW by completing vendetta missions, conquest missions, paying with Mirian(in-game currency), or paying with Gold. These loot boxes are separated into loot chests, war chests, vendetta chests, conquest chests, and spoils of war chests. Loot chests, vendetta chests, and conquest chests give equipment, whereas war chests and spoils of war chests give orcs and training orders. Honestly, these chests are unneccesary early-game and only the war chests are more relevant in Act IV of SoW, but you don't have to use them. You will still be racking up these chests whether you use them or not. I don't see anything wrong with loot boxes being in a game as long as it's not hiding content away, which this isn't, unless if you consider reassignment orders, which sends a follower Uruk into the garrison so that you can bring him into another region, which I can completely understand.
What about Gold and microtransactions? Well, sorry to burst your bubbles but once you unlock daily challenges, you'll be given a daily challenge that will give you 500 Gold, from there, each daily challenge will give different items like chests or gems or 50 Gold. What can you buy for 500 Gold though? A Gold loot chest worth 150 Gold, Gold war chest worth 200 Gold, Mithril Loot chest worth 400 Gold, and a few other chests. But do you need to? No, you don't. Not at all. I still have my 500 Gold in the game and have not even thought about using it at all.
"So you get Gold from the game, fine, you can still pay for them." you might say. Yes, you can still pay for them, but if you do, well... sorry to say but you're just not good at the game then. I would say an average player will be able to go through the game without wanting to purchase Gold because they will come to realize that you don't need to, they're optional. They're there, sure, but they're not forced down your throat.
"But the 50 hour grind..." No, the supposed 50 hour grind is more like 7 hours or 10 hours at most, maybe even less if you're a better player than I am. (Not hard to surpass)
"But that's still pretty long" Understandable, 7 - 10 hours is still pretty taxing, but it's 10 stages of defending forts. Each stage from 1 to 6 will have you defend one fort each. The next few forts will require you to defend multiple forts sometimes, but the last stage will have you defend all 4 forts. So let's assume stage 7 to 9 requires 2 forts each. You have a total of 16 fort defense missions. Each fort defense might take you maybe 15 minutes or 30 minutes max, whether you were victorious or not. If you failed, well, you'll have to take over the fort the old fashion way.
That being said, I do think having microtransactions in a fully-priced game is a bad practice, even if it's not hiding content away.

The puzzles are probably a little too easy for point-and-click adventure game veterans - finished it in around 6 hours and I didn't attempt to rush through it. So if you're expecting a challenge, look elsewhere.
In all other ways, it lives up to expectations as a Tim Schafer game. The setting is adorable without being outright twee. The dual PC/split POV narrative has promise and some really fantastic bits (can't say more here without spoilers). The writing is never as outright hilarious as, say, a Monkey Island game, but it does stay consistently amusing throughout.
Also because of its pedigree, the gameplay is gratifyingly streamlined. As an example: in older games, getting from one side of the map to the other was a chore, consisting of watching your character amble along each screen. In this game, if you double click an in-room destination, the character will jog there. Double-click an exit and you warp to the next room immediately, bypassing the walk animation completely. This may be one reason the game is so much quicker to complete, but I'm a huge fan of the feature and others like it. Adventure games should be challenging, but never tedious.
Is it worth full price? I received the game as a gift, so it's hard for me to say whether you will get $20 worth of fun out of it. But now that I'm hooked on the setting and story, I'll be picking up the rest of the game without a doubt.

This isn't right.  You know these floors.  You used to come here. You and a few friends.  Like that motorcycle guy who was always inviting you to his house parties, playing darts with a set of throwing knives he had bought as a joke.  Why did he stop leaving messages?  You got along well with him. He wouldn't want to see what's happened to you.  He wouldn't even recognize you in that mask of bloody rage you wear.  It's strangely liberating to put it on and have your identity, your humanity forgotten. The music pounding in your ears seems to give you strength and speed you never had before as you charge toward them, as you swing your axe in a pirouette and bathe in hot blood.  You arch your back, you crow in ecstasy as you bring your axe down on one man who was still moving, twitching.  Then you puff and shake yourself off, and charge up the stairs, the wattles of your mask sticky with gore.  You're not done yet tonight, though.  Not until the last neck is broken, when the bloodthirst evaporates in an instant -- and you're left alone and silent, the weapon dropping from your hand as the music disappears from your veins. And then, all that's left to do is to take off the mask and go back home.  You hope it'll just be a dream, but you always wake up with the mask clutched in your hands, looking you in the eye, waiting for more...

I was skeptical that a crowd funded game with a 60 dollar initial pricetag would actually end up being a solid title. Thankfully, I was proven wrong. I picked up the game for 40 dollars and so far it has been worth every penny.
Gameplay-
This isn't a game that holds your hand every step of the way, often times you need to think about what you are doing or saying (dialogue) and if you mess up it might give you an undesirable result. Personally, I enjoy it since I feel like everytime i go anywhere new there is a chance to find some need little tidbit or item that normally would not stand out.
Characters-
While it is unusual to find an RPG these days that allows the creation of a party (only other one i can think of is might and magic legacy), it provides an opportunity to make characters specialize in different fields. For example, I have a hand to hand bruiser that has meathead skills (break, hard♥♥♥♥♥and mechanical repair (not meathead but the best i could do)). Then another character has sniper computer science and smart♥♥♥♥♥ Another cool aspect is that you can assign characters religion, nationality and even their favorite pack of smokes- who knows maybe there is a little easter egg somewhere if you have a jewish asian etc. Also there are optional companions along the way, which can add 3 more faces (max) to your party.
Combat-
Being as it is turn base, it takes patience, but at the same time it allows the methodical approach. A lot of people don't like weapon jamming (requires an action similar to a reload), but i like it considering it adds more variability. If you have like Classic Turn-Based combat then you will enjoy this.
Loot-
I dont like how treasure was dealt with in this game. I find myself normally picking up heaps of junk or 6-7 of the same crappy gun i've been using. It also seems a little odd that there is such an abundance of ammo in an apocalytic wasteland. There are also some hidden items that can be turned into npcs for rewards, so keep an eye out!
The World-
The game utilizes a travel mechanic that places the part on a "board" in which they have to travel to different locations all the while you can be attacked by raiders and be mindful of your water supply. As for whether the game is open ended or not, I would say yes to an extent. Even though there are optional side objectives, the path always leads you in the direction of the mission. It is similar to the Mass Effect Series as both have the option for exploration and side missions, but the story missions are required to advance.
Overall-
Have you played Divinity: Original Sin (check)
Have you played Shadowrun Returns (check)
Have you played Fallout 2 (check)
Did you like any of them (check)
Then you will love this (check)

Dispite the Fallout-esqe setting the game plays more like X-Com. If you wanted a emotional or light hearted juant through a lovingly crafted gameworld... this is not it. This is the sort of game where you must be perfect. You must die over and over untill you find the right thing to do. This is a tactics game with RPG elements, not an rpg with tactical elements, which is the oppisite of what it advertises. The appeal of this game is Strategy and eventual Victory, which isnt really my bag. But dont knock it if others like it! However the game is marked by poor design... Let me give you an example of the poor combat and a glitch in the release version.
I have started my game on the LOWEST difficulty and proceded to what I assumed would be a tutorial area. A group of raiders demended a toll for passage to a mission critical area and have clearly murdered a passing family who didnt pay. I was having none of this. I attack them and they wipe the floor with me a bit. As a veteran of the original 2 Fallouts and the original Wasteland I found this battle a bit odd. A few of the raiders charged me with machetes and ended thier turn RIGHT NEXT to one of my characters without attacking. "Well they are doomed" I thought to myself as I moused over one with my assualt rife. 0% chance to hit. "What?" I thought. Apperantly weapons have a minimum range so if your ranger is too close they cant fight with their assualt or sniper weapon at all. So I switch to my fists and try to wail on 'em. I miss three times. Then the turn flips to another of my rangers, equipped with a pistol which CAN be fired in a melee. I run him the one space required to fire point blank and use my action points to fire twice with 63% chance to hit. I miss both times.
Cursing my luck, I end my turn and a raider with a gun runs up and shoots through the two melee raiders hurting my rifleman for a paltry 4 points of damage. After a few more turns I manage to fight off the raiders in sight with some moderate damage to two of my rangers, as well as a dog that got involved for some reason. When the fight is over my rangers stand there, still in combat mode waiting for another dog that apparently is attacking me... but isnt. The dog is nowhere in sight. I cyle turns waiting for this dog to show up when i remember "OH! Fallout had that little end comabt button that made stuff like this easy, il just look for that!" Guess what! There isnt one. If the game thinks there is an enemy, but you cant see or find it, that your out of luck! Afer a few dozen turns running around trying to find both this dog or Waseland 2 version of the end combat button, I relize the game is glitched and I am boned. It is at this point that I quit and restart, remembering to give all my ranger melee skills this time!
To make a summery of my BRIEF experince with this game... Its frustrating, but some people like that. Its also definitly not a game to play if you expect ANYTHING like Fallout 1 or 2s gameplay, dispite that being soemthing they use to sell the game. All in all I will give this game alot more time BUT I must be slightly erked by the fact that it gives me a game experince it didnt advertise. I feel a bit lied to.
Perhaps if the game was simply more forgiving on the easiest difficulty then some of the problems wouldn't of shown through, but as it stands now it needs a determined tactical gamer not a rpg enthusiest like me.

Following up the delightful and unexpectedly self-aware Unhack, it’s astonishing how far developer Invert Mouse has fallen with the pitiful Bermuda, an underwater alien thriller that is so dysfunctional I wanted to shut it off to spare it anymore embarrassment.
Invert Mouse’s main goal with Bermuda seems to be to try something more serious than the developer has done in the past, but rather than settle for conventional drama Bermuda jumps straight into science fiction absurdity. Plot devices are invented off hand and then left suspending in space as if to serve as window dressing for the explosive non sequiturs which cap off each act. It’s as if in its feverish obsession to create “emotional moments” Bermuda forgets everything that took place before that scene, unconcerned with how far it has vered off course so long as it arrives at the next juicy twist.
But I couldn’t even find a way to enjoy Bermuda ironically because its flat writing leaves no room for camp or unintended hilarity. Characters are boring, single faceted shells for the equally uninspired plot which drone on and on, unaware that their audience has long since dozed off yet seeming just as bored with their lines. It doesn’t help that there are a lot of things about Bermuda which are more than a little weird. The religious undertones feel pigeoned in almost for the sake of being able to present Bermuda as a bizarre piece of Christian media, and the fetishistic relationship between two characters left me feeling dirty and creeped out.
It’s just an immensely unenjoyable experience all around, and one that seems intentionally so but without anything interesting with which to fill the black hole that seems to have enveloped Bermuda to ensure nothing joyful or humorous finds its way in. And so Bermuda comes and goes, full of drama yet lacking any presence and leaving me grasping for even the tiniest justification of the hour I just lost.

Do you enjoy reading? Are you a fan of choose your own adventure books? Are you a fan of fantasy settings? If you answered yes to all three then chances are you will find what DuCats Game Studio have presented here appealing. Bonus points if you like earning quick and easy Steam achievements. Swordbreaker the Game. The game definitely reminds me of the old fantasy adventure choose your own adventure books that I loved so dearly as a child but whose adult texts were often aimed at people several years older than I was (I began reading these books at about the age of ten). Regardless, it was an experience that I was more than willing to take on. It certainly proved to be a different type of visual novel than the largely Asian variety that has come to be popular on Steam. Not that there’s anything wrong with them just that there is a notable difference.
One critique that I will offer DuCats is to please make English your default language in your next game. I am certain that you will find that a greater percentage of Russians are at least somewhat knowledgeable about the English language than you will find native English speakers who can read Russian. Starting the game to Russian text and subtitles proved to be a disorienting experience. In fact, I accidentally closed the game and looked for the language settings in the out of game options menu, which was set to English, before heading to the Steam discussion forums to find that the simple answer was to click the ‘Eng’ button on the bottom left hand corner of the main menu.
The achievements come quick and fast as do the deaths. Take a wrong option and you can kiss goodbye to that life. Thankfully, you do have three of them. I would have liked to have had a better idea of what was going to happen next as some of the options felt as though they very easily could have gone the other way or that they should have. However, arguably that’s something that constitutes a good story – you should never know what is going to come next even if some of the deaths felt a little cheap. It’s more than a little unfortunate that you have to start over once you have lost that third and final life but there are so many different angles to take – some of which have multiple successful (as in you will not die) to move the story in different directions.
The art work is beautiful. The artists are masters in their field. If I could I would simply scroll through the different images in this game and enjoy them without having to play the game they are that good. It’s different than the usual type that you’ll find in visual novels and gives helps the game its distinct taste and flavor. The music was suitable for the game although I believe that some would find it grating and repetitive.  The game is technically sound and plays very well. There’s not much to critique from that perspective at all.
I would definitely recommend Swordbreaker the Game to old school adventure game fans – whether that be by book or by video gaming. There’s a lot to like here. There is definite value for money with this title.

The goals and number of guards change, but this does little to make it less boring. It just felt like a tedious stopgap between story segments. The game would undoubtedly have benefited from a more traditional point-and-click or choose-your-own-adventure style to its storytelling.
For being only a 3 dollar title, the story is surprisingly good. It had enough mystery to it to keep me interested, but never seemed like it was making an♥♥♥♥♥pull when it threw in plot twists. My only gripe is that Eddie can't seem to go more than a few sentences without throwing in a reference to God, and I'm not saying that just because I'm not religious. Especially once Mukan started angrily declaring that she didn't believe in God, all I could do was roll my eyes. It struck me as trying to insert controversy where none was needed. Leave the battle of the religions to the♥♥♥♥♥end of the internet where it belongs; I just want to enjoy a good story.
Gripes aside, I still enjoyed the game. Despite being a weaker entry than Unhack, I would still recommend this to anyone who enjoys a good mystery. It's pretty cheap, and while the gameplay is boring, it's not difficult, nor should it take you but a couple minutes to run through.

Swordbreaker, developed by DuCats Games Studio, is a unique visual novel with some of the strangest, yet interesting designs I’ve ever seen.
The story is fairly simple. You play as a nameless adventurer who goes by the title Swordbreaker. After an evening at the pub, the weary adventurer witnesses a murder. The killer escapes, yet the dying victim hands Swordbreaker an old map before sputtering his last. The map leads to an ancient castle, packed with a limitless supply of treasure! Like most adventurers would, Swordbreaker sets off on a journey that’ll put his skills to the test, and change his life forever.
The entirety of the game takes place in this castle, and it’s got to be the most bazare castle ever portrayed in gaming. Just about anything you can think of dwells here; Giant arachnids, aliens, ghosts, orcs, killer squids, warlocks, princesses, zombies, skeletons and so much more. There are over 300 different scenarios to encounter throughout the castle, all of which result in different outcomes. It’s addictive as hell, and each new playthrough will unveil new fights, encounters and choices.
But, this game’s true saving grace is the artwork. Every single picture, from the most mundane death to a breath-taking fight sequence, throbs with detail. Creatures look frightening and the castle’s twisted interior will make any adventurer soil themselves. The amount of effort and dedication put into this art is unfathomable.
Apart from its random story and breathtaking visuals, it’s hard to believe how much replay value Swordbreaker contains. With hundreds of different encounters and possible ways to die, topped off with over 60 achievements, you’ll be surviving this game’s brutality for quite a few hours. Just playing through once would be a huge disservice to what Swordbreaker achieves.
Translation from Russian to English is fine, and it won’t be the most enticing thing you’ll ever read, but it gets the job done. Sadly, it’s Swordbreaker’s pure reliance on luck that irritates me. Almost every decision made can get you killed, and to survive… well, you’ve just gotta hope for the best. You’re normally given two or three different options to make during scenarios, and it’s never clear which one will keep you alive. You’ve got three lives, and once they’re all depleted, you restart from the beginning. It can be pretty aggravating at times, especially when the game cheats you during a climactic boss fight, but with Swordbreaker’s endless amount of replayability, I’d say that makes up for it.
It’s cheap, it's innocent, and it’ll make for a fun pastime. I see no reason to miss out on something as cool as Swordbreaker.

Sad to see so many players begin their review with, "its a great game, an improvement over the first game, BUT...microtransactions" and ultimately give it a thumbs down just based on that ideology.
These kinds of games have continued to get more and more complex and expensive to create...which is what we all want...yet, we, as a consumer base tend to act like we are entitled to paying the same price that was being paid for games 10 years ago. $59.
If there is not some way for a game developer to make more revenue, one of two things will happen...that game developer will need to be bought out by a bigger, more financially secure company that can front the MASSIVE costs for an eventual payout while paying people and keeping up a building and equipment necessary for making games...or they just go out of business. I am sure you can think of several examples of both of these things happening.
Listen, there is no alternative to those outcomes if we, as a consumer, refuse to pay any more than $59 for ALL games of ALL time. Perhaps game developers could just make games that fit the $59 budget we seem to insist they work with but I am sure we all can understand what those limitations will do to the games we look forward to playing eventually.
While we all operate in the mindset of playability and fun, they have to operate under the pressure of market potential, market projection, upfront costs and maintaining the development of a product that produces zero profit until it is complete. It is a huge gamble to the tune of 100s of millions of dollars with no guarantee they will sell enough to get into profit. Especially when a large portion of consumers, potentially interested in buying the product, tend to use their ability to review the product not based on the merits of the game itself but solely on any attempt made to increase revenue.
It is not pay to win here. The game is perfectly playable without paying a single cent over the original purchase price. Additional content, however, is available if you choose to purchase it.
I think the game is an improvement over the first and I enjoyed the first one very much so this game is made well and does exactly what I would reasonably expect it to do based on the price I paid...even more so.
A whole lot of elitist, entitled behavior in the gaming community that obviously has no idea what it takes to make a game we all want to play. If an alternative route towards increasing the capability for developers to recoup their expense doesn't make its way into the future of gaming in a way that we all can accept, there is no future for gaming. Its that simple.

Shadow of War is an immensely fun game. The dramatic, relatable storylines are a step above other mainstream games. The combat is insanely immersive. Each battle with an Orc Captain is wildly different. There are so many fine details at play during these battles, it would be rare to fight one Captain and be fully reminded of another. And new Captains seem to ambush you out of nowhere.
If you enjoyed Shadow of Mordor you will be in awe at all the cool stuff they've added for you to do. SoW has the best combat mechanics I've ever seen (especially melee), much improved and polished from it's predecessor. Sometimes I'll look at a zone on the map and think, "Hmm, it's kind of small," but then I'll get into the action and forget where I am. There's always a new angle with a different feel.
This game is massive and there's so much to accomplish and explore. Not to mention it's action packed all the way through. I don't want to get into detail about all the crazy things you can do because you can watch trailers and twitch, you know. But I will say:
If you've ever dreamed of flying around on a dragon and burning halpless groundies like Daenerys Targaryen, this game is for you.
That being said, there are two major complaints about this game and they have nothing to do with the gameplay experience. I will outline the chief complaint and explain why it is unfounded. I won't detail the "Forthog Orc-Slayer DLC controversy" because at the time of this writing WB has recognized their mistake, made the DLC free and sent a donation to the family.
1. Microtransactions:
The scope of this game is huge. The storylines, the battles, the dialog and all of the little things. Wow. Honestly, this game is worth way more than $60. I'm at 85 hours (on hard mode) and still loving it. 70 cents an hour for premium entertainment? That's one hell of a bargain.
Mainstream games have been selling for $60 for quite some time now. Set aside development costs. Let's think about inflation and growing player demands. Games have been getting better and better but the price has remained the same. There's only one way to keep that price where it is and that's microtransactions.
For those of you who haven't played this game, you can buy gold loot crates with cash and silver loot crates with in-game currency (free). Both types give you followers that you can position to your liking around the world or in one of the various forts you've conquered. You get slightly better rewards with gold crates, but they're the same type of rewards as in silver crates.
If you're a true bawss however, you can get followers by hunting them down and mind @#!%ing them into submission - in other words, by playing the game. And let me tell you, each encounter is going to be exciting, unique and worth your time and effort.
Of all the time I've spent on this game, not once have I felt the urge to purchase gold to buy loot crates for the simple reason that I'd rather play the game as much as possible. One important thing to note: it's not multiplayer, you don't have to buy these things because there's no one to get ahead of. Even still, you can complete online single player challenges to earn gold to buy gold loot crates.
____ In Closing ____
Middle-Earth: Shadow of War has seen a ton of bad press for all the wrong reasons. No one's out there bashing Blizzard games for their microtransactions in games such as Hearthstone or Overwatch. The loot crates in SoW don't help all that much and the game is not even multiplayer. Don't feed the frenzy and miss out on an amazing game experience. Because it is truly a badass game.

First of all, I have to admit that I really enjoyed the first 3 acts, so let's start from the pros of the game.
The game is a much better version of the first one. If you're into going around gathering the collectables, you'll hear interesting lore and interaction between Talion and Celebrimbor.
The level-up traits are interesting and fun. If you want to, you can really play the way you like and aren't forced to stick to one specific way.
The visuals or the armors are really improved and interestind. Really glad they put that in since in the first game you could only change your skins and there were only 2-3 actually good skins that pretty much looked very similar.
The siege system at the begining of the game is really entertaining. It makes you feel like you're really making an impact on the world.
Overall, anyone who likes LoTR and the first game is going to also enjoy this game. At least at first.
With all of that I cannot recommend this game right now, one week after release.
The game is way overpriced, the base game being 60$ and the expansion pass another 40$. That is 100$ for the full game that feels like it was bug-tested by Bethesda.
This game doesn't have many minor bugs, but the bigger ones will straight up force you to restart the game and often happen during the sieges, so it will make you restart it. Now if this only happened once in a while it would be okay, but I had to restart roughly 1/3 sieges because of some bug, most commonly getting stuck while climbing buildings or during the introduction of orc captains.
These two things have to be adressed on their own. The parkour system is straight up terrible. I didn't think of it that way at the beginning, but 10+ hours into the game I started feeling how clunky it is. I replayed the first game before this came out and somehow, the parkour from the first game was actually smoother than in this one. In the cities you constantly run up buidings, carts and whatever is nearby for no reason at all. It's almost like that game is forcing you to run on the roofs, where there are no objections in your path.
My guess this is because of the character perks that you unlock with leveling up or gathering collectables and side objectives (and this was probably what I enjoyed the most while playing), but when you get most of the perks a problem occurs. There are not enough keys if you're playing on the keyboard. I know that might not make a lot of sense but listen. Most keys they start to share 2-3 perks, depending on how you press the key (instantly, or if you hold it, or if you press shift or mouse 2 another effect occurs). These perks are fun to use but in late game a lot of them are pretty useless and you end up using only the main 1/3 or so. BUT the game often prioritizes the secondary perks and their uses that will get you killed more than once. The second chance system is also something I just can't really grasp. Some orc captains have a trait that won't let you use second chance and it is a good thing, it makes you want to be more prepared for the fights, but I had normal orcs kill me without giving me a second chance too.
Lastly on the game mechanics, the orc introductions get really annoying and I don't understand how could they not put a "skip" button. Now I have to say this was interesting and gave character to the orcs that I enjoyed, but during act 4, where in 20 -30 minute sieges I had around 20 orcs introducing themselves each time I wanted to kill myself. They can talk anywhere from a few seconds to a couple of minutes. You end up listening to the same thing for 5+ minutes in one siege, at which point you had already listened to like a 100 orcs while playing the game. Not to mention that sometimes the orc just left during his introduction in my game, leaving just an empty scenery and the game waiting for him to end. But since he left, no matter how long I waited it wouldn't end, so I just started restarting the game when this would happen.
Now to finish this, the whole act 4 is bull****. They made it way too long. SPOILERS: act 4 is just 20 sieges that you need to hold out. This can take anywhere from 5 to 15+ hours, depending if you're going to buy the loot boxes. (Now a lot of people vere angry because of the  loot boxes but they aren't neccecary. What they do is just make you finish act 4 faster. If you wanted to, you could get anything from them while playing the game with some more grind, since legendary orcs aren't really that rare to get and can actually even be farmed (lol)). This ~10h gameplay is very repetative as you do the same thing over and over. Nothing new happens, no new mechanics are inpremented at this point. Now to mention the siege mechanic itself is pretty buggy.
The game has online sieges, but after act 4 most players will be sick and tired of them anyway, not to mention the game has almost no replay value, unless you'll want to come back and replay it after a year or so when you'll have completely forgotten it.
Overall, the game is not worth 100$ the way it is now and probably will never be. I'd say get it if you like LoTR and the first game IF this game goes on 50%+ discount during winter or summer sales. Otherwise even if I enjoyed the game overall, I cannot recommend buying it.

Short: This is a really good idle game and you learn something about chemistry (high school level id say). Also, in contrast to many other idle games, it doesnt have too long waiting periods.
Long: In this game you "build" a world by collecting atoms. This is done by putting so called "extractors" on elements on the periodic table and/or hovering your cursor above them. With these atoms you can buy upgrades or invest them into "evolution" which grants you bonuses. Over time you unlock the whole periodic table. To advance you have to complete so called "missions" which are for example "extract 5 elements with boiling point <0°C at once" etc. This means you get a basic feeling for the periodic table if you havent already. Sometimes molecules appear on the screen and you can click them and see what they are (and get bonus on the respective elements) which I believe is nice for "visual learners" as I am. Its not that you have to learn something by heart but I think it can give you a basic feeling about how common compounds (water, sulfuric acid, methane,...) look like. As I wrote before this is rather high school level (Bohrs atomic model) so dont expect any high level chemistry here. But its really fun and not too boring if you know what I mean. You do sometimes have waiting periods but they are like minutes and not hours as in many other idle games. So its something you can actually play actively.
Usually educational games are really boring and not even worth being called "games" but this ones really fun if you like idle games. 5 euros as a price is fair in my view.

Let's start with the good:

The story is pretty interesting and I enjoyed revealing it bit by bit, playing some time as Shay and then as Vella, it's useful when you get stuck on a puzzle to switch to the second charater.
As I hoped the second part took me longer to beat and overall Steam says that I played the game about 15 hours, I took my time, although the actual time should be a bit less it's still a nice amount, the average time to beat should be about 10.5 hours or so.
And for the bad:
I kinda hoped there would be a bit more to the story and somwhere in part 2 I could guess where it goes.
Most of the puzzles where fine but there were a couple of kinda hard to guess puzzles that really took me time to figure out, one of which was a really bad choice in my opinion and I'm sure that many players got stuck in that place, it was kinda annoying and I decided to use a guide just for that one puzzle (still not sure if I'de get that one without it! they needed to add some kind of hint there, I was just clueless on what I needed to do next and wandered around the screens looking for a hint).
Also some puzzles were a bit tiring (fetching things, going from one place to another and back again several times etc'), mostly on act 2.
To sum it up, as I said I enjoyed the game overall, I'm happy that we got the game but indeed it could have been a bit better, the first part was shorter and easier but more interesting and fun to play. Still if you like adventure point and click games you should give this game a try, I thought it was worth the 15$ I paid for it, but you can get it on sale for much less (lowest so far was 6.24$).

The classic is reborn with some new content, plus revived and revamped multi-player!
This is the quintessential flight simulator!  It is the most accurate, in-depth, and authentic flight simulator available.  So realist, I have seen this software used in flight sims in museums!  Whether you are looking to pilot a hand-glider, a helicopter,  a prop plane like Cessna, or a jet airliner like a Boeing 747, it is here; and true to life.  From the control panel layouts and aircraft operation, to Air Traffic Control and flight planning.  If you are looking for a non-military flight simulator, you can not go wrong with Flight Simulator X:Steam Edition.
The Steam Edition adds the ability to play in multi-player environments; where you can play as a pilot or co-pilot to an air traffic controller.  There are also different races like Red Bull Air Race and Reno National courses, and even more!  There are also the original missions from the game plus many more, providing 50+ hours worth of single-player missions; or just pick an airport, pick a plane, and take off!  You will be playing this game for years.
In addition, if you really become addicted to this game, there is a plethora of accessories that you can get.  You could literally have professional grade flight simulator with life-like throttle levers, panels, headsets, and more.
PROS:
I could say everything but...
Added multi-player and single-player content, stunning visuals, realist (or not so much, if you prefer) flight conditions and aircraft controls, ridiculous re-play value
NEUTRALS:
Aircraft selection-While there is a variety in the types of aircraft you can pilot, it still feels like one or two aircraft were selected from each category of aircraft and that's what you get.  Some may have some color options, but for the most part, if you want to fly a prop plane you have these 2 or 3, if you want fly a jet plane you have these 2 or 3, and so on.
CONS:
I don't have any cons for this game, what there are cons for is from Steam.  This is not a con in the non-Steam version of this flight simulator, since it can be resolved.  Sorry guys; love ya but this is on you...
Add-on Content.  If you own the original Microsoft FSX game, there is FREE add-on content; literally by the hundreds of thousands.  From texture and airport upgrades, to improved visuals on landmarks, and I couldn't even begin to list all the options.  But NOT with Steam Edition.  The game description blames it on compatibility, which I concede may have a level of truth to it.  However, to charge over $1500 for DLC is truly...rediculous...outlandish...unbelievable...I think those are even understatements.  I don't understand this pricing on any level, period.
Overall
If you are looking for a flight simulator, you need not look further.  This is the pinnacle of consumer-level flight simulator.  In regards to the DLC pricing issue, my recommendation would be this.  Buy the Steam Edition, for two reasons. First is the online multi-player content, this is not available on the original game.  (*There is a multi-player option on the original game.  However, it is LAN multi-player meaning you don't play online, and I don't have any experience with it.)  Second, if you really like the game and find that you want to improve the experience, buying a copy of the original game isn't too expensive and then you can download all the free add-on content until you heart's desire.  I stress this because if you want to put some time into it, there are a countless number of beautiful fly-bys you can do in this simulator; and in fairly realist graphics with add-ons and high settings.

Guns and Robots can best be described as World of Tanks meets Loadout. Let me explain why:
It uses the World of Tanks method of resolving objectives. If you blow up, that's it, you're out. If everyone on one side dies, the game is over. The objective rarely is considered in most matches because of this. It also uses the idea of disarming an opponent based on where you shoot. Shoot the feet, you slow the opponent. Shot the arms, you disarm it. Shoot the head, you impair it's vision.
It's like Loadout in that, in order to succeed, you have to experiment with your build. There are a sea of different parts, whcih are used to make modules, the components of your robot. Each robot is made up of one chassis, one engine, one body type, one battery (or two), one head unit, and 2 to 4 weopons and weapon frames. This means you can tailer the bot to match your strategy as much as you wish. To make this more absurd, you can equipt up to two devices, which allow you to pull the game to your advantage.
Also like loadout, you ave to buy every part. Unlike Loadout, however, there is a limited inventory for each part, and each part can only be used on one robot at a time, so you are encouraged to just have one, with a few spare pieces to mmix it up a few times.
In short, it's intense, it's annoying, but once you deal with it, it can be a really good game. Or a really bad one.

TL;DR: It's basically the same simulator that Microsoft published in October 2006. See the chapter about differences if you're not new to FSX.
Those who don't know the series, should know that Flight simulator X is called FSX by short.
I've been using flight sim software for a long time now, and actually got the FSX: Gold edition for free from Microsoft in 2006, so i have spent some hours (about 1500-2000) in this before it was released on steam.
In this review i will focus on FSX: Steam edition as a game presented for new users, and then point out the differences between the Steam edition and the regular one that was published in 2006.
To be fair, if you only want to play FSX for casual arcadeish gameplay, crashing planes and so on
.
If you have checked out FSX on youtube and found HD videos of big living Airports, shiny ultra realistic planes, and other things that look very realistic, and think that this is what the "game" is, then
. These videos is a result of many add-ons, a beast of a machine, several short clips, and a lot of editing. They look incredible, but doesn't represent FSX for what it is.
But if you are new to flight simulators and want to learn the basics of flying, and/or want to learn how to fly by instrument rules, or knows how to fly and want to fly from/to locations you know, you should buy this!
Pros:
- It includes the whole world, with almost every airport (some big cities, but mostly blocky buildings at airpots).
- Decent flight model (How the airplane reacts to the world)
- Extreme rate of customization (see add-on chapter below)
- Many settings that allow anything from basic to advanced flights
- Decent amount of stock airplanes.
Cons:
- 32-bit architecture/VAS (See Add-on chapter)
- Poor performance (Very CPU demanding, and not forgiving for AMD users)
- Stock planes (very basic and does not represent the real aircraft very good)
- Add-ons (see chapter below)
Flight simulator must be the sim with the most add-ons in the world. It's amazing how many developers that make things for FSX. Without the add-ons i would NOT recommend this simulator. An example of what add-ons you can buy/get is:
-
Anything from basic free planes, to really advanced and realistic airplanes like the Majestic Dash-8 Q400 or PMDG 737 NGX.
-
Anything from free fan-made stuff, to professionally made add-ons from companies like Orbx FTX, Aerosoft, Flight1, and so on.
-
Like with Airplanes and Scenery you can get a lot of other software to boost the quality of the weather system (new textures and possibilities to get the real world weather), ground and water textures.
-
You can also get a lot of mission-packs, and other tools. Both freeware and payware.
Even tho FSX is nothing without it's add-ons, it's still many problems with them. Often to get what you really want, you need to pay a lot of money to buy all the good add-ons. And there is also the fact that the more add-ons you add to FSX the slower it loads. Some add-ons also cause problems with other add-ons installed (from minor bugs to FSX not starting at all). This happens more often with freeware add-ons than payware add-ons.
Also because of the poor performance in FSX, and the fact that it's heavy CPU demanding (I got an 4Ghz AMD 8-core processor) you might not get to a playable framerate if you have combine a detailed airport with for example the PMDG 737 NGX (6-10 FPS). If you run Intel you will get a much better performance because of the logical cores in the intel processor.
Also; Remember that this version of FSX is called FSX: Steam edition. Even though every add-on for FSX should work on FSX:SE, some might have problems if not optimized for FSX:SE

The biggest achilles heel that haunt allmost every FSX user is VAS (Virtual Access Space). Im not going to go in detail on what it is and how it works, but i will tell you the basics, and it's limitations.
VAS is basically virtual memory (Note: this does not equal RAM, nor harddrive space). Each program you run gets it's own chunk of VAS that it can fill up. If the VAS limit is exceeded the program will STOP WORKING with the well known "Out of Memory" (OOM) error.
FSX is built on the old 32-bit architecture. This limits the programs VAS to about 4GB. This becomes a major problem when you start putting add-ons in FSX. Too many add-ons, or add-ons that is poorly optimized will push the VAS limit and cause an OOM.
The VAS will fill up over time. An example: FSX base game will take about 1,2 GB. When loaded into the world you will be at aprox 2 GB VAS. You then have a fancy add-on airport that takes about 300MB, and an add-on airplane that takes about 350MB. You then start flying with a VAS at 2,6GB. No problem you think? You take off and fly towards the destination, that is on the other side of the country. On your way you fly over 4-5 other add-on airports, and your VAS is suddenly 3,7GB. Then you reach your destination, and on final, about to land you hear a "DING", with a message telling you "Out of memory", and FSX quit.
Another problem with the VAS is that it doesn't clear it's memory when you don't need it anymore. So if you fly a short trip from airport A to airport B where you reach 3,2GB VAS usage, and then start another flight from airport C, your VAS will still be 3,2GB.
FSX Users have several solutions to avoid this error, like for exampel using a program to monitor their VAS so they can save the flight and restart FSX. Another solution is to deactivate all the scenery you don't need for the flight. Also, the AI traffic fills up the VAS, so be sure to have this set to 0%. Some developers also run the core of their add-on in windows and not FSX to save VAS usage.
Other than that, it is NOT possible to fix this issue, other than developing a new simulator that uses a 64-bit architecture and allow higher VAS usage.
If you are a long-time user of FSX and wonder if you should buy the steam edition, the answer is maybe.
I will list the main differences i've found between FSX and FSX: Steam edition:
- FSX:SE is a re-released FSX: Gold edition, so all servicepacks are included
- FSX:SE uses Steamworx for multiplayer. FSX used gamespy (no longer supported after february 2013)
- FSX:SE can be installed on every computer you own using steam, and no CD-key required. Every FSX disc have a maximum installation limit of 5 before the disc is useless, and you had to save the CD-key.
- FSX:SE is still supported and receives updates. Microsoft doesn't support FSX anymore.
- Some bugs from FSX is fixed, and FSX:SE is tweaked to run better on modern computers.
- FSX:SE does however NOT include the SDK that's included in FSX.
There might be even more differences that i haven't noticed/forgot about when i wrote this.
Overall it runs slightly better than FSX, and when i finally had to reinstall FSX i landed on using the steam edition.
I recommend FSX:SE because of all the add-ons from FSX, and that there are few other decent options out there. You should also check out x-plane 10 and P3D (Lockheed-martins version of FSX).

First things first. DEADPOOL ISN'T IN IT. GET OVER IT. DOWNLOAD ONE OF THE VARIOUS MODS TO GET HIM IN GAME AND MOVE ON. The reasons why. Marvel Studios doesn't have the right to Deadpool and Spider-man's rights were still up in the air at the time of development for this game. Ergo no Deadpool. The End.
