That said I personally love this game. And how can I not? I stayed up until 2 a.m. New Zealand time playing until i completed at least the first movie. The story is from movies I love. As a comic book nerd I knew already I was going to at least like this game and I can proudly say that I love it. Sure it seems lazy getting clips from the movies but they are not going to hire the movie actors to re-do their lines and lose a lot of their budget. Instead they hire a couple of people to do the voices and get some main stay voice actors like Hayley Atwell (Agent Carter), Clark Gregg (Agent Phil Coulson)(booyah), Cobie Smulders (Maria Hill)(I was shocked by this one), Stan Lee and Lou Ferrigno(1970's Hulk. Not Bruce Banner, just Lou and the Hulk) and Ming-Na Wen for Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D..
I love how there are characters that nobody really knows and then prompts research behind them, because that's what TT does. They take fairly unknown characters and chucks them into a Lego game. When I was younger, "Choose your own Adventure" books were a great source of entertainment. The stories probably weren't particularly great, but the endings always were. While there were always a few good endings - the kind where the protagonist saves the day/gets the girl/becomes a billionaire - most of the time he (or she) was killed. I call it one of the benefits of growing up in the 80s. Not only did your parents take you to see
, but you also got to read books, where the authors thought up dozens of brutal and hilarious deaths for the main character. After playing through Swordbreaker, I'm feeling the urge to buy up a load of Edward Packard books.
As the titular Swordbreaker, you'll enter a giant castle in the search of the greatest treasure. There's not much to say about the hero except that he reminds me of Dirk the Daring. What? You've never heard of
? Well, just picture a hapless shmuck with a sword. As the player, you must lead Swordbreaker through the castle to his ultimate fate. Will you obtain the incredible treasure? Or will you suffer over 100 untimely deaths? Hmm..I guess you'll have to find that out on your own.
The game begins with you outside of the castle. At every point, there are at least two decisions you can make. Sometimes these decisions lead to alternate routes, or they just lead to death. You get three lives and then you have to start over. This is done to encourage replay-value. The decisions are never changed or randomized in anyway, so as long as your memory is sound, you'll eventually make it through the castle. That said, it's worth taking the time to try everything, even if death is guaranteed. Some of the ways the hero meets his end are flat-out hilarious. They're not as imaginative as the stories I read growing up, but they're all illustrated and definitely brutal.
Along the way you'll meet other characters. In these situations, you can choose to help them, kill them, or run away. This morality system determines the "good" ending you can receive. By "good" I mean an ending where you aren't viciously massacred in a humiliating fashion. You'll see what I mean if you pick this game up. The number of times the hero dies by tripping and falling is ridiculous. If he can't handle walking and running, maybe he shouldn't be an adventurer. Thankfully, these constant deaths are balanced out, by the fact that getting back to where you ran out of lives, only takes a minute or two.
Once you've seen everything in this game, there's little reason to go back. Looking through the gallery is nice, but you can't expect anything in the way of replay-value. It takes a few hours to unlock most if not all of the scenes. Considering that the game is priced at $3, I think it's a fair value. If you're a completionist, getting the few remaining scenes can be frustrating. There is a map of the castle that tracks every scene, but it doesn't tell you how to reach every area. It might be worth the effort to jot down a few notes. The only other complaint is that the music gets old very quickly. On the bright side, I can catch up on my music backlog.
There's only so much I can say about Swordbreaker without resorting to spoilers. If the concept interests you, then give it a look. You may discover that it isn't a terrible way to spend an afternoon or two.

This game excels in many ways and in short -- you should buy it.
Most captivating is the atmosphere. This game was developed by Microsoft and it is very apparent that they took inspiration from their home state of Washington. The vast temperate rain forests containing abundant lakes coupled with cloudy skies truly strengthen the setting. Taking on a vibe of mystery and horror the story of Alan Wake is also quite interesting. I'll be honest I mostly play games for the story much like one would read a book or watch a movie. In this regard Alan Wake was incredibly fun but at times I also found myself "grinding" through the game in a sense, wishing to simply continue the story. I suffered from one or two "rage quit" moments but ultimately pressed on and I am glad I did. Another refreshing strength of this game is the unique gameplay. The combination of the flashlight weaponry with unique puzzles and challenges is very refreshing compared to other games and made the game less monotonous. All in all, while not perfect, Alan Wake is a very enjoyable game and everyone should play through it once.

Alan Wake is one of those games that you'll love, or you'll have a mild dislike of. The game starts out as Alan goes on vacation after being blocked in his writing for years. From there, things go from bad to worse very quickly. It's a very Stephen King/Lovecraft type of story. But rather than horror, it's a Thriller story with supernatural elements. You probably won't be scared, but there are bits that can leave you a bit on edge.
The biggest complaints that I've seen from people are the story is sort of meh and the combat is repetitive. Both of these complaints have some truth, but they are also very personal. I loved the combat, the gun play feels awesome and while the enemies never really grow much, they are still fun to fight. The story is kind of meh, but it gets the job done well and has enought twists and turns to keep your attention. I've completed the game four times and still have an itch to go back and play through it again
One thing I think everyone can agree on is that the graphics are stunning. I bought an xbox360 basically just to play this game after years of waiting for it to come to PC. I thought it looked nice then, but the PC copies blow it away. Lighting is well done, the world feels expensive and alive. You feel like you're exploring a small town and it's surrounding areas, something few games have done well.
The sound design is another great in this game. The only time I felt really nervous and uncomfortable came from walking though the woods and stepping into the dark fog that covers some parts of the world. It sounds like a freight train and some strange monster are going at it. It's just weird and it does it's job of putting you on edge.
The game is worth your money. It was worth it when it first came out and it's worth it now. I suggest a xbox360 controller though as it seems to play best with it.

Cookies vs. Claus:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Who doesn’t love cookies? I haven’t found too many people who don’t. Who doesn’t love Santa Claus? You know that old guy dressed in red with a long white beard who makes a round once a year to deliver presents to everybody. Let’s be honest, the guy is an icon! Until one Christmas Eve, when Santa meets Cookies, and it isn’t like when Harry met Sally, it’s deadly! The question is, are you going to be a Cookie or a Claus? Let’s get the cookie . . . or . . .  Claus to crumble!
Cookies vs. Claus is an action game where you take control of a cookie, Santa Claus and other Christmas related characters and eliminate your opponents as fast as you can to collect three well- earned golden stars.
In the main menu, you’ll be able to access single player, online and custom modes. In the single player mode, you’ll be able to play Santa, Rudolph the Reindeer and Cookies missions. There are currently 96 levels to clear. Your goal is to eliminate all your opponents as fast as you can without suffering too much damage in order to win three stars. The first four stages will be unlocked, but you’ll have to accumulate a certain number of stars in order to unlock the other ones. There are twelve missions per character. Bear in mind you have six different types of cookies to play, as well as Santa and Rudolph. In this mode, you’ll be playing in a combined kitchen and lounge room with a big Xmas tree right in the middle. The room will be full of toys which you can pick up if you play Santa, or use if you play cookies. I thoroughly enjoyed jumping in a plane and dive bombing Santa (that’ll learn ya for giving me the wrong Chrissy present!) Mind you, I like the tank and flying saucer too. Anyway, there are plenty of goodies to pick up and use in this room. Also, ninety percent of the levels will be finished under sixty seconds, but it doesn’t mean that you’ll earn three stars at all. For example, Rudolph is a difficult character to eliminate. His nose is a powerful laser beam and inflicts severe damage. Santa has a candy cane that shoots white balls, and as for cookies . . . well, it would depend which cookie you’re playing. The Ninja cookie has a katana and shuriken and can become invisible. What of a bugger of a cookie!  I’ll let you discover the other five by yourself.
The online mode currently has two maps available which includes the one I mentioned above and the North Pole map. In this mode, you’ll be part of a team of cookies (four in total) or playing Santa. The goal is to eliminate Santa as fast as possible. The tricky aspect for the cookies is that they’ll only have fifteen lives available between them. Use all the lives and you lose the battle. In the last mode you can customize a battle.
Nice colourful graphics. The soundtrack is cheery, festive and fun! You’ll be able to find an online game very quickly; people are playing this game - it’s a lot of fun! In regards to the controls, you’ll be able to use your mouse and keyboard, or a gamepad. Personally, I would like to see more maps added for the online mode. Mind you, this game is an early access and I look forward to seeing more updates.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Colourful and cute graphics
-	Fun and easy to play
-	96 single player levels to clear
-	Online mode with players
-	Love my cookies
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No achievements or trading cards at this stage
-	Need more maps
Regardless if you play a cookie or Santa Claus, it will be Xmas every single day!
7/10

I'm not sure what can be said about Life is Strange that hasn't already been said.
The game is great, even if some mechanics are a little frustrating, like zooming in and out of a photo to get it in focus. My strategy for that tends to amount to button mashing. Max starts off a quiet, mallable protagonist, but grows with the player. I loved her character development, and she's my favourite character in the game, even with her humble beginnings. The story is interesting, and has a few plot threads that maybe run too independently of each other. The dialogue is awkward at times- it's teenagers speaking like adults think they talk like, which should give you an idea- but there's a charm to it's awkwardness, and it doesn't bother me past a few cringe moments (but it's something to know, going in). There are little secrets littered everywhere in the world, if you care to look, and the photo challenges are awesome fun.
Life is Strange, overall, is just a lovely game, which tells a story that will captivate a lot of people.

This is my favourite game.  Bar none.  I've never played anything more fun than this.
The story, immaculate.  Rather then shove it down your throat, they let you decide how engrossed you want to be.  You want to just kill a load of blokes, then get to the end?  Brilliant.  You want to piece together what exactly the crazy guy you're controlling is doing?  Even better.  Nothing is spoon-fed to you here.  You make the most out of this games story yourself.  Ive played both games all the way through, and am still trying to decipher what the hell happened, exactly.  There really isnt anything else like it out there, where you honestly could become so engrossed in whats on the surface a Violent Sociopath Sim.  There's just so much more to this game.
Then you've got the gameplay.  Smooth and addictive, like a mentholated cigerette.  When you die, most times its your own fault, and in no other series should 'Patience is a virtue' be taken more to heart.  Whether you run in guns blazing, or pop in without a sound, the gameplay always seems frantic.  The graphics tie in so well with this too.  I've never played a game more violent.  Sure, you can say that it's pixelated, but the first time you execute someone on the ground with the boiling water or the hammer, you can't really help but cringe due to the implications of it all.  It's incredibly well done.
The Music of this game is the frosting that keeps the moist, delicious cake othat is this game together.  I read that the creators just picked out what sounded good, and to me, that's astounding.  Some of them feel like a violent rythym game, with every bludgeon going with the electronic beats of the music.  It creates a to die for package that I've yet to find emulated well.  It's really one of a kind.
I know this isnt the best game that's ever been made, and I wouldn't try to make that argument.  But in my opinion, there is no comparrison to anything else.  It is the best game I've ever had to good fortune to play, and I'm glad for every hour I've played.  Buy it.

This is a game I wouldn't hesitate to recommend to anyone who has interest in space or exploration. Vehicle construction works like Legos and is very intuitive. The modding community is HUGE and there are lots of tools that make designing the perfect vehicle easier, such as delta v and thrust to weight ratio calculations. This sounds educational, and it is, but it is incredibly fun and gives an immense sense of accomplishment when you learn how to reach your next milestone. The feeling of landing on another celestial body the first time is an unparalleled sense of satisfaction.
This is Early Access done right. The game is fantastic and has infinite replayability. This is the most bang (literally) for your buck you will get out of any game.

I've had this game for a long long time now. I've never written a review before, but I feel like now is the time.
Firstly, I'll just quickly describe what the gameplay is like:
There is a sandbox mode with no limits, but that ruins the challenge, so I'll only talk about 'Campaign'. There is a third mode much similar to campaign called 'Science' which is like the usual campaign but without having to worry about money. I find that I enjoy placing limits on how much I can spend because otherwise the game feels a bit too easy. So, on to campaign:
Essentially, you start with a little booster and capsule and a parachute, you try and fly. On your way you'll collect some 'science' which will allow you to buy better parts so you can explore further. You'll complete 'contracts' and you get to decide how they're done. Want to complete 5 contracts in one go by tying four satellites to the side of your Moon lander and basically just launching them off the side? Sure thing, go ahead. You do all the thinking and all the piloting. Good luck.
Eventually, you'll make it to space. Then you'll make it to orbit. Then eventually you'll start dreaming up your own missions to try and land on other planets. You design, build and fly your own craft. You can get out and explore entire moons, or planets. (To be honest though, planets are *big* and usually just boring. That goes for real life, too, though). This isn't No Mans Sky where you'll find so much crap on every planet, but that's okay - the fun is in the journey and the career progression.
I have never learned so much from a game. This game demands that you learn, and you'll god damn enjoy it. Ridiculous things will happen along the way:
- you'll travel halfway to Duna only to realise you don't have enough fuel to slow down and be captured into orbit,
- you'll almost *certainly* deploy your parachutes at the same time as your main engine at some point. If you haven't already done so: try it.
- You'll de-orbit a space station just for fun.
- You'll gleam with pride once you manage your first Mun landing, and you'll be ecstatic if/when you manage to land on another planet.
Pros:
- Really deep game with lots of hours of fun to be had. I've spent days outside of the game thinking about my missions, and sometimes I just sit and watch my ships orbit with pride.
- learn astrophysics in a way that you can see, and have fun with
- build ridiculous rockets, robots, space stations and moon bases - MANUALLY. You literally will have to land two modules (that you designed) on a moon and try to connect them MANUALLY. The satisfaction when you achieve this is unbeaten in gaming, IMO.
- HUGE amounts of modding, with a really dedicated modding community. You can make the game how you want, for example: Different rockets, ship parts, overhauls on graphics, gameplay mods etc. There really is a great collection.
Cons:
- Sometimes in career mode there are contracts that begin to get repetitive. There's only so many times I can run a fairly routine satellite launch to Kerbin orbit. I tend to accept these and use the cheats menu to just mark them as complete: I know that sounds cheap, but I feel like it massively reduces the grind, and it helps me get on with the more challenging aspects of the game
- Sometimes, very occasionally, there will be a glitch if you're running the game too fast that makes your rocket spin out of control or miss a re-entry. I've literally flown through a planet because the game (and my ship) was travelling at such a high speed that (presumably) the game engine didn't have a chance to check for collision. This is easily avoided: Don't run your game at 100000 times the speed when you're a little too close to a planet.
All in all, I'd buy this game twice.

One thing that really stood out to me with Wasteland 2 is the depth of the game. I have played a lot of RPG games over the years and I now realize that the character development and story is getting thinner and thinner and the action getting richer. I do not mind this at all. On the other hand I think that if you want to run and gun, do not want to do much reading and do not really care about the background stories then you will probably not find this nearly as rewarding.
There are some negatives with the game. Some of details in the character development can be overwhelming and unclear. Most of this is clarified in the game manual which you should read. Also some of the UI controls can be a bit unintuitive for example trading items between characters. Finally the camera can get a bit frustrating to have to keep moving around to get the best angle. On the other hand it is nice to have the freedom to position the camera yourself.

Is Wasteland 2 up to spec?  No, sadly, it is not.
As a squad-based RPG, it feels more like FO:Tactics than Wasteland.  There is a storyline, but the actual roleplay suffers from the lack of a central character.  You end up with less of a Fallout-style Jack of All Trades and more of a set of specialists that feels stale.
The game also seems unfinished, with many bugs still present and most problems have one real solution and a bunch of approaches to it.  The conversation choices are just garnish and a lot of interactions will result in being attacked without a chance to explain or talk it out.  Prepare to be frustrated by a game that looks more modern, but lacks depth (plenty of breadth, though).
It's been covered in other reviews, but here are the basic issues with this over-specialization:
-You have to constantly switch between party members for each task (lockpicking, safecracking, defusing, disabling) and wait for each to have a small loading icon to complete the task.  The delay between selection, the poor controls, and having to swap between them makes it tedious.  All for an old teddy bear, a used polaroid, and some scrap metal (not a joke, this is the kind of loot you will be seeing a lot of).
-Success at these skills yields XP, but only to the party-member who does it.  This means that your demo guy will be getting a lot more, as almost everyone in the wastes seems to have the knowledge, supplies, and desire to trap everything.
-Some weapons types are so situationally specific as to be obnoxious (looking at you shotgun and heavy weapons).  Others have handicaps that don't make sense (an assault rifle suffers a penalty to hit when a target is adjacent, which the AI exploits by rushing a group of heavily armed people with an axe).
-You have to micro-manage prior to combat to ensure that your weapons are optimally employed, but it is often a matter of getting interrupted by the enemy spotting you (no, there is no "sneak" option either) and having combat kick off prematurely while you awkwardly select and move your personnel.
-NPCs (to include hire-ons) have a tendency to go rogue, ruining your carefully-crafted team composition and plan.  This usually means rushing out of cover and often shooting past teammates, hitting them in the process.  Tag-alongs (like animal friends or story characters) are always in this AI pattern, making you leave your positions to take the heat off of them.
Now let's talk about design.
-Levels are often open areas with little or nothing to do in them.  A few stashes (with locks, tumblers, alarms, and traps... whee!) or cliche'd NPCs and a lot of walking in-between.  You keep looking, using your perception skill, to try to find SOMETHING there, but the return is rarely worth the effort.
-The AI.  It's horrible, devolving into people with guns rushing into range and often sharing cover with the enemy (in some cases, side-by-side).
-Difficulty.  Harder levels just mean more HP and armor for the enemies and higher levels required for defusing, unlocking, etc.  Just a waste of time, as it makes the game tedious and not challenging.
-Combat is disappointing.  While they did add "headshot" as a choice, the fights seem to be somewhat formulaic and the level design does not make for interesting cover-based shootouts or flanking.  It feels somewhat stale and would have benefitted from the location-based targeting of the Fallout series.  Also, the incidence of shooting friendlies is too high, making it a common occurence when AI starts rushing.  APs are too few to attempt to run around and you really don't have many options or any selectable skills to make it tactical.
-The UI is clunky.  Rather than have selectable portraits at a fixed point, when you open the inventory/skill screen, it pops up a new set.  Baldur's Gate did not suffer from this issue, so why move in this direction?  When you open your skills screen to level up, the bars don't always load and you have to scroll to force it to do so.  There is also a delay when opening this screen, despite the relatively simple nature of its display.
-The engine has issues with mouse-based selection, with items blocking your click with a transparent "hit box" (this happens with both terrain and mobs).  There are also times when the game does not register a click.  Not a deal-breaker, just makes the game feel less polished.
-Movement honestly feels worse than in Wasteland.  I preferred the grid-based precision that the original had to the click and watch a throng of morons push past each other.  The ability to set up formations would be a welcomed solution (again, Baldur's Gate had this...).
I'm disposed to complain, but here is the up-side:
+The game seems pretty long and there are a lot of locations to visit (even if their maps are too bland).
+There is a weapon mod system in which you can recover parts of a weapon (though it seems odd that it's random what you get).
+The conversation system shows you what skills you would need to select what options, setting it up for future play-throughs in which you can make informed decisions regarding new NPC skills.
+No crashes to date.  Despite some clunkiness, they seem to have made it very stable.
+Some elements of the original remain and it is kinda neat to see how things have changed since.
+The millieu is interesting, if limited.  There remain a lot of quests, both cliches and refreshing.
If you liked Fallout Tactics, you will be right at home.  If you like Fallout 1&2, you might be a little underwhelmed.  If you're looking to recapture that Wasteland feeling...  Well, it's there in some storyline nods, but the gameplay has changed significantly.
The sum is greater than its somewhat-flawed presentation.  You will get your money's worth if you stick with it, but there will be moments of aggravation.

I love visual novels quite a bit. So when an visual novels come to Steam, I usually purchase them to support said games. It doesn't help that I this game was made by the same people who did "Unhack," a game which I adore immensely. However, the problem lies in multiple aspects, making it confused as to what the true culprit is which makes this game not pass.
Let's break down the elements on the game, starting with the music. This section will be short because, to be frank, the music is pretty forgettable. Normally, with another game, I wouldn't focus to heavily on this but, with a visual novel, there is a lot more riding on the music, It conveys what the game can't so the music needs to convey every emotion just as well as the character's dialogue and voice cast, if there is one. With "Bermuda," the music felt static. It never felt like it was anything special and, once the scene was over, the music vanished both from the game and my memory.

Next, let's look at the story. The story provided is rather silly in concept and is too rushed to be anything special. It also doesn't help that this seems to be a character driven story but fails in execution, which I will discuss later. The plot is sort of there because it needed to be, that's all.
Before moving onto the characters in question, let's address one of the major problems with the game: the gameplay. To be fair, not many visual novels have a gameplay aspect so, the fact that this one does makes it a tad more interesting for having one. With that said, the gameplay is boring. If it was difficult but well-made, I wouldn't be able to complain. If it was very easy but well-made, I'd complain on difficulty but that's it. However, "Bermuda"'s  gameplay finds a way to be  simple, boring, and pathetically easily. You move the main character, Edward, on the same map, accomplishing whatever  goal is given to you. Whether that be going to the top floor, buying time for someone, or bringing guards to their untimely demise. The problem is that it's the same thing, not really changing at all. It's boring is the best way to put it.
The last point and the largest problem are the characters. There are only about five major characters, not discussing one for spoiler reasons. The first is Finyomu, the acting commander of the ship. She's only about seven years old but acts much older than that. She wishes to know more about the surface world, studying humans to learn more about them. Besides some things that come up later, that's pretty much it. She's a basic character, as if copy and pasted. The second-in-command, Mukan, has even less character. She's the atypical tomboy, liking girly things (poetry, romance novels, etc.) but having to be a hard♥♥♥♥♥on the ship. She's overly protective of Finyomu though she is her best friend. That's it. Then the human characters. First up is Paul. He's a tough guy who went to jail for protecting another character, Joanna, and is currently in a relationship with her. He's the guy who the reader might identify with in this situation. He happens to also be the most developed character in the story. The second human is Joanna. I hate this character. She's barely in the story but has such a pull on the Paul and Edward. She is clearly in love with Edward but is dating Paul because he asked. She is the only human teleported back to the surface before something goes wrong . That's all we know! Lastly, we have Edward/Eddie, the main character. He's bare bones, nothing special to him at all. Though he loves God...a lot. Exaggerating here but it's almost like every other sentence is about God. That bothered me immensely and made me start to hate him a bit. It's tiresome, hearing about God non-stop. That's all there is to it.
In case you couldn't tell, the main point in that massive section above was this. The story is too short for the characters to shine. No matter how bland a character might be, they can be exciting in some way throughout the story. Especially in a character driven story, the length can hinder the characters. Many stories, however, don't have this problem but I finished this game in just under two hours. That's too short. Visual novels like "Saya no Uta" or "Little Busters!" thrive on their characters. Though the latter is muchy longer, the former visual novel is fairly short, only about two to ten hours as listen on VNDB. However, unlike this game, "Saya no Uta" has characters which can shine, even if they aren't the best or most well-written. This game just didn't take the time so the characters fall flat, killing it along with it.
One last point before the wrap-up: the voice acting. Though these voice actors are amazing, having a deep love for Christina Vee and Kyle Herbert, the acting is fairly stiff. I don't know if it's because of the material given but there's something off with these performances. Well, except Christina Vee, who sounds very good and emotional. Everyone else is stiff.

I'm so glad I decided to buy this game on launch despite all the controversy. It's one of the most amazing open world games I've played. There's so much content, so much to do and with a ton of variation, unlike the previous title (Shadow of Mordor). You'll not get bored of killing orcs so easily here.
Player progression upgrades are essentially revamped with some skills returning and others having been modified or removed. However, you don't have to unlock everything in a specific order like you had to in the last game. This time around you can pick and choose from a customizable skill tree, or six different branches, with 6 main skills and 2-3 skill upgrades, per skill, of which you can only have 1 upgrade active at any time. There's enough variation there to allow for all sorts of gameplay styles.
The new and upgraded Nemesis system is fantastic and I recommend (as does the game) you to play it on nemesis difficulty if you truly want to enjoy it. I've been ambushed by♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off blood brothers (they come looking for you if you killed their blood broothers) and obsessed orcs so many times, and they all have unique dialogues fitting the situation in which you are ambushed. In fact some of the blood brothers will tag team you if you engage with any of their brothers recklessly. The orcs also adapt to your fighting style much faster on higher difficulties so you'll have to constantly think before you act. This ensures that every encounter is unique and doesn't get repetitive.
The new fortress attack (offline) quests are a welcome addition. Conquering fortresses with your upgraded army is so much fun. You can lay siege to the enemy with siege graugs or unleash drakes upon your enemies (they attack the enemy, but your troops are not fireproof). Once you conquer a fortress you can upgrade its defenses with Mirian which is the in-game currency (not the micro-transaction one). However, this is where things get a little iffy. Mirian is earned through in-game quests, nemesis missions, and random treasure carrying orcs who also carry gems you can use to enchant weapons and armor with. The problem with Mirian is simply that you earn too little through active quests and story missions to upgrade your fortresses  with (3000 and 7500 upgrades), so expect a little grind there - mark a captain or warchief with death threat, kill him, do the challenge for his dropped loot (weapons and armor) and then salvage it for Mirian.
There's a lot of story missions this time around and they are all beefy segments with a good deal of orc mudering, sneaking around and also quality (4k) cutscenes. I am not a huge fan of Tolkien's written lore. I watched the movies and read The Hobbit, so I don't really care (at all) about all this pointless talk of "lore r**pe." This game is not canon to books, it's canon to the jacksonverse. Just leave it at that.
Micro-transactions: not necessary, still a questionable decision by the publisher (and perhaps the developer), you 100% do not need them. You get a ton of legendary orcs for the end game through just being active with the nemesis system. So please don't read those silly "don't buy this game because micro-transactions" reviews. Yes, they suck and shouldn't be in a $60 game but when you don't buy the game you don't hurt the publisher. You hurt the developer. They might be forced to put this franchise on hold, be reassigned to work on other projects for the publisher, or even have layoffs. This is a great game, 9/10 game. Buy it and play it if you are a fan of the previous title. Don't buy the lootboxes.

Basically the only gripe I consistenly see about this game are the loot boxes and the "grind" that "strongly encourages" you to buy loot boxes.  First off, Shadow Wars isn't a grind.  It's shockingly easy to keep your followers leveled up, and the turnover of orc captains makes finding new and improved potential allies very easy.  Secondly, the regular loot boxes (the ones you use Mirian  to buy), are actually pretty decent once your character is in the mid 40's.  You'll commonly get captains with one or no weaknesses (perfect for fortrerss defense or assault).  Not only that, but the game literally throws Mirian at you.  There's no other useful place to spend that Mirian (after you max out your fortress upgrades) except for the market.
TL;DR: Stop freaking out about microtransactions.  There is no need for anyone to use real money to buy the loot boxes, just use the in game currency that Shadow of War showers upon you.

Until now, I've never been able to play a game all day while working. I'll get an alert from a friend on gmail, by the sound of a beep, but it's not a friend on gmail, it's a mountain in space, sharing mildly philosophical musings by the chord of a distant piano. Like other works from David O'REilly, seemingly random, low-poly characters interact. This is the first time though, the characters are inanimate. They share as much quirky personality, just the same. It brings to mind the inanimate rock we live on, which continues to slowly turn. If someday animate characters become inanimate corpses, burrowed on its surface - like barrels, traffic cones, or a thumbtack - it would still be a planet turning in space. My mountain once asked me, "How can I prove I exist?" Well, I look forward to continue watching my mountain, thereby proving its existence.

While playing this game, I felt like I was back in chemistry class. Everything is related to elements on the periodic table and/or forming molecules with those elements, but the game refuses to even give you the common courtesy of showing an overlay of the elements on the periodic table - instead, you're presented with a blank version of the table with which you have to guess blindly until you find the right spots for what you want.
Quests are often related to picking out the correct set of elements on the periodic table. An example of this system is "be harvesting X number of elements with electronegativity value Y". I would just place harvesters on random elements until I got the right combo, which ultimately just wasn't fun. I prefer games that don't feel like school work.

[OLD REVIEW: When only the first part was out]
Now to the actual critisisms of the game. The game is incredibly short and since this is supposed to be about half of the game, I am very worried for the total length of this game when it's complete. The puzzles are very simplistic and straight forward which means that the story, characters and enviroments is what has to be good to carry this game.
And they are. The game oozes of atmosphere with great characters, great enviroments all realised with a beautiful artstyle. The story is also good so far but I can't put down a real opinion there as the game is not finished.
[UPDATE: May 02 2015]
The second part is now out and I have to say that the game all in all, is a disappointment. The first thing that is important to mention is that there are very few new assets or anything new to experience in the second part. All characters and enviroments are reused although re arranged and modified a bit to be the setting of the new story and the story in it self is not very good. It doesn't make much sense and the end doesn't manage to satisfy in any way.
The length of the game, as I was afraid of the last time I reviewed the game, is indeed very short and is mostly hold up by some puzzles that will take a long time to figure out. This is because the difficulty spike in the second part is enormous. While the first part was way too easy, the second one can be frustratingly hard. All in all there is one word I would describe Broken Age with and that is disappointment. It might be worth to play if you catch it on a sale for the art and atmosphere alone but otherwise, stay far away from it.

- - -THE LOOT BOX CON - - -
A lot of people are bent out of shape simply because of the inclusion of the boxes in the first place, but what if I told you the end-game is actually built around making things easier if you just buy a crate?
In Shadow of Mordor, I liked to start up the challenge modes and simply run around and Dominate the cool looking orcs and execute the rest, then start the challenges over.  In this game it's not that easy...
Since the game has a leveling system and orcs level with you, a majority of the orcs starting from level 45+ appear to spawn with the "Iron Will" trait (at least in my game so far).  This means they cant be dominated unless you first shame them in an attempt to remove the trait.  But, doing this has a chance to ruin their mind, and it's still not even guaranteed that you will remove the "Iron Will" trait from them.
If you do successfully remove the "Iron Will" trait from an Orc, you still have to hunt them down again, dominate them, and then level them back up.  In short, the only reliable way to dominate an orc at or near your level after 50+ seems to be to hope he is one of the few who spawn without "Iron Will", or to simply purchase from the Market.
- - -THE REVIEW - - -
This the first game, but they took the concept and made it "More".  Then added a handful of other things.
Not exactly better or worse overall.  Some aspects of the game are better, some are worse.
THE GOOD:
The Story is pretty decent, small issue here or there with the Plot, but nothing significant.
The combat can be fun, and it's a good game to just start up and kill some time orc hunting.
The online mode adds a bit of a unique challenge to the game, especially considering you can "Invade" friends.
I also enjoyed that they incorperated the Wraiths into the game.
The Appendix shows some of the background to the world or lore that's interesting to read.  I dont remember if this was in the first one.
THE BAD:
The motto for the game was "Nothing will be forgotten" - Except Talion forgot all of his skills from the last game, and you must relearn them.  Also, neither my "Nemesis" or "Follower" looked the same as from the last game, but both of those orc appearances are in this game, so I'm not sure what happened there.  Not really a big deal, but that part obviously looks "Forgotten" to me.
The concepts it does have, you do over and over - this pads the gametime, but cant really be called "Extra Content".  It can be enjoyable, or it can be annoying depending on your preference.
The quest-lines are tiered behind completing certain "Checkpoints" in the areas, but it's more of the same concepts you'll already need to be doing, ie. "Dominate X Followers in this area to unlock", "Capture the Fortress in this Area to unlock", "Learn this Skill to unlock", etc.
Talion moves like you're trying to steer a boat.  If you're trying to sprint through an area, you'll sometimes run up walls you werent aiming at, or when attempting to use an ability on an orc (Execute, Combat Brand, etc), he'll sometimes cast in the complete opposite way that you're aiming.
Hit tracking is also an issue.  I cant count the times I used an execute or an attack, and Talion would sprint 100 yards in a direction to just land a hit.  The enemy orcs do this also; some will attack the air a mile away from you, but if you dont hit that counter or dodge, you'll still take damage, because hit tracking is going to find a way to move them ALLL the way to you in time to hit you.  For the "Charging skills" the Orcs do, this makes sense, for everything else it doesnt.  I really think this needs to be nerfed/patched a bit.
Additionally, I dont understand the point of "Ring" in this game.  It seems like all of your abilities in game are the same with or without it.  Maybe it's the "Branding Skill" that's the difference or it doesnt matter because you have the Elf, but I'm not 100% sure.
The End-Game is set up to be a tedious grind.  It's probably also really feels intended for you to suppliment this with the loot crate system.
There is no replayability. - Well, there is, but it's artificial as in "They're attacking my fort again" or "I lost the fort they kept attacking, now you need to take it back".
It's really up to the Orcs regarding how "Dominated" their mind really was by your Ring of "Power" especially since they canturn on you whenever they want..."Dominate mind"? More like "Politely encourage loyalty" instead.
The Carnan Quest-Line:
The first half is what you expect.  From the second half on, it is 100% trash IMO, and drastically takes away from what was enjoyable about the game.  Again, here the Orcs are somehow the most powerful thing in LOTR Lore...There's a necro orc and his allies that infinitely res during the encounters unless you break the nearby totem, This wouldnt be a bad thing, but the totems for this quest line, unlike every other totem in the game, require you to "Dominate" them, intead of climb to the top, which means standing still casting while mobs are coming back to life or trying to hit or shoot you.  If this wasnt annoying enough, during the later phase of this quest you have to fight the boss and about 40 orcs while trying to destroy 4 totems.  Then on the very next part of this quest, you have to do the same thing with 6 totems, except this time each totem is also guarded by a champion who you have to listen to gargle for 30 seconds.  For me, the majority of these guys had "Death-Defying" as well, so most of them were adapting to everything over the course of the fights and this really turned this into a tedious quest grind for me.
HIT OR MISS:
If you thought the first one was hard, I'd argue that RNG can make this one harder.
Because they added a system where orcs can "Adapt", and some of the traits line up in a way that already limit how you can attack some of the orcs, it makes me wonder why Sauron isnt serving them...
In my game, because of this Adapt mechanic, two of the orcs already seem to be invincible:
For starters, neither have any mortal weaknesses; the first is a savage who I cant perform normal attacks against, is "Vigilant to Stealth, Immune to Executions, "Can heal himself during combat through sheer willpower", has adapted to shoulder charge, vault and the wraith punch.  - The only thing I can hurt him with is ranged, and 9 headshots only take him down to about 60% HP.  By the time I run and collect more Elf-Shot, he's already used his heal ability (Even if I interrupt it, he immediately starts it up again - no CD on it).  The one time I did manage to get his HP down, before he had adapted to the vault, he had death-defying.  I'm pretty sure Sauron will be one of his Warchief's soon.
The second one has a shield, and I cant get beyond the shield.  Everything that you would use on a shielded orc (Pin, Vault, etc) he was either immune to or had adapted to.  The only damage I can do is if I run away and run back into him and somehow land a hit on his "Back".  He also had death-defying though, so it felt like too much effort.
You could make the blind argument of "Get gud", but I've actually only died 2-3 times in this game in about 35 hours.  The difficulty really seems hit or miss.  I steam-roll most orcs, or know how to utilize the moves you can use on them, but some of the encounters seem like you're not meant to win them without cheesing.
All in All; If you liked the first one or you like the LOTR lore, you'll probably like this.  If you're just looking at this for the first time, pick up the first game before this, it's cheaper now and has a majority of the same content.  If you really like that, then try this.

This game would be fun for an existing chemistry hobbyist, but if you have only a passing curiosity in chemistry you may not have fun when the game asks you to google chemistry topics.  The game feels like it is built with the "I am not doing your homework for you" attitude you occasionally get on the more pedantic science forums.  This feeling persists through navigation through the unique user interface that is subsequently confusing as hell.  I have played hundreds of games and used all kinds of software in my life, and while the UI in this game doesn't rank near something like ZBrush in outlandish design, it is definitely on the far side of awkward.  This would be fine if there was some help in understanding it, but that is not the way this game works.
I think a useful way to understand what this game is or where it stands in the landscape of video games is to compare it against the game Spore.  For me, Spore was a fun adventure that anyone could enjoy.  It was also a game about evolution, but it didn't ask you to study anything.  Rather than a fun adventure, I think this game, Idle Evolution, fits best as a time-killer companion to a General Chemistry college class.  This is of course with my UI arguments notwithstanding.  I could see this as being something a chemistry student would use to ease off some of the pressure gained from studying without actually departing the world of chemistry.  What this is not, is another game like Spore for the casual gamer.

This is a good example why there should be a difference between idle (incremental) and clicker games on Steam.
Those are the complete polar opposites of gameplay.
A clicker is a game where you are supposed to furiously click the same button thousands of times to progress or earn points.
In Idle Evolution clicking doesn't earn you anything. There is a hover mechanic, but you can alt-tab while hovering and it'll still count.
This is a game designed to be put away for some time (in fact, some missions straight up require you to do that), so you can go do something productive knowing that there will be something interesting waiting for you when you get tired.
The game sure has its flaws (grindy minigames, missions that lie to you, weird design for higher difficulty, appendix upgrade that does nothing AFAIK), but it's good enough as a productivity tool.
It's also useful to learn some real scientific numbers along the way. At least definitely more useful than learning numbers like "blue laser damage", "green dragon hp" and "bear butt drop rate".

So, I'm here writing a review, because the game has asked me to stop playing for 30 minutes. I will progress my level a little bit, if I don't play it for 30 minutes. Quite an odd request, but hey, here I am.
To be honest, I really feel like I have no idea what I'm doing, though I'll chop that up to not having played very much. I know I'm building a planet, using chemical compounds created out of harvested elements. I'm also helping to push evolution along by earning chemical bonds by creating more elements needed to create specific bonds.
If that sounds a little daunting, that's because it is.
The thing is, even though I feel kinda doubtful as to whether I'm actually doing it right nor not, I'm still progressing.
I
I'm doing it right, but I still don't feel sure.
This is not your average clicker game, not by a long shot. That being said, it is still quite entertaining, and I feel pretty sure that I'm going to get it all figured out within time.
It's actually kind of nice to play a clicker/idle game that truly does require thought, througout. It's not just mindless clicking, you won't progress by opening it and just leaving it running for 300 days in a row. You have to do stuff, and that stuff does require at least a little bit of chemistry smarts.
I would surely recommend this to someone who likes the genre (clickers and idlers), but who also doesn't mind a bit of a thought challenge.
If that sounds like you, you'll probably enjoy this game.

Let me just put it this way:
This and LEGO(R) MARVEL Superheroes are two equal and opposite sides of the same coin.
One is open city play Manhattan. One is open PLANET play Earth, plus a piece of the Nine Realms thrown in for fun.
One is utterly Original Story, with all the Classic Characters LEGO-ified from the Fantastic Four to Deadpool, the other is Carbon-Copy of the Cinematic Universe.
It Includes as much of the Netflix and ABC shows as possible while neglecting some obvious things from the previous game including the lack of return of even Deadpool Red Bricks, which is super obviously due to this game being prepared before everything was finalized for MARVEL to be allowed to make Deadpool and get Spider-Man into Civil War. Yes, this game is a MARVEL game with no Spider-Man, but with a team of 'Defenders' that includes neither Namor, Hulk, nor Doctor Strange.
Does that make it bad? NO! This to me makes one game simply Timeless, and one simply a Period Piece. A Historical Artifact. The first game took place in a strange Tesseract-Aether created Alternate Amalgam Universe, the LEGO Universe. This is the reverse-engineer process, A Basic LEGO game, MARVEL-Cinematic Universe-ified.
There are Three Kinds of People:
Those who love love love what Game 1 is doing and hate what Game 2 is doing;
Those who love love love what Game 2 is doing to get to the point and didn't stop as much to smell the roses for Game 1 (Game 1 lacked Infinity Stones or Eternity, come on!)
And Those who......having seen what Game 1 and Game 2 look like......strongly believe that Game 3, which is so, totally coming, is going to be the all-time-record Best MARVEL game in the History Of Ever.
LEGO MARVEL: Infinity War is going to have Spider-Man. It's going to have Deadpool. It's going to have Thanos and the Infinity Gems. It's going to have at the very least the Cinematic Universe's take on the Cosmic Powers that Be. It's going to not be so gummed up by a zillion X-Men-verse characters, and lack of Magneto is going to be a sad thing, but we will have space for a zillion other characters that we wouldn't have got that have their own charm, and we will have who knows what else. We can even strongly hope that by the time it's time for LEGO MARVEL 3, MARVEL will at least be able to negotiate for the use of Fantastic Four characters for the game, whatever happens film-wise. Which will be great and awesome.
I have had some glitch issues and it took me a while to fix them.
I wasn't able to get the DLC the same day I got the game, but as soon as I could, I did.
It's LEGO. And it's MARVEL.
If you have played basically any games at all, there is something in this game for you, and while you might be reluctant to pay full price for it, you know you wish you had more money to justify impulse buying it even if you have doubts. Of course you will miss Spider-Man. But you will love flying around the Planet landing on the Hub Worlds.
As with many games of this nature, the Secrets and Extras are not only harder than you would expect after a slew of easy ones, but sometimes your own controls get in the way and make it seem physically impossible to ever get something.
Be honest. You knew what you were getting into. You are HOPING for that experience, so you can say, I got THAT character-whose-name-I-don't-know-and-doesn't-appear-in-anything-I've-ever-seen-ever-and-even-my-dad-doesn't-know-this-insane-pointless-obscure-character.
You know that character? The one with ZERO good stories about them? Well now they HAVE a Story about them. The Story of YOU getting their Character Token in LEGO MARVEL's Avengers.
Captain America (Sam Wilson) Falcon can partner with Captain America (Civilian) Steve Rogers who is just in a Jacket and Shield, to explore Washington DC's Mall together, and just running side by side each other gets an Achievement. Know what it's called?
ON YOUR LEFT.
You do realize that right there is worth the price of admission, yes?
Also, there's like, a whole game to play, and stuff, besides the zillion ''OMG SQUEEE!" moments like that.
Does Arnim Zola (Classic) look stupid and not fit this game at all? Yes, absolutely.
Is that a problem worth complaining about? Not when finding him is one of the hardest things you'll do. He's not hard to reach, but he's HIDDEN. Really Well. Very Secret. Much Stealth. And his Hideout is one of the best parts of the game.

This is my favourite game.  Bar none.  I've never played anything more fun than this.
The story, immaculate.  Rather then shove it down your throat, they let you decide how engrossed you want to be.  You want to just kill a load of blokes, then get to the end?  Brilliant.  You want to piece together what exactly the crazy guy you're controlling is doing?  Even better.  Nothing is spoon-fed to you here.  You make the most out of this games story yourself.  Ive played both games all the way through, and am still trying to decipher what the hell happened, exactly.  There really isnt anything else like it out there, where you honestly could become so engrossed in whats on the surface a Violent Sociopath Sim.  There's just so much more to this game.
Then you've got the gameplay.  Smooth and addictive, like a mentholated cigerette.  When you die, most times its your own fault, and in no other series should 'Patience is a virtue' be taken more to heart.  Whether you run in guns blazing, or pop in without a sound, the gameplay always seems frantic.  The graphics tie in so well with this too.  I've never played a game more violent.  Sure, you can say that it's pixelated, but the first time you execute someone on the ground with the boiling water or the hammer, you can't really help but cringe due to the implications of it all.  It's incredibly well done.
The Music of this game is the frosting that keeps the moist, delicious cake othat is this game together.  I read that the creators just picked out what sounded good, and to me, that's astounding.  Some of them feel like a violent rythym game, with every bludgeon going with the electronic beats of the music.  It creates a to die for package that I've yet to find emulated well.  It's really one of a kind.
I know this isnt the best game that's ever been made, and I wouldn't try to make that argument.  But in my opinion, there is no comparrison to anything else.  It is the best game I've ever had to good fortune to play, and I'm glad for every hour I've played.  Buy it.

Look at my name.  LOOK AT IT!  And tremble before the fearful countenance that is my Desert Dweller portrait!
Yes...I'm an old Wasteland 1 fan.  Loved it then back on the old C=64.  Loved Fallout 1, 2, Tactics and Fallout 3, all of which were inspired and modeled after Wasteland.  So I am admittedly a little biassed in this brief review.
Some things I like about it so far:
- Depth of choice
- Consequences and world alteration based on those choices
- Deep character customization
- The atmosphere created by the visuals and audio
- There is 'enough' eye candy and ear candy without going overboard
- Multiple approaches/solutions to many problems
- Challenge and reward levels feel apropriate
- There is 'enough' realism to add in planning and tactics that help immersion without being burdensome
- Lots of nods and references to the original that actually fit into the story and make sense
- There is 'enough' voice acting with apropriate emotion that isn't too cold/dry or too flowery/dramatic
- The written story is deep, interesting, concise and easy to follow so you can move on quickly
Some things I would like to see improved:
- Character creation needs more detailed notes for newcomers.
- It is not clear HOW or even IF most of the C.L.A.S.S.I.C. attributes alter your skills.  Derived stats, yes.  Skills, I can only see one stat that will impact some of them.
- Screen edge scrolling/panning of the area map is a little slow.
- Would like a little more freeness in the camera controls.  Rotation, zoom and angle.  I don't care if I see map edge.
- Sometimes hard to tell what is and is not cover in combat.
Overall though, it is great fun and stays very true to the original.  Even with the few lumps it has, it is very polished, rock solid stable, and seems optimized well for multicore CPUs and multi-GPU setups.  Characters and quests make sense and are well scripted and laid out to be intuitive and challenging.  There is some fun exploring little nooks in the areas to find hidden loot and bonuses.  And while it is fairly linear, the branches you can take are divrese and plentiful.  I see a lot of replay value just from the choices you can make.  And your choices will have impact, sometimes in unexpected and even unplesant ways.
So, grab your Proton Axe and Meson cannon...and don your best suit of Pseudo-Chitin armor.  It's time to go out adventuring among the muties.  Just be careful, so you can come back to camp and share your stories around the fire over a bottle of Snake Squeezins.  Radioactive glow and 3rd arm optional, of course.

The story is interesting, and has a few plot threads that maybe run too independently of each other. Life is Strange, overall, is just a lovely game, which tells a story that will captivate a lot of people.

Just a note: I am not one of the many people who have played the free version on Kongregate. This is my first time even hearing of this title.
That being said, my first impressions of this title were positive to say the least. When you first start a game there are three difficulties—normal, chemist, and Heisenberg--with the last being unlocked by completing the game on any difficulty. The higher the difficulty, the less help you'll receive, so if this is your first foray into this title, normal is your best bet. You can also select how the HUD will look between basic and full; the former is short and sweet, showing only the minimum options, and full allows you to control every aspect of your atom production. Are you a Chem major or are you new to the whole science thing? The game can be tailored to suit your scientific know how. Off to a good start.
From there, the game begins a long, in-depth tutorial. Rather than do this all at once and overload you with game mechanics and menus, the game eased you in, easing you in one step at a time through a series of objectives meant to nude you gently in the right direction. Wonderful.
The objective of Idle Evolution is to evolve planets through the various periods--from the beginning of time, when there was no life in a barren landscape up through the atmosphere developing water creatures evolving into land dwellers and so on with the help of compounds valuable to life -- compounds that you create. Basically, it’s playing God on a molecular level.
The first step of your sciencing is to gather atoms by placing extractors on a square marked Hydrogen, the only element available to you right off the bat. These atoms act as your currency for purchasing upgrades, making compounds for evolution, and activating different passive bonuses.
And then, you wait. Because this is an idle game, you will spend a lot of time, well, *idling*. Still, there are a few things to do when you have enough atoms/
.
The heart of every idle game. Evolution upgrades net you more extractors and makes them more effective actively (when cursor is over it) automatically the general production rate without any added bonuses or modification, and when you’re idle (close the game); it also allows you to increase storage of atoms, increase the exchange rate between atoms by percent, create and use compounds in greater quantities for a quicker evolution, and the like.
Evolution is achieved by using requested compounds. If you have the atoms necessary to make that compound, they will be combined for you with a click of a button and you can then increase the evolution percentage with a click of a different button.
Zones are separated into groups like noble gases, akali metals, and transitional metals. Having an extractor on each element in a zone activates a passive bonus that can be increased in the zone menu by using points accumulated simply by having active zones.
The Zones screen is the only place you won’t spend atoms. Instead, your atoms passively gain points every second and you use those instead.
Accessing this menu allows you to play a mini game where you control a bot and the goal is to shoot green tiles by clicking them. Each shot costs atoms in an increasing amount and when you get to 16%, you unlock the next atom in the table. If you shoot all of the tiles, all of the important information for the atom—boiling point, atomic number, etc—is revealed and you get a 1% increase in an overall atom production boost.
Eventually you’ll unlock the ability to shoot all of the tiles automatically, but this is costly.
Here you can exchange one type of atom for another. You can increase the rate of exchange in the upgrades menu.
The reserve menu allows you to set aside a percentage of your atoms to dedicate to passive upgrades via points. The percentage set aside for reserve cannot be used for upgrades. The more atoms you have in reserve, the more points you’ll accumulate; then they can be allocated to improvements like shorter cooldowns for quizzes, more chances to retry mini games, etc.
Quizzes are where the game exhibits its education aspects the most. They are available every half hour of time spent in game and ask a range of questions from who is the scientist who discovered [this] to what the name of an element is, for which you’re given an image of the atoms it’s comprised of.There are also minigames--classics like brickbreak and match 2--but these are few and far in between, requiring you to click on an on-screen object that appears at random to activate them.
The game is very minimalistic and the dioramas for the planets/evolutionary periods being the most graphically intensive things you’ll encounter. As such, it should run smoothly on even older potatoes. The UI is clean and provides all of the information you’ll need at a glance. Need more info? There are tooltips for that. The music for Idle Evolution is great. If you intend to leave the game running in the background while you’re doing other things, it’s very nice-- not to mention catchy -- background music that runs the gamut from smooth jazz to upbeat futuristic electronica.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
I can't recommend Idle Evolution more--to the right audience. It's a very niche title, so if you're interested in the sciences, pick this one up. It will educate AND amuse you and, to me, that's worth the price of admission.

It has several different things to do -- you have the normal upgrades you would expect from a idler game, but also you can apply zone bonuses to an entire zone (such as "Noble gasses"), play a shooting mingame to 'know' elements to get an extraction bonus, find 3 hidden mini games, ....
If you do all of the achievements, you will spend noticeably more than the "10 hours of gameplay" mentioned in the store description [at least at the time I write this review]. So it delivers good value for the money even if it is not something I see my self returning to often.

Never got round to reviewing this when I played it, but I thought I should do it, since, in retrospect, it was one of the best games I ever played. In short, I remember that it struck me, that this is like Silent Hill 2 meets Max Payne 1, in a TV series kind of thriller presentation. There's hardly a thing wrong in this game. The stronger point is that the story is very good, narrated very well, that hooked me right from the and kept it very interesting and gripping right to the end. It takes place in a northern-ish, foresty setting that provides an immersive atmosphere, brought to life by the often stunning and impressive visuals. All the characters and sub plots are interesting and the voice acting is good across the board. The gameplay itself is like a 3rd person shooter, nothing too out of the ordinary, but the light/dark, sanity/insanity mechanics keep things tense, ominous, and mysterious. The pacing is good, unraveling the story in a quite gripping, thriller-esque, manner until the very end where everything ties together wonderfully. It left me with a memorable experience.
The lack of content in the game is scary. Do not waste your money on it.

If you want to paraphrase Hotline Miami, I'd say "gamedesign from hell with terrible controls, yet addictive"
The game has massive problems, yet somehow it gets you addicted.

the good:
- interesting, trippy "story"

- kinda skillbased combat mechanics

- price below 1€/$/£ when in sale

the bad:
- very random enemy AI. Sometimes they see and shoot you while being far out of your max vision reach. Othertimes they stand next to you and do nothing.
- special "stealth mission with no killing" is very annoying
- some enemies are magically invulnerable to certain attacks - w/o any explanation
- can't save mid-mission; so it's easy to lose 10+ minutes of gameplay if you have to leave
the ugly:
- FPS lock
- mousecursor is virtually invisible with all the trippy colors and stuff going on
- terrible controls. not only because you can't rebind keys, but the character moves as he's on ice, sliding and not being very precise.
- same silly, semi-unskippable cutscene plays in certain levels. As you might have to retry maps dozens of times, it really gets annoying fast.

Time for another review from me! So, here is Broken Age -- Tim Schäfer's first true Point n' Click adventure since Grim Fandango. It's been a while but it's amazing to see him return to the form. This is his hometurf and what he does best. But does it hold up to his usual standard. I'd certainly say so. Now some may say that the game's puzzles (which adventure games are so famous for) are fairly straigtforward. To a degree, they are, but I found myself thinking a bit every now and then.
Disregarding all that  -- The comedy and charm is as strong as ever -- You play as 2 characters this time, in 2 different settings, but both of them are related to the other in some way, which you'll discover as you play. First of we got Mr. Frodo, going by the name of Shay, who's a rather ordinary teenage boy, trapped in what most 10-12 year old boys might consider a Utopia, but Shay considers it a dull routine of nightmarish proportions.. because everything is done for you (You know, like how the gaming industry of today is -- Hurr, hurr) or in other words, just dull (like how we all felt during our mid-teens). Shay gets to live in futuristic space-ship, alongside an overprotective AI Motherbrain, who sees to his every needs (Feeding him with a spoon, tucking him in bed, turn every day adventure into easy mode --lol--). His life is basically devoid of excitement in an otherwise adventurous-looking setting --  Shay, getting bored of this ridiculous pretense, decides to flee from it, and accept an invitation from an ominous looking wolf-dressed man named Marek, ready to show him the true hardships of life and how sucky it can be sometimes. Meanwhile in a rural village is our other protagonist, Villa, who's just about ready for the traditional Maiden's Feast, involving her getting eaten by a Lovecraftian monstrosity. Neat.
In true Tim Schäfer style, all of the characters feel and act rather mundane but to an absurd degree. They all seem to think of the Maiden's Feast as an exciting celebration, like it was Christmas, despite it revolving around sacrificing innocent girls to be eaten by a cosmic monstrosity. Villa being the protagonist, asks what we are all thinking.. "Why the bleeding hell don't we just kill the damn thing?". But no, that would be going against a tradition that no one seems to bother changing because new things are scary, just like in real life -- And there you got it.
So as the tentacle beast devours the Maidens, Villa being the only rational human being left, decides to flee and learn how to kill the monster and save her village. It doesn't take long 'till Villa comes across an array of interesting caricatures, whom she has to help in order to proceed -- Among my favorites is the rather 'baked' lumberjack fellow named Curtis & the leader of the Cloud society, Meriloft, voiced by Jack Black.
True to its adventure roots, the game has various interpretations of keys for various interpretations of doors, which the player has to figure out in order to proceed. The puzzles are definitely still there but they are not at the league of more complex puzzles like that of the Silent Hill 2-3 games or older Schäfer adventures. What really sells this game is the humor, the characters, the artwork and especially the music. It's all very, very, gorgeous and this is how Adventure games are done -- Where Schäfer shines and Telltale does not. It's recommended to do Shay's story first, then finish it with Villa since her story is a bit longer. An actual negative I can give about the game is the fact that what you're getting isn't the whole game -- Act 2 is still in the making, but it'll be for free whenever, and thus obviously the game ends on a cliff-hanger, but an intriguing one nevertheless. Lastly, I musn't forget.
On the audio side you might notice the voicing talents of Jennifer Hale, Will Wheaton, Jack Black (returning from previous Double Fine game Brütal Legend and of course Elijah Wood himself -- Mr. Frodo). All of them do a superb job of enriching the adventure game experience by adding their sharp voices to the humor. Schäfer's voice director has done a splendid job to utilize all of the famous voices correctly. So a thumbs up for that and you'll have to forgive me for not mentioning the other voices, because there are certainly a few noteworthy ones. From a spaceship with talking cutlery, to a cloud society of sky people living with birds -- What you're getting is the Tim Schäfer experience that you'll recognize. So if enjoyed previous Double Fine games or the old LucasArts adventures, then don't cheat yourself out of this experience. While the game isn't complete yet, it is still very much worth it. But it might adviceable to wait a bit before one delves into it when the whole game is complete.

This is not the game you want if you want everything streamlined and obvious what to do next. This is the game for you if you like actually making choices and exploration.
- So many choices and stats. Or you can just go with pre-canned chars and not worry too much about it.
- Lots of text! So much text. Well written, and quite a bit of it is pretty funny, too.
- There's so much side-stuff to find that it's almost overwhelming. Don't get overwhelmed! You can find it on your next playthrough.
- The combat is like Fallout 2 and X-Com had a love child.
- I love Fallout 2, but be honest, the UI is absolutely horrible. This is quite intuitive.
- It looks painterly 2D, but it's really 3D, so you can zoom and pan and rotate the camera to your heart's content!
My only caveat is that I haven't finished it, so everything could go to hell, but I doubt it because this is the game inExile has been waiting 30 years to make.
If you like the old isometric overhead RPGs like Fallout 1 + 2, Arcanum, and even Baldur's Gate series, you need to get this.
Controls made it unplayable for me. Bored by the time I got to the first enemy.

Broken Age is very different in that it isn't what we're used to in video games, or at least it isn't common. If you're looking for a more action-oriented game, I'll probably point you twoards Double Fine's other title, Psychonauts. Broken Age is like an interactive popup book, moving the main characters around with a simple point-and-click, and choosing what to say through on-screen prompts.
This doesn't mean it isn't a good game. Oh no. I rather enjoyed being able to sit back and relax with it. The art style is absolutely gorgeous and does feel like the entire game is a painting, and the music is pretty and builds the settings. The writing is also very spot on with unique characters and witty comments. It does feel a little short, but don't forget that this game has two stories within it, and this is only the first Act. The next one you won't need to buy again, so be patient.
I'm not about to go and spoil the ending of the first Act for anyone, but it's one of those "the more you think about it, the more it blows your mind" endings.

Only recommend on sale.
FACTS:
- It runs smoothly on i7-6700, GTX1060 6GB, 32GB RAM and Win10 64 bit (60+ fps). My old LCD monitor can only go up to 1680x1050, but with most of the settings on ultra, the game looks great and loads pretty fast.
- No crash and no game breaking bug found.
- Wired X360 controller works great.
- The gameplay has received some tweaks and improvements from the first game. Combat feels more fluid. Beast riding is better (especially the drake). Stealth doesn't change much. There are good amount of skills to unlock, but once you get all the ones that suit your style, unlocking more doesn't matter much.
- In-app purchase isn't really affecting anything in single player. War Chests can save you a little grinding time, but that's about it. You don't have to pay real money if you don't want to. I haven't and I won't. Just destroy unused items (which are plenty) to get the in-game currency and you'll have more than enough to buy silver chests.
However, if you're serious about seeing your name up high on the leaderboard, then yes, the loot box economy will affect you. It means absolutely nothing to me though, so I don't complain about it.
CONS:
- It really gets criminally repetitious. Act 4 drags on way, way, way, wayyyy too long. (I have very high tolerance for repetition, so when I say it's too long and boring, I don't say it lightly.) This makes me want to be done with the game as fast as I can and I don't care to play any DLC campaign any more. Faction DLCs don't add much to the game anyway. It's just more of the 'kill that orc captain' missions.  Thus, DLCs aren't really worth it unless you get it cheap.
- Camera sucks in combat. It keeps swinging into weird angle and behind objects. It's fun fighting orcs; it's not when you have to fight the camera at the same time. This didn't happen at launch but after some patches it does now. Bravo. What a genius "fix".
In conclusion:
It's an improved 'more of the same' that isn't worth the full price and I regret pre-ordering it.
If you like Shadow of Mordor and you can tolerate serious degree of repetition, get it on sale.

Before I start, I want to say that I do not believe this is a bad game. This game is fine and im sure there is a niche market for fans of this, however I do not fall into this group. Scroll to the bottom for a pros/cons list.
For a long time I have enjoyed playing Idle and Clicker games, and have put likely thousands of hours of my life in them overall. I saw this game, thought it looked interesting and did some research. I found out there was an older version that was completely free to play online and I tried that out. After only a few minutes (I wasn't expecting too much to change throughout and the general concept of the game seemed clear enough) I decided I would purchase this game and see how it would work out. It starts out simply enough, and the tutorials are clear enough to get you where you need to be. It starts slow, like every one of these games, but I feel like the pace never picked up much since the beginning. The concept seems great, the gameplay was fine, but overall this game left me feeling like I wasn't doing much. You can argue that I only have 5+ hours played, which is true, but you also need to consider that time "idling" (not having the game launched) isn't counted for.
Pros:
-Great Idea, basing an idle game off the perodic table
-Not a mouse clicking spam fest
-Some education/testing of what you remember from school
Cons:
-Extremely slow progression, with way more content unlocking than I can manage
-This game is not free, if you are looking for a classic idle/clicker game there are many out there for free
-Some of the hints get annoying quickly if you're watching the screen waiting for something (such as some quest requirements)
Overall, I do not recommend this game because I do not think this is the type of game for everybody. As I said I consider myself a huge fan of this genre and this game just did not cut it for me. To anybody out there who loves this game, I hope you continue to enjoy it. For anybody looking for a new idle game, please take your time to try out other games first (including the free to play version of this online).
