I don't think a lot of people don't see the value in Mountain, and when people do they tend to simply overcomplicate the game for what it is. It's not meant to be a 'game' exactly. The developers of the game purposefully say this originally: "Leave it open - it's designed to run in the periphery of your life. Only interact with it when you feel like it. You can play Mountain while playing other games. If you are not playing it, it will play itself. ". Again Mountain is just mean to be left open and you can return to it when you feel like it. You might not see the aspect of it originally but you can find it later… hopefully. But then again, what are the standards of a 'game'? Are we to simply segregate Mountain simply because it is possibly outside of the norm? On the contrary! Different experiences lead to different viewpoints which make you more open-minded. So can people truly state that Mountain is not a game but a screensaver? There are many ways to view Mountain and seeing it as a screensaver is one of the more popular demoralizing viewpoints to which many have so acquired. So one can only view Mountain as simply a standalone and not compare it to more contemporary issues. Or one can compare it but by doing so one loses the face value of the game itself. I think I've settled for now the dispute that this 'game' might be a screensaver or simply not a 'game' at all.
On another note, the developers stated this: "If you're having an annoying storm or boring night, play a melody (using your keyboard) and time will accelerate." Mountain is there for you when you decide to return to it and play it. I think that is a common misconception. It's not as much meant to be a 'game' but rather a subsidiary and supporting game next to you. Yet there are many ways to view Mountain as with any form of issue in life. But the Way Mountain was constructed, at times unappealing to the eye, allows it to show you a different path and possibly one you may not have seen before hand.
But you don't have to follow what the developers say. A 'game' is meant to be played whichever way you feel like it. If you feel like you've been cheated off by buying this game, then take two steps back and think about the aspects of this 'game' and the elements. Perhaps you begin to notice that wonderful ambient sound that plays amidst the night, or perhaps you fall in love with the way the streaks of the sun touch your Mountain. But you might not have to like all these things to truly enjoy the game. Perhaps you have all these games and you developed a love for the game. Or perhaps you try to ridicule the game but in turn you've actually Grown accustomed to the game. I for one cannot answer that question of whether a gamer should like this or not, but it is all up to the gamer who buys it, and whether he is willing to open up his heart and mind.
Now is the Mountain truly your Mountain and your own property? I think that is in the conception of the gamer alone for the gamer can make notion whether the Mountain truly is a self embodiment, or the player truly controls the Mountain. Does the Mountain not speak to us and tell us of its thoughts? Or is it conveying a hidden message to where we might be its own spawn and it is the master. Whichever way you see fit, there are quite a lot of ways to see Mountain, as with any game. Mountain might not have a storyline, no shooting, no love triangle (unless you begin to make one up between somehow the items, the Mountain, and the sky in which case you probably might have gone a bit too far), but Mountain contains a moment of solitude in which you might notice things in games that can be recurrent in Mountain. Perhaps Mountain might contain all these elements in which you create the story. Mountain can always be a storyline in which you, the gamer, is going along a path with the Mountain to a destination into your subconscious. There is much to do in Mountain and blocking your imagination and logic will only hinder it. But if you so choose to do so than you have not hurt no one but yourself in denying the possible powers in the 'game' itself. This review cannot display my neutrality toward the game but I only wish to explain to the gamer that Mountain can only be accentuated by only the gamer.
And another thing many question is the role of the keyboard in the game. Although at first it may seem like the keys simply advance time and increase it in a way the human eye can perceive, Mountain is inevitably omnipresent and time is of little importance to him. Binding ourselves to this thought, we can perceive the passing of time as not one full of dread and dreariness, not one full of change and a different scenery, but becoming part of the universe and its infinite realm of possibilities. What we perceive as a minute can seem as nothing more than what has occurred to the Mountain. What we perceive as the future is simply the happening in the Mountain. What we perceive as the past is imply seen as the done by the Mountain.
And another question still remains as to what is the value of the items that the Mountain contains and at times loses. Are those pieces of our memories or life lessons that we must cope to accept? Or are those as somewhat like to put it as simple items that simply 'fall' on the Mountain. No they are granted upon the Mountain and delivered first hand to the Mountain or possibly to you. And what is of this item leaving our grasp and floating off into space? Have we broken your heart, Mountain? Have we done some unforgivable act too which I've lost my pony? That alone can be answered only by the gamer and his affiliation with the mountain.
And what of this inevitable destruction that reaches the doorsteps of the Mountain ever so often. Are we to simply ponder over the oblivion of the Mountain or sputter key notes to protect the Mountain? Or can we observe the Mountain and it's destruction in all its gloom and tidings of change too which a new Mountain is brought forth to bring new waves of joy to the gamer, too which the cycle is repeated. Why do we have the ability to protect the Mountain or is it even in our ability to protect it? Is it predestined that we protected or is it by our own free-will? That is something that neither I can answer you and only you can resolve either by justifying it or believing in something.
This setting that surrounds the Mountain is quite serene and yet the darkness around it is quite opposite. Is this serving as a contrast between dark and light? The battle of how light destroys the darkness. Or perhaps the story has been switched and light is simply a harbinger of this cycle of death that is ever so dreaded upon. Again, I am not in any sort of ability to answer that question, and it alone can be sought through the Mountain.
So if you ever feel hurt or saddened than perhaps a tune on the fashioned keyboard can mend your heart. Or perhaps a stressed out day simply requires a concerto done by your own imagination. And maybe in the end when you've discovered the infinite combinations on the keys that by which you alone and the Mountain as well contains in the hidden locks of memory, you realize all this and then come to think in terms of the Mountain, and how time is not congruent, but simply an assortment of things by which we alone can process and that by which we alone can control. Mountain is infinite and it is up to the gamer only to perceive the game as he wishes.

This is a good game and has a lot of potential but it doesnt really live up to what I wanted.
The PROS:
- Great music. Tons of classics and hidden gems from that era.
- Fun combat with good AI. Good fighting and weapons handling.
- Driving is good. Driving fast cars is nice, slower cars are not very fun to drive.
- Nice world design. Rich with details, just not as pretty as I would like.
- Decent steath system, has some flaws. Like when swimming, you cant swim steathy, but it doesnt matter cause they wont spot you anyhow.
The CONS:
- Graphics leave a lot to be desired.
- Little thing about character movement and the game in general are just not there. An example is how Clay just falls into water, like he wasnt trying to jump in, just falls.
- Story is alright, but no put together well. Feels like its missing cut scenes. CIA buddy just shows up no questions asked and gathers intel so you can fight a mob war?
- Very slow start to the game. Really wanted a hit the ground running start like in Mafia II, a vietnam combat mission would have been ideal!
- Repetative combat. Sneaking around is fun, but basicly the same on each mission.
- Yet to see any type of character customization.
- Police system feels outdated, get out of the bubble and your off.
- Really no damage to cars. Smash into a light pole? Hardly a scratch.
- Some missions are more of a bother than a good time. Drive like a mad man...
- Hard isnt that hard. Still little room for error, but doesnt seem like their are any more enemies than normal.
My advice, is wait to buy. The core game is good, but lacks polish. Combat is for sure a step up from Mafia II, but really the graphics are not much better and the whole thing feels incomplete. Its like owning a nice car but it is rusted on the sides and the windows dont roll up. I will keep playing until CIV IV comes out lol I sure do hope the devs behind this see what an unfinished product they put out and try to bring it closer to its potential.
In its current state I give it a 7/10.

Idle Evolution is a polished idle game that centers around the periodic table of the elements. It's good. It's cheep. Buy it.
It is culturally a clicker but isn't quite one because there isn't really an option to speed up gameplay by wearing out your mouse. You can speed (at least) one thing up by hovering over it, but clicking does nothing.
The gameplay is rich with complexity that is slowly introduced and built upon as you play the game. This complexity is heavily based on Chemistry. You don't need a strong background in Chemestry to enjoy this game; however, you may have to reference things ingame or just a couple of different configurations to something to work. For example, you might need to place something over all the elements that make up Phosphoric Acid. This means you need to place a thingie over Hydrogen, Phosphorus, and Oxygen.
I haven't experienced any bugs, glitches, or just obvious poor design. On the contrary, everything feels about right and there are lots of obscure things included. For example, hitting M on your keyboard while ingame will display information about the currently playing background music. This is not at all necessary for a game but is a mark of well thought out games.

TLDR: Audio guy ruins day. Film rips are smelly turds in otherwise clean audio.
I adored the first lego marvel game. It was polished brilliance (if keyboard controls weren't the smoothest, it never interfered enough for me to be annoyed by it). I saw a couple of steam reviews saying 'if you loved the first you'll love this', and grabbed it at a sale price.
I... kinda regret it. I want to love it. I really do. The sheer joy I got out of the first one and the huge numbers of hours I put in getting 100% completion made me sing it's praises but I've struggled to play two hours of this one. I have repeatedly quit over and over because I have become so damn frustrated with it. Let me elaborate, as I know two hours isn't a lot to judge a game by.
First off, the little gripes; it's laggier and buggier than it's precedessor. My hardware is fairly low end, but unless I was playing multiplayer on the previous lego marvel, it looked great and ran great. This has low framerate on the /startup/ menu and no matter what settings I tweak it always feels like it's struggling.
Cap's shield extinguisher for fires also is ridiculously finicky. Sometimes it'll jump straight to the fire being put out before even pressing (J), other times I have to repeatedly tap between (K) and (J) for it to work. God help you if any enemies are remotely nearby because the (K) prompt for the extended 'fancy' takedowns are so much more intrusive in this game than the last and somehow take up even more of your time as well as having them rammed in your face constantly.
The game doesn't know what it wants to be. It's too serious for a lego game, yet too silly for anything else and feels like the team were divided as to which direction they wanted to go and instead dragged it kicking and screaming in both directions.
Now, onto my main gripe which is the reason I'm actually reviewing this.
The audio.
Oh GOD the audio.
Some genius thought it would be a brilliant idea to use audio clips ripped (and when I say ripped, I mean they sound /ripped/, background noise and everything) from the films, but record original VA for other stuff. It breaks immersion completely and is horribly jarring as the levels of them are all over the place (if it weren't for the fact I have subtitles on, some of the lines I would have thought were my sound card glitching out) and the reverb doesn't match any of the sounds produced by the environment. It's horrible. It's honest to god horrible.
This also means that the main characters I loved playing as in the last game (Stark, Widow, Hawkeye etc) say /nothing/ other than the storymode direct-from-reel stuff and the same awfully integrated lines over and over and over and *over*(If I have to hear Cap's fuzzy♥♥♥♥♥TFA lines again I swear I will go crazy).
Aside the ripped audio, the voice acting is generally good, but for some reason they went with old school comic Bucky sound (I half expected him to go 'gee whizz!!") which is, again, really jarring when you've got Sebastian Stan's rugged stubbly appearance strutting around with this schoolboy voice chirping out.
I have never ever /ever/ heard audio in a game so poorly done and the fact it's come from such a prominent studio and one that has been consistently excellent in the past just... really gets my goat.
So no. No I wouldn't recommend this game unless they patch the god damn audio.

- - -THE LOOT BOX CON - - -
A lot of people are bent out of shape simply because of the inclusion of the boxes in the first place, but what if I told you the end-game is actually built around making things easier if you just buy a crate?
In Shadow of Mordor, I liked to start up the challenge modes and simply run around and Dominate the cool looking orcs and execute the rest, then start the challenges over.  In this game it's not that easy...
Since the game has a leveling system and orcs level with you, a majority of the orcs starting from level 45+ appear to spawn with the "Iron Will" trait (at least in my game so far).  This means they cant be dominated unless you first shame them in an attempt to remove the trait.  But, doing this has a chance to ruin their mind, and it's still not even guaranteed that you will remove the "Iron Will" trait from them.
If you do successfully remove the "Iron Will" trait from an Orc, you still have to hunt them down again, dominate them, and then level them back up.  In short, the only reliable way to dominate an orc at or near your level after 50+ seems to be to hope he is one of the few who spawn without "Iron Will", or to simply purchase from the Market.
- - -THE REVIEW - - -
This the first game, but they took the concept and made it "More".  Then added a handful of other things.
Not exactly better or worse overall.  Some aspects of the game are better, some are worse.
THE GOOD:
The Story is pretty decent, small issue here or there with the Plot, but nothing significant.
The combat can be fun, and it's a good game to just start up and kill some time orc hunting.
The online mode adds a bit of a unique challenge to the game, especially considering you can "Invade" friends.
I also enjoyed that they incorperated the Wraiths into the game.
The Appendix shows some of the background to the world or lore that's interesting to read.  I dont remember if this was in the first one.
THE BAD:
The motto for the game was "Nothing will be forgotten" - Except Talion forgot all of his skills from the last game, and you must relearn them.  Also, neither my "Nemesis" or "Follower" looked the same as from the last game, but both of those orc appearances are in this game, so I'm not sure what happened there.  Not really a big deal, but that part obviously looks "Forgotten" to me.
The concepts it does have, you do over and over - this pads the gametime, but cant really be called "Extra Content".  It can be enjoyable, or it can be annoying depending on your preference.
The quest-lines are tiered behind completing certain "Checkpoints" in the areas, but it's more of the same concepts you'll already need to be doing, ie. "Dominate X Followers in this area to unlock", "Capture the Fortress in this Area to unlock", "Learn this Skill to unlock", etc.
Talion moves like you're trying to steer a boat.  If you're trying to sprint through an area, you'll sometimes run up walls you werent aiming at, or when attempting to use an ability on an orc (Execute, Combat Brand, etc), he'll sometimes cast in the complete opposite way that you're aiming.
Hit tracking is also an issue.  I cant count the times I used an execute or an attack, and Talion would sprint 100 yards in a direction to just land a hit.  The enemy orcs do this also; some will attack the air a mile away from you, but if you dont hit that counter or dodge, you'll still take damage, because hit tracking is going to find a way to move them ALLL the way to you in time to hit you.  For the "Charging skills" the Orcs do, this makes sense, for everything else it doesnt.  I really think this needs to be nerfed/patched a bit.
Additionally, I dont understand the point of "Ring" in this game.  It seems like all of your abilities in game are the same with or without it.  Maybe it's the "Branding Skill" that's the difference or it doesnt matter because you have the Elf, but I'm not 100% sure.
The End-Game is set up to be a tedious grind.  It's probably also really feels intended for you to suppliment this with the loot crate system.
There is no replayability. - Well, there is, but it's artificial as in "They're attacking my fort again" or "I lost the fort they kept attacking, now you need to take it back".
It's really up to the Orcs regarding how "Dominated" their mind really was by your Ring of "Power" especially since they canturn on you whenever they want..."Dominate mind"? More like "Politely encourage loyalty" instead.
The Carnan Quest-Line:
The first half is what you expect.  From the second half on, it is 100% trash IMO, and drastically takes away from what was enjoyable about the game.  Again, here the Orcs are somehow the most powerful thing in LOTR Lore...There's a necro orc and his allies that infinitely res during the encounters unless you break the nearby totem, This wouldnt be a bad thing, but the totems for this quest line, unlike every other totem in the game, require you to "Dominate" them, intead of climb to the top, which means standing still casting while mobs are coming back to life or trying to hit or shoot you.  If this wasnt annoying enough, during the later phase of this quest you have to fight the boss and about 40 orcs while trying to destroy 4 totems.  Then on the very next part of this quest, you have to do the same thing with 6 totems, except this time each totem is also guarded by a champion who you have to listen to gargle for 30 seconds.  For me, the majority of these guys had "Death-Defying" as well, so most of them were adapting to everything over the course of the fights and this really turned this into a tedious quest grind for me.
HIT OR MISS:
If you thought the first one was hard, I'd argue that RNG can make this one harder.
Because they added a system where orcs can "Adapt", and some of the traits line up in a way that already limit how you can attack some of the orcs, it makes me wonder why Sauron isnt serving them...
In my game, because of this Adapt mechanic, two of the orcs already seem to be invincible:
For starters, neither have any mortal weaknesses; the first is a savage who I cant perform normal attacks against, is "Vigilant to Stealth, Immune to Executions, "Can heal himself during combat through sheer willpower", has adapted to shoulder charge, vault and the wraith punch.  - The only thing I can hurt him with is ranged, and 9 headshots only take him down to about 60% HP.  By the time I run and collect more Elf-Shot, he's already used his heal ability (Even if I interrupt it, he immediately starts it up again - no CD on it).  The one time I did manage to get his HP down, before he had adapted to the vault, he had death-defying.  I'm pretty sure Sauron will be one of his Warchief's soon.
The second one has a shield, and I cant get beyond the shield.  Everything that you would use on a shielded orc (Pin, Vault, etc) he was either immune to or had adapted to.  The only damage I can do is if I run away and run back into him and somehow land a hit on his "Back".  He also had death-defying though, so it felt like too much effort.
You could make the blind argument of "Get gud", but I've actually only died 2-3 times in this game in about 35 hours.  The difficulty really seems hit or miss.  I steam-roll most orcs, or know how to utilize the moves you can use on them, but some of the encounters seem like you're not meant to win them without cheesing.
All in All; If you liked the first one or you like the LOTR lore, you'll probably like this.  If you're just looking at this for the first time, pick up the first game before this, it's cheaper now and has a majority of the same content.  If you really like that, then try this.

The concept behind the game is simple enough and quite appealing: build a goofy robot out of random scrap and junk, strap some equally goofy weapons to it like dynamite launchers, bootleg laser guns and acid filled water balloons, and then send it out to go blow up stuff. It's rather cartoony, doesn't take itself all that seriously, and in theory would be a fun quick-fix sort of game.
In practice though, there are a lot of imbalances and glaring issues that ruin the fun. The main offender is the upgrading. You have to upgrade your robot's parts and weapons to stay competitive, but it's not just a matter of paying some coins and waiting for the upgrade to finish like other games of this type. You also have to have upgrade components which can only be found randomly as post-match rewards or bought outright with premium currency (aka the cash shop), and if you don't feel like buying them then you're going to be stuck waiting a very long time for enough components to do anything. This really kills the experimenting that should be a part of any game about robot building, as it makes you not want to invest in new parts or weapons. Having the timesink alone is more than enough to slow down upgrading, adding in the extra element of components just comes across as a very cynical cash grab attempt.
Weapon balance is also another problem, as too often one player can steamroll an entire team by themselves just because they managed to build a heavy bot with four launcher arms. Supposedly battery power and weight limits have a limiting effect, but since launcher rounds travel in a straight line and not an arc, it seems all too easy to just build something that can tank all the opposition's fire and spray AoE misery right into their faces.
And finally, there are a number of overall fit-and-finish oversights that left a sour impression. The tutorial gives only the very barest of detail on how to build a robot and doesn't give even a basic explanation of how weight limits, battery power or engine choices affect your movement and ability to use your weapons. A lot of features can only be found by just clicking around and stumbling onto them. Even some very basic functions aren't working right: there's an achievement for renaming your robot, but at the time of writing this you can't even do that. Shouldn't the things tied to achievements at least be checked to make sure they're not broken?
There's a fun idea here, but the game loses its appeal quickly and still feels like it needs a lot more work before it's ready to be played more than once out of curiosity.

Updated Review for Post Week 1 Patch
A week has gone by and a lot of stuff has changed for the better with Guns and Robots.
Half of that was the developers rebalancing of how you earn sparks, and the other half was me learning more about how the game works and how I should be playing it.
In order to save time I am just going to go over each of my "Bad" points from the last review and explain why it’s not an issue anymore:
The Bad:
- Only 5vs5 players - Well this actually makes the game quick and sweet and feels really balanced.
- 1 LIFE PER GAME - Again I was wrong about this, after playing this game for several more hours I can honestly say the game is over so fast it doesn't matter.
- Game starts you with a full inventory - Now the devs give you multiple ways to get a lot of sparks when you start playing the game (daily challenges, round rewards, and with every achievement) and you can spend them all to get a decent number of inventory slots out of the gate.
- With the limited inventory it makes it almost impossible to buy parts and experiment - I now realize that the way the game is MENT to be played is that you buy parts, try them, and if you don’t like them, sell them and try something else. I have only played a week and now have well over $50 000, and each part is usually $200, so it is not an issue to buy and sell parts to keep your inventory clean.
- The interface for making your robot is cumbersome – I did say you get used to it, and I have.
- When you combine parts into "modules" the part is considered IN USE. And you cannot use that same part on another robot that you make – This is still an issue which I touch on in the video… If I like the head, chest and legs of a robot, why can I not use them to make a second one just to change up the guns? It would save time assembling & disassembling them etc.
- YOUR ROBOT IS LOCKED INTO A MATCH UNTIL ITS OVER – The matches usually last 3 minutes, so this was never really an issue, just my first impression.
- I am getting matched up with players that seem to have hundreds more health than me and way more powerful weapons – This isn’t really true… There are many classes of robots and gun types… some robot builds still do tare through me, but I tare through other as well. It is one of the good things about this game :)
So there you have it! I was wrong about some of my early impressions, and the devs made a great move when they started giving people sparks early on through achievements so that they could increase their inventory.
All in all, in its current state I can recommend this game as a fun and addictive casual free to play shooter.

I have only played this game for 2 hours. So I don't feel comfortable reviewing it. But I will post some of my observations here.
The Good:
- Robots have personality
- You can customize every part to make the robot of your dreams
- Many different kinds of weapons, feet, chests, heads, and devices (gadgets likes mines, etc.)
- The clubhouse where you make the robots is a cool place for the main menu
- You get 1 cash currency every couple of matches to lessen the hurt (explained later)
- HATS
- Levels/maps are varied and look nice
- The overall game has personality bursting from it really
- The leveling up is satisfying and you get currency, and materials needed to upgrade equipment when you level.
The Bad:
- Only 5vs5 players
- 1 LIFE PER GAME - this game more than anything needs to allow you to fight and die over and over again to see what is good/bad about your build. But much like World of Tanks, you only get 1 life per match AND your robot is locked until the match finished. But alteast WoT gives you multiple tanks to start, this game... only gives you one.
- Game starts you with a full inventory, and you need to use the real cash currency [sparks] to expand it.
- With the limited inventory (which requires real cash currency [sparks] to expand) it makes it almost impossible to buy parts and experiment with making new robots without playing hundreds of rounds to get "sparks".
- The inerface for making your robot is combersome and takes longer than it should making it a chore. (You do get used to it though)
- When you combine parts into "modules" the part is considered IN USE. And you can not use that same part on another robot that you make.
- You only start off with 2 slots to make robots and again, YOUR ROBOT IS LOCKED INTO A MATCH UNTIL ITS OVER, so you're left sitting there until its over, which really sucks. Atleast in World of Tanks they give you 5 tanks to screw around with, not just 1.
- Its Day 1, I should be being matched with new players, instead I am getting matched up with players that seem to have hundreds more health than me and way more powerful weapons.
- Leveling up equipment takes real world time. This sucks but is in a lot of F2P games...

Alan Wake is a 3rd person shooter/action-adventure game originally released for the Xbox 360 and ported over to the PC. The PC port is done well, with all the graphical options you could want, and the DLC from the console game included with the purchase.
The story for Alan Wake is the real standout. Your character, Alan Wake, is a famous writing who is struggling with writer's block. You go on a vacation to the Pacific Northwest with your wife, where things begin to get supernatural. The game is split into 1-2 hour segments called episodes, like a TV show. At the end of each episode, there is a closing song and title screen. Each following episode begins with a "previously on..." segment. This breaks the game up into nice 1-2 chunks of playtime, and also allows for a natural jump to exploring some back story at the beginning of each segment. I really enjoyed how this aspect played out, and would love to see it in other games. The story kept me engrossed all the way through, and did not overstay its welcome. I was anxiously anticipating the end, not to finally be done with the game, but to find out what actually happens. I couldn't ask for anything more from a game in that regard.
The gameplay does leave a bit to be desired. There is a very limited selection of weapons, and you will be fighting the same enemies over and over again. The Taken, as the baddies are labeled in this game, are not especially varied. There are the normal kind, the strong kind, and the fast kind. You will see combinations of these throughout your time with Alan Wake. Be prepared to fight plenty of lumberjacks as you run through the forests of the Pacific Northwest. There are several types of collectables to look for along the way. Most have no effect on the story, however the manuscripts tie in to the game and show you what to expect next. It's a shame that the game requires two playthroughs to collect them all.
The graphics are fairly good when you consider that the game was originally released in 2010 on console. The animation of the main character could have used some work to appear more lifelike. The environment looks great, but you will be seeing a lot of forest. I was growing a little tired of that setting by the end. The FMVs are jarring when they come on, since the graphics take a notable step down from the main gameplay. That may be a result of the graphics getting a small bump when moved to PC.
The controls are adequate for what you will be doing the most of, running and shooting. I used a 360 controller and had no issues. The only difficulties were in some of the platforming sequences. I found myself missing some jumps or running off the edge of small platforms. I would not have missed those sections if they were not included.
The music is fantastic, and plays a minor role in the story. At the end of each episode, a song plays over the title screen. It has some connection to what you have just seen. A mix of licensed and original songs are used, with the original songs really fitting in nicely in tone and quality.
Overall I would wholeheartedly recommend Alan Wake for a playthrough. The story is engrossing, and the gameplay, while repetitive at times, moves quickly along to keep you interested. I do not see a lot of replayability in this title, since the story is the main selling point. However, there is enough length to keep you satisfied with your purchase on one playthrough. I recommend playing the special episodes after finishing the main game, since they add a bit more closure to the experience. Those can be found under the episodes option on the main menu.
Grade: B+

TL; DR = A great idea that, given a little more love, could turn out to be an indie classic.
I really enjoy the idea of Mars 2030. I think the most apt comparison I can think of is it's a barebones Oregon Trail....IN SPACE!
What I particularly value about this game is how deliberate everything is. There are few embellishments, no fluff. The mechanics gel neatly with what I've come to understand as the underlying theme and message of the game: that a realistic journey to Mars is a long-haul slog rife with equal parts tedium, uncertainty, and eventually triumph. The whole monochromatic aesthetic and MIDI soundtrack remind me of being an 8 year old playing games on floppy disk on my auntie's PC. It helps that Fallout is probably my favorite series of all time.
In its current state, that's a bit of a double edged sword, however. I personally love games that do things differently. It's why I support Greenlight, Kickstarter, and crowdfunding in the first place. If gaming is to be taken seriously as an artistic medium, developers need to take risks. They need to deviate from the status quo of shooty-bang-bang FPS and iterative Sportsball games.
As it stands, however, I definitely get some of the criticisms of Mars. There's a lot of dead space (PUNS!), a lot of sitting around not doing much. Again, I'm kind of a pretentious a-hole; I get the point and I really dig it. But apart from the occasional decision point about choosing equipment and what to do when Spock gets space-dysentery, the interactive/gameplay aspect isn't really there to hook the average person who wants to just sit and play. I personally just had the game running while doing some work from home or listening to podcasts.
Where I can definitely see some room for improvement is adding mini-games or FTL-esque RPG/choose-your-own-adventure-like  mechanics into the mix. I think the devs can definitely add some more "gamey" mechanics without detracting from their intended message of a realistic Martian expedition.
Ultimately, however, I think it would be an awful shame to pass this game up because of its current state. It's reasonably priced, it's experimental, and I have a feeling that the devs are in it for the long haul (their own Martian journey, if you will). I'm proud to have supported these folks and hope that they get the support to do some really cool things in the near future.

Lego Avengers is what I would call a "spiritual succesor" to Lego Marvel Superheroes, which is the best Lego game of all time
So how does this game compare?
The best parts of Lego Marvel return such as the awesome Open World (some of) your favorite Marvel characters and great humor.
So I'll start out with the open world
The huge open world New York from Lego Marvel returns, and it's almost exactly the same as in Lego Marvel. The only difference is that some of the landmarks like the Baxter Building Daily Bugle and the X-Mansion are gone. But the world is still fun to explore with tons of side missions. They also added random crimes, people will be robbed and cars will be stolen, but that's it. I really wish they expanded this feature, like stopping a large scale bank robbery or a stopping a big fight between the criminals and the cops, the current crimes tend to get old. There are also several other hub worlds, but all the other one's are small. Espicially Washington D.C, I wish instead of having a ton of tiny one's that they would have just put in the city that AAOU takes place in and have be the same size as New York.
Now I'll talk about the characters
Since they're using the MCU for this game we only get characters that appear in the MCU, meaning no X-Men Spider-Man Fantastic Four or Deadpool. Yet this still has more characters than the last game, and a lot of them are just filler, there's a million "Agent" characters and just civilians as characters. But I do like what they did with some of the characters in this game. In Lego Marvel Hulk was just ok, he could run around and punch cars, that was about it. In this game Hulk has an awesome super jump and can climb on buildings, Quicksilver is also fun because he can run up buildings. I would also like to mention that the character creator has improved.
Now I'll talk about the story
I actually really liked the story in Lego Marvel, the voice actors were great and it was funny, Lego Avengers' story is based off of movies from the MCU, while there's nothing wrong with this it's just not as funny as Lego Marvel, don't get me wrong, this game is funny, I actually laughed at several of the jokes, and they also use lines from the movies in different ways, overall the story is great.
Overall I give it a 8/10, a must have for fans of the MCU or Marvel or Lego Games in general

Updated Review for Post Week 1 Patch
A week has gone by and a lot of stuff has changed for the better with Guns and Robots.
Half of that was the developers rebalancing of how you earn sparks, and the other half was me learning more about how the game works and how I should be playing it.
In order to save time I am just going to go over each of my "Bad" points from the last review and explain why it’s not an issue anymore:
The Bad:
- Only 5vs5 players - Well this actually makes the game quick and sweet and feels really balanced.
- 1 LIFE PER GAME - Again I was wrong about this, after playing this game for several more hours I can honestly say the game is over so fast it doesn't matter.
- Game starts you with a full inventory - Now the devs give you multiple ways to get a lot of sparks when you start playing the game (daily challenges, round rewards, and with every achievement) and you can spend them all to get a decent number of inventory slots out of the gate.
- With the limited inventory it makes it almost impossible to buy parts and experiment - I now realize that the way the game is MENT to be played is that you buy parts, try them, and if you don’t like them, sell them and try something else. I have only played a week and now have well over $50 000, and each part is usually $200, so it is not an issue to buy and sell parts to keep your inventory clean.
- The interface for making your robot is cumbersome – I did say you get used to it, and I have.
- When you combine parts into "modules" the part is considered IN USE. And you cannot use that same part on another robot that you make – This is still an issue which I touch on in the video… If I like the head, chest and legs of a robot, why can I not use them to make a second one just to change up the guns? It would save time assembling & disassembling them etc.
- YOUR ROBOT IS LOCKED INTO A MATCH UNTIL ITS OVER – The matches usually last 3 minutes, so this was never really an issue, just my first impression.
- I am getting matched up with players that seem to have hundreds more health than me and way more powerful weapons – This isn’t really true… There are many classes of robots and gun types… some robot builds still do tare through me, but I tare through other as well. It is one of the good things about this game :)
So there you have it! I was wrong about some of my early impressions, and the devs made a great move when they started giving people sparks early on through achievements so that they could increase their inventory.
All in all, in its current state I can recommend this game as a fun and addictive casual free to play shooter.

I have only played this game for 2 hours. So I don't feel comfortable reviewing it. But I will post some of my observations here.
The Good:
- Robots have personality
- You can customize every part to make the robot of your dreams
- Many different kinds of weapons, feet, chests, heads, and devices (gadgets likes mines, etc.)
- The clubhouse where you make the robots is a cool place for the main menu
- You get 1 cash currency every couple of matches to lessen the hurt (explained later)
- HATS
- Levels/maps are varied and look nice
- The overall game has personality bursting from it really
- The leveling up is satisfying and you get currency, and materials needed to upgrade equipment when you level.
The Bad:
- Only 5vs5 players
- 1 LIFE PER GAME - this game more than anything needs to allow you to fight and die over and over again to see what is good/bad about your build. But much like World of Tanks, you only get 1 life per match AND your robot is locked until the match finished. But alteast WoT gives you multiple tanks to start, this game... only gives you one.
- Game starts you with a full inventory, and you need to use the real cash currency [sparks] to expand it.
- With the limited inventory (which requires real cash currency [sparks] to expand) it makes it almost impossible to buy parts and experiment with making new robots without playing hundreds of rounds to get "sparks".
- The inerface for making your robot is combersome and takes longer than it should making it a chore. (You do get used to it though)
- When you combine parts into "modules" the part is considered IN USE. And you can not use that same part on another robot that you make.
- You only start off with 2 slots to make robots and again, YOUR ROBOT IS LOCKED INTO A MATCH UNTIL ITS OVER, so you're left sitting there until its over, which really sucks. Atleast in World of Tanks they give you 5 tanks to screw around with, not just 1.
- Its Day 1, I should be being matched with new players, instead I am getting matched up with players that seem to have hundreds more health than me and way more powerful weapons.
- Leveling up equipment takes real world time. This sucks but is in a lot of F2P games...
Final verdict: Like I said this is not a review. I've only played for two hours so if you don't feel that you can trust my words on it, well there you go.
I honestly feel like the game is limiting you with the limited inventory. I feel like the inventory is needed to allow player to truely customize their robots freely.  And since that is the main draw of this game, I feel bad :(
The good free to play games out there don't do that, they don't ask for money for gameplay required items, and inventory in this type of game is a MUST. I don't know, I love its charm but hate it limits so early on while playing it (2 hours).... as of right now, I can't recommend it.
If you had 100 slots, or unlimited slots this game would be a light hearted casual shooter that I would recommend to everyone who needs to kill 5 minutes at a time, but ... yeah.

I've played it for around 2 hours so far. Mostly solo, but a couple of my friends joined when they were around. I reeeally like this game so far.
Matchmaking is really fast, I never had to wait more than a few seconds to get into the action. There doesn't seem to be any issues with lag which as I am located in Australia and I was worried that there may not be servers in my region. Controlling your robot is very easy, weapons on your left are bound to your left click and vice versa. I think you can also fire weapons individually with number keys. So you basically are allowed a lot of versatility e.g. you can have your long range weapons on one side and your flamer thrower or shotgun on the other side for close quarters. I found that it was really fun to play. Only problem I found was that you weapons don't fire from you perspective, so often my projectiles would clip into objects even though I had a clear line of sight of targets. Also because my weapons sat low on my chassis I couldn't fire over certain cover. It's something you just need to get used to. You seem to get plenty of the base currency from playing matches. I was quickly able to buy components and set up my robot in the basic configuration that I wanted after just playing just a few matches. You have a limited amount of inventory space for robot components. You need to use premium currency to increase it's capacity. But I found that you can just sell components that you don't want to use anymore to make space for replacements. With all the base currency you earn it's easy to afford new components in case you want to switch back or try something else. There appears to a large variety of options when it comes to build and equipping your robot. The modules you assemble together to build your robot are made of multiple components. This basically allows you to customise them e.g. a base component may apply a damage modifier to your weapon at the cost durability etc. You have a player level which progresses as you complete matches and unlocks upgrades for modules i.e. for chassis, weapons and so on. Upgrades require special components which I had trouble earning as rewards for matches. You can buy them with the premium currency which I thought could sort of force you invest money to avoid a grind, because you don't seem to earn a lot of it through matches. However I did notice that you can actually convert the free base currency to the premium currency and as I said getting the base currency seems to be pretty easy. So getting enough of the premium currency might not that hard at least in order to acquire low to medium tier upgrades.
For a game that is described as cartoony I really like how it looks. Yes some of the designs are pretty silly, but some of the robots look really really cool. There is quite a large amount of variety and interesting examples in the designs created by players. The most memorable build which I saw was a big heavy one that slowly glided around. And personally I built a heavy weapons platform with four guns and tank tracks. It was really slow but it felt cool as hell to move into the fray with it =)
This game is absolutely worth playing so far. Not a single major issue. Even better with friends which by the way are easy to form a squad and play alongside with.

At the end of the day this is a third person shooter with what appears to be a variety of customizable parts, cool weapons, and strategic maps.
However, after playing for a while you'll realize that there's actually very little customization at all and mostly combat ends up being two teams of people smash eachother together hammering their fire buttons until the tide turns in one direction or the other due to focused fire.
Weapons and components appear to have lots of stats, but more or less all end up being the same. One gun may have 10 damage for 3 shots per second, another 30 damage for 1 shot per second. They'll use about the same amount of energy per second and so on. There are differences but they're mostly minor. Different chasis have different speeds and some other stats, but mostly you're deciding if you want 4 arms (for higher DPS and lower sustained DPS) or 2 arms. That's about it. Light mechs dont seem to have much advatnage over heavies (they go faster, but not really MUCH faster).
All in all there are simply better games out there that deliver a higher degree of customization and strategy, ranging from more complex games like Mechwarrior Online to more similar ones like Robocraft.

Shadow of War is a very strong follow up to the excellent Shadow of Mordor. There are some issues I had with the game that I think ultimately hold the game back from being great. That being said, it still is a solid title and well worth a play especially if you enjoyed the first game.
I'm going to address the microtransactions kerfuffle at the opening of this review and then I will not be mentioning them again. The fact that MTs are in a 99% single player experience is short-sighted and unnecessary. They should never have been in this game in the first place. That being said, there is no reason whatsoever to purchase anything to play this game to its entirety at an enjoyable level. You can largely ignore the microtransactions for the most part. You may want to spend the in game currency that you earn or any gold you may earn on some of the loot boxes, but you largely can ignore the "Market" section of the menu  entirely. The game does not nag you to buy anything aside from some menu mentions and you can earn Gold (the paid currency) by doing challenges. WB could've avoided a lot of negative press by never putting them in this otherwise good game.
Here are some tl;dr Pros and Cons...
Pros
+ Very strong technologically. Great graphics, voice acting/sound, and music.
+ Lots of varying regions to discover.
+ Raiding forts is a lot of fun.
+ Strong set pieces. The big moments are memorable.
+ The Orcs are hilarious and varying.
+ Flying a dragon is one of the most thrilling and satisfying moments in any current release.
Cons
- The story is shallow.
- The first 6-8 hours of the game are convoluted in almost every respect.
- Defending forts (unlike attacking) is not so much fun.
- Gear/gems system is never fully explained, but at least easy to figure out.
- Controversy around the game could've been avoided.
I'm not going to cover the minutiae of the game in my review because if you are familiar with the first game, you get what the second is about. You're here to smash some orcs and have a laugh doing so. The game delivers this in an impressive design that is gorgeous in places.
The biggest minus to the game is the story. While there are aspects of it I enjoyed (mainly around the character Bruz and anything have to do with the Nazgul), the story comes off disjointed and in pieces. There's no cohesion behind a lot of the motivation that Talion has. The game starts with a group of Gondorians as the central focus and it lacks depth and there's no foundation for empathising with their plight. There are a few splinter stories that are interesting but most of them are just slices and lack depth for obvious reasons. At the very least a lot of fun gameplay is in the splinter stories, and that helps out a lot. However, unlike the first game, I never felt the same motivation to know what happens since that began so viscerally in the first game. If Mordor is the Lord of the Rings series, War is the Hobbit series in terms of quality of story. If you're a Tolkien traditionalist, this game may not be for you as it takes dramatic liberty with some of the lore. For the most part I did not mind this and in some ways it really works, but consider yourself warned.
I currently have 45 hours in the game at the time of this review. I have completed all of the scripted stories and am at stage 4 (of 10) of "The Shadow Wars" which is the end game act. The Shadow Wars involve the mechanic of defending forts and invading if necessary and that is basically it.
Despite the controversy, Monolith deserve a lot of credit for Shadow of War. It plays well and has some really awesome moments. There is criticism that could and should be levied. But, if you enjoy third person action, this delivers on a lot of levels. There's a lot more going on in this game than in the first which is important for a sequel.

Firstly, I'd like to preface this whole review by saying that I love this game, and it's improved on almost every aspect of its predecessor, which I go into in the following paragraphs. Unfortunately, in retrospect I feel like a message needs to be sent to WB, that microtransactions in AAA games are NEVER okay and that's why I'm going to be giving this game a negative review.
Secondly, I'd like to point you towards the BDG's review that refers you to the loophole whereby refusing to accept the terms of service allows you to bypass all of the online bullcrap such as the market and "invasions". I still hate the fact that WB, being the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ publishers that they are (see above) decided to shoehorn in the AAA industry's latest fetish for making money, and I had cancelled my pre-order initially after the lootboxes' reveal. Come release day however, and all the major review outlets were praising this title with the strong overall theme being, that if you liked the first one - you were probably gonna love the sequel. Further research online revealed the supposed grind that comes in the final act, as an incentive to buy lootboxes most likely (though I must admit, opinions have been quite contradictory on the matter), yet the glowing reviews of the game itself stuck in my mind, and as someone who loved the first game - I finally caved and bought it the day after it launched.
Combat is much improved over the first, with improvements that can be applied to each skill, to yield vastly different effects and cater to different playstyles. It's still the "arkham" system of combat, so if you weren't a fan of it in the first game, there won't be much different here for you. Despite the accusations that can be levelled at the combat I still find it hugely enjoyable and that is mostly in part to the gorgeous animations and oh-so crunchy sound design. Talion can be likened to a ballet dancer in combat, since he dodges all over the place, moving from enemy to enemy with satisfying speed and the sound an orc's bones make when skewered/sliced/stabbed is almost cathartic.
Graphics have improved, but are still fairly average - with the main improvement being the size and density of the maps this time around. The opening area in particular is very impressive; touting an entire Gondorian city, surrounding woodland and a cave system underneath filled with all sorts of nasty creatures. Subseqent maps add a great deal of variety to the game, with a snowy/mountainous area and grassy/jungle map - just to name a few.  Lip syncing is not perfect to say the least, but is still an improvement over its predecessor. Blood effects seem to be improved, (I swear it sticks to surfaces more than it did in the last game).
Enemy variety is improved: the hulking ologs add some much needed depth to the combat, due to their increased health pool, which means that they can't be so easily vanquished, along with the fact that their attacks are generally more AOE in effect and high damage in nature. Beast variety is something that they improved subtlely, with new, rare types of elemental graugs available to be hunted in the different biomes. Naturally, the headline new beast type would be the dragons, and I've got to admit, they are super fun to fight, and even more fun to control.
The nemesis system has been greatly expanded here with more characteristics, e.g. blood brothers, different classes, e.g. assassins that will frequently sneak up on you, and plenty more that I wouldn't want to spoil. It's a delight discovering all of the new features and quirks of the reiterated nemesis system and is well worth experiencing first-hand for yourself.
Since I talked about the nemesis system, I should share one of my most interesting stories, where I ended up feeling really ♥♥♥♥ing bad for an orc:
Hoshgrish was a crossbowman who I'd recruited to join my army. He was a proud orc, who I then sent to kill his blood brother in a duel. When the duel began, Hoshgrish was getting beaten up pretty badly, so I had to step in and murder his brother to stop him from getting killed. After seeing his blood brother's death at my hands, Hoshgrish snapped and betrayed me, raining down fiery bolts as he grieved. I took him down and dominated him, preparing to once again brainwash him into joining the BRIGHT LORD. Unbenownst to me however, the traumatic event of  losing his blood brother, steeled Hoshgrish's will against me and he refused to succumb to my power. As a result, I shamed him, burning the side of his cheek with my mark - breaking his mind and making him deranged. Subsequently, I sent my Olog commander after him to kill him off at a ceremony. When my Olog burst out of the bushes, Hoshgrish let out the most pathetic and heartbreaking series of whimpers I'd never thought I'd hear an orc utter and ran away sobbing. Hoshgrish had become terrified of practically anything - and that was the night I found myself feeling tearful for an orc. ;(
Difficulty levels are something new for the series, and were a much needed feature in my opinion, since in the first game it certainly felt like after reaching a certain point/power level, you'd have to *try* and get yourself killed on purpose if you actually wanted any semblance of a challenge. I've been playing this game on hard (nemesis difficulty) and I'm very happy to report that this game will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ You really have to plan carefully when taking on enemies and it forces you towards making strategic decisions to make a fight easier, e.g. removing archers. Also, since you die more often, it makes you engage with the nemesis system more heavily - and I personally feel that nemesis difficulty is the ultimate way to play this game.
One issue that I have with Shadow of War is how grindy it can feel, as well as the tutorial feeling like it overstays its welcome excessively - and naturally if the combat and nemesis system don't keep you engaged, you're likely to feel the repetitive nature of it all more keenly than others.
Overall, if you liked the first game, you will love the sequel - though I don't blame any of you for waiting for a sale, or maybe for the microtransactions to be patched out.
EDIT:
So I completed the first couple of siege battles and I must admit that I'm very happy with this new component of the game. Firstly, they definitely captured the feeling of pure epicness that accompanied any LOTR battle in the film. The way they visually represent every one of your selected unit types cheering behind you is great and the dialogue your generals have with you before the battle is even cooler - varying based on their personality and loyalty towards you. The checkpoint capturing system itself may feel a bit basic, but the overall feel of these sequences are unparalled for immersing yourself in these battles that have taken 20 hours to build up to.

The Binding of Issac is a roguelike zelda dungeon game.
At first start you play as the protagonist who drops into the basement and then you immediately go into action. I think at this point you will naturally decide either you love this game or you don't feel like playing it because of the visuals. Its delicate hand drawn art style can be grotesque at times, but personally I don't feel that it is an issue for me.
After a few runs (dying a few times), once you get the hang of it (learning how not to die too soon), you can start enjoying the exploration aspect of this game, which I believe you will enjoy if you like this aspect of  roguelike games. There are over 300 collectible/usable items in the game (with Wrath of the Lamb), each with unique buffs and debuffs. The game doesn't tell you what the power of the items are, but then again, if you enjoy roguelike games you most likely will appreciate this system. Enemies are varied at every level set, which adds more depth to the procedure generation system.
The con of this game is its story, as with most roguelike games, its story is weak. It has its certain theme, thus the level design and weapon design, but I'd say you probably still could enjoy the game without its background story if you are that type of person who doesn't care about lores.
Final verdict: although its art style may put some people off, if you like roguelike games, then you should buy this game as it is an interesting and unique twist in this genre. Even at its full price The Binding of Isaac is still recommendable.

[TL;DR: Recommended with caveats. Get it on sale, and only if you don't have LEGO Marvel Super Heroes already. If you don't like LEGO games, or Marvel stuff, there is nothing here to change your mind. Pass on it if that is the case.]
You should really know by now if LEGO games are your cup of tea or not. That being said, rather than explain everything about them, I'm gonna focus on what this one does differently than some of the others.
There is a lot of combat in this game, and as you probably know, combat in LEGO games is awful. Your AI team mates will constantly get in your line of fire, and you will "lock on" to random objects that the game thinks you are trying to punch instead of the bad guys that are in the process of killing you. Luckily, there are still infinite lives and you only lose 1,000 studs upon death.
You can turn off hints in this game, which is a welcome addition. Still, I wish it do more than that, and stop taking control of the camera to make sure I see exactly what item it wants me to interact with next.
The Manhattan hub from LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is back as your main hub. There are also a few other tiny hubs with a handful of collectables each. This includes Asgard, Tony's Malibu Home, a Shield Base, and some others. The X-Mansion is mysteriously missing from the Manhattan hub. If you go to where it should be, there's just a boring building.
The levels all follow the Avengers movies, which isn't really a problem, but I would have liked to have seen a game with its own story like LEGO MSH had.
I know this is branded as an Avenger's game, but the lack of X-Men characters and stuff is really sad. I mean, even Wolverine and Spider-Man were in the Avengers.
Other roster complaints: Nova is the older Nova and not Sam Alexander, the current Nova. Not a big deal, but they have some other current heroes like Squirrel Girl's Unbeatable outfit, Jane Foster as Thor, and Kamala Khan as Ms. Marvel. Speaking of Ms. Marvel, why the hell is Carol Danvers in this game as Ms. Marvel instead of Captain Marvel? Were they just too lazy to make a new skin for her? She's been Captain Marvel for years now in the comics, come on guys.
Remember the black cosmic bricks from LEGO MSH? They're back, and still called cosmic bricks, but I have no idea why. Here's a list of some cosmic characters that cannot interact with cosmic bricks: Nova, Ms. Marvel, Captain freakin' Universe. So who can? Ultron. That's the only person I've found who is able to interact with these "cosmic" bricks. I get they wanted to gate them off until the end of the game, but why not just rename them if only Ultron can use them?
Speaking of Captain Universe, there is something about the character I really like. So one of the spots you can interact with is an area with hidden bricks. You usually have to play this dumb minigame to detect the bricks, but if you use Captain Universe, because of her cosmic awareness, the bricks just show up. She gets to skip the minigame completely. Nice attention to detail.
This game has a serious lack of hidden levels. Remember how in LEGO MSH you used gold bricks to build doors to bonus levels? Yeah, that's gone. What are gold bricks for, you ask? Who knows, I can't find any use for them at all. The game does unlock three more levels after you finish most of the story, but these are just other Avengers themed levels, and don't feel like the wacky or pure LEGO bonus levels of the other titles.
While it's a shame to see them continue to just scrape by on these cookie cutter mediocre LEGO titles, it's still a decent purchase if you enjoy the series.
That being said, maybe you should wait for a sale, or pick up LEGO Marvel Super Heroes first.

There's absolutely way too much gristle here before you get to the real meat, and the only palatable portions of this game. Everything about the story campaign is poorly planned, poorly audio mixed, poorly executioned and purely a grind. Constantly stealing your camera to show interminable 'Here's Where You Should Go' cutscenes, dialogue that is brought into extreme relief by the goofy animations (it's UNREAL how bad Loki and Ultron's dialogue is, I'd forgotten that about the movies), AWFUL unskippable battleship-like decoding puzzles among literal dozens of other things make it impossible for me to recommend this game to anyone. You'd be much, much, much better off getting the previous LEGO Marvel game or literally any other LEGO game on the Steam store page.
The saving grace to this tarnish on Traveller's Tales' record is the open world, unlocked after the story is over. With its original writing and voice acting, which was sorely missed in the story mode, along with the actual pure joy that is super jumping all over town as dozens and dozens of characters that would otherwise not get any representation in a video game, it's almost enough to get you to ignore the overall abysmal faults.
Bullet List Time:
-I loved having all the women characters in the open world, it was great getting to use Sif and Jessica Jones and Hellcat and America Chavez
-I loved not being hamstrung to using the main Avengers team for the puzzles and challenges, with each having a female counterpart.
-I loved super-speed. This is a great game to just run around in and stop and do whatever mission or quest is nearby. Having all three speedster characters be able to run up buildings was an obvious, yet genius, move and it always brings a smile to my face.
-THANOSCOPTER
-I have a really hard time deciding on the worst chapter in story mode but I gotta tell you, I had zero fun throughout the entirety of the Avengers 2 campaign. All the missions were tedious, the presentation confusing at best, and the way the final level could end without your say-so REALLY made it tough to replay it to 100%.
In short, don't buy this game. At least not until its $5 on sale like the rest of the catalogue.

I saw this game in late 2012/early 2013. It was a live-archive on youtube. I didn't like it. Back then, it seemed like a game that grade-schooler could create in his free time. So I didn't like it.
As youtube recommandations are flawless, as we all know, I saw this video two years later. Thought to myself "What was that about?". Watched it. Absolutely loved it.
It was during the times I was an edgy teenager (yay yay middle-school) and concept of game where you brutally murdered everyone seemed brilliant. I bought it for $3 or something like that, I believe. Got bored shortly later.
Then again, came back when HM2 was released, so a quarter later, I believe. Then, I fell absolutely in love with this game. Why? Okay, now - review time.
The art style and music are geniuely amazing. These two made me love 80s with my whole heart. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ VHS quality became the prettiest. Trashy synthesizer music became loveable.
Story is goddamn.. cool. It's just cool. A silent killing machine, Jacket, swimming through pools of blood of his enemies. While making a meat stew of their faces using only fists. Marvelous. On top of all, story has its depth, that I don't really care about, but is as mysterious as it can be. And that's really awesome.
Gameplay... It's hard. It's frustrating. It's bugged as hell (bullet mechanics are my absolute favs). It's really freaking rewarding. Beating the poop out of the same enemies over and over again and when, finally, you got through the one guy that was unable to kill... It's an awesome feeling. Then you get another guy just like the guy before and fight him till he or your will to fight dies.
And the A+ at the end is a sweet reward for your sweat.
Generally, game's awesome. Do you love 80s?
If yes, go play it, you're gonna love it (most likely)!
If not... well... go play it, you're gonna love 80s AND the game! Isn't that a sweet deal?

When asked what it is I enjoy most about a game, the best I can come up with is "the experience", as vague as that is. Whatever I mean by that, Hotline Miami captures it in every way. With the sickly bright visuals, the unflinching and brutal violence, the hypnotizing soundtrack, and the surreal plot, it sets itself apart as one of the most distinct experiences in indie gaming. It's comparable to drugs, getting under your skin and becoming a game you play by feel more than sight. You'll get into a flow and completely lose yourself in the violence, only for the last enemy to die. Then the music cuts abruptly, a dull buzzing plays, and you slowly walk back to your car through the trail of maimed bodies.
Everything moves so fast, you don't even have time to think, you just have to react instinctively. The feel of the action very much compliments what's going on in the protagonist's head. No time to stop and think, only to act, and react, as fast as possible, no matter the consequences. The best games don't just have you play as a character, they make you feel like you *are* the character, and the gradually deteriorating mental state of a brutal killer wouldn't look like anything else than what you see in this game. The violence, intensity, and difficulty aren't going to be for everyone, but this is among my most loved of indie titles on the market.

Mafia 3 is a beautiful game. Let me say now i am only about 8 hours in and will be redoing my review at a later time. The game's story is gripping and actually interesting which really gets you into it from the very beggining. Despite people saying the driving mechanics are clunky or whatever it may be (there are two different driving settings in the settings menu) i found the driving to be very smooth and responsive while using a controller.
The game's setting itself set in the fictional New Orleans, it's breathtaking really. Although the map size may not be that attractive at first, this game really made an interesting and real to life open world by allowing players to roam anywhere and having a large number of open buildings and stores to explore. Combining that with the story makes it a great experience so far. And honestly the story has it's stale moments but unlike most games Mafia 3's missions and side missions not only provide an actual reasoning behind them to do it but also provides you with mulriple ways to complete them.
However, at the time of this review there has been no patch or bug fixes to the game and the game is still capped at 30fps. This is not a huge complaint at the moment for myself but does impact the game significantly.
The gameplay itself is an amazing improvement from the last intallement. The cover system can be annoying at times but overall it works good. With a wide range of weapons and a decent amount of upgrades to play with it holds it's ground. The movment system is suprisingly very good, the AI on the other hand not so much as the seem to be a little too easy and unresponsive not to mention the vehicle AI.
All in all, this game has a decently long and interesting story that makes you to not want to stop playing and great gameplay to add to it.

- Great open world to explore and replayability
- Collectibles and rare items to find throughout the map
CONS-
- Significant need for patch with 30fps cap increase and settings update
- AI can be unresponsive and too easy

What follows is a break-up of the different things I experienced in game, in a bullet-point, non review-esque style.
+ COMBAT: a solid combat system:
10 different weapon types, including 3 melee weapon types (blunt, blade and brawl) and 7 close (shotguns, pistols, SMG) to medium (assault rifles, heavy weapons) to long (sniper rifles) range. With an extra emphasis on armor and some weapon types being very effective against heavy armor (energy weapons, a category in which there are weapons of all ranges) and some less.
A cover system which sometimes bugs a bit.
A crouch to aim better system.
A headshot system that trades accuracy for extra damage.
A "when you shoot someone lower (in terms of altitude) than you, you get a bonus in accuracy" system
Some hit ratios may seem a little low, the more you spend skill points in a weapon type, the more precise you become in your shots with it.
+ EXPLORATION: Another well thought out system
You will need to upgrade 11 different skills to survive in the wasteland, and by that I mean to efficiently explore every single area by destroying walls and lockpicking doors and gates and loot every single chest, safe...
Don't forget to level up your perception skill to spot traps and mines and your demolition skill to disarm them.
Your surgeon and field medic skills can help you a lot in the wastes, or rather, it can help the people around you a lot.
The vision circle around your characters will be blocked by high objects, forcing you to move behind them making the game much more realistic.
+ STORY:
There are lots of different paths you can take throughout the main story and the side stories, which all affect each other in a way.
To unlock different paths, don't forget to upgrade your 3 convincing skills, Hard-A-s-s, Kiss-A-s-s (which I think should've been called seduction but yeah whatever), and Smart-A-s-s
And believe me, youll need them or you'll really be locked on one path instead of having the liberty to choose.
* message to the creators of this game, an A-s-s is a donkey. The bottom is A-r-s-e not A-s-s!!! *

Ultimately it just wasn't for me and I think it's fair to say it may not be for others too.
Nuclear Throne gets a lot right. A lot! Visuals are off the charts, sound is fun, and the gameplay is as smooth as silk and satisfying to wield (I went with keyboard and mouse, but controller didn't feel half bad for a few rounds either). Now I hate comparing apples and oranges but you immediately get this sense of it being some sort of glorious love child of two fan favorites; Binding of Isaac and Risk of Rain. I was downright giddy after my first few runs. Unfortunately it lacks something vitally important that make both of those mainstays; There's just no sense of progression here. I may be getting worse at gaming but I just didn't feel like I accomplished anything after my first run. A first run that throws all sorts of character unlocks in your face and gives you a false sense of how the game will progress. It just really doesn't after that. Well, not for a long time anyway. The only thing that kept me going besides self loathing was that I received an "achievement" for killing a boss that I had not. So I felt obligated to end him at least once. And this alone gave me the bulk of my 15hrs of playtime. Because well, the game is a punishing hectic mess and that's how long it took to off the dude! Which I will say is not a bad thing on it's own but as I said, there is just no rewards or progression for your truly futile efforts.
You unlock a character now and then when you notice a funky secret, but they rarely bring anything to the table that gets you over the next hump or obstacle in your way. For me, they never did. Its just you versus the cruel world of the game. 15hrs of playing and I have the same equipment at my disposal as I started with. You just get better on your own. Or in my case, you don't. And the biggest problem is that the brunt of this equipment comes in the form of random number generation. Your level upgrades are a roll of the dice and chances are, much more often than not, you won't get a chance to pick the upgrades you'd prefer. This makes the bulk of your runs a large step in quality below the runs featuring a perfect dice roll. And you better believe you'll make a stupid mistake and ruin your good setup should you get it! Pure punishment.
I dunno, I guess I'm a wimp, but I'm tapping out. There was just something lacking for me. Much like the developers other title LUFTRAUSERS it gives you instant satisfaction but if you're in it for the long haul you better have some serious dedication and be an absolute glutton for punishment. I love the idea of what Vlambeer can accomplish with a program like Game Maker: Studio and it should be taken as inspiration to those aspiring. It is well worth a purchase in that regard. But no matter how smooth and pretty they keep making these titles I'm left with feelings of unbalance and lacking of progression. I wish I could "git gud" at this and see some of the later level stuff, but there's just no motivation to do so. Every one of my steps forward has 150 steps backwards in between with no new lessons learned. Beyond being a bundle game I can't recommend it. The fun just ends after 30mins and the punishment and praying to the "RNG Gods" begins.
Proceed with caution.

Now I hear a lot of people saying Enter the Gungeon is supposed to be better than this game and Isaac. Enter the gungeon is 60 fps while this game is 30 fps. However there are two main reasons why I prefer this game more to Gungeon. First is that the game feels a lot more skill based than gungeon. Whenever I play gungeon, it feels like how you do on the first boss widely depends on the items you get on the first floor. If you have not such a good loadout, the first boss feels like it takes forever to destroy. And most of the time, the loadout you get in the beginning isn't so great. In this game, that's not really the case. Usually by the time you reach the first boss, you have a lot likely adequately equipped, in which you can fight the boss without it overstaying its welcome. As for enemies in this game, it also feels like while you can kill enemies easily, they can kill you easily too, so how long you really last in this game depends on your skill.
The other reason I prefer this game to Gungeon, and this is a big one, is because IT HAS ONLINE CO-OP. Well, unofficially. You have to download a mod to get it to work, called "Nuclear throne together". Believe it or not, this mod does have a fair share of users active. And after playing it for around an hour, I have to say that it is one of the best co-op games I've ever played. Enter the Gungeon could have also greatly benefitted from co-op but sadly it's not available in that game. Not to say that Gungeon isn't a bad game. What gungeon has in itself is solid. But this game feels like you win more with skill, not with the gun you're holding, and really, if you don't mind 30 FPS, you're going to have a hell of a time with this game.  Also you have many characters with different playstyles, craploads of guns, probably around the same amount as gungeon, and online play. Seriously, why are you still reading this? Go out and buy this game!
