So it's Saturday afternoon and I'm studying for a December history final, and I noticed this gem was on sale. 33 whole cents, off!? Hell yes! I mean I was aware it's like satire and all (or so I thought). Makes a good screensaver at the very least, right? I buy the thing and have it installed in 2 mins. Mhmm... ok... what's this? Ok... ah I see, draw a picture. Hey, it's like therapy or something. Generates a mountain. Oh, that's cute. The first thing that I immediately notice is just how much of a CPU hog the mountain is. My new rig now runs like a truck. Great. Well, put it on the lowest settings and it's tolerable. A decent compromise. The ambient soundtrack isn't too shabby, either. Soothes the senses... mmm... relaxing. The perfect environment for an esoteric mind. After all, I am god. God is the mountain, god is Mountain, Mountain is God. Wait, what?
6 pm. It appears that the mountain is immune to the effects of alt-tab, that is to say, I'm not willing to do it. You really do get attached to this thing. Sorry, did I say "the mountain"? I meant Mountain. Just Mountain. It's like a pet! Your best friend! Really! Think about it. You check on it once a while for its well-being. When it gets cloudy and moody, you give it a shake; really brightens its day. Need I mention it comes with accessories? Free accessories? Brilliant! You only need to wait between intervals of 30 minutes or so for another baseball or coffee mug or some other piece of crap to land on the side of Mountain's face. Totally worth the wait.
Now I'm not even studying history. I am totally unprepared for the exam. I can just imagine my prof asking some inherently complex question about the capitalist, free-trade economy of the British Empire. I know! I shall consult Mountain. Mountain must know about Britannia in all her imperial, glorified past. Mountain responds in some intuitively philosophical jargon that one does not simply comprehend. I am not prepared. Yet, strangely, I am at peace. Contemplation... contemplation. Then it hits me, as it shall hit you: I am Mountain! There is no other other explanation. I know this. The hidden connections that I have been experiencing for the past 3 hours. You will realize this as well. You, too, are Mountain. Mountain isn't some toy to be trifled with. The entity of Mountain is the very core of your conscience. They weren't kidding on the store page. You really are Mountain, and not simply via some superficial dichotomy in which you play an omnipotent deity who hurls divine wrath at his/her mortal subjects (who are, by the way, completely non-existent here). You are faced with real, life-changing dilemmas in your role as Mountain: there is no true escape from them. Such is life. Such is the life of an adolescent male living in his parents' house, as is the life of a spinning hunk of rock hurtling through the vacuum of empty space.
For instance, why is Mountain spinning? What does this mean? Is Mountain simply obeying the laws of physics? Does Mountain orbit a greater being? If so, why does this greater being refuse to make an appearance? Why? And how, in drawing aforementioned connections, does this relate to you? Does your life, like Mountain, actually revolve around an individual whom you presently consider to be of little significance? Or perhaps it revolves around an idea that is central to your character, your personality. Perhaps kindness, generosity, love. Or perhaps greater goals, such as ambition, power, and authority. The choice is yours. For me, beneath the idyllic demeanor of Mountain, there may lie such ambition. I can hear Mountain whispering to me just now: carpe diem. Seize the day!
But all ambitions require small steps. Mountain tells me to rest. It is 2:40 am on Sunday. I shall return to quiet slumber once again after I have finished my bowl of Kraft Dinner, the staple food of every Canadian student's diet. And then, maybe next morning, I will actually start studying history.
Or, you know, you could always just consider this game a screensaver.

4 Hours into Marvel Avengers, I still can't confidently say whether or not it's a recommended purchase. I don't think this is anything more than DLC that could of been attached to the previous Marvel Lego game. Batman 3 had the Arrow, Man of Steel and Dark Knight DLC and that is what they should of done with this instead of a single full price release.
The open world is very much identical, theres a lot of level reuse and all characters have been ported over, though if anything they've been made worse. The combat has been tweaked and not for the better, a lot of hit or miss attacks occur and some characters feel too slow during fighting especially Cap who suffers most. The Thor and Loki fight during the first Avengers section is a tough slog, using button mashing that recycles the animation over and over as you mash the buttons on screen, this happens a lot. It's hard to tell during these sequences if it's actually doing anything or it's stuck on loop.
The inclusion of the one button for mutiple uses is frustrating, if your using an xbox controller 'B' can be used as double team attack, fire extinguishing, targeting and building all at the same time. Leading to some deaths that never should of occured, while you frantically try to get the character to do the right action. Cap's fire extinguishing is much worse than the last game, having now to do a two button weird jump animation to put them out rather than hold a button for Cap to place his shield on the ground.
The 'B' button finsihing moves are just the end of the combo from the previous game, made as a finishing move. If you played the last game as i have, it doesn't really make any sense as it breaks the flow of the combo and looks janky on animation.
Graphically it's not very different from Lego Batman 3 or its predecessor, not a bad thing because there's not much more you can do to a lego game to make it look great anyways.
Audio dialogue is taken from the films and honestly i wish they hadn't bothered. It sounds out of place and a lot of the times, poor. The dubbing of effects they've tried to use to make it fit in actually make them stand out.
There was a lot of hints to the MCU and characters straight from the movies in the last Marvel Lego, there really was no real need to base an entire game around these two Avengers movies. Maybe it would of been worth the money if it was MCU based and we got to play levels from all MCU films but that's not the case. This really is high priced DLC, unfortunately falling the wrong side of worth the money.
If you like Lego games this will keep you entertained, it sucks to be harsh on it but after 4 hours and having 100% the last one, it really doesn't stand up on its own well.

(TL;DR at bottom)
Lego Marvel Avengers, although it has it's flaws, is a solid entry into the Lego games Series.  If you're a fan of either Lego games or the Marvel Cinematic Universe, you'll likely enjoy it and should consider picking it up.  If you're like me and are a fan of both, you need it.
First off, let's just jump right into what is expected and known about a Lego game.  Game mechanics are still relatively the same, no major leaps forward from Lego Marvel Super Heroes.  You're still going to spend a lot of time punching things , building thing, and solving puzzles.
However, there are a few new mechanics that were a small fresh take such as team ups between the characters.  When fighting, if you get close to another character, a button will appear and initiate a combo between the 2 characters.  Because of the vast number of characters, the number of combos are huge!  Not all are amazing, but some were just visiually brilliant and just awesome.
Next graphics,  I'll make this short and sweet.  This is the fisrt lego game that really has stepped up it game visually.  The environments really look polished and have great textures and well done lighting.  Cutscenes run well and are often redone scenes from the movies, done shot for shot beautifully and I really enjoyed them.
Let's talk sound.  The soundtracks from the movies are used here again and work perfectly with the game, no problems there.  However, those voices... Lines have been pulled directly from the movies, which would be nice, except they sound like they've gone through 100 filters of effects for this game to get rid of background noise.  They work pretty well for cutscenes, but during the gameplay they are just gross and don't fit.  I hate dying as hawkeye just cause I dread to hear the gameplay sounds fade out to hear him whisper, "Do you know what it's like to be unmade?"  Ugh... Just gross.
The Character selection, in my opinion, is still solid.  Its taken a hit since losing all non MCU charcters since Super Heroes (Spiderman, F4, xmen) but very rarely do I actually miss them during gameplay.  The number of characters in Lego Marvel Avengers is still huge and I like learning the new characters and unlocking all of them.
I did have a few glitches happen in my playthrough that halted my progression.  A couple times I had a character land inbetween  boundaries and unable to leave so I had to restart the level.  Another time, a puzzle that required me to jump on buttons in a sequence just didn't register me jumping on the buttons.  I had to restart the game and I got it working.  Nothing gamebreaking, but still irritating.
Overall, I am thouroughly enjoying Lego Marvel Avengers.  It may not be worth $40, but it's easy to find on sale for PC, so get it then.  I'd give it an 8.5/10.
Pros:
-Heroes can team up and make awesomeness happen
-Well Done Graphics (Improved since Marvel Superheroes)
-Still many characters to unlock, most fairly unique
-Nice soundtrack and the lines pulled from the movies sound good during cutscenes
-Classic lego sense of humor that remains entertaining
-Open world and unlockables give great replay ability
-To pick an Ironman suit, you zoom into Tony's HUD and it's freaking awesome.
Cons:
-Lines from the moving sound horrible during gameplay
-A few glitches

Paladins is one of the best up-and-coming games of the last two years. Hi-Rez Studios have taken the character-based first-person shooter, a genre attributed to Team Fortress 2, and combined it with all the strategy of a MOBA, including in-game items that allow you to counter-build your opponents, and card-based decks that augment each character's abilities in unique ways, allowing you to enhance the elements of a champion that you most enjoy working with.
There's currently two dozen 'Champions' to choose from, split into four classes, and many more on the way. On top of the run-and-gun action of every good first-person shooters, each character comes with three unique abilities and an ultimate that can swing the game in your favour. Paladins truly captures the complexity of a strategy game, but with the excitement of a shooter.
The game has a fantasy aesthetic, and features elves, goblins, orcs, and other anthropomorphic fauna/flora playing on all manner of snow, forest, castle, etc-themed maps. The Champions are all delightfully well-designed, each with very distinct personalities and idiosyncracies, including comprehensive voice acting featured in Hi-Rez' famous 'Voice Guidance System', that allows users to speak to their team through their Champion's voice.
Hi-Rez is also the king of cosmetics, and this free-to-play masterpiece makes its money from some of the best cosmetics on the market. The game is updated fortnightly, and there's always something new to see with every patch. Best of all, the purchasable items are entirely cosmetic, and you won't need to pay a cent to unlock all the Champions and cards they can equip, as is Hi-Rez' anti-pay-to-win custom.
I can't recommend this game enough. It's free, it's perfect for all ages, and it has a thriving community, esports scene, and constant updates.

Rather than complain about the optional loot box system, I'm instead going to tell you why Shadow of War failed to live up to the legacy of Shadow of Mordor.
Let me tell you how this game ruined the nemesis system and your interactions with it.
1. Despite the marketing plan for the game being amazing (Up until the lootbox reveal) the orcs on your side do not develop... They rarely betray you, and they DO NOT develop if you save them, or help you out in a pickle. Once you dominate an orce, they become a shadow of their former selves.
2. Because of how rarity works, Orcs are no longer as potent as individuals. If you get repeatedly killed by a common orc, he doesn't become epic or legendary... He just keeps being himself. Orcs do not improve... They remain stagnant.
3. The orcs just... They look so bland. The same armor and weapons keep popping up over and over again, and orcs are SIGNIFICANTLY easier to kill... They're just cannon fodder now.
4. Olog-Hai are tokens. Olog-Hai are just sort of slapped onto the roster to give the illusion of more variety. Olog-hai only have 3 weapons... A club/sword, their fists, and a flamethrower. And they don't cheat death like uruks. Olog-Hai are just a poor attempt... They don't fit in amongst the uruk captains.
5. Remember those videos showing off the "epic" fortress assaults? Yeah... Those are just lame 3-point capture quests where captains and warchiefs show up to slow you down. If you're skilled enough, you can take a fortress without a single captain on your side, and you STILL get a capable army of NPC uruks. It's just SO lackluster.
6. Tribes are purely cosmetic outside of combat and loot. Tribes do NOTHING... They merely give you an idea of what abilities they have in combat, and they tell you what the fortress will look like if they become warchief. Aside from that, they just let you know what legendary loot they will drop. That's it. Buying the silver edition of this game simply gives you 2 new armor sets to farm for, and makes it harder to farm the previously existing tribe armor sets.
7. Mounts have become trivial. Remember when seeing a Caragor made you change your tactics in combat? Now you just need to hit them in the head once to shadow mount them, or hit them a second time to completely eliminate the captain's mount advantage... Speaking of which... Captains with moutns are actually LESS capable in combat vs. Talion... They're more of a nuisance.
8. If you DO want to farm an army of legendary uruk captains, you will have to grind... A LOT. Remember when you could make a captain more powerful by letting him kill you? Well now, unless he's legendary, that's irrelevent... And your captains will be unable to be more powerful than you, which means if you DO try to empower them, you will have to shame them to make them low level enough to be dominated. Not only does this leave a scar on their face that reminds you that this stupid feature exists, but it also has a chance to make the uruk deranged, meaning that any personality they had before, will be replaced with insane gibberish noises... I found an awesome uruk named "The Tower", and in an effort to recruit him, I had to shame him, which made him deranged. Seeing his awesome voice and personality vanish like that made me so sad. I wanted him on my side! But no... Stupid level caps.
9. GRINDING. So yeah, uruks are now bland, and their value is dictated by rarity rather than personality and your experience with them. No longer can you find an uruk who will repeatedly murder you, then lead you to realize that he'd make a better ally than enemy... You will instead seek out legendaries and epics, killing any common captains you find, even if they are genuinely interesting... They'll just die to a more rare captain.
10. Upgrades. There is a solution to this! Want to show a common or epic uruk that you are attached to some love? Give it a legendary upgrade scroll! The uruk will become legendary and become a force to be reckoned with!... But. To get this scroll... you'll have to buy golden loot boxes... Yup. If you want to show appreciation to an uruk you built history with, you have to pay real money in the hopes that you get a power up for it.
11. Regions. Despite the game having multiple regions with very different locales, the uruks residing there all look the same. It'd be so much better if the uruks had different armor and personalities based on where they came from. A fire lord in the cold mountains just isn't all that interesting.
12. Cursed uruks. Remember when the marketing videos made the cursed status effect look like some epic story device and ailment that made combat more difficult? No. It's just a buff on weapons like fire, ice, and poison. There are 4 types of weapon modifiers... Curse, poison, fire, and ice. And ice is only available to you, not the uruks.
13. Cinematics. Again... Cinematics just aren't cutting it. Captains and warchiefs just don't comment on anything around them. The only time they say something interesting is when they take action. If you kill an ally or cast them out of your army, they say NOTHING. Furthermore, uruks do not interact with each other outside of events that you set up.
14. Feuds/blood brothers/friendships. Uruks do not comment on you if you treat them well, and there is no way to tell if who an uruks is blood brothers with, or who they dislike. It's just an excuse to have an uruk ambush you.
15. The game peppers you with captains in "Ambushes" while you're sneaking about or doing something to give the illusion of depth. The game isn't letting you create anything... It's giving you the illusion of depth and choice.
16. Shadow or Mordor is vastly superior in its ability to tell custom stories. In that game, uruks were unique, they were all individuals. Fighting them was harder, and There were no stat restrictions... An uruk could be way higher level than you, and you had to fight your way up to finally take him out. You made your own choices and had tools to help you combat the challenges ahead of you. The story evolved around you, and your enemies were forces to be reckoned with.
Uruks are simply not individuals. They do not interact with you, they don't pose a challenge, and they don't evolve or react as vividly as we were promised. The game feels like an empty shell. This is not what we were promised. We, the gamers, want to form meaningful bonds with our enemies and our allies, and we want to feel like the game reacts to our choices. This is not that. This is a small contained sandbox with microtransactions corrupting the childlike wonder and playful nature of the gamers who loved the first game.

1988, a pivotal year towards the close of the last century.
Arnold Schwarzenegger discovered that Danny Devito was his long lost twin.
Tom Cruise encouraged Dustin Hoffman to play a little blackjack and George Bush senior had just been voted into office.
A fact which I'm sure had no bearing on the emergence of a brand new gaming genre, the post apocalyptic RPG.
The original Wasteland was a ground-breaking title back in the day with recruitable NPC's populating a persistent world. This is something we take for granted in RPG's today, but back in the pink and blue neon haze of the 80's this was unheard-of.
Even if you haven't heard of the original Wasteland, I'm certain you'll be familiar with the Fall Out franchise. A franchise which would probably not exist had wasteland not come before.
It was nearly 10 years after Wastelands release before we got our hands on its spiritual successor Fallout.
Sequels were planned for Wasteland but they never quite came to fruition, but now thanks to a little thing called kick starter and loyal fans with long memories ...
... We have the imminent and long overdue release of Wasteland 2.
After 26 years lost in the wilderness, expectations are high, but are we in danger of placing Wasteland 2 on a pedestal, expecting too much and inevitably about to face disappointment when September 19th rolls around?
After hitting the play button for the first time you'll find yourself at the character creation screen.
Here you'll find more stats and options than you could shake an iguana on a stick at, with skills ranging from animal whisperer to toaster repair.
Prepare to spend an unhealthy amount of time agonising over the attributes and skills sets for your posse of wannabe rangers.
Not that this isn't fun, It's a good kind of agony trying to build your perfect team but if this kind of stat tweaking isn't for you, there is a roster of pre-built characters all lined up like puppies in a pound waiting for you to give them a new home in your squad.
Once you've settled on what you hope is a complimentary skill set for your four rangers you'll be treated to a highly atmospheric cinematic which cleverly fills in a little of the back story for the desert rangers and leaves your group standing around the fresh grave of a fallen comrade.
The writing on the makeshift coffin reads "Born a man, died a desert ranger"
It's here that the game starts as "Ace" is laid to rest and you're team picks up his failed assignment.
It's this assignment that will be your first thread of the main quest that you will follow through Wasteland 2.
After some interesting conversations with the NPCS at the graveside you'll head off on your first mission and it's here that the first moral choice hits hard and fast.
There's a distress signal from Highpool, a community under attack, they need your help, then almost immediately another from the nearby agricultural centre that's having some "plant problems", you'll only have time to try to save one, but which....
It's decisions like this which really make Wasteland 2 come alive, whatever you choose will have repercussions, you're a part of this dying world and your choices matter.
The tough decisions don't all come in the form of moral choices either. The turn based combat present here will test your tactical decision making too. You'll be glad you spent all that time tweaking your stats and skills and matching your weapon load outs to your strengths when bad guys, gals, animals and plants come for you.
When they do come, they'll look great. you'll find crisp detailed graphics and atmospheric audio in Wasteland 2 which makes every encounter a vivid experience.
The end of the world never looked so good.
The experience InXile are creating here is shaping up to be one of the most interesting RPG's in a very, very long time.
At the time of writing the game is still in Beta, although you wouldn't know it, the experience to be had in the first few hours of play is already highly entertaining and very polished.
If you remember, earlier in this preview I expressed my concern that anticipation for this release is too high and that it can only lead to disappointment.
So how do I feel about this now, after I've actually played the game?
From my experience with the beta, the answer to this question is a resounding No. Wasteland 2 is everything I'm looking for in a crunchy RPG and I love it.
This is going to be something special. I'm genuinely excited for the release of this title and I'm certain I'll be sinking an ungodly amount of time into the wastes over the coming weeks.
It's time to rediscover the Wasteland

The fact that this game was made at all fills a corner of my heart with great joy -- Games like these (turn based rpgs) of good quality are often far-between, and I have no regrets playing this one. Very true to the wasteland of old, part of what I love is how you don't need to have played the ancient classic, but if you have it breathes life into many facets of the story. the gritty feel is spot on, and the skill system and character building is intriguing -- though perhaps not as fun as fallout series. It is interesting to note that Wasteland is THE game that inspired so much that came after it in the post-apoc rpg genre... so it is interesting that when it's sequel finally arrives, some of it's successors have already pushed the horizon beyond what it appears (thus far -- haven't finished yet) wasteland 2 will be able to take us. The "robots rising from the ashes of the past to take back the earth" premise has been done so many times since wasteland 1 -- at least twice in the fallout series alone, I'm kind of sad that wasteland 2's synthetics seem to be shaping up to be more of the usual as well... still, I can't write out the idea that this is a red herring as of the time of this review, but lets just say I'd be slightly sad if it's not. Wasteland 1 was revolutionary in almost every respect -- for Wasteland 2 to rise from the ashes, like the numerous armies of robots of whch I've spoke, only to not deliver something new would be unfortunate. Otherwise, great game -- solid RPG, great story, great mechanics, great atmosphere/world... nuff said.

LEGO Marvel Super Heroes was good, but a lot of people felt kinda lost because it was based on the comic universe, and not the cinematic universe. LEGO Avengers is not only based on "Age of Ultron" (as the cover or even the game's icon will sugest), it covers "The Avengers", "Age of Ultron", "Captain America - The First Avenger", "Captain America - Winter Soldier", "Iron Man 3", and "Thor - The Dark World". The cutscenes recreates the most iconic moments of those movies in LEGO style, and they did a pretty good job with that. Also, the game has audio clips from the movies, that means you can hear Chris Evans, Robert Downing Jr, Chris Hermsworth, etc. This is a great feature for the kids. Gameplay wise, this is the first LEGO game that introduced some new features, like co-op actions, some special finishers, and all the characters actually feel really diferent from each other. Puzzles are the same as always, but at least you have some variation on the fighting parts. Music was taken straight out of the movies, so is great. Unfortunely, the dialogues are very low, and every time your character does an special action, it says some one-liner from the movies, and this gets old...fast. Despite this few things, game is great as all the LEGO ones, and is perfect for kids that only know about the Marvel movies. As always, you have good humor, and a lot of replay value. I still think LEGO Batman 3 is the perfect LEGO game, but this is the best you'll get with Marvel characters. Also, there is future DLC planned to adapt "Ant-Man" and the upcoming "Captain America - Civil War", so there is more content coming. If you are not into Marvel, you might wanna wait some time until a sale, but if you are a Marvel fan, or have kids that most likely love the movies, you should buy this game right now, the effort they put into this game deserves your money.

A great throwback to the golden age of adventure games; Broken Age is proof positive that the old genre still has some life in it. The art style is absolutely gorgeous; it's like a pop-up book come to life. The story is tightly written, and is one of the best examples of storytelling in gaming. The game is quite funny, but that's to be expected from the minds behind Psychonauts and Brutal Legend.
As for difficulty, the game isn't too hard by adventure game standards. Generally speaking, most puzzle solutions are logical, and only a few managed to stump me. The dual protagonist setup is well thought-out; if you get bored with a protagonist, or fed up with his/her current puzzle, you can easily switch back to the other protagonist for a change of pace. My only complaint is that the game is a bit on the short side, and being an adventure game, the replay value is limited. Of course, that could change with the release of Part 2 later this year (which will be available as a free update), but the game is definitely worth buying in its current state.

I think if you watch Youtubers play this (I found this via Jesse Cox), you'll probably get the gist of whether you'll like it or not. It's a goofy little election simulator. The game is much more fun with friends, though, especially if you're both being total goofballs, like my friend and I were.
There are some minor nitpicks. Third parties might be a good addition, especially if it becomes more than a two-player game. It would be fun to take down both the Democrat and Republican parties as some party I made up. Also, it's possible to be screwed over by which topics are most relevant, although that might be to avoid blowout wins. (I only experienced this when I was doing much better than my opponent.) The biggest gripe, however, is that talk show appearances can blow up in your face, and it's not even your fault. Your candidate can say downright stupid things you didn't want them to say, and you have to say it because it's the only option you have. Some damage control would be nice, because currently I think it's better not to go on at all.
All in all, I think it was money well spent, especially since I think I bought it on sale. I mean, what other game would allow me to have a Jesus vs. Satan election with my friend?

There's no better way to enjoy the nuclear fallout than to spew thousands of bullets right into the skullls of little mutated rats with your brand new quadruple machinegun. Nuclear Throne promises that and a lot more mutants and guns. Taking the fast-paced combat of a bullet-hell and item diversity of a rogue-like, Nuclear Throne lets you take the role of a mutant seeking power over all, with a lot of firepower. Each character posseses different abilities and can obtain more upon leveling up after gathering enough radiation. Your arsenal is definitely not going to be small, as flamethrowers, smart guns and double miniguns will help tear through any enemies you encounter. However, don't think for a second that your journey to reach the "Nuclear Throne" is going to be piece of cake. With the lack of phasing, a well timed projectile barrage can end your run in an instant, so will a poorly timed explosion. Death is 100% assured within this wasteland.
Great rogue-like x bullet-hell breed, offering you non-stop action and lots and lots of guns!

Well, this was disappointing... So, I don't play ALL the games out there, and maybe I don't play all that many games period, but this is the worst writing I've ever seen in a video game. Seriously, it's incredibly bad. Especially, since the entire game is a character-based drama with long stretches where characters just talk to each other.
The weird part is that the underlying story and characters are actually quite alright, might even have been really cool, but the dialogue within the game ruins it all completely. Everything is explained to you in excruciating detail as if you are too stupid to understand what's going on. It breaks characters, it breaks tension of individual scenes and it ruins the overall flow of the story. Imagine a selfish and bratty teenager, suddenly turning to you and explaining how selfish and bratty they are, as well as all the problems in their life that made them the way they are, only to turn around and go back to being selfish and bratty in the next scene. Or having a character on the verge of a break down suddenly start reminding  you out loud of every minute detail of your previous interactions to "subtly" demonstrate how your previous choices are affecting the current situation. (That "subtly" deserves a lot more quotation marks around it.) Oh yeah, and don't even try to forget those minute details – they would be spelled out to you at least a dozen times over, just in case you somehow missed how your actions affect people.
This happens in the game all the time. Sorry. I haven't stressed it enough. This happens in the game ALL THE TIME!!! The game doesn't trust you to make a single most obvious conclusion by yourself, and instead insists on spelling out every last detail. And the worst part – there are so many other opportunities to deliver that same information to the player, if you think they cannot possibly comprehend the amazing complexity of your story. The main character has a diary with an ungodly amount of text in it. The voice over narrates everything you see and explains all the key choices to you. There is absolutely no need to also have characters within the game "coincidentally" point out the game's mechanics to you.
Personally, I found this writing incredibly annoying, to the point where it sucked out all the enjoyment of the game for me. (Really, all I did was yell 'SHUT UP!!!' during every key dialogue in the second half of the story and I still couldn't miss any important details, since everything is made so obvious and repeated to you several times.)

I started out in Minas Ithil as a lowly level 8 ranger, still inexperienced to the new ways of Mordor, and was slain by a hunter named Puklu the Gouger with a no chance ability (meaning your extra lives are rendered useless) and some serious burst damage from triple throwing daggers.  Frustrated by this unexpected mechanic, I came back and decided to take revenge, starting with a worm to get intel on Puklu.  Upon discovering his fear of fire and being pinned, I pursued him with renewed vigor, only to be ambushed by two of his best friends who were tipped off by my curiosity in Puklu's weaknesses.  Needless to say, I died again.
By this point, Puklu had gone from Puklu the Gouger, a lowly level 8 captain to Puklu the Slayer, a legendary level 15 warrior with some serious talents and forces at his disposal.  With firm resolve, I adjusted my tactics from attempting to fight Puklu head on, where he is strongest, to more hit and run, ranged, and using the environment to combat my now much stronger nemesis.  This time, I finally succeeded against him and acquired some very nice legendary loot.   Thinking this unpleasant chapter of my life over, I moved on to pursue his friends only to be ambushed by the now titled Puklu the Survivor.  He was missing a good chunk of his face, but that didn't seem to slow him down at all as we battled.  I finally achieved victory and received another nice piece of legendary loot.  Maybe this time Puklu's story was over?
Hardly.  He reappeared again as part of a traitor's trap, swearing his eternal revenge against me.  After cleaving Puklu in half, I wondered could his revenge really be eternal?  Now enter Puklu the Reforged, more machine than Uruk with his missing limbs replaced with metal hooks and blades with metal staples keeping him together.  Perhaps this was the end of Puklu's story after his beheading at my hands?  If only.  Puklu the Damned, an undead abomination brought back by necromancy, his disfigured body unable to even form words rose from the dead and continued his quest for revenge against me.  With his purification, I have yet to see him again, but I know somewhere out there, Puklu plots against his (im)mortal nemesis.
Overall, the story is pretty good and makes some interesting additions to the Lord of the Rings lore.  However, the majority of your time in Shadows of Mordor will be spent messing around with the nemesis system, which dominates almost every aspect of the game.  I enjoyed it, but it does get slower killing captains as they inexorably become harder and harder to fight.  No need to worry though, you won't reach that barrier for some time.

I can't give this game enough thumbs up.
LEGO Marvel's Avengers is the DEFINITIVE Super Hero game by LEGO. It features a massive core hub (Manhattan) and seven smaller hubs for you to explore at your leisure, including the SHIELD Base and the famous realm of Asgard. There are several characters that can be unlocked just by playing the stories (more on those in a minute), and over a hundred more to be found scattered through Free Play levels and the open world.
Each hub has characters unique to that location. For example, a few character tokens you might find in Tony Stark's Malibu penthouse are Iron Monger, Happy Hogan, and (if I remember correctly) the Mark 5 Iron Man suit.
The gameplay is a vast improvement over LEGO Marvel Super Heroes. The combat feels much better, and the new tag-team attacks are a blast. The combo system takes some getting used to, and the targeting can be a bit funky, but overall combat is very fun. Each 'main' Avenger can team up with another 'main' Avenger to perform unique tag-team moves, and which move you get depends on who initiates the combo.
For example, let's say you have Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver. If you initiate a tag-team with Scarlet Witch as Quicksilver, Quicksilver will run off screen and come back with a bunch of red LEGO blocks. Scarlet Witch then lifts them into the air (as Quicksilver dashes around in excitement) before causing them to erupt in a rain of energy. However, if you intiate a tag-team with Quicksilver as Scarlet Witch, Quicksilver picks her up and spins her around as she fires a beam of energy across a wide area.
For 'side' characters, the tag-team is the same, with one person grabbing the other's wrists and performing a synchronized air slam. A bit grating after a while, but by no means a detriment to the game.
The story is split across six (technically seven?) Marvel movies: Avengers, Iron Man 3, Thor: Dark World, Captain America: Winter Soldier, Avengers: Age of Ultron, and Ant-Man (in the upcoming DLC pack, that is).
Some people criticize the lack of an original story and the use of direct voice-acting rips from the films, but I actually rather like both of these. Many favorite lines are repeated, with some clever new dialogue to help fit the scene thrown in. The lack of an original plot doesn't bother me either, as the ones that the game DOES cover are all very well written and fun to play through.
The game is drop-dead gorgeous. It's a bit heavy on mid-range laptops like mine, which surprised me a bit. However, even at 1280x720 (not my current resolution, mind), the game still looks significantly better than it's predecessor.
However, the game is not perfect. It does have a few rough spots, such as the occasional friendly fire. The voice acting does get a bit tired after a while, as does the generic tag-team for other characters. The story is also a bit short, but the Free Roam makes up for that. The side mission 'Into The Aether' is a bit bugged, but that may just be me. Finally, the game is fairly easy.
Despite these very insignificant shortcomings, this game is excellent and definitely worthy of a solid 9/10.

Update upon completing Act 2:
Hm... this game... I enjoyed Act 1 when it came out over a year ago. It wasn't the best adventure game I'd ever played, but it had a lot going for it; and I was really excited about the direction of the story after the conclusion of Act 1. There were obviously a lot of issues surrounding the crowd funding and the release schedule, but I'll leave it at that and stick to the game itself.
Act 2 was disappointing in pretty much every way. I went into it interested in where the story was going to go, and by the end was just using a guide to finish it as quickly as possible so I could move it to my completed list.
So what's wrong with Act 2 when Act 1 was pretty solid? Well, first off, there really aren't any new environments. Act the end of Act 1 the characters switch places, which means almost all of Act 2 takes in (slightly) modified versions of the Act 1 environments, so there isn't much new to see. On top of that, the characters don't seem to be even slight confused/intrigued/excited/put off by suddenly being in a world that is completely different than the one they've know their entire lives. Just pretty ho hum about the whole thing. In this way, they reflect the player well because I wasn't excited to be in those environments either.
I mentioned in my earlier review that the puzzles were easy, but that certainly isn't the case now. The difficulty curve from Act 1 to Act 2 isn't so much a gradual increase as it is a brick wall that you slam into face first. When I started playing Act 1 and realized that you can switch back and forth between the characters at any time (similar to the classic Day Of The Tentacle), I expected that to play into the puzzles in same way. But no, it's just two completely separate games that have no connection until the very last cut scene. Fine, those are mechanics established in Act 1 and it's completely acceptable in terms of game design. Act 2 says "the hell with good game design, the rules are now completely different!". Not only are there instances where you need to be bouncing back and forth between the characters and completing actions to proceed, there are puzzles that require you seek out incredibly obscure bits of information in one character's world to complete a puzzle in the other's. And in case you're wondering if it makes continuity sense for one character to learn a piece of information and it benefit the other character, it does not. Oh, and did I mention that not only are most of the puzzles and sequences very difficult, they are also often nonsensical and extremely tedious? Well they are.
Speaking of continuity, the story is my other big complaint. Act 1's story had 2 interesting narratives, both with their own sense of mystery, and ended up coming together in a surprising but totally believable way. Act 2 on the other hand introduces new concepts from out of no where. The answers to the questions from Act 1 are so from left field that they aren't interesting and turn the latter half of Act 2 into a difficult grind to the credit screen.
So what's to like about Act 2? Unfortunately not a lot. The art is still fantastic and the voice acting is still top notch, unfortunately it's pretty much all the same art and voices you've already experienced in Act 1. The puzzles have turned into a drag and the story loses all of it's luster. In fact, Act 2 was so unpleasant to play that I'm changing my recommendation from a Yes to a No. Keep in mind, this has nothing to do with the long delay or any of the  other issues people have raised, but has to do with the experience of playing Broken Age in it's entirety.
Old Act 1 Review:
Recommended if you miss old school point and click adventure games (Monkey Island) or interactive narrative "games" (Walking Dead, Gone Home), but with some caveats.
First off, the story are characters are interesting and the art is solid. The voice acting is also great and the dialogue is well written. It's a very enjoyable experience overall.
My real qualm with the game is that it has the feel of the old point and clicks I fondly remember, but no where near the challenge. The "puzzles" are fairly obvious and finding the solutions isn't terribly interesting. You wont find yourself trying to use every item with things in the environment because you'll usually only have one or two items in your inventory and their usage will be pretty straightforward.
It's definitely worth playing, just don't expect the challenge one normally associates with point and click adventure games.

Should I care for my Mountain? Or should I let it accumulate with trash? Will there be real consequences of what I draw in the openning screen?  Was that baseball there 5 minutes ago? In 'Mountain'There's a persistent sense of "I wonder if something is about to happen..." Occasionally it does. In Mountain, you don't play. You expect, you question, you get hopeful, you get disapointed, you get inspired, but most importantly you think. The creator of Mountain specified that this game is best left running for you to occasionally check in on. I left mountain running for 6 hours while I did work. Every so often, I would hear the chyme indicating my Mountain was about to express its pure existential thoughts. What's the point of that thought? Why would a mountain care about the sunrise? Maybe it's not about that, maybe it's a statement. Maybe it's demonstrating the joy of pure life. Maybe not though, maybe it's touching on the cynicisms of life and time?
Art is what makes people think. This interactive piece of art will let you poke at it all day and you'll never be satisfied with any conclusions you may create regarding its purpose. You will keep poking, keep wondering. I managed to get a dwarf planet to destroy my mountain - I was killed and the game offered me a 'retry.' Does this imply I failed a goal? What is my goal? Who IS Mountain? I may never find an answer, but I don't think I'll stop asking any time soon.
"I don't really know what I am, is that weird?" Said Mountain just as I typed the last sentence. Don't worry, Mountain, I'm doing my best to find out.
If you've ever read the Catcher in the Rye, you know that someone's entire story and entire personality can be revealed through the way they observe the world around them. Not in their actions, necessarily, but the way they think. That's mountain. Don't buy for gameplay, you won't find it. Buy it to experience something new, to think, and to ask questions.

Paladins is one of the best up-and-coming games of the last two years. Hi-Rez Studios have taken the character-based first-person shooter, a genre attributed to Team Fortress 2, and combined it with all the strategy of a MOBA, including in-game items that allow you to counter-build your opponents, and card-based decks that augment each character's abilities in unique ways, allowing you to enhance the elements of a champion that you most enjoy working with.
There's currently two dozen 'Champions' to choose from, split into four classes, and many more on the way. On top of the run-and-gun action of every good first-person shooters, each character comes with three unique abilities and an ultimate that can swing the game in your favour. Paladins truly captures the complexity of a strategy game, but with the excitement of a shooter.
The game has a fantasy aesthetic, and features elves, goblins, orcs, and other anthropomorphic fauna/flora playing on all manner of snow, forest, castle, etc-themed maps. The Champions are all delightfully well-designed, each with very distinct personalities and idiosyncracies, including comprehensive voice acting featured in Hi-Rez' famous 'Voice Guidance System', that allows users to speak to their team through their Champion's voice.
Hi-Rez is also the king of cosmetics, and this free-to-play masterpiece makes its money from some of the best cosmetics on the market. The game is updated fortnightly, and there's always something new to see with every patch. Best of all, the purchasable items are entirely cosmetic, and you won't need to pay a cent to unlock all the Champions and cards they can equip, as is Hi-Rez' anti-pay-to-win custom.
I can't recommend this game enough. It's free, it's perfect for all ages, and it has a thriving community, esports scene, and constant updates.

What can I say?  Tim Schafer has done it again.
Broken Age is an enjoyable point-and-click adventure with the right mix of character dialog, puzzles, and humor.  This all leads into decent character development throughout the game, and sets up the ending of this First Act perfectly.
The dynamic of shifting between the stories of two characters worked well throughout the game.  The two stories were balanced in terms of content, and I really didn't favor one over the other.  While it's important to play and appreciate both stories you aren't forced to switch throughout most of the game.  This allows the player to enjoy each story and character independently, and not be arbitrarily ripped out of the experience.  I enjoyed being able to switch between the stories when I wanted to, without consequences.
And the ending of this First Act?  I won't spoil it, but it's brilliantly executed and memorable.  It certainly makes me look forward to Act Two.  As far as which story to finish first, I will say that I finished Shay's story first and found the ending very profound.  It was truly an 'OMG' moment where the two stories merge, and suddenly everything makes sense and shocks you at the same time.  Please take your time and enjoy both stories before you get to the ending, as you'll appreciate the results.
I highly recommend Broken Age to both fans of point-and-click adventures and first-timers.  Tim Schafer and Double Fine have delivered a high-quality experience that is well worth the money.

First things first:
This is a game with loot. Loot means that you have to grind to get better things. So, If you don't like loot in games, or grinding...you probably won't enjoy the game very much.
I won the game, a 100% in about 70 hs because I took it slowly, I enjoyed every single thing it had to offer, and got almost all sets to max level.
Now, to the other matter:
Does this game have Loot boxes? Yes.
Does this game have Micro transactions? Yes.
Does the game compel you to buy them? NO.
Do you REALLY need them to win the game? NO.
You can buy them with in game currency? Yes. (In fact, I bought a couple just to try it out...No difference from the orcs you get just by playing, only thing are orders to give them a fire weapon for example...and that's not game changing)
To the game itself:
The game is just excellent, the story improved a lot since SoM, the gameplay too and of course the Nemesis System is now ramped up to 100. Each orc with their own personalities and traits are just amazing. Fortresses assaults are just GREAT (tho I'd like more of them). Regions are very well designed and now you have a gear system which actually changes the look ingame and sets with the special bonuses for completing them.
There is however something that a just found a bit lazy from the devs, yes I'm talking about Act IV.
You have 10 stages of the "Shadow Wars", where you have to defend your fortresses against assaults....a LOT of times, after which you get the real ending of the game. The main issue I found is that...that's it, that's what you do the whole act, each time more and more difficult. That's where most people say it's blocked behind a "pay wall" because you need stronger orcs, It's NOT true. All you have to do is level up your orcs...and let's face it, it's not hard. I find the loot boxes here, and excuse for lazy people, of course, it will take some time, frustration and so on...but you'll do it without spending money, and the feeling is good.
There isn't much to say about the game that hasn't been show in gameplays or streams in terms of overall content, you got the fortresses, you got your orcs, you got your Nemesis System and boy, it's even better this time. This review is more focused in shaking that belief that you need to pay extra money to finish the game.
If you bought the game because wanted to see the Nuclear Throne on your first run, well, I have some bad news for you...

Hotline Miami is a very difficult game. If you rage quit easily, it is not for you.
If you do, however, enjoy bashing your head against a wall over and over again until the wall breaks, only to find another, thicker wall on the other side, this game is for you!
Seriously though, it controls EXTREMELY well, and while the RNG will bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥once in a while, most of your failures will be because you messed up. Levels are short, but you'll likely be spending a decent amount of time trying each one again and again, trying to figure out the best possible way to get through it. And on a similar note, the game has an arcade-style point system, giving you some incentive to keep returning to levels you've already beaten, so that you can get that new high score you've been craving.
The downside to this game, for me at least, is that unlike many trial-and-error games, it just doesn't give that huge sense of accomplishment with each benchmark reached. With Dark Souls, for enstance, I left each area feeling accomplished; feeling like I'm king of the world (until a new even BIGGER demon punched my face in and put me back into my place, that is). But with Hotline Miami, I never got that feeling. Beating each level just sorta felt like a chackpoint, where the next step was to do more of the same, only harder this time around.
That said, I wholy admit that that issue might lie simply in my personal tastes, and that others may not experience it the same way.
In all, I would give this game a 5/10
It's worth a try. It has a great atmosphere, and controls very well. I absolutely feel like the low score I gave is due mainly to it simply not being my personal cup of tea. So, try it for yourself! You might just like it!

A quick glance at the negative reviews reveals grievances with the developer for abandoning the project years ago. Since I don't know what commitments the developer originally made, I'll leave that aside. LF is best described as a combination of
and Soldak Entertainment's excellent dungeon crawler
. Perspective is entirely isometric, with tools and weapons progressing from stone to metals, mobs of undead and spiders spawning in darkness, and multiple biomes with different resources available for harvest.
The twist is in base building: You can craft town buildings that attract vendors selling items and leveled equipment. Vendors change their inventory frequently and typically offer a few items above the player's current tech level, e.g. if you're using copper equipment, tools and weapons merchants might sell iron tools and weapons.
It's clear that quite a few gameplay balance issues were left unaddressed since release. In particular, while underworld mob levels match the underworld map level (e.g. level 1 mobs at underworld level 1), overworld mobs always match or exceed the player's level. This means that a 20th level player can survive indefinitely at underworld levels 1 through 19 then get slaughtered within seconds of walking around the overworld at night. Also, the
-style click-to-attack mechanic is seriously flawed, especially when facing multiple attackers. It's qute easy to lose a winnable battle by clicking just outside the hitbox of the intended mob or accidentally clicking a nearby object, causing the player to walk around blithely while getting beaten to death. There's even a glaring visual bug in which some walls connected in build mode don't actually connect.
That said, I've enjoyed the 10+ hours I've spent with this $10 game. I've found
to be far more fun and interesting than the much more popular
. I'd like to see LF's source code released without any art assets, enabling the community to improve the game while still requiring the original game files.

This is my first game review.  I loved the original Mafia.  I liked Mafia II.  Had better graphics, but the story line didn’t grab me like the 1st one did.  This one’s story line seems pretty good even though I’ve only played a short time.  Unfortunately, this will also be my first refunded game.  I was so excited to see a 3rd Mafia was being worked on and had high hopes, but you know what?  If we don’t start taking a stand with the way these games are being released, it won’t change for the better.  I didn’t pre-order this one, and after this, I think I will vow to never pre-order a game in the future.
With all my settings set to high, the cinematic scenes look pretty sweet, but for sixty bucks and a whopping forty gigs, I’d expect the gameplay graphics to be pretty sweet too.  Sorry, but this is hardly that.
Many things irked me from the get-go, starting with the setup screen with little directions on how to adjust the gamma and hud.  It’s ok though, I just press keys or buttons until I figured it out.  Not a big deal, but that was the very first impression I was faced with on this game. First impressions are pretty crucial too.
Made it through the setup screen and started the game.  I’m using an Xbox controller and the controls, movement and driving felt a little quirky, but that’s just something I think I’d adjust to after a while.  Within minutes into the game, I was already just a little disappointed with the game and just thought maybe my expectations were too high.
The frame rate seemed pretty stable, and I know there’s a patch coming to unlock it from 30, but damnit, why release a game before it’s finished, or at least is going to leave a good FIRST IMPRESSION?
The thing that pushed it over the edge for me was reading other reviews about crashes.  I have a pretty good system running here and I can’t tell you the last time I’ve had a game crash on me, but, after just 1 hour into the game during a cinematic scene, this did.  I’m sorry, but I just can’t justify paying this much for something that seems like a lot of work went into it, but didn’t deliver.  Maybe someday, they’ll release another forty gig patch to address the graphics and crashes.  If I played this longer, I’d probably have a larger list of issues.
Oh, also, if I’m using a controller, please be consistent on which buttons to press instead of telling me to press keys on my keyboard some of the time.

The lighting is awful, textures are washed out, all surfaces look like plastic, and why is everything is so damn blurry?!  It's incredibly hard to focus on what you're doing while playing this game.  It puts so much strain on my vision that I've found myself rubbing at my eyes constantly just to try and cope with the haziness and blur that's smeared everywhere.  Night time driving is nearly impossible.  Light sources only travel about 3 feet at night, so vehicle headlights and street lights literally just look like white circles made in microsoft paint that float around you as you drive by them.  Rain or weather just adds to this problem and makes all aspects of game play unenjoyable.  I've watched television shows that were recorded in 1968 that had better image quality than this game has.  (Maybe that's what they were going for?)
And why -- just why -- did the devs decide a 30 fps cap was a good idea on anything other than a plebstation or a potato box where it was probably struggling to hit 30fps anyway?  It is crystal clear how much more attention and care went into ensuring the console experience was optimal while the PC port got the shaft, yet again.  The UI and menus almost demand that you use a joystick -- if I'm playing on PC, I don't want to have to press Enter or use my ♥♥♥♥ing arrow keys to navigate menus that were obviously not designed with a PC player in mind.
No amount of great writing or engaging story lines can make up for the fact that the PC experience has been an afterthought.  If it looks and feels like dog♥♥♥♥♥♥and I can't find myself enjoying even the minute to minute experience, what good will a story do for me?

I had played a demo of Alan Wake a couple of years ago, and knew roughly what it was about. But I'd put off playing it because I'd had other, "more interesting" games to play. I sat and played about 30 minutes of Alan Wake one night, and thought "myeh, it's alright, I'll keep it installed". So I did.
Then, a couple of weeks later, I fancied a quick bash on it.
11 hours later, I'd completed the main game and was just about to start the "Special Episode" when I realise that, actually, I had to go to work soon.
If you're interested in psychological horror, pulp horror, Lovecraft, or the art of writing, this is quite the potent game to play. It isn't without its flaws, but any non-MMO game that can make me sit and play it for 11 hours without taking a break deserves considerable accolade.
Add to it the 2 "Special Episode" DLCs, which are essential parts of the storyline and, thankfully, included in the PC version, you have a great, story-driven package.
If you just want to shoot things, I recommend checking out Alan Wake's American Nightmare instead, though the story of that game won't really make a lick of sense without having played Alan Wake first.

A unique but flawed concept. I'd actually say the price is somewhat reasonable, but there's a lot of potential here you aren't exploiting, so I can't recommend it right now. Improve it a bit and I will gladly change my review. Here's some things I would say you could do to improve it:
* There's a pretty good base here for pixel art, but you should allow your artist to expand the palette and work with less limitations. Portal proved you can have a minimalistic art style that still worked well.
* Either make every weapon draw from the same energy pool or make them each have their own ammo type; its esoteric and hard to understand when ammo only replenishes the weapon you're currently wielding.
* Don't require ammo for breaking through obstacles; its another design flaw that arbitrarily slows progress and makes the player feel like they have to guess what the designer was thinking. I would suggest putting in switches to open new areas or something similar instead.
* You've got some grammatical errors in your intermission screens. Fixing that will give players a better first impression.
* Make the player less of a meat shield and more mobile and make enemy projectiles slower; this will help players dodge more projectiles and reward skillful play, while increasing the overall challenge.
Overall, I think it's a great start but it feels a bit more like a playable alpha than a fully-fledged game. Even for $3.99 you should consider fleshing out the game more.

Today on
: Lego Marvel's Avengers.
First off, it's a Lego game. If you don't like running around, smashing everything in sight, janky controls poorly ported from consoles, and inexplicable chickens, this changes very little in the formula. But that's not necessarily a bad thing. If it ain't broke, don't fix it and all that.
Second, it's improved. (Graphically.) If you played Lego Marvel Superheroes, almost all of the characters that made the jump to this one have been made better in one way or another, even if it's just graphically. Thor, perhaps, was one of the most fun to play with, now that Mjolnir stays electrified and easily deflects projectiles heading your way. They also made up for Hawkeye's relative uselessness in the MCU (I love you, Clint, but it's true) by giving him several more block types to interact with than the previous game. The graphics are actually very nice and I can still run it maxed out on my definitely-not-a-gaming-computer. That's always a nice feeling.
Third: open world. Grand Theft LEGO never fails to amuse me, but I'm easily amused and if you give me the opportunity to have the Hulk steal a car and drive it around New York City until it explodes, I'm going to take it. They took what was already the best part of the previous game and made it even better, IMO, and I've barely had a chance to play it. (UPDATE 2/2: Make sure you check out some of the other hubs besides Manhattan for more content -- also Coulson doesn't bug you about some guy stealing a purse every two minutes, which is nice.)
Four: the heroes. While Spider-Man, the X-Men, and the Fantastic Four are notably missing from the roster (blame FOX), this gave Marvel the chance to pull out some of its lesser-known roster of heroes. I'm not sleeping until I unlock Kamala Khan, because I'm just so excited there is a video game with Kamala Khan in it. Also, the Young Avengers will always hold a place in my heart for being the book that got me into comics to begin with, so I'm pretty excited about them, too. (I'm guessing the game will
explain how Scarlet Witch, in her mid-twenties, has teenage twin sons also running around fighting crime?)
This isn't to say it's not without its flaws, because it has lots of those, too. Maybe I'm romanticising it because of the content that it's based on, maybe I'm biased, maybe I should just sleep and replay it in the morning when I haven't had coffee yet and see how frustrated a children's game can make me.
There is no original story in this game unless you decide to play out your own in the open world. If you've seen the movies, you've seen the plot for this game. While it draws mostly from the two Avengers movies, there are sequences from many of the solo films as well. On the bright side, the fact that this is a Lego game means no one dies, so
are fine, on vacation in Tahiti.
They also made the Bruce/Natasha relationship in Age of Ultron make a little bit of sense, which is a miraculous achievement I didn't think was possible. So props there.
Because the game uses the original audio from the movies, things feel... off. Some lines are delivered too seriously for any Lego game, others are taken out of context to be used as chatter while you play, and it all sounds very quiet at times. For some inexplicable reason, they had a different voice actor record new dialogue for Bucky Barnes in the Captain America: First Avenger level, who sounds more like the original kid Bucky from the 1940s than the soldier portrayed in the movies. ("I'm with you 'til the end of the line!" he says enthusiastically! For some reason I have taken offense to this and I'm not entirely sure why.)
That being said, Hayley Atwell, Clark Gregg, and Cobie Smulders all recorded additional dialogue for their characters (Agents Carter, Coulson, and Hill respectively), and when delivered well (which it not always is), are amusing and make this game feel like it's supposed to be -- a Lego game in the MCU.
You're thrown into the game's opening sequence with absolutely no instruction as to how to play. Fortunately, if you've played any Lego game on the PC in the past, absolutely nothing has changed. Unfortunately, if you've played any Lego game on the PC in the past, absolutely nothing has changed. The controls suck. They always will suck. This time, they just suck and you're given very little information on how to use them. There are puzzle sections I spent ten minutes on because things were just not clear.
There are bugs -- I can't get the Steam Overlay to work, and sometimes the characters just won't do what you want them to (Tony, you're making Clint ashamed by how poorly you're aming your laser beam. Just hit the gold bricks, that's your only job).
So far, it's a cute game. It's a Lego game. It's a Marvel game. And it's fun. I can't really complain about that. Is it worth $40? Not really, but yet again, it's not money I regret spending (yet).
UPDATE (2/2/2016): I've finished Story Mode, and I have to say, I'm more underwhelmed than I was when I started out. While it's not necessarily enough for me to give it a not recommended rating, I'd definitely say that it's subpar as far as Lego game and pales in comparison next to the previous Marvel game. It's still fun though. Stupidly so. And it's not like people play Lego games for the excellent, original stories. So, yeah. Wait until this one goes on sale. But it's still fun, and it still has Kamala Khan, and that's good enough for me.

Honestly, Mountain is a game that I cannot recommend to anyone.
You: But then why does your review say that you recommend it?
Me: Zip it for a sec, and I'll tell you!
TLDR: I can't tell you whether or not you'll like Mountain.  Take a look at the info for it, and if you buy it, go in with an open mind, and don't expect it to be something that you're constantly watching for changes.
So, as many of the Steam reviews have already made evident, Mountain is not exactly a game.  It is slightly more interactive than a screensaver, but it's certainly not about to set the world on fire with deep gameplay mechanics, cutting edge graphics, or a particularly engaging story.
However, I still found it oddly compelling.
Something about just loading up the game for the first time, generating a mountain, and then leaving it running in the background while working on homework was just very pleasant.  Perhaps it's because I'm rather fond of white noise, and as a result, I found the sounds of wind, rain, and crickets in the background, punctuated by the occasional *ping* of a new message to be very relaxing.  Maybe it was the mystery of it all, not knowing what my mountain would look like the next time I opened it up.  Maybe it would be a new season!  Maybe there would be some new object on the mountainside!  Who knows?  Whatever the reason, I have enjoyed my time with it so far, and plan to spend a great deal more time seeing what it has to offer.
If I have any complaints about the game, it is the following:
1. As many others have commented, the resource usage for this game is ridiculous.  While my CPU is by no means beefy (An AMD A10-4600M), the fact that this game is constantly using around 50% of my CPU's capabilities is a huge nuisance.  I would love to leave it running in the background all the time, even while playing other games, but it just slows everything else to a crawl.  I would love it if a fix (if one is even possible) for this were released.
2. After a while, the messages start to get a bit repetitive.  I suppose this just gives a reason to ignore them, but it is still somewhat annoying when the vast majority of them can be boiled down to, "I feel (emotion adjective) on this (adjective)(time noun)".
So to clarify my position, I do not recommend Mountain to anyone.  I would not walk up to someone and rant and rave about, "OH MAN, YOU HAVE TO TRY THIS GAME!!!", because I think it would set false pretenses for what the game is, and ultimately lead to disappointment.  I could not tell someone that it is something they would enjoy, because it is a completely different experience from any other game I've played (if one can even consider it a game).
It is for this reason that I say, make your own decision.  Read the store page description, check out some screenshots, and decide if it's right for you.  It's only $1, so in an age where going to a movie can cost upwards of $10 or $20, it's not a huge loss.
If you buy it, don't expect that you can sit down and stare intently at it while your mountain changes.  If you go in expecting this, you will think the game is the biggest waste of time in the world.  Just let it sit in the background while you read a book, make a meal, or study, checking back every now and then to see how the landscape has changed.
This is how I have been "playing" the game, and it's how I've been enjoying it so far.  It's up to you to decide if you will too.

Edit for OB44 update.
Hi-Rez added a third currency, the only purpose of which was clearly a cash grab. They shipped the update with severe bugs, didn't deliver on some promises, and overall killed community confidence. Was fun while it lasted. I'll check it out in a few months but for now I'm looking at Overwatch.
---
Great game. People call it an Overwatch clone, and while Overwatch and this game do share a few common traits keep in mind most of those traits existed in past games. Specifically, games made by Hi-Rez studios. Global Agenda and Tribes: Ascend are game Hi-Rez has made in the past and a lot of the inspiration for this game came from those games, not from Overwatch. Overwatch and Paladins were also released fairly close to each other so obviously Hi-Rez couldn't have made a clone in 4 months. Paladins was in development for 4 years before it was released.
Anyway, now that I got that out of the way. This game is great. Mechanics are smooth, and even though it's in beta the balance feels nice. Maeve is a new champion and while she feels a little overpowered at the moment it's important to keep in mind she is new so there needs to be an adjustment period.
Game Modes: I do wish there were more gamemodes. There are only two at the moment. A pure payload gamemode and a KOTH/Payload hybrid. A pure KOTH or control point gamemode would be awesome. But the two gamemodes with the sizable amount of maps makes it so that most matches are completely different.
Champions: Great roster of champions. They're all mostly balanced and have their strenghts and weaknesses that don't outshine another champions. Everyone has their place.
Bugs: Haven't run into any yet but I don't have that many hours into it.
Money/P2W-ability: There is no way to spend money and automatically be better than another player in this game. Spending money will only give you XP/Gold boosts, and get you cosmetics. You can spend real money to get "cards" (which are used to change how your champions abilities act) but the cards are already cheap enough that even playing games casually will net you enough gold for a full deck. Not to mention you are given a full deck for every character to start with. You use gold to also buy champions, which again can be bought with money too but they're also fairly realistically priced.
Overall I give this game a solid 8.5/10. Excited to see where it goes.

Hotline Miami is a unique game in which you break into various buildings and proceed to violently murder every single inhabitant inside and once you are done, you walk back through all the carnage and death you have caused, trying not to trip over all the corpses or slip in the blood, feeling like a bad a s s but also maybe even a monster at the same time, and drive away in your car, never looking back. A very interesting experience I must say.
The gameplay is both strategic and also fast-paced, as groups of enemies are stationed in various areas of the map and you must find the best way to eliminate them all before being killed yourself. Enemies at a distance with fire-arms must be engaged at short distances (mainly due to the fact that all enemies essentially have aim-bot and thus kill you very swiftly), unless you have a firearm yourself, so positioning becomes vital. However, discharging a gun alerts nearby enemies and causes a rapid rush towards your location, causing you to think and act quickly. Due to the fast "die and restart" system that is implemented, death does not slow you down that much at all, and thus the gameplay becomes much more fluid and exciting. There is something extremely satisfying about tactically and violently dispatching foes left and right, constantly picking up and throwing weapons with very little breathing room, like something out of an action movie. That is what makes Hotline Miami so appealing, the determination to kill everyone as efficiently as possible or string together a higher combo until you have mastered the level or utilising different techniques such as rushing in with guns or quietly with melee weapons. The masks also offer many completely different styles of play, such as killing throws or fists only. The gameplay of Hotline Miami is by far its best quality and will keep you entertained for many playthroughs.
The story is not really that fascinating on the surface, but if you put in the extra effort and collect all the collectible puzzle pieces and solve the puzzle, the story takes a bit of an intriguing turn and you may even find out a bit about the reasons behind the slaughter. Then again, maybe you're just doing it for fun. Maybe you enjoy murdering people.
Anyway, there are also many fun achievements that aren't too hard but are still challenging enough to make you feel good about completing them. Getting A+ on all chapters is one of the most difficult, requiring a lot of practice and stringing together combos in order to be successful. Getting a kill with every single weapon can be labelled as the most tedious, as there are many weapons you may not even have known existed even after playing through the game multiple times, and require some luck and a lot of time/commitment to finish. Overall, it took 30 hrs to 100% and I feel with the exception of the "use every weapon" achievement, it was quite worth it and felt very rewarding.
The soundtrack is also a highlight and fits with the theme of the game perfectly, with electronic beats accompanying you throughout the levels and making your experience all the more fun.
If you are looking for an original, fast-paced and hectic heap of enjoyment, you cannot go wrong with Hotline Miami. Will remain one of my favourite games of all time for a while, if not forever. It is a must-own game and well worth the purchase.

This game is a rough (gem)stone with bright/worked and flawed/unfinished sides:
The bright sides:

- Fitting music & sound

- no goals/quests nor bosses/challenges, just sandbox builiding, exploration & crafting
- combat aiming (use <shift> to stand still and aim easier)

All in all, I had my fun with it albeit the inability to see/visit all biodomes & the graphic bugs.
Building your cosy home (& outposts) with annex gardens/pens/walls/toolsheds/... is fun.
But the end is there sooner than later as there are no real challenges to be had.
Just some building, exploring & crafting fun . . .
That's it!
Recommended at a Sales period.

I've played two Vlambeer games now -the other one being Super Crate Box- and I've noticed a common theme: insertion of the mainstays of an old-school FPS (lots of guns, lots of enemies, cathartic gameplay, basically whatever Serious Sam does) into other, older genres to see what happens. With Super Crate Box, the genre in question is an 8-bit platformer, along the lines of the original Donkey Kong. In Nuclear Throne, it's a top-down bullet hell shooter (with RPG elements), which is a wonderful choice for combination with an old-school FPS. However, doing so means that the game has to take away the FPS ability to tank absurd amounts of damage, which is where the roguelite elements come in.
Nuclear Throne's main issue for me is that, upon death, no matter how far you are, you're sent all the way back to the start. I'd expect nothing less from a roguelite ('roguelite' for me meaning it has randomization and permadeath), and this wouldn't be a problem but for the fact that the first levels will soon become VERY familiar, because they only vary so much, and contain the least interesting weapons and enemies. I can see why the decision was made; if you could save, you could finish the game in about 20 minutes, and being a roguelite means that the devs don't have to balance the massive amount of weapons and enemies, both of which are spawned randomly and vary widely in terms of power. Still, managing to kill Li'l Hunter (the game's other issue) and then being blown up by a random car because you weren't being careful with your explosives, only to be sent ALL the way back to the start, can be...disheartening, to say the least.
That's essentially my only problem with the game, though, and judging by the fact that I've put 206 hours into it at time of writing, it doesn't stop me from playing. I love Nuclear Throne. I love its adrenaline-soaked gameplay, I love its crushing difficulty, I love its increasingly bizarre arsenal, I love its variety, and I could talk about it for hours.
I won't here, though, because these reviews are disjointed and rambling enough already. Suffice it to say that I like to play Robot, my favorite mutation is Gamma Guts, and my favorite weapons are the Eraser and the Seeker Shotgun.
Anyway, yes. I love Nuclear Throne, and I recommend it to everyone. It's my favorite roguelite of all time. Sorry, FTL. To quote Saints Row 2, you lost to the best.

That haitus then turned into a complete absence, only broken by their sudden return to post a community discussion thread asking players for suggestions for an upcoming update.  They returned exactly twice to that thread to reply; once to tell a player to hold shift while clicking left mouse button if they didn't want to move while collecting items or attacking enemies, and the second time to write a single sentence reply to another poster.  Any updates after their initial offering on Steam have largely done nothing to improve either gameplay or bugs and glitches.
So I deem this abandonware, like so much other Greenlight and Early Access junk.
