Lantern Forge is a nice little game with endless possibilities. It's a building/survival type game that I'm glad I bought. The beginning was a bit clunky, but that's mostly because it doesn't use the usual control setups so the finger movements are unfamiliar. That's not neccesarily a bad thing, though. Once you get used to the controls, the game's great.

First things first:
This is a game with loot. Loot means that you have to grind to get better things. So, If you don't like loot in games, or grinding...you probably won't enjoy the game very much.
I won the game, a 100% in about 70 hs because I took it slowly, I enjoyed every single thing it had to offer, and got almost all sets to max level.
Now, to the other matter:
Does this game have Loot boxes? Yes.
Does this game have Micro transactions? Yes.
Does the game compel you to buy them? NO.
Do you REALLY need them to win the game? NO.
You can buy them with in game currency? Yes. (In fact, I bought a couple just to try it out...No difference from the orcs you get just by playing, only thing are orders to give them a fire weapon for example...and that's not game changing)
To the game itself:
The game is just excellent, the story improved a lot since SoM, the gameplay too and of course the Nemesis System is now ramped up to 100. Each orc with their own personalities and traits are just amazing. Fortresses assaults are just GREAT (tho I'd like more of them). Regions are very well designed and now you have a gear system which actually changes the look ingame and sets with the special bonuses for completing them.
There is however something that a just found a bit lazy from the devs, yes I'm talking about Act IV.
You have 10 stages of the "Shadow Wars", where you have to defend your fortresses against assaults....a LOT of times, after which you get the real ending of the game. The main issue I found is that...that's it, that's what you do the whole act, each time more and more difficult. That's where most people say it's blocked behind a "pay wall" because you need stronger orcs, It's NOT true. All you have to do is level up your orcs...and let's face it, it's not hard. I find the loot boxes here, and excuse for lazy people, of course, it will take some time, frustration and so on...but you'll do it without spending money, and the feeling is good.
There isn't much to say about the game that hasn't been show in gameplays or streams in terms of overall content, you got the fortresses, you got your orcs, you got your Nemesis System and boy, it's even better this time. This review is more focused in shaking that belief that you need to pay extra money to finish the game.

Simple but surprisingly deep, there is nothing about this game I don't like. A fantastic art style; a soundtrack so good I have it on my iPod; addictive gameplay, with very high replay value; explores themes of religion, childhood fears, growing up, and death.
All up, it plays like a great randomly-generated RPG, and feels like an extremely personal game from Ed McMillen. We grow to know Isaac on a far deeper level than any other video game character out there.

While Lantern Forge could certainly benefit from some fine tuning, especially with the UI, there are no gaping flaws or immersion breaking moments in the game. This said it also lacks anything amazing enough to floor you.
The framework of the game is built upon traditional rpg tropes. You have familiar goblins and spider enemies who inhabit familiar procedural generated environments which you'll explore with one of three familiar hero archetypes that all work in a familiar fashion.
One of Lantern Forge's more innovative and stronger experiences comes from your town. The game itself puts you in the role of building it, or rather strongly suggests that you build one. It gives you a lot of room to be creative, allowing you to either making your town a work of art with individual shops, gardens and style or a small functional space to cram everything you need into. At the moment you don't need to worry about protecting your town, its simply there for you to gather and process loot. There are a number of elements that work together well here, from making simple shops, trading with your merchants, farming crops, crafting and just decoration. From your new town, the game allows you to decide if you want to gear up by hunting monsters and selling/buying loot from merchants or by gathering raw mats and crafting it yourself. Both crafting and fighting generate exp to level and improve your load out.
If you're not into it for the creativity or town building the game does offer traditional dungeon crawling. You begin by building stairs down which generates a whole new underground map each level you explore and there’s nothing apparent limiting how many levels down you want to go at any time up to the cap of 90. You do this again and again, every staircase down increases the difficulty and generating a whole new area with better loot and material. Though each level is different they aren't very unique, you'll quickly find that if you've seen one level you've seen them all and it slowly becomes frustrating as each staircase adds one more load screen. Although its a quick load, the number of staircases add up and it gets frustrating until you can get warp stones, after which it's not so bad. Once you get there, if there are any surprises, boss fights, secrete treasures or other gems I've not found or heard of them, its simply another layer and load screen. When you start to level up from the grind you'll have the option of the three traditional classes, melee guy, range guy, or magic guy with a sprinkling of an all encompassing utility option. At first glance it doesn't seem like you'll want to mix builds as each 'class' lines up with one stat and one ability tree making cross classing a likely waste of potential.
The interface is one of the weaker points. It will take time to learn as it's not immediately intuitive and can be frustrating as you adjust to a lack of WASD for movement and a combat/build mode toggle. The game relies strongly on the mouse for most things, the keyboard seeming to be more an after thought, the only keys used besides hotbar is shift which simply holds you in place for ranged attacks. You'll need to slowly figure out how to navigate around obstacle with the mouse as your character sometimes isn't sure if he's walking, using a workbench, or punching something. Once you figure out how to navigate around bushes and bodies it all starts to flow.
Overall I do recommend this game because you're getting a 10$ game, not a 2$ + 'IOU for 8$ worth of content to come' game. It's a collection of a lot of safe ideas mixed together rather well. A very appealing art style, functional mechanics, and 'passable' UI.
If I had any strong suggestions for the game it would be to dress up dungeon crawling a little. Limit my ability to easily move between Z levels, make it feel like an achievement to progress further down and not just another loading screen. Hide stuff in the dungeons, collectables, secrete rooms, rare monsters, most of all you can hide cool stuff I want to put in my town to show off. Make me wonder what's lurking in the darkness, remove my ability to see whats there with better fog of war. Currently its to easy to see dungeons or to see ores by scanning the darkness with my mouse, make it scary and not just risk management to explore.

It is a fun sim game, and it is worth the $10.  However, it suffers from serious balance issues.  Once my mage got the "fireball" spell at lvl 10, I was easily able to solo monster camps.  Four monsters spawn, and they all die from the fireball.  This gives about half a level of exp, which rocketed me to lvl 40 very quickly.  Monsters scale to your level and so does their loot.  They were dropping copper gear (tier 2) at 10, but were quickly dropping the best gear in the game (tier 6, I believe) at 40.  I didn't need to mine or grind or craft any more.  There are 90 levels that you can dig down to, but I never needed to dig down more than 8.
TL;DR
It is a fun crafter/sim game, but the balance is severely broken.  If you want to take your time with the game, then don't kill mobs outside.  Kill the mobs underground because they scale to level depth and not your level, but everything up top scales to your level and is too easy to kill with magic, which powerlevels you way beyond what you should be.

At launch I would have given this game a 6/10. I played a lot that first week and enjoyed it, but it was unpolished. There were many bugs and performance issues. I stopped playing after 27 hours knowing that I'd come back to it after it was patched up a bit.
The story and game world made such an impression on me that I just started thinking of it again, out of the blue. I checked the store page today and as chance would have it, happens to be the same day the first paid DLC, "Faster, Baby!" launched. Intrigued by this I did a little research to see if the expansion might be worth it. After seeing the work the devs have put into the game since launch (bug fixes, new weapons, new outfits, car customizations, racing, etc.) I decided to get the Season Pass. The expansions look really promising and seem to have a lot of value. So I'm diving back in and will be updating this review based on what's new since I played last year. If all goes as I expect it should with this year's updates, Mafia III will jump from a 6 to an easy 7.5/10...maybe even higher.
Even with it's rough edges and lack of certain content at launch I think it's always been underrated. The reviews of Mafia III remind me of Mad Max. The way many people talk you'd think these games are utter garbage not even worthy of a 1/10 rating (some even go so far as to use those exact words). That's going way too far the other direction...as I said in my opening sentence, this game started off worthy of a solid 6/10, which is slightly above average. Even at it's worst, it's never been a bad game. Can it get repetative? Sure...as do most games. Mad Max got that reputation, but there were several distinct things to do, just like in Mafia III. Tired of the story missions? Go collect some Playboys...that's always fun! Or go cause some mayhem and out-run the cops, which is one of GTA's (for example) main selling points. There are several types of missions though...it's not as repetative as some people say. And then if you're truly bored...FIRE UP ANOTHER GAME FOR GOD'S SAKE!! It's not like you only have one game installed on your PC at a time, so go play something else for a while! Then guess what...when you come back to Mafia III, it's enjoyable for another few hours. Wash, rinse, repeat!

Alan Wake was mediocre.
Edit: Gonna flesh out this review, because I think it'd help if I was more descriptive.
Alan Wake is a fully functional horror game, that is creepy for about the first 5 hours of Stephen King aping. At a certain point, however, large portions of the gameplay become Alan battling hostile inanimate objects. This isn't scary at all. Speaking critically, Stephen King's "Inanimate Objects Turn Evil" plots have never adapted well to visual media. Be it games or movies, the second a Stephen King project starts throwing around satanic cars and phones, it wades too far into comedy and slapstick to elicit horror.
I'd still like this game if it actually went in a comedy/slapstick direction with this kind of thing, kinda like Deadly Premonition, which is a great game. It doesn't though, and the inanimate object haunting is played entirely straight and ruins the mood of a game that was really good up to that point.
This is a 5/5 AAA game budget and quality wise, but as an actual gameplay experience, it's a 2/5.
P.S.
I've heard whisperings that the game was originally supposed to be a lot less linear, which would have also helped.

I was originally a little harsher on this game before I did some digging into the game itself. I now find it quite inspiring. Minimized was developed using the "Raycaster game engine". Which is a freeware raycasting engine you can find on ModDb(and probably a few other places) IT is a very primitive game engine, but it gets the job done none the less.
The fact that  Minimized got this far is more than deserving of a digital high five. IT could have just as easily never gone beyond some ModDB page that 99% of the internet could not have given half a♥♥♥♥♥♥about but here it is on Steam taking money from me that could have been spent on my kids future college tuition.
now on to the brass tacks.
PROS:
Great visual concept(if not the most flawless execution)
Great soundtrack that meshs perfectly with the theme.
Level design is non-linear but not a frustrating labyrinth.
CONS:
Sometimes you can overlook entire rooms because of the way the visuals bleed together.
Other than that most faults are more the simplicity of the engine and beyond the fault of the devleper.
-All weapons share the same ammo pool
-there does not seem to be a way to have a melee based enemy
-No AOE weapon attacks or enviromental damage.
I do hope whoever is makign the raycaster game engine eventually adds in this kind of stuff and the developer Minimized patchs some cool♥♥♥♥♥♥into the game.
Old school fans are the sort not to take to much notice of things that don't feed directly into the gameplay or visual aesthetic and Minimized is a compelling bare bones example of that mindset.
Buy it.

Well, this was disappointing... So, I don't play ALL the games out there, and maybe I don't play all that many games period, but this is the worst writing I've ever seen in a video game. Seriously, it's incredibly bad. Especially, since the entire game is a character-based drama with long stretches where characters just talk to each other.
The weird part is that the underlying story and characters are actually quite alright, might even have been really cool, but the dialogue within the game ruins it all completely. Everything is explained to you in excruciating detail as if you are too stupid to understand what's going on. It breaks characters, it breaks tension of individual scenes and it ruins the overall flow of the story. Imagine a selfish and bratty teenager, suddenly turning to you and explaining how selfish and bratty they are, as well as all the problems in their life that made them the way they are, only to turn around and go back to being selfish and bratty in the next scene. Or having a character on the verge of a break down suddenly start reminding  you out loud of every minute detail of your previous interactions to "subtly" demonstrate how your previous choices are affecting the current situation. (That "subtly" deserves a lot more quotation marks around it.) Oh yeah, and don't even try to forget those minute details – they would be spelled out to you at least a dozen times over, just in case you somehow missed how your actions affect people.
This happens in the game all the time. Sorry. I haven't stressed it enough. This happens in the game ALL THE TIME!!! The game doesn't trust you to make a single most obvious conclusion by yourself, and instead insists on spelling out every last detail. And the worst part – there are so many other opportunities to deliver that same information to the player, if you think they cannot possibly comprehend the amazing complexity of your story. The main character has a diary with an ungodly amount of text in it. The voice over narrates everything you see and explains all the key choices to you. There is absolutely no need to also have characters within the game "coincidentally" point out the game's mechanics to you.
Personally, I found this writing incredibly annoying, to the point where it sucked out all the enjoyment of the game for me. (Really, all I did was yell 'SHUT UP!!!' during every key dialogue in the second half of the story and I still couldn't miss any important details, since everything is made so obvious and repeated to you several times.)

I played a hell of a alot of Lego Marvel Super Heroes which was extremely fun and not too challenging. This game is pretty much what you'd expect from a "sequal" of sorts. It still has the story missions, freeplay, collectibles, lots of characters and plenty to do. The only major addition I can recongise this time over is a bit more polish and some really nice animations for combat.
This time the story follows the Avengers as they go through multiple film scenarios such as Avengers, Avengers: Age of Ultron, Captain America: The First Avenger, Iron Man 3, Thor: Dark World and Captain America: Winter Soldier.
They have added voice clips from the movies which at first is a nice touch, but then you realise how chopped and changed the dialogue is and how bad quality and quiet the clips are. Personally it is starting to annoy me but a decent idea I guess; there are also some good and original Lego moments and humor.
If you are a Marvel fan, buy it.
If you are a Lego video game fan, buy it.
If you are on the fence, wait for a good old Lego Steam sale.
Graphics: 8/10 - Usual lego graphics, crisp on higher resolutions but suffer on lower. Regular clipping issues.
Audio - 5/10 - Usual soundtrack mostly taken from Lego Super Heroes. Horrible movie audio clip quality.
Controls 8/10 - Use a gamepad if you can, works perfectly. I still find the flight mechanics unrefined personally.
Story 10/10 - If you like the Marvel films or would like a quick run through of some MCU events it is perfect.
Overall: 8/10 - Highly Recommended!
TLDR; Same as Lego Marvel Super Heroes. MCU story. Bad movie audio clips. Good Lego video game and Marvel fun!

Full review:
This is a review of ACT 1 of Broken Age, act 2 is currently unreleased.
Broken Age - Act 1, an excellent point-and-click adventure. This is coming from someone who usually avoids the genre. I don't know how, but Double Fine somehow kept me entertained whilst playing their latest adventure. I despise point-and-click games, but this, this was a treat.
Broken Age's existence is entirely due to the success of Double Fine's "Double Fine Adventure" Kickstarter, which in my opinion, is the reason why Kickstarter is so popular today. The game's credits list all of the backers, all of them. It took quite some time for all of those credits to roll.
The game employs a colorful, stylized world, all in 2D. The art is fantastic, retaining that signature Double Fine feel to it. The music was also great, combining well with the game's overall style.
The game's story however, is what I enjoyed most. The story is what probably kept me playing. Normally, I wouldn't even play a point-and-click game, and if I did, then I'd quit it within say.. 30 minutes? With Broken Age however, I never felt bored and the puzzles didn't keep me stumped as long as I would have expected from a game in the genre. Actually, I would have preferred the puzzles to be a bit harder. Most of them were rather straight-forward and easily solved. I may have gotten stumped once or twice, but I felt like they could have been a lot more challenging while retaining my attention.
The story is broken into two parts: Shay's and Vella's adventures. Two entirely different characters that the player can switch to and from at any given moment. I found myself going through with Shay's quest first, rather than Vella's. I enjoyed Shay's story more than Vella's, but I played through the whole game wanting to know if the stories connected somehow, possibly one of the reasons why I found this game so enjoyable. The constant desire to see how the stories connect, or if they do at all.
Voice acting in the game is incredible, well, aside from one character. It felt like Vella's voice was... off. It just sounded out of place. That may just be me, but it constantly bugged me throughout her journey. All of the other voice acting is simply amazing, no complaints there.
All good things said, Broken Age does not bring anything new to the table. This may be disappointing for some, but I certainly overlooked this fault purely out of interest for the game's story. Although I may dislike point-and-click games, I've played quite a few of them in my time, and Broken Age doesn't seem to differ from them, aside from the art style. Broken Age was actually much easier than a few of the point-and-click game's I've played, because, as I said, the puzzles are rather straight-forward.
There are many reasons for me to recommend Broken Age. I urge you to try it out for yourself. I certainly can't wait for the next act in the series.

while i only payed a dollar for the game and got more then what i payed for i have to say the reviews of improvements of this game are greatly exaggerated. the hit boxes of the dinosaurs are something even red 5 would laugh at. first off i bought the LMG assuming it was a large machine gun... apparently LMG = burst rifle..... thats a simple error to fix in 30 sec.. you dont have an LMG you have a burst rifle.  bow was fun but kind of impractical. (however bow weapons tend to be heavily connection dependent to be practical). using the mouse to steer the vehicles when most controls for tanks rely heavily on the wasd keys and using the mouse for turret control was aggravating (but tolerable... tom clancy games have button mapping that was worse) .
settings are set to all optional parts enabled (motion blur, bloom, etc) and high settings. disabling most of the optional settings makes the game playable but connectivty issues and wonky hitboxes are never good for a game no matter how pretty.
the hats.... just.... just no.... i mean if the hat replaced the helmet instead of being on top of it maybe .... other wise... no. even tf2 knows better then to allow clipping of cosmetic items.
however.... this game isnt something from the bowls of hell.... its kind of a fun idea though i was never into being a sci fi dinosaur killer and this game has raised a slight interest.  I also have to give props to the developer still putting the time and effort to at least try to make the game better. something we dont see enough of these days in an age where companies like hi rez and activision make a game cash the paycheck for a year then abandon it for a new project in a different genre.
In fact id love to see this game on a new engine with  updated charcter models.... and working hit boxes -_-....and a more intuitive UI.
people are arguing its worthy of an 83 or an 80 on the meta critic score... after my expereince that is not the case. the game has definitely made steps forward from the 30 it originally received but not worthy of a 82. this game  id have to say a 63 would be a much more accurate score of the game. its no triple A title and with a setting such as sci fi soldiers  killing dinosaurs i already had low expectations... which surprised me in good ways and bad as well. there are large areas for improvement just to make the game a 75 worthy score and even an hour of gameplay is enough to see that. it was fun for a dollar and i hope it gets put into their next project. these guys have a nice idea.... just need to do a bit better job of executing it.
if ya got a spare buck give it a shot for a couple hours have a little derpy fun.... and never speak of it again.

I've played two Vlambeer games now -the other one being Super Crate Box- and I've noticed a common theme: insertion of the mainstays of an old-school FPS (lots of guns, lots of enemies, cathartic gameplay, basically whatever Serious Sam does) into other, older genres to see what happens. With Super Crate Box, the genre in question is an 8-bit platformer, along the lines of the original Donkey Kong. In Nuclear Throne, it's a top-down bullet hell shooter (with RPG elements), which is a wonderful choice for combination with an old-school FPS. However, doing so means that the game has to take away the FPS ability to tank absurd amounts of damage, which is where the roguelite elements come in.
Nuclear Throne's main issue for me is that, upon death, no matter how far you are, you're sent all the way back to the start. I'd expect nothing less from a roguelite ('roguelite' for me meaning it has randomization and permadeath), and this wouldn't be a problem but for the fact that the first levels will soon become VERY familiar, because they only vary so much, and contain the least interesting weapons and enemies. I can see why the decision was made; if you could save, you could finish the game in about 20 minutes, and being a roguelite means that the devs don't have to balance the massive amount of weapons and enemies, both of which are spawned randomly and vary widely in terms of power. Still, managing to kill Li'l Hunter (the game's other issue) and then being blown up by a random car because you weren't being careful with your explosives, only to be sent ALL the way back to the start, can be...disheartening, to say the least.
That's essentially my only problem with the game, though, and judging by the fact that I've put 206 hours into it at time of writing, it doesn't stop me from playing. I love Nuclear Throne. I love its adrenaline-soaked gameplay, I love its crushing difficulty, I love its increasingly bizarre arsenal, I love its variety, and I could talk about it for hours.
I won't here, though, because these reviews are disjointed and rambling enough already. Suffice it to say that I like to play Robot, my favorite mutation is Gamma Guts, and my favorite weapons are the Eraser and the Seeker Shotgun.
Anyway, yes. I love Nuclear Throne, and I recommend it to everyone. It's my favorite roguelite of all time. Sorry, FTL. To quote Saints Row 2, you lost to the best.

Oh boy where do I start with this game?
Let me tell you, this game is HARDCORE. You know Dark Souls? You play Dark Souls to relax after playing Nuclear Throne, that's how hardcore it is.
You start out playing Nuclear Throne and you're like "yeah, whatever, some shooter or somethin', I guess this is a little fun". But then you die. Over and over again you die, and start getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at how bad you are at this, and force yourself to get better. As you progress, you start noticing that this little harmless shooter was not as shallow as it first seemed. It it DEEP, it has SO MANY THINGS in it. Guns, enemies, maps, bosses, secret little things to do and unlock that make you go into a secret-seeking frenzy. You think you're done when, after countless hours, you beat the final boss? Psh, you haven't seen ANYTHING yet. This is the kind of game that you have to experience for yourself, so I'm not going to spoil anything. I only recommend that you try playing this along with friends if you're not into searching for secrets on the internet, they might find something you overlooked and vice-versa. Now, for the Pros and Cons section of this review:
This game is absolute must-play. If, after giving it a real and long try, you end up not liking it, so be it. Chances are, though, if you're a fan of roguelikes, shooters or just FUN GAMES, you'll most likely love this one. Its price may seem a little too high for someone who hasn't played it yet, as it would with any other indie shooter, but the level of detail and content in this game way surpasses that price-point. Not to mention the countless hours you'll spend playing (and dying on) this game. Buy it, try it and, hopefully, love it.

Minimized is an interesting idea that is good for the most part. It has good controls and gameplay, but thats about it. The only thing you do is go from level to level shooting enemies until you happen to find the level exit, all the while just picking up colored shapes that are just sort of there. It's not bad, just repetitive. It feels like the developers put in filler levels to make up for it's rather large price tag for a game of this kind. Plus, since all weapons ahre the same ammo type, it is really easy to run out and be stuck with the wimpy laser-hand melee thing.
It's good, but tedious and feels like filler. This would be a good Gamejolt game in the state it is, but not much else. Here are a few reccomendations:
1. have each weapon use a different ammo type. you would think that having all weapons shoot the same ammo would be easier, but you burn through your ammo so fast it hardly matters. Having seperate ammo for each weapon would allow the player to moderate their usage, and leave them with enough ammo to take out the harder enemies.
2. PLEASE, GET RID OF THE BULLET SPONGES. Some of the bigger enemies in this game take an arseload of ammo to knock down just ONE of them. And in the later levels you are often boxed into small spaces with these enemies. And if they trap you in a door? RIP. You can't open the door to run away (idk why, maybe a glitch. you just can't) and since the enemies do tha old Wolfenstein trick of shooting through each other to melt you. If you haven't saved, THIS COULD SEND YOU BACK LITERALLY HOURS.
3. Maps. This game is, like Wolfenstein, a giant maze. you need to find these yellow keys that open a red door that sends you to the next level. But sometimes the keys and doors are spaced apart so far you lose track of where your going.
4. Make the Melee destroy props. this might not sound big, but it is. Some keys or paths to the exit are trapped behind destructable props in the world (exploding barrels, boxes, desks, pipes, etc.) and these props can be destroyed by shooting them. But you cannot destroy them by meleeing them with your laser hand. What does this mean? it means you have to always have at least some bullets on you to ensure that you can get these keys or doors. If you have no ammo and you come across one of these, guess what? you have to either find an ammo box or restart the level. Don't you love it when a game punishes you for not savingenough ammo to break a friggin cardboard box?
5. I really hope this isn't true, but the starting menu say you have to collect 500,000 POWER CELLS TO WIN. 500 FREAKIN THOUSAND. I don't know if this is a typo but if it isn't, DEVS. NO ONE IS GOING TO PLAY LONG ENOUGH TO GET THAT MANY POWER CELLS. NO ONE. How about, like, 500 power cells? 1000? even 10,000 is still ok! but 500,000 is WAY TOO MUCH.
In the end, Minimized has potential, but in its current state its mor eof a chore to play rather than a game. if the above changes are made, then yes, this is a game worth playing.

What a odd little duck this is.  First and foremost, I enjoyed it.  Am enjoying it, rather -- I've every intention of continuing to play it further.  While simplistic at first, don't mistake the game's unwavering dedication to absolute minimalism as a cover for a lack of talent on the devs' part.  This is a well-realized idea and a game that harkens back to some of the most noteworthy titles in PC gaming history.
Initially, I was extremely disoriented.  It took me a bit of playtime to learn to understand the visual language of the game, and there's nothing so crass and modern as an automap or mini-map function to help you along.  By the time you complete the first level, though, you've become engrossed in the design language of the world, your eye able to use the negative space and blackness to see what isn't being explicitly drawn.  It actually started to remind me a bit of the Virtual Boy -- the ill-fated, monochromatic Nintendo console from the late 1990s.  Both are similar in that they try to do so much with so little -- though, in Minimized's case, these limitations are self-imposed.  It works, though.  Once you get into it, you start to notice how the world is set up, how the objects in the game use simple colors to differentiate them at a glance.
In terms of gameplay, Minimized feels like a polished-up Wolfenstein 3D mixed with more than a pinch of Blake Stone and seasoned with Rise of the Triad, all mixed through a ZX Spectrum monitor -- a comparison I suspect the developers were deliberately aiming for.  Maps are composed of blocks and squares, arranged on a grid of four cardinal directions, doors open by sliding sideways, and treasure (in the form of "energy" needed to complete the game) is scattered about on floors alongside power-ups such as health and ammunition.  Enemies range from simple spheres which slowly drain your health at close range to soldier-robots which attack you from afar with energy weapons.  Circle-strafe and lead your target -- this is a dance you should be familiar with by this point.  Still, there's something refreshing about having only two dimensions to worry about.  There's no sniper ledges, no QTEs, no stun-the-boss-and-hit-his-weak-point-three-times rope-a-dopes.  There's just you, your gun, and the bad guys.
The sound design is excellent, especially the soundtrack, and for the paltry extra price, I recommend downloading the music for your own listening pleasure as well.  Chiptunes augmented with digital samples or real instruments are the order of the day here, mostly sounding like they could've been mixed with an original NES sound chip.  There's some interesting instrumentation, though, and you'll hear a handful of old tricks that sound pros used to use to get around limited channels -- fast-trill arpeggios to simulate chords, for example.  It has a very European PC feel, channeling the best of the MSX and ZX Spectrum era, but with some modern touches mixed in.  The sound effects in the game are mostly period-appropriate bloops and blips, but they work and work well.  Anything more "realistic" or "high-fidelity" would clash with the aesthetic of the game.
If I have to level criticisms against Minimized, well, it's hard to do so without running up against the walls the devs have deliberately erected for themselves.  For instance, as a player, my first instinct is to ask, "Why no map in-game?"  And yet, after having played for a few more levels, I'm brought back to that feeling of originally playing Wolfenstein 3D or Eye of the Beholder as a young'un.  We didn't have maps back then, no; if you wanted such a luxury, you got out the graph paper and did it yourself.  I find dusty, unused corridors of my brain lighting up again, for the first time in a very long time.  Remember this room -- it connects to the other one, which goes to the hall, which leads to the red door.
The only thing that I feel needs addressing has to do with the trappings surrounding the game.  For instance, the Settings menu needs some work -- on my copy, the "Graphics" slider instead controls the music volume, and the Music slider seems to do nothing.  The translation and text could also use a once-over from a native English speaker -- although, having played my share of poorly-translated NES games, I would also be willing to chalk this up as a stylistic quirk.  Certainly it doesn't harm your enjoyment of the game.  Everything else that's core to the experience -- running and gunning against waves of enemies while collecting treasure and power-ups -- is tightly executed and feels well-made.
So bravo to Minimized, I say, and bravo to the tiny team that brought it into the world.  I wish you all the success in this and future projects.  Now, I'm going to go back to navigating neon corridors...

Animations are janky, player textures frequently disappear mid-match (leaving behind their primary-colored models), hitboxes are off (why is a shot to the crest of the neck of a raptor considered a headshot, but shooting them in the head isn't?), levels are uninspiring copy-paste affairs (how many times am I going to see the same wrecked drill in a level?) with incredibly linear objective design (Base 2 is always the same spot, as is base 3, etc).  Capturing the bases in Survival mode itself does nothing but progress the game to the next wave of dinosaurs, as even the vehicles spawn at the start of the match - you could have a buddy run to Base 3 for the Mech while you turn on the generator to start Wave One!
That's not to say the game is /bad/.  Are there performance issues?  Yes.  Is the attention to detail lacking?  Absolutely.  Is it incredibly linear to the point of boredom after a while?  You betcha.  But until you really start to notice those things (about thirty minutes in, for me), the game is still fun in a mindless sort of way, especially with friends.  That said though, for $15, I expect a lot more for my money than copy-pasted levels and textures, braindead AI, movement animations from the original Tribes (in terms of "skating" over terrain), and a linear level experience.
For the $1 I paid for it, it feels like a discounted iPad app.  Shame that when it's off sale, the developers are still asking for $15 for this thing.  I'd like to see a lot more polish (and better netcode) before plunking down that much cash, especially when you're competing against similarly priced titles like Killing Floor, Starbound, etc, that are way better experiences overall.

Dennaton Games released this little indie gem in 2012. Hyper-violence through pixel art, this game puts players in the role of a nameless anti-hero who receives strange phone calls directing him to commit unspeakable acts of graphic violence. Set in 1989 Miami, the techno soundtrack thumps away in a monotonous throbbing pulse as a perfect soundtrack to the extreme violence and chaos. The colours are all hypnotic 80's vibrant fluro reds, pinks and greens and fit with the time period perfectly. There's a real sense of uneasiness about this game as you converse with faceless people in pig and horse masks, asking you questions like, "Do you enjoy hurting people?". The games difficultly harkens back to the old days of brutally hard Sega and Nes titles where one hit means you're dead, that's it, start the level again. There's an achievement for dying 1,000 times, I hit it at just over 5 hours (mind you I also hit the achievement around the same time for killing 1989 enemies so it's balanced out). The graphics are delightfully retro pixel art that beautifully complements the disturbing nature of the games themes. Proof that you don't need big budgets and high end processing power to deliver a truly enjoyable and thought provoking gaming experience.

When I played the beta of this game in 2013, I was not impressed. I was frustrated with the UI, the art direction, the scripting, and the way combat was weighed. I played the original in the late 1980s, and loved the surreal and unforgiving world it created.
I came back, this month, hoping that the issues I'd complained about had been fixed. I genuinely love this series and was pessimistic about its survival. I owe the devs an apology--the beta I've played this month has been everything I could have wanted (though I could always use more toasters and mutants, if anyone is listening).
I can recommend this game to fans of the first game, as well as fans of dystopian and apocalyptic games. However, it is distinct from other entries in this genre, including the often-cited Fallout series.
Closer to the roots of such games than the more recent entries in the apolcalyptic genre, Wasteland 2 is tactical and played from above your party's head. You can pause between turns, and sometimes you'd better think about it first.
It also has the charm of being more appropriately unforgiving--it's the !@#(*% apocalypse, the stakes are high, and I APPROVE of punishing button mashing and careless playing.
Know your save file, love your save file. The game saves less often than you might want it to, so you'll want to stay on that yourself.
Your characters will have to specialize, and no single character will be able to be everything. You will want to think hard about how you want to allocate specialties.
It is very possible to make in-game mistakes that kill you and your party instantly, though you'd have to be pretty oblivious to make them. If the button says "do not push me," do no--actually, if you push it, you deserve what you get.
The wrong comment to the wrong person can touch off wars between groups, closing whole story sections to you. The appropriate choice in dialog is not always obvious, and the best choice is not always available to you, without specializing.
Depending on your level of difficulty, making use of the ability to create ambushes and lead people into them will become very useful, as is developing a character able to scout ahead.
The game is still being developed, and has some on-going and minor technical issues, including an optimization problem I ran into on my rig that required me to turn down the refresh rate and render quality considerably. From reading the forums, this problem is not exactly common, but happens often enough to merit mention.
The half of the game available for play right now also seems a bit short--I'm hoping that the final product will be much longer (gimmie!)
It's hard to evaluate a story when you're missing the denouemont, but to this point, it has a familiar and interesting arc. Given the development, I'm fairly confident the finished product, based on the skill I've seen, will have been worth backing the project.
A word of advice: do not buy this game expecting Fallout: New Vegas, or expecting a completely open, huge world filled with 1950s kitsch, naivete, and classic sci-fi allusions.
Expect, instead, a world hemmed in on all sides by radiation and death, with the disaffection, paramiliatry themes, and violence of the 1980s. The devs have done a particularly good job of recalling the first game without simply recreating it.
And devs, at the risk of spoiling something, the Brothers patrolling the mountain pass are just about perfect. If there's any fear close to our current, collective hearts, it's contamination.
Don't believe their lies. It's a third-rate Unreal Tournament 3 mod, with tons of jank and like, one looping music track. It's worth 99c, but not a penny more.

SCORE: 9/10
First off, the game is an improvement in every way from Shadow of Mordor - better combat, more varied environments, better graphics, better world building, better use of your followers, and no QTEs. It is a derivative game - combining the parkour of Assassin's Creed, the towers of Far Cry and Assassin's Creed, with the melee combat of Batman and the bow combat of Tomb Raider or Horizon Zero Dawn, There are times with investigations - similar to The Witcher 3 and Batman. It combines all these aspects into the lore and world of Tolkien. It isn't canon by any means, but it is an enjoyable story and only the most die-hard fans would have a problem with it. My favorite book and movie ever is The Lord of the Rings, and I'm fine with the liberties this game takes.
As for the microtransactions and loot boxes that people have complained about, it is far overblown. You absolutely do not need a single thing, and I have seen multiple gaming publications repeat that same things. When I read Metacritic and some forums, I would swear that the people complaining have never actually played the game. That said, I wish they weren't there because I don't like them in general and don't like where the games industry is headed with them.
The game is super fun, looks to have 40-60 hours of extended gameplay for just one play-through, and offers ultrawidescreen gaming that performs very well at 3440x1440p on ultra everything with a 1080ti.

Broken Age Act 1 is a beautiful adventure game where you follow two different people in storylines that feel quite different to each other. It's got an art style that feels quite unique, the voice acting is on the level of Shiny's Sacrifice - in other words high profile names doing their best quality voice acting giving their personas a very distinct character. The story is really well written and funny, and the world adds to that - there are also lots of hilarious things about both the environments and small side things happening.
Shay's story is like a teenager stuck in a spaceship where the computer treats him like he was still three years old, and the environments are full of props to that effect. Also, lots of things seems to be vowen, knitted of crocheted, like the yarn buddies, the arms of the computer, the warping effect when travelling in space, the present, the weaver etc. It's also quite heavily lampshaded. The story does a good work of giving the feeling that you as a character are bored and need to find a way to get out of the grudge while still not boring you as the player. It also gives you a great feeling of wanting to be doing something to help others.
Vella's story is the tale of a girl who is chosen as sacrifice to a monster to save the village, but who instead wants to fight the monster. The setting is such that nobody except her grandfather sees anything wrong with the sacrifice, instead seeing being sacrificed being a great honour, but you can see in it moments of despair about losing daughters or those daughters dying while still being an honourable sacrifice. The setting is more a renaissance faire with some fantastic elements to it, and a good lot of humourous dialogue.
What is the game missing? Well, in the LucasArts games of old, you generally had tasks like Monkey Island's sword fighting puzzle, where you first had to do an item quest, then you had to do a collection of lines, to eventually beat the Sword Master. It felt like you were actually achieving something by solving it. There were also moments in the game where you got stuck for a while and had to search for a solution, trying to figure the puzzle out. In here, the solutions are always really close by the problem, and there is no procedure to figure out you need to go through to solve it. There was not a single puzzle that made me stop and actually think about how to solve it, everything was obvious from the outset. The good thing about it though is that there is no pixel hunting, no missing items far away and having to backtrack, no banging your head on the table in frustration of not being able to get past a point and eventually dropping the game in frustration.
Despite those faults, the first act is storywise about as great as any point'n'click game has ever been, in looks, dialogue, humour and music it's spot on. The game throws a few screwballs at you, and I feel that depending on your game play order you will get a very different experience. If you play Shay's story first then Vella's story, you will suddenly get a shocking reveal that casts your actions in Shay's story in a very different light. If you play Vella's story first you will at the end of Shay's story get a different screwball where you at the end suddenly realise that an assumption you will probably make in her story's later part was dead on wrong, but not the shock of the reveal about your actions as Shay. If you switch characters at natural boundaries, and this is probably best done with playing Shay first, then switching when quest giver changes to Marek, and for Vella changing between Sugar Bunting and Merriloft, then Shay for the linear quests given by Marek, then Vella changing after escaping Merriloft, then play Shay to the end, then finally Vella to the end. The big picture of the story will be revealed way earlier, but it will not have any great reveals. It ends with a great cliffhanger that makes you really anticipate the second act.
If you wonder about the inspirations for the story, Tim Schafer has pointed to 1948 story The Lottery by Shirley Jackson, with a spoiler warning if you read it.
Over all, it's a very good and humorous story experience, if you're a lore fan you will probably really get into the game, but if you're looking for hard thinking nuts to consider, the puzzles of the first act will not give you full satisfaction, but I think you will have a hard time finding somebody that played the first act that is not eagerly anticipating the second act.
A warning though: Don't view any let's plays of this game, or you will spoil it utterly.

Sadly, this is a rather mediocre hidden object game that was developed by "SpinTop" rather than PopCap (who only published it) - wish I'd noticed that before purchasing as PopCap themselves make excellent games.
There is a simple story-framing piece of text at the start, then it's the same New York-themed screens (with like 10 objects to find in each) over and over and over, with each grouping of 2-8 (of the 25) screens separated by simple match 3, word find, jigsaw or rotation puzzle, with no actual story (unlike, say, Pirateville from MumboJumbo, where you have story setups for every screen you play).  Got about 12 "clues" (levels, out of 25) in before giving up in boredom, so I don't know if they bothered with anything other than a simple text outro once you find the will...
In short, not worth the effort or the price - and *always* check to make sure PopCap's the developer as well as the publisher before buying. :/
EDIT: Oh, and worst of all, if you leave your mouse on an object while you're searching for others (to remind yourself where it is so you can get multiple in a row for a speed bonus), it will pop up a big panel, that you have to click away, once per scene telling you that you can use the hint button (no matter how many times you may have used that button in the past).  So incredibly annoying.

Lego Marvel Avengers is the second Lego Marvel game in the series, developed by TT Games and published by Warner Brothers, releasing on PS4, PS3, PS Vita, 3DS, Wii U, Xbox One, Xbox 360 and of course, Steam in January 2016.
As with all Lego games, you are going to get stellar gameplay. Run around whacking enemies using your super heroes special power, be it Hulk’s strength or Captain America’s shield, you will get to play as your favourite heroes in style here. I am about three levels into the game thus far and have had a good range of different puzzles and action to take part in. Your inner Lego builder will absolutely love smashing all of the scenery and objects to get that magic 100% brick mark on every level too.
I am playing the game on 4k and the game looks exactly the same as the rest of the series. You can drop it down to lower resolutions but you will lose the crispness of the models and textures. As with the rest of the series, all of the animations are absolutely flawless. Unlike the previous Marvel game in the series, Marven Avengers uses original voice acting that is pulled straight from the six films this game is based off. There are also a couple of lines from a few characters that have been specially recorded just for the purpose of this game.
The story of the game is based off The Avengers, Avengers Age of Ultron, Captain America, Iron Man 3, Thor: Dark World and Captain America: The Winter Soldier. Meaning you are going to get an absolutely stunning plot. I am like a little kid again following this story as I haven’t seen a few of the films; I am looking forward to seeing how it all plays out.
Don’t expect to get a massive challenge in this game, dying doesn’t really come with any penalty, and the puzzles can normally be figured out pretty quickly. That doesn’t take away any of the fun though, you will find yourself spending hours just running around in awe at the structures and objects in this game that are made out of Legos!  Level design is always the Lego games stronger points, with sooooo many collectibles, and hundreds of side missions to feast on.
There is also a lot of replay ability in this game, you will need to go back and replay levels if you want to unlock everything, as some parts of the stage will require a certain hero which you may not have unlocked yet. This is one of my favourite things to do once I finish the main story as you get to replay old content while still being rewarded.
As said above, I am running on 4k with the texture quality set to high and I am getting a silky smooth 60 fps. I have suffered from one freeze in game play that lasted about five seconds, not sure what will have caused this so I am going to assume it is a one off. The game plays perfectly with a game pad and I would recommend you do to. The ease of a second player dropping in and out of gameplay is again a major strong point making couch co-op relevant.
Even though I am only about an hour and a half into this game, I can easily highly recommend Lego: Marvel Avengers as a brilliant game. I love the Lego series, and this game is going to probably be one of its most popular releases. The game’s retail price on Steam is £24,99, I would say that is a fair price, but you can find it a lot cheaper elsewhere and Lego games do go on sale fairly regularly, so you may want to bear that in mind.

Well, this was disappointing... So, I don't play ALL the games out there, and maybe I don't play all that many games period, but this is the worst writing I've ever seen in a video game. Seriously, it's incredibly bad. Especially, since the entire game is a character-based drama with long stretches where characters just talk to each other.
The weird part is that the underlying story and characters are actually quite alright, might even have been really cool, but the dialogue within the game ruins it all completely. Everything is explained to you in excruciating detail as if you are too stupid to understand what's going on. It breaks characters, it breaks tension of individual scenes and it ruins the overall flow of the story. Imagine a selfish and bratty teenager, suddenly turning to you and explaining how selfish and bratty they are, as well as all the problems in their life that made them the way they are, only to turn around and go back to being selfish and bratty in the next scene. Or having a character on the verge of a break down suddenly start reminding  you out loud of every minute detail of your previous interactions to "subtly" demonstrate how your previous choices are affecting the current situation. (That "subtly" deserves a lot more quotation marks around it.) Oh yeah, and don't even try to forget those minute details – they would be spelled out to you at least a dozen times over, just in case you somehow missed how your actions affect people.
This happens in the game all the time. Sorry. I haven't stressed it enough. This happens in the game ALL THE TIME!!! The game doesn't trust you to make a single most obvious conclusion by yourself, and instead insists on spelling out every last detail. And the worst part – there are so many other opportunities to deliver that same information to the player, if you think they cannot possibly comprehend the amazing complexity of your story. The main character has a diary with an ungodly amount of text in it. The voice over narrates everything you see and explains all the key choices to you. There is absolutely no need to also have characters within the game "coincidentally" point out the game's mechanics to you.
Personally, I found this writing incredibly annoying, to the point where it sucked out all the enjoyment of the game for me. (Really, all I did was yell 'SHUT UP!!!' during every key dialogue in the second half of the story and I still couldn't miss any important details, since everything is made so obvious and repeated to you several times.)

OK, this shows promise and as a fan of the first Wasteland I really like the walk down memory lane.
The first few hours of game play were,however, a bit frustrating to say the least.
***MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS***
So you get this mission to check out a radio tower. The problem is if you don't go there straight away and roam a little you trigger this new quest line of either going to Highwater or some agricultural station. Your 'boss' tells you that these calls have priority over you initial mission, so off you go!
Problem is, you automatically fail one of them. While you're exploring some hydro-plant which is about to fail you get this desperate radio calls from the other mission, how they're overrun but you can do nothing about it as the hydro-plant is about to explode. Moreover, prior to the power plant mission you get some side quests which ALL fail if you don't do them first. Basically, I saved the town's power plant from destruction but the grateful people of Highwater kicked me out of town because I did not kill the bandits first, found a dog and put out a fire for them. Consequently, the wrong person gets the votes to be the new mayor. He's all in with the bandits and tells me to get the hell out of town.
Basically, after six hours of game play I'm a total failure. Is this a feature? I don't know. Maybe this game is about priorities but the jumps in the quest system seem contrived and lack immersion this way. Non-linear is OK but if you simply say 'If you don't do missions A,B and C before D then they must have failed!' is a bit sloppy in terms of story-telling to me.
***END SPOILERS***
Apart from that you pretty much get a product as advertised: An isometric sequel to Wasteland 1. It is all there! The setting, the desolate arid lands, the radiation zones, the bandits and mutants and all those old-school turn-based combat fights. The skill system is almost pen&paper-like but does the trick. The item system is working as intended. I really like how easy you could set up hot buttons and point and click your way to skill checks and interactions.
I did have a hard time getting used to camera controls and setting up teams of party members but that might be my inexperience at work here.
Bottom line: As a fan of the original Wasteland, you will not want to miss this, but the game does confront you with certain constraints you might not consider acceptable in a modern open world setting.
But what do you get if you deduct the fandom? Not sure about that at this stage of development. I will restart the story with my utter and complete failure in mind and update my verdict.
As for now I think you get a better chunk of post-apocalyptic America for your bucks from Fallout 3/New Vegas games.
We'll see.......

Now, here's a tought. I like this game in concept, and if I'm not mistaken the engine is programmed ground up [Clarification: It's not, it's a ready engine called apparently "Raycasting Game Maker"], and all I can get behind. I also applaud the fact that the game is minimalistic as in there is nothing extra, and every once and a while, that is what I'm looking for.
However... Even as there is not too many controls, I weap for AZERTY keybard users, as the keys are hard coded and cannot be changed (not hard to program in, btw), and does not even have duplicates. In example, the 'open door' key is Space, which is normal for your Wolfensteins etc, when youre using arrow keys to move, but on my WASD+mouse, I prefer that key to be E. And that said, there is interestingly a way to turn with keyboard using the arrow keys like in the good old Apogee/ID '3D' games, but you can't move forwards and backwards using arrow keys. But well, that is an issue I can (witt a WASD keyboard) cope with. Little less with the fact that you can't adjust mouse sensitivity (again, not too hard to program in).
What I can't cope with is the forced resolution and apparently 15fps gaming, that causes nausea during gameplay especially if turning fast (this is a thing. This was a thing with Wolfenstein 3D also, but then it was due to real technical limitations). The resolution is something that unneccessarily obscures the game, when the enemies (that are presented by an outline) can't be seen as the pixels they are consisted with are deemed too small to render by the engine (and yes, there are levels where this is a serious issue). Now, in reality there is no reason for rendering the game in such a small resolution, since it's not too hard to stretch "bigger than" pixels without destroying the artstyle.
Oh, and just to note, this game has similar ammo pickup system as Digital Homicide's "Slaughtering Grounds", as the ammo is universal, but you will pick up ammo for the weapon that is in your hand. This is never disclosed in the game (or atleast not clearly), and is a game design choise I would never stand behind, as it results people first of all learning this hard way when trying to find ammo for the better weapon, and using the backup in the progress, AND it renders the backup useless as you will never get ammo for any other weapon than what you are currently using. It also needs to be noted that in Wolfenstein 3D the ammo plicy was that it was universal ammo, but plyer was motivated to use variety just in order to conserve ammo, or opting to sheer DPS depending on situation. In this game, you will have most ammo on the weapon you have in hand, and very likely no ammo on any other weapon.
TL;DR: The fps of the game causes nausea, and the options are lacking, if issues are fixed, the review will be revisited.

Hotline Miami is an 8-bit top down game where you play as an assassin that is systematically obliterating the Russian gangsters. This game doesn't hold any punches when it come to violence and gore. I guess the 8-bit style and the fact that most of the people that you're killing are criminals take away the sting of slaughtering them with anything you can find.
Story:
The story may seem a little lacking your first playthrough, but that only because you'll be distracted with the killing and dying every 5 seconds. The game revolve around an unnamed assassin (closest thing you get to a name is Jacket) receiving cryptic message on his answering machine from mysterious individuals. Each of these message always contain the address to Jacket next target. I don't want to spoil much, especially since I'm playing through the game again to get all the little details I missed. But just know you'll probably overlook some things going through your first time.
Gameplay:
When you arrive to a level you'll be face with numerous enemies armed with melee weapons (knives, baseball bats, golf clubs, etc) or guns (shotguns, assault rifles, etc). Initially you'll start off with your barehands each level (unless using a mask). You can pick up weapons and use them on enemies and discard them by throwing them at your enemies which will knock them down. Down enemies must be executed otherwise they will get back up. It should noted that you'll die after 1 hit (as do your enemies). So be prepared to restart a level over and over again after each death.
As you beat each level you'll unlock new weapons and masks. Each masks provide certain abilities or weapons, for example: The dog mask will keep dogs from attacking you, the tiger mask make your punches deadly, the wolf mask start you off with a knife, etc. These mask really encourage you to go back to play the level again to see if a mask could have made the level easier. Not to mention since you get more points for stringing your kills together and the style by which you kill your enemies will have you replaying level over and over again for a higher score.
There are 3 generic enemies type, lets call them: grunts, heavies, and dogs. The grunts are you're generic enemy you will see every level. Their weapons ranges from whatever they can get their hands on (from baseball bats to guns). Dogs are the same as grunts, their only difference is how quickly they can zip toward you to bite your throat out. Heavies unlike dogs and grunts, they don't go down from being melee to death. You gotta either shoot them otherwise they will bash your head in with their bare hands.
One thing all enemies have in common is a set patrol route or pattern of movement. When you first enter a stage enemies will be on a certain patrol route, when you start your attack their routes may disturb, but once they lose track of the player they will quickly return to their old pattern or just start patrolling the current room.  Now there are bosses to the game, but I don't want to spoil them and their fighting style are still similar to the enemies types I name off. The only difference is that they have unique patterns.
Whether by accident or purpose, it always pleasing when a game can have such a simple concept  (kill all enemies in the level) yet find ways to keep those elements engaging (such as new weapons or masks).
Final Comments:
While this game may seem like a reflex game, you gotta use strategy to learn the enemies routes and to decide which masks and weapons will give you the best advantage. I know I didn't touch on it but I gotta say the music fit extremely well with the atmosphere and all the colors you see throughout the game. For a top down 8-bit this game was really colorful and felt like you was on some type drug filled trip. While some may be put off by the violence of this game, I encourage them not to let that be the reason they past up this great 80s game.

This game is frustratingly difficult, occasionally hard to control and sometimes confusing. But you know what? I had a blast with it throughout it's entirety. For me (I got the game on sale for 2.50$) this game was worth every penny, and would've been worth it even if I got it full price. Hotline Miami is a top-down beat em' up with a great soundtrack set in Miami in the 80s. This game was super fun to play, I found myself getting frustrated as enemies rushed me from every direction to kill me, only to not be able to put the game down. I would go through every level probably at least 20 times before I beat it, but it is so rewarding when you finally do beat it. Enemies are smart, they patrol the area in groups, if they see you they will rush to the place you just were, they will shoot you through glass even you didn't see. They are very challenging but never unfair. Using weapons is a trade off, guns give you range, but attract many enemies to your area, melee weapons are completely silent, but you have to get close to an enemy to kill them. There are also many ways to complete a level given the masks and your own personal preference. These masks (you unlock them by beating missions) give you a different stat boost, such as starting with a knife, more ammo, more guns, faster running, etc. This makes the levels extremely replayable, as on one run you can run faster and rush people with a melee weapon, on another you can spam a machine gun because of the extra ammo. This gives this short adventure many more hours than originally, and I'm sure coming back to play this game in the future would be amazing. I have to also commend the art-style and the music. Good god, both of these are SUPERB, as many indie games these days tend to be. The art-style lends itself a nice cartoonish style that is simple and easy on the eyes, yet still gets everything done, and done well. The music is also extremely great and fits the style of this game very well. I recommend purchasing or downloading this soundtrack because it it so dang nice. It fits this game as well as the FTL soundtrack fits that game. The control aspect is done alright, but it was a little weird to get use to. Locking on is almost essential for guns, but it is extremely tough to lock on to an enemy that is rushing you, which can lead to some annoying deaths. I'm not sure what could be done about this though, so I guess it was done the best it could've been. Last thing, the story is also very nice, confusing and inviting questions like the Five Nights at Freddy's, but with interesting characters and characters that you don't understand at first. No spoilers, but the ending is satisfying, you will be angry at characters in the game, and you will be confused by many of them. Hands down, this game is amazing, but if you get frustrated really easily this game might not be for you.

Okay, so for the about 300 hours (I know it says 160 something but I sometimes launch it without steam) i've been playing this game, i've been bewildered beyond my comprehension.
Kerbal Space Program is a game about building rockets with the aim of getting somewhere that's not a flaming ball of fire beside the launchpad. You build your own rockets, add some fuel and whatever else you might need and launch. It's not rocket science.
This is a list of the pros and cons of this game, however I think the most important pro about this game is that it fits every single playstyle you might want to have, not just because of all the mods you can install, but because of the sheer amount of gameplay it includes. You want to just make big♥♥♥♥♥rockets that get to nowhere? More power to you! Do you want to follow in the path of Voyager 1 & 2 and build probes to launch to the planets farther out? Go ahead, the parts are there. Maybe you want a different, more realistic approach? There's that too, with the right mods!
Pros
Sheer amount of gameplay:
-----------------------------
Kerbal Space Program includes 16 different celestial bodies you can explore and land of, ranging from tiny moons with pathetic amounts of gravity, to big planets which are extremely difficult to get to and back from. However, nothing is truly impossible, as with the huge amount of parts in the game, you can build almost anything (assuming you have a good enough CPU and aren't afraid of accidentally setting your computer on fire). While the game won't offer specific tasks like styudying a planet, mods are an extremely easy fix. And even without them, you can send probes to the outer reaches of the Kerbol system, or put a Kerbal on Kerbins nearest celestial body, the Mun. Or perhaps go all out, and visit the Joolian system and it's moons. Visiting the planets themselves isn't the limit, the planets have what they call "Anomalies" places of interest that may house some unexplainable rock formation, or suprisingly a Kerbals face sticking out from the ground on another planet. With or without mods the game has enough gameplay to make you wish the days were longer, and that school essay you have to complete will just write itself.
Easy to learn:
--------------
Kerbal Space Program's seemingly difficult features like orbits and non-existent words like "Apoapsis" (it's not like we've been sending stuff to space for over 50 years and have no idea how anything works), they're actually quite simple concepts to learn. While the in-game tutorials don't seem very helpful, steam guides and popular KSP YouTuber's such as Scott Manley will help to put you on the road to become a true rocket scientist (at least the in-game equivalent of one). The moment you understand the fundamental parts of a certain feature, you can immediately do it with enough patience.
Community:
------------
This game has an incredible community. As mentioned before you have YouTuber's like Scott Manley, or Bob Fitch if you're into series. Or Matt Lowne if you're into huge over-engineered rockets that seem to strain your CPU to the max, but are fun because at one point or another they blow up anyway, and you can't help but laugh. (Unless it's your 5th attempt at a Saturn V replica and you're seriously getting tired of it all). If videos aren't your thing browse the steam forums or the official KSP forums, there is bound to be an interesting craft someone has built, or a suggestion that you'd love implimented into the game.
Negatives:
-----------
There aren't too many negatives in KSP. The only minor issues are that updates roll in extremely slowly, and that big updates tend to cause bugs that aren't solved until another patch comes out.
All in all, I highly reccomend the game.

Absolutely fantastic.  In the last decade, the importance of storytelling in games has died almost completely.  Stories were replaced with explosions, special effects, and gore.  Though such things are by no mean unnecessary, they do not a tale make.
Tim Schafer has been out of the Point-And-Click phase of games for nearly two decades.  His company's work from then 'til now has been fairly up and down.  For some games, like Stacking and Psychonauts, the company tried to use new angles at traditional tales/archetypes.  Others, such as Trenched and Brutal Legend, did little to stand out from the crowd.  To the least, Broken Age is of neither category.
Broken Age is a homage to the beginning of Tim Schafer's legacy.  However, it's not just filled with references to former glory to earn an extra dime, it is a true extension of the writing brilliance of the team at Double Fine.  The game is absolutely, positively refreshing.
Both tales begin with a load of tension, encapsulating the player with a goal from the get-go.  The stories feel like expansions of some of the short story greats such as "The Lottery" and "Other People."  Not only inspired but some of fiction's greatest twists that cover the taboo of history, but the game expands on the concepts and questions the root of not only the character's but the player's belief system.
Whichever path you begin your journey on, you will be thrown almost immediately into a breathtaking story that will make you have no buyer's remorse.  Be warned--you may want to make sure you don't work the day after you start, you're likely to forget about the concept of time.
Don't waste your timed, dated and aged like bread.

Kerbal Space Program is hands down the most fun I have had with a video game in quite a while. The core premise of the game is fairly simple: build some rockets, try to fly them to places. That might sound pretty straightforward, but where Kerbal Space program really shines is in HOW that is done, and how it is done is with SCIENCE. The game perfectly encapsulates one of the best ways of looking at science.
It really is a hell of an experience, and you can really feel it in full force thanks to the fact that there is very little hand holding in the game. In all liklihood, when you first sit down to play it you WILL mess up. Badly. You will have rockets flip over, burn up in the atmosphere, and explode. You will forget key parts, mess up staging, and accidentally deploy your parachutes at the same time as your engines. You will bolt things together at random because you have no idea what to do, run out of fuel stranded in space, and crash into moons at 2000 m/s. It will be a disaster, but you will keep at it, and eventually you will learn. As your Kerbals gain an understanding of their world and grow, so too will you, and believe me when I say that the feeling of accomplishment is tremendous. When you are flawlessly burning prograde at your apoapsis to circularize your orbit around some god-forsaken rock on the edge of the solar system, you will feel like a colossus bestriding the universe. It will be glorious.
I cannot recommend Kerbal Space Program highly enough. Buy this game right now and get started sciencing your way to the stars through a series of horrific explosions.

"I'm Alan Wake. Author. Dreamweaver. Visionary. Star of the video game with the same title. You're about to enter the world of my imagination. You are entering the Dark Place."
There's no avoiding it: this game wears its influences on its sleeve from the very beginning. If you're aware of the works of Stephen King and Stanley Kubrick, this game *revels* in their tropes, and insights, and atmosphere. Alan is a big-shot author with writers' block, and so of course he ventures off with his wife to the mountain town of Bright Falls to relax and unwind; and, of course, his latest project starts becoming too real.
Although the meat of the gameplay is a simple third-person action game, where you travel from puzzle to puzzle while managing crowds of monsters, with a story you can follow from a mile away - the narration by Alan, and the isolation of the mountain-town setting, and the Dark Presence that turns ordinary surroundings into something strange and malevolent, means the gameplay is pushed forward by the narrative. Like EA's Dead Space, if you charge through Alan Wake slaughtering monsters indiscriminately and skipping cutscenes, you're missing the glue that binds the game together.
What I really liked - and what not many other games do, come to think of it - was how Alan Wake is separated into six individual 'episodes' (and two bonus features), each with their own sub-plot within an overarching plot. Each begins with a recap of the previous episode's events and ends with a credits song, so again you're encouraged to soak in the game's atmosphere and let events sink in, rather than marathoning through.
I found the 'light' gameplay mechanic interesting, too. Enemies are invulnerable until you banish their darkness with a light source, so in encounters you'll be dodging attacks until you can get a clear shot at them. Alan's healed not with med-kits, but by finding a strong light source - so 'following the light' is both a gameplay pointer and a viable strategy on higher difficulties, or if you're overwhelmed and out of ammo.
Alan Wake embraces its influences without delving into self-parody, and is a perfectly competent action game to boot. I'd definitely recommend if you're a fan of Western existential horror, or feel like something spooky and interesting to play.

Recommend Nuclear Throne is not an easy task, you must first recognize if you have a deeper problem of compulsive masochism, if you like to suffer, this is your game.
Nuclear throne is a shooter with overhead view and Roguelike elements such as randomly generated scenarios, economy inventory and high difficulty, in which we have to shoot everything that looks like a threat (a "Shoot and then asks" full-fledged). For this purpose we use an absurd amount of weapons (+100) which are as useful as multifarious (guitars, lasers rays, bazookas, crossbows, etc.) and a concept called "Mutation", which is a type of modifier which is activated when you level up your character; there are all kinds of modifiers such as increasing life points, make enemies drop more likely to make or increase shooting accuracy, to name a few.
Nuclear Throne have a lot of charismatic characters with different intrinsic skills; Crystal is a piece of purple quartz whose special ability is activate a shield that bounces from enemy bullets for 2 seconds, Steroids can use dual weapons or Chicken and his ability to throw their weapons at enemies.
The main virtue of Nuclear Throne lies in the constant randomness and our ability to adapt to these situations, sometimes in the less pleasant ways and perhaps an unfair randomness in some sections, but never fault the game itself but rather by the failed approach we give to our plays. Our mission is to reach and defeat the Nuclear Throne, yes, but much matter how, the weapons I have, the mutations I have chosen, the character I'm playing, the arrangement and number of enemies and obstacles on stage. Everything under the halo of a subconscious immutable fluidity and rigor that enables playing with almost no major surprises to a true bullet hell situations.
Perhaps Nuclear Throne is the highest point of Vlambeer as video game developer and in which their dual philosophy of direct fun and almost obscene depth is clearly note, it is a game that can end in 5 minutes, or get stuck for hours trying to discover new weapons, situations, enemies, characters, etc.
Nuclear Throne is hard drug, so beware.
