Whenever I look at reviews for games, I always look at how long the individual has played before I read the review.  I wish Steam had an option to sort negative and positive reviews by playtime.  Some people are quick to judge negatively or positively before seeing what a game really has to offer.  Have you ever met someone that you liked initially, but upon getting to know further didn't like so much?  People that have spent more time on a game are better suited to fairly judge it.
Nuclear Throne isn't quite like any game I've played before.  It's a stage based twin-stick shooter with high levels of randomization.  You play as one of many mutants trying to make it to the Nuclear Throne.  Why?  It's never really stated.  The game doesn't have an in game story line.  You can go out on the web and search for information that the developers commented about if you like, but in game there isn't very much to go on at all.  Ultimately this doesn't matter much, as most people probably aren't playing this sort of game for the story.
As you play through each stage and make your way to the Nuclear Throne you gain experience, level up, and find weapons.  Every time you level up, you select a mutation (upgrade) from a random list up until the final level where you get to select an ultra mutation which is unique to the mutant you are using.  Each mutant has a special ability and the vast majority of them are useful in one way or another.  You can eventually unlock different/slightly enhanced starting weapons for the mutants. It is also possible to unlock crowns for each character, each crown makes various gameplay changes.  It's a neat idea, but unfortunately many of the crowns are outright bad to the point of being detrimental.
The individual stages are very short, and randomly generated.  This is both positive and negative respectively.  The short stages enable very fast games.  You can reach the throne in less than 10 minutes if you are going at a good pace.  The randomly generated stages give the game a high level of replayability but also end up being its greatest flaw. Games with randomly generated levels often do so by having a large number of premade segments and attaching a handful of them together to create the level.  This doesn't seem to be the case in Nuclear Throne, and the end result is inconsistent stages with almost no level design.  You can start a stage in a great location, and the next run you could start the same stage in a completely awful location.  After playing for a while you will have an idea of which stages are particularly egregious offenders of this and be mentally prepared for what might await, but in the end it may or may not work out depending on what you encounter.  One other issue with the stages is that they feature a very low number of unique enemies.  The three ice levels, for example, have four enemies: tanks, snowbots, robot wolves, and snow bandits.  This might not sound bad but the game crams so many of the same enemy on the screen that it evokes thoughts of an mspaint picture where a five year old learned how to use copy and paste for the first time.
The aforementioned issues become especially apparent when you loop the game.  I'll give fair warning here and say that I don't like looping as a feature in games, and I know it's something many players appreciate. When you loop everything hits the fan, and it's ugly.  The game abandons the modicum of level design that was present and flings stages absolutely filled with enemies at you.  This pours the coolness of weapon variety and mutation selection down the drain.  The farther you go, you'll discover that some mutations are extremely important, and that a small number of weapons are actually viable so late in the game.
The graphics are mostly unimpressive. I wouldn't describe them as good or bad, but I will say that I didn't find them to be very pretty.  I did think that the fact that characters don't turn to face the direction they're moving in was an odd choice.  The soundtrack is great and each song fits its stage well.  The music choices in the sewer, palace, and throne room were notably good.
Nuclear Throne has many flaws, but it is also a lot of fun at times.  The action is fast paced and the runs can be short enough that people without a lot of free time to spend playing can have a quick run between other activities.  For anyone on the fence about buying this game, I suggest you search Google for Wasteland Kings.  It is the original prototype for Nuclear Throne and similar enough that it should give you an idea of whether or not the game is for you.  One warning though: I don't believe Wasteland Kings has gamepad support and the full release of Nuclear Throne does, so don't let that affect your opinion.  I feel that with a handful of changes and a small amount of polish this game could be something truly remarkable, but as it is I cannot recommend it at the current price of $11.99.

After the First War in Darwinia, the virtual world was altered forever.  Suddenly, violence was embedded in the minds of the Darwinians, and they split themselves into factions to vie for control of the realm.  In Multiwinia, you play as these factions trying to gain territory or launch a rocket or WMD before the other factions.
Unlike its predecessor, Multiwinia has almost no story to speak of.  All the lore is contained within the little snippets that describe each level, but there’s no order to them.  This is truly exactly what the title describes: Multiplayer Darwinia.
The controls are largely the same as in Darwinia, though now you can directly command individual groups of Darwinians, as well as promote captains to give them standing orders while you attend to matters elsewhere.  The difference here is that there are many different game modes to play.  King of the Hill, Rocket Building, and even an Assault mode where one player defends a base and the others have to attack it by any means necessary.
Again, you’ll grow attached to these little guys, but they’re not as innocent as before.  They will happily slaughter any opposing forces they come across, and you won’t have too much time to grieve them if they die, because they are replaced almost instantly.
The action is fast-paced and hectic, though the battles are won in minutes, not seconds.  You’ll need to think out your choices minutes in advance, and hold territory as best you can while waiting for reinforcements.  Though if you fail, it isn’t very disheartening.  Just fire up another round and try again.
This is a fun little game, though it is not very deep.  It’s a passable RTS for fans of Darwinia, though you’ll be hard-pressed to find anyone online to play with nowadays.

This is the first game I bought on Steam, and where to start?
I've seen other people play the game (mainly Youtubers), but actually playing it for yourself is a different experience altogether. For one thing, I found myself becoming more immersed with each episode, and I was reluctant to take a break in between. You really have to put thought into the majority of decisions you make and the actions you perform, which I think is quite clever. I've seen games before where the choices you make barely matter, so this makes a nice change.
The main thing I truly admired about the game as a whole is the storytelling. Throughout the episodes, there were moments where I longed to be there with the characters - in some cases, I wanted to be inside Arcadia Bay just for the views. As infuriating as it was to learn some of the controls (looking at you, photograph focusing minigame), I think that the concept of rewinding time was handled very well. It's an especially useful game mechanic if you regret your choice and want to change it.
One fault I do find is some of the animations. They seemed somewhat repetitive at times, almost robotic, but this didn't get to me too much. The dialogue is realistic and well-written, the art style and visuals are gorgeous, and it's a game I can see myself playing over and over again. I really look forward to Before The Storm, and I hope that the same great qualities of the original will be present there too.

Finally broke 100 hours with this gem.  This game is EXACTLY what was promised, and delivers where it counts.  Fans of the original game and the post-apocalyptic genre should eat this right up.  There's at LEAST 25 hours of content in the Arizona portion of the game.  With that being the halfway point we're looking at a 50+ hour game which is more than most games today will give you for the pricetag.  There were no corners cut or shortcuts taken and it's very evident in the late beta.  The game is highly polished and the bugs are (almost) gone!  The expectations are very high for release (Sept 19th?) and I fully believe InXile won't disappoint.
Synopsis:  You are a freshly recruited Desert Ranger in the post-nuclear wastes of Arizona, USA.  Welcomed and rushed straight off to investigate a prominent ranger's death and complete his critical mission, the game wastes no time showing you the harsh and dangerous environment that is the Wasteland.  Through use of skills, combat, dialogue, and cunning, you will forge a unique path through the wasteland and write your own story as a member of the Desert Rangers.  Of course there's mutated plants and animals, killer robots, raiders, cannibals, thugs, and radiation clouds to keep you company along the way.
The Game:  Unlike most games that ease you in with kiddy missions and tutorials, this game slaps you in the face.  ADAPT OR DIE is the theme for the first few run-ins with the bad men and creatures of the wastes.  If you're unlucky enough not to recruit a special friend before setting out, you'll be lucky to survive to the first real location without a ridiculous number of reloads.  On my first playthrough I was losing team members in the first 10 minutes.  Then I realized the coolest thing about this game:  You have to actually THINK.  About Everything.  The combat is highly tactical, and the choices have real consequences.  There's actually no way to do everything in one playthrough.  With each location you visit you'll make decisions that affect the rest of your game.  And the consequences don't show up until later, making your choices semi-permanent (you REALLY don't want to reload and replay the last 1.5 HOURS to fix that dialogue choice).  This is one of the most immersive top down TBC RPG games I've ever played.  It is very much a spiritual ancestor of the Fallout series, but the playability is very much with the times.  You can also have a party of up to 7 members, which is much more than other games have allowed, but furthermore in my playthrough of just the Arizona area, I encountered 6 recruitable NPCs and I know for a fact I missed at least 1 due to a choice I made.  So there's probably upwards of 12-15 characters you can add to your party throughout the game, which is a  TON!  And there's so many ways to do everything!  Locked door?  Pick it, bust it down, or find the key.  Broken robot? Fix it mechanically or hack the cpu.  There's a real sense of reality applying in this world.  If it makes sense, you can probably do it.  I must commend the developers for that specifically, as it's frankly an amazing thing to see in a game.  Also, in many situations you can avoid combat alltogether, or you can choose a side and manipulate the outcome, so there's just as much variation to the game strategy as there is to the skill use.  It feels very complete in the way of forging your own path.
Combat:  The combat in this game is a bit more complicated than your typical tactical turn based game.  Aside from the usual Action Points system for movement/weapon use, you also have to deal with weapon jams, your NPCs going rogue and doing whatever they want for their turn, and rampant friendly fire if you don't watch your angles.  The only way to avoid this (and you can't ever avoid it entirely) is to invest survival points into your weapons and leadership skills to minimize the chance of jams/rogue turns.  Some may find this a frustrating addition to combat, but I find it adds a great depth and believability to it.  To compare the combat to something, I'd say it's similar to XCOM but with more of a Fallout RPG focus, so it's not nearly as hard once you get the hang of it.
Overall this game is what Post-Apocalyptic gamers have been waiting for since Fallout 2.  If you enjoy turn based games and love the genre, it's bound to become one of your favorite titles for any number of reasons.  The story is huge, the choices are real, the combat is deadly.  Do you have what it takes to be a Desert Ranger?

This game is frustratingly difficult, occasionally hard to control and sometimes confusing. But you know what? I had a blast with it throughout it's entirety. For me (I got the game on sale for 2.50$) this game was worth every penny, and would've been worth it even if I got it full price. Hotline Miami is a top-down beat em' up with a great soundtrack set in Miami in the 80s. This game was super fun to play, I found myself getting frustrated as enemies rushed me from every direction to kill me, only to not be able to put the game down. I would go through every level probably at least 20 times before I beat it, but it is so rewarding when you finally do beat it. Enemies are smart, they patrol the area in groups, if they see you they will rush to the place you just were, they will shoot you through glass even you didn't see. They are very challenging but never unfair. Using weapons is a trade off, guns give you range, but attract many enemies to your area, melee weapons are completely silent, but you have to get close to an enemy to kill them. There are also many ways to complete a level given the masks and your own personal preference. These masks (you unlock them by beating missions) give you a different stat boost, such as starting with a knife, more ammo, more guns, faster running, etc. This makes the levels extremely replayable, as on one run you can run faster and rush people with a melee weapon, on another you can spam a machine gun because of the extra ammo. This gives this short adventure many more hours than originally, and I'm sure coming back to play this game in the future would be amazing. I have to also commend the art-style and the music. Good god, both of these are SUPERB, as many indie games these days tend to be. The art-style lends itself a nice cartoonish style that is simple and easy on the eyes, yet still gets everything done, and done well. The music is also extremely great and fits the style of this game very well. I recommend purchasing or downloading this soundtrack because it it so dang nice. It fits this game as well as the FTL soundtrack fits that game. The control aspect is done alright, but it was a little weird to get use to. Locking on is almost essential for guns, but it is extremely tough to lock on to an enemy that is rushing you, which can lead to some annoying deaths. I'm not sure what could be done about this though, so I guess it was done the best it could've been. Last thing, the story is also very nice, confusing and inviting questions like the Five Nights at Freddy's, but with interesting characters and characters that you don't understand at first. No spoilers, but the ending is satisfying, you will be angry at characters in the game, and you will be confused by many of them. Hands down, this game is amazing, but if you get frustrated really easily this game might not be for you.

I LOVE this game!
The mechanics are simple and straightforward so you can get straight into the action with very little fiddling around. While the gameplay is essentially quite simple, ie kill all the bad guys, it's also rock hard, but never in a way that feels cheap or unfair. Frenzied button-mashing won't get you very far, it requires quite a high degree of skill and precision, which makes it all the more rewarding when you pull it off. Every kill is satisfying, and I feel a genuine sense of accomplishment when I finally clear a stage. The variety of ways to dispatch enemies, along with the vast array of weaponry and masks that give you different attributes are loads of fun and keep things interesting.
The aesthetics of Hotline Miami are stunning. The retro 16 bit graphical style is gorgeous and clearly shows an affection for the era of the SNES and the Megadrive. The environments are beautifully designed, it's obvious how much care and attention has been taken with every little detail. The game's world has genuine depth and atmosphere, it feels real and fleshed out. The propulsive, synth-heavy soundtrack is equally fantastic and adds to the sweaty, keyed-up, unhinged feel of it all.
I hardly need to mention that this game is EXTREMELY violent. Even with the retro graphics some of the action can be genuinely unnerving in its gleeful sadism, so if you don't like that sort of thing you might not enjoy it very much. But if over-the-top pixelated ultra-violence is your thing, you should absolutely check it out without delay!

The Binding of Isaac is perhaps one of the most poorly coded games I've had the pleasure of playing and, despite that, I would heartily recommend it over most AAA titles.
The game operates on the premise that your mother is out to kill you and you are trying to escape horrible, horrible death. So, you jump into the basement. This is where the game earns its keep. Isaac is a 2-D Top Down Shooter with randomly generated levels where death means the end of a run and your success can largely depend on the luck of the items randomly generated within those levels.
The game is pretty much about avoiding damage while clearing rooms while finding upgrades so you can win the game. It rarely approaches the level of bullethell dodging, but mostly just relies on sheer variety of enemies & bosses to kill you, whether through that one bullet you walked into or the one fly who you ignored who rammed into you. Still, it's pretty much all dodgeable at the end of the day, with a few unfair moments. Still, that's what makes this roguelike so much fun.

"I'm Alan Wake. Author. Dreamweaver. Visionary. Star of the video game with the same title. You're about to enter the world of my imagination. You are entering the Dark Place."
There's no avoiding it: this game wears its influences on its sleeve from the very beginning. If you're aware of the works of Stephen King and Stanley Kubrick, this game *revels* in their tropes, and insights, and atmosphere. Alan is a big-shot author with writers' block, and so of course he ventures off with his wife to the mountain town of Bright Falls to relax and unwind; and, of course, his latest project starts becoming too real.
Although the meat of the gameplay is a simple third-person action game, where you travel from puzzle to puzzle while managing crowds of monsters, with a story you can follow from a mile away - the narration by Alan, and the isolation of the mountain-town setting, and the Dark Presence that turns ordinary surroundings into something strange and malevolent, means the gameplay is pushed forward by the narrative. Like EA's Dead Space, if you charge through Alan Wake slaughtering monsters indiscriminately and skipping cutscenes, you're missing the glue that binds the game together.
What I really liked - and what not many other games do, come to think of it - was how Alan Wake is separated into six individual 'episodes' (and two bonus features), each with their own sub-plot within an overarching plot. Each begins with a recap of the previous episode's events and ends with a credits song, so again you're encouraged to soak in the game's atmosphere and let events sink in, rather than marathoning through.
I found the 'light' gameplay mechanic interesting, too. Enemies are invulnerable until you banish their darkness with a light source, so in encounters you'll be dodging attacks until you can get a clear shot at them. Alan's healed not with med-kits, but by finding a strong light source - so 'following the light' is both a gameplay pointer and a viable strategy on higher difficulties, or if you're overwhelmed and out of ammo.
Alan Wake embraces its influences without delving into self-parody, and is a perfectly competent action game to boot. I'd definitely recommend if you're a fan of Western existential horror, or feel like something spooky and interesting to play.

Okay, so for the about 300 hours (I know it says 160 something but I sometimes launch it without steam) i've been playing this game, i've been bewildered beyond my comprehension.
Kerbal Space Program is a game about building rockets with the aim of getting somewhere that's not a flaming ball of fire beside the launchpad. You build your own rockets, add some fuel and whatever else you might need and launch. It's not rocket science.
This is a list of the pros and cons of this game, however I think the most important pro about this game is that it fits every single playstyle you might want to have, not just because of all the mods you can install, but because of the sheer amount of gameplay it includes. You want to just make big♥♥♥♥♥rockets that get to nowhere? More power to you! Do you want to follow in the path of Voyager 1 & 2 and build probes to launch to the planets farther out? Go ahead, the parts are there. Maybe you want a different, more realistic approach? There's that too, with the right mods!
Pros
Sheer amount of gameplay:
-----------------------------
Kerbal Space Program includes 16 different celestial bodies you can explore and land of, ranging from tiny moons with pathetic amounts of gravity, to big planets which are extremely difficult to get to and back from. However, nothing is truly impossible, as with the huge amount of parts in the game, you can build almost anything (assuming you have a good enough CPU and aren't afraid of accidentally setting your computer on fire). While the game won't offer specific tasks like styudying a planet, mods are an extremely easy fix. And even without them, you can send probes to the outer reaches of the Kerbol system, or put a Kerbal on Kerbins nearest celestial body, the Mun. Or perhaps go all out, and visit the Joolian system and it's moons. Visiting the planets themselves isn't the limit, the planets have what they call "Anomalies" places of interest that may house some unexplainable rock formation, or suprisingly a Kerbals face sticking out from the ground on another planet. With or without mods the game has enough gameplay to make you wish the days were longer, and that school essay you have to complete will just write itself.
Easy to learn:
--------------
Kerbal Space Program's seemingly difficult features like orbits and non-existent words like "Apoapsis" (it's not like we've been sending stuff to space for over 50 years and have no idea how anything works), they're actually quite simple concepts to learn. While the in-game tutorials don't seem very helpful, steam guides and popular KSP YouTuber's such as Scott Manley will help to put you on the road to become a true rocket scientist (at least the in-game equivalent of one). The moment you understand the fundamental parts of a certain feature, you can immediately do it with enough patience.
Community:
------------
This game has an incredible community. As mentioned before you have YouTuber's like Scott Manley, or Bob Fitch if you're into series. Or Matt Lowne if you're into huge over-engineered rockets that seem to strain your CPU to the max, but are fun because at one point or another they blow up anyway, and you can't help but laugh. (Unless it's your 5th attempt at a Saturn V replica and you're seriously getting tired of it all). If videos aren't your thing browse the steam forums or the official KSP forums, there is bound to be an interesting craft someone has built, or a suggestion that you'd love implimented into the game.
Negatives:
-----------
There aren't too many negatives in KSP. The only minor issues are that updates roll in extremely slowly, and that big updates tend to cause bugs that aren't solved until another patch comes out.
All in all, I highly reccomend the game.

Kerbal Space Program is hands down the most fun I have had with a video game in quite a while. The core premise of the game is fairly simple: build some rockets, try to fly them to places. That might sound pretty straightforward, but where Kerbal Space program really shines is in HOW that is done, and how it is done is with SCIENCE. The game perfectly encapsulates one of the best ways of looking at science.
It really is a hell of an experience, and you can really feel it in full force thanks to the fact that there is very little hand holding in the game. In all liklihood, when you first sit down to play it you WILL mess up. Badly. You will have rockets flip over, burn up in the atmosphere, and explode. You will forget key parts, mess up staging, and accidentally deploy your parachutes at the same time as your engines. You will bolt things together at random because you have no idea what to do, run out of fuel stranded in space, and crash into moons at 2000 m/s. It will be a disaster, but you will keep at it, and eventually you will learn. As your Kerbals gain an understanding of their world and grow, so too will you, and believe me when I say that the feeling of accomplishment is tremendous. When you are flawlessly burning prograde at your apoapsis to circularize your orbit around some god-forsaken rock on the edge of the solar system, you will feel like a colossus bestriding the universe. It will be glorious.
I cannot recommend Kerbal Space Program highly enough. Buy this game right now and get started sciencing your way to the stars through a series of horrific explosions.

Whenever I look at reviews for games, I always look at how long the individual has played before I read the review.  I wish Steam had an option to sort negative and positive reviews by playtime.  Some people are quick to judge negatively or positively before seeing what a game really has to offer.  Have you ever met someone that you liked initially, but upon getting to know further didn't like so much?  People that have spent more time on a game are better suited to fairly judge it.
Nuclear Throne isn't quite like any game I've played before.  It's a stage based twin-stick shooter with high levels of randomization.  You play as one of many mutants trying to make it to the Nuclear Throne.  Why?  It's never really stated.  The game doesn't have an in game story line.  You can go out on the web and search for information that the developers commented about if you like, but in game there isn't very much to go on at all.  Ultimately this doesn't matter much, as most people probably aren't playing this sort of game for the story.
As you play through each stage and make your way to the Nuclear Throne you gain experience, level up, and find weapons.  Every time you level up, you select a mutation (upgrade) from a random list up until the final level where you get to select an ultra mutation which is unique to the mutant you are using.  Each mutant has a special ability and the vast majority of them are useful in one way or another.  You can eventually unlock different/slightly enhanced starting weapons for the mutants. It is also possible to unlock crowns for each character, each crown makes various gameplay changes.  It's a neat idea, but unfortunately many of the crowns are outright bad to the point of being detrimental.
The individual stages are very short, and randomly generated.  This is both positive and negative respectively.  The short stages enable very fast games.  You can reach the throne in less than 10 minutes if you are going at a good pace.  The randomly generated stages give the game a high level of replayability but also end up being its greatest flaw. Games with randomly generated levels often do so by having a large number of premade segments and attaching a handful of them together to create the level.  This doesn't seem to be the case in Nuclear Throne, and the end result is inconsistent stages with almost no level design.  You can start a stage in a great location, and the next run you could start the same stage in a completely awful location.  After playing for a while you will have an idea of which stages are particularly egregious offenders of this and be mentally prepared for what might await, but in the end it may or may not work out depending on what you encounter.  One other issue with the stages is that they feature a very low number of unique enemies.  The three ice levels, for example, have four enemies: tanks, snowbots, robot wolves, and snow bandits.  This might not sound bad but the game crams so many of the same enemy on the screen that it evokes thoughts of an mspaint picture where a five year old learned how to use copy and paste for the first time.
The aforementioned issues become especially apparent when you loop the game.  I'll give fair warning here and say that I don't like looping as a feature in games, and I know it's something many players appreciate. When you loop everything hits the fan, and it's ugly.  The game abandons the modicum of level design that was present and flings stages absolutely filled with enemies at you.  This pours the coolness of weapon variety and mutation selection down the drain.  The farther you go, you'll discover that some mutations are extremely important, and that a small number of weapons are actually viable so late in the game.
The graphics are mostly unimpressive. I wouldn't describe them as good or bad, but I will say that I didn't find them to be very pretty.  I did think that the fact that characters don't turn to face the direction they're moving in was an odd choice.  The soundtrack is great and each song fits its stage well.  The music choices in the sewer, palace, and throne room were notably good.
Nuclear Throne has many flaws, but it is also a lot of fun at times.  The action is fast paced and the runs can be short enough that people without a lot of free time to spend playing can have a quick run between other activities.  For anyone on the fence about buying this game, I suggest you search Google for Wasteland Kings.  It is the original prototype for Nuclear Throne and similar enough that it should give you an idea of whether or not the game is for you.  One warning though: I don't believe Wasteland Kings has gamepad support and the full release of Nuclear Throne does, so don't let that affect your opinion.  I feel that with a handful of changes and a small amount of polish this game could be something truly remarkable, but as it is I cannot recommend it at the current price of $11.99.

The good: I love party games.  Chalo Chalo is a great party game.  Had a blast playing it for about half an hour on a friend’s machine with a group of seven people at various levels of intoxication.  The game was everything that was advertised.  Easy to pick up, everyone could get the controller app, and connect in under 5 minutes.
The bad: We had a few issues with disconnects mid-game and players' dots would just wander off the screen.  Also, I get that the devs are probably going for some aesthetic with the pastels for each player’s dot, but half the players had a hard time picking out their dot.
The unacceptable:  One of our players was colorblind.  The player couldn't tell the difference between the fast (green) and the death (red) tiles.  Considering that around 1 in 20 people are colorblind and the game is made for 8 players, the likelihood that someone at your party is colorblind is fairly high.  It is completely unacceptable that there is no colorblind palette option.
Add a colorblind mode.  Add a mode with more distinct colors for the dots.
TL;DR: Chalo Chalo is a fun party game.  It needs a colorblind mode or you won’t be able to play it at parties.

Multiwinia is a RTS game, but it is NOT the kind of RTS you would think it would be.
Multiwinia is probably (if not), IS the most unique RTS games I have ever played in my life.
What makes Multiwinia a one-of-a-kind game? Well let me tell you:
1. Unlike most RTS games, Multiwinia features one main unit: The Darwinian.
2. Despite there being only one unit, there are CRATES that can give many different power-ups that can turn the tide of the battlefield. Whether you get reinforcements, turrets, viruses, NUKES!, and even Dragons!
3. Multiwinia also features different game modes, like Capture the Flag/Point(s), Domination, Assault, and a few more.
4. All Multiwinians are the same, nothing counters another. In Multiwinia, the only thing you need, is a STRATEGY.
Ok, I said some things that make the game unique. Now I'm going to tell you some other things you need to know if you plan on gettings Multiwinia:
1. Multiwinia is the MULTIPLAYER version of Darwinia. There is no campaign for Multiwinia because Darwinia has the campaign, if you want story mode, get Darwinia.
2. Multiwinia is FUN. Whether you get addicted or not, is beyond me. But one thing is for sure, if your bored, play this game!
3. Multiwinia is cheap. The game is really old, so I mean that's probably why it's cheap. BUT, your paying for plenty of fun content!
Would I recommend this game?
OF COURSE!
Multiwinia is 10 bucks, but on sale, it gets as cheap as 2 dollars!
But I recommend you get Darwinia + Multiwinia, so you have the campaign AND multiplayer. It's probably 4 or 5 bucks on sale.
TL;DR Multiwinia is a multiplayer version of Darwinia, which has the campaign. Multiwinia is a very fun and unique RTS game. If you want a RTS with simple mechanics and fun gameplay, get this game!

It might be best to sum Wasteland 2 up as a more modern version of the original late 80's PC game. Unfortunately, I'd say about 90% of their player base probably wasn't even born when the game was originally published, so sadly a good many of the references to the original game are lost.
While it's nice to see a more updated version, the sad reality is that the game is pretty disaapointing overall. Don't expect to find a massive open world to explore in a "choose your own adventure" style like the Fallout series, Wasteland 2 is anything if not very, very linear with limited choices for the protagonist to choose from, and ultimately not having much bearing on the game. Timeliness is emphasized, and rather than the player being able to think about whether or not they'd like to take a particular action, it's pretty much either having option A or B crammed down your throat. It's best summed up as a "damned if you do, damned if you don't" scenario's.
My advice would be to hold off until the official release, and while the most current patch has helped to revamp a few of the areas, improve graphics, and solve a slew of bugs from the original, for the time being, it's buggy enough to make you wonder if Bethesda had a hand in it.

Bought this game about 2 weeks ago and I just cannot get off from it! It's just really fun to build and launch the spaceships into the space to explore the Mun(moon) and other planets.
So far I could only reach to the Moon and that took me loads of tries(I even killed 3 of my crew which actually made me really sad =<)  just land a damn rocket on top of its hills. Then I found out that you can quicksave(F5) and try it over and over again until you success(yaayy).

There is a career mode in which you can earn money and reputation as you select missions and accomplishing them. (For example; plant a flag to the moon which gives you 100k money). At first, you will struggle getting into an orbit around earth but you will essentially gain science points by doing experiments and unlocking new components and eventually it will be possible for you to get to Moon. Not only rockets, but also you can build planes which are kinda harder to build since you have to balance it very precisely.
I highly recommend this game if your are patient and love physics based stuff. Very fun game! You won't notice how time flies in this game =P

This game! It is addictive. I was hesistant for very long to buy this games and watched the discussions every now and then, but I really didn't expect too much, when I finally purchased it. And was I wrong!
This game isn't your run of the mill space game. It is actually much more like a physics simulator (with some extras... like building up your spaceprogram, unlock new techs, and of course upgrade your facilities). But the core of it really is flight and maneuver planning, learning how the physics in space work on a intuitional, not theoretical level. Want to get to the 'Mun' (yes, no typo)? Burn prograde at the right time und thereby raise the apo of your orbit to an encounter. You want to go further? You better plan in a little gravity assisted slingshot maneuver to save delta-V and make sure you can get home on your fuel. That's it. Not like in other games: get in your ship, fly straight to wherever you want and stop... that is not how maneuvering in space works. It might sound boring, but after a while you find yourself sinking two real life hours to build a rocket, that can lift your precious com-satellite and get it into a stable polar orbit around Minmis without noticing.
It can be frustrating at times, too, granted. Especially when your own stupidity is at fault, returning from your first lunar flyby without a heat shield only noticing it, when you are about to re-enter and can't do anything against that anymore, or forget those damn solar panels (when playing with mods, which make this very good game outstanding, this can easily turn lethal...). And sometimes, when the Kraken attacks... well, that's just bad luck then, I guess.
This is one of the best purchases I ever did. I bought it at discount for 18 €, but it's easily worth the 40 € on which it is right now.

The game had a rough start. Right after launch the overall rating was 33%, now, a day later, it's 52%. That's saying something. And it's that you shouldn't rush a game, not even when it's as good as Mafia III.
If you start to read through the negative reviews you'll find they mostly complain about the frame rate lock, which restricts (as of now) the game to run at 30 fps. Allegedly a patch is on the way to enable the game to run at 60, or even more, but this also only put up the question: why 2K couldn't wait a few more days? I admit I don't know anything about the business side of releasing a game, but postponing release by a few days doesn't seem to mess up all financial plans for the fiscal year.
But whatever, the game is here, at 30fps and it's awesome. There were some complaints about aim assist, but it can be set low, high or can be turned entire off, so it isn't an issue either. Some mentioned that the game look awful. I'm not that sure about that, because the quality of the main characters is jawdropping. Lesser characters may not be that detailed, but looking at Sammy's face, even from very close, I could forget for a few moments it is only a real-time rendered bunch of polygons. The city looks better in GTA, but that doesn't mean this game is ugly, and in fact traffic seems somehow more realistic than in Rockstar's games.
The game is perfectly playable with mouse and keyboard; it's responsive and your fingers won't tie a knot on themselves while playing. I have two complaints though. First is that during driving the engine brake is too strong in my opinion, so your car decelerate rapidly, and I haven't found option to turn on cruise control (haven't really looked for it though). Second is the same as with all GTAs: for some reason the devs like to keep the camera as close to the ground as it's possible without making the unplayable. That means, you don't see the front of your car and thus you have no idea when you will bump into another car without moving the camera manually. Even more so with trucks... I'll never understand why they don't let us set camera height during driving.
Oh, and I must mention something else.
Some lunatics (especially this guy: /id/iron-born/recommended/360430) may try to convince you this game is anti-white propaganda, which is utterly ridiculous for more than one reasons. You play as a black man, in 1960's America, in the south, and you're a gangster. It shows. Harsh language, racism everywhere, and you are out to avenge your family and friends. With the help of white men, by the way... Trying to tie this to today's Black Lives Matter movement is along the lines of claiming that Earth is flat. But, in fact, reading these masterpieces is at least as entertaining as the game itself :-)

:Spoiler free:
16 hours in and I have a pretty good understanding of the story, gameplay, world, characters, mechanics. Not going to discuss the 30 fps lock since devs said it will be fixed soon. So going through the pros and cons of the core game.
Pros :
The World: It's very well done, full of atmosphere, and interesting commentary around every corner. The map is probably about 60-65%? size of GTAV but has far more interiors in the first two ditricts then almost all of GTA combined, so what it lacks in size it makes up for not just being complete window dressing.
Story: It's fantastic so far, you really sympathise with the characters. Which was one of my primary worries, I was afraid a straight up revenge story, as the trailers suggested, would leave me not being able to connect with them. The exception being Vito, whos story we all know.  Luckily the writers hit all the right notes, for me atleast, and I resonated very strongly with Lincoln very quickly.
Gameplay:
Driving is well done for Keyboard and mouse, I havn't tried controller since I havn't felt the need. Unlike GTA were I have a controller plugged in for driving and keyboard and mouse for roaming and shooting. I would still imagine controller would be best though.
Stealth is alittle OP im my opinion, but great fun, I would suggest playing on the hardest difficulty if you want any sort of a challenege. This could just be because I'm still in the early game though and perhaps things havn't ramped up yet.
Underbosses: This is what makes it a Mafia game for me. Would I have liked a traditionally Italian mob story, sure, but the ingrediants are there and I think they fit great. In fact I really like building my personal Mafia from the ground up, with the your underbosses all having differant visions, and the constant head butting and rivalry for territories. The threat of betrayal and consequences, a great dynamic in my opinion.
Music : Really not to much to be said on this front, it's amazing and pulls you deeper into the world, and I find great satisfaction running over people with "Somebody to Love" blasting on the radio
Cons:
Texures: Quality isn't all that great and I do hope that is one of the PC addition updates that 2K might add in the future, but as of now they're just decent. Though the textures aren't the best they actually are made worse by my next con.
FXAA : Or what I assume it to be, If it is, I've never seen FXAA quite so agressive. FXAA generally smudges textures to make them look better, but this cranks it up 11, at times its like playing the game looking through a foggy mirror. Setting this from high to low diminished this for me, but not the degree I would like.
Overall It's a solid game with a few minor issues, one major if you count the 30FPS (Which I'm in that camp aswell, driving in particular has given me a sea sick like nausea at 30 fps) Though the fact that I'm still playing even when it does that, could be used as an endorsement in of itself.

Quick and Simple: Did you love Shadow of Mordor enough that you'd pay $60 for another run at it? If so, then you already own this. If not, then Shadow of War is best described as "The Same, but More." Decide how much that's worth to you.
The Review: Once Upon a Time in Mordor, an inseperable couple get their special ring stolen by a sexy hag, and need to start up their Human Resources Firm again and make sure that the right Orcs get into the Right Position so they can get their ring back and fulfill their vows.
Well, mostly.
The Story of Shadow of War is completely nonsensical and for the most part forgone (Because LoTR *happens*, you know that things don't work out for Pimp Daddy Calabrim-badass and Talion the Meat Puppet), but the star of the show is and has always been the Orcs. An absolute endless parade of unique personalites and weird encounters for you to bash sword, arrow, and spell against as you pick the guys with the funniest names or best intro quips and press-gang them into your hell army.
That's the heart and soul of the Mordor series. And it's very much still there.
Months of bad press about sexy spider girls who aren't spiders, the game being Pay-To-Win, WB trying to monotize a freaking developer tribute, and another paid review scandal over-shadow what is perhaps a strangely safe, samey, and very 'normal' sequel. The Nemisis system is in place and still glowing hot. The Combat has not changed at all since the previous game. And even what you DO is still primarily about grabbing funny orcs and making them fight. There's VERY LITTLE CHANGE here.
Which is why the Loot Box system, while scary, really hasn't affected the way I play the game. Yes, it's stupid you can pop orcs out of boxes, but the game is so flush with in-game currency, that it's hard to ever really feel the squeeze. And that's sort of how it felt to me "It didn't really change my game experience". Levels and Skill points come fast and furious, so I never felt compelled to pop an XP Boost, and you'll have the "Important" upgrades within 6 hours.
So...that's it. Shadow of War: It's Shadow of Mordor! Again!

Life is Strange is an adventure game with minimal gameplay and simple puzzles, so it basically plays out like a "choose your own adventure" novel.
The story is a character driven mystery that is similar to the movie "Butterfly Effect" in both substance and execution. Like that movie, it primarily explores choices and their broader consequences through a time-travel gimmick. This is a great choice for the medium and the game is full of meaningful choices that are left to the player to decide and reap the consequences for. Unfortunately, again like "Butterfly Effect", the story often fails to resist getting itself into overdone scenarios when the narrative would of had more impact if it was more restrained and subtle. Unlike the "Butterfly Effect", the majority of the cast of characters here have interesting and deep personal narratives which, combined with the interactive nature of the game, maintained my interest throughout the game despite the overall plot getting more ridiculous as the episodes progressed.
All-in-all I enjoyed the ride and seeing how my various decisions played out. The first episode itself serves as a good demo. If you enjoy that episode, you'll likely enjoy the rest of the game even though the overall story doesn't hold up to its initial promise.

A multiplayer remake of Darwinia. It's slightly better but is still unplayable. It explains the basics in 2 tutorials, like, controlling the units, making a formation, capturing stuff. However, as soon as you try the single player mode vs the AI (there are no players online to play against) immediately you get questions you don't know answers to and you always lose because you don't know what's happening. Like, where the hell those grenades (or whatever, you just see explosions) come from and wipe out half of your formation. Can you use grenades, too? If so, what button does that? Or where the hell from do ships appear and send rockets from all sides at a location? Why suddenly the battle slowed down etc etc. It seems that the AI takes some bonus crates which have all kinds of special effects, but it's not clear what those effects do, how many of them there are etc. It's not even clearly visible who a spawning point belongs to - there are small colored dots indicating that but in a huge colorful mess of particles this game is they get lost completely.
There is still the same strange camera control system: moving the mouse rotates the camera (!?), and the cursor is fixed at the center of the screen as if you were controlling a minigun on a helicopter with the task of shooting targets on the ground. The mouse wheel zooms in/out in the same reversed and unconfigurable mode as in Darwinia. Deselecting units is done with Space. It should have been right click (or left click, if right-click is for giving a movement order - depends on whether you like C&C or AoE system better)... Formations work clumsy, as it's not possible to send a formation a bit forward - the destination point must be in front of the whole formation. Selecting groups of darwinians with a long mouse-down is a novel idea but works not so good as it spends too much time. Why didn't they just let people use the old good dragbox or double left-click to select, say, 50 darwinians?
Btw, the basic gameplay here is much like in "virus rts" type games, where you have a set of points on the map, spawning tiny units of one fixed type at a regular rate, and you can pick 50% of them from one point and send to another connected point - there are plenty of mobile games like that now. Surely, Multiwinia is much more complex, and there are more modes, but the basic idea is just that. If you get it (almost) for free in a bundle, it's maybe worth a look. Just don't expect much.

Ultraviolent, stylish, satisfying, and hard as all hell, Hotline Miami is a brilliant action game. With the constant balance between being reckless for higher scores and being subtle to stay alive, Hotline's constant action requires you to use your wits and your reflexes to get through impossible situations, as one wrong move will leave you dead.
No matter how absurdly difficult the game feels at times, it never feels unfair. When you die, it's your own fault, not the game's. And even if you do die, so what? Checkpoints aplenty keep the action constant and encourage you not to fear death, letting you find out new ways to maximize your score and new approaches if the last one wasn't working. The wonderful sound design, with appropriate "oomph" to all your attacks backed by an absolutely outstanding electro soundtrack blaring in your ears constantly, contributes to the adrenaline-fueled haze the game so clearly wants you to indulge in.
I can't recommend this game enough. Buy the hell out of it and enjoy the ride.

Top notch game and highly recommended. The new update of candidates is great - any game which allows for you to beat Trump as Nancy Pelosi is definitely a must buy.
There are, however, a few recommendations to make it even better:
1. Third Party Candidates/Parties/Run as Independent. This is spoke about quite a bit and would fully transform the game. It would obviously be brilliant as you wouldn't be forced into just a two party route, but more importantly it would be great online. Currently, it is far easier for Democrats to win than Republicans, which is not great for multiplayer as one person has a lot more good candidates to choose from than the other. This leads to point No.2...
2. More Candidates! Now there has just been a great update, but the GOP side is still fairly weak (probably due to the necessary inclusion of the many 2016 candidates). Ideally there should be more ex-Presidents and ex-Presidential candidates from the past and far past, but really just some C20th ones will do e.g The Bushes, Reagan, Nixon, JFK, FDR. Maybe even include some First Ladies or notable VPs in there too, it would definitely add more range and keep the game dynamic.
3. Set the Agenda. Now whilst this is a 2016 simulator, it would be great if you could set which issues you wanted to be the most important in the election (this would also help remove the bias against the GOP, as the Dems do far greater with Independents on issues such as Gay Marriage and Marijuana). Also, this would be great to simulate PAST elections (e.g Bush vs Gore, Obama vs McCain), which would be extremely fun and great for online play.
4. Music. This is a minor issue, but sometimes the music loops poorly or barely loops at all.
5. Workshop? Not as necessary as the ones above but the addition of the Workshop would be great to share Custom Candidates with other people. For example, fictional Presidents such as F.Underwood or real political figures that the creators of the game might not have time to make but the players could share. in fact, this could actually solve the need to spend time making new candidates all the time when really the public could make them.
At the end of the day it's a great time and none of the above issues will stop me from playing it, they would just take it over the edge and turn it into an even greater game. You have until November guys!

I bought this game looking for an alternative to President Infinity. I like PI, but it also gives me a headache: it's not only incredibly complicated and arcane, but it also is visually unappealing. The interfaces are static and include way too many numbers and words, requiring far too much decoding. I wanted a game that was near to (but still slightly below) the complexity of PI with a more dynamic interface.
Political Machine certainly has a more dynamic interface, but has almost no complexity. The whole process is incredibly dumbed-down and simplistic. So, add me to the list of people perplexed by the fact that this game doesn't include a primary process.
Another area where the game lacks is the endorsement system. The small amount of organizations (and lack of politician or media endorsements) takes out much of the replay value of the game, where, essentially, each game you'll end up endorsed by the same people (because you get to choose who endorses you). This points to how unlike real elections the game is: whereas real elections involve a lot of chance and uncertainty, this game allows you to control most of the outcomes.
The game is fun, and is great at its occasional satire about how elections work in the real world. However, it has no lasting power. I've won two games, after about two hours of playing, and am already getting bored. The difficulty doesn't really matter to me: I don't think this game needs to be more difficult and it has plenty of difficulty settings. There just isn't much to do. It really just functions as a game for those people who want to see their candidate of choice win the presidency over and over again.

Bought this game about 2 weeks ago and I just cannot get off from it! It's just really fun to build and launch the spaceships into the space to explore the Mun(moon) and other planets.
So far I could only reach to the Moon and that took me loads of tries(I even killed 3 of my crew which actually made me really sad =<)  just land a damn rocket on top of its hills. Then I found out that you can quicksave(F5) and try it over and over again until you success(yaayy).
Anyways back to the game, as people says, it indeed has a very steep learning curve. It took me a while to find out what is what how gravity works and how to build a proper rocket. You have to factor in your center of mass, center of thrust and center of lift. Moreover, air resistance must be factored in so your ship wont slow down while going up in the atmosphere. The game is all physics based.
There is a career mode in which you can earn money and reputation as you select missions and accomplishing them. (For example; plant a flag to the moon which gives you 100k money). At first, you will struggle getting into an orbit around earth but you will essentially gain science points by doing experiments and unlocking new components and eventually it will be possible for you to get to Moon. Not only rockets, but also you can build planes which are kinda harder to build since you have to balance it very precisely.
I highly recommend this game if your are patient and love physics based stuff. Very fun game! You won't notice how time flies in this game =P

Broken Age has set out to revive our love for point-and-click adventure games - titles such as Grim Fandango, Monkey Island, and the like.  Have Double Fine delivered on this front?  Personally, the answer is a resounding 'YES'.

:Spoiler free:
16 hours in and I have a pretty good understanding of the story, gameplay, world, characters, mechanics. Not going to discuss the 30 fps lock since devs said it will be fixed soon. So going through the pros and cons of the core game.
Pros :
The World: It's very well done, full of atmosphere, and interesting commentary around every corner. The map is probably about 60-65%? size of GTAV but has far more interiors in the first two ditricts then almost all of GTA combined, so what it lacks in size it makes up for not just being complete window dressing.
Story: It's fantastic so far, you really sympathise with the characters. Which was one of my primary worries, I was afraid a straight up revenge story, as the trailers suggested, would leave me not being able to connect with them. The exception being Vito, whos story we all know.  Luckily the writers hit all the right notes, for me atleast, and I resonated very strongly with Lincoln very quickly.
Gameplay:
Driving is well done for Keyboard and mouse, I havn't tried controller since I havn't felt the need. Unlike GTA were I have a controller plugged in for driving and keyboard and mouse for roaming and shooting. I would still imagine controller would be best though.
Stealth is alittle OP im my opinion, but great fun, I would suggest playing on the hardest difficulty if you want any sort of a challenege. This could just be because I'm still in the early game though and perhaps things havn't ramped up yet.
Underbosses: This is what makes it a Mafia game for me. Would I have liked a traditionally Italian mob story, sure, but the ingrediants are there and I think they fit great. In fact I really like building my personal Mafia from the ground up, with the your underbosses all having differant visions, and the constant head butting and rivalry for territories. The threat of betrayal and consequences, a great dynamic in my opinion.
Music : Really not to much to be said on this front, it's amazing and pulls you deeper into the world, and I find great satisfaction running over people with "Somebody to Love" blasting on the radio
Cons:
Texures: Quality isn't all that great and I do hope that is one of the PC addition updates that 2K might add in the future, but as of now they're just decent. Though the textures aren't the best they actually are made worse by my next con.
FXAA : Or what I assume it to be, If it is, I've never seen FXAA quite so agressive. FXAA generally smudges textures to make them look better, but this cranks it up 11, at times its like playing the game looking through a foggy mirror. Setting this from high to low diminished this for me, but not the degree I would like.
Overall It's a solid game with a few minor issues, one major if you count the 30FPS (Which I'm in that camp aswell, driving in particular has given me a sea sick like nausea at 30 fps) Though the fact that I'm still playing even when it does that, could be used as an endorsement in of itself.

This game! It is addictive. I was hesistant for very long to buy this games and watched the discussions every now and then, but I really didn't expect too much, when I finally purchased it. And was I wrong!
This game isn't your run of the mill space game. It is actually much more like a physics simulator (with some extras... like building up your spaceprogram, unlock new techs, and of course upgrade your facilities). But the core of it really is flight and maneuver planning, learning how the physics in space work on a intuitional, not theoretical level. Want to get to the 'Mun' (yes, no typo)? Burn prograde at the right time und thereby raise the apo of your orbit to an encounter. You want to go further? You better plan in a little gravity assisted slingshot maneuver to save delta-V and make sure you can get home on your fuel. That's it. Not like in other games: get in your ship, fly straight to wherever you want and stop... that is not how maneuvering in space works. It might sound boring, but after a while you find yourself sinking two real life hours to build a rocket, that can lift your precious com-satellite and get it into a stable polar orbit around Minmis without noticing.
It can be frustrating at times, too, granted. Especially when your own stupidity is at fault, returning from your first lunar flyby without a heat shield only noticing it, when you are about to re-enter and can't do anything against that anymore, or forget those damn solar panels (when playing with mods, which make this very good game outstanding, this can easily turn lethal...). And sometimes, when the Kraken attacks... well, that's just bad luck then, I guess.
This is one of the best purchases I ever did. I bought it at discount for 18 €, but it's easily worth the 40 € on which it is right now.

UPD: I finished the game and seriously the gameplay is amazing and this game didn't diserve all the hate that it's got for the microtransactions because these are not needed at all. I finished the game on Nemesis difficulty (highest one) without having any need in any of the lootboxes that I had. I had a ton of legendary gear and legendary followers.
Speaking about the "secret ending": basically to get it you need to take part in sieges (not online), to be exact in 10 stages of sieges which are 3 times 1 siege, 3 times 2 sieges , 3 times 3 sieges and 1 time 4 sieges which are 22 sieges in total. I could say that doing these 22 times in a row one after another in one evening got a tiny bit annoying (its the only thing that I did in chapter 4 because I finished all the sidequests and found all the collecrables). But seeing the ending was worth it because it left a pleasant feel after I watched it and honestly after seeing the ending I felt a bit sorry that I've beaten the game. Once story DLC comes out I'll gladly play it because like Shadow Of Mordor this game is totally fun and you just can't get enough of it. And in case if you are afraid that lootboxes will be a paywall for a "true" ending - don't be. Like I said I didn't even open a ton of boxes that I had because I didn't feel any need in these. At some point you will have more orcs that you can count, legendary or not. But honestly I didn't see that much difference between normal/epic/legendary orcs. They all have weaknesses and strengths and it is always about abusing them. Or dominating all their bodyguards for them to kill their former masters while you hide away because they can one-shot you and you are stressed enough already.
P.S. Speaking about "grinding" that some of you crybabies were afraid of just as much as "paywall" on the game ending - it took me 2 or 3 hours to get the "true" ending. Which is not much of a secret or true or bonus or whatever ending so to speak. Game leaves you at chapter 4 after a short video (at the end of chapter 3) and tells you to defend your forts and after you do it a bunch of times (like I said before) you get the endgame cinematic which finishes the story of Thalion.
Original review:
People complain about grinding.
But it is the game in which it's fun to simply go to a random direction and kill everything you see on your way. So while you enjoy doing so you won't even bother with the word grind.
People complain about microtransactions, saying that they are forced onto you if you want the "true ending" and "endgame".
But "true ending" is a bonus for playing the endgame which you might do because you like killing orcs. Most of people who complain about micotransactions ruining the game won't even bother to finish the story, which is needed for the "endgame" (that's the whole point of the word endgame). When it comes to story progress you would NEVER ever think "Boi I need to buy a lootbox to progress" or "I should invest more into the game to continue playing the story quests".
SoW is a great game which expands on SoM in every aspect. Nemesis system 2.0 is totally fun and feels personal. Combat is tiny little bit reworked compared to the first game - no more oneshot executions after 5 hit combos, now you need to fill up a special bar for it to happen. SoW now has a skill trees and an actual space for character builds. Loot with set bonuses, gear objectives and even sockets. There are daily quests and objectives, online vendetta missions (like in first game) and online siege missions too. Plus there is a sweet little "Photographic mod" which allows you to pause the game and fly around in a freecam taking screenshots with no UI.
In other words if you loved the first game you will love the second. The hate bandwagon this game has is just about people being intimidated by the big price and optional microtransactions, really. People always do that. For example look at how much of a negative impact and downvote spree Bethesda had with Skyrim (back in the day) and Fallout 4 (recently) ingame mod markets and it doesn't make any of these two games bad.

This has to be the most realistic game I've ever played: Alan can't run, Alan can't jump, Alan can't aim, Alan doesn't plan ahead and keeps losing his weapons, Alan is booring, Alan keeps getting into trouble.
Then there's the other side, the unrealistic side where the game keeps spawning enemies just for dificulty sake, where you are punished for exploring, where AI is given an unfair advantage, where you only have the ONE path.
All that make this game very boring and the "It's a horror genre game" excuse doesn't cut it.
I was ready to ditch this game by hour 3 but after so many "It get's better later on" comments, I've completed the game and I can say: THAT'S A COMPLETE LIE! The game only get's more frustrating as it progresses.
Try the demo to see if you like it first, but I can't recommen this game. It's just too frustrating, especially coming from Rockstar.

After playing this game the night before it launched having been extatic about all the hours I was gonna pour into this, Shadow of War unfortunatly leaves much to be desired especially being as cocky as to have an expansion pass which has dlc content not released yet.
That being said this game is definetly a major improvement on it's predecessor with the nemisis system back and better than ever. The sieges are hectic and the best part of the game. They can get really crazy with a bunch or Captains running around and explosions left right and center. The forging your army is definitly one of the highlights of this game and a great marketing technique used by developers, which unfortunatly leads into the controversial "Microtransactions". Yes they can defiantly help you grind through the game in a day or two which is unfortunate. Especially in Act IV. I only stayed with the Silver Chests and the a Mystic chest that I was gifted. I haven't used the Legendary Champions War Party Chest or the Gold chest I got from the Gold edition because my Uruk's died way too fast. I didn't want to risk wasting my Legendary Uruk's so early in the game.
The Uruk's themselves are more varried and have dialogue from very intense sounding, to funny and hysterical. The Nemisis system is improved upon greatly and each Uruk is unique, eerie and awesome looking, to a certain extent where you have so many Uruk's that you will find some same skinned ones.
The story tries desperatly to fit into the imaginative world that J.R.R Tolkien gave us, but with a good try, still manages to come down low. Well, at least not "quick-time event" low. There are alot of things in the story that I had a problem with but without giving too much away, it's hard to comment.
Having said that by developers claiming the game is much harder introducing a difficulty setting was pretty exciting. Still I managed to complete the game in under a week. Having completed the game however I spent most of my time in Act II and alot of my effort and enjoyment comes from there. However I felt that Act's III and IV were rushed and sloppy. I felt that there was no care in what was put in. I also felt that with the inclusion of difficulty settings that there should have been a "New Game Plus". There is not a lot you can do after getting 100% completion besides the repetitive online Vendetta's and Sieges.
It is early on and has only been a week since release but I did run into game breaking bugs with cutscenes being freezed and dialouge skipped. As well as getting stuck during combat and having to leave the mission. I also experienced glitches with the Silver Chests where I got Legendary Uruk's (I only mention that as a glitch because I heard that you can only get them from Gold and Mithril chests which cost real world money). I was happy though with that glitch. All possible to be fixed in future patches.
I didn`t really have a problem with the Standard, Silver, and Gold editions of the game (I am in Canada so it`s priced $80, $100, $130 not counting the $400 Mithril Edition) coming out for pre-order because that what games are nowadays unfortunatly, but leaving out a Cut Region that is in the game but Red and you can`t travel too is ridiculous. As well as the two Orc tribes being left out? The Expansions I get but none of these things are even in the game yet with myslef buying the Gold Edition. I felt betrayed that I spent how much I did on the this and didn`t get my money`s worth.
I do have to recommend this game because it is a solid game. Just a few rants here and there but that is because I care. I am excited with what`s coming out and hope that this game reaches higher grounds.

Now only a few days from release, I can easily say that this game is well worth the high price. Brian Fargo's latest work is a crater-deep, atmospheric tabletop-style game, bringing back the best aspects of Fallout and the original Wasteland while leaving behind the clunky interface. This is what a turn-based RPG should be, what Fallout 3 should have been. This nonlinear game somehow manages to have better storytelling and immersion than games that actually try to pull the player along any kind of linear path. You know how a lot of people advertize their experience as being full of choice and freedom? Here is the game that actually means it. No tutorial, no big opening scene, you get about a minute of instructional dialogue for your first mission and then you can go wherever the hell you like, and the game spontaneously punish you for trying to explore so early, like others might.
Genius turn-based combat system, inventive characters, perfect DnD Campaign fuel, oddly colorful post-apocalyptic world, and a haunting soundtrack to back it all up. I'm definitely gushing, yes, but this is the one experience in an RPG I've had that has been the closest to absolutely flawless.

Nothing is truly scary when you can shoot it in the face, which is why it's bad horror.
Speaking of shooting things in the face, this games combat is not particularly good.  You have to shine a flashlight on your enemies to make them vulnerable, which takes time.  This feels more gimmicky than Dead space's limb-cutting, and far less cathartic, which is why it's not particularly good action either.
It short, it felt like it couldn't make up its goddamn mind.

Very good.  I am quite impressed.  I do recommend Lantern Forge.  (Why it is called that I know not.)  However, the recommendation comes with some... reservations.  That is to say, I have thoroughly enjoyed the game but I'm not sure if some of the things that I have appreciated will go over well with the majority.
Pro's:
- Isometric view.  Check.
- Multi level underground environment.  Check.
- Procedurally generated maps with multiple "biomes."  Check.
- Plot.  Completely absent.
- Sandbox Game with multiple activity types.  Check.
- Quests, missions and side quests.  Completely Absent.
Con's:
- Player pathing is...  well it needs work.
- Player mouse control... I do tend to attack stuff accidently.  A lot.  And by stuff I mean EVERTHING.  Walls Cows Fences...  The move to button is the same as the attack button is the same as the harvest button.  Not so good but not a game breaker.
- Combat.  It works it's just a bit basic.  So if you are looking for a Mine Craft type you will be right at home.  If you want Diablo 4... try Full Mojo Rampage.
Now, by now, I know a lot of you are wondering, "Did Selva say the absence of plot and missions was a good thing?"  Why, yes, I did say that.    See, in my humble opinion, a sandbox game like this doesn’t need narrative elements to be a good game.  It doesn't have to have a "story to tell" to be enjoyable.  So far as I can tell the plot is "You are in a forest.  There are Monsters.  Try not to starve to death."  From there, you do what you bloody like.  Wish to be a nomadic hunter?  Good on you.  Want to build a town or a farm?  Go for it.  Want to dig deep into the ground searching for rare minerals or dungeons?  Just do it.  You do not need some NPC telling you to do these things, or when or how many of these things to do.  That's your business.  No one else's.  To many modern games get caught up in having to tell a story.  It's good top know that some game makers haven't forgotten that the stories came later.  So, yes, not burdening the player with Narrative and structured quests missions etc, is a good thing.
Thanks for listening.

First of all, I'd like to say that story and story missions have been entertaining and the open world, while not that large, is fun to explore. But there are many technical issues that drag this game down.
Graphics.
Since at release Mafia 3 is locked at 30 fps it's not a smooth experience. Game's textures seem really low res and everything is very blurry. That is probably to mask textures and help with aliasing. Also the options menu is basic and offers little for tweaking settings. And there are no texture options. Looks like everything is identical to console versions graphics wise.
Also I don't know what the hell is wrong with game's lighting system but driving around during the day I got a few seconds of "sunny" lighting followed by "overcast" and back again and it kept repeating. I thought that had something to do with clouds but they never moved. Never happened during story missions, just when doing open world stuff. Also the skybox is quite poor.
On top of all that sometimes I had strange graphical artifacts follow me around.
There's a minor thing with peoples' eyes. They are very reflective and I find them really creepy looking.
So overall there's a lot of things to fix in patches. It is weird though, sometimes the game looks great and other times it's a blurry, shiny, reflective mess.
Gameplay.
Glad to say that the actual gameplay is solid. Cover works like it should, shooting is nice, silent takedowns are brutal, everything pretty much works.
Driving feels okay. Tried switching between Normal and Simulation driving modes and Simulation feels a bit better for me. Cars felt like they had more weight that way. Very similar to Mafia 2 or GTA IV (less so).
Now what bugged me was the stealth system. You crouch a bit and suddenly you're almost invisible. It takes time for unaware enemies to notice you. There's an "awareness" indicator which fills up after a few seconds and that is plenty of time to go around knocking people out. And if you're spotted and run away, everyone forgets about you after they search the spot you were last seen.
Sound.
From what I heard, music and voice acting are great and so are other sounds except cars. Some cars sound really cheap and "one note" and have no subtlety.
Overall.
There is a fun game in there if you like open world games and can ignore technical problems. Personally, I would not recommend it as it is now.

The easiest way to describe this game is imagine Mafia 2 mixed with Assassins Creed Syndicate set in New Orleans 1968.
While it makes for a great game it unfortunately loses a little of what made Mafia unique in a sea of GTA clones, such as being wanted for what you are wearing (you can't even change clothes as far as Ive played), or license plates being wanted. There are car upgrades but they are universal. You dont have a garage (as far as ive played) to modify cars looks or store them. Police presence is tamed down quite a bit and they havent hassled me once for a traffic violation. It doesn't look like you can bribe them at all (as far as Ive played at least).
The story is really unique, the setting and world is incredibly detailed, the original and licensed soundtracks are phenomenal, the driving (on simulation mode at least) is good fun, and the shootouts feel visceral.
Minor tech issues aside on PC,  I'd say its worth a buy to anyone interested in an open world crime game with a unique setting. Just dont expect anything other than the story and setting to be significantly different/better than any other open world game out there.

text:
I was in the middle of a 10 pages review when I accidentally kicked the power cord and the computer turned off. So I'll make this brief.
Yes, I recommend it. Buy the game.
Strong point: story. Very clever and surprising.
Broken Age ditched all those verbs from the first adventure games. I think that's actually an advance, these things always felt hacky, sometimes there were redundant verbs and you never knew exactly what to do, do I USE a door or OPEN it? Eventually the verbs shrunk to less actions, like full throttle's intuitive wheel. But it was still questionable, what does HAND means I'll do? punch? pick it up? OK, I am glad we got over that but the fact is that more options than simply clicking gives more dimensions to the puzzles and Broken Age feels easy and linear in the puzzle department. Maybe there's a sweet spot between plain click and verbs that makes sense.
I may be swimming against the stream here but I don't like the voice acting. It's not bad acting though, I think they don't know how to deliver Tim Shafer's very dry humor writing, everything sounds like a children's cartoon and it's not as funny as it could be.
UPDATE FOR EPISODE 2:
Everything I said before still holds but I want to make an extra comment on the voice acting. I HATE VELLA'S VOICE. Most of the voices are pretty bad, missing the jokes and all, but serviceable, except hers goes the extra mile and makes me hate the parts of the game I have to play as her. It's like they wrote all of Vella's lines in a book and had someone read it to children as bedtime story, recorded it, and called it voice acting. It's bad. Really, really bad.
I still like the story. It got a little messy and confusing near the end though (still better than several classic adventure games). There were some clever puzzles. I laughed on occasion. Besides my dislike for the voice acting (and hatred for Vella's voice in particular) it's a good adventure game.
