This game looks as though it could be entertaining from the screenshots/video, so when it came on sale I was tempted to buy it as I like a craft/build em up.
The problem is that it's just a little bit boring. There is no real 'survival' element to it, it's just very much about collecting resources and creating what quickly becomes an impenetrable 'home' to save you from the few easily avoided monsters that are kicking around on the surface.
Underground is essentially more of the same, just with different items/resources to collect.
There's no reason to upgrade your 'home' other than making it look prettier (aside from the crafting stations) and building is limited to a single story, unless you go underground. There are oceans, there is no point to advancing that I am aware of and eventually, there is no point in playing because you feel like you've seen everything that's on offer.
If you like creative only games; there are better ones. If you like survival-builder games, there are better ones.

Alan Wake is less a horror game and more of a story experience. The horror aspects are all but lost unless you are playing on the hardest difficulty, which takes two or three playthroughs to unlock, and the difference is palpable.
On anything but nightmare mode, a shadowy man will pop out on occasion and after going shine shine shine, glack glack glack, the threat is gone and you can continue with the story. On nightmare mode the game is completely different. Hordes of shadowy abominations of our reality will pour from the woods while you desperately sprint towards the next pinprick of light only to have it wink out as you near it. Then you pop a flare and continue the full tilt sprint to the next shining becon of hope, only for Wake to get tired and then get an axe in the back of his head.
Nightmare mode seems to be the way the game was MEANT to be played, but you can't access it without 2 other plythroughs, which is simply asking too much. Personally I play through a game once and am done with it unless theres some crazy alternate endings that I HAVE to get, wich there aren't here. Which brings me to the story.
Alan Wake's story is a cross between Stephen King and Twin Peaks, with a heavy dose of lovecraft mixed in. I will not spoil anything in this, but the story is truly the best aspect of this game. It keeps the player thinking about what will happen next and where this♥♥♥♥♥♥storm of nightmares will end up.
In the end, Alan Wake is not a particularly scary game, unless played on the highest difficulty. The story and immersion are it's strong points, but one playthrough is probably enough, unless you are a completionist, then this game has plenty for you in the forms of thermoses scattered around the playing areas. This game is a definite 8/10, nothing♥♥♥♥♥♥your-pants amazing, but still enough that everyone should play it one time through.

Have difficulties rating this game. On the one hand I think this game is an improvement over the last game. On the other hand it has some flaws which I dont remember from the last game.
The nemesis system is still the strong point of the game. It has been expanded upon so you can now be betrayed so a Captain switches sides. Another funny addition is when you are suddenly attacked by a Captain which can be very inconvenient at times. This makes it interesting although after a while you will become used to it.
The bad side of the Nemesis system is that it will be possible to engage captains which are (almost) impossible to kill or turn to the Bright Lord. The strenghts and weaknesses are chosen at random but sometimes this leads to a Captain which has such a niche of chances to be drowned of health that it feels impossible. Expected this in end game but even half through the game this can occur.
When looking at the skill tree and the fighting system at such there are some nice improvements made to the system but there are also some things that are less likeable. When fighting a group of Orcs in the previous game it was possible to fight off a group of Orcs, countering Orcs and then strike the Captain within the fight and it was possible to keep most of your health. In this game however the symbols of counter are eather shown to short for me or the system doesnt allow me to engage in counter quickly enough when Im in the middle of striking another opponent. This can make it very frustrating to fight and the choice is often to just run away and come back health replenished instead of having the option of slaughtering the orcs as in SOM.
Another point of frustration is the parkour elements. The level design sometimes stops me from running further with only a little elevation in sight. It makes you go into a full stop to go into climb mode to advance. Some elements wont even permit this and only stop you without any evidince of why this object is any different. Not a show stopper but more of an annoyance.
Last point of concern is the levelling system. I am not opposed to a levelling system as this is an action RPG but the levelling feels completely useless. It's the same uselessness that is prevelant in games like Borderlands. You keep on levelling but enemies level as well with gear levelling at the same pace. For me the levelling doesnt add anything to the game with the randomness of the loot being just another useless micro management task added without any value. A system like Fallout 4 without any gear levelling but a crafting system would have been preferable
Don't think the game would be very different without loot crates. As gear is attainable through regular gameplay regardless of using loot crates it doesnt matter that these exist. With Daily quest objectives it is even possible to attain the payable loot crates. There is no pay-2-win applicable as far as I can judge. The main bad thing on the loot crates is that these exist in the market which takes a time to load with buying and opening stuff taking additional time.
The bigger map with different areas is one of the better steps that Monolith has taken. Dont really mind a smaller map but having the option to switch region makes it more fun. It allows for a new environment to explore with it's own eco system. This last thing might be improved upon as well. For the progression it's probably decided to not let orcs get from one area to another but for immersion it would be preffered if it was possible. It would be nice to get a fully levelled Orc from one area with mad skills to another area for a castle siege.
This was the thing that got me to buy this game. To play the sequal to the much loved SOM was already awesome but being able to raid a castle makes it even better. The fun of the castle siege however isn't as big as I expected. Conquering a castle means occupying certain points for a period of time after which you can challenge the Overlord of the castle. This then brings you to the main hall of the castle surrounded by the Overlord and his closest friends. The ability to ammend your conquering force is possible by adding some upgrades, but it is more limited than I had hoped. There is no strategy possible by holding certain forces back to open the gates yourself preventing defense mechanisms to cut your forces way back. The stealth approach to the castle siege isnt something that has been possible yet. I have some reservation here as I am in Act II of IV and this might be possible further in the game.
It's a good game. The thing is I was hoping for an excellent game or an extra ordinary game. Got hopes up and feel a bit disappointed. It doesnt make it a bad game but leaves some items to be desired for that could have made this so much more. As Steam doesnt allow nuance it's only Yes or No. In this case I have chosen No to allow the negative review readers to read some nuance instead of only loot boxes are bad.

I hate to write a bad review on this because the devs have obviously poured their heart and soul into this game.  But to be completely honest, it tries to emulate so many games that it doesn't know what it wants to be.  Basically you start in the woods with nothing and have to survive, build things, and explore dungeons.  Sounds good on paper, but all parts of it are bare-bones and nothing is really fleshed out.
It doesn't focus on the survival like Don't Starve
It doesn't focus on the sandbox stuff like Minecraft/Terraria
It doesn't focus on the dungeon-crawling like Torchlight/Diablo
It's got incomplete bits of all of those without specializing or expanding any of those and it ends up as kind of a bland, forgettable mess. It gives a bad impression right from the start with the controls. It has "W" moving you towards the cursor...but no full WASD controls, which it SORELY needs. Gathering resources has a pretty crazy range, so you'll find yourself chopping trees/grass/rocks from 10 feet away with the same bland animation, which makes it feel really bad as well.
The survival aspects aren't challenging at all.  Night brings monsters, but you can easily craft a bed.  Once it's crafted, you just need to right clock and bam...no more night.  Food is insanely easy to craft as well.  There might as well not even be Hunger and Fatigue meters because they're ridiculously easy to get filled and move on. There's no point in the sandbox stuff because there's no multiplayer and thus no one to ever really see or use what you've built.
And the dungeon crawler stuff is pretty limited to clunky-feeling combat in one of the 'big 3' paths of melee/ranged/magic, where splitting between them just hurts you in the long run.
So in the end, it's really repetitive/grindy and I'd say avoid it, unfortunately.

I remember when I was younger, back when I used to play games on the Xbox360...those were the dark days, but there was this one game that I got for my birthday that really stuck-out in my Xbox collection, and that game was Alan Wake.  I friggin' loved this game when it came out, and was my favorite game during the time the game was released.  Alan Wake does something really well, and that's atmosphere.  Atmosphere is the game's strongpoint, and it takes this strong point and uses this for most of the game.  Alan Wake is great at making creepy dark forests super creepy, with its fantastic grasp at writing and gameplay.
Now, the story for this game heavily borrows from Steven King's style of both writing and characters.  Apparently, the writers for this game have a real hard-on for Steven King, so-much-so that they name-dropped the man in the very first line of the game!  Steven King was obviously a very big inspiration for this game's existance, it even has the same stories as most of Steven King's books like: The Mist, Misery, Bag of Bones, and other books that are the same!
I've always loved the concept for this game; a Steven King-inspired horror game about a writer fighting forces of darkness, and to fight the darkness, he must shine light on the dark creatures with a flashlight and then shoot it with any weapon he happens to have at the time.  It's a somewhat fun and intense gameplay mechanic that makes fighting the baddies a fight for your life.  It's kind of an iconic image, seeing a man in a hoodie, with a flashlight shooting men with darkness coming out of their asses.  I never get tired of shooting these guys in the face with a shotgun, and I feel like the weapons handle so satisyingly.  It feels so damn good to shoot these guys!!  Even after all of these years of not playing Alan Wake, this never gets old!  Other reviewers would disagree with me on this one, as most people feel like the shooting these guys gets boring after a while, but not with me, I love shooting these bad guys.
And then there's the writing that I keep raving about.  If you've played the Max Payne games (which I have), you should feel right at home with this, as this game was made by the same guys who wrote and designed Max Payne 1&2.  The narration and the names Alan Wake and Max Payne are two names that are both fitting for both of these characters.  Alan is about waking up, and Max is about pain.  Hell, there's even an easter egg that features James MacCaffrey, who is the voice of Max Payne who makes a voice appearence in one of the game's many manuscript pages.
I dunno, I just really like this game.  Yeah, the characters' faces look like they've been violently run over by a truck.  Yeah, the references are very blatant.  Yeah, sometimes it feels like the game is trying too hard to be a Steven King-themed masterpiece.  Yeah, this game was a bit too hyped.  And yeah, this game can be kinda pretentious in the way of its writing, but I still love this game.
It's a great game that is intelligent, fun and it has a hard-on for Steven King, and that's why I recommend this game.

Where to start... The game is awesome. I'm an early backer and I've played every beta that has been released, as far through as I can. Many of the bugs/issues noted by previous reviewers just simply aren't there anymore so a lot of the Cons of the reviewers just aren't correct.
If you loved the original wasteland and you like turn based combat and actual movement strategy (think X-Com where if you move the wrong position you're toast) and a place where choices have real consequences then you will love this game. If you like all action and no brains then don't get this game. While it isn't a deep cerebral game, you do have to think about the solutions to problems (there are almost always two solutions or more to every problem). The isometric view isn't for some people but for those of us who came from the original world of RPG's it's an old friend that gives you a better view of the battlefield.
Some in-depth points. This is a deep story and if you played the original you will appreciate a lot of the subtle humor. The NPC's almost all have a background - you don't though and you don't ever "grow" into a personalilty with a back story. I happen to like this approach where you get to explore your world without worrying about yourself too much. However, almost every path through the story will shape how other people view you and it will either help you accomplish missions or make it much more difficult.
Pros: Everything. Basically if I was going to wait for a sequel then I would want it to be this.
I don't really have any Cons for this game. Everything is beautiful and well done. It is a very replayable game (I've mapped out about 9 different paths that I want to (or have tried) try. In addition sometimes having certain NPC's with your party allows you to unlock areas or conversation paths that you could not otherwise discover.
The team did a great job and I hope to write up a complete walkthrough in addition to the getting started guide which I'll update once the game goes live.

This is a fantastic, well-made, pretty accurate game. I'm impressed with how thorough and expansive this game is. I'm not here to criticize this, as in my almost 20 hours this week of this game I have only found one pressing issue. I just want to give some suggestions to potentially better the game. Pretty fantastic idea, having custom characters btw.
1. Add the option for a third-party candidate.
Maybe create a conglomeration of parties for this? Libertarian, Green, and normal Independent. This could add an interesting and fun alternative to the normal process.
2. Add debates! This would add such a fun and potentially game-changing aspect to the election cycle. You could put the option on the game setup screen, where you could set the number of debates from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of say, 6?
3. I don't know how practical it would be so this is a tentative suggestion. Maybe add an option for a three-way election? Pit all three parties (assuming you add a third party) against each other! Or two of one party against one of another! Or three people from the same party! Just a cool thought, if you couldn't implement it that's understandable.
4. Make the point system for issues better. This is my one issue with the game. When creating a custom character, there are 20+ issues that you only have 100 points to spread over. Maybe lessen issues, or add more points, or make it require less points to strongly be for or against an issue. It's not game-ruining, but it can get a bit frustrating when trying to truly customize a character.
5. This is to potentially help diversify gameplay even more. Maybe, when you get the option to randomize issue importance, have a customize option? I'd understand if you don't allow games with customized issue importance to go on leaderboards or something (too easy to tailor issues for you to win) but I think it would add a cool element to elections. For example, I made an Abraham Lincoln and Jefferson Davis character and have been trying to randomize issues to include Ending Human Trafficking, BlackLivesMatter, and Confederate Flag Display, or issues related to the civil war. Obviously, with the depth of issues in the game it's nearly impossible to get the election centered around exactly what I want, and it made me think of adding that kind of option.
So that's it. I think this is an amazing game, and I'll be playing it a lot in the months to come. Hope my review and suggestions helped!

There are many things I can say about this game. It is technically functional. It is nominally playable.
It is not, by any metric, much fun.
If you really want to slum it with some bottom-barrel commerical-grade rpgmaker titles, might I recommend City of Chains? It's by the same developer, using the same stock tileset, and it's markedly better in every way. CoC is worth the .60 cents on sale. This...is not.
All Outrage's buzzwords sound like good things. Party-building, dungeon crawling, cyberpunk roguelike should mean you're in for a delicious hamburger of a game, but the chef's only moderately skilled and the materials they're cooking with are extremely subpar. Every portrait and texture in the game has an ugly-stick-shaped dent in its face. The menu colors are garish, and the dialog prompt that lets you navigate the dungeon feels more restrictive than novel.
The plot is a loose, somewhat context-less string of happenings wherein your characters shoot a billionaire in the head because he's trying to be a vigilante. Which *they* already are.
I guess the moral event horizon is when you start using a robot suit for your vigilanteism?
Game balance is a tenative step in the right direction, with different classes of weapons all being sidegrades from each other, and with the player nominally having to balance high damage bullet-use against low-damage melee attacks. but even on the harder difficulty levels there's more grind than actual challenge. And in a nominally plot-driven game, the plot simply isn't good enough to incentivize putting up with that.
If you want something done in a much* better fashion with the same stock tileset, I suggest you pick up City of Chains.
Otherwise, give this one a miss.
*which is to say, somewhat.

So after much thought over the past few days I thought I would write a review for this game, and I figured I would start it off right:
Broken Age is nostalgia, artistic, creative, and so much more wrapped up into a game. The even better news: it is only Act 1.
Now I grew up on point and click adventures. They were the first games I was ever introduced to as a kid, and they have a special place in my heart. Ironically Secrets of Monkey Island was my first introduction to this simple, yet entertaining genre of games. So when I was shocked to find that Tim Schafer, a creative mind behind Secrets of Monkey Island, was directing this game, it made me jump for joy! I just had to see what this game was about, and I am glad I did.
Broken Age is not like many other point and click games I have played before, in such that it has a dual story line, following two main character: Shay, and Vella. Shay, is quite, wity, and just looking for adventure while stuck on the incubation ship he calls home. While Vella on the other hand is adventerous, and always curious about her life style. The two characters are set up with a dual story line, which is said to intertwine, ad little hints are given as such as to how they do so as you play through each storyline.
Now I will sadly stop with the character/story description to prevent from spoiling stuff as for I don't think it is right of me to destroy the beautiful twist that has been given to end Act 1.
The gameplay though is what is important here, and it is phenonmenal. Was great to start up and see that classic cross hairs pointer on the screen, you are kindly greeted in both storylines to the beautiful sound track and voice acting as well. The music flows throughout the game, and is calming yet exciting. The voice acting is amazing as well with an allstar cast from talents like Jack Black, Elijah Wood, and Wil Wheaton, all who play the parts of their characters so well it is clearly obvious whoever chose the voice actors had some clear insight into who they wanted. Both games start you off with simple puzzles, one that are semi tedious, but are welcome and inviting due to the wity storyline that goes with each one. After those beginning ones the puzzles pick up a bit, with some work and strategizing going in as to how to solve each one, and ideas as to what items would be needed in order to do so. The entire time you are running around though the enviornments themselves are extremely interactive, and are witty, with voice acting and small quirks seeming to be at every turn.
All in all Broken Age manages to do what I think many point and click games I have played in the last few years have struggled to do. It has beautiful art, and exciting storyline that has a mysterious edge, beautifully done voice acting, and gameplay which is so simple yet so beautifully executed. I enjoyed every minute of this game thus far, and I am even more xcited to play Act 2.

Have difficulties rating this game. On the one hand I think this game is an improvement over the last game. On the other hand it has some flaws which I dont remember from the last game.
The nemesis system is still the strong point of the game. It has been expanded upon so you can now be betrayed so a Captain switches sides. Another funny addition is when you are suddenly attacked by a Captain which can be very inconvenient at times. This makes it interesting although after a while you will become used to it.
The bad side of the Nemesis system is that it will be possible to engage captains which are (almost) impossible to kill or turn to the Bright Lord. The strenghts and weaknesses are chosen at random but sometimes this leads to a Captain which has such a niche of chances to be drowned of health that it feels impossible. Expected this in end game but even half through the game this can occur.
When looking at the skill tree and the fighting system at such there are some nice improvements made to the system but there are also some things that are less likeable. When fighting a group of Orcs in the previous game it was possible to fight off a group of Orcs, countering Orcs and then strike the Captain within the fight and it was possible to keep most of your health. In this game however the symbols of counter are eather shown to short for me or the system doesnt allow me to engage in counter quickly enough when Im in the middle of striking another opponent. This can make it very frustrating to fight and the choice is often to just run away and come back health replenished instead of having the option of slaughtering the orcs as in SOM.
Another point of frustration is the parkour elements. The level design sometimes stops me from running further with only a little elevation in sight. It makes you go into a full stop to go into climb mode to advance. Some elements wont even permit this and only stop you without any evidince of why this object is any different. Not a show stopper but more of an annoyance.
Last point of concern is the levelling system. I am not opposed to a levelling system as this is an action RPG but the levelling feels completely useless. It's the same uselessness that is prevelant in games like Borderlands. You keep on levelling but enemies level as well with gear levelling at the same pace. For me the levelling doesnt add anything to the game with the randomness of the loot being just another useless micro management task added without any value. A system like Fallout 4 without any gear levelling but a crafting system would have been preferable
Don't think the game would be very different without loot crates. As gear is attainable through regular gameplay regardless of using loot crates it doesnt matter that these exist. With Daily quest objectives it is even possible to attain the payable loot crates. There is no pay-2-win applicable as far as I can judge. The main bad thing on the loot crates is that these exist in the market which takes a time to load with buying and opening stuff taking additional time.
The bigger map with different areas is one of the better steps that Monolith has taken. Dont really mind a smaller map but having the option to switch region makes it more fun. It allows for a new environment to explore with it's own eco system. This last thing might be improved upon as well. For the progression it's probably decided to not let orcs get from one area to another but for immersion it would be preffered if it was possible. It would be nice to get a fully levelled Orc from one area with mad skills to another area for a castle siege.
This was the thing that got me to buy this game. To play the sequal to the much loved SOM was already awesome but being able to raid a castle makes it even better. The fun of the castle siege however isn't as big as I expected. Conquering a castle means occupying certain points for a period of time after which you can challenge the Overlord of the castle. This then brings you to the main hall of the castle surrounded by the Overlord and his closest friends. The ability to ammend your conquering force is possible by adding some upgrades, but it is more limited than I had hoped. There is no strategy possible by holding certain forces back to open the gates yourself preventing defense mechanisms to cut your forces way back. The stealth approach to the castle siege isnt something that has been possible yet. I have some reservation here as I am in Act II of IV and this might be possible further in the game.
It's a good game. The thing is I was hoping for an excellent game or an extra ordinary game. Got hopes up and feel a bit disappointed. It doesnt make it a bad game but leaves some items to be desired for that could have made this so much more. As Steam doesnt allow nuance it's only Yes or No. In this case I have chosen No to allow the negative review readers to read some nuance instead of only loot boxes are bad.

I wish there was a neutral review but there isn't so it's going to be negative.
The game expands a lot on the first one: adding drakes, sieges, orc clans, gear system, skill branching, arenas etc. and by itself it's a good thing. The problem is that while expanding it doesn't really improve much. For example:
- Gear system seems great but feels really weird since you'll be changing your equipment a lot and therefore won't be able to stick to a single prefered build over long time. As you level up, the sword you liked so much for it's passives will become weak and you will either have to change it for something with a different passive that might be completely useless for you, but with higher damage or stick with what you got and accept the fact you'll have to smack orcs for twice as long.
- Orc clans at first glance bring diversity to the game, but when you'll realise that for you to get a complete set of prefered legendary gear you need a very specific set of orcs it becomes a nightmare. In my game i really wanted to get a dark legendary set, but there are simply no dark orcs around: plenty of marauders, warmongers and machine orcs but next to no dark orcs. Having spent 50 hours ingame (at the time of writing this review) i still have not seen a single dark tank and as a result i can't get the legendary chestplate i want. At the same time during my playthrough i met 8 gluttonous ologs that were from the same clan and looked EXACTLY the same.
- Skill branching seemed like a great idea at first, but after reading every single variation for every single skill i understood that there will be only one set of skills and their mods that i will ever use, and i was right. Around level 25 i had everything i would ever need and after that i was just blindly spending skill points for whatever got under my mouse.
- Arenas got to be a great addition though, right? I remember enjoying improvised fights that Uruk's Hollow made for his youtube channel, so these arenas have got to be great. Nope. Most of the time orcs in the arena either just stand and watch each other or they repeat the same move again and again. Watching a fight of two destroyers is just infuriating to no end. You meet an orc and he is just a killing machine: he swings and hacks at you with immense vigour and, surely, abnormal strength, there is just no end to his attacks and they are all varied too - he uses hooks, throws axes, goes for combo attacks, summons a cursed dagger and teleports behind your back with it. So OF COURSE you'll make him work for you and try him in the arena..... just to watch him stand around most of the time, throwing basic attacks from time to time.
- Drakes are awesome though. No argument there.
I also should probably mention that there is, once again, no FOV slider in the game and some actions can't be rebinded to a separate button. For example:
- no matter what you do "jump down" and "dominate" will be on a same button which is a pain given there is ledge domination and archers standing on roofs that you might want to dominate while near them (while also near a roof edge))
- "dismount", "kill and dismount" and "special ranged attack" are on the same button regardless of what you want (too bad if you accidentaly kill your drake while trying to make it spit fire)
- "drain" and "stun" are on the same button no matter what (want to fill that HP of yours? sure here's an orc. how about you stun him 17 times instead of draining?)
It's also importand to understand that I really want to like this game, and i certainly do, from time to time. But the longer i play it the more frustration i feel while playing it. If i were to write this review 20 hours of gametime ago - it'd be positive, because frustration from all the little things wouldn't have accumulated yet. It's great till end of act 2 and all downhill from there.

UPDATE - 21.05.17 - This game is to be seen as *finished* but alas, there are many of us who beleive it was released in an unfinished state - whether or not that is a true statement it is a personal opinion - this review is still a possitive one - cheers
First impressions:
Oh god! not another clone!!!
But then i decided to take a risk (well, at 6 quid, why not?)
And it paid off, BIG TIME!
Yes, it is another one of those clones! But wait...
Pros:
Farming: you can find, harvest and plant your own food, plants, trees for survival, build materials and profit.
Building: You can build hundreds of items, such as a bed (which binds you to the bed's location), tools, weapons, armor, decorations, cookers, smelter, labs, workbenches, the list is almost endless!
Fighting and Leveling: you can build weapons to fight mobs, roam throug dungeons, etc. You can level up with skill trees and stats (yes, its an RPG GAME WOOHOOO!!!!)
Exploring: You can explore a vast, open world (yes, it has a border, but i haven't reached it yet) it has various biomes in one world (dessert, snow, tropics, fairy land, forests etc) you can walk for hours in one direction and not reach the edge.
Shops and Buildings: You can build a town centre, shops, houses, paths etc.
Enchanting and Potions: You can build enchantments and *sockets* for your armor and weapons, you can build potions to help you survive.
Cons:
I don't see these as Cons in a sense, but...
Exploration: You can walk hours in one direction and not reache the resources you actually need (it is a randomised world each time)
No Tutorial (as such): you come into the game completley *Naked* you don't know anything about it, most of it is trial and error/survive or die, although there is a *lip service* tutorial in the main menu.
Random Mobs: The reason why this would be a con is because, when you start your first world, you might spawn right next to a bees nest, and die horribaly... Also, once you figure out how to build and use a staircase (going down) you might land right on top of a goblin barracks in the centre of a dungeon.
Final thoughts:
All in all, an amazing game, not many faults to it appart from those listed.
If you don't like taking risks, there is always the demo on the dev's website, but please, please, please take the risk! you will be rewarded! :D

I remember when I was younger, back when I used to play games on the Xbox360...those were the dark days, but there was this one game that I got for my birthday that really stuck-out in my Xbox collection, and that game was Alan Wake.  I friggin' loved this game when it came out, and was my favorite game during the time the game was released.  Alan Wake does something really well, and that's atmosphere.  Atmosphere is the game's strongpoint, and it takes this strong point and uses this for most of the game.  Alan Wake is great at making creepy dark forests super creepy, with its fantastic grasp at writing and gameplay.
Now, the story for this game heavily borrows from Steven King's style of both writing and characters.  Apparently, the writers for this game have a real hard-on for Steven King, so-much-so that they name-dropped the man in the very first line of the game!  Steven King was obviously a very big inspiration for this game's existance, it even has the same stories as most of Steven King's books like: The Mist, Misery, Bag of Bones, and other books that are the same!
I've always loved the concept for this game; a Steven King-inspired horror game about a writer fighting forces of darkness, and to fight the darkness, he must shine light on the dark creatures with a flashlight and then shoot it with any weapon he happens to have at the time.  It's a somewhat fun and intense gameplay mechanic that makes fighting the baddies a fight for your life.  It's kind of an iconic image, seeing a man in a hoodie, with a flashlight shooting men with darkness coming out of their asses.  I never get tired of shooting these guys in the face with a shotgun, and I feel like the weapons handle so satisyingly.  It feels so damn good to shoot these guys!!  Even after all of these years of not playing Alan Wake, this never gets old!  Other reviewers would disagree with me on this one, as most people feel like the shooting these guys gets boring after a while, but not with me, I love shooting these bad guys.
And then there's the writing that I keep raving about.  If you've played the Max Payne games (which I have), you should feel right at home with this, as this game was made by the same guys who wrote and designed Max Payne 1&2.  The narration and the names Alan Wake and Max Payne are two names that are both fitting for both of these characters.  Alan is about waking up, and Max is about pain.  Hell, there's even an easter egg that features James MacCaffrey, who is the voice of Max Payne who makes a voice appearence in one of the game's many manuscript pages.
I dunno, I just really like this game.  Yeah, the characters' faces look like they've been violently run over by a truck.  Yeah, the references are very blatant.  Yeah, sometimes it feels like the game is trying too hard to be a Steven King-themed masterpiece.  Yeah, this game was a bit too hyped.  And yeah, this game can be kinda pretentious in the way of its writing, but I still love this game.
It's a great game that is intelligent, fun and it has a hard-on for Steven King, and that's why I recommend this game.

After some extensive play, I'm going to give it a thumbs up.  The graphics are awesome, I loved the different biomes that made each game unique.
There were minor bugs that were usually corrected by restarting the game.  Some gameplay issues I saw that would make things more enjoyable:
1. Give us access to a starter weapon like a stone sword.  The first few minutes can be rough until you start mining and collect copper/copper forge.
2. There's too much ground clutter.  You could cut the amount of rocks/twigs/trees by 75% and there would still be plenty. This would also encourage people to plant all those saplings that drop.
3. Slow down the leveling process.  I found myself constantly fighting stuff way below my skill level by the time I got enough ore to create the next level pickaxe.  For example, a little while ago  I was level 14 and trying to scrape up enough iron to make an iron pickaxe.  Slow it down so we have time to explore each level, gear up, and be fighting mobs our own level.
4. Portals.  I love the idea, but you have to mine down ten levels to get to the silver you need to create them.  That's a lot of load times.  Maybe make them accessable earlier in gameplay so by the time the player gets to level five and starts getting sick of the load screen, they have access to it?
5. Loading map deaths.  Most of my deaths seem to occur when the game lags while loading a map.
The above are little complaints.  I still recommend this game and can't wait to see what comes next.

Running on Linux, with the radeonsi driver.
Both of my xinput controllers didn't work at all in this game, and the controller/resolution configuration menu that starts before the game had approximately 40 entries for "Cancel", all mapped identically. This configuration menu actually detected both of my controllers, but they were completely useless in-game, so I was forced to use the mouse.
Gameplay with the mouse wasn't honestly bad. I was surprised. it ended up like a mashup of SNES Mario Paint's "Fly Swatter" game, along with Space Invaders and hints of Galaxian thrown in.
There are graphical issues. All the models are pink until they explode in to pretty little triangles, then they look like they're supposed to. I'm not sure if this is different in other drivers, but on radeonsi, every enemy (and your ship) are just pink shapes.
The game has a REALLY uneven difficulty curve. First level is a cakewalk for even the most inexperienced gamer. Second level is noticeably more difficult, and level three is impossible if you don't have the right upgrades. it keeps getting harder after that, to the point that I wondered aloud how someone would actually be able to play this game well with a gamepad; it'd be End-of-Ikaruga hard by Level 4.
All of the above stated, it was less than a dollar when I bought it. How can I not recommend it? I've received less entertainment giving street performers/buskers $2 coins than I have from this game so far. I'll likely play it a lot, even with the glaring problems. I just wish it didn't have the problems.

A story game with an original plot!  Although the hero has a special power, the story is set in what often seems like the everyday life of school. An immersive world, that takes you in. Although in my play through a character died, I left it that way, and did not replay it to save the character by following the 'correct' choices in a walkthrough, as I wanted the feel of keeping to my choices.  Yet, the 'choices' are not always clear to the player as the developers would have liked, given that the short phrases for each choice undercommunicate what each implies.  If you are looking for something different from an action game, give this one a try.  Thank you to the developers.  It's a great gaming experience.

Wasteland 2 is a throwback but it never feels outdated. The interface definitely needs some work but overall, it is an involving experience. The tactical combat feels similar to what XCOM did recently. It is satisfyingly brutal and also quite challenging. I love that your choices are impactful, and if one of the followers you pick up along the way dies, they stay perished unless you revive them in time. This makes for tense battles akin to old-school rpg's.
The graphics are smooth and polished, with some pretty great colors and lighting. You will come across a wide range of environments and npc's. Enemies vary from infected violent animals to trigger happy raiders, environments from vibrant woods to dreary basements and "dungeons". There is a lot to take in here, and that is quite refreshing to see.
Overall, with some polish and feedback taken, this game would be a breath of fresh air and surprisingly so. It feels quite derivative at times, but all of the pieces fit together masterfully. I would reccomend this to any rpg fan.

This is the first RPGMaker game I actually liked.

This game feels unfinished. First the good: The combat is fun (although simple), and the RPG mechanics give it a little extra flavor that other similar games lack. Now, the bad.
- There is only one surface level, so you can't build 2-story houses.
- There's no reason to explore the surface. Anything you find there can be found underground. But the surface is featureless anyway. The only terrain feature is water, and it just acts like another tile type.
- Farming is fairly useless, because you will always have plenty of food from killing enemies.
- There may be 100 levels underground, but when they are all the same, what's the point? I've gotten down to about level 50, and haven't seen much different from the first 10 levels.
- Combat isn't balanced, Mages will kill you a lot quicker than you can close on them.
- Pathing is terrible. You character is constantly getting stuck on corners in the tunnels and on small trees on the surface.
- No WASD movement. (Seriously guys?)
- There's no reason to build a house. Monsters attack at night, but you can use a bed to instantly turn it to day time, so you never really have to face the night.
So, that's my opinion. I hope the game gets better, because it is kind of charming, but right now I simply can't recommend it. This game really should have been labelled as early access.

I'm going to start this off with the TL;DR version of my review:  BUY THIS GAME.
For those folks still reading, here is why you need this game.
I am a twenty-something year old gamer. If you are too, and you grew up playing a lot of the old school PC rpgs, you will fall right in love with Lantern Forge. Don't get me wrong, gamers of all ages can find something to love about this game, but in my opinion it hearkens back to the days of yore. Those days of RPG classics such as Diablo, Diablo II, Ultima VII, Ultima Online, etc. It has taken elements of all those games and mixed them in a pot with Minecraft, Harvest Moon, Rune Factory, and Terraria to name a few.
You can build a base/ house/ mansion/ entire town. You can build shops that will attract merchants to buy/sell. You can tame animals and keep them close to home so you can collect their furs to craft ever more supplies. You can grow crops of all different types, (there are a ton, and they all have different growth cycles). You can build stairs into the ground that will take you down into a dungeon that is might as well be infinitely huge. There are rare and unique weapons and armor. Hell, there are even rare and unique tools, which are what you use to till the land, cut down trees, mine ores, and harvest crops. It literally has elements of every cool RPG/survival sim/hack and slash/ dungeon crawler ever made. To avoid a massive wall of text, I'll stop there, (because I could go on.......and on).
The graphics in the game aren't the greatest, but this is yet another case of content and gameplay > graphics. Let's face it, most mainstream games are all graphics and no content. They are like watching a movie rather than playing a game. That is why many people are turning to indie developers, and the developers of this game are great. You can really tell that they are fans of the games that inspired Lantern Forge. You can also tell that they are fans of their own game, because although their are some UI woes, everything is fully functional, fully immersive, and most of all, fully fun to play.
I sincerely hope that this game catches more steam, (get it?) and that a ton of people purchase it, because I'd love to see it continue to get developed. Oh, I didn't even mention how every world is procedurally generated. That equals infinite replayability for a measly ten bucks.
So to summarize my gaming brethren.....what are you waiting for? Show support for awesome indie games and buy this gem.

The game itself is interesting. There's a lot of reading, remembering key words, critical thinking (should I send my team in fighting? Or should I try a more diplomatic approach?) and storytelling. Quests and advancement is a little lackluster, but not bad, and every choice has a consequence. Graphics are decent, sound and music are stellar, and some of the game (easter eggs, dialogue, and random loot) are a little corny, but not bad.
I would recommend this game to anyone that enjoys any kind of Role-Playing game.

Wakey wakey Alaaaan. This game has a dark, eerie setting that predominantly takes place in a forest surrounding Cauldron Lake where you come across an evil force known as the Taken. This evil can possess both human beings and inanimate objects in a bid to put Alan to sleep, for good. Thankfully, one of Alan's weapons is a torch light, which literally burns the darkness layer protecting the possessed. Once this layer is burned, then it's weapons free till the assailant fades to nothing.
The AI is very good. They'll come at you in numbers, throw weapons at you, spread out and try to flank you and even call in the heavies that can take twice [if not more] the damage. You can try dodging their attacks or run away, though you will not get far at all - they will catch you and hurt you plenty. SO! That leaves you with an offensive defense option - FIGHT. Other than your torch, you have an arsenal of weapons such as a revolver, shotgun and hunting rifle as well as tactical equipment such as flares and flash bangs. Not to mention the flare gun. Choose however you want to attack. Ammo is readily available [I played Normal game mode]. There are no med packs and your health bar renegrates slowly. So if you're not careful with your six, you could be in trouble. Finally, you have some safe havens, such as a lit lamp post to catch your breath.
The graphics are fantastic. The setting is beautiful. The lighting is very good, though can hurt the eye so you may need to turn that brightness down or play in a well lit room. Although, I would highly recommend playing in the dark with the headphones on. Huge emphasis on the story and is an interesting story. Definitely has that Japanese horror feel to it. It did feel as though the developers dragged on a bit with the gameplay to prolong the game, but I think the story covered it well. A must play. 9/10.

All thigns considered, I LOVE this game. The story is excellent, the NPCs are memorable, and the gameplay is just right. I backed the game at the $30 tier on Kickstarter, and if Act 2 is as good as act 1 I will count this as one of my best purchases in recent history.

I originally wrote a long-winded review on this title, with the developer actually replying in an obviously scripted manor.  Needless to say, in the months since nothing has changed.  Starting out with the game, don’t let the title fool you because this new "edition" is the same Flight Simulator X that’s been around for over 10 years.  There is nothing additional added.  There are no additional default aircraft, the scenery isn't better, it' only some minor workarounds that have been done.  Let me explain that further…
While Microsoft is still the developer of FSX, Dovetail Games has taken over as a “publisher” for this title.  Now, it might sound a little unclear but here’s the facts surrounding Dovetail’s involvement.  They’ve done some work on the multiplayer aspects of the game, making it once again “functional”.  Not that you couldn’t play multiplayer before Dovetail got involved.  You just needed a 3rd party program and a little instruction from a Google search to get connected with your friends.  Now, due to Dovetail's involvement, that method of multiplayer has been blocked so they can provide a centeral hub for all games.  They also made the game “Steam Compatible”, which is another way of saying they modified the game so DLC could be directly installed by Steam.  That said…
When you discuss the core of the game, nothing has changed.  The scenery is still the same.  The default aircrafts are still the same.  The interface is still the same.  It’s all the same as it was 10 years ago.  Nothing has changed or been added to this new "edition".  There have been no noticeable improvements, quite the contrary.  New bugs have crept up that cause the game to occasionally crash.  This coming from someone who has had the original FSX since it originally launched.  So why would Dovetail resurrect a game that is 10 years old when Microsoft itself doesn’t see fit to keep on the store shelves?
To answer that question you only have to browse other simulation titles by Dovetail.  The company is the kings of DLC content.  Look at their Train Simulator 2016 game.  There is very little content included with the actual game yet the cost of all the DLC for it, 232 items, comes in at close to 3 THOUSAND DOLLARS!  The DLC for Flight Simulator X is a little more tame, only around $650 for all of it, but that's still fairly ridiculous considering nothing has been added to the new "edition".  THIS is the main focus of Dovetail bringing FSX to Steam.  It’s not to make improvements to the game.  It’s not to fix the glaring bugs they've added and fix the outdated graphics.  It’s to sell DLC so they can make a quick buck off an old (and relatively dead) title.
If you already own Flight Simulator X… DO NOT BUY!
If you’re on the fence… DO NOT BUY!
If you expect new scenery… DO NOT BUY!
if you expect more aircraft… DO NOT BUY!
There is ONLY ONE reason you should ever consider buying this Steam version.  It’s the same reason I bought it.  Because I already have a large library of free FSX content that I’ve gathered over the past years, my DVD’s were damaged somehow, and this is the only way I can now reinstall FSX.  Don’t let my play-time fool you.  If I could have avoided buying this buggy Steam version and stuck with my original FSX, I would have.

Playing this game is alot like starting a project. Unless you have a clear idea of what you want to do, it'll be rather hard to figure out the best way to enjoy this. Fortunately, they have alot of variety to the game and what you are able to do with it, as well as giving you a chance to enjoy all the skills and classes you want to take or experiment with!
Lantern Forge can be classified as a basic RPG, but with quite a few twists. There are no real classes there, since you're not limited to only choosing one set of skills. Your equipment can be mixed and matched, so if you like to wear a mage's armor, but prefer to go Gandalf and swinging swords around, it's all good. There are some npc's to start with after you gather all the materials for a town center, so you'll have more ways to earn money, like selling crops or ditching extra gear you don't need.
The community of players for this game is large enough that they won't lead you off into the deep end if you ask any questions, and you'll find lots of post and screenshots of how people are doing. Once extra content like bosses, base-destroying monsters and extra events pop up, things will be getting interesting.
There are a few pros/cons to this game, so I'll go ahead and list them all off as I've seen them.
Pros:
Fairly Infinite Re-playabilitiy
Lots of variety in building things, like castle towns, manors, small towns, etc.
Various and assorted monsters
Pick and choose the skills and playstyles you want
Easy to understand controls
Very friendly gamers to help you out with questions
Cons:
Lots of loading screens
It can be very difficult to get some of the items you need to progress further into the game
Money is too abundant
The surface has monsters that are scaled to your level, so leveling up is easy
Dungeons are too small and easy. They need way more variety, as well as traps and harder monsters.

The game is split in two parts, the boy's part and the girl's part. Both parts are too short, even though it's just the first half of the game. I finished it in 6 hours, and I'm sure you could do it in four.
The boy part is very babyish. The puzzles at the beginning are extremely simple, which is of course intended, but still I think it would bore even a child of 12. Even when the boy meets the wolf (which actually looks more like a fox), things stay rater simple. The graphics on the screen of the "rescue machine" are horrible, this whole rescue thing doesn't feel real, but is very abstract and silly.
The girl part is much better. I even actually like this part of the plot. There are some jokes (finally) and even some puzzles that aren't just trivial. (They aren't very hard either, but that's OK.) The part tastes a little too girlish for me, but that's just my opinion. I liked the two sentinels and the puking tree best.
The graphics are quite nicely painted in general. This is even the case in the boy part of the plot (apart from the rescue machine's screen). The problem with the scenery in that part is that everything looks so baby-like, I can't help disliking it. In the girl part, I especially like the slow animation of plants in some screens, or the birds in the sky at the beach. When there is a closeup, however, graphics become very blurry. Also, apart from some smoke and a laser ray, there's almost no special effects.
I like the fact that the music was played by a real orchestra. Unfortunately, it doesn't make much difference, because the game lacks of a recognisable theme. There is no opening sequence, no central score, so the music stays just in the background. The thing with background music is that it tends to get on your nerves after some time. I would have liked it better if there was one score that appeared in cutscenes, while the rest of the game would stick to ambient sound effects.
The overall impression of the game is not very good. It's too short, babyish, girlish, unchallenging, uninspiring. I'm not sure if I am going to be willing to invest six more hours playing the second part when it's out.

Nuclear Throne is like a post-apocalyptic Groundhog's Day adventure, where the only way off the loop is basically to not play the game. Of course that's not an option, because this game has been fine tuned to perfection. From an eclectic soundtrack to really punchy sound effects, tons of screenshake, colorful environments, funny characters, and a world full of mystery, each playthrough gives you something different, but familiar. You'll learn the path to the throne, but you won't quite know what's waiting for you on it. If you're looking for a game that will challenge your hand-eye coordination, your patience for starting over, and your mouse's structural integrity, Nuclear Throne is the game for you.

The Political Machine is a decent game with quick gameplay, easy-to-understand rules, and probably one of the best simulations of American politics out there.
However, the main reason that last statement stands is because there just aren't that many political games out there, so the field is thin. While The Political Machine can scratch that itch, it's not without its problems.
But first, the good stuff. The game gives you the opportunity to play as your favorite candidate. You engage in the sort of things that are expected of politicians on the campaign trail: you create and run ads, you give speeches, you hire consultants, garner endorsements, etc., and each have a direct impact on the game that you can easily visualize.
The game also has real-life issues, ranking of said issues, and reflects the demographics of each state appropriately. You'll find that you're often fighting over the states that it makes sense to fight over--Texas is almost certainly going to go Republican while California is almost certainly going to go Democratic unless you fight an uphill (and futile) battle to get it. And while you *can* get all mathy and pick apart the raw data, you don't have to--the game gives you a pretty good idea of what to do without having to fuss with all the details.
That said, it is a value game--you're only paying ten bucks, and the games are over in about ten to fifteen minutes (unless you crank up the stats to play a looong game, and even those rarely crack a half hour). This is clearly designed to be a casual game.
All this is pretty good, and quite frankly the down sides are mostly missed opportunities.
The one concrete bad thing is that if you own any of the previous Political Machine games (they've been making them since the 2004 election) it's a hard sell to even count $5 worth the upgrade. You're literally getting a handful of new candidates, a new set of issues, and some extremely minor tweaks in the rules. If you've played PM 2012, PM 2016 is almost literally the exact same thing.
It's also a little disappointing that there isn't more variety in the randomization of issues (which we will get to in a moment). "Fighting ISIS" is always going to be the #1 issue each game, so it does get repetitive.
But I do feel the need to point out some missed opportunities.
Some are easy to implement: the fact that you can't randomly have a candidate selected is weird. It's an obvious feature that should take practically no effort, but it's never been included. It would be nice to have candidates randomly chosen.
That said, the game *does* allow for random electoral votes, random wealth, and random issues...but it's *completely* random. That's not really fun; who wants to figure out the issue rankings of all 50 issues in all 50 states? It would be nice to have an option somewhere in the middle: issues still are based on real life, but just shuffled around slightly. So each issue might go up or down one rank in each state, but not completely random. You still know that "Fighting ISIS" will be important, but may this game "Addressing Climate Change" will be slightly higher. As it stands, I know that "Marijuana Legalization" will always be the most important issue in Colorado, Washington, and Oregon, and I can easily snap those states up with a few well-placed ads. It would be nice if I know those were important in those states, but maybe not as important some games over others.
(And it's weird that "random electoral votes" literally means "random" as in there may be 1000 electoral votes. Why not make it still 535, but they are randomly distributed?) There are some weird decisions like that.
It would also be nice to have more variety in the endorsements: as it stands, the endorsements always help the same issues (in the same states) and it's almost always a war of attrition to simply snap up your own endorsments to make sure your rival doesn't get them. And in the end it's a wash: as long as you both get your own everything sort of evens out. It's just not very interesting. (Thankfully, PM2016 added a new rule where you can get a National Endorsment which you can get repeatedly--previous games, once you got all the endorsments all the political capital went to waste. It's a step in the right direction, but I'd like it if there were more options--maybe getting to choose one issue and getting a +5 bonus to that issue only, or something like that.)
There are other things: the VP candidates do very little aside from raise awareness; it would be nice if they granted some other bonuses. A debate would be nice. And so on.
I hate to say too much bad about the game, since it's really a good game and the "bad" things are more of a wish list. But it's also valid--when you re-release the same game every four years, you expect there to be a little more development each time, especially since a lot of these requests would be incredibly easy (and cheap!) to impliment and seen rather obvious.

*DISCLAIMER: I have never played Overwatch, nor do I intend to, so I'll be judging Paladins solely as its own game*
Pros
+ It's free and defnitely not P2W
+ It runs well on older machines
+ In-game gold gain is very fast
+ You can also earn gems to buy cosmetics with quests and daily log-in rewards
Cons
- Client is a little buggy, often getting kicked before the match or being unable to select a champ and getting a 'deserter' penalty for a few minutes.
- PUG games can lead to unbalanced teams
- Don't expect your average player to know how to play
Paladins is fun, fast and plays much like a Moba where character picks/counter picks and a balanced team are more likely to lead to victory as you cannot switch characters mid-game a la TF2. Picking a support or tank character doesn't lock you into a specific role though. Some characters excel in different roles in the hands of a good player.
Like a MOBA, some characters are often regarded as OP, typically because a team lacks a counter pick or understanding of the character, or the player is just very good. Also like a MOBA, most PUG players will ignore objectives completely in favour of a fight, though the community so far seems quite well mannered.
Paladins currently has two currencies: gold and gems. Gold is earned from playing, and is spent on characters (currently 5000g to unlock), some cosmetics (some are gem-bought or unlocked in chests only), and loadout cards which improve champion abilities in a number of ways, typically by reducing cooldowns or adding benefits to that ability. Gems are bought with real money or earned slowly through promotions, log-in rewards and quests.
After about a week of playing in the evenings, I've unlocked several characters, loadout cards and a few cosmetic items all through gameplay alone. You can buy a founders pack for about $20 that unlocks all champs, plus future releases, as well as giving you a few other items.
I've encountered a few bugs, some minor like the texture setting defaulting to low every time I start a match or character loadouts not saving if I disconnect, but generally gameplay is smooth and consistent and haven't noticed any in-game lag or latency issues (aside from the disconnects).
It's worth a few hours of anyone's time.

I originally wrote a long-winded review on this title, with the developer actually replying in an obviously scripted manor.  Needless to say, in the months since nothing has changed.  Starting out with the game, don’t let the title fool you because this new "edition" is the same Flight Simulator X that’s been around for over 10 years.  There is nothing additional added.  There are no additional default aircraft, the scenery isn't better, it' only some minor workarounds that have been done.  Let me explain that further…
While Microsoft is still the developer of FSX, Dovetail Games has taken over as a “publisher” for this title.  Now, it might sound a little unclear but here’s the facts surrounding Dovetail’s involvement.  They’ve done some work on the multiplayer aspects of the game, making it once again “functional”.  Not that you couldn’t play multiplayer before Dovetail got involved.  You just needed a 3rd party program and a little instruction from a Google search to get connected with your friends.  Now, due to Dovetail's involvement, that method of multiplayer has been blocked so they can provide a centeral hub for all games.  They also made the game “Steam Compatible”, which is another way of saying they modified the game so DLC could be directly installed by Steam.  That said…
When you discuss the core of the game, nothing has changed.  The scenery is still the same.  The default aircrafts are still the same.  The interface is still the same.  It’s all the same as it was 10 years ago.  Nothing has changed or been added to this new "edition".  There have been no noticeable improvements, quite the contrary.  New bugs have crept up that cause the game to occasionally crash.  This coming from someone who has had the original FSX since it originally launched.  So why would Dovetail resurrect a game that is 10 years old when Microsoft itself doesn’t see fit to keep on the store shelves?
To answer that question you only have to browse other simulation titles by Dovetail.  The company is the kings of DLC content.  Look at their Train Simulator 2016 game.  There is very little content included with the actual game yet the cost of all the DLC for it, 232 items, comes in at close to 3 THOUSAND DOLLARS!  The DLC for Flight Simulator X is a little more tame, only around $650 for all of it, but that's still fairly ridiculous considering nothing has been added to the new "edition".  THIS is the main focus of Dovetail bringing FSX to Steam.  It’s not to make improvements to the game.  It’s not to fix the glaring bugs they've added and fix the outdated graphics.  It’s to sell DLC so they can make a quick buck off an old (and relatively dead) title.
If you already own Flight Simulator X… DO NOT BUY!
If you’re on the fence… DO NOT BUY!
If you expect new scenery… DO NOT BUY!
if you expect more aircraft… DO NOT BUY!
There is ONLY ONE reason you should ever consider buying this Steam version.  It’s the same reason I bought it.  Because I already have a large library of free FSX content that I’ve gathered over the past years, my DVD’s were damaged somehow, and this is the only way I can now reinstall FSX.  Don’t let my play-time fool you.  If I could have avoided buying this buggy Steam version and stuck with my original FSX, I would have.

It's Obsidian's worst, but their worst is better than a lot of people's best.
This game has some of the most deep and impactful choice and consequence in any game, the characters are likable, and the story is interesting.
But the gameplay is terrible
The game is mostly non-linear for the meat of the content and actions taken in one section will affect the other sections and the game as a whole. As well, enemies can be charmed and won over or talked out of fighting in general.
But the gameplay is terrible.
The game overall expresses the feeling of being a secret agent better than any other I've seen, with a suite of tools and aides allowing uncountable approaches to all of it's problems. You can seduce and charm your way around, dicking everything on two legs and some things that aren't. You can play the hardline no nonsense spy willing to kill at a moment's notice.
But the gameplay is absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing terrible. The stealth system objectively is more luck than skill based, even when leveled up the gunplay is limp and noodle-y, boss fights are an absolute headache when they can't be talked around, and the margin for error is unforgiving to the point where getting detected is most appropriately met with a quickload.
If you love choice and consequence, if you like Obsidian's writing and game writing in general, and if you want to see some of the best content out there; I would recommend this game.
But I can't stress enough that the gameplay in this game is TERRIBLE. If you think that'll turn you off, play something else by these devs.

I took a chance and thought 'if there are any game breaking bugs then hopefully some skilled and kind modder has fixed this issue' but to my surprise there weren't many game breaking bugs(the checkpoint system the game has doesn't always function properly for instance). To those of you who have watched Angry Joe's review and thought 'is it really as bad as he makes it out to be?' the answer is no, it's mostly because that Joe played it on Xbox360 and that Joe was maybe thinking that Alpha Protocol was a 3rd person shooter. See, the complaint he has with the guns was that they shoot wildly and are inaccurate, but to the game's credit, it plays like an RPG and less like a 3rd person shooter so in order to aim better with guns then you'd need to know what weapon specializes in what field(pistols for stealth/close-range, shotguns for close, rifles for medium range), build your character around that, and aiming and waiting for the reticle to get smaller when focusing on enemies. The best description on the top of my head would be the gun system in Vampire: The Masquerade.
tl:dr, if you've watched Angry Joe's review and think this game sucks, it doesn't... not on PC anyways, and it's true Obsidian RPG

There’s a tiny little airfield down the road from the house called Sandown Airport. It’s far too short for airliners to land or take off from, but I sure as hell tried it with a Boeing 747-400 in this game! To make a long story short, I ran off the runway, ran over several houses, finally limped into the air, forgot to use my flaps and slammed into the ground. I loved every minute of it.
Almost any airport you can think of (and many you don't know about) are in this game, and there are also plenty of aircraft included with the game to tide you over until you set off to the Internet to look for a massive variety of freeware and Payware jets and helicopters!
This is a game which is definitely worth playing if you want to have some fun, and a useful learning tool if you're seriously into simming. Flight Simulator X is also far less taxing on many computers, making it a perfect alternative for computers who can't run the fiendishly-large X-Plane 10. FSX is used by everyone from total newcomers, like me, to professional airline pilots.
In conclusion, I wholeheartedly recommend picking this game/simulator up, because no matter how serious people can be with it, you can find many ways to amuse yourself in the vastness of Earth's skies.

I play a lot of sandbox, city-building, and simulation games.  This one drew my attention as I was looking at the newly available games.
I wanted to like this game.  I tried hard.  It's pretty, has enormous depth and goals which I have yet to achieve, and I'm sure a lot of re-playability.  But it has some flaws which prevent me from achieving happiness with this game, which made me quit earlier than I would have liked because they were so central to the game play experience.
One, the lack of ability to rotate the perspective of the character, is fatal for me.  Once you put up walls, the only way to see behind them is to demolish the wall, build what you wanted to build, and then rebuild the wall and hope that the engine lets you put the wall back in the right place.  For example I built a fort with log walls and then wanted to build farms up close to the walls so as to utilize my available space.  I can't precisely place torches or other lighting sources on the inside of walls on the bottom part of the fort.  So, the southern walls of everything that gets built will not be able to be decorated.  It's probably a minor annoyance to some, but as a sandbox builder, I want that rotate control.
Two, I somehow managed to zoom out.  Whatever controls I had hit in frustration to do so, I could never figure out how to recover as the in-game help was well, no help at all.  I had to delete that save game and rebuild.  Annoying.
Three, no WASD support??  I finally figured out that I could hold down W and move the mouse to achieve some pathing, but that's a big red flag and terribly annoying.  The entire industry has already made us gamers accept WASD as the movement keys, and heck, my keyboard has 4 red WASD keys.  So don't make me learn a new interface.
Four, no hotkeys?  See WASD above... lack of hotkeys (or at least the ability to find a hotkey reference) made this game very taxing to keep mousing around the user interface.  At least "I" for Inventory seemed to work just fine.
Now, for the things I did like... bows.  Lots of food to find, grow, cook and eat.  Bunnies that drop furs that you can use to make fur clothing.  Grass beds in the beginning.  Apple trees that drop apples.  I like the rustic-ness one can achieve with all of the wood items and grass.  I like the feel of starting out as a hunter-gatherer and then moving into agriculture.  The ability to crate up tame animals and carry them back to base to release them (unlike another game which makes you lead the animals by taunting them with food).
This game could be a 10 - but instead I have to call it a 6 or 7 overall.  Big, deep world, lots of things to do, but lacking fundamentals in terms of expected user interface.  These are the equivalent to me of having a spanking resume for a high-paying job but noticing as you sit down for the interview at the number one company in the world that your resume is filled with spelling, grammar and punctuation errors.
I'd be willing to spend more time playing the game if these items were fixed in future patches.

If you play games for the game play mechanics, then you might like this title. Alan Wake is a third-person survival horror mystery. The main character is a writer, so he is portrayed as not very athletic. This translates into the feeling of slugish and unresponsive movement. Enemies must first be cleansed of darkness by shining a flashlight on them for varying amounts of time (3-10 seconds). I found this mechanic to be a bit frustrating later in the game. The flashlight also acts as the targeting reticule. There are 5 different guns available: revolver, double-barrel shotgun, pump-action shotgun, hunting rifle and the flare gun. The flare gun acts as a rocket launcher since all of the enemies are weak to light. There are also flashbangs and road flares. Ammo is somewhat scare, and there will be times when the player will be out of ammo if care isn't taken. There is no upgrade system in this game.
If you play games for the storytelling, then you will probably like this title.  The main character and his wife go on vacation to a small pacific northwest town in an attempt to cure his writer's block. I found the characters to be mostly interesting. I also though that the dialog and voice acting were very good.
The design of the world and the characters is very good in my opinion. The lighting is mostly dark, though. There are a few sections of the story that take place during the day, but most of it is during the night.
I was annoyed by the frailty and sluggishness of the main character, and the fact that most of the game takes place at very low light levels. This obviously gave a sense of urgancy to everything, but this changed to annoyance for me towards the later parts of the story. I also foung the game to be more challenging than I would have expected on the lowest difficulty setting.
Overall, I enjoyed my time with this title. Aside from the annoyances, I found the story to be well worth it.

The fundemental flaw in the YES OR NO recomendations in steam reviewing platform really starts to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off when you review Early Access or alpha build games.  The problem is like many alpha and early games the changes that can and will come can drastically alter your entire experience.  In some cases an entirely new build may completely destroy what you got use to over the last 5-6 months of playing.
Wasteland 2 I waited until it was on sale for, 60$ price tag was justified by not spitting in the faces of their kick starter backers, and I do respect that.  Was the $40 (on sale) I paid to play this game a few months before release worth it?  I would say yes.  While not an MMO and i won't get points for getting to x, y, z before anyone else, it still is a really solid return to classics.
It shows that classic systems implemented correctly into newer engines can play really nice together.  Now I must admit i don't remember much if ANYTHING from the original wasteland, but I do remember Fallout and playing that.  This game feels more at home with an isometric Fallout (to me at least).  It plays really well, but for some it can be described as "too slow".
Wasteland 2 doesn't hold back on a classic experience by giving you a bunch of tools at your disposal, and giving you the freedom to resolve conflicts your way.  Save a few game breaking bugs (again early build beta), the game is overall really solidly done.  Now while playing I felt like I have in most RPGs eventually your character becomes a hoarder and you are able to basically buy anything without it having it hinder you in any real significant way.
For being survivors of a wasteland these guys sure as ♥♥♥♥ stockpiled the ammunition up.  It became overly easy to have an abundance of ammunition, also after recruiting 3 extra characters ontop of your 4, you become a small wrecking crew that is essentially an unstoppable killing force.  There are moments that will give you some pause and trouble, but for the most part i was able to breeze through the content without too much trouble, hell barely even used my medic skill yet continued to skill it up.
Despite this, as you progress you start to want to ♥♥♥♥ with the wasteland's inhabitants more and more.  From the Rail Nomads and their rediculous fued, to the Red Skorpions in the prison, even the lowly little Wreckers.  All in all the game presents itself well, plays well, and has a story that is interesting enough to keep you wanting to play more.
I do recommend when it releases, but I would not recommend the game for $60.  There is speculation if the game will be 25$ - 40$, and I'd recommend around those prices, but for just playing early on / few extras the $60 is up to your own budget.  A solid and promising title, with a good amount of polish and a hopeful final push before release date this could shape up to be an amazing title.
Also the promise of the mod tools after release is a killer bonus as well.

Do you dare lead poor mutliwinians into battle?
This game's concept is simply beautiful. This game takes an RPG perspective except every base you get spits out units every so often. You as the controller are given special powers such as transports or air strikes to help your troops in battle. The battling is simplistic (none the less entertaining) and you are allowed to assign one of your soldiers as a major who can control a brigade. This makes it useful when trying to corner an enemy. What adds a bit of depth to the game is the fact they include certain additions to your arsenal. You may have an armoured transport, air strikes, dark forests which engulfs enemies, nuclear strikes and even defensive turrets you can control. There a few different game types : domination, king of the hill, capture the statue, rocket riot, blitzkrieg and assault. All game modes are great, my personal favorite is domination.
Visually, the game sets its own standard. It's neither good nor bad, but these graphics specifically define what multiwinia is. I really enjoy the path the devs took regarding the appeal to the game. The sound is basic but varied (which is good). Whether your launching a nuclear attack or an alien abducting your dead multiwinians, there is a sound for each action.
Overall, a good game and I would recommend a buy on sale. It's a neat little breakaway from other strategy games and really pits you against your online opponents.
RATING : 7.5/10.
