I only played
of the first episode of this game, so I feel that this review is no better than judging a book by its cover. Ignore me if you want, but I have my gripes about this game based on my tastes.
I had supposedly exhausted all the possible actions you could do after hitting the fire alarm and going outside to talk to people. After heading to see Warren to hand him the flash drive,
after I spent my time forcibly butting my nose into two-and-a-half girl dramas, I had to stop playing. My completionist attitude ruined me: I had missed a few of the memento photos Max could take if you did certain actions, and I wanted to rewind to get them. (Maybe I'm being petty here, but going into this game without knowing how it works ruined the experience.) Of course, that's not how the game works. "Rewind" just means "undo your last significant action," and if that doesn't include moving to the next area because an invisible narrative (and temporal) wall prevents me from doing so -- if the game wants to force me to go back to the beginning, just to get those photos, I'd ask for a refund so that my time wasn't for naught (joke's on me; this was free). Completionists might not agree with me on this, but a lot of things you collect in other games are unimportant or supplementary -- it's just to put a trophy on your wall -- but no one appreciates having their work thrown out the window. The mechanics are not my only complaint, and it certainly isn't the most important.
I know they're supposed to be stereotypical/archetypical high school students (though why from a private academy?), but almost every person you can interact with comes off as some facet of the word "a-hole." These conversations were unbearable, not because they're cringey since I'm past high school now, but because they make it seem like you're wasting your time talking to these people. This is likely the persepctive you're supposed to adopt playing as Max, but even Max is a problem! She is literally sitting on the moral fence for most of the choices that matter, and given your time rewind powers, shouldn't she get a different perspective and decide from there? Like, give the player another option to choose?... Who, me? I'm supposed to make the binary decision for her since
the player? I get to make her as much as a pushover as everyone else is because she's just a dumb, antisocial high school girl? This is more polarizing than Mass Effect's paragon/renegade options! Thanks, devs, for genuinely making me feel how and what Max feels, but I don't like this kind of character. I guess I prefer blank slates over loaded or insiginificant backgrounds, but Max has far too much on her plate to deal with and too few utensils for you to eat it all up.
I don't believe I entered the game with false expectations. Everyone says this game will make me cry if I play in its entirety, and I bet it would because, according to my predictions, Max won't be able to save X person since her powers can only do so much or they stop working -- she has to live with the consequences and now hangs around in mental limbo, beating herself up (boohoo). However, I can't say that my tears shed for the first episode were empathetic. Now this review makes
sound like an angsty teenager. God, how I wish that weren't true.
P.S.: I didn't want to include this in the meat of my review, but goodness gracious, the graphics are horribly old. I suppose the polishing budget was spent on the film treatment-like visual effects, which were admittedly very nice.
(Begin edit) I should also note that though I appreciate the devs' attention to detail, so much more could have been done with all the things with which you can interact. Additionally, I didn't want to complain about all the social pandering either, yet it's worth noting how this game is far too representative of modern society for my liking. (End edit)

No PROS , but No CONS either

2. The graphics - don't get me wrong IT'S NOT BAD AT ALL - the problem is that it reminds of the Fallout 4 engine rather than the Witcher graphics. 3. Shadows - that's something that really need some development - when moving from dark zone to highlighted ones - you'll see what I mean.
OVERALL:
Game's good and think I will enjoy every dime invested into it and the season pass. I hope you will enjoy it too.

UPDATE:
After around 80h in Mafia III and beating it on hard I should add few more notes:
More CONS:
- the AI  - it is unfortunately really dumb - you may kill all mobs in a certain mission using only your knife because they are dumb enough to come one by one even when they know u are in the area because u shot someone, or you enter a restaurant full of people and mobs , u kill a mob , people start screaming - run out, but the mobs dont give a **** because the murder / corpse is out of their sight.
- The missions are really repeative, you just change the object of your assault - liquer store, drug store, casino store ...
- (that's not maybe a CONS but still) : The game is Mafia after all - I mean - even pretending to be an open world there is not much u can do aside from the main story missions which are - "take this area" and the respective side missions which are  "increase the income of the taken
area". Then move to the next
More PROS:
- You can decide how to beat a certain mission in varios ways - play rambo style shooting everyone or play splinter cell by taking all the mobs using your knife / silenced gun one by one using the decoy bombs or sneaking around.
- The fight is not that bad - u can hide and shoot and when a mob approaches u can kill him using your knife, the choice of weapons is good, grenades also bring fun.
- The attention to the details deserves credit - for example how your car behaves on a different surface, when playing the radio and enter tunnel or undeground the signal starts fading.
- The overall city design is really good and the different districts show really different architecture.
- After beaing the whole game I should say the voice acting was one of the best I've seen in a game so far.
- The kill finishers animations are also nice and in a quite a big variety - using your knife, using your Ak47 as a baseball bat, using your pistol to smash someone's head, etc.
The variety of vehicles is also good - u can drive everything cars, boats, trucks, vans.
- There is a small connection with the Mafia II game as one of your underbosses is the main characted from the Mafia II game - Vitto Sc.
- whatever bugs I've encountered were minor - maybe 2 -4 game grashes for the entire 80h of game play. Few minor problems when a side mission marker dissappear from map, which however was easily solved by reloading checkpoint or restarting the game. The developers released 1 or 2 patches to address most of the early problems, which deserves nothing but a credit.
Overall :
Still I recommend the game - it was fun, the story was not worse compared to the previous Mafia games and played on hard difficulty may bring some challenge - at least you may be killed with 2-3 shots, the same way u kill the mobs (except bosses) with a single head shot.

Having put a full day's-worth of time into this game, I figured it was about time I wrote a review. First and foremost, you will die. Not in a Dark Souls kind of way. More in like a Dark Souls "I WAS FIVE FEET FROM MY CORPSE AND I'M DEAD AGAIN" kind of way. Nuclear Throne is like a post-apocalyptic Groundhog's Day adventure, where the only way off the loop is basically to not play the game. Of course that's not an option, because this game has been fine tuned to perfection. From an eclectic soundtrack to really punchy sound effects, tons of screenshake, colorful environments, funny characters, and a world full of mystery, each playthrough gives you something different, but familiar. You'll learn the path to the throne, but you won't quite know what's waiting for you on it. If you're looking for a game that will challenge your hand-eye coordination, your patience for starting over, and your mouse's structural integrity, Nuclear Throne is the game for you.

Alright. Let me explain a few things, as a person very intrested in politics, I was very interested in this game when I first heard about it. I thought, "Oh wow! A simulator of the road to becoming president! That sounds fun!" Well, it really wasn't.
The game starts you off and says you need to pick a side: republican or democrat, there is no independent, or third party. A little dissapointed, but still optimistic, I carried on to see what I could do.
I will give the game credit, the character customization, although limited, is pretty fun to mess around with. It's the only time its an option to wear your head or not in a campaign. Literally.
In the game, it gives you certain issues to deal with, which are understandable, and you decided how you feel about them. This part was ok.
An issue, however, was that it's a 1v1. There are only two competitors, 1 republican, 1 democrat. There was no mention of having multiple campaigners at the same time.
Another issue was something probably not intended, many times I experienced bugs which disabled me from continuing my turn, requiring me to leave the game and then reenter in order to continue.
And the last and final issue: the game just doesn't seem that interesting. Sure, I bet some people love it. Myself, I could only contain my excitement for one game. After that, it's easy to lose interest.
It is notable that I may be a LITTLE biased because I lost the election by electoral vote, not popular vote, to Hillary Clinton (Screw you Hillary) because of California (you too, California, you traitor) which switched on me at the last minute, but all in all, I don't recommend this game. If you enjoy it, sure, go ahead and do so. Just beware those purple states. Those will hit you hardest.
Don't buy this game, it's not worth it in my opinion. Use that $10 on what's really important:
Buying electoral votes.

It's a really good game overall, but here's the breakdown:
1. Combat:
The combat is almost identical to SoM with some new abilities and upgrades to old skills. Flurry Attack is called Snowstorm now and has Freeze element on use. In addition to putting an Orc on fire, you can Freeze, Poison or Curse them now.
2. RPG elements:
Sword, Dagger, Bow have numerical value on Damage now like most RPGs and you can change your weapons and armor(Cape, Chest piece, Ring) from inventory.
Legendary Gear gives you set bonuses for matching pieces.
Different bows have different arrow capacities, from 6 to 14 from what I've observed.
3. Nemesis System:
Lot more variety among Captain traits now, also there are trolls known as Olog besides Orcs.
Orc wering Tower's armor are my favorite besides the Crazy ones.
4. Online features:
You can avenge other players by killing the Captains or Warchiefs that killed them in Vendetta Missions.
THere's also Castle Siege missions to attack castles of other players with your Uruk and Olog army.
The only con so far has been the lootbox system, and even though you can buy the lootboxes with premium currency you can earn from Daily and Community Challenges, and the cheaper boxes from coins that orcs drop randomly, the feature is unwanted in a paid AAA game. It's no different from MGSV TPP's microtransactions. The boxes only give you gear and follower Uruks, which you can just find in the open world of the game itself.
Between "No Man's Sky" and "The Witcher 3", I would give this game a "Dark Souls 3". It's way above average to a new player, but incredibly enticing for someone who enjoyed Shadow Of Mordor.
Solid 8.5/10 for those who like numbers.

That's all I ask for an rpg and this game delivered. It allowed me to become invested and I had a constant desire to know what would happen next that easily propelled me through the less exciting combat.
The story is something to have fun with. This is a trope-filled superspy story - recognise it for what it is and enjoy it like you would any James Bond, Jason Bourne, or Jack Bauer adventure!
I picked this one up on sale and I heartily recommend any rpg fan or lover of the superspy genre to do the same.

This game is early-access for a reason, it's not perfect. However, even without the polish, Lantern Forge still offers an immersive, satisfying gaming experience. It lacks a comprehensive tutorial for the newcomers, but the developers and community are chock-full of advice and posts for those struggling with the initial get-go. Although, with just a bit of experimentation, it doesn't take much to figure out the gameplay mechanics and come up with your own strategy for how to get going in the world.
Controls can occassionally frustrate with pathing problems during combat, but holding down SHIFT will lock your character into attack mode and prevent you from just walking off toward your pointer. Combat isn't possible without some kind of weapon (no running up and fist-fighting your friendly neighborhood goblin), which limits your options severely until you're able to gather the first tier of advanced materials for class specialization. Before then, it is possible to use your starter tools (stone whatever-you-make) as a form of defense. (Not recommended for mobs). There is also a lack of bosses in this world, but the developers have stated they are planning on implementing them.
Leveling up yields you points for stat calculation and skill tree building. The list of skills is not extensive and with only five points to cap out a skill, it doesn't take long to build your strength. Which leaves acquiring gear matched to your level to deal with enemies (also at your level) the basic challenge for combat. Which leads to trading.
The option to create shops for trade does seem to take some of the challenge out of the game. Copper (the in-game currency) is pretty easy to acquire, so trading with the shops can be almost too lucrative at times. It makes finding the gear you need just as easy as a visit to the merchant you've created, which unfortunately levels with you and allow you to acquire gear before you've reached the necessary underground level that would yield the same material.
This is a 2-dimensional isometric world, which limits your movements to a standard 2-dimensional format. But the graphics are engaging with a charm that has quite an appeal.
As a final product, I wouldn't recommend it. But as a work-in-progress with a dedicated development team who have stated that there is still work to do before the game can be considered final, I say the price is right.

As someone obsessed with sandbox survival games, I really wanted to like this one. Unfortunately, broken gameplay, poor design decisions, and a buggy client make it really hard for me to recommend Lantern Forge in this stage of development. The game isn't marked as Early Access - it really should be, since very little about its gameplay or aesthetics feel polished enough to be a final released game.
Essentially: Lantern Forge's combat system is crippled by its own controls on top of balance issues, while its survival aspect lacks challenge. The game has limited content to explore, and story-wise, the game provides no plot, no choices, and no sense of urgency to motivate me to keep advancing.
Gameplay Problems:
Movement issues: Controlling your character is awkward at best in both movement schemes. Mouse-based movement, which was the only form of movement available when I first wrote this review, was completely broken due to bad click detection (leading the character to start mining if you clicked anywhere near a rock), bad collision detection (getting stuck on thin trees that the character didn't seem to be anywhere near) and a complete absence of pathfinding (walking into a wall when a door is less than a block away).
The devs later implemented a W-for-forward-movement-based-on-mouse-position movement scheme. Although it's *better*, it's only preferable in the same way that getting the flu is preferable to getting pneumonia, because in exchange for fixing the click detection and pathfinding issues, it hamstrings your ability to move effectively in combat. More on this in the next point.
Combat, Part 1: All combat is click-based. You have to hold down the cursor over an enemy to continue attacking, but due to the poor implementation of click detection, it's trial and error to figure out where you should be clicking to actually hit an enemy, and good luck if the enemy is moving. Now recall that all movement is *also* mouse-based. Because you have to click on the enemy to attack, there's no way to strafe around and get into a better position without interrupting your attack. Playing as an archer or mage? Tough. You're going to start running towards the enemy anyway if you misclick, might as well as put on heavy armor.
Combat, Part 2: Combat Mode and useless hotkeys make your combat skills painful to actually use. This game relies on the Diablo II control scheme, where left-click attacks and right-click uses a single registered skill; while you can register a skill to a hotkey, hitting that hotkey doesn't activate the skill - it just switches your right click. This was tolerable 10 years ago; it feels absurd today. Worse, you have to be in Combat Mode to even activate skills; if you're in Build Mode, which you will be for the majority of the game, right-click performs context-dependent actions on the surrounding landscape instead (building, farming, mining).
In effect, to even use your character's skills instead of bashing enemies, you have to 1. make sure you're wielding a weapon and not just swinging your currently equipped tool, 2. make sure you're in combat mode, and 3. make sure your current right-click skill is actually usable by your equipped weapon type (so no bows for sword skills). This needs to happen every time you run into an enemy.
Combat, Part 3: Enemies are both unbalanced and cheap. All melee enemies in the game rush you as soon as they enter the screen, as long as they have a path to you. The prevalence of mob spawners in this game means that's usually 3-4 enemies at once, and the problem with this is that at the same level as you, each enemy does about 5x the damage you do to it per hit, since all your weapons have absurdly low damage-per-hit (if high attack speed). Your character's regeneration rate is high, but not that high, and the lack of usable AoE skills in this game mean that while you bash ineffectually at one mob, three others are chewing on your face.
(Knights, the ostensible melee class, have only 1 AoE skill which costs 50% of starting mana if you don't have any mana-boosting items. It's also based on your weapon's damage-per-hit... you can see the problem with this.)
The end result of this is that when dungeon-delving, you'll usually be stuck grinding against enemies 5 levels below you because anything higher is too hard, and getting appropriately low-level equipment drops. This gets tedious rapidly, and the problem is this is the entirety of the game.
Design Problems:
1. All progression is grinding. Past the first two tiers of items (copper and iron), I realized there was absolutely nothing new that would be added by digging deeper and hunting for later tiers. No skills to unlock, no bosses, and no new mechanics, besides a numbers boost and even-more-absurdly-overpowered enemies. The game's complete lack of story or even a framing device just makes this worse, because while you *can* build your town and collect all the vendors, there's no reason to.
2. Survival is a cakewalk. Once you have even a small-sized farm set up, the survival aspect of the game becomes trivial, and you can probably feed yourself entirely off wild respawning apple trees. Furthermore, there's zero consequences for dying that I've noticed besides moving to your spawn point, not even an item drop.
Other Issues:
1. Aesthetics and UI are poorly implemented. There's no minimap, with only a (x, y, z) numbers-based position marker indicating where you are, so good luck finding your way back if you get lost deep underground (or you could just die and respawn, but how cheap is that). The crafting window is difficult to navigate for several reasons, and shortcuts for moving items are not indicated in any documentation. There's also no way to remap controls.
2. Bugs. I've crashed to desktop once, and noticed memory leaks in the form of slowdowns after a few hours. Background music seems to be buggy in that the daytime music starts playing at midnight instead of dawn, and every so often, a weapon you're trying to craft will spawn with 0 attack.
I've come back to Lantern Forge twice since I first started, and each time it's disappointed me greatly with how little it's improved on what I'd think are fundamental problems. Although I'd have sincerely enjoyed this game with some fixes, I can't recommend it to anyone at this point in time.

Unlike any other adventure I’ve ever played,
is a beauty. Everything fleshes well thematically and almost everything feeds into the story.
There are many ways where TSDFA:BA:A1btSoDFaIbaB does not push adventure gaming forward. In many ways, it’s pretty standard. There’s an inventory. One-click, one verb. Not really all that impressive, and I’ve been spoiled by other indie adventures when it comes to innovations. There aren’t any novel little touches to the mechanics, as, for example, I’ve grown to expect in each new Wadjet Eye game. Resonance memorably used scenery and memories in the inventory, and another (which escapes my memory) used dialogue in the inventory. This dialogue-inventory thing was, frankly, was sort of a refinement of the sword dueling in the first Monkey Island game, a sequence more directly stolen in The Shivah. Still, Wadjet Eye added an interesting twist to the soup of mechanics—- sounds delicious!—- and there are no twists in TSDFA:BA:A1btSoDFaIbaB.
This game is also very pretty, and very well produced, even if the gameplay is really on the easy side. Then again, that’s no innovation for Double Fine this side of the Meat Circus. Saying Double Fine has beautifully, impeccably polished flavor hindered by simplistic gameplay is sort of like saying that Bethesda makes large sandbox RPGs, that Rockstar has a potty mouth, or that Obsidian is Latin for “rushed by publisher.”
No, where TSDFA:BA:A1btSoDFaIbaB is one of the great adventures is in how carefully it examines, in every aspect of the design, the difficulties of growing up, of coming of age. That’s why its art stands out. Though Bagel’s paintings are storybook perfection, it isn’t the kind of art you’d see in a children’s storybook. It has shadows lurking, and the right kind of sophistication, hinting at the increased burdens of adulthood. Its soundtrack, worth a purchase by itself, is in turns intimate and epic. Its puzzles usually mean something to the story, because, as another reviewer pointed out, they often involve helping someone else, an important element of any coming of age story. These puzzles rarely if ever distract from the overall experience, and always—- and I mean always—- logical. There’s one situation which comes close to contrivance, but it, almost too conveniently, gets explained away.
All of these elements feed into what is so far one of the most complex coming of age stories in recent memory. Like a Pixar film, it challenges easy storytelling conventions to create a thematically rich and well-fleshed-out story, with ambiguities, with subtleties, with surprises. This richness is really only appreciated on multiple playthroughs, making this game one of the rare adventures worth replaying. This is the sort of element which is independent of having only the first half of the story released—- each of the characters tries to make their way, rebelling against what’s thought best for them, only to find a deeper reality than they ever expected. This haunting subtlety lends itself as even a theme to the story.

For example, whether parents have the best interests of their children in mind is actually a question in this story. That is astonishing only in a sense, because there is a sense where coming of age stories routinely question parental authority. However, in TSDFA:BA:A1btSoDFaIbaB, it actually feels like a question, seriously considered, if not analyzed, by Tim Schafer and his legion of designers. As of the first half of the story, the answer to that question has not already been answered, and there is reason to suspect that a Momputer really does her boy’s best interests at heart, and her concern over him his leaving his cradle seems genuine and not at all cynical, not at all calculating. There’s also reason to believe she was, at one point, in precisely the same situation as the girl character, sacrificed for a greater good. The boy, working without the supervision of his Momputer, believes he is doing good by some innocent victims—- yet he’s stealing girls from their families. The girl believes she’s killing a ravenous beast, only to realize that the tentacled monster is piloted, somehow, by a boy her age.
This moment, carefully built up to by a number of hints, in its way represents not just the literal sense—- the boring sense—- of a plot twist. Even this climax—- a cliffhanger for Part 1 of 2—- has direct relation to the theme, to coming of age. What boy did not treat girls as things to be saved, and what girls did not treat boys as monsters to be avoided? What boy did not ache for danger or challenge, against being coddled? What girl was not angry at being forced into doing something at odds with who she was? Even the title serves the theme: Looking at it sideways, “Broken Age” summons the awkwardness of adolescence, the age of breaking childhood and emerging into adulthood. Man, that’s a good title—- you’d think they’d go with “Broken Age” instead of TSDFA:BA:A1btSoDFaIbaB. Hindsight, I suppose.
These few examples, and I’m sure they’re only the barest, most obvious examples, underscore the beautiful cohesion of all elements of this game in service to a story. It does not just tell the story of a boy named Shay, a girl named Vella. It tells the story of what it means to grow up, what it’s like to finally notice the opposite sex, to rebel against parental authority, and what leaving the safety of that authority means. Not a thing seems out of place, and not a moment draws the player out of the experience. As a result, it’s more than just the most beautiful adventure game ever created—- it’s also the most true.
Tim Schafer still has a chance to fall into the Dread Pit of Cliches in the second half, I suppose, but after this first half, and after all the hints towards the far-reaching disaster these characters cause, I have no cause to believe he will fail this game, or fail the story.
Forgive its brevity, forgive its ease, and forget its simplicity. Broken Age has a lot to say, and it says it enthrallingly, and—- this is its innovation—- it says it with every part, in every moment.

Well as a fan of RPGs i couldn't walk away from this one. I mean this is a real hardcore, oldschool RPG at it's best! Early access brought on us many bugs, glitches and many times after another patch game would not run... but, now it's made a whole, there are some minor fixes left so what will Wasteland 2 can give you?
Graphics: Decent. It's not masterpiece in graphical state, but it's not the polygons that make game looks, it's artstyle. And it's there! You think Wasteland 's a big sandbox? With some rubble piles here and there? Destroyed houses and cities? yes all that, but also plenty more! Gen labs, terrariums, farms, villages; there are enough places and variety to feel like home (if you're a fan of postapocalyptic).
Gameplay: True oldschool. Do not touch this game if you're JRPG\console raised or school lad\lass. You probably feel lost, because game require brains to play. From Charecter creation to Wasteland jorney. You allowed to create up to 4 charecters, and will meet some more on ye joprneys, team can be 7 people max. And it is important what stats and skills charecter posses. Many times to find alternate root or to unlock secret, or simply to snoop around you will need some particular skill; One charecter will not be able to be master of everything, so think, do math... still you will probably will have to start game all over after first 3 hours. Stats btw are connected, so if you want fast or strong charcter you will have to sacrifice something in order to build that charecter. So it's important to understand what do you want, not blindly jumping into a game (stats btw can not be increased with level up, only skills can. Though you will find little trinkets here and there that will amplify particular stat). And the most awesome of all -- you can write your own biography for charecter! And use random avatars! As the game starts, well it's you standart RPG; World map, quests, exploration, fights... but with a certan twists here and there. For example, while wondering through the desert your charecters will need water and rad protection (or they will die) water can be refiled in Oasis or on base still you need to plan ahead. Combat can be very hard, or simple (depends on your charecter combatant skills and difficulty level), there are a variety of enemies and some of them can be really chalenging, or will require a certan tactic to defeat. Finaly a lot of secrets, alternate roots, quests that go against each other: Right from the begining you will have a choise to save X or Y and this WILL, I repeat WILL affect game, not like in JRPG or modern adventures. No, you WILL suffer the consiquences of ye choise... High replayability value.
Music and Sound: Musik is... well it support atmosphere still you will probably won't even notice that it exist. Sound on the other hand is great.
Final verdict? If you love Fallout 1 and 2, if you love oldschool RPG that require brain for play, if you hungry for challenge and want game that will give you freedom while restricting you gently. This is Wasteland 2 lady and gentleman: a game that every hardcore player and every oldschool gamer must own.

Not often does a game set in the future take one back to the past. The original Wasteland was the first RPG that I was able to finish, with a bit of help from my friends. We would get together and discuss strategys, clues, characters, and story. Though our characters and the way we played them were different, we still had the same goal. Defeat the impending robot menace while trying to avoid being reduced to a thin, red paste.
My first playthrough of Wasteland 2 ended with all of my characters dead during the second mission, indicating that the same learning curve of the original game applies to the sequel as well. This provides multiple opportunities to explore new gameplay styles and lateral thinking not found in most other games. "Are my characters well-rounded or specialists?" "Do I save Ag Center or Highpool?" "Should this NPC join my party or should I explode him like a blood sausage?" These choices will affect how the game progresses, and may make it easier or harder to achieve your goals.
In the new age of online strategy guides and walkthroughs, a game like Wasteland 2 has no single way to win. Any walkthrough would only encompass the writer's experience. A strategy guide would at best be helpful suggestions, and should in no way tell you "how to beat the game." It's all up to you, Desert Rangers.

Alan Wake, this was a game that I was really excited to play. I was unable to purchase this game for quite some time due to financial funds but I have it now and I am thrilled to write review of Remedy Entertainment’s Alan Wake.
Alan Wake is a third person survival horror about… you guessed it right, Alan Wake. A famous writer, who has been having troublesome nightmares do to his writer’s block. Because of his writer’s block, he and his wife have decided to a vacation to Bright Falls. Which seems to be ironic because the game is all about darkness.
Upon arriving in Bright Falls things go bad fast with Alan’s wife being kidnapped after an argument with Alan. Immediately after his wife goes missing, Alan makes his best efforts to track her down. Throughout his time of searching for his wife, he starts to have trouble telling the difference between his nightmares and reality.
Now, of the survival horror games that I have played, Alan Wake is very different almost very aspect. The biggest and most important difference is the narrative. The story is being told by Alan Wake as you are playing through the game. The game takes on a audio book type feel. This helps the player feel more connected to Alan and gives a better understanding of Alan’s character development. The story is not only told by Alan but also through tv rewinds. As you begin each episode of Alan Wake, a “previously on Alan Wake…” cutscene will start telling what occurred in the previous episode.These two narratives truly make Alan Wake have a unique type of storytelling compared other survival horror games. While most other horror games just want to try and scary the pants off of you, the creators of Alan Wake actually wanted to tell a story and make the player feel as one with the character while still making the player feel uneasy as they play.
Alan Wake uses a flashlight and revolver to kill the Taken, the people or objects that are taken by the dark. Through out the game you will find other tools and weapons such as improved flashlights, flares, etc. that will have you get pass the swarms of Taken. You encounter several different types of Taken, powerful in their own way but still weak to light.
When encountering Taken there were many times where I found it challenging to kill or even run away. I wish I could blame it on the combat mechanics but it worked so well even without a melee feature. It was difficult to kill the Taken because while I was trying to purify one there would three or four other Taken that spawn and start throwing axes or that run up to me and start hitting me with what seemed to a never ending combo. It got to a point where, I couldn’t seem to kill all of the Taken that attacking me so decided to run. That did not seem to work, not even half the time. I was unable to escape them either because Alan got tired from sprinting, the Taken were faster than me, or because when I was running to a light that would ironically blow out.
The only other thing that made this game frustrating was the clunkyness of controlling Alan Wake. There were moments when I went to grab an item and I would fall off a ledge because I needed to turn or when I wanted dodge and I would end up sprinting, because my default sprint and dodge key were the same shift key. Theses issues do not ruin Alan Wake’s story or thag the but they do cause it to be frustrating, so just be prepared to die…a few times.
Now when it comes to the visuals of Alan Wake, you will be anything but frustrated. The game is run on a Havok engine, the same as L.A. Noire, which means they are clean and seamless cinematics. The cinematics aren’t the only thing that looks good but the actual gameplay visuals themselves are unbelievable. It was amazing when I was standing on the side of a mountain and I was able to clearly see the neon lights of a gas station and know that it was a gas station, not look like an 8-bit jpeg gas station that you could barely tell was a gas staion. Even if you do not usually play survival horror games, you should definitely play Alan Wake for its visual greatness.
Alan Wake is an outstanding game. The story is in depth, different and yet still scary while never losing focus of the character development of Alan. The visuals are unbelievably shocking. The narrative of the story will suck you in and have you wanting more. The clunky controls were the only negative, even though they were not enough to ruin the game, they do tend to cause some frustration. Alan Wake was definitely worth the purchase, so if you have the chance to add this game to your library, do it.

Steven King the game. That is the best way to describe Alan Wake. Once an Xbox360 exclusive title, Alan Wake writes its way to the PC with incredible graphics that hold up even to todays "next gen" standard of graphics. The textures are deep, physics are dynamic and have a reason to exhist in the game world, and the lighting is fantastic.
The gameplay is not the most involved 3rd person gameplay you can experience. Most of the game has you running from one light to the next shooting any dark pocessed enemies you might encounter inbetween by shining your flashlight at them to weaken them, then blasting them repeatedly with some simple guns. There's little variety in level design or enemy design so it's very easy to get bored with this game's gameplay.
Thankfully, the story saves the game from ever getting boring. Just like a Steven King novel, this game features a story with tons of twists and turns that'll keep you wondering what the heck is going on. Very deep psychological horror elements that touches on the essence of thought, what's real and what's not real. Essentially the "Inception" of video gaming stories. If you're afraid that this game might be too scary for you, don't be. While it claims to be a psychological horror, the only thing even remotely scary is the occasional flashback of an old ladies face. You'll be more scared playing a Bioshock game.
I'd recommend this to anyone who enjoys pretty graphics or likes a good story to make them think.

They may be little pixel men but once the battle starts and you see them die by the hundreds and their scream fill your ears you'll know it's more than a bit retro-cute. (I owned this long ago, before I used Steam, I have many more hours than listed here.)
Multiwinia isn't a direct control RTS type of game so to speak, they have a bit of their own mind. They will battlewhen near enemies, and mill about when without orders. Yet they loyally follow the orders of their own commanders. That's where you come in! Now you can grab a few or group and give them a general move order, they do the fighting needed there and along the way. But for better results you can upgrade individuals to leaders marked with a simple flag. Now those guys can lead a tightly orginized group with direct marching orders. Or they can simply create a movement vector marked by an arrow on the flag and a small pulsing line across the ground.
So you set up a line of movements to get those coming into the area to head out to a rally point or simply swarm an area. Once the "pulsing line" movement order is on the ground they will follow it like ant, and as long as it's active they wander nearby, as other movenear the path they take up the order too. In any place you can quickly put together a formation, and these will have better fighting skills and will automatically resupply its troops from nearby unassigned troops. Basically it's ant trails and battle lines for movement and warfare.
There are some support itmes and "data" to retrieve during battle.  Bombers, troop transports, turrets, and even some resource collectors which basically collect the little glowing digital souls of all those fallen. And fall they will!
Multiwinia is a hands-on and hands off-game in a way. You will most certainly be involved in your efforts to win or hold a battle line, but you will also find yourself gladly zooming in to watch the epic little retro digital warfare! You WILL hear theri screams! You'll see men running on fire! Bodies fly through the air as a Bomber run lays waste to an area! Hold a ridge or hilltop and fight off swarms of AI. Control the flow of battle by locking down choke points, controling spawn points and grabbing all the field drops you can. And enjoy the wonderfully colorful retro arcade epic battle graphics.
No need to worry about massive tech-trees or specialized units. Not major economic structureto build up. Just get the spawn points, resources you can and take the high ground. They will do the rest! Sit back, relax and enjoy!
And remember: no matter how many adorable little lives are lost, or the endless digital screams that fill your gamer nightmares, it's all okay; they are just pixel men. See, look at them march, oh... that's cute. And...they're all dead.

This is a good game. The gameplay feels familiar to anyone who has played open-world games, the setting makes it stand out though. In a very good way, the world is very vivid and feels alive. It's downright brutal in it's approach (which I love, going stealth kills until spotted is always my approach), I do miss a few things from Mafia II. Maybe I haven't encountered it yet but I liked how cops came after you for running a red light, which I haven't seen here. The story is great, it was confusing at first how the game jumped around between events but you get caught up very quickly and as far as I can tell it only happens in the begining.
There are some bugs, nothing major but at release very few games are without issues. Many issues relate to textures or graphics (at least on my end, though only on objects in the world). There are a few mission bugs which no doubt will be fixed in time but nothing game breaking. 30 FPS isn't an issue for me, like for so many others and the devs have already stated this will be fixed in a patch very soon.
I highly recommend this game, it captures the era it is set in perfectly. It's brutal and doesn't hold back in any way, my most fun experiences is only using the knife for entire sections of the game (even when spotted). The driving is awesome, just like Mafia II, you feel the weight of the cars way better than most games like this. A good follow-up to an awesome series.

One of the best if not the best VTT (Virtual Tabletop) out there. It easily accomodates all types of RPG's and does it with a very nice and powerful interface. Die rolling and the possibility to create your own themes makes it the VTT that's truly a close aproximation of a face-to-face game at the kitchen table at home.
With DnD 5e, Pathfinder, Call of Cthulhu, Savage Worlds and more officially supported with rulesets, modules and a whole community supporting other rules and themes you cannot go wrong with this program.
The program comes with three levels of purchase, The Ultimate edition which allows you to host games with Demo users, Standard Edition which allows you to play with Ultimate users as well as other Standard edition users and finally the free (Demo) version which allows you to play with Ultimate Edition owners.
Without the rulesets Fantasy Grounds is powerful enough to let you use it for any game you want be it GURPS or Mutant Year zero so you do not need to buy anything else, but the options are there for all the more powerful experience.
I cannot recommend this program enough, try it, buy it, play it!

Mountain was nominated in the 2014 Game Awards in the category "Games for Change".  Don't let yourself be fooled however: It is not a game that can be played. Mountain is a zero player game; an animated wallpaper.
You are born a Mountain, floating through space. You experience the turning of time and seasons. Things crash into you on occation. And you ponder on your existence. You can, to a very limited extent, affect what happens on-screen, but this doesn't extend beyond different animations.
The ambient music (mostly wind or rain) is atmospheric, the imagery is pretty, and you can play tunes using your keyboard.
I can't say I regret buying it because I had some fun with it and it was only 66c, but it's not something I would recommend anyone buying.

Often refered  to as 'the overwatch rip-off' Paladins is a fun 5v5  hero shooter. Most of its characters resemble characters from overwatch and both were released near the same time but Paladins is free, and it is really fun for a free game. There are some reasons I prefer this to overwatch: my first reason being that this is on steam, if overwatch was on steam I would already have it but I cant be bothered to by games that aren't on steam because steam makes buying games so easy, secondly, Paladins has a ratherinteresting card system that allows you to reduce cool downs and allow your character to specialize in certain attributes, third, the uograde system at the beginning of matches that you can use to increase damage, movement speed and reeduce damage which can allow certain heros to shine in different situations depending on the upgrades, fourth, to get into comp, you have to get level 4+ in 12 different heros which is much better than overwatch because instead of maining one hero until level 25(?) in overwatch, the game incourages you playother heros and last but not least, your health regenerates.
But because its free, the graphics aren't as good as overwatch and it doesnt feel as well polished and still has some rough edges (glitches) but it is unfair to compare any game to another, even if there are lots of similarities.
All-in-all, Paladins is a nice, free game that you can spend hours on, the game always has people playing it and it doesn't require as much skill as most modern day fps games *cough *cough cs:go *cough *cough.

Hotline Miami. A top down 80s stylized game that is extremely violent and full of satisfying amounts of blood and gore. It presents these traits in very difficult levels that are well thought out and are among the best levels I've ever seen in a game. They are extremely fun to do, while retaining a truely challenging difficulty. Just one small mistake or hesitation and you're DEAD. This makes the game very addictive, but rarely making it a chore to play. Advice: Make sure your keyboard has a working R key, you'll find yourself using it a lot. The color pallet is amazing with bright, neon colors every where on screen and the pixel art style only adds to this. This is of course referencing the 80's style of gaming where everything was pixelated. The sound design was pure perfection with music that also sounded like it was from the 80's, even sporting artists that have the music on places like soundcloud which is good because you'll want to hear this music again and again. Next to this music the sound design sported explicitly real sounding noices for bashing a skull in, slicing through flesh and other gory things. Finally, the story. I'm not going to spoil anything because that would be a crime, but it is amazing. It skips around towards the end and at times confuses, but it's the good type of confusion. All in all, this game is just great. It nail the atomosphere, gameplay, music and everything else. 9.7/10.

Agent Michael Thorton performs his rookie mission for the ultra Top Secret Intelligence organization Alpha Protocol and stumbles upon a conspiracy which causes his superiors to attempt his immediate termination. Obsidian showcases their talent for writing choice driven RPGs and left their competitors in the dust once again with Alpha Protocol. I was worried going in that I would encounter a swarm of bugs, but the only bug I encountered was an issue withmemory overrun after playing for a few hours. As it only occurred after several continuous hours of play and was easily resolved by restarting the game I don't consider it a big problem.
Having finished the game I would really love to dive into a sequel. By setting a few of the possible ending variables in stone there is a wealth of possibility for a direct sequel to the events of Alpha Protocol. Or they could write a new story with little direct relation to the events of AP. Either way I would love to see Obsidian put their writing chops to work on an Alpha Protocol 2.

In a fit of nostalgia, I decided to replay Alpha Protocol and was surprised to find that it hasn't aged that badly. It's badly flawed in a lot of ways, but it's still one of my favourite action-RPGs, if only because it's one of the few RPGs to take on a modern setting, and even rarer, actually makes a decent, authentic stab at being a Bourne/Bond-'em-up.
The storyline is fairly derivative of spy thrillers (a lot of the reviews upon release criticised it for being on the bland side), but it's certainly functional and is interesting enough to stand up to being replayed. The best thing is that your choices in dialogue and action do make a big difference throughout the game, and there are reportedly 32 different endings that you can set up. So it is absolutely worth replaying, not just to try out different NPC alliances, but different play-styles, too. Some of the characterisation is a little off (SIE, I'm looking at you, darling), but it is impressive that so much effort went into creating a genuinely branching narrative that responds to what you do in game.
The mechanics may be a bit of a required taste for some: the computer hacking mini-game can be on the frustrating (infuriating?) side until you master it and like many modern day RPGs, the guns pretty useless until you've put at least 3 skill points into them, and a couple of the Boss battles are genuinely hateful. The Stealth mechanics are pretty good (not nearly so annoying as some RPG games), the gadgets are actually useful and the hand-to-hand combat has a nice weight to it. While I would have preferred an open world rather than a mission hub structure, at least the level design of individual missions gives you more than a strictly linear route to your objectives, and the safehouses themselves are littered with nice touches (watch out for the Sega Dreamcast consoles under the TVs).
I may replay it again as an utter psychopath, because some of the NPC responses are quite fun if you have zero qualms about murdering everyone in sight. If you've not played it, it's worth picking up on sale. (I recommend that you specialise in Stealth, Pistols, Toughness & Martial Arts on your first play through)

Lantern Forge reminds me a lot of a version of Rogue that I played on my first Macintosh back in 1984 - and that's good - very good.  I used to play that game day after day for months because it was so easy to get into even if you just had a few minutes to play, yet so addictive you'd usually be there for hours.  There's something about the play and pacing that's just right.
The part that's so much like Rogue is the multi-floor procedurally generated dungeon chock full of mobs, loot, and persistent modifiable terrain.  Rogue had more character customization, but in both games you may end up struggling a bit if you try to force the game to play in one certain way; instead if you step back and just think about what abilities and resources you
have, you can sometimes discover to your delight a totally different way to play.
What's been added to this formula is an equally engaging surface world to explore, and practically another full-blown game building things and leaving your mark on the world.  Here also you shouldn't let the limitations of other games trap you into thinking there's only one way to play, i.e. survive the night, build a shelter, find some food, start a farm, farm the farm, get some weapons and tools and start exploring the dungeon, blah, blah, blah.  Once you figure it out, you can skip farming if you want, and you don't even need to build shelter - you can live like a nomad and carry your camp with you.
The game isn't without problems.  The pathfinding really needs some work, and the UI could use a lot of improvement.  The big issue for most people of course would be the crashes, and certainly these need to be fixed.   I've had a few dozen crashes so far myself, but it's only been a minor annoyance - restarting the game takes less than a minute and I find I've usually been rolled back no more than a minute or two of play.  Definitely a problem, but not enough to make me want to stop playing - I'm just having too much fun.

UPDATED JULY 2016: I enjoyed this originally, back when I made a video on it and it held the promose of something I was very excited to see. I really wish it was still in development, but it appears that is no longer the case. Here's my original video on the game, for those interested...

Act 1 was a joy.
Positive + + +
The storytelling is phenomenal.  The sort that resembles the kind found in a children's book. The character designs are unique, simple, yet beautiful.  The varying Maiden costume designs alone are an imaginative wonder.  Probably the strongest point one should praise this game for is its abundance of absurd humor.  Many jokes are down to earth, help elaborate each character telling them ( versus hinder them ), and most importantly are actually funny!  The puzzle-solving is well-thought out and designed early on to help the player understand the scope of their ability.  As it progresses the puzzles become more abstract, however using common sense, imagination, and if all else fails...cycling through your items until the right thing happens...will not only help solve many of these, but also reward you with unique and hilarious dialogue.  Literally no detail was looked over in designing this game, dialogue-wise.
The duo-stories complement each other perfectly.  Although Shay's story is shorter, it is filled with more complex puzzles to solve.  Once again, cycling through your inventory and exploring every crevice is key to solving them.
Both stories give a good feeling of accomplishment when puzzles and tasks are finally completed.
Negative - - -
Many of my negative review points are entirely speculative, and really are inappropriate until the entire thing is released.
However, I will review the negative points based entirely on Act 1.
First, if Act 2 is the precise length of Act 1 (and ONLY if it's the precise length), then the game is simply too short.  Playing through while putting actual effort in puzzle-solving, I managed to complete Act 1 in just less than five hours.  While those five hours were incredibly fun, playing a game which realistically can be completed entirely in only eight to ten hours is disappointing.  Be aware that this game is the epitome of quality over quantity, however there is a desperate need to have more quantity of such quality, if only because of how amazing the world experience is to live through!  There's so much that needs to be explored.  What are the other villages like!?  What are the stories behind many of the other characters!?  Is this world hiding a whole other continent of amazing people!?  If Act 2 is just as short as Act 1, then the game missed an opportunity to elaborate on an amazing, thought-provoking world.
Second, some of the talking dialogue is strange.  As an example of this,  on some options where Vella is responding, the things which the voice actress must say seems both awkward and inappropriately executed.  This, however, should be ignored because the natural flow of a conversation can't truly be established when you can repeatedly select random dialogue, which might or might not be an appropriate response in the hierarchy of scripted responses.  For what it is, the game does a fine job, and the witty and hilarious dialogue is spectacular.
Finally, it is not made clear what will happen to my soundtrack download which I purchased.  Will I be receiving it in an email download link!?  Will it be available only after Act 2 is released!?  Some elaboration beforehand would be nice.
Other than those small points, this game is a spectacular and relaxing experience.  I would not recommend it to the Neanderthalic COD players that populate much modern gaming; however it's made thoroughly clear that this game is not meant for them anyway.  For anyone looking to sit down, enjoy a well-written story, and teat their puzzle-solving skills...this game is right up your ally.
On a final note:  Everything above, positives and negatives, are made all the more impressive considering how it was backed on Kickstarter by 87k people ( the names of which are revealed at the end of the credits.  Every...single...one...You can, however, use the mouse scroll to rush through each of them ).  This game is the best example of what happens when the people ban together and independently support amazing talent to create a unique and amazing game, which in the current gaming client would simply not be possible otherwise!  This is a success for indie game supporters, indie game developers, and for unique artistic merit that deserves to be talked about for years to come!  Let's hope with XBone, PS4, WiiWare, and of course...Steam and Kickstarter respectively, developers will be able to bring to life unique and exciting gameplay, stories, and experiences for many years to come!
I would highly recommend this game to those looking for something different than generic tired old shooters can provide.  Thank you Double Fine for the privilege to experience what is, thus far, a welcomed and memorable gaming experience which in this player's overall opinion far outweighs the few negatives.  Here's to an exciting Act 2!

Alan Wake should garner many positive reviews that will focus on the story and its "unusual" presentation and style. Know this; it would make an excellent book or movie. The problem is that even the best novel can be turned into a bad video game and that is essentially what has happened here.
The story unfolds over the course of 20 hours as you run from one well lit area to the next, fighting waves of the exact same 4 monsters, using the exact same 4 weapons and the exact same strategy all the way to the end. The Enemy AI is rudimentary. The soundtrack is non-existent. Alan Wake will occasionally narrate and explain a new revelation, or what he is feeling or what you need to do next.
The game lacks tradition incentives to keep you playing. There are no choices, no dialogue trees, no weapon upgrades, and no level-ups. Even Alan Wakes own survival is tied to the plot and thus never seems to be in question. The game thrusts you into the action without spending sufficient time on character development and then tells you that you need to do X, Y and Z if you wish to save various people you don't care about. This might work in a book or movie were we are simply spectators along for the ride, but it is asking a lot in a game where players must invest 20 hours of their own time to progress the story. I constantly found myself asking the question, "Do I really care about these people? Do I even care what happens to Alan Wake? Why do I need a key to open this door when I have a shotgun in my hand?" As a result, it is easy to lose interest.
This might be one of the few games that you will have on your plate that you have to force yourself to finish.

Alan Wake is an episodic psychological-thriller action game that follows the titular author on his 'vacation' to the fictional Pacific Northwest town of Bright Falls. Alan has fallen on hard times, after writing his very successful Alex Casey crime-drama series, he hasn't been able to write another book for the last two years, and has become far more well-known for his violent out-lashes at the press. He and his wife, Alice, are hoping to get away from it all, away from the bustling city of New York that they're accustomed too to the small and peaceful Washington town ... However, this goes terribly wrong after a series of odd occurrences at their resting cabin ends up with Alan waking up a week later with no memory of what happened in the last week, his wife missing, and strange shadow people coming after him in the darkness of the woods.
Alan Wake at its best is an immersive trip both into the rather colorful and well-realized town of Bright Falls, and the more sinister and campy lurkings that pull from everything from Stephen King to Lovecraft to David Lynch. At its worst its a repetitive combat game where you'll often get lost in the woods.
Maybe more appropriately stated is that Alan Wake is a huge love it/hate it game. There are elements of Alan Wake that it pulls off beautifully, while other elements wear rather thin over its course. Honestly how much you enjoy the game deals completely in how grand you enjoy what it does right, and how much you can deal with what it does wrong.
Alan Wake is a rather gorgeous game. It has fantastic art direction, a well-done lighting system, matched with fantastic optimization for PC and probably some of the best realized forest settings and night lighting realized in games. Its visual flair suffers a bit from some weird facial animations from the characters, but during sections of the game where you stand on mountains overlooking a valley below full of details, it can be kind of breath-taking. Bright Falls feels like a real-place, and the way they connect everything and how it all fits together as an overall map is impressive. It does feel like a vibrant, lived-in place often during the daytime sections of gameplay where you get to explore and take everything in.
It also has a very elegant soundtrack to it. The compositions really switch between three tones; beautiful symphonic pieces for the more relaxing and emotional scenes of the game, low-keyed and sometimes a bit sinister down-time music to match exploration and dreary environments, and rather thunderous 'struggle' music of when the action gets going. From this, the beautiful symphonic pieces definitely stand-out, but none of it is really bad. On-top of this, a variety of licensed songs have been chosen for the game, which play on radios and during episode endings. And sound-design is rather top-notch, with atmospheric forestry sounds, creaks in rustic homes, and little sounds that really help make the atmosphere and world. The sounds of shining light on enemies, shooting your gun, and your flashlight turning on, are all also suitably satisfying.
The gameplay of Alan Wake is really split into two modes; Exploration mode, where you're in a location without enemies with a variety of small tasks you can do, both for progression and for fun, and Night Time, when often you're isolated and alone (or with someone who you question how long they're going to last) as monsters come out at you from the woods. The night time takes up probably about 80% of the game, while exploration mode happens about 20% of the time.
The combat system is fairly simple, though with a few tricks to it. Enemies are covered in shadows which make them invincible to bullets, so the first goal is to disperse the shadows with your light. You can focus-down a strong beam of light that will chip more at the shadows of an enemy, but rapidly consumes battery power, or do a normal light, which does a lot less damage to Taken but slowly recharges the battery. If you use up a battery, it will go out and be off for about 10 seconds, unless you put in a new battery, but of which come in limited supplies. You can also use light to also stun enemies by flashing them with a strong beam quickly, which is useful if you decide to flee rather than fight. The guns feel rather samey, but you also get flashbang grenades, which will kill in one-hit weaker enemies and damage stronger ones, and flares, which you can light to ward-off enemies or deplete at their shadows.
Alan's final form of dealing with Taken is to flee from encounters, but this can be a bit tricky at first. Alan has very limited sprinting (he'll tire out after about 15 seconds and lower his pace to a light jog), and the enemies can catch-up to you without some intervention. The real art of fleeing in Alan Wake isn't just running, but to manage your stamina meter (it's better to stop before you tire-out to recharge it than letting it run out), and managing the enemies with your light by briefly flashing a strong light on them to stun them for a few moments.
All-in-all, it can be satisfying, but as the game goes on it can also be fairly repetitive. There's only about seven types of enemies through the course of the game, and three of them are rather similar. The limited selection and the amount of times you face the enemies can be a bit tiring.
Also a good portion of the game is set in forests., especially early on. The game throws you into a lot of forests where if you're not good at keeping direction in mind or marking landmarks, it can get very easy to get lost.
But there is some good mix-up here. A variety of set-pieces and moments lay littered through the adventure to help break the tedium of combat, ranging from atmospheric and moody caverns, stage show showdowns, a variety of exploration and daytime sections, police chases, car driving segments, and more. In some parts of the game you won't be fighting alone, and notably during Episodes 4 and 5 especially, they tread you away from the forests to much more interesting locations.
Alan Wake may test on some gamers patience, but there is also a lot to love here. The characters are colorful, and through the game's course are very easy to like. Optional side-stuff, including interesting radio broadcasts and black-and-white Twilight Zone parodies you can watch on televisions through the world are enjoyable.
There are a total of 8 episodes in Alan Wake, and to beat them all should take you somewhere between 12-24 hours. The breaking point for many comes during Episode 3, which is notably the longest episode in the whole game, and with less story developments than most of the other episodes as well.
On a personal level, I really enjoyed Alan Wake. It has flaws, the biggest one being repetition, but the overall package I found to be immersive, to have enjoyable TV-show like gameplay segments (fun characters, cliffhangers, location design), and I got rather wrapped up in the story and world of the game. There's stand-out moments in gameplay, and I can honestly say there is no other game quite like Alan Wake. While it pulls from a lot of sources, it manages to be unlike any other game, and quite unique.
But there is drudgery here, and if you're less a fan of camp, world-building, and more dragged down by repetition of combat, you may very well not enjoy your trip to Bright Falls. To some, the game comes off as a mediocre game with flashes of brilliance that it unfortunately does not ever quite live up too.
Alan Wake will either strike with you or will not, a rather polarizing game. However, if you're a fan of horror authors, television programs like Twin Peaks or Happy Town, or want a believable Pacific Northwest setting, this may do you in.

While I originally played Alan Wake on the Xbox360 and have only subsequently picked it up for the PC (during one of those crazy 90% off daily deals), many of the same pros and cons exist in both versions of the game.
The game has very good mid-generation graphics and the soundtrack is likewise. One major problem with the game, and this has to be excused to some degree because it is necessitated by the storyline, is that it is so very, very, very dark. In a lot of ways the almost complete darkness does more to hinder the effects of the horror storyline than it does to help it; during the interlude periods where it is day time you will come to realize that you are completely safe, whereas during the nighttime sequences enemies will seemingly pop out of the ground from nothingness.
While the combat is relatively simple to master and the puzzles in the game are barely puzzles at all as much as they are quick-time-events, the game does suffer from a serious dose to repetition as a side effect. Boss fights, if they can really be called that, are typically just a slightly bigger dude that you have to chip away at a piece at a time until you have him away from his minions.
The story is kinda unique for a videogame but it very obviously borrows heavily from John Carpenter's In The Mouth Of Madness and David Lynch's Twin Peaks, so take that how you will. Perhaps the only other really noteworthy item is the voice acting, which I actually quite liked and I have extremely high standards since the days of Dragon Quest VIII and Koudelka.
All-in-all a fun game that is a touch too long and repetitious for its' own good.

I love this game!  It's a typical RPG in many ways, but it has a fully developed food and hunger and farming that most games lack. There are many different biomes which hold different resources which gives a good reason to go exploring above ground. I think $10 is a very fair price on this little gem and will bring many hours of fun.  If you like gathering and crafting and building and farming and tending animals, you will love this game!

The North Hollywood shootout, sometimes also called the Battle of North Hollywood, was an armed confrontation between two heavily armed and armored bank robbers and members of the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) in the North Hollywood district of Los Angeles on February 28, 1997. Both perpetrators were killed, twelve police officers and eight civilians were injured, and numerous vehicles and other property were damaged or destroyed by the nearly 2,000 rounds of ammunition fired by the robbers and police.[1]
At 9:17 AM, Larry Phillips, Jr. and Emil Mătăsăreanu entered and robbed the North Hollywood Bank of America branch. Phillips and Mătăsăreanu were confronted by LAPD officers when they exited the bank and a shootout between the officers and robbers ensued. The two robbers attempted to flee the scene, Phillips on foot and Mătăsăreanu in their getaway vehicle, while continuing to engage the officers. The shootout continued onto a residential street adjacent to the bank until Phillips was mortally wounded, including a self-inflicted gunshot wound; Mătăsăreanu was killed by officers three blocks away. Phillips and Mătăsăreanu are believed to have robbed at least two other banks using virtually similar methods by taking control of the entire bank and firing illegally modified automatic weapons chambered with intermediate cartridges for control and entry past 'bullet-proof' security doors, and are possible suspects in two armored vehicle robberies.[2]
Standard issue sidearms carried by most local patrol officers at the time were 9 mm pistols or .38 Special revolvers; some patrol cars also were equipped with a 12-gauge shotgun. Phillips and Mătăsăreanu carried illegally modified fully automatic Norinco Type 56 S-1s (an AK-47 variant), a Bushmaster XM15 Dissipator, and a HK-91 rifle with high capacity drum magazines as well as a Beretta 92FS pistol. The bank robbers wore heavy plate mostly homemade body armor which successfully protected them from handgun rounds and shotgun pellets fired by the responding officers. A police SWAT team eventually arrived bearing sufficient firepower, and they commandeered an armored truck to evacuate the wounded. Several officers also appropriated AR-15 and other semi-automatic rifles from a nearby firearms dealer. The incident sparked debate on the need for patrol officers to upgrade their firepower in preparation for similar situations in the future.[3] An officer was heard on the LAPD police frequency approximately 10-15 minutes into the shootout, warning other officers that they should "not stop [the getaway vehicle], they've got automatic weapons, there's nothing we have that can stop them." [4]
Due to the large number of injuries, rounds fired, weapons used, and overall length of the shootout, it is regarded as one of the longest and bloodiest events in American police history.[5] Both men had fired approximately 1,100 rounds, while approximately 650 rounds were fired by police.[6] Another estimate is that a total of nearly 2,000 rounds were fired.

Fantasy Grounds has become my favorite platform for virtual table top gaming with long distance friends and connecting with new players.  I play 5e primarily as a player and have recently dived into DMing.  The tools and options are top notch for both options, but really shines for DM's.  Creating a campaign or game story is faster and very streamlined with the tools and tables.  Although it takes a little bit of learning, the UI and program mechanics are fantastic for automating mundane calculations which speeds up game play.  Although the virtual table top communities are pretty good at welcoming and helping new players, my experience with FG was the best.  It didn't take long to hook up with a group and its always easy to get advise when I need it on how to run the game or use the program.
Keep in mind that FG is a program that has built in rulesets for players and GM's to build their games and it is somewhat limited, but you can manually add content to it or purchase rulesets and reference material.  There are options for players to share these resources/content by participating in sessions with a DM that has an ultimate license if you play with a demo version.  Standard license players can also share resources in sessions with other players with standard licenses.
That said, the functionality of the program sets this product apart from other similar programs despite the learning curve and the price point for game licensing and products.   Check it out and hit me up if you have any questions about the program.

Currently I have access to the beta and here are the notes I am forwarding to Inexile.  In general:
This beta is stable, more stable than many "finished" game releases I have dealt with in the past.  Not one slow down, not one hang, not one crash.  Amazing for a beta.
The game is exactly what I wanted.  Something very similar to the old school FALLOUT games.  Lots of dialog, mature subject matter in some places (not suitable for children though no swearing yet), and no funky dialog like you sometimes get with translations from some other language into english.
Though I am attaching my beta notes which suggest several issues, I give this game a 4/5 stars in its beta state, and hope beta problems I did find are addressed.  None of the things I note prevented game play.
Build #42098
#1  Inventory Review (right click on mesh top).  The descriptive text has a spelling error.  "This laced top will have to fellas tying themselves in knots".  Might warrant a review of item descriptions for correctness.  Maybe the user community can help with this.
#2  No obvious way to transfer items between characters other than tediously dropping items to the ground and having a different team member pick them up.
I was wrong with this one.  If you notice the cursor icon when left clicking an inventory item, in the upper left corner is a little white arrow.  This arrow needs to be in the icon window of target PC, the item will transfer to that PC inventory when you drag and drop.  My bad.
#3  Fraps keys do not seem to work so getting screen shots does not work.  Was hoping the game would have a hot key for screenshots too.
#4  Rotate of camera is not particularly smooth and seems to get stuck at times requiring a continued restart of mouse movement.  This makes working your way through some maps very difficult.
#5  Do not see a way to change the angle of view.  One can zoom and rotate but not change the angle of view in order too at a greater distance or less distance.  This is certainly not a requirement and for most will likely not affect gameplay but most games that allow rotate and zoom allow angle change to the view.
#6  Pictures in inventory after right clicking to get additional info have jagged edges.  What happened to AA?
#7  The overall feel of the interface is not as gritty as I would have liked.  It is difficulty not to compare this game to the likes of Fallout and Fallout2, and I will refrain from doing so as much as possible.  In this case though it is an excellent way to describe what I mean.  The fallout interface had the feel of the game.  This interface does not.  It is too clean and lacks details and imagination.  The interface is functional for game play but could have been far more visually appealing.  I believe this significant because of the amount of time spent in the inventory and character screens so time spent updating these interface elements would go a long way to improving the feel of the game.
#8  Either audio is having problems with dialog, or some of the dialog has not been done.  For example, entering Highpool, half the dialog you have over the radio is not audible; you can only read it.
#9  9mm and .39 ammo look the same.  Caused me to run out of ammo by accident on one of the PC.
#10 Very dissappointing textures in some places.  For example, a raider encounter on the way to the prison.  Looks like some buildings burried in sand?  But are these visuals the best you could do?  They are rather poor, lacking interest and detail.  I am chalking this off to this being a beta with some areas not yet completed.
#11. After doing goat hill, and dealing with some scorpions raiders, one of the dead raiders was blinking in and out of existence.  Not a problem for game play but an interesting bug maybe.

Even though Alpha Protocol is a bit of an oldtimer by now, I still remember it fondly as one of the few Espionage FPS games I liked. I played this one back when my main source of getting games, was still buying them in the store than in Steam. So adding it to my Steam Library a bit later, so my current time on the game belies, how good it actually is.
I really liked the games narrative back in the day, although it was rather straight forward. What carried the game for me was the rather well executed stealthing about. Spotting enemies from afar, planning your route to the room and naturally before the mission you have to decide which equipment you take with you. There are some obvious twists in the story now in hindsight, but the game has a lot of replay value just due to the fact that you can decide on how to approach each mission.
Certainly you could just strap the biggest guns to your back and go in guns blazing, but the level designers took care that you can get through each level utilizing Stealth to your advantage, except for a few Story parts where it gets rather messy. It diminishes the fun I had stealthing about a little and feels a bit like the game is punishing me a bit for using stealth routes and equipping myself as well as putting points into the stealth category, but I still look back at this game fondly.
If you can stomach some older looking graphics and a few quirks here and there, for a fun stealth Espionage RPG FPS ... well ... now that I've said it seems a bit ambitious now right? Anyways ... I had a great time and can recommend it to anyone that's into the genre.
