Nuclear Throne is a top-down shooter in which your goal is to fight your way through a post-apocalyptic world stuffed with hordes of enemies in order to reach the eponymous Throne and stake your claim as king of the wasteland. You play as any one of a variety of mutants, each with their own unique abilities that lend themselves to subtly different playstyles. The game drops your character into a randomly generated area populated with a variety of enemies; only by completely clearing an area of these can you progress to the next stage. As you kill enemies, you recover rads, NT's analogue to experience points. Collecting rads allows you to level up, at which time you choose from one of four random mutations which bestow your character with new passive abilities to help you to survive the ever-increasing onslaught of baddies.
Another facet of the gameplay is finding new weapons among the arenas in which you fight, and making a decision on which two will be carried with you through to the next stage. NT features a huge variety of weapons that strongly influence how you will approach battles, from your bone-standard Revolvers, Shotguns or Crossbows, all the way up to Laser Miniguns, Gatling Bazookas, Energy Swords, and the always insane Super Plasma Cannon. As you fight through the game you will need to keep an eye on your supply of ammunition - a weapon going dry during a gunfight almost inevitably leads to a disappointing death.
Selecting the proper abilities that match with your character's playstyle and your carried weapons is the key to success. There are a small handful of endings, but generally you don't aim to simply end the game - defeating the final boss in a certain way allows you to "loop" the game, dropping you back in the very first area of the game to make another run at the Throne with all of your weapons and mutations carried over, but with the difficulty cranked to an unforgivingly hard level. Looping the game is where the real fun and challenge of Nuclear Throne shines through, as you use ridiculous weapons to deal with the dozens (or hundreds) of enemies swarming you at a time - and there is no limit. Looping the game and defeating the Throne again allows you to loop the game again and again, theoretically forever, with the difficulty continually ramping up, until you finally die. Further, even if all this is not challenge enough, there are also several optional Crowns (similar to the Skulls in the Halo games) that alter gameplay in different ways.
So, what do I think?
It's fun, certainly - 100 hours in any game for me is a pretty rare feat - and intensely gratifying to survive the huge battles the game provides, the screen positively lousy with enemies in all directions. However, there are several extremely frustrating elements to the game. Your character is very fragile, able to survive only a handful of hits before dying - the number of times I've been killed by I-don't-even-know-what during the chaos of battle are too many to mention. Certain mutations improve your survivability, leading there to exist several distinctly "god-tier" mutation selections that are almost necessary to reliably loop the game. RNG, as it does, can often leave you high and dry when it comes to getting that one certain mutation or weapon that you really, really need.
Secondly, the level generation sometimes spawns you directly in the center of a swarm of bad guys with no place to avoid enemy fire (these infamous "safe spawns" of which any veteran of NT is familiar are often an enormous source of frustration), and certain enemies have the ability to lethally teleport right on top of you with very little or no warning. Some deaths distinctly feel like they are beyond your control; compare to other games in the genre, such as The Binding of Isaac or Enter The Gungeon, in which deaths always feel like your own stupid fault, and totally fair in that regard. Nuclear Throne, by design, is unfair - but incredibly rewarding once you have an idea how to leverage the odds in your favor.
These criticisms aside, Nuclear Throne is, at its best, an intensely fun shooter that is well worth the low asking price ($11.99 USD at the time of this writing) that has provided me with a hundred hours of enjoyment and is easily likely to provide hundreds more. I could only recommend passing it up if you're the sort to bust up your gaming peripherals when suffering a frustrating loss - a younger me would probably have replaced a couple of gamepads by 100 hours. If you can laugh off the often annoying deaths and have the tenacity to improve enough to really get into the meat of the game, it's a must-buy.

While I originally played Alan Wake on the Xbox360 and have only subsequently picked it up for the PC (during one of those crazy 90% off daily deals), many of the same pros and cons exist in both versions of the game.
The game has very good mid-generation graphics and the soundtrack is likewise. One major problem with the game, and this has to be excused to some degree because it is necessitated by the storyline, is that it is so very, very, very dark. In a lot of ways the almost complete darkness does more to hinder the effects of the horror storyline than it does to help it; during the interlude periods where it is day time you will come to realize that you are completely safe, whereas during the nighttime sequences enemies will seemingly pop out of the ground from nothingness.
While the combat is relatively simple to master and the puzzles in the game are barely puzzles at all as much as they are quick-time-events, the game does suffer from a serious dose to repetition as a side effect. Boss fights, if they can really be called that, are typically just a slightly bigger dude that you have to chip away at a piece at a time until you have him away from his minions.
The story is kinda unique for a videogame but it very obviously borrows heavily from John Carpenter's In The Mouth Of Madness and David Lynch's Twin Peaks, so take that how you will. Perhaps the only other really noteworthy item is the voice acting, which I actually quite liked and I have extremely high standards since the days of Dragon Quest VIII and Koudelka.
All-in-all a fun game that is a touch too long and repetitious for its' own good.

TL;DR


The game is a lot of fun and the Nemesis System can get you hooked in a gameplay loop that makes you forget about time. The Nemesis System has been expanded and some of the additions will preasently surprise you. They will ambush you a lot(it will get anoying after a few times) and comment on what you did outside the sotry missions. Taunt you and if they kill you revenge will be the only option. I has that Civilisation "one more turn" mentality.
The basic Arkham combat is still there but there are lots of alternate option to tackle encounters and the new skill augments support this "play the way you want to play" approach. It can be really chaotic and the camera can and will be a pain.
Most of the bosses are either quick time events, really easy scripted sequences or random orcs from the Nemesis System. All of them feel rather underwhelming when playing and the random orc can feel out of place and completely unrelated to the story. Overall the story missions are weak and it's clear the developers had to pick between better developed story missions or the Nemesis System.
The story was ok. I'm not a LotR fanatic but there will most likely be people who will grab their pitchforks and want to burn Monolith to the ground.
The fortresses are all the same and having different orcs defend or attack them changes nothing. They are repetitive but the 20 defense marathon at the end is completely optional. Just watch the final cutscene on youtube. It's not like it matters anyway since after you do all of that and free roam unlocks you get a message that the story continues in the DLCs.
As mentioned before the camera can be really bad and to make things worse the screen can be cluttered with enemis, icons and counter prompts and during sieges it's best to just stand on a roof away from the fight. Maybe Shadow Pull or Shadow Brand a captain here and there.
The most anoying things were the captain introductions/retreats/deaths that are again unskippable. During most of the game it's acceptable but during the sieges you get bombarded with captains and they all have to introduce them selves. Sometimes they seem to be talking for ages. They can introduce more in the same cutscene and some of them even commenting that they are here to fight not talk but they still do it. At one point I just wanted to punch the screen. Some captains have 4 decoys that play a slow motion death animation for each when they die. And when your captains bleed out durng the sieges they also play slow motion animations of them falling down for like 8 seconds. Doesn't sound like much but when they chain like 5 in a row you'll be staring at the screen wondering why are you not playing. There will be 6 or 7 of them bleeding out at different points on the map at the same time and soon you will stop caring. You can always brand the ones attacking you that are higher level anyway.
The performance is good. It runs rather well on my mediocre hardware and looks good to boot. Not as good as in the reveal trailer but that is to be expected these days.
As for the microtransactions they are completely unnecesary. You get either orcs, xp boosts or training orders that can give your orc a flaming weapon or a caragor to ride on. None of this matters and you can finish the games final act by simply branding the orcs that attack you. I finished defences where my orcs were half the level of the attacker.  I got one loot box(you can buy them with the ingame currency that I had way more than I needed just by selling all the junk items that dropped from most captains) just to try it out for the last defense. I got 2 orcs one normal the other Legendary. The Legendary was bleeding out 2 minutes into the mission. The orcs at this stage are complete fodder and if someone pays money for these loot boxes just to have the orcs die 5 minutes later should see a psychiatrist.

A sandbox game that will test your creativity, engineering aptitude, and ability to learn from your mistakes. It has a virtually infinite skill ceiling and tons of things to do. Even after you touch down on every planet (if you can!), you could make SSTO spaceplanes to do the same, or a massive frigate that mines asteroids as it goes. A helicopter for interplanetary travel? It's possible! Return back home from an outer planet using nothing but your built-in jetpack? Possible! Capture an asteroid and throw it at your space station? Possible!
To accomplish the above in the stock game legitimately could easily take hundreds of hours. But even if that's not enough stuff for you, there is a rich mod community around this game. Mods extend the game in ways like adding realistic food/water/oxygen needs for your astronauts or replacing the entire Kerbol system with our real-life solar system (full-scale!). My favorite are BD Armory and North Kerbin Dynamics, which add munitions to weaponize your crafts- everything from machine guns, laser-guided bombs, actual lasers, nukes, and artillery cannons.
In short, a great game that will give you hundreds of hours of fun.

I have to say that the game itself is great, if a little too easy shortly in, but the controls need serious help. Having the movement control be the same control used to mine objects was probably a very bad idea, and combined with a complete lack of pathing (you will have to manually click to get to a corner THEN go around it, otherwise your character tries to walk through a wall) and control can be frustrating. The lack of any real in game help is also frustrating.
That said, if you can get use to the controls and get past the initial learning curve, the game is actually a great deal of fun. It plays like a mix of Minecraft and Diablo with the ability to set up a merchant right outside your front door thrown in. Getting your first real weapon is a pain, and until then you're stuck using your pick to fight off anything you encounter because you can't craft weapons without a workbench that requires copper to make, but once you have it and one or two levels the game is a tad overly easy. It is however still a lot of fun.
I would recommend it to anyone who likes Minecraft and/or Terraria. The Diablo-esque aspect is fun but the overly easy combat and heavy emphasis on crafting makes the game less fun if you're expecting that sort of thing, especially early on. But it really shines as a Minecraft-like experience once you get past the terrible control scheme and complete lack of in-game tutorial to teach said controls. There is a help function but it only teaches the basics of crafting.

*Warning, ONLY a first impression. I intend to update later after more game time and info*
While Lantern Forge could certainly benefit from some fine tuning, especially with the UI, there are no gaping flaws or immersion breaking moments in the game.  This said it also lacks anything amazing enough to floor you.
The framework of the game is built upon traditional rpg tropes.  You have familiar goblins and spider enemies who inhabit familiar procedural generated environments which you'll explore with one of three familiar hero archetypes that all work in a familiar fashion.
One of Lantern Forge's more innovative and stronger experiences comes from your town.  The game itself puts you in the role of building it, or rather strongly suggests that you build one.  It gives you a lot of room to be creative, allowing you to either making your town a work of art with individual shops, gardens and style or a small functional space to cram everything you need into.  At the moment you don't need to worry about protecting your town, its simply there for you to gather and process loot.  There are a number of elements that work together well here, from making simple shops, trading with your merchants, farming crops, crafting and just decoration.  From your new town, the game allows you to decide if you want to gear up by hunting monsters and selling/buying loot from merchants or by gathering raw mats and crafting it yourself.  Both crafting and fighting generate exp to level and improve your load out.
If you're not into it for the creativity or town building the game does offer traditional dungeon crawling.  You begin by building stairs down which generates a whole new underground map each level you explore and there’s nothing apparent limiting how many levels down you want to go at any time up to the cap of 90.  You do this again and again, every staircase down increases the difficulty and generating a whole new area with better loot and material.  Though each level is different they aren't very unique, you'll quickly find that if you've seen one level you've seen them all and it slowly becomes frustrating as each staircase adds one more load screen.  Although its a quick load, the number of staircases add up and it gets frustrating until you can get warp stones, after which it's not so bad.  Once you get there, if there are any surprises, boss fights, secrete treasures or other gems I've not found or heard of them, its simply another layer and load screen.  When you start to level up from the grind you'll have the option of the three traditional classes, melee guy, range guy, or magic guy with a sprinkling of an all encompassing utility option.  At first glance it doesn't seem like you'll want to mix builds as each 'class' lines up with one stat and one ability tree making cross classing a likely waste of potential.
The interface is one of the weaker points.  It will take time to learn as it's not immediately intuitive and can be frustrating as you adjust to a lack of WASD for movement and a combat/build mode toggle.   The game relies strongly on the mouse for most things, the keyboard seeming to be more an after thought, the only keys used besides hotbar is shift which simply holds you in place for ranged attacks.  You'll need to slowly figure out how to navigate around obstacle with the mouse as your character sometimes isn't sure if he's walking, using a workbench, or punching something.  Once you figure out how to navigate around bushes and bodies it all starts to flow.
Overall I do recommend this game because you're getting a 10$ game, not a 2$ + 'IOU for 8$ worth of content to come' game.  It's a collection of a lot of safe ideas mixed together rather well.  A very appealing art style, functional mechanics, and 'passable' UI.
If I had any strong suggestions for the game it would be to dress up dungeon crawling a little.  Limit my ability to easily move between Z levels, make it feel like an achievement to progress further down and not just another loading screen.  Hide stuff in the dungeons, collectables, secrete rooms, rare monsters, most of all you can hide cool stuff I want to put in my town to show off.  Make me wonder what's lurking in the darkness, remove my ability to see whats there with better fog of war.  Currently its to easy to see dungeons or to see ores by scanning the darkness with my mouse, make it scary and not just risk management to explore.

TLDR: A wonderful adventure game, with perfect writing, graphics and voice acting. A little easy and possibly short, depending on the still to be released second act.
Broken Age is a great adventure game and don't let the angry people tell you otherwise.
Let's get the "bad" out of the way. Yes, Broken Age is quite easy, especially if you're an adventure game veteran. If you are an adult who played a ton of adventure games you probably won't get stuck for hours on a puzzle. Also, presuming the second act will be as long as the first, the complete Broken Age will not be too long.
Apart from that, though, it's a great adventure game. The angry veterans will lament the fact that it's not "classic" as Monkey Island. Well, I am an adventure game veteran too, and if you think what made games like Monkey Island great were a ton of action verbs and the fact that you got stuck for hours on a puzzle, well, you are missing the point. What made those games great were the setting, the humor, the fantastic characters, the fact that the game brought you in an awesome fantasy world. Broken Age does that wonderfully.
The graphics, the writing, the characters and their voice actors are all perfect. Broken Age actually gave me a "classic adventure" game feeling, whatever that means, and I can't wait to play the second act.

Not going to sugar-coat it: what you see in the trailer is pretty much what you get. Whether you think it's worth a dollar or not is for yourself to think.
As only introduced on the game's Store page, Helenna the protagonist has to grab falling objects to keep her cool and get a highscore. Shinies bring points, hearts and potions are health and skulls give out lots of points in exchange for health. Additionally, the health decreases (or your "fear level" rises) constantly, so keep grabbing those happy hearts!
Really, there's nothing else to the game - it's that casual. There's no progression or variation of any kind (granted, the item drop rate changes with your health). The only thing you struggle for is the highscore. As your health fluctuates, the game merely becomes an act of balancing between health drops and grabbing the high-valued skulls to reach those elusive achievements.
Initially, I thought there was a bug in items randomly disappearing mid-air, but I finally noticed that the bats flying around would collide with the items and both would get destroyed. Still, this took me a while to notice. I experienced no other "bugs".
Keep in mind that the trailer gives off a somewhat optimistic look: the difficulty level has been increased since the release by reducing health drops, so it's a bit more challenging to reach high scores. The balance feels quite good now, but it doesn't take lots of practice to reach a point where it's easy to keep scoring ever higher while keeping the health in check.
As a score-based game, the achievements kept me interested for an hour, after which I had grinded the 1-million total accumulated score. There's no list of highscores (global nor local) but your top-score will be shown on the screen at all times.
With no progression nor other content to keep me playing, the only reasonably cool feature worth mentioning is the eerie music that works well for the casual item hunt.
I did have fun trying to reach 100'000 points score and grabbing all the achievements, except for the grindy 1M one. So it gets
from me. Just keep in mind it's rather basic casual: as a gaming experience you could probably find a free browser-game with very similar gameplay with little effort.

Ever since I got it in 2012, this game has never ceased to amaze me. The game features great physics. If you enjoy physics sanboxes, I highly recommend purchasing this game, as you'll spend countless hours exploring both physics in atmosphere, and also in microgravity in space. Because of this, however, there alos features a steep learning curve that makes it challenging to make it out of Kerbin's gravity pull, but once you get the hang of it, the game gets way more fun and rewarding.
Overall, a great game that ages extremely well. Doesn't need to be the most beautiful game out there to surpass expectations. You'll lose track of time with your creations, and every new accomplishment will leave you hungry for more. If you're uncertain, go watch some videos online. I recommend Scott Manley, but there are many other YouTubers who regularly play KSP.

I've been using Fantasy Grounds for about a year now. A lot of play time, but a solid 50 hours of that time is probably for porting 4e content so I could use it. While it is a product I use when I play D&D, it is also an annoyingly bad purchase that pisses me off when I have to ask others to get it to join my campaigns. I'm going to have a pro/con list that I believe sums up my problems with this "game", but I don't believe it is all of it since I will not purchase the dlc due to it's price and stupidity of the whole affair of this.
Pros--
o FG is most definitely the #1 option for accessibility and ease of understanding, it feels comfortable when you have played with it for about an hour.
o The icons and token system feel good and allow map combat to benefit a lot since you can make icons connect to PC's and NPC's so that damage is calculated by the game and input onto sheets (as well as effects).
o They give you some monsters and items for 5e to use without having to write them out yourself.
o Rolling is easy and can be done by clicking or rolling directly on the chat window. It does the math and will specify damage type in the text window alongside the rolls.
o The notes and story tabs are useful for longer-term games. I dig them and use them.
Cons --
o There is no map building feature and you have to obtain every image and token for youself unless you are willing to spend hard-earned dosh to get their images.
o The game costs $30 more than it should for what it is, which is essentially a husk that asks you to paint it to make it look nice.
o DLC... look at the prices and come back to me saying that is an okay thing to do with what they give you the the base kit. The acceptable ones are the modules, but some of the DLC just feels like money grubbing for the most basic scraps.
o The system is old and that is certain from the boot and any time you need to update. FG has some sort of personal site and log-on that it asks for but you don't need to update it. It just generally feels like it got lost to time, but never tried to catch up (likely because it would be "too big" an opportunity cost).
o NPC tokens do not have a border and you need to use an art app to make one so that the whole deal doesn't look garbage. A great deal of FG is trying to make it look good with a system that doesn't give you much help in that department.
o Small gripe, but the password system is random and you need to use one of their passwords for some reason. I don't know why this is.
Final words: I love playing TTRPGs, but I very much dislike asking people to buy this game and always say to wait for it to be on sale (and even then I feel bad). The biggest problems with this "game" are money-oriented. This is because FG is for the money, not the players. Having a pit in my stomach for asking somone to buy this is all that I should need to say.

29 June 2014
Introduction
Wasteland 2 has been Early Access for some time now and those of you who remember the awesome Fallout 1, 2 and Tactics, I can confidently say that this is the true successor unlike Fallout 3 which was Elder Scrolls Oblivion with guns.
Graphics
The first thing classic Fallout veterans will notice is the transition from 2D to 3D and it’s great to finally explore the Post Apocalyptic world and watch all the action from any angle you choose. The world itself is suitably detailed and the animations are great and more than adequate for the job. Although there are games with better graphics, Wastelands 2 is all about the gameplay which I’ll cover later in more detail.
Sound/Music
Voice acting is great and the music fits nicely with the theme. Sound effects including weapon effects, enemies during encounters and items are again more than suitable.

So far so good but this game is £39.99 in Early Access and it seems to be okay so far .... so why would anyone pay such a large amount of money for a game that’s not yet complete?
Gameplay
This is where Wasteland 2 more than earns the right for such a high retail price. When you first start the game you have the choice to create your team (highly recommended) and the list of abilities that your character can develop in are great,
Barter, Pistol, Shotgun, First-Aid, Heavy Weapons, Surgeon, Weapon Smithing, Toaster Repair, Melee, Blunt Weapons, Safe Cracking, Alarm Disarming and more. All of which require skill points to master that are awarded upon levelling up.
Characters can be equipped with 2 weapons, primary and a secondary (Sniper Rifle and a Pistol side arm  for example) and be fitted it with various Armour and Trinkets (Literally thousands of combinations). There are over 150 Weapons in the game and the fire-arms can also be modified with the use of weapon smithing to increase accuracy or decrease the chances of stoppages.
The Wasteland world has lots to interact with too (Objects highlighted in Green), even more points of interest to add to the immersion (Objects highlighted in Brown) and how you interact is up to you, use a lock pick to open the door or a rocket launcher the choice is always yours.
The desolate world is also filled with NPC’s and some are offering lots of information via an interesting chat system (certain words will be highlighted and added to your vocabulary to enquire about as the conversation proceeds).
Wasteland 2 is also full of decisions and consequences, some are small like attempting to pick a lock early on with low skill level can destroy the lock forever to much bigger decisions that will decide the fate of entire towns and NPC’s, who you decide to  save or let die is up to you but you’ll inevitably have to face the consequences later on.
Now onto Enemy encounters, this is probably my favourite part as I’m a big fan of tactical combat. Once you encounter Enemies the game will switch from free roaming to turn-based where you’ll have a set number of AP (Action Points ) to use on movement, crouching, reloading, unjamming weapons, single round shots and burst fire.
Different weapons have a different effects too, Shotguns have a wider spread to hit multiple enemies whilst Sniper Rifles will have the ability to penetrate and hit another enemy  in depth, killing two with one round and let’s not forget the animations, lots of gore and I was able to blow one guy clean in half with a Shotgun and watch him crawl around on his hands.
I’ll be honest in saying that I’m only about 7/8 hours into the game so far but it’s got me hooked which is a rarity as I tend to bounce back and forth from game to game (I even annoy myself sometimes), the game is also not without bugs (the odd graphical glitch) and some of  the voice acting is still to be added but that’s Early Access for you.
Pros so far
1 True successor to fallout 2
2 Character customization
3 Game altering decisions
4 Great turn based combat
Cons so far
The usual bugs normally found in early Access
Conclusion
Fantastic game but is it worth £39.99........ If like me you loved Fallout 2 then definitely, it’s the sequel I’ve been waiting years for, luckily for me I picked it up during the Steam Sale for around £25 which I’m more than happy about, feel free to comment and I hope you enjoyed my review.

Nuclear Throne is a top-down shooter in which your goal is to fight your way through a post-apocalyptic world stuffed with hordes of enemies in order to reach the eponymous Throne and stake your claim as king of the wasteland. You play as any one of a variety of mutants, each with their own unique abilities that lend themselves to subtly different playstyles. The game drops your character into a randomly generated area populated with a variety of enemies; only by completely clearing an area of these can you progress to the next stage. As you kill enemies, you recover rads, NT's analogue to experience points. Collecting rads allows you to level up, at which time you choose from one of four random mutations which bestow your character with new passive abilities to help you to survive the ever-increasing onslaught of baddies.
Another facet of the gameplay is finding new weapons among the arenas in which you fight, and making a decision on which two will be carried with you through to the next stage. NT features a huge variety of weapons that strongly influence how you will approach battles, from your bone-standard Revolvers, Shotguns or Crossbows, all the way up to Laser Miniguns, Gatling Bazookas, Energy Swords, and the always insane Super Plasma Cannon. As you fight through the game you will need to keep an eye on your supply of ammunition - a weapon going dry during a gunfight almost inevitably leads to a disappointing death.
Selecting the proper abilities that match with your character's playstyle and your carried weapons is the key to success. There are a small handful of endings, but generally you don't aim to simply end the game - defeating the final boss in a certain way allows you to "loop" the game, dropping you back in the very first area of the game to make another run at the Throne with all of your weapons and mutations carried over, but with the difficulty cranked to an unforgivingly hard level. Looping the game is where the real fun and challenge of Nuclear Throne shines through, as you use ridiculous weapons to deal with the dozens (or hundreds) of enemies swarming you at a time - and there is no limit. Looping the game and defeating the Throne again allows you to loop the game again and again, theoretically forever, with the difficulty continually ramping up, until you finally die. Further, even if all this is not challenge enough, there are also several optional Crowns (similar to the Skulls in the Halo games) that alter gameplay in different ways.
So, what do I think?
It's fun, certainly - 100 hours in any game for me is a pretty rare feat - and intensely gratifying to survive the huge battles the game provides, the screen positively lousy with enemies in all directions. However, there are several extremely frustrating elements to the game. Your character is very fragile, able to survive only a handful of hits before dying - the number of times I've been killed by I-don't-even-know-what during the chaos of battle are too many to mention. Certain mutations improve your survivability, leading there to exist several distinctly "god-tier" mutation selections that are almost necessary to reliably loop the game. RNG, as it does, can often leave you high and dry when it comes to getting that one certain mutation or weapon that you really, really need.
Secondly, the level generation sometimes spawns you directly in the center of a swarm of bad guys with no place to avoid enemy fire (these infamous "safe spawns" of which any veteran of NT is familiar are often an enormous source of frustration), and certain enemies have the ability to lethally teleport right on top of you with very little or no warning. Some deaths distinctly feel like they are beyond your control; compare to other games in the genre, such as The Binding of Isaac or Enter The Gungeon, in which deaths always feel like your own stupid fault, and totally fair in that regard. Nuclear Throne, by design, is unfair - but incredibly rewarding once you have an idea how to leverage the odds in your favor.
These criticisms aside, Nuclear Throne is, at its best, an intensely fun shooter that is well worth the low asking price ($11.99 USD at the time of this writing) that has provided me with a hundred hours of enjoyment and is easily likely to provide hundreds more. I could only recommend passing it up if you're the sort to bust up your gaming peripherals when suffering a frustrating loss - a younger me would probably have replaced a couple of gamepads by 100 hours. If you can laugh off the often annoying deaths and have the tenacity to improve enough to really get into the meat of the game, it's a must-buy.

This second season of The Walking Dead is even more perfect than I could have asked for. Telltale fixed all the issues (which were all minimal) I had with the previous game and was still able to catch my heart strings at the end. Being able to play Clementine is all anyone could have asked for because it makes you understand the sort of stress this can put on a 9-year-old child, and allows you to reflect on her life when she was with Lee. The moral decisions you need to decide can be extremely tough as you need to balance the odds of each and can be especially hard when your trust with one character can be altered due to a choice (screw you, Bonnie).
Sometimes the story did feel a little slow, especially with the fourth episode. There was really only one choice in that chapter that needed some consideration. But each chapter allowed you to bond or find out about what is going on inside the characters minds. Kenny was definitely a character I loved a lot, despite some of his actions. For those who wanted to know, I stuck with him till the end and I don't regret it. Sure, Jane seemed like a better choice for Clem's survival, but Kenny absolutely adores Clem and the last conversation you have with him brought me to tears. He has his issues but he's a good man.
Anyway, I have loved The Walking Dead series so far and I look forward to playing the third game (when I eventually buy it) and the spin-off: Michonne. I especially can't wait to see Clem and Kenny again.

Would I recommend this game? Absolutely, if you would like a shooter game that has a lot of character and a lot of replayability. It has a lot of playable characters that can drastically alter how you play, and tons of weapons you can try, a lot of which are fun.
However that recommendation comes with some caveats, as this is not an entirely fair or skill-based game. It's better at it than say, Binding of Isaac, but you are still going to suffer a lot of cheap deaths. Things exploding on you, guys charging in from off-screen, or just getting bad weapons or bad spawns (I'm aware Hammerhead is a thing, but I feel if you need a specific perk to show up to counteract a situation, that's still a flaw even if there's a fix for it - plus there are still enemies that don't really much about what cover you have).
The game's not entirely balanced, either. There's weapons you wouldn't want to use, like the Toxic weapons, which are impractical and can hurt you since there's no way to negate toxic damage, or the Screwdriver, by far the worst melee weapon in the game which is only useful for one secret; seeing it drop after you can get that secret feels like a joke on you.
It also feels like there's a big disparity in mutations, as well, since there are ones like Boiling Veins, which protects you from dying to explosions (and this game has a LOT of explosions), and Strong Spirit, which gives you a mulligan from death once per stage; really practical things as you go through the game. Then there's say, Lucky Shot, which can give you ammo of a random type when you kill an enemy - except that you usually won't find yourself switching weapons all that often, and the game tends to naturally drop ammo for stuff you don't have anyway. Or Extra Feet, which makes you faster (something one of the character does already), and negates the effect of terrain...but there are only instances of that in two areas, one of which is only a single stage long. I understand this is meant to encourage different builds, but there's a good reason some of these are considered 'core' mutations and others aren't.
I should say this isn't the case for the characters, though, as every one of them feels distinct and appeals to a different kind of player. You want to be good on Ammo, pick Fish. You want to be careful, Crystal or Eyes. Pure damage? Steroids or YV. Want the game to abuse you like a dog? Go Melting.
I don't know how many of the reviews bring this up, but I also love the game's sound. Pretty much every enemy has a bunch of unique soundbytes for attacks they use, which is helpful for reacting, as well as when they die, which is useful for knowing when you've killed something offscreen (and is also immensely satisfying for several foes - looking at you, Lil' Hunter). This isn't always foolproof though, as sometimes a bunch of sounds can happen at the same time.
I hope I haven't implied I dislike the game by criticizing it, because if I genuinely didn't like it I wouldn't have played as long as I have. It's a great game. But playing it is pretty much tough love, and you'll need to keep that in mind a lot.

Straight up, one of the best games of 2017 thus far. Likely a GOTY for many, especially those who enjoyed the prequel, as it's essentially more of the same, albeit with a great deal cut and pasted from the original game. The core gameplay is quite similar, with a re-worked weapon and skill system, and the combat is the same mash-fest as many WB produced games from the last decade.
It's a graphical marvel, especially on beefy systems, and contains faithful recreations of many iconic scenes from the LOTR universe, taking a lot of inspiration from the Peter Jackson movie trilogy. Battles feel epic, and the scale of the world is much larger than ever before.  Sadly, having played the preqel just before this, many of the animations have been directly copied across from the first game, which did feel a little lazy to me - they still look and feel as good as ever though, which is really just a minor niggle in the scheme of things.
The Uruks are, as expected, the stars of the game. Each captain and warchief have interesting quirks about their characters, and hearing their name chanted as they enter the battlefield is an amazing touch, and really shows the attention to detail Monolith put into this game.
Microtransactions are ♥♥♥♥♥♥. But that's a fact that I'm not sure we can ever change. This shouldn't detract from the awesome game that lies under all the negative press surrounding an optional system, however - at the time of writing I've played for eight hours and have not even touched the store feature, nor have I opened any of the chests given to me at the start of the game for pre-ordering. Simply put, the game rewards you enough to dissaude you from paying extra, which is a nice touch.
8.5/10

The Political Machine 2016 is the fourth game in the series (the earlier three being The Political Machine, The Political Machine 2008, and The Political Machine 2012) and I'm sorry to say the game hasn't matured much, if at all, since it's original incarnation back in 2004.
TPM2016 is a turn-based strategy game where you play a candidate running for the office of President of the United States. You can adjust the game's length, difficulty, and starting wealth, but assuming you're aiming to play a full run for POTUS, you're looking at 52 weeks (or turns) of gameplay.
You can choose from a mix of recent politicians (from both the Republican and Democrat parties) and even choose historical presidents, such as George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, and Teddy Roosevelt. You can also create your own character, which is nice since it allows you to tailor your candidate's political attributes, as opposed to using whatever was preset for real politicians.
When creating your own politician, I would've liked the capability to choose "independent" as my party choice, instead of being stuck with either Democrat or Republican. Granted, someone from one of those two parties always wins, but part of the fun of video games is seeing what you can do, even if the end result is hardly realistic.
While playing you can establish various offices, hire operatives (some of whom boost your own ratings and others who reduce your opponent's ratings), gain endorsements, have print or television ads made, and give speeches on numerous subjects. In addition to promoting your own platform, you can also attempt to discredit your opponent.
You might also gain some operatives (none of whom you could hire normally) through special events, and get invited on to TV shows. The news shows are parodies of real political talk shows and require you to answer questions within a set time limit.
As a light-hearted attempt to portray the mad rush of a presidential campaign, TPM2016 succeeds nicely. Unfortunately, that's where the game's positives end.
1. The graphics are atrocious, although this has been a problem since TPM2008. All the characters look like deformed bobble head dolls. I realize that's to keep the overall theme jovial, but it ruins the immersion. This is made worse by the character creator being absolutely awful in how it integrates the characters, so instead of the game realizing that hair needs to adjust its height and depth based on head shape, the player has to do it all manually. It's tedious and completely unnecessary.
2. Certain actions, like giving speeches, inexplicably fail after a while. At first your speeches will probably net you a small gain in state approval (something like 2% or so), but as time goes on, you'll get stuck at 0%, regardless of how much the voters agree with you.
3. Certain operatives, like the Fixer (who is supposed to remove a targeted opposing candidate's operative in that state) doesn't work properly. The instructions say to left-click the Fixer and then right-click him on an opposing operative to remove him, but all it does is move the Fixer around. That's it.
4. TPM2016 is very black or white in its approach. You're either a full-blown Republican or a die-hard Democrat. There's no room for anything in-between. Admittedly, politics in the US can be like this at times, but nobody is 100% one side or the other. Perhaps if an independent option were added this wouldn't be a problem.
So, would I recommend The Political Machine 2016? If it were just a case of "I don't particularly care for the game's design," then I'd still vote yes, but it's more than that. The game seems broken in some ways, so I can't recommend a product that doesn't work like advertised. Maybe a few patches will be released and if that happens, I'll amend this review, but until that occurs, I'll have to say "no, I don't recommend it."

Out of all the previous games I have played in the past year, I'm most certain that Middle Earth: Shadow of War is one of the best gaming experiences I've had in a long time. There's a lot of things that I could talk about in the game, ranging from the combat system, stealth system, nemisis system etc. But to me, the main thing that stands out the most and has had me hooked to the very last minute was the evergrowing, branching out story and narrative. Also, this review isn't like practically all of the others that I've seen, with countless amounts of people bombing the game over the controversial 'Microtransactions' and 'Lootboxes'. The game doesn't force them on you, you're not forced to pay ACTUAL money for them. You get an abundance of in-game currency that you can use to buy the war chests from the market, and you get boxes for free from completing online Vendetta missions for other players. No you don't have to pay for gold war chests to get Epic and Legendary Orcs, I've had plenty from the silver chests that I paid for with the in-game currency. On top of that, the in-game currency that you get is literally everywhere, in main missions, dropped from random enemies, side quests, challenges etc. Theres no way for you to NOT recieve the game's currency. The 'Gold' currency that you get to pay for gold and blue war chests you can earn through online Vendettas and Seige missions too, as the first one you complete you recieve 500 gold right off the bat. I haven't spent a single penny of my money on this game, I just don't have to and neither do you.
To get to the combat and stealth; yes the game has recycled animations from the first but that doesn't mean that's really a bad thing. In my opinion, those animations are already really good on their own, and for Monolith to ADD to those and refine them makes playing this sequel even better. I adored the combat from Shadow of Mordor, it felt like the Arkham series and Mad Max, which is a good thing as that combat system is really the only good system in games today. The combat has been worked on a lot, and there's SO much more skills to use as the skill tree is huge compared to the first game. Stealth is still a good and exciting way to get around an environment when hunting a captain or warchief, and with the new skills that you can unlock makes it even better.
The gameplay overall is a lot of the same things from the first game, but has been worked on and added to so much that it makes the game much more enjoyable than the first. The graphics in almost all areas are a lot better, sharper and just visually more appealing. It helps that you're not just stuck with two maps anymore, and the game has around 5 regions that you progress through, each with their own distinctive look and feel. My favourite porbably being Gorgoroth.
Lastly the narrative itself and the story the game wants to take you through felt incredible and made me itch to play more after every cutscene. The first game almost had me there, I did watch the cutscenes the first 10 hours or so in but then it got to a point where I just wanted to play instead of listen. This game, not once, made me feel that way. I was intrigued and felt as if I HAD to listen, to watch what was happening on screen. I've not really been much of a Lord of The Rings fan, although I do have a Mum that loves the books, films and the earlier games that released on the PS2. The story this time round I felt was an incredible step up compared to Shadow of Mordor, and the fact that if you put a little more effort in to the end of the game you can get an ending that ties into the films is just amazing. I've got just under 40 hours on the game so far, in which I have completed every main mission, side quest and every single collectable and not once did I feel bored or that the game felt repitive. The plot twists where amazing due to me being so sucked into the story, and  I didn't even see it coming. I mean it wasn't even hinted at in the trailers at all and I hadn't seen it mentioned anywhere online, so for me to witness it first hand and spoiler-free was mind blowing. Obviously we all know about the 3 movies and what happens so I was kind of expecting the ending to stick true to that. You'll know what I mean at the end.
(Side note: The attention to detail and continuity at the end of the game from the Orcs is incredible. As well as when you open up the region map after finishing the game, you'll notice something that I thought was incredibly well done and well thought of, it's near Mount Doom...)
The game does have a 'True' ending that you can after you complete act 4 called 'The Shadow Wars'. I won't really get into that other than saying it's a 20 stage seige mission for your fortresses and that's all I'm going to say. I haven't finished them, as a matter of fact I've only completed the first one which took me about an hour and a half, maybe 2 hours to prepare for. But it was really fun and at least there's something to do after you finish the game.
Overall my verdict for the game is a solid 9.8/10.
There was a few small hiccups along the way that were quickly fixed, and I'm sure overtime they'll be patched out. But from the gameplay to the narrative, everything about the game was amazing and an unforgettable experience for me. Also I'd like to mention the game's soundtrack, especially the main menu and map theme. Absolutely adore that song, just thought I'd throw that in there. But I digress, the game was a solid experience, well worth the money and I know for a fact that I'm going to continue playing it and very much looking forward to the future of the game.

First off, Shadow of War does what a sequel should do. In just about every department everything is polished, tightened and improved in just about every way. The Nemesis system is more expansive than ever, giving quite a number of possibilities when either encountering or creating Orc captains. Combat feel tighter all around with a revamped skill tree that helps keep Talion from becoming too overpowered, while still providing the much needed edge to take down hordes of enemies and the captains. The graphics aren't a massive improvement, but this is acceptable given the already excellent detail given and the high amount of graphics effects that can be going on in the heat of the moment. Overall, they took what they had and really put the spit shine to work.
A new feature here is the siege mode. A fort in every region that can be taken over with your Orc army can be somewhat challenging, but nothing overwhelming. Though the Nemesis sytem can potentially produce some rather wild results in just what captain, or overlord in the case of forts, can end up facing you down. But the siege mode is a welcome addition that comes along with an online mode in which you can test your abilities against forts other players have customized in a ranked ladder and take on the Orcs they've appointed to defend the fort, along with whatever other defences they've installed.
As for combat, nothing has changed too much. Like the other games from WB, such as the Batman Arkham series, it improves just about everything combat wise. However, unlike Arkham Knight for example, you will find yourself more often than not putting all the different skills and such to use. It's far more balanced this time around, keeping Talion from becoming almost ridiculously overpowered when your not even half way through the game. Along with that, the skill tree has been expanded upon, giving a variety of new skills and a more tactical setup, allowing secondary skills which act as buffs to your main skills, giving not only a bit of extra customization, but something to help vary your combat a bit, say in an instance where you need to change an attack from dealing fire damage to ice damage when dealing with captains that have unique elemental buffs.
Oh. And there are effectively ZERO quick time events. None. Nada. Zip. They threw that trash out.
The story if much much much more fleshed out, with several narratives going on over the course of the game in not just two regions, but five major regions, each almost the size of the original two maps from Shadow of Mordor. Characters seem a bit more inspired this time around and Talion doesn't come across so much as a drag. As for whether the story is canon or not to Lord of the Rings lore, I honestly couldn't say myself, but it does heat up to a certain degree, more than enough to be far more engaging this time around and give some interesting backstories to some of the Nazgul and even the great spider Shelob.
As for being optimized, things seem pretty tight on that end too. Don't fret to much of your on the lower end when it come to your CPU, the game doesn't seem to draw to much power. As for GPU, I was using an EVGA 6GB 1060 on ultra settings with textures on high and the frame rate almost never dipped below 50 through my entire playthrough. And even if you need to turn the graphics down, you shouldn't be too dissapointed, the game still looks plenty fantastic.
I've seen a lot of people angry about microtransactions, however when it comes right down to it, this doesn't seem to effect the main game in any real way. It seems more focused on people who would have a higher interest in climbing the leaderboards in the online siege mode. My only argument against people who have an issue with microtransactions is any good company is ALWAYS looking for an extra revenue stream. The game itself is worth it's price alone and if you don't want to pay extra money for microtransactions, then do what I do. Ignore it. It's that simple. I suppose I don't see what the fuss is about.
Not sure what else to say about the game. I will say however, it has more content than I expected, along with an entire post game chapter after the story is completed using the new siege mechanics, along with some other mechanics I can't mention due to plot spoilers. But if your already interested in buying the game, I can guarentee some of these plot mechanics will raise an eyebrow and peak some interest.
Overall, Shadow of War was a bit more than I expected on several fronts, storyline inparticular. So is it worth the $60(USD)? I'd say so. It definately has a good bang for the buck to it.

I have always wanted to play this game during my childhood, but at the time I couldn't get this game. So, this is my first time playing the game (However, I have played Army Men and Army Men Toys in Space before).
Here are some pros and cons comparing to Army Men I.
Pros:
- The controls are better than Army Men I :
> You can use your mouse to aim and also to move by left-click (in Army Men I, you have to use keyboard to rotatate/aim).
- Better squad controls/system :
> You can order them individually (attack, defense, hold) but you can not fully control them like Sarge.
> In campaign, your squad member can level up, which increase their HP. Not sure about other stats.
> In campaign, at the end of a mission, if your squad members are alive, they will go with you to the next mission with their improved stats.
> Squad mates are smarter, more useful, easier to control. And they comes with variety of weapons.
- Improved graphics.
- Difficulty options
- Great story potential and news characters. but.... (see cons)
Cons :
- Game is shorter, I think.
- Weird music choices, I don't know how to explain this (lol), but it's not that bad.
- Story sounds interesting and has high potential, but executed poorly and has little impact on missions.
<<<<<< SPOILERS  ALERT>>>>>>>
> There are 4 antagonists: Major Maylars, Dr. Madd, Rogue Green colonel, General Plastro.
> The introduction of MM is very interesting but his role is only that he took over the Tan army and that is only implied. At the time I don't even know that, I still have to fight the Tan army like usual. No impact to the story. What was the point of this guy???
> Dr. Madd is a guy from Grey army who creates zombies and other technologies. This character is good in his way.
> Rogue Green colonel. His arc is good but the only problem is that it is implied that something/somebody makes him go rouge but in the end there is no answer to that.
> General Plastro, it is implied that he was taken over by MM. So, it make sense that he is not mentioned in the game that much, I think.
> Few back story dialogs/radio/in game voice to explain the current situation on Major Mylar take over. I don't mind few CG cutscenes (it's an Army Men game not MGS) but if they are going to have some more complex story, they should do a better story telling.
> At the end of the day, the overall story is ok. But may be, I was expecting too much from a game from 18 years ago.

Oh boi, now this will be a long one but Imma try to make it as simple as possible. Will contain some spoilers
I only want to point out some major flaws in the game as I actually really like it but it might not be worth $60 as of now
- Attacking and defending fortresses. Every siege you will play will be basically the same. The fortress might look different, the Warchiefs and their upgrades might vary, but gameplay doesn’t really change, as you every time have to capture 3-4 points within the fortress and kill the Overlord. In any interview with Monolith you would hear how they wanted to make the game practically endless by being able to siege forts of other players, but i’m not sure if I wanna do that anymore at this point since I’m already rather sick of ‘em just within the storyline
But defending fortresses… Upon reaching Act IV and starting the defence of my fortresses, it’s laughable how many times I had to come out just to kill enemy warchiefs which are ♥♥♥♥ing stuck beneath my walls, like, I have an army of orcs ready to fight anyone who enters the fortress, but well too bad that the AI is so dumb that sometimes NOT A SINGLE enemy orc actually makes it past the gates/walls
- Grinding and Microtransactions. Act IV is basically grinding 99% of the time because you will need better orcs and better upgrades since this act is all about defending your fortresses, I can see how someone thought ‘hey, now this part will take players lots of time doing repetitive things, over and over, why not include some microtransactions?’, most of negative reviews were all pissy about those but this ain’t the worst about this game. You have loot boxes which will do nothing else but save your time. That’s really why you have loot boxes in this game, to spare you from all that grind. It’s not like it’s hard, it just gets repetitive and therefore boring, so I can understand why would some go ‘♥♥♥♥ it’ and just buy whatever they’re missing with Gold
- Animations, very few innovations. Seriously, if you played the first game then you’ll quickly realize that there’s not all that many new animations, most of them have been simply taken from Shadow of Mordor. They have indeed improved core gameplay a bit but overall it's barely different from the previous title
- Amount of content. Grinding aside, how much does the game really have to offer? Act 1 has been my absolute favorite by all means, the way the story has been put there made actually care and feel like I’m actually fighting for something important, but it only goes downhill from there. Act 3 came close to that but it has been too short. And I don’t know if you can even call the grind of Act IV actual content

I've been playing this for awhile now and I have to say I'm really enjoying in. There are a few game breaking bugs and the UI in general is not great. I really hope the creators continue to update it and fix it.
Exploration:
The biomes are all very different.
There is no map that I could find. Though in it's place there is X,Y coords of where you are and where your bind place is.
The path finding is not great. When you click to go somewhere most the time you end up stuck on a block or tree with your character trying, unsuccessfully, to get around it.  You also end up hitting trees, logs, and rocks on accident.
Survival:
I think this part of the game is almost too easy. Maybe I'm just used to Don't Starve and I think after this first day I shouldn't be able to have a pack full of food. Also almost every tree dropping a sapling is over kill. I wish food and trees were a little scarcer, only because:
I really enjoy the farming in this game. Each plant has it's own grow time so if you plant two carrots next to each other one might grow in a couple game hours and the other in days.
Combat:
The combat is a little clunky. I think that the UI could be improved so when you go into combat mode you can't accidentally select an item to use that's not a weapon. Also I wish that when your current weapon breaks that it would switch to your next weapon automaticly.
As I've played both ranged classes it's easy enough to have monsters follow you down a hall and kill them as they come at you.  Sometimes when going from your special abilities (right clicking) back to normal attack your character wont do anything few seconds.
Crafting:
There is alot to craft in this game weapons, armor, gems, enchantments, decor. When you make certain items they have sockets to gem. You can also add enchantments to your items.
The Crafting UI leaves alot to be desired. If you are using the smelter to make pitch for torches you then have to close the ui the reopen to make the torches. There is also a bug where the stations don't show you everything they can make and you have to re-open them.
Other than than the UI being unfinished and the crashing. I am really enjoying this game a lot.

Hmm. I've been playing Kerbal Space Program a lot recently, and it's left quite an impression on me. The impression is as follows:
AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH
This goes on for about five more pages, but I'll spare you. Look, KSP is not a game for the faint of heart. Er, faint of brain. There is a lot, and I mean a LOT, of careful planning that one has to do in order to do anything successfully in this game. Unlike other games, even ones about spaceflight, the game isn't working for you. It also isn't working against you. It says, "Here are the rules. They're pretty much the same as in real life, so if you know those, you might do a little better than most." Then it sits back and laughs as you inevitably learn why the Apollo missions used free return orbits instead of direct insertion.
It's not easy. And it will never BE easy. But that's the point. Because after hours and hours of grueling gameplay, frustrating accidents, and an utter lack of knowledge about spaceflight, the moment you hit touchdown on the Mun and for the first time, see that famous Kerbrise, then baby, it was worth it.
I love you, Kerbal Space Program. Don't ever change.
Unless you like fix bugs.
Please do change that.

Mediterranean Chicken and Pasta
Makes: 4 servingsPrep: 5 mins Cook: 15 mins Carb Grams Per Serving: 38
Ingredients
1 6 - ounce jar marinated artichoke hearts
1 tablespoon olive oil
12 ounces skinless, boneless chicken breast, cut into bite-size pieces
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1/4 cup chicken broth
1/4 dry white wine
1 teaspoon dried oregano, crushed
1 7 - ounce jar roasted red peppers, drained and cut into strips
1/4 cup pitted kalamata olives
3 cups hot cooked campanelle or penne pasta
1/4 cup crumbled feta cheese (optional)
Directions
Drain artichoke hearts, reserving marinade, and chop them.
In a large skillet, heat oil over medium-high heat; add chicken and garlic. Cook and stir until chicken is brown.
Add the reserved artichoke marinade, broth, wine and dried oregano.
Bring to a boil; reduce heat. Simmer, covered, 10 minutes.
Stir in chopped artichokes, roasted peppers and olives.
To serve, spoon chicken mixture over pasta. If desired, sprinkle with feta cheese.

Servings Per Recipe: 4

Broken Age is a fabulous point-and-click game. Though I'm only over an hour in I can safely say it reminds me of my childhood for I grew up on Spyfox, Freddi Fish, Pajama Sam, Carmen San Diego. Plus the art style feels like you are watching a children's book acted out by the characters, a very unique style which gives the game it's own character.
This game is not only entertaining but it really leaves you wanting to play more because of the immersion. Shay being in a mundane routine of someone else's accord and Vella being a thinker who is opressed and looked down upon. Characters are very human and have depth, and that doesn't just apply to the main characters. The characters all are wonderfully voiced by many talents which really brings out the personalities even more.
But the voice acting isn't all it has to offer for sound. The music is splendid and I had bought the soundtrack along with the game. I don't regret it. No, I'm so happy that I have the soundtrack and it adds so many layers to the game.
The puzzles are fair so far. I don't think I had much of a problem with the amount of time I spent on them at all. Most of the time it was me being unobservant or I had a pitfall in logic, not the game. Some games require a ridculous amount of obscure going around and collecting and combining. But I had a clear idea of my objective, without knowing too many details on how to achieve it and it clicked... Eventually.
The game does have a few flaws. Like all point-and-click games it will get linear if you play it for a long period of time, so you may just want to play it in little secessions. Walking speed is a bit slow for some people.  I know from several other people that yes, it's short. However, this is only Act I out of two and I hope the second one is much longer than the first.
In short
Pros:
Fascinating story
Quality art style that is unique
Smooth gameplay
Remarkable music
Astounding voice acting
Worth the price
Cons:
Linear (as expected with most point and click games)
Choices do not affect story (not that it had to but it would be a nice touch)
It's short (as stated it's only act I)
And this falls a bit between both depending on who you are.
It's different. If you are apprehensive to buy it now, wait for a sale, but if you really want it, get it as soon as possible.

From what I've played so far, the game is based upon the old FATE game engine which was copied from Diablo's earlier series. It's a mixture of Harvest Moon with FATE and admittedly doesn't feel too good in both areas due to the numerous bugs I've encountered so far. One of the most prominent is the random times your character seems to be blurred out by a white block by equipping certain tools or armor. {For me, it was a copper axe, then copper greaves}. The game lacks any sort of tutorial and is a bit of a deep leap when trying to figure out how to begin unless you watch players on youtube. It does however boast a rich enviroment of building. The other thing that irks me about this game is  it feels as if the walls do not properly connect. Also, quite a few items boast no pictures in the inventory or play screen {Bricked Items, Iron Curiass}. This game needs a lot of spit and polish because I would recommend it to anyone because I've decently high standards when it comes to "Role Playing Games". The interesting thing about this game though, if you put up with the bugs, is the ability to build a town center you can teleport to, teleporters you can place underground, and merchant townspeople. The townspeople however do tend to overcharge. You can't sell most items for very much but it's still good to play around with. Not sure about the item refresh rate. I can't say I'd recommend it, at least not until it is a fair bit more stable as it also tends to crash randomly and for no reason. You lose large amounts of items in this fashion.

This is an extraordinarily useful resource - if you take advantage of the fantastic community behind it.  All of the negative reviews seem to focus on the fact that out of the box all they see is a blank screen with some dice on it.  This is mostly true, it only starts with fairly barebones rule modules for a few common RPGs.  Oh no, they say, now I'm forced to buy expensive DLC to use this thing I just bought!  Well not so fast.
There is a ton of completely free community-made content for Fantasy Grounds.  Shadowrun?  Got it.  World of Darkness?  Yep.  If you can think of a system, there's a very good chance that someone's made a module for it, all you have to do is take the time to get it and plug it in.  The professional modules being sold for real cashola have extra polish and time-saving automation, but their purchase is NOT required to run a game.  It's up to you to decide whether having the snazzy presentation and extra resources ready-made for you is worth dropping the money on; if you decide it isn't it's easy to go out and snag maps and tokens and portraits online to do it yourself.
I bought this because I was going to run a Star Wars Edge of the Empire game.  I looked at Roll20 first, because it's free, right?  Well, no, it turned out that making the dice system for Star Wars work in Roll20 would require that I pay ten bucks a month for the API access of a Pro account.  Forever.  Then I looked at Fantasy Grounds, saw that a user had made a great Star Wars module for it, shelled out the money for a lifetime license, installed the module and went along my merry way.  Haven't paid a penny since.  Maps and tokens have been easy to find online and import into the game as needed.  At this point I would've paid MORE for Roll20 than I did for Fantasy Grounds.
All that said, here are my complaints about the program: It has no VOIP, music, or sound effect functionality.  All of those things would be great to have, but right now you have to fiddle around with third-party programs to make that work.  The interface is very unintuitive.  Don't just buy this an hour before game time and expect to be running a great game, it took me a good deal of fiddling around with stuff on my own to work out how to display maps with masked areas, set up encounters with all the NPC stats and tokens, and generally get everything working smoothly.  They're working on a new version of the program with snazzier graphics capability and I'm hoping that some of my issues will be fixed with that, but as of now they're not saying very much about what features are being added, so that may just be an empty dream.
Short version: It's not perfect, but it's still very good and has a ton of talented people coming out with content for it.  It remains my favorite virtual table top program.

For what it is, I got a fair amount of play out of Multiwinia but it certainly isn't anything spectacular.  Actually, it's about as simplified as an RTS game can possibly get.  There is only one type of unit, and the only real control you have is to give a vague direction to them.  Occassionally you'll use an item or pull off a clever pincer attack, but Multiwinia is very simplistic.
Despite being simplistic, or perhaps because of it, a large chunk of the gameplay is a grind.  Send your 100 units to kill the enemy's 100 units and try to stop them from spawning more, so you can send in more and take a base that they can no longer defend.  Of course, you'll be sending these units in waves, usually immediately after they spawn.  As far as gameplay goes, there really isn't a lot there: you'll end up automating most of your units' movements.
There are a few different game modes but only a few of them really work well.  King of the hill and generic base capturing are fine.  There's a mode that involves capturing bases to fuel a rocket as well, but it's similar to the general base capturing mode.  Another mode features capturing statues and returning them to your base (permanently) and while different enough, doesn't really get away from the base/king of the hill modes much.  The last type I wouldn't recommend to anyone.  It involves capturing a heavily fortified position.  One army gets very frequent respawns while the other doesnt, but as there is little to no strategy in this game, it's very painful to play.  The attacking team either sits and hordes units, or sends them in as he gets them.  Either way, they almost all die for little to no progress against the defender.
There's online vs and it works well enough, but like I've said, the lack of any unique units or strategy really bogs this game down to a grind and you probably won't have a lot of fun with your friends.  It's good for a game or two but after that you'll probably want to move on.
On the plus side, the AI is competent enough that playing against it isn't boring, especially if there are several enemy teams.  Watching enemy teams duke it out is quite entertaining.
Oh, some really cool/scary things can happen if the aliens or darkwinians get out of control.  ♥♥♥♥ those aliens man, they are god damned ridiculous.
Final note?  The way items are distributed is pretty biased.  I do like the idea that if you want the items then you have to send units to go collect them because you have to decide whether or not the reward is worth the risk of leaving an area unguarded or unharassed (pro tip: it usually is).
I liked it but I think I'm also in a very small minority of people that would.  It's just so basic.

I bought this game on launch day (for PS3) and I have no regrets over having done so, which is something I can't say most of the time. I was hyped because it was an Obsidian game with Chris Avellone on it.
Fortunately, the game lived up to the hype. Sure, you have some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ minigames that can be a pain, especially when you encouter the higher difficuly ones, but it's a roleplaying game first and foremost, and minigames are "peccata minuta". You play a spy, and you build your reputation as you go. There aren't "wrong" choices in this game, only choices with different effects that can be boons or hindrances depending how you want to go about it later on - e.g.: you can make a major antagonist fight to the death in a situation that's advantageous for you if you make him hate you earlier on, when he would normally retreat, or you can turn him to your side if you build a relationship of respect and uncover certain pieces of information and make some specific conversational bonuses.
It also offers a "challenge" starting choice (the Rookie) that begins with less skills, but is somewhat compensated by the Rookie conversational options that give unexpected results, as well as the Veteran class (unlockable by beating the game with Rookie) which starts with extra skills as well as "Veteran" options that allow you to perform feats such as completing two objectives that would be exclusive otherwise, as well as giving you extra conversational options.
The NPCs all have their own kind of charm, with some very memorable ones (especially one potentiall ally in Korea), as well as very memorable romance options (getting right what Mass Effect couldn't). Speaking of which, there is some influence from Mass Effect in this game, but it's mostly on the interface and controls. Don't be deceived: this game stands head and shoulders above ME as a roleplaying game (the action is somewhat better in ME, though). There are no "wrong" sides in this game and you won't get shorter questlines or ♥♥♥♥♥ier outcomes for choosing the "bad" side, which is something you can't say about most games out there, where you are expected to be goody-two-shoes most of the time.
These days this game can be bought for very cheap for most of the year, and you'll get a lot of fun out of it for very little money (if you are not the type to be easily aggravated by silly puzzles), so I don't know what you are doing not buying or playing it. Buy it for your friends, too.
It is more of a story then a game. And it is truly deep and brilliant. Highly recommended.

(I owned the game prior on Desura before the game was greenlit on Steam. Add 20+ hours to the actual playtime shown.)
Pros:   This has the basic crafting element with your other 2d/3d indie sandbox games but with a twist. First off the game has just as much emphasis on survival as it does crafting. However, unlike Don’t Starve when your hunger meter gets down to zero you don’t die. Instead you have less than 10 HP and are very fragile.  This allows you to still craft, build, farm, etc. at your house but will keep you on your toes.
You can make your own farm by planting the seeds and harvesting them. Then you can cook food from crafting ovens. In addition to that you can trap animals like, cows, sheep, etc. so that they can produce milk, wool that can be used as crafting materials. That in its self is a fun meta game.
In addition to a hunger system if you take the mage path there is meter for mana regen. You ether need to sleep in your bed to refresh or you can make teas, etc. This balances out magic as it is powerful.
Also, everything from swords, armor, wants, etc. has a durability. They get worn over time and unlike other game you have a reason to make the same pick axe or armor over again. Also, when you die you take a durability hit. This really adds another layer of dynamic strategy to the game.
There is a nice RPG element and you can chose, mage, warrior, archer, or adventure path. There are no classes just a skill tree system.
The game is fully launched but the developers are continuing to make updates and improvements to the game all the time. Tones of replay value here and worth the asking price of $10 USD.
Cons:   While the bird’s eye view is a nice touch, sometimes it can be difficult to see certain angles when playing blocks while building your house. Game used mouse instead of WASDE controls. At times this can make combat annoying but after a while you will get used to it. Combat through doorways while in dungeons can be annoying when you right click it closes the door instead of combat. This can be resolved by letting the enemy pass through the doorway first.
