At the moment, I can't decide whether I love this game or hate it.
Alpha Protocol is an interesting RPG, brought to us by Obsidian Entertainment of Fallout New Vegas, Knights of the Old Republic II, and Neverwinter Nights 2 fame. People might also recognize these guys as the bunch behind Pillars of Eternity. But Alpha Protocol isn't like any of those other games from a gameplay standpoint.
In Alpha Protocol, you play as Michael Thorton, a newly inducted agent of... what else, Alpha Protocol, a top secret organization with the mandate to protect America, and presumably the world, from total disaster. So, basically, Cerberus from Mass Effect crossed with XCOM, only without the whole ends justify the means shtick, at least from what I've played so far. Michael himself, is a voiced protagonist whose personality the player can shape at their own whim being aggressive (Renegade Shepard), suave (James Bond) or Professional (JC Denton/Adam Jensen). And just like in KOTOR 2, how Michael acts towards his companions will affect their view of him through an influence system. The story is very well written, and so far has kept me intrigued.
And now, the gameplay. Oh boy, where do I start... Alpha Protocol seems as though it wants to be both Deus Ex, and Metal Gear Solid at the same time. In the sense of it being a stealth game, it succeeds at this brilliantly. The game is at its best when you are sneaking around, knocking out guards from behind, hacking terminals, lockpicking doors, and trying to find the not-so-obvious routes to your objectives. However, once the bullets start flying, the cracks start showing. While the shooting feels nice and somewhat responsive, the aiming is some of the worst I have ever seen in a video game. The crosshair is freaking huge, taking up nearly the entire center of the screen, and it doesn't matter if you have the center dot aimed at your enemies head, the shot can end up to the left, right, up or downward of where you intended. If you hold your aim, the crosshair will shrink to a more managable size, allowing you to make a more accurate shot. Out of all the things to take from the original Deus Ex, I really don't think the aiming system should have been it.
That aside though, the only other issue I have with this game is the fact that it uses a checkpoint system instead of manual saving. This game really needs it. As far as optimization goes, for me, the game runs smoothly at 60 FPS on my Windows 10 machine, with no crashes or any noticeable bugs game breaking or otherwise thus far.
At the beginning of this review, I said I didn't know if I loved this game or hated it. I suspect that the more I play, the more I'll warm up to it. The shooting might be wonky, but the stealth is great, and the story is intriguing. This feels like my own James Bond movie, and I'm curious to see how everything ties itself together.

Straight up, one of the best games of 2017 thus far. Likely a GOTY for many, especially those who enjoyed the prequel, as it's essentially more of the same, albeit with a great deal cut and pasted from the original game. The core gameplay is quite similar, with a re-worked weapon and skill system, and the combat is the same mash-fest as many WB produced games from the last decade.
It's a graphical marvel, especially on beefy systems, and contains faithful recreations of many iconic scenes from the LOTR universe, taking a lot of inspiration from the Peter Jackson movie trilogy. Battles feel epic, and the scale of the world is much larger than ever before.  Sadly, having played the preqel just before this, many of the animations have been directly copied across from the first game, which did feel a little lazy to me - they still look and feel as good as ever though, which is really just a minor niggle in the scheme of things.
The Uruks are, as expected, the stars of the game. Each captain and warchief have interesting quirks about their characters, and hearing their name chanted as they enter the battlefield is an amazing touch, and really shows the attention to detail Monolith put into this game.
Microtransactions are ♥♥♥♥♥♥. But that's a fact that I'm not sure we can ever change. This shouldn't detract from the awesome game that lies under all the negative press surrounding an optional system, however - at the time of writing I've played for eight hours and have not even touched the store feature, nor have I opened any of the chests given to me at the start of the game for pre-ordering. Simply put, the game rewards you enough to dissaude you from paying extra, which is a nice touch.

Out of all the previous games I have played in the past year, I'm most certain that Middle Earth: Shadow of War is one of the best gaming experiences I've had in a long time. There's a lot of things that I could talk about in the game, ranging from the combat system, stealth system, nemisis system etc. But to me, the main thing that stands out the most and has had me hooked to the very last minute was the evergrowing, branching out story and narrative. Also, this review isn't like practically all of the others that I've seen, with countless amounts of people bombing the game over the controversial 'Microtransactions' and 'Lootboxes'. The game doesn't force them on you, you're not forced to pay ACTUAL money for them. You get an abundance of in-game currency that you can use to buy the war chests from the market, and you get boxes for free from completing online Vendetta missions for other players. No you don't have to pay for gold war chests to get Epic and Legendary Orcs, I've had plenty from the silver chests that I paid for with the in-game currency. On top of that, the in-game currency that you get is literally everywhere, in main missions, dropped from random enemies, side quests, challenges etc. Theres no way for you to NOT recieve the game's currency. The 'Gold' currency that you get to pay for gold and blue war chests you can earn through online Vendettas and Seige missions too, as the first one you complete you recieve 500 gold right off the bat. I haven't spent a single penny of my money on this game, I just don't have to and neither do you.
To get to the combat and stealth; yes the game has recycled animations from the first but that doesn't mean that's really a bad thing. In my opinion, those animations are already really good on their own, and for Monolith to ADD to those and refine them makes playing this sequel even better. I adored the combat from Shadow of Mordor, it felt like the Arkham series and Mad Max, which is a good thing as that combat system is really the only good system in games today. The combat has been worked on a lot, and there's SO much more skills to use as the skill tree is huge compared to the first game. Stealth is still a good and exciting way to get around an environment when hunting a captain or warchief, and with the new skills that you can unlock makes it even better.
The gameplay overall is a lot of the same things from the first game, but has been worked on and added to so much that it makes the game much more enjoyable than the first. The graphics in almost all areas are a lot better, sharper and just visually more appealing. It helps that you're not just stuck with two maps anymore, and the game has around 5 regions that you progress through, each with their own distinctive look and feel. My favourite porbably being Gorgoroth.
Lastly the narrative itself and the story the game wants to take you through felt incredible and made me itch to play more after every cutscene. The first game almost had me there, I did watch the cutscenes the first 10 hours or so in but then it got to a point where I just wanted to play instead of listen. This game, not once, made me feel that way. I was intrigued and felt as if I HAD to listen, to watch what was happening on screen. I've not really been much of a Lord of The Rings fan, although I do have a Mum that loves the books, films and the earlier games that released on the PS2. The story this time round I felt was an incredible step up compared to Shadow of Mordor, and the fact that if you put a little more effort in to the end of the game you can get an ending that ties into the films is just amazing. I've got just under 40 hours on the game so far, in which I have completed every main mission, side quest and every single collectable and not once did I feel bored or that the game felt repitive. The plot twists where amazing due to me being so sucked into the story, and  I didn't even see it coming. I mean it wasn't even hinted at in the trailers at all and I hadn't seen it mentioned anywhere online, so for me to witness it first hand and spoiler-free was mind blowing. Obviously we all know about the 3 movies and what happens so I was kind of expecting the ending to stick true to that. You'll know what I mean at the end.
(Side note: The attention to detail and continuity at the end of the game from the Orcs is incredible. As well as when you open up the region map after finishing the game, you'll notice something that I thought was incredibly well done and well thought of, it's near Mount Doom...)
The game does have a 'True' ending that you can after you complete act 4 called 'The Shadow Wars'. I won't really get into that other than saying it's a 20 stage seige mission for your fortresses and that's all I'm going to say. I haven't finished them, as a matter of fact I've only completed the first one which took me about an hour and a half, maybe 2 hours to prepare for. But it was really fun and at least there's something to do after you finish the game.
Overall my verdict for the game is a solid 9.8/10.
There was a few small hiccups along the way that were quickly fixed, and I'm sure overtime they'll be patched out. But from the gameplay to the narrative, everything about the game was amazing and an unforgettable experience for me. Also I'd like to mention the game's soundtrack, especially the main menu and map theme. Absolutely adore that song, just thought I'd throw that in there. But I digress, the game was a solid experience, well worth the money and I know for a fact that I'm going to continue playing it and very much looking forward to the future of the game.

Ever since I got it in 2012, this game has never ceased to amaze me. Since I got the demo that many years back, the game has continually gotten better, thanks to its active development team that listens closely to its fanbase. The game offers a wonderful sanbox mode whereby all parts for both spaceship building and plane building are open to you, and also a challenging career mode whereby you slowly progress as a space agency, unlocking parts and missions as you go, all while balancing your budget, and maintaining a steady influx of science points for research.
The game features great physics. If you enjoy physics sanboxes, I highly recommend purchasing this game, as you'll spend countless hours exploring both physics in atmosphere, and also in microgravity in space. Because of this, however, there alos features a steep learning curve that makes it challenging to make it out of Kerbin's gravity pull, but once you get the hang of it, the game gets way more fun and rewarding.
Overall, a great game that ages extremely well. Doesn't need to be the most beautiful game out there to surpass expectations. You'll lose track of time with your creations, and every new accomplishment will leave you hungry for more. If you're uncertain, go watch some videos online. I recommend Scott Manley, but there are many other YouTubers who regularly play KSP.

I feel as if The Political Machine 2016 has a good mindset on what they want to achieve, but I don't think it is executed properly. I can't stress how annoying it is to play on normal and get my head shoved up my @ss everytime I play. Most of it is realistic, except for how the states play. When I'm playing a campaign, there are states in every election that will always basically vote for your party like Kansas for Republican. In the game, there is a constant need to drive attention away from the battleground states, just to save a state like Texas from ever falling to the Democrats. Really, I see what they are doing in trying to add diversity, but it takes away the feel from fighting neck to neck in a state like Ohio or Pennsylvania. Instead, we are given an AI that will always convince natural conservative states easily by visiting them once or twice. I just don't feel the need to campaign in Oklahoma to regain the vote when there are swing states I need to win. Also, the game lacks diversity in terms of creativity. There is a limited character creation process that only includes a small amount of features; as well as creating your own party or running as an independent. Yes, the game is $10 and it is pretty decent for $10, but the game doesn't have much to offer than running against an Democrat AI who can somehow win Texas even though they always vote conservative IRL with little campaigning. Basically, the game lacks some balance issues with the AI and how the function of the states play out as well as creativity. I wouldn't recommend this game to others, due to the fact that I'd rather pay an extra $10 or $20 for the game if it was improved upon compared to what it is now. I hope this was helpful in your guide for trying to recreate the 2016 Presidential Election.

Hmm. I've been playing Kerbal Space Program a lot recently, and it's left quite an impression on me. The impression is as follows:
AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH
This goes on for about five more pages, but I'll spare you. Look, KSP is not a game for the faint of heart. Er, faint of brain. There is a lot, and I mean a LOT, of careful planning that one has to do in order to do anything successfully in this game. Unlike other games, even ones about spaceflight, the game isn't working for you. It also isn't working against you. It says, "Here are the rules. They're pretty much the same as in real life, so if you know those, you might do a little better than most." Then it sits back and laughs as you inevitably learn why the Apollo missions used free return orbits instead of direct insertion.
It's not easy. And it will never BE easy. But that's the point. Because after hours and hours of grueling gameplay, frustrating accidents, and an utter lack of knowledge about spaceflight, the moment you hit touchdown on the Mun and for the first time, see that famous Kerbrise, then baby, it was worth it.
I love you, Kerbal Space Program. Don't ever change.
Unless you like fix bugs.
Please do change that.

I purchased this game based on certain positive reviews.
“Act 1 of Broken Age is a gorgeous, impeccably written adventure that simultaneously tugs at my nostalgic core, while ushering in a new era for the point-and-click genre.”
9.5 – IGN
“I haven’t felt this surge of nostalgia and excitement about a game in a long time, and I truly think Broken Age will be looked back fondly as one of the greats.”
9.5 – Destructoid
Having beaten it in roughly 4 hours, I have to ask: Was I playing the same game?
Nostolgia?
New Era for Point and Click?
The Greats?
This game offers nothing to the genre. The Greats had action menus. large explorable worlds, plenty of red herrings (both as objects and characters), along with memorable personalities and dialogue. Broken Age has none of this. Instead, interctive action menus have been replaced by a single mouse cursor which works for all Look\Interact\Pick Up type activities. Clicking on a piece of the world causes the character to simply interact with it in only one way.
The puzzles are laughable. Some of them literally require nothing more than getting to the end of a dialogue tree.
I suggest you all save your money and wait for a real adventure game.

This is my favorite horror game. It plays completely differently from other horror games where the player is mostly helpless, such as the Amnesia series or Clock Tower. It is instead an action game with a master class narrative (as far as games go) that plays like an old, lost Stephen King novel with a nod to Rod Serling and The Twilight Zone. The dark forests of western Washington state provide fantastic immersion and a unique setting, especially since the game's vast levels bring life to the game's world in the way that smaller corridor-based games cannot. There are many movies that wish they had the kind of setting and cinematography that this game has. Remedy provides a pretty good soundtrack, and the gameplay by the former Max Payne devs make it pretty gun heavy as a third-person shooter. It has a lot of downtime in between action so that the game's story can pull you in, but it makes it all the more intense when night falls and you are no longer safe. There is not much enemy variety or even a variety of ways to kill the horrors that you will fight and run from, but the game is short enough that it is not that much of a problem. A continuation of this series or a spiritual successor in the same style is one of my most looked for games.

This is a free game kind of, their business model is wierd but the idea is that the demo gives you access to the game PERIOD.
There are 3 types of ownership:
Demo - Access of the game but cannot expand on content, you get partial access for regular owners and full access w/ Ult.
Regular - You get access to everything and you never have to worry about who the host is to get full access.
Ultimate - You can do anything pretty much.
The key difference between the types is if you are going to be a DM or not.
If you are with a group with a set DM it's best to just pool resources and get that DM the stuff then everyone just uses the Demo version and link to the DM's ultimate.
If you are changing DMs a lot then everyone would probably be better off with Regular.
If you DM a lot then Ultimate is your best bet, you wont have to worry about what status your players are.

In this review I would like to first clarify what Fantasy Grounds is, and is not.
Fantasy Grounds isn't a traditional game. In fact, it isn't a game at all. It is a virtual tabletop that allows you to play traditional role playing games over the Internet.
By default it supports a variety of tabletop games. By supports it means that if you buy the prewritten modules (highly recommended) or type in the rules yourself (time consuming and not recommended) you can play these games online, with other people.
It is certainly functional without buying a single module, but I think you'll agree that buying a premade module for your game is a better use of your time. Unfortunately due to licensing costs, modules from some publishers such as Wizards of the Coast (Dungeons and Dragons) are rather expensive.
One of Fantasy Grounds great strengths is that it can automate many of the tedious tasks that bog down traditional games, things like automatic experience point calculations, applying combat effects and so on. Once you get over the initial learning curve, it becomes quite easy for the Game Master to design and run an encounter.
There are 2 options with Fantasy Grounds, a regular or ultimate license. If you have the same Game Master for every game, buy the ultimate license. It is a site license that allows unlimited free (Demo) license to connnect and play. Players never have to spend any money.
It is very important to realise that only modules owned by the Game Master (who is hosting the game) can be used. Players CAN NOT share modules with their Game Master.
If you are looking at this as a player, I would suggest having the Game Master buy the Ultimate license, and the players gifting the needed game modules to the Game Master. Players should then use the free Demo license to connect.
Happy Gaming.

First off, Shadow of War does what a sequel should do. In just about every department everything is polished, tightened and improved in just about every way. The Nemesis system is more expansive than ever, giving quite a number of possibilities when either encountering or creating Orc captains. Combat feel tighter all around with a revamped skill tree that helps keep Talion from becoming too overpowered, while still providing the much needed edge to take down hordes of enemies and the captains. The graphics aren't a massive improvement, but this is acceptable given the already excellent detail given and the high amount of graphics effects that can be going on in the heat of the moment. Overall, they took what they had and really put the spit shine to work.
A new feature here is the siege mode. A fort in every region that can be taken over with your Orc army can be somewhat challenging, but nothing overwhelming. Though the Nemesis sytem can potentially produce some rather wild results in just what captain, or overlord in the case of forts, can end up facing you down. But the siege mode is a welcome addition that comes along with an online mode in which you can test your abilities against forts other players have customized in a ranked ladder and take on the Orcs they've appointed to defend the fort, along with whatever other defences they've installed.
As for combat, nothing has changed too much. Like the other games from WB, such as the Batman Arkham series, it improves just about everything combat wise. However, unlike Arkham Knight for example, you will find yourself more often than not putting all the different skills and such to use. It's far more balanced this time around, keeping Talion from becoming almost ridiculously overpowered when your not even half way through the game. Along with that, the skill tree has been expanded upon, giving a variety of new skills and a more tactical setup, allowing secondary skills which act as buffs to your main skills, giving not only a bit of extra customization, but something to help vary your combat a bit, say in an instance where you need to change an attack from dealing fire damage to ice damage when dealing with captains that have unique elemental buffs.
Oh. And there are effectively ZERO quick time events. None. Nada. Zip. They threw that trash out.
The story if much much much more fleshed out, with several narratives going on over the course of the game in not just two regions, but five major regions, each almost the size of the original two maps from Shadow of Mordor. Characters seem a bit more inspired this time around and Talion doesn't come across so much as a drag. As for whether the story is canon or not to Lord of the Rings lore, I honestly couldn't say myself, but it does heat up to a certain degree, more than enough to be far more engaging this time around and give some interesting backstories to some of the Nazgul and even the great spider Shelob.
As for being optimized, things seem pretty tight on that end too. Don't fret to much of your on the lower end when it come to your CPU, the game doesn't seem to draw to much power. As for GPU, I was using an EVGA 6GB 1060 on ultra settings with textures on high and the frame rate almost never dipped below 50 through my entire playthrough. And even if you need to turn the graphics down, you shouldn't be too dissapointed, the game still looks plenty fantastic.
I've seen a lot of people angry about microtransactions, however when it comes right down to it, this doesn't seem to effect the main game in any real way. It seems more focused on people who would have a higher interest in climbing the leaderboards in the online siege mode. My only argument against people who have an issue with microtransactions is any good company is ALWAYS looking for an extra revenue stream. The game itself is worth it's price alone and if you don't want to pay extra money for microtransactions, then do what I do. Ignore it. It's that simple. I suppose I don't see what the fuss is about.
Not sure what else to say about the game. I will say however, it has more content than I expected, along with an entire post game chapter after the story is completed using the new siege mechanics, along with some other mechanics I can't mention due to plot spoilers. But if your already interested in buying the game, I can guarentee some of these plot mechanics will raise an eyebrow and peak some interest.
Overall, Shadow of War was a bit more than I expected on several fronts, storyline inparticular. So is it worth the $60(USD)? I'd say so. It definately has a good bang for the buck to it.

I feel as if The Political Machine 2016 has a good mindset on what they want to achieve, but I don't think it is executed properly. I can't stress how annoying it is to play on normal and get my head shoved up my @ss everytime I play. Most of it is realistic, except for how the states play. When I'm playing a campaign, there are states in every election that will always basically vote for your party like Kansas for Republican. In the game, there is a constant need to drive attention away from the battleground states, just to save a state like Texas from ever falling to the Democrats. Really, I see what they are doing in trying to add diversity, but it takes away the feel from fighting neck to neck in a state like Ohio or Pennsylvania. Instead, we are given an AI that will always convince natural conservative states easily by visiting them once or twice. I just don't feel the need to campaign in Oklahoma to regain the vote when there are swing states I need to win. Also, the game lacks diversity in terms of creativity. There is a limited character creation process that only includes a small amount of features; as well as creating your own party or running as an independent. Yes, the game is $10 and it is pretty decent for $10, but the game doesn't have much to offer than running against an Democrat AI who can somehow win Texas even though they always vote conservative IRL with little campaigning. Basically, the game lacks some balance issues with the AI and how the function of the states play out as well as creativity. I wouldn't recommend this game to others, due to the fact that I'd rather pay an extra $10 or $20 for the game if it was improved upon compared to what it is now. I hope this was helpful in your guide for trying to recreate the 2016 Presidential Election.

Oh boi, now this will be a long one but Imma try to make it as simple as possible. Will contain some spoilers
I only want to point out some major flaws in the game as I actually really like it but it might not be worth $60 as of now
- Attacking and defending fortresses. Every siege you will play will be basically the same. The fortress might look different, the Warchiefs and their upgrades might vary, but gameplay doesn’t really change, as you every time have to capture 3-4 points within the fortress and kill the Overlord. In any interview with Monolith you would hear how they wanted to make the game practically endless by being able to siege forts of other players, but i’m not sure if I wanna do that anymore at this point since I’m already rather sick of ‘em just within the storyline
But defending fortresses… Upon reaching Act IV and starting the defence of my fortresses, it’s laughable how many times I had to come out just to kill enemy warchiefs which are ♥♥♥♥ing stuck beneath my walls, like, I have an army of orcs ready to fight anyone who enters the fortress, but well too bad that the AI is so dumb that sometimes NOT A SINGLE enemy orc actually makes it past the gates/walls
- Grinding and Microtransactions. Act IV is basically grinding 99% of the time because you will need better orcs and better upgrades since this act is all about defending your fortresses, I can see how someone thought ‘hey, now this part will take players lots of time doing repetitive things, over and over, why not include some microtransactions?’, most of negative reviews were all pissy about those but this ain’t the worst about this game. You have loot boxes which will do nothing else but save your time. That’s really why you have loot boxes in this game, to spare you from all that grind. It’s not like it’s hard, it just gets repetitive and therefore boring, so I can understand why would some go ‘♥♥♥♥ it’ and just buy whatever they’re missing with Gold
- Animations, very few innovations. Seriously, if you played the first game then you’ll quickly realize that there’s not all that many new animations, most of them have been simply taken from Shadow of Mordor. They have indeed improved core gameplay a bit but overall it's barely different from the previous title
- Amount of content. Grinding aside, how much does the game really have to offer? Act 1 has been my absolute favorite by all means, the way the story has been put there made actually care and feel like I’m actually fighting for something important, but it only goes downhill from there. Act 3 came close to that but it has been too short. And I don’t know if you can even call the grind of Act IV actual content
Act 2... I wouldn’t call it bad, but I was at very least disappointed with how they executed fighting with the Balrog. Like, if you’ve seen the LoTR movies you know how tough one might be, but in this game defeating most of the captains would be more complicated than the Balrog himself, and you come out of the fight like it was nothing, what?
- Fully priced $60 game. As of now, the game just lacks enough content for it’s price, I really hope they will make decent DLC because I actually ♥♥♥♥ing like the game despite all the flaws, but it’s again simply overpriced. Monolith will seriously have to continue working on the game and add FREE additional content on top of DLCs. The story wasn’t the best, fine, but there are so many missed opportunities that could still be executed whether in new or existing regions, at the moment the only things that could be keeping you playing (besides grinding) are either Pit Fights or Fort Sieges, which both suffer from lack of variety and get boring fast
Again, yes I do like the game, I hope that whatever can still be fixed WILL be fixed, but I still can’t recommend it since what you’re paying for is simply not worthy of $60 and you might wanna wait for a sale or until more content will be added

A new version of the US Presidential elections brings out a new version of the Political Machine. On sale for two bucks and fifty cents, I couldn't resist goosing the economy and picking it up. For that price it is a fun little game.
It is a turn based strategy game where you pick from existing candidates who are represented by bobble head dolls or create your own candidate. Once in the game you are presented with a map of the 50 states that shows the states who are locks for one party as either blue or red and the states still in play as grey. You can easily filter the map to show rich states for fund raising or take a look at the map by electoral college votes. Your candidates move between the states launching ads, giving speeches or establishing campaign headquarters.
The headquarters are interesting as they come in three types. The traditional one is good for fundraising and increasing awareness of your candidate. The other types give you currency to get endorsements from say the gun lobby or operatives who can increase the effectiveness of your speeches or your advertising.
There are also random events that can hurt or help your campaign. The most interesting of these is the chance to appear on national TV shows and answer two questions. The biggest missing item are any form of debate between the candidates and independent candidates. Still it is fun this time of year to pick from the various bobble headed candidates and try to win the voters over to your side.
Quick, clever and fun this is a nice cheap game for those who like politics and light strategy.
Rating: B-

Broken Age is a beautiful game, with an interesting premise. I was incredibly excited to boot this up, and I began the game with Vella's story. The dialogue is charming, the gags amusing, if sometimes a little unsophisticated, but the puzzles aren't nearly complex enough. I was hoping that since Tim Schaefer was at the wheel, Broken Age would feature Grim Fandango or Monkey Island style gameplay. Ultimately everything comes down to 'get item. put item in slot. puzzle solved', and there's no subtlety there at all. That's a tad disappointing, but the art style and story carried it for me enough that I finished the game as it is. I'm looking forward to the next act, but I'm glad it's free or else I likely wouldn't bother with it.
If you're looking for a charming, story-driven romp through fantasy lands with intriguing, beautiful character designs - I highly recommend Broken Age. If you're looking for a challenging, rewarding adventure game, then I'd advise you to look elsewhere. Not once did I feel a thrill of satisfaction for solving a puzzle that I remember so keenly when playing something like The Secret of Monkey Island or Edna and Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes.
I'd give it a 6/10. The voice talent and soundtrack shine, but I'm left with a sour taste in my mouth, like I've been patronised by the gameplay.

1 tablespoon olive oil
12 ounces skinless, boneless chicken breast, cut into bite-size pieces
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1/4 cup chicken broth
1/4 dry white wine
1 teaspoon dried oregano, crushed
1 7 - ounce jar roasted red peppers, drained and cut into strips
1/4 cup pitted kalamata olives
3 cups hot cooked campanelle or penne pasta
1/4 cup crumbled feta cheese (optional)
Directions
Drain artichoke hearts, reserving marinade, and chop them.
In a large skillet, heat oil over medium-high heat; add chicken and garlic. Cook and stir until chicken is brown.
Add the reserved artichoke marinade, broth, wine and dried oregano.
Bring to a boil; reduce heat. Simmer, covered, 10 minutes.
Stir in chopped artichokes, roasted peppers and olives.
To serve, spoon chicken mixture over pasta. If desired, sprinkle with feta cheese.
Nutrition Information
Servings Per Recipe: 4

The game meets a lot of basic functionalities to work as a fun casual diversion at times.  The art is suitably fun and light-hearted.  The game's mechanics are light as well, but they are more designed with a strategic game, rather than a more authentic political simulator.  Indeed, the game's mechaicnes are more ofo a generic strategy one on the gameboard of a USA map rather than a poltical one.
Now havign said that, the game is still fine.  I've owned and played every iteration of the game.  I've never asked for my money back or anything.  And this time, there is an addition of multiplayer for those interested.
But the game's engine lacks a lot of depth, and more importantly, very little change.  The first version of the game had the same basic graphics, engine, concepts, and such.  You spend your time colelcting various currencies you can use for purchasing things.  Dollars and political capital can be spent for ads and endorsements as such.
But I'm going to leave the franchaise alone, barring major changes in the game of a deeper level.  I don't need a new skin every few eyars with a new group of candidates that are currently in teh news.
Let me give you an example of one game mechanic that's simple, but could have been more.  Endorsements:
In this game there are 11 endorsements.  Ten are nromal, and one is a pseudo-endorsement to invest in your campaign structure that you can do later on after the ten are gone, so you won;t waste your points.
Five endorsements are related to each party - Republican and Democrat.  If you have a Democrat candidate, then you have to spend double the capital to purchase a Republican affiliated endorsement, and vice versa.   A simple game develops where you race your opponent to collect endorsements, and try to get them first.  Simple mechanics result - you look at the map to figure out where the best endorsements will help you pull states, try to bring those in from your foe, and then hold serve on your own turf.  But the concept is very simple, pure strategy.  You could easily reskin the concept to anything else and it's have the same depth.
But you could flesh it out a lot more:
Take Jim Webb as an example.  He's nnot a normal Democratic candidate.  He's pro-gun, and he was an Under Secretery of Defense under Reagan for 3 years and Secretary of the Navy under him for another.  However, in a debate, he stated that he was more "all lives matter" than "black lives matter".  So you could give him teh Republication bonus to pull the gun lobby, but give him teh Republication penalty to pull the minority/black lobby.
And you could do this with others.  Ben Carson could be easier to grab the black/minority endorsement, Rand Paul the civil rights one, and so forth.  You could layer them in, and have more than just normal cost or double cost.  Maybe it's 50% harder for a Rand Paul to get the Christian Confederation, or perhaps Bernie Sanders needs a 2.5 cost for pulling the US Chamber of Business rather than the normal penalty.
That would help.
And that's just one mechanic.  You could similar flesh out the others.  If this game had been really pushed between releases A(nd there's a lot of time between them, so that'd have been very likely) then you could have had a game that evolved with the times and was a real nice game today.  But nope.  It's the same game, but now with Donald Trump.  Does it have 3rd parties or Independant folk?  Nope.  Does it have debate mechanics where you can try to go after your opponent live?  Nope.
Hopefully you get the point.  It's a quick game that you can pick up in a few minutes, win on your first go through, win one or twice more, and then put it down and finish with, "Is that all there is?"
Yes, that's all there is.

I was leery of buying Broken Age.
I was one of the people who didn't know Kickstarter existed when the Double Fine Adventure got kicked off, and cursed myself for my inability to donate at a later date.  But then I heard about Tim Schafer's "Oops, I accidentally made the game too big out of excitement" and the resulting decision to release the game in two parts.
I was leery of buying such a Broken Age, broken into pieces.  But I bought it anyway because I believed in the man behind the Age.
And I was right to do so.
I will only touch upon the beauty of the designs and the watercolor style artwork.  How it transforms the world into a living, breathing, stylistic entity that adds to the gravity and majesty of the game.  You can see that just from the advertising previews.
I will only offhandedly mention the beautiful music, and how it aids in captivating the strange and enchanting art, holding your attention and increasing your desire to see what's over on the next screen.
I will speak about the voice cast.  About how Curtis (Wil Wheaton) just made my day, and Shay's (Elijah Wood) desperately struggling morality trying to escape it's infancy made me really, really care.  About how the entire cast is Grade-A and there is not a sour note amongst them I could even try to harp upon.
I will talk about the length of Part 1.  It is short... but it is just right.  There was no filler in it, and it felt like Shay's story was shorter than Vella's, but neither side of the adventure had any spam in it.  No filler to make you sigh in boredom of somethign that should not be there.  Every bit of the game was something to be important, either in setting the tone or setting of the characters or the world.  Nothing too much, and it delivers you to...
The Twist.
There is a reason that Tim Schafer chose to end Part 1 right where he did, because there is no better spot to end Part 1.  The Twist changed my entire perspective on EVERYTHING.  And I will have to play the game again in reverse order to make sure I understand it this time for it's true self.  Just like Fight Club, you have to see it at least twice to really get it.
And the time from now until the release of Part 2...  Let that Twist stew in your gut.  let it capture your imagination and leave you asking, How and Why.  All in preparation for Part 2.
Part 1 was just the closing of the First Act in terms of the laws of writing.  The Second and Third Act are yet to come.

Life is Strange is one of my favorite games of all time, dispite the small amount of "game" there is to be found in it.
The game is largely dialogue focused, with ocassional puzzle-elements that take advantage of specific time powers aquired early on in the story. The story-telling, soundtrack, and general tone of the game is where the game truly shines. Life is Strange's soundtrack is a shmogesborg of beautiful sad indie tunes from bands like Foals that perfectly complement emotional climaxes in the story. You will probably find yourself adding many of these songs to personal playlists.
The story revolves around a high school girl, a murder mystery, and the problems that inevitably result from time travel. It is heartbreaking in a way that I've never seen done in a game before. It possesses a style of tradgedy you don't think games as a medium are capable of capturing.
This is a game that will stick with you for a long time. I beat Life is Strange over a year ago, and I still think about it fairly regularly. It's the kind of game that un-ironically includes the number of depression and help hotlines because it's fully aware of how heartbreaking the content is.
I recommend this game the same way I recommend people read a book - not to have fun, but to come away from it with a new level of empathy that you didn't have beforehand.

Even though Multiwinia is mostly a multi player upgrade to Darwinia, it is an immensely better game than its predecessor. Nearly all aspects of the game have been improved to the point of near greatness in short bursts. In this iteration of the series, the focus is placed on multi player style game modes, which could also be played against the CPU. Multi player servers are available, but the amount of people playing in public games is scarce to none. This is not a problem, as the single player mode provides much entertainment, challenge, and excitement. Unit placement, movement, and orders have been polished beyond comparison to the nearly broken Darwinia. Everything is fluid, fixed, and sleek. There are also many power-ups and surprises that enhance the game play to the extent of limitless replay ability. In everything Darwinia went wrong, Multiwinia corrected and got right. There are so many maps to play in, and several game modes that will guarantee the almost permanent installation of Multiwinia on your system. You will go back to this game time and time again. The fun and excitement it provides is timeless. There is no reason to play the defective Darwinia if you have Multiwinia. The controls are outstanding, especially when you compare them to the controls and path finding disasters of Darwinia. Each game plays differently, as the variety in maps, game modes, random power-ups, and AI will change your experiences throughout. All difficulty levels are challenging and fun to play, even if you lose. Each match takes between five and twenty minutes, and time flies by quickly, as you are constantly paying attention to your enemies, your units, and ordering them around the map. The action is non-stop. Unfortunately, Multiwinia does not keep track of your personal statistics besides Steam achievements (which I do not care for). There is also a lack of leaderboards of any kind because of the non-inclusion of statistics keeping. It would have been extremely nice to have access to both, even if it were for single player only. Sometimes, you may be losing by a considerable amount, and you will still be able to pull off the win. Power-ups are important at times, depending on the luck of the draw. You will develop a liking to some of them, and apathy for others. While Multiwinia is a short-lived gaming experience, it is Introversion's best effort so far. This game is a perfect example of something you keep installed for years to come, always going back to it for quick matches action packed with fun and entertainment.

Having enjoyed the first season of
immensely, I put off playing the second one for a couple of years - mostly out of concern that after so brilliant a game, the sequel could only fall short of its predecessor.
I am very glad to report that I was completely wrong: this second season is just as captivating as the first one; it dragged me into its story and managed to get under my skin effortless. Just like in any Telltale-game, the story receives main forcus and the success of the game mostly depends on it. This second season picks up a couple of months after the end of the first one and continues the story of the young orphan Clementine, who tries to survive in a world plunged into ruins due to a zombie outbreak and - even more so - to the cruelty and madness of some of the survivors. The story is original, well told and doesn't involve too many distracting twists and turns.
Clementine is a very particular kind of game-protagonist. Being a young girl, she is likeable, even cute on first sight, and evoked strong feelings of compassion during the early stages of the game. But as she gets confronted with more and more (especially human) cruelty, she definitely hardens up and quickly develops a tough, even harsh part of herself. During the game the player can of course through all kind of decisions direct the way in which Clementine not only lives through the story, but also develops as a human being, up to a certain degree.
Even if one would choose all the "sweet" and "understanding" options in the dialogues, at a deep level the development of Clementine definitely is one away from being a little, depending girl towards a more mature character. This by itself is quite a thing to achieve in any work of story-telling art, being a book, a theater play, a game or an opera. Characters are all too often one-sided, either good or bad, something which definitely doesn't apply to Clementine in this game. The other characters are a mixed bag. Some are believable and interesting, while others are too one-sided, or make too short an appearance to make much impact on the game. This might be my only point of real criticism: there are probably too many side-characters, whose story in only very briefly touched upon. This is something which is probably done on purpose to show how fleeting encounters are in a world like this, but it doesn't always work in a game.
For the rest, the game shows all the strong points of a top-notch Telltale-product: excellent, sometimes even superb voice-acting, sober but effective comics-style graphics, perfectly suited music and an ominous soundtrack. There is not much else to say to anyone who hasn't played it yet: just do so, as it won't disappoint in the slightest. Playtime might be a tad shorter than the first one, but there is definitely room for a second, differently oriented playthrough.

This is not so much a review as an explanation of how Fantasy Grounds has enabled me to play RPGs for the last 12 years...

Twelve years of updates and no charges is value to me.

I have to be honest I bought it because you could actually roll the dice. I convinced the players to buy a license each and our d20 campaign continued.
I had to make the ruleset with people I "met" on the forums but we learnt the xml (not as hard as some people make out), we did the grahics and we had a blast. I won a copy of the Ultimate edition when I posted my first Youtube video (now I have a 151 subscribers which is not alot in Youtube turns but still amazing to me).
Over the years I have run or player D20 Modern, Savage Worlds and Pathfinder games. I have run games with completer strangers in the many FG Cons and FG Daze we have. I have made DLC for many Savage Worlds products.
I have used this product for thousands of hours regardless of what Steam states (that is just how long I have clocked up using my macbook at hotels when I am working away from home, player only not GMing).
I have spent hours asking questions and answering them on the forums (well worth a visit)
If you want to use this product download the demo and play with it, look out for the GMs who run sessions (like myself with Ultimate Licenses so you can join us and play without need to have bought the sofware), ask questions on the forums, and enjoy this product.

This program is amazing. I will talk about its use for presential sessions, as this is the use i have given to the program with one minor exception. I will first list the pros and cons.
Pros:
-planning encounters with automatic xp and challenge level calculations
-tracking of players, levels, HP and initiative all in one place (no more running 6 apps at the same time)
-Campaign sessions saved so you can remember what you did last time and what you planned forward
-library, with ability to create and change monsters, items, and rules in general.
-Running encounters in maps
Cons:
-Expensive
-Have to buy separate libraries to have full experience
-Setting up a server is a hassle
I have used Fantasy grounds for one quick one player session (to try it out) i made a one shot adventure for my GF and she loved it, she said although the program takes a bit to get used to. After about 30 minutes she got the hang of it and it run quite smoothly. Encounters are a bliss running monsters is a lot more intuitive than keeping track on a playmat since when they hit one you dont mix up who got hit on a piece of paper. Also she told me that not having to remember all the rules by heart, and having her character auto roll for damage with all modifiers was awesome.
When using it in a physical session, it is also great help, you can plan fast encounters, keep track of all player hp and monsters at the same time without hassle. Also for me keepong all my sessions and story written parts saved is awesome, also you can keep maps interactive and use them as a dm to keep track of traps, mosnter locations etc.
All in all awesome program, if you can afford it definitely get it, it will make your life as a dm easier.

This is a great game, and has quickly risen to one of my favorite games of all time. There are many good things about this game. It has numerous weopons that are all a blast to use, different characters to fit all types of playstyles,it has multiple endings thorugh different bosses, but one of the best part about this game is the progression system. The first time you will play, you will die within about two or three levels depending on your skill level, which will unlock you melting. Within a few hours, you will be reaching the labs, and unlocking steroids, and before you know it, you are looping regularly, trying to kill Mom with a golden weopon to get the golden frog pistol and unlock frog or attempting to defeat the captain rith rogue to get her b-skin. The best part about this game, to me at least, is how it focuses on th gameplay over the story. Too many games nowadays try to either have a super deep story presented through dialogue heavy cutscenes or hide it through little sprinkles of information to get you to dig deeper. While this game does have some sparse lore, it never takes center stage over the main attraction, which is the balls to the wall fun gameplay. This is the first game in a while that I've seen focus on the fun the player is having over a super deep story. Lastly, the game is balanced very well. For every crap run you have where you get terrible weopons like the wrench and laser pistol and die on lil' Hunter, you will have an amazing double loop run with the fully powered up energy sword and the super crossbow. However, there is a minor gripe I have with it. There are texture glitches that occur every once in a while, that tamper with gameplay severely. Every few runs, I will have a texture glitch, where the texture that covers the level boarder shows up without hit detection. Usually its not a big problem, but multiple times i've had a run ended due to and enemy that i couldn't see such as one of the ice robots that I couldn't see throwing a car at me and ending my run instantly. That is really the only major reoccuring problem I have with the game. I reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys hard games and twin-stick shooters. 9/10

This is a casual game, and I owned 2008 and skipped the last one... anyway, for a casual game it delivers and is a good bang for your buck.  There's not a whole lot you can change in the series, though I think that the bobble heads are a bit worn out now, and there could have been better graphics in the design of your own candidate.  It's a bit cartoony the way it is... but it is what it is.
I played 4 short games of 26 week turns.  I played them pretty much the same way to see what sort of results I would get.  3 of the games I ran as Republican and lost all 3 games by slim margins.  When I played the game as a Democrat it seemed to me that the states fell in line with the Democrats much more easily, i.e., the states would react more positively to a speech by the Democrat than by a Republican.
Knowing how the electoral votes works is key, and you can of course campaign the big states of California, Texas, Florida and New York and then work some of the mid-west and southern votes.  Hawaii and Alaska are pretty much swing states, and it would not make much difference.
A longer game could allow you to do better in terms of election, because with just 26 week turns you can only have enough time to focus on the larger states, and that's probably why the swing was more in favor of Democrats, so I will likely play longer games to see if longer strategies work better.
Overall it is a fun game and worth the $20.  It would be great to see better graphics of the map and especially the candidates, perhaps be able to re-play in other past election years, create new parties would be an awesome improvement so you can run as Independent, Tea Party, Green or just make one up.  Lastly, I wish there was some way to add more issues to the game, and create a different political environment.  Perhaps an editor???   And it would be great to have a version that plays not the final election but getting the parties nomination with primaries, and other such features... IF that could happen you would have a truly awesome game, though now I'd give it a 6 out of 10.

As I sit here considering how best to describe Alan Wake, the image that springs to mind was Lenoidas' final moments in the film 300: standing there in a captivating environment, looking pretty right up until he is swiftly cut down by an inescapable tidal wave of several thousand arrows...
**************
I have not made the acquaintance of anyone at Remedy games, yet I am certain not a single employee is familiar with the concept of "subtlety," or at least how to execute it successfully. This game is a fire-hose of pop culture references – Twin Peaks homages being the most egregious – and nearly every last one of them is clumsily implemented. The story has some intriguing elements regarding the themes of creation and the internal conflict that inevitably arises within the creator(s); however, it's executed in a fairly uneven manner that seems more interested in playing the mysterious "is it all real or in Alan's head" angle, and lacks a resonant through-line of a vastly superior title such as Silent Hill 2.
The controls are also disappointingly loose, and the resultant gameplay is sloppy. Such issues are commonplace among survival horror games, often defended as "enhancing the tension" among apologists; yet loose controls need not be antithetical to good gameplay, as other survival horror entries such as Amnesia: Dark Descent ably demonstrate. There are plenty of moments in Alan Wake with ample tension that are not aided in the slightest by the easily-exhausted sprint function or the awkward aiming and character movements. Nor does it help matters that the jump function works about a tenth as well as it should; though, as luck would have it, this does nothing to stop Remedy from tossing in a number of platforming-based segments that wonderfully illustrate the blundering majesty of the game's physics engine.
And on top of it all, the game is absolutely obsessed with speed ramping (THERE's that 300 connection) and wresting control of the camera away from the player to show you something any time it feels bored with what's happening in the game, which is all the time. This obsession with fashioning the game in a cinematic vein is incredibly detrimental to both the gameplay and the overall experience. I don’t need to be shown with an elaborate zoom that there is a threat looming ahead; I can already see it because it is directly in front of my f*cking face, obstructing my forward progress.
The world of Alan Wake is indeed an impressive one to behold and explore. It’s just too bad it’s tanked by clunky gameplay, ham-fisted dialogue and story, and all-too-knowing references. (Maybe don’t start the next game off by name-dropping Stephen King in the opening seconds.)

I have been using FG as a GM for 4 years now - at the table! I know FG is designed largely for online play, but I prefer face-to-face-roleplay and toe-to-toe-combat! My review is in that context and no other.
First: My requirements were to have a system that worked off-line.
Next I wanted to stop having to carrying around massive books as the game sessions were at a player's house
It would be cool if it  gave me maps and character placements on them
It needed to allow for story elements and descriptions,
I wanted as much as possible of the game mechanic to be automated
I desperately needed cross-referencing so I could easily access spell descriptions, item stats, monster stats, etc
Finally: If any player was unable to make the session I wanted a means of them joining in fro ma distance.
A tall order. So how did FG2 stand up under such pressure?
Off-line: FG2 runs perfectly fine off-line. I have found that starting it up at home where I have web access, then driving to the session helps if there's no internet available there. In the past I've had problems - this is most probably because I use the MAC version in Steam.
No Books: t allows me to leave most of the books at home. I say 'most' because a lot of the modules I'm running are non-SRD and not yet available as DLC. But with the community (currently) providing loads of extra modules and extensions for my preferred RPG (Pathfinder) and FG's inbuilt module creation facility I can overcome much of that. I still take a rulebook in case a player needs one to refer to but hasn't brought their own. I sometimes bring the Adventure Path with me for just-in-case backup.
Maps and Characters: Others have said that FG struggles in the maps area. This is a shame, as this is such a cool feature. However, other than a non-intuitive way of handling images, I've had little ofr no issues with maps. As I'm using them for reference purpose I suppose I'm using low-quality versions. (See later.) I could import maps, place a grid, and place characers on the grid. I still haven't used this feature to it's fullest for a number of reasons. Mainly because I play at the table, I'm forever drawing the map and then the players control their figure. At the end of the session, if the encounter is still active and the positions of pieces is important then I'll take a photo of the table. (Ore even a video!) I'd like to be able to transfer the pieces  to the map in FG and then I wouldn't need the photo! But this means extra work for me - especially as I sometimes change the map as I GM....
Characters: FG has a sweet set of Chaarcter sheets that are nicely laid out. I get my players to use PCGEN exports of their characters after they level up and then import them into FG. As we play at the table, I let them use paper copies of tablets. In fact I get them t maintain their own sheets all thetime. If they forget something and suffer for it, they'll learn for next time. If they 'cheat' then they have fun, but will get found out soon enough when I get their elecrronic version. My main point for having characters in FG is to keep tabs on initiative order in the combat tracker - which is superb.
Tokens: Placing characters and npc/monsters on the map is simple enough in FG. However, the issue of token images is still a bother for me. I balk at having to pay for these as DLC - but getting my own set up is fine. Caveat: As I play at the table we use mini's or markers so tokens on a map are not such a great deal at the moment. And with FG not providing Line-of-Site or Fog-of-War this part of FG isn't so important.
Story: FG has a superb system for story elements allowing for descriptive parts, encounter groupings, and more. It takes a while to get used to, but it's great once you work within its quirkiness. Setting up story elements can be time consuming - DLC saves a tonne of that tedium - but you can add your own encounters, locations, and more. This is one part of FG I rely heavily on.
Automation: This is an area of FG that is fantastic and frustrating at the same time. Cross linking to spells, counting wand usage, rolling hit and damage, etc - all is great. But sometimes I want the character sheets and stats to update automatically and FG doesn't always do it. I want to be able to speed through the tedium of combat and skill rolls - sometimes I can, sometimes not. I get frustrated by it at times, but only say 15%. Mostly the players are unaware of what I struggle with. And my GM stye is laid back - sometimes if it's cool and fun I'll allow it. Sometimes if a player is pressing my buttons the wrong way I want a system to put the brakes on.
Cross-Referencing: This is great - as long as the info is in the system. You can set up a load of modules that can contain all you want. You have to load the module up before you get to see the info. I sometimes forget, and FG will just sit looking at me and do nothing until I remeber - then it's quick and easy to overcome. Creating your own items, spells, feats, etc is a bit awkward and I'd like to be able to easily insert cross references. As I said earlier, FG has its own system of hyperlinking that could do with some work - but it works. I just want more flexibility.
Remote Player: This is an area I haven't had success with. We have one player who is miles away and plays by Skype. Fortunately he's honest enough to own up to his fumles and crits! The major sticking point in FG for me here is connectivity. As I have no access to the modems at the player's house where we meet I cannot set up the connectivity FG wants. Also, the price point for multiple players using FG is prohibitive. Yes, I should get the ultimate version, but I can't justify the expense for one remote player (everyone else is at the table!)
Other comments: FG has a great interface but gets cluttered real quick. I want to be able to turn the chat box off altogether, as well as the dice, as they're not used at the table (I roll real dice - the players get jittery if I say I rolled a hit and either they don't see it or even hear the dice clattering!) Map movement and scrolling is awkward. Using a Mac trackpad is a pain as FG will open 'windows' when all I want to do is scroll. Showing players images and handouts is awkward, so I have to prepare those pefore hand. One day I'll get a flat screen set up and lay it out instead of my chessex mat, but then we'll loose the fun of saying 'the white counter with the feather is the undead-orc, remember?!' (And I like the spectacle of the table.)
So there we have it. I'm very pleased with FG at the moment and would rate it 9/10. There's room for imrpovement. There's loads I use it for. (If it doesn't run at the table - one week it failed to launch on my MAC notebook - then I'm lost. That's how much I've come to depend on it.) I'm watching the future of FG development closely, especially with the Unity version and their recent partnering with Paizo. Will the price of modules increase? will the community generated material be banned? will we finally get line-of-sight and a decent fog-of-war? will there be a TPK button? (mwa-ha-ha!)
FG is highly recommended by me, for use at the table, with your mates, prezels, pizzas and cola's!

After putting over 4 hours into the game it I've reached the conclusion that it's trying and failing to be too many things at once.
The controls go funky on me quite a lot.  I have swung my mouse to the right going straight up and it registered as a left loop, which got me killed running into someone. My dash has also been locked in the on position, making a quick boost become an uncontrollable skid into 3 other players.  I would chalk this up to a fluke, but it kept happening.
The arenas are super tiny.  While this encourages action to take place, it is so small that new players have barely any time to collect mass before having 5 other new players fling themselves at you hoping to score quick mass.
Very bad hit boxes. While other games like Slither.io have a small hit box on the very tip of your snake, Worm.is's hit box is the entirety of your head. Two snakes smashing heads in a straight line, the one with the most mass automatically wins. Very frustrating when trying to make any progress in the game, since a larger worm hitting you will most likely also hit your head, in which the most mass rule applies and you pop.  So how do you kill larger worms?  By stealing from Agar.io and putting buzz saws around the arena that you can shoot mass into. After a few shots they become fly off in the direction that you hit it with.  This has worked ONCE in all the times I tried, since it has to hit the center of the head to kill the worm. Not to even mention if any other player sees you trying to do it you'll immediately be attacked since you are shooting points out of your body for them to collect. (And they will see you since as I said the arenas are tiny.)
So how do you get quick and easy mass?  My best tactic to gain 40k mass was to go along the edge for the first few minutes (since the boundaries are hard barriers and will kill you if you so much as look at them for very long) to gain enough mass to begin going into a circle and watch as other players throw themselves at me and collect  the mass as I go around. Since I won head on collisions I just sat there and kept going around until a new player spawned in with invincibility and kept his tail on my nose when it went away, killing me.
Chat is also questionable, since half of the chat messages were just spawned players begging the top 3 to team up so they give them mass and the other half was people complaining about newbs stealing the mass of people they killed.
Hunger games was a novel idea, but after waiting a half hour for a second game to load and only having 8/20 players, I gave up on playing it more than once.
Finally, going back to the mass shooting... Why on earth make that the default left click?  It's a bad feature in the first place, making it what's the default dash button in Slither is just asinine.
Can this game be salvaged? Loosen up the hit boxes, open the arenas a bit and remove the stupid mass shooting and it could be more fun. As it stands now? I'll just go back to slither.io

"Mountain is a kind of visual silence"
Game developer David Oreilly
So, this is not a review, if you are reading this, no need to take it seriously, rage at me or anything like it, it is more about personal insights I've had while watching my mountain change rather than giving the game a number to theorically represent if it's good to be bought or not.
(sometimes I may refer to the mountain as a her, because I thought my mountain had a very feminine personality)
The mountain is more about watching, wondering and hearing, than it is about interacting. Even though we are instructed early in our gaming paths that good interactions, polished gameplay and good story writing are good for videogames, sometimes, things can just be calmer and more about you and the computer ahead of you.
At first I wanted to see possible interactions with the mountain, trying to click, play music for it, and see how it changes, if time passes faster, do objects appear more often? Do objects have a higher chance of appearing if the mountain is not my main task and is alt-tabbed?
While at it, I convinced myself that any interactions are useless, and I started watching it for some minutes, and I could noted how intricate and well-done is the design of it all.
The mountain "roots" are a reverse version of the mountain itself, just like a tree has roots that branch over the reach of itself on the underground, the mountain has roots which go about the same size as the mountain itself, it also has a mind on its own, when the mountain sends a text about any recent thoughts it had, it looks like the mountain has some existential thoughts, things like "Am I the only one seeing this black night?" are commonplace for it, maybe the Mountain wants others like her close to her, she feels alone and wants to know if she is the only Mountain in the galaxy or the universe, maybe other peoples mountains may feel that too, but due to the immense space between them, they cannot interact.
When you zoom out, you see the emptiness and beautifulness of the space, the mountain is just a mere dot in the great expanse of the university around it, but when you zoom close to your mountain, you see the sky, the clouds and the mountain itself, you see the world as the mountain sees it, The mountain talks about things that mountains would talk about, it talks about the weather, it's the closest thing that the mountain knows that'll change, it's the common subject between the watcher and the character, the most common conversations are related to the weather, comments over rains, nights, days, snow, and once in a while the existentialism may pop-up on the mountain's head.
Objects may appear on the mountain while you are not looking, you cannot know where they came from, and they seem to appear as random human-made objects on random places of the mountain. I look at this as a meter of how much have you watched your mountain, since sometimes it takes long periods for objects to pop-up, mountains with lots of objects may have interacted with us humans for too long, and has become desecrated by our eyes watching it.
Some of the Mountain's issues are the same issues that we have, sometimes she will question why is she alone, if she's doing good, why no one comes to her, among other things, it has a inner life, we don't know what is her past, but we do know that she has a past, as we can see that trees have grown on her and fireflies fly near the trees in the night, she needed time for these things to grow on her, for this genesis to happen above her, while the lower half is mainly dead, the upper half is living and pulsating with the climate changes that may happen to it. Sometimes when the mountain questions if she's alone, that's also a human question, if we are alone in the universe, if Earth is the only planet that has "life" as we know it, if we are the only humans around or if there are other planets similar to ours with people wandering about these same things.
My mountain (or should I say, the mountain I met) enjoys fresh days with the sun shining over her, she expresses her joy when she sees a good day and she dislikes snow a lot, I won't know if any other mountains out there like snow or not, because I won't be able to watch them the same way I watch mine, I can only see my mountain, and this is the mountain I know, I know her bumps and her trees, the most recent objects and the oldest ones to inhabit her, and I feel a sort of connection about knowing her without her ever being able to acknowledge my presence, just like a God would do when watching someone think about its own small and meagre existence here on Earth.
I came into this game because it's so cheap, and I wanted to know what it's all about, I tried not to read about it in the past trying to dodge any kinds of preponderations that people would give me by reading their reviews or texts about it, at first, I was pretty skeptical about it and I thought that I would rage and become anxious at the lack of interactions available, but I ended up enjoying it more than most of the games I played recently.

So I bought FG just a few days ago (Saturday and it is now just Wednesday).  I have never used a VTT before and the only other similar program I have ever heard of was d20 (but not sure that is a VTT) which I know almost nothing about.
Anyway, I am loving this software.  I am excited to get my first module complete so I can play my first session with my children.  They are already excited about it as well.  This is so much better than playing at the actual table.  Just the automated Character bookkeeping was enough for my kids to be interested in playing D&D again.
I did a lot of research about the software before purchase.  So I had seen all the comments about a steep learning curve.  Trust me it is steep.  Also unless you intend to buy modules it will take a long time to set up your own in order to play your first session.  However, if you are aware of this going in and stick to it, I believe this software is well worth the cost.
I jumped in and went full monty with my initial purchase.  I bought the ultimate license (as this allows my kids to use the demo version when I DM; and I have at least 4 children who will play and more might join after watching our first session).  I also bought the 5e DM Guide, PHB, and Monster Manual.  I had been using 2/2.5e until now so this also has increased my learning curve as the D&D rules have changed significantly.  So $300 later I am all in and happy with it.
I haven't even played my first session yet.  Only one small test session. I am still creating my first module.  Also another big plus for me was the FG community.   If you buy this, make sure to sign into the forums and ask questions.  The help there is almost immediate.  They also have a dedicated TS server but unfortunately not a single person has spoken to me in it.  Everyone seems to be in dedicated sessions, so is probably too busy playing to bother with someone sitting in tech support channel.  LOL
After playing my first session I will add to this review.  But I love it so far and doubt that will change.  The more I learn the more I like it.   So my recommendation is a resounding "Hell, yes"....LOL

Have you ever dreamed to control a mech?
Do you dare to dream further? Do you dare to dream about controlling a Sapphire mech?
If the answer is yes , sorry bruh all I can offer is a fun little twin stick shooter type of game with upgradeable mechs.
You can upgrade 3 parts of your mech - legs , body and guns. These parts have 3 categories , fast moving/shooting but lightly armored/low damage , medium , and slow moving/shooting but heavy armored /damege (which means you can basically turn your mech into a tank if you choose all heavy parts). Each type of legs gives you a special perk - the typical two legs give you a barrier that you can activate , sort of like a shield but it stays in place instead of moving with your mech exploding when its duration is up , the rat-track legs give you bullet time (which is nice sometimes as rat-tracks are hellaslow and bullets tend to be hellafast) not sure about the arachno legs as I never saw the need to use them or the medium body/weapon for that matter.
The game is a little on the short side , with only 12 missions , replay value is almost non existent , as the collectables are not that hard to find. That being said , I consider the asking price of 8 € too high (I got it as a gift) for a game that was once free to play browser game , as far as I know.

I really need to point out the unnecessary review bombing and how much everyone is complaining about the microtransactions and loot boxes. Don't let those people stop you from missing this game if you enjoyed the first game. Yes microtransactions are BS and they are absolutely an affront to the gaming industry but this isn't even close to EA levels of greed. The loot boxes are entirely unnecessary and you will pick up much better stuff just playing the game. It is NOT pay to win. There are also daily challenges that reward you with the in game currency so you can mess around with the evil lootboxes without ever spending a dime of your real money with P2W scams.  You can also disable the marketplace features entirely if you are still seething with a sense of injustice...To give an example - I just completed the "Kill 25 enemies while riding a drake" for 50 gold,"perform 5 aerial archery kills" for 50 gold, and "Kill a fortress commander" for 500 gold daily challenge. I also got about 165 Gold today by completing other online challenges like vendettas and I picked up some gold in a spoils of war chest I believe. To put it in perspective it's 20$ for 2000 in game gold and I got 865 gold "free" for playing through the game like a normal person. Microtransactions and gambling lootboxes are still bad and I do not support them at all but seriously chill out...
Moving on to the game: If you loved the nemesis system, beautiful arcs of Uruk blood trailing from a spitaling severed head in slow motion, and the amazing journey through Middle Earth you got in Shadow of Mordor then you will not be disappointed. As far as sequels go so far they are knocking it out of the park in my opinion. When a developer screws up a long anticipated sequel you expect a lot of disappointment and cut features. Not this time. Every successful game mechanic from the last game has  been kept and very often improved upon significantly. The combat is as beautiful as ever, the scenery is MUCH better this time around with a lot less drab and dreary Uruk fortresses in ash country. The "Build your Army" aspect is completely overhauled with TONS of awesome new features and management options. Night and day difference from the last game and its already fun system. Seriously - Do a little homework, take each review with a grain of salt, and give this a shot if you're a fan of the series. Wait for a sale if it eases your conscience. I came into this game with low expectations and dread after reading a lot of negative reviews and I was very pleasantly surprised. But hey, see for yourself. Thanks for reading. I'll probably get a bunch of unhelpful ratings for pointing out the people hyperventilating and calling them "LITERALLY WORSE THAN EA LITERALLY HITLER GAME DEVELOPERS HURRRR" but screw it.
