If you go back to the isometric 3D-games of the late nineties and early 2000, you would encounter games such as Wasteland, Fallout, Fallout 2, Jagged Alliance 2, and similar. Those types of games set a prescedent and would influence dozens of other games including the sequels to Fallout (Fallout 3 and New Vegas). They were all open-world sandbox games where the first and foremost factor was player choice, and decisions and their consequences.
What Wasteland 2 gets right is all of this AND a highly detailed RPG-experience that is almost unique today (check out Shadowrun Returns for another title with similar content). Expect a highly hard-core player experience though, this is not for the impatient.
Updated 2014-09-14
Wasteland 2 - beta impressions
I have been playing Wasteland 2 off and on since just after Wasteland 2 became publicised and have seen it grow from a really buggy game to a somewhat buggy game.
The core of Wasteland 2 is the same core as Fallout 2, you're in a post-nuclear world where radiation clouds common, and where people die like flies. In fact, this is the original post-apocalypse game series; believe it or not, but where Fallout 2 comes with a 50'ies style and tongue-in-cheek sense of humour, Wasteland 2 is pure unfiltered social realism.
Not that there aren't things that are humorous, I unfortunately believe that they haven't been designed to be such. One of the earlier challenges you might face is encountering a situation where mutation has happened, mutated plants and insects, and getting attacked by gigantic fly larvae and flies that graphically appear... shall we say, funny... doesn't match at all with the general theme and art style which tries to be built on realism.
This style-mismatch occurs on several levels, and where I don't have an issue with toasters (which is a Wasteland-classic) I do have an issue with some of the art which seems funny or silly in a bad way. This interferes with the authenticity of the game in my opinion and seems sloppy or not so well thought out to me.
Gameplay
Gameplay on the other hand is very well worked out, the combat is classic turn-based (á la Fallout 2) and tactics, using cover, and a large variety of different weapons. The combat and the effects of combat is very well worked through. You can even use skills against non-human opponents to distract or even scare animals away, which, when you fight "honey badgers" (yes, unfortunately they're in the game, and are almost as lethal as deathclaws in Fallout 2) are very welcome. Area of effect weapons are incredibly effective, and the encounters are challenging to say the least. Expect to have to do some fights over and over again until you figure out a way to win the fight with as little wounds or deaths as possible.
Death is a big part of Wasteland 2 and there will be situations where you most likely will lose a character or two. Consequences are a factor in this game, fortunately there are plenty of new characters you can recruit along the way. From hobos to indians and doctors. Having a wide variety of skills in your party will be essential to making it in the wasteland, and (for example) only focusing on weapon skills in your party will immediately lead to your demise. Thus you will most definitely make use of every attribute and skill point spent, and get punished for every gap you have in your skill set.
Wasteland 2 is big on consequences for your actions and many scenarios come with multiple possible outcomes. Expect to be faced with challenges where your decision to help one town over one other will come back to bite you in the butt. Water is essential to your survival in this game, and affects you directly. If you fail to help a city which provides you with water, you will suddenly find yourself in dehydration-station. Ammunition is also something which tends to run out, which means that having a secondary melee-weapon can be the difference between a complete loss and a victory. Also expect to pay through the ears for rare ammunition, so whilst having a sniper in most situations is a game-changer, paying to resupply that sniper with ammunition instead of buying medkits will be a tough nut to balance.
Bugs and choices
Unfortunately with a lot of complex mechanics, small side-quests and multiple-choice scenarios there are bugs galore, still in the late beta. Some which will be minor (like you being unable to end your turn in combat, thus having to load a save to start the encounter over [DON'T FORGET TO TURN AUTO-SAVE 15mins ON!) to major game-breaking ones where certain choices breaks things. In the beta I've run into at least three game-breaking things that made everyone in a town attack me on sight because a certain script triggered the wrong consequence. Similarly a situation where I was supposed to get certain gear from a quest that would make a dire situation better simply didn't, because the dialogue options stuck, and thus I had to play through a nightmare scenario where I couldn't complete a certain scenario without losing characters with a hitpoint amount lower than 70. Which meant for a lot of the game I didn't have a medic/surgeon and a survivalist... basically forcing me to fight every encounter, and be unable to heal.
I really hope that the big patch that comes next week that takes us out of beta and into release will fix these bugs, because this IS a really good game. I have probably enjoyed it more than I enjoyed Divinity: Original Sin, which I was convinced was GOTY and the best RPG I played in a long time. But where Divinity was much more linear, and came with little changes in the story regardless if you played a "bad" guy or a "good" guy, Wasteland takes a completely different spin and makes you feel that your choices have impact, it feels more open world, and while there is a "main storyline", you can easily deviate from this if you choose to.
Conclusion and my advice
Given how the development has progressed during beta, I think that this game will be released in an unpolished state. In beta there has been at least 2 instances where fixes to game-breaking bugs have broken all save games. I think you SHOULD buy this game, but I think you should wait for some time AFTER release, particularly if you are impatient and are prone to temper-tantrums over the game messing things up for you. In beta I have simply "played past" some of the game-breaking bugs, ignoring the fact that the game didn't work as it was supposed to after making certain choices.
This game will probably not receive top scores like Divinity, which was a polished game and graphically a lot more consistent and superior in stability. What Divinity lacked though this game has in larger amounts; is non-linearity, strong causality (choices matter), and a more open world. Where Divinity essentially limited where you could go at what level (which made progressing in divinity more linear) Wasteland 2 instead allows you to go everywhere, and whilst you might be more prone to miss with shots at lower levels, most fights are still possible to win even with a well-defined level 1 party. There is also random encounters, and changes in who you become friends if if you did what-effects making the world in Wasteland 2 much more dynamic.
Unfortunately that's not enough to win the GOTY, I probably still think that Divinity: Original Sin is GOTY and probably the best RPG of the decade. But Wasteland 2 in a polished state would probably dethrone it. Unfortunately it is far from polished, and that's especially frustrating given how much potential the game has got.
Do not buy.

Context for myself:
Been using FG for four years (maybe 5).
Am a ultimate license holder, and I GM multiple games using it.
Also experienced the player side and have played in multiple games.
Have used other vtt's; battlegrounds (shudder) and roll20.
Fantasy Grounds is by far the best virtual tabletop program on the market.
Sadly, that statement means very little. If I was to ask someone who was semi-aware of their options, they'd probably name Roll20, and not realize that Fantasy Grounds even existed.
That is the extent of the competition sadly, while the others are not worth mentioning if you are serious about getting into a online game either as a player or a GM.
While this review is about FG, I will give mention to Roll20 only so I can accurately compare the two.
FG Pros:
Cleaner Interface - This is the most important aspect, second only to online functionality. Having a nice clean attractive interface is a massive bonus. FG achieves this and is highly regarded as the vtt with the best interface. I've got players who have experienced the roll20 side of things (including myself) and it is just far superior and easier to manage your characters, dice rolls and other essentials.
Functionality - FG has nice and easy placement of hotkey management via a hotbar at the bottom for quick and easy dice rolls. It's dice mechanics are realistic and impressive. Character sheets are clean with easy to navigate tabs, compared to the horrendous sheets of roll20.
Automation - FG's official rulesets, namely DnD ones, are mostly automated. There will always be a need for manual input in some from the GM so do not go into FG expecting a sophisticated automated ruleset. It can't function without a GM after all! Whole point of the automation here however is to act as an aid and for ease of use, and I have personally found it very helpful.
Chat function - Chatbar is nice and usually lagfree. It also features (in some rulesets, not all) a language function. Can your character speak draconic? Well if he can, and if someone spoke in draconic using the language extension in chat, only he will be able to understand it. Very nifty!
Ruleset Selection - FG has a nice selection of rulesets ranging from the official ones to the free community ones that don't cost a cent. The official ones also have extensions (mods basically) that add further features.
Cons:
Memory - FG uses a lot of memory if you plan on using some of the big rulesets like DnD. It's memory footprint will be around 4gb (my average) which is no big deal, right? If you start adding tokens and lots of handouts/images, expect the footprint to increase tenfold. I had it reaching 8gb at one stage, and not because I had 8gb worth of stuff in FG, I didn't. But FG's memory management isn't great. A work-around to this is to simply have your tokens outside of FG and only import a few that are essential, and keep the rest out until you need them. But this is not a solution I personally like cause I run multiple games, and you can imagine the headache in having to insert and remove tokens from time to time.
Program Crashing/Masking - FG thankfully doesn't experience much lag. And comparing it to roll20, its far less troublesome. But using the inbuilt Masking feature could be asking for trouble. It is usually fine on small maps (I mean like, really tiny maps) but FG has trouble handling big map files, even ones that meet the recommended sizes for FG. Masking isn't done well in FG, and FG does not have a dynamic fog of war/lighting system like Roll20 has. From to time, using the masking feature can crash your program. A bloody pain in the middle of a session!
Networking.
Mapping - This ties into the above. FG should never limit the ambition of a GM through the limits of its program. Unfortuntely it does, rarely but it happens. Want a nice big dungeon map? Well, you might want to tone it down a bit. Coupled with FG's bad memory management and ability to handle large image files, it can get very crash-happy. Fortuntely for myself I have found the sweet spot to stop this from happening (most of the time) but it does happen now and aagain.
Price Point - This is something that nearly every review points out as a con/negative. It's nice that FG is free if you can bag a game with an ultimate licensed GM (if he doesn't ask you to pay/sub!) but if you plan to GM yourself, having an ultimate license is more or less required. The other licenses are in a sense, a waste of time. The standard license is basic and simply requires that all those who are going to play, pay the same cost. Far as I'm aware, you don't get any of the dnd rulesets as you do with the ultimate, and I don't think there is any limitation on players (could be wrong). I've often heard it stated both officially and non-officially that the price of the FG Ultimate License is good value. Most common arguement for this is that you save a lot of money in terms of the books or PDF's you'd fork out otherwise.  I disagree.
Lets use DnD as an example; Nearly all the core set (players handbook, monsters guide, core rules, etc) can be gotten around 30 dollars (quick check on amazon showed some at 24 etc). Lets not rule out buying second hand books in good condition, plenty can be found on Ebay and such and great deals can be found. In total, could end up forking out around 60-80 for a complete core set. If you don't shop around and just impulse buy, lets increase that to around 110, there abouts. FG costs 149, for the ultimate edition and I'm not even going to bring in the subscription options cause you'll only end up wasting money on that in the long run, so lets keep it practical. With the ultimate edition, you might think your getting a good deal with it including all the dnd rulesets and pathfinder. That's what I thought, originally. However let me point out that they only include the SRD content. Not ideal, not at all if you plan to be serious about running a long-term game. That means you'll have to digitally buy the Core Class pack which is 49,99, the complete core monster pack which is the same price, and the other modules are priced around the same. Your paying a higher mark-up for them than book format, which makes sense; after all these modules contain a lot of handy VTT features to make your life easier. Add all that on TOP of your ultimate license fee, and your well over the 200 mark already. Get me?
I would argue that the price point is good value only if the dnd rulesets didn't contain limited content such as the SRD, which is not practical as I said for gming a long game. I do understand why the price point is what it is, I just don't agree with it, nor do I see it as good value.
Competition is sadly lacking however. Roll20 is certainly more mainstream (cause its free) and FG is only just starting to break the market. But it's high price point is a deterent for many who prefer to go to Roll20. Hopefully in time more VTT's will come available and that might put extra pressure on FG to change its ways. I'd even argue that the upcoming future unity update could see changes in this regard.
Another issue I want to mention before I call it on this review is the very confusing marketing of FG. I've lost count of how many times I've heard a new player not familiar with FG get confuse over their license functionality and purpose. I've had more than one player who I was in the process of recruiting for my game say to me they are not interested cause they have to pay for FG. Then I have to point out in detail why they do not, and that having an ultimate license negates their need to pay. Not to mention FG's 'demo' version is highly confusing, labeled wrong and I've often had to explain the function of FG's free version. Their other licenses don't do a great job at explaining their differences either and can be somewhat misleading.
All-in-all I do recommend FG, believe it or not! It's not perfect, it has a long way to go, but its the best VTT around.

I absolutely love Fantasy Grounds!
I've played D&D off an on since I was a kid (about 20 years ago now). I skipped 4E altogether but have played 2E, 3.5 and now getting into 5E.
The group I DM for is a group of folks I've met through MMOs, and we all play lots of other games together. Someone asked if D&D would be fun to try, and I got to divulge to them my lifelong passion of D&D. First, we started playing a campaign I homebrewed for them in Roll20. It was fine, but we found Roll20 to be cumbersome for our online-only group.
I did some research and decided to drop the cash on FG Ultimate License. The players I DM for, also pitched in, so that was how it worked for our group.
I will never ever ever go back to Roll20. Fantasy Ground does everything we wanted it to, and more. Attack a monster and the damage is done to it automatically! Get new gear, your AC is automatically fixed up! Assigning loot, XP etc to players is a walk in the park. Creating encounters, linking things on the maps, story entries, handouts, literally everything is so easy to do in FG, its amazing, and I wish I had gotten it even sooner.
The best part is being able to edit, copy, customize just about everything with the click of a mouse (or a drag of the mouse in most cases :P). Our homebrew campaign world is constantly evolving and its so easy for me to reflect that or reference stuff from past adventures inside Fantasy Grounds. Something I couldn't really do, or at least do well, in Roll20.
The icing on the cake? The community. The Fantasy Grounds community forums are amazing. A wealth of information can be found there, and if you can't find what you're looking for, you can ask, and someone will point you where you need to go. There's boatloads of extensions for you to add to your games to make them even better.
I absolutely recommend this to folks looking for a way to play D&D online with friends. If you're like me and had a group of folks ready to play with, you could easily just get the Ultimate license, split the cost among your friends, and be ready to go.

Much human thought and culture has been dedicated to explaining the unknown and thus making it safe. Videogames have too rarely explored the themes of the unknowable inspiring creativity but Alan Wake wants to make the effort. It is a game about an artist changing reality with his gift and facing the darkness, both inside and outside the mind.
Alan Wake, the titular novelist, has attained success precious few novelists can even imagine including a downright luxurious apartment in New York City and high visibility in the talk show circuit. He is also a dark, brooding man with only his wife Alice and agent-and-best-friend Barry being his only windows to the humanity in general. A vacation to the mountains and forests of Washington state becomes a nightmare for our hero when his wife is taken by the darkness sending Alan on his quest. The story is central to the game but it is unfortunately impossible to discuss it in detail without posting spoilers. Suffice to say that it is a mixed success. Alan comes off more petulant than tortured and his disdain for people in general renders him unpleasant, especially considering his winning hand in life. What makes this worse is that the writers are on Alan's side and the people he hates turn out to be hateable. The cast has an another Achilles' heel as well in Barry. He is one of those hustling agent types familiar from many, many movies about Hollywood. It makes no sense that someone like that could be on the top of the literary food chain and his career-boosting ideas are inept indeed. His attempts at comedic relief are also a mismatch for the sombre tone of the game in general. Since Alan and Barry get most of the screen time a thickness of skin is recommended.
The first and most important rule in depicting genius artists in fiction is always the same: do not show their work for genius cannot be replicated. Alan Wake the game apparently does not approve of this rule for Alan Wake the novelist has pages of his fiction scattered throughout the game as collectibles. The prose is so incompetent that I would have preferred Alan reciting from The Lusty Argonian Maid instead. Sadly these are not the only collectibles for the intense nightmare also has room for beer can pyramids, coffee thermoses and more. You cannot start a generator without passing a QTE test either. The ladders are also something of a mystery: why do I have to first press the action key to mount and then the movement key to climb the damn thing -- with a prompt appearing to tell me what to do? Why can't I be allowed to disappear into the game instead? Alan also has a highly irritating tendency to narrate the events, in effect repeating the things the player is already experiencing or making utterly baffling remarks such as: "I had fallen off so many cliffs it was ridiculous."
There is still reason to shut out all this (and a few other things) and focus on the strenghts, the ones that make Alan Wake a game worth experiencing. The forests at night are otherworldly and threatening and I have not seen ones like them elsewhere in gaming. I was most relieved to be allowed to switch off the HUD to complete the atmosphere. The town of Bright Falls also has proud Twin Peaks influences which were highly pleasing to see. Graphics may have some Xbox 360 ruggedness but the nighttime sights are still powerful. The main gameplay element besides experiencing the story is the combat. Alan needs to peel away the darkness protecting the Taken before using his guns to end them. The arsenal consists of a revolver, two varieties of shotguns and hunting rifle which fits the setting perfectly. You also have to reload them one bullet at a time which adds to the intensity of the encounters. The other group of equipment are the light sources you carry, from flashlights and flashbangs to the flare gun which is here the BFG 9000 superweapon it rarely gets to be. Alan isn't particularly nimble either so the process of avoiding enemy attacks, firing and reloading weapons and knowing when to use light requires a steady hand. I found this all pleasurable to do and felt skilled but not invincible after defeating a particularly dangerous group.
Alan Wake would certainly have benefited from tough but fair editing. Had the designers been free from the pressures of fitting into the general design of console gameplay of the time and had the writers focused more on presenting questions and invoking mystery than churning out language something unique could have been achieved. But while Alan Wake is a mixed triumph it is still a triumph. The feel of wandering in someone elses dream is palpable in the best sequences as is the intensity in many battle scenes, and the contrast between light and dark is used in many creative and thematically appropriate ways. Those looking for pleasure in nightmare should find some in Alan Wake and I can recommend the game for anyone in the mood for exploring the unknown.

10/10 crash simulator.
Seriously though, this game is fantastic if you don't mind the steep learning curve, kerbals who can survive high falls, learning about space and failing...A lot of failing. “I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work.” Who doesn't love failing? What was I doing? Oh yeah, my ship just crashed and burned, back to the VAB. Flight's going well? Alt-tab and come back 5s later, well look who's on their way down to the cold hard ground. But really, failing is just a part of the game, and you get to learn what works and what doesn't. It gets much better once you understand the concepts required to handle and build the vehicles as well as space exploration in general. Then you go on building things that just works and it really gives a sense of achievement; you did it, you. You got Bob up in space. Great job, now he's stranded...because all you wanted was to get to space and you forgot to include the return trip.
The game supports mods to enhance the experience, features several modes depending on what you want to do. Play sandbox if you want to build ridiculous rockets with enough funds to run an entire nation just to have it crash into mission control 5 seconds later as you laugh manically. Science for those who do not want to manage funds but still go through the science develoment and career for the management of all aspects of building your own space program.
Also remember that F5 is your best friend. It's the only one who can come clutch for you when all else seem to fall apart.

It's a good game if you want to muck around with the default aircraft or go flying around your town, but if you want to go hardcore and do more realistic procedures and flights, then money is a must as most addons for this game are quite expensive, but a good game and update to FS none the less.

This is not a game, it is a piece of art that has very limited interaction. If you enjoy looking at something beautiful and the emotional representation of this, then I would say $1 is a nice supporting price to pay for this kind of thing. After awhile random objects like anvils and soccer balls will show up that you can move around, but nothing else really happened, except changing weather. You can play your mountain tunes using the keyboard that act like basic piano notes, and the mountain will send a soft single note to let you know it's going to say something in writing on the top left of the screen. It can be interpreted as the changes in you or emotions that you can experience.
This product is definitely not for everyone and some people will be confused by it or angry at the limited interactions, while others will find it beautiful and calming, enjoying the presence of the little mountain in the background of their computer.
Pros:
- Beautiful
- Music and sound effects are calming, beautiful, and simple
- Relaxing and emotional
- Only $1
- there are very subtle interactions that are really calming
Cons:
- Very limited interactions, it would be nice if you could sculpt your mountain or move the trees around
- Most people will not like this game, as it is more art than a game.
I am recommending this to you if you are an art person or somebody who enjoys relaxing sound effects and beautiful things, otherwise, I would recommend not buying this as you will most likely just be disappointed.
If you like these types of things, I would suggest it be an 7.5/10, if you do not like these types of games, I would say a 1/10, it is hard to give a rating too.

I love horror games and I love the Cthulu Mythos. I did not care for this game very much.
Pros:
+Beautiful graphics and fitting eldritch scenery
+Great sound design and tension-building soundtracks
+Solid lore (almost everything had a place in the mythos)
Cons:
-NOT SCARY. While tension was high most of the time, nothing was ever at stake. I took my time with the game and explored every nook and cranny. There was only one or two occasions where I could actually get hurt, everything else was just 'All in your head'.
-NOISY PROTAGONIST. Even with the kindly-added 'Silent Mode' feature enabled, the whiny MC takes every opportunity to cry and TELL you how scared he is at all times. Bad for immersion.
-BAD PUZZLES. Puzzle elements go hand-in-hand with the horror/mystery genre, but not this time. Items required for progression are generally littered around the nearest 'Mental Spook-Zone' and snap into place for you, saving you any mental effort.
Scaring people is hard in an atmospheric horror game, I get that. But when all that seperates you from 'Dear Esther' is a few poorly-made puzzles and the odd illusion then you really need to step your game up.

Let's get one thing out of the way: If you're a creative type, especially a writer of any persuasion, Alan Wake is worth a playthrough just for the subject matter, namely the nature of dreams, the unconscious, and the creative process, and how they are all tied up in each other. Any professional fiction writer will tell you that they often don't know where their "ideas" come from -- they might as well just come straight out of the proverbial ether, and to anyone else it sounds like superstitious mumbo-jumbo. But the truth is, it often really does come out of left field, left field being that ocean of subconscious impulses and images that is constantly roiling in everyone's heads. A writer's job is paying attention to those images when they do show up, when most people can comfortably ignore them, and that makes it a tricky business. That's the gist of what Alan Wake deals with, and if anything, it's worth it to see what the game devs have to say about it.
Is it a GOOD story? Well. That is entirely up to your interpretation of the events in the game. And I'll mostly leave it at that. I'll give some of my impressions in no particular order: If you like the show
, you'll like this. If you like David Lynch's stuff, you will like this, particularly for some of the music and very obvious homages to things like
,
and perhaps
. That is to say, if you want things to make sense in a linear way, forget it. It's actually a little bittersweet to play through this if you are a big fan of Lynch, because while Alan Wake is very very obviously a love letter to the "weird stuff happening in a little town" genre, and it really does nail some of the spooky imagery that Lynch is known for, the characters and the dialogue fall disappointingly flat. It's a very rough imitation of the unforgettable dialogue of
,
, etc. I can't fault them that much for that, because at least they tried. Enough of that.
Gameplay is pretty technically tight with satisfying, challenging gunplay mixed up with light-source mechanics -- you weaken things with your flashlight, and then blast them. It's fun and keeps you on the edge of your seat most of the time. But, and this just may be my low tolerance for the same damn thing over and over, there are many times later in the game where you wish you could just get it over with. The pacing is a little annoying and predictable at times; when you would appreciate a chance to just wander around in the more story-oriented areas, suddenly you're back in the gauntlet of enemies running through the nighttime forest. And there is a LOT of nighttime forest. You've never seen so many trees! But they certainly look pretty. One of my biggest gripes would have to be the fact that the game occasionally does not follow its own rules, which inevitably leads to some frustrating reloads. The enemies will sometimes cheap-shot you, for example falling on you while you're in the middle of opening a chest; most of the time you cannot break out of certain "cinematic" moments fast enough and it will screw you fairly mercilessly. Thankfully reload times are fast and the checkpoints for the most part are plentiful and logical. Just minor annoyances when it comes down to it.
It's a fun ride for the most part. I wish I could say that "this is, excuse me, a
fine cup of coffee," but for several reasons it's just a pretty good cup of joe. You take what you can get, though!
love it

This game has beautiful visuals and environments, which is probably why you're even looking at it. I'll tell you right now it's not worth $20, or even $10. Maybe $1-5, depending on how excited you are about H.P. Lovecraft. I do like the overall atmosphere, other than the protagonist's voice, but I'm just going to go over the parts I didn't like so well:
This is a walking simulator, and definitely not what most would consider to be horror. If you watched the one trailer and thought you might spend any amount of time running away from apparitions because they might "get you", well, you'll be disappointed. The focus is instead on figuring out where to go and solving puzzles. Most of the puzzles in the game are so simple you'll probably spend more time trying to find some easy to miss object used to solve the puzzle rather than figuring out the puzzle itself. There were several times I had to ransack an area more than once because I didn't get close enough to something to realize I could open or take it. It probably would have been better if you didn't have to be nearly point blank next to things in order to see that they are interactable.
There are only 2 short game play sections where you can die to something other than just being really silly, and while they aren't too difficult, they feel cumbersome compared to the zero challenge of the rest of the game. Contrary to another review, one of these sections is NOT "RNG-based". Once you even understand you have to actually do something to survive, it's not hard to figure out how to get past it. As soon as I figured out the solution, I immediately cleared it.
(Another review mentioned getting stuck and not being able to move. I had this happen once, maybe twice, but I was able to fix it by crouching. So, if you get stuck somewhere, try hitting LCTRL and moving around before you reset. So, yeah, there are some bugs, also.)
In general, the pacing of certain events are far too slow, and I don't mean that you take forever meandering through areas solving light puzzles. That's fine, for what it is. I mean, whenever there's a scripted event that occurs, it usually takes so long for it to complete (or even to get to the point of the sequence), it sucks any horror or suspense right out of it. In the few instances where it's not so painfully slow it's comical or boring, it's so fast you still can't care. Another thing that is insanely slow is the load screens on "death". They take sooo long, and are boring black screens for most of it. Any time you fail, you want to get back to it as quickly as possible, not stare into the pitch black abyss, bored out of your mind, waiting for the chance.
Once you finally see what the people who are talking throughout the game look like, you'll wish you hadn't. No one's face seems to match their voice, and the facial animations and head movements for "humans" are so poor it will break immersion instantly. And yes, for those who have played,
While we're on the topic, the protagonist talks way, waaay too much. And if you click on a thing thinking he'll say something different or that you need to sit there and investigate it, 99 times out of 100, you get the same long line of dialogue you got the first time, and continue wishing this guy would never talk.
This is my personal opinion, but I don't feel like reading long notes or journal entries while playing horror games. Or atmospheric games. For example, in BioShock, I'd much rather get the audio clips than the files. The voice adds to the creepy atmosphere. This is one of the times it might have been ok (if he had a better voice) if the protagonist actually talked more, to read out the files. There are sooo many of these. If you just want to read all this stuff, you'd probably be better off just reading in general. Say,
?

Conarium is a well crafted and thematic walking simulator with some decent puzzles.
Going to be very clear on this. Conarium is first and foremost a walking simulator but an excellent one.
The game looks very polished and just oozes with the Lovecraft Mythos.
It is in effect a Lovecraftian walking sim.
Which unfortunately makes this game a rarity. Would love to see more games like this and would highly recommend this game espcially for Lovecraft fans.
Pros
- So Lovecraftian it blew my mind. They don't hold back every minute is pure eldritch goodness
- None of the puzzles were frustrating and rarely were they too simple. Good pacing.
- Polished gameplay and graphics
- The attention to detail in terms of lore and the environments is very impressive
- Intersting story. You will feel the urge to finish the game and see how it ends.
- Well considered trophies and collectibles
- Two endings possible (nice surprise I wasn't expecting)
- Very varied sections everything looks gorgeous. Lovecraft's tales come to life.
Cons
- A little short, not as short as some walking sims for sure. I really really took my time and stretched it to 6 hours including idling. Some sections could have used more time to allow them to breathe and allow us to descend deeper into the world the devs have so lovingly crafted for us.
- Only slightly creepy this will vary person to person but a scary game this is not.
- Voice acting wasn't awful but was certainly a weak point.
Recommendation: Worth your money if you like the Lovecraft Mythos and either like or tolerate walking sims. At sale it's a steal.

An unbelievably awesome program! I have waited years to find something like this. It is a VTT (Virtual Table Top) system for playing any RPG you can imagine. Many of the most popular systems (and their various editions) are either pre-loaded or available for a competitve price. All VTTs have that capability but only Fantasy Grounds has the rulesets LICENSED from publishers like WotC and others. So it is the OFFICIAL stuff and not what some greasy dude half put together and loaded to a forum as on other VTTs.
Plus the presentation is epic! Some VTTs have a few bonus gimicks, but once you play FG you will see that the maximum fun and playability is applied with ALL the features you need and more!
However, be aware that the learning curve is sharp for the first two hours. You will open it and be WTF do I click, as it isn't setup like someone's VB app dice roller. Watch a few youtube videos and read a bit of the manual. Once you get a few of the icons down, it's fine after that. Any new sections you come to will be easy because you understand the formating and layout of FG. So hard at first, easy forever.
And the forum on their website is awesome! So many great people looking to help and looking to run games.
100 hour update: Still going strong and the games have been AMAZING! Top tip: watching a couple tutorial videos helped many get over that early learning curve.

Fantasy Grounds is a great tool for role playing online.

While it may be considered a bit on the pricy side, it's price is very comperable to the cost of the books you would normally be buying to play the games, it gets updated quite often, and if you simply don't want to pay for it - download the trial, and play with a game master that has an Ultimate License.  That gives you a fully functioning client and you play for free.  The amount of built in tools and automation for games like D&D 5e is amazing as well.  You can use as much or as little as you like.
The conversions I have purchased have been very well done and worth the money I paid for it.  Having everything ready for me in the program, but fully modifyable is very much worth it.
If you decide to give it a try, do yourself a favor and go to the forums and get involved.  There are a lot of great people that play, there are events like FG Con, and lots going on that you can be a part of.
As someone that doesn't have the ability to sit down around a gaming table with a group irl much anymore, this has allowed me to enjoy one of my favorite pasttimes again.  If you are a tabletop rpg enthusiast, I highly recommend it.

I just finished Broken Age Act 1, the first part of what was previously known as Double Fine Adventure, Tim Shafer's infamous Kickstarter game. It's a beautiful game, and I found myself taking many screenshots which I've now made into a desktop background slideshow. ^_^ The story looks like it's going to a pretty interesting place, and after finishing it, I feel like I might want to replay it to get a better perspective on some things that happened earlier with the information I now have from the end. The characters are fun with plenty of the humor you would expect from Schafer and Double Fine, and the voice acting from Elijah Wood and Masasa Moyo was superb (not to mention Jack Black, Jennifer Hale and Wil Wheaton).
It took me about 5 hours to get through the whole thing, the puzzles for the most part are pretty logical, and not terribly difficult, but there were still plenty of aha! moments throughout. There was only one point where I got really stuck and that was basically just a terrible case of tunnel vision on my part. Overall, I really enjoyed it, and yet I recommend it with slight hesitation, due to not knowing how the second half is going to go. I feel like $25 is near the upper price limit for a shorter game like this one (~10 hours, assuming both parts are around the same length), and while I'm impressed with what I've seen so far and eager to see where the story goes next, it's still an incomplete perspective. If you already love adventure games or Double Fine, I doubt you'd regret it, but if you're on the fence maybe wait for a sale or until Act 2 comes out for the full verdict.

Strapped a kerbanaut to a chair and a chair to a solid fuel rocket. Skipped the instructions manual, called it Coffin 1 and hit the launch button. What?!? He survived!
Some manufacturer got interested enough to pay us to test their stuff. So we made our 1st ground testing vehicle: Dynamite Stick. Performed as expected.
More test contracts! Except these had to actually leave the ground. Plenty of duct tape later, Boom Stick was born. Also performed as low as expected.
You know that story about a guy who jumps off a tall building's roof and as he falls past each floor goes on repeating to himself "so far so good..."? Inspired by that story, but in reverse, we created Blind Flying Brick to test the waters of suborbital trajectories. It made a splash (At least some parts did!).
"We got this!" we thought. "We're ready for an orbit!" and "How hard can it be?" were thrown around at staff meetings. Time to get serious. Some new girl measured some angles or something with her fingers and, after nearly setting her hair on fire with some mind melting calculations (or maybe it was the smell of Jebadiah's toast), we started building Overshooter 1. At Overshooter version 8 we were running a little low on morale, altitude... and kerbanauts.
Enter Pirouette 1... and 2, 3, 4 and 5. We were getting close... to the red line on our budget. Reluctantly, we sold our research and begged the government for a bail-out, which obliterated our already failing reputation. This was do or die! At least for kerbanaut Maltrey Kerman aboard Pirouette 1006 (we added more digits to look cool). 3, 2, 1, ignition! And we got our first orbit!!! A few minutes later, amidst the chaos of cheap champagne spilling over the control consoles, Base was talking to orbiting Maltrey: "What do you mean you got no more fuel?!" "sigh... well, relax and enjoy the view with some tea and biscuits". We will rescue Maltrey, eventually. For now we hired our new ace pilot: MatGun Kerman.
OK, we got to orbit but could we get there and back? Maltrey named our next vehicle: the Orbital Sarcophagus. Great success... at version 107. It was actually version 7 but remember: got to look cool for the sponsors.
Had a contract to escape home planet Kerbin. Just point up and add loads of bang, right? Not quite, we found out. After the trauma of leaving Maltrey stranded in orbit, we weren't going to just send someone into the cold space aboard One Way Ticket. We installed a Stayputnik control probe on top instead of the usual kerbanaut pod. All fine and dandy until we find out, mid flight, that this thing has no stability control! That was an interesting flight, to say the least, but, somehow, we pulled it up, and off.
Then we expanded (or diluted) and got into Tourism and Science with the vehicles Tourist Kebab, Science Blaster and Blewllet. Eventually, tourists weren't happy with suborbital flights and wanted to go rad and risk Maltrey's fate. It became a thing and we started a lucrative business selling Maltrey's Fate t-shirts. Anyway, we upgraded to Tourist Blender and the money was flowing like spilled champagne.
With all the upgrades around the base we wanted to get serious about planes too. The earlier attempts at generating any survivable plane, Pigglet and Ostrich just had too few parts and fewer still that would hold in place during takeoff. We made Duct Taped and had some success with it but we wanted to go further and higher. How could we get across to the other side of the planet or up beyond 10k altitude with our puny jet engine powered planes? Add rockets!
This idea triggered a few of our most daring designs such as the runway launched Rickety Rocket and the pad launched Worse of Both Worlds and YACI (Yet Another Crazy Idea). On hindsight, YACI should probably have been baptised YASI, with an S for Stupid. Rickety turned out to be a great belly lander and YACI/YASI managed to fly half way across the globe despite running out of fuel a few meters from target.
All the while, Fingers Crossed and Fire and Forgotten kept our technology testing programme alive and taught us that, unlike MatGun’s Minecraft sculptures, really long contraptions bend and wobble when you apply ludicrous amounts of thrust to them.
All these adventures and we haven't even reached for the Mun! Just imagine what the future can bring if we have the kerballs to tempt Mattrey's Fate.

It’s predominately explorative with truly admirable atmosphere. The atmosphere has that spot on unsettling and alien feel. All the while spelunking an ancient caverns and tombs filled with mystery of an eon race. Along the way you’ll be presented with vivid dreams and encounter hallucinations. These are mainly to flavor the Lovecraft mythos and story. There’s plenty of trophies that reference Lovecraft’s work ranging from iconic relics (such as the Elder Thing) to his written works.
Throughout the game your journal will record any documents, notes and secrets you collect. However the tasks, which you’re prompted briefly in what to do next, aren’t record in your journal. So, if you want to recall the task, it won’t be there. You’ll be blindly guessing in what to do next to progress but, depending how you play, you may encounter this a few to several times. Still, it would’ve helpful for tasks to be recorded in the journal.
The controls are rather simple: most of the actions revolve around the mouse from interactions to opening your inventory. Dozens of objects in the game can be examined and gyrated, but most neither serve a purpose nor meaning. There’s some of hands-on puzzles to solve during your play through. Majority of the puzzles are quite simple and the rest may require minor intellectual effort. In other words, the puzzles are weak in this aspect of the game.
The story itself is passable and the voice-acting is mediocre but isn’t neither great nor bad. However the story, as I’m going to say emphatically, is rather short. If you’re like me, who leaves no stone unturned, explore every nook and cranny, you’ll probably finish roughly around five hours. Otherwise if you prefer to play in a steady pace, you’ll likely finish in less than four hours.
As of build 1.0.0.5, there’s a movement bug in the game. May or may not encounter this but here’s a link to my topic with the solution if you encounter it:
It does contain spoilers, you’ve been warned.
Alas, the puzzles are easy to solve, you’ll get lost here and there, and a short passable story but Conarium is still an enjoyable Lovecraftian experience. Upon finishing the game, you may start anew (or load a previous saved game) to collect any missing trophies, achievements, secrets, documents and notes. However it isn’t really worth replaying just to collect them all. What hurts this game’s score is the asking price, which is $19.99. A more suitable asking price would be half that or $11.99 at best. I recommend this game, only when it’s on sale, to any Lovecraft fans and newcomers to get a sample of the Lovecraft mythos.
My verdict for Conarium is a 7/10.

Fantasy Grounds feels old, but it certainly has done well in making running D&D5E games much easier. Certainly not friendly to new users, there are certain quirks that you simply must pay attention to. Some "order of operations" are vital in getting the most out of this utility, and while it is expensive if you want "everything 5E", you're really only paying $40 for the program, and the prices for the WotC books are pretty much the same as you'd get retail.
After running a campaign using Fantasy Grounds, I found that the number of tools useable certainly lets the game move forward.  As a DM, the only real complaint I found myself fighting with was the lack of real-estate on a lower resolution. The tablet I am running this program on runs at 1280x800. While usable, I intend to use a secondary monitor for more space to hold things so I'm not having to shuffle stuff around as if I were playing "Papers Please".
With an Ultimate License, my players only had to grab the demo version and connect. It was pretty simple on a local network, and most were very positive about it as it let us focus on what was being done and not the actual math behind it all (though at times we did do manual calculations for giggles when manual rolls were desired.)
In the end, it let us progress quickly through the game, and I'll happily use it again.

WARNING: I recently finished the game on easy mode, so this review is not reflective of the higher difficulties. Keep that in mind. I am posting a positive review to slightly offset the negativity the game has received, which is not entirely warranted in my opinion. While the game is not perfect, it was an enjoyable experience.
The plot is a twist on the conventional spy uncovering a consipracy plot, and there are a variety of choices that can be made on how the main protagonist reacts to a given situation. These choices can affect the plot depending on the choice, and it feels like they matter which is a big plus. I won't spoil the tough choices, but you can be professional with your colleagues, or act emotionally, which can lower your reputation and potentially make things difficult in the long run, such as having no backup.
When I mean long run, I mean about 14 hours, which was my finishing time, although there is potential replay value, and a harder difficulty playthrough would most likely take longer. The characters could have been fleshed out more, and I would like to have been given more information on what happened with the characters in the past, but I'm guessing that would have been in a prequel (if they made one!)
In terms of game mechanics, I experienced no major bugs throughout my playthrough. The graphics are decent by 2010 standards, and I had no issues with framerate and textures, unlike other reports. The gunplay is good if accuracy is improved in the skilltree, and if weapons are used as intended. The accuracy of the guns can be a little low relative to how much they're upgraded (e.g I had a pistol with 5 upgrades that was very inaccurate), but it is only a minor issue, and to be fair I should have upgraded the pistol more, if I wanted it to be more reliable.
The missions have a great amount of variety, ranging from Moscow to Taipei and a lot in between. The late stage bosses, while interesting, are a little tricky, but that is to be expected, and difficulty alone should not be used against a game. The melee feels a little clunky across the board, but again, I am nitpicking. Also, the hacking on easy mode is a cinch, so anyone struggling in that area should turn the difficulty down, since I would be surprised if anyone could fail at the hacks in the generous amount of time they give on the lower difficulties.
Alpha Protocol is by no means a bad game, and even though I am typically a casual, impatient gamer, I did not want the plot to finish. It is likely I will play the game again in the future, and would recommend it anyone who likes FPS games. Additionally, even if you don't like role playing, stealth or hacking, you should try it since these elements do not overwhelm the game, and add depth to an otherwise generic game (sorry if that sounds harsh).

Let's get one thing out of the way: If you're a creative type, especially a writer of any persuasion, Alan Wake is worth a playthrough just for the subject matter, namely the nature of dreams, the unconscious, and the creative process, and how they are all tied up in each other. Any professional fiction writer will tell you that they often don't know where their "ideas" come from -- they might as well just come straight out of the proverbial ether, and to anyone else it sounds like superstitious mumbo-jumbo. But the truth is, it often really does come out of left field, left field being that ocean of subconscious impulses and images that is constantly roiling in everyone's heads. A writer's job is paying attention to those images when they do show up, when most people can comfortably ignore them, and that makes it a tricky business. That's the gist of what Alan Wake deals with, and if anything, it's worth it to see what the game devs have to say about it.
Is it a GOOD story? Well. That is entirely up to your interpretation of the events in the game. And I'll mostly leave it at that. I'll give some of my impressions in no particular order: If you like the show
, you'll like this. If you like David Lynch's stuff, you will like this, particularly for some of the music and very obvious homages to things like
,
and perhaps
. That is to say, if you want things to make sense in a linear way, forget it. It's actually a little bittersweet to play through this if you are a big fan of Lynch, because while Alan Wake is very very obviously a love letter to the "weird stuff happening in a little town" genre, and it really does nail some of the spooky imagery that Lynch is known for, the characters and the dialogue fall disappointingly flat. It's a very rough imitation of the unforgettable dialogue of
,
, etc. I can't fault them that much for that, because at least they tried. Enough of that.
Gameplay is pretty technically tight with satisfying, challenging gunplay mixed up with light-source mechanics -- you weaken things with your flashlight, and then blast them. It's fun and keeps you on the edge of your seat most of the time. But, and this just may be my low tolerance for the same damn thing over and over, there are many times later in the game where you wish you could just get it over with. The pacing is a little annoying and predictable at times; when you would appreciate a chance to just wander around in the more story-oriented areas, suddenly you're back in the gauntlet of enemies running through the nighttime forest. And there is a LOT of nighttime forest. You've never seen so many trees! But they certainly look pretty. One of my biggest gripes would have to be the fact that the game occasionally does not follow its own rules, which inevitably leads to some frustrating reloads. The enemies will sometimes cheap-shot you, for example falling on you while you're in the middle of opening a chest; most of the time you cannot break out of certain "cinematic" moments fast enough and it will screw you fairly mercilessly. Thankfully reload times are fast and the checkpoints for the most part are plentiful and logical. Just minor annoyances when it comes down to it.
It's a fun ride for the most part. I wish I could say that "this is, excuse me, a
fine cup of coffee," but for several reasons it's just a pretty good cup of joe. You take what you can get, though!

Upon installation, you might notice that the text in the game is garbled, unplayable at first. The game is encoded in Japanese, so you need to change some settings to see the Japanese text. In order for the game to work on Windows 10, go to: Control Panel\Clock, Language, and Region, then click on Region. In the Region popup, click the Administrative tab, click on Change system locale to Japanese (Japan), and restart your computer.
Now, here's the tricky part. I don't know Japanese. And if you don't, either, it can be pretty frustrating to play. I remember messing around with it when I was little, so I sort of know what to do. But for those of you who don't know what things to click, go download Google Translate on your smartphone, select Japanese -> English, Then take a picture of the screen, highlight the words, and it'll be instantly translated. Then, remember what those symbols meant, and enjoy the game!

The interface is great and well laid out, with the ability to apply a custom skin to enhance the mood. The functionality also matches the interface and is robust and very polished.
The way that the adventure planning pieces feed encounter data into the map/tokens and combat tracking is great. I was able to flow seamlessly between narrative time and combat encounters, and as a DM, I had everything I needed where and when I needed it.
The combat tracker is basically a one-stop shop for DMs. I can see all the relative stats and statuses for each creature in the encounter, including monster stat blocks. There’s no need for virtual “page flipping” to use multiple creatures, and when presented within the initiative tracker, this makes it very easy to play multiple monsters without slowing down the pace of play. Combined with the easy maps and tokens, FG enables a very smooth encounter management experience, which results in faster, more immersive combats.

I'd say Alpha Protocol was average. I expected more out of it. I've read praise on this game for it's dialogue choices and how they actually impact the game. I agree with this statement but only to an extent. There is really only one ending to this game, and depending on some of your choices earlier the various characters you've encountered will be copy pasted appropriately. This was a let down, though I enjoyed the conversations and how you had to decide the proper way to manipulate the different characters in the game. I wish the dialogue options weren't timed
I liked how the players are able to decide how they want to complete a mission. From what I remember none of the missions forced you to be stealthly or to go in guns blazing other than the boss fights. I spent some points leveling up pistols and assault rifles, and I must say the pistols especially were overpowered. Being able to aim a critical hit while being in cover was too much. Chain shot got crazy too. I could win any fight while using no more than 7 bullets. The pistol was way better than the assault rifle also which made no sense. The AR was so ridiculously unable even with upgrades.
I wish choosing to wear civilian clothing was utilized more. There are only two missions that slightly change depending on whether you chose to wear civilian clothing or not, and even then it's only a slight change in the conversation with no effect on the outcome. Also for other missions where you meet with people, sometimes civilian clothing would be automatically chosen for you. I think forcing you to decide the appropriate attire for a mission would have been more immersive.
I appreciated the fact that you could do the missions in any order. After Saudi Arabia all of the locations open up to you. The order you choose does have an effect on your future missions and encounters which I thought was awesome. It makes me want to replay the game later and do everything differently. I just wanted the environments to feel a little more lively. Searching rooms for safes, computers, and other loot was fun, but most of the areas in Alpha Protocol felt dead. They were lacking that oomph.
Buy Alpha Protocol if you like action RPGs. Despite it's flaws, I think it brings something special to the table that I hope other games adopt.

I have the ultimate license, so that anyone can play in my games without having to pay a dime (they can use the beta version). It took me over a year to get the courage to try out the program, as it seemed very intimidating, but after I looked at tutorials online and tried it out for myself with some friends, I found that it is very easy and fun to use.
I have used this and Roll20, and I must say that Fantasy Grounds is far superior for a number of reasons. First is the price. With Roll20, the free version is okay if you're just a player, but as a DM, you need to upgrade. With Roll20, you don't buy the program and it's yours. Instead, you must "rent" it by the month or year with a subscription. With Fantasy Grounds, once you buy it (at once, or through monthly payments), it's yours to keep. One thing I will say about Roll20 is that as it uses Google Hangouts, you can see and hear each other in chat, where Fantasy Grounds does not have a chat function yet. My group uses Razer Comms, a free team voice chat program by the company who makes gaming peripherals. One of the many cool functions is the ability to speak in a racial tongue, and the words will be seem by others who speak the same language. Those who don't will only see strange glyphs which match the language. For example, Dwarvish and Elvish match the runes that were on the code wheel from the original SSI Gold Box game, Pool of Radiance(!). It's got a very nice combat system, where players can simply drop their attack die onto an enemy, and the program will automatically add modifiers, know if they hit, and even deal damage and conditions. It can even do the critical hits and fumbles for you.
Something else to keep in mind is that if you want to be the DM, you will have to have at least the $39 version of the game. With that one, you can play in games with others who have paid for the $39 version, as well. If you get the Ultimate license for $149, then you can play in anyone's games, and you can host the game for people with the free demo version. Also, you'll need to purchase the rulesets for the games you want. For example, You can get the D&D 5E basic rules for cheap (or maybe free), but you're better off getting the full core books to get all the races and classes. At about $40 - $50 apiece, it isn't cheap. Also, the official modules cost around $35 each. I will say, as I own all the offical books and modules, that it's worth it in the end. Sure, it's easy to make your own adventures with PDFs and understanding the format, but all the work is done for you with the purchases.
All-in-all, it may seem a little costly and intimidating at first, but me and my group who live thousands of miles away are having a blast every Monday night. Your best bet is to get the free trial, watch some of the videos online, and jump in someone's game as an observer. You'll be hooked. Just remember that it isn't a "video game" of D&D. It helps keep track of rules, and it's still just a tabletop for playing with friends. Definitely recommended, if you have the extra money.

I initially wrote off Life is Strange as a game I had no interest in playing. Why on earth would a game about teenage girl drama interest me; a 25 year old guy? Then it just so happened that I started watching a playthrough of the game on YouTube and discovered that there was much more to Life is Strange than the vaneer of teen angst had led me to believe. Needless to say, I had to play it for myself.
Whilst the game still has a light drizzle of cringe on top (the dialogue can be wonky in places), it doesn't at all detract from what's underneath. Life is Strange is the premier iteration of the "Telltale Adventure Game," DONTNOD having stolen that crown right out from under the titular studio.
While Telltale games are more than happy to tell you that; "Your choices WILL have consequences!" before inevitably ending the same way no matter what you choose, Life is Strange actually makes good on this promise, with events drastically changing depending on what you've done leading up to them. Of course, the ending is still going to go in one of two distinct directions, but I didn't feel at all cheated when the end finally came.
The real star here is the time travel mechanic, which you'll use to either solve puzzles in creative ways, or alter the flow of conversations with an array of memorable characters. It elevates that game from what would be a dime-a-dozen Telltale-like game, to one I'd recommend above all others.
If you like Telltale games, or are looking for games with engaging stories, then you owe it to yourself to give Life is Strange a whirl. If neither of these apply to you, then you can safely give this game a pass.

The Political Machine 2016 is a fun satirical political simulator that allows one to navigate the Electoral College with their favourite Presidential hopeful. Below is a short PRO's and CON's with the game, as well as a tl:dr
PROS:
* Though satirical, the strategy is very deep
* Cartoonish presentation is eye-pleasing
* Character Creation
* Great chance to Role Play as Trump/Sanders etc.
* Playing on either political side feels different. You won't be exploiting the same political strategy as both a Republican and Democrat
* Fun Multiplayer
* Devs are adding additional characters to the game (eg. Michelle Obama, Nancy Pelosi) as well as new game features like Random Events
* Able to randomise political issue importance, state wealth, voting power etc. = Great Replayability
CONS:
* UI Bugs (This review was published in the final days of early access so they may be gone by the time you read this)
* Those who played TPM 2012 say this is a lazy reskin (I never played 2012 so cannot comment on that)
* Inconsistent Difficulty for beginners- Bumping up the difficulty on games slightly (eg. Challenging -> Tough) can make the game very difficult
The Political Machine 2016 is a greatly enjoyable strategy/simulator of the trainwreck that is the Electoral College. Many of the negative reviews are from those who played the 2012 Political Machine where not much has changed in this version. Though this is lazy, the developers are adding new content in the form of updates. I reccomend the Political Machine 2016 for those who are new to TPM series and those who have an interest in basic US politics.
tl:dr
Fun, strategic reskin of the Political Machine 2012. If new to the series, buy. If you played PM2012, wait for sale.

- Driving feels good, not perfect, but gives the whole 'action movie' aesthetic the game was going for, and I like that.
- Great Soundtrack
- Combat feels amazing compared to most games in the genre. Guns feel like they have some heft behind them, and the takedowns are really well animated. They truly do portray a man with nothing else to lose and a vendetta against everyone who stands in his way.
- Ammo is fairly limited, which makes you play a lot smarter. Whilst in Mafia II cops dropped ammo, they do not in Mafia III. While you can shoot up mobsters in distilleries and warehouses all day long, get into a prolonged gunfight with the cops and you're gonna need to make good use of melee takedowns.
- Stealth plays a lot better in Mafia III than in Mafia II. You can play stealthily pretty much whenever you want, rather than only at key points.
- The story is phenomenal. It's really well told, all of the characters are believable and the interviews of various characters are a nice touch, too. Bringing back the playable character from Mafia II, Vito Scaletta, was a good move, too, tying in all 3 Mafia games.
So clearly there is a lot I like about the game. Here are some cons, though.
- The FPS is locked at 30FPS, though it's already been announced that this is getting fixed, so if you're buying this game any more than a week after release, you can most likely ignore this.
- Still only 3 radio stations :/ I think for a game on this scale there should have been at least another couple of stations...
- Civilian AI is thick as sh*t. Drivers will pull U-turns at annoying times, crash randomely for seemingly no reason, and pedestrians react unrealistically to someone firing shots. They will run towards the nearest telephone to call the police, even if that means running towards you. Also, only civilians that are very close to you will react to gunshots. People who are a fairly short distance away will continue as normal.
- The 'Wanted' system from Mafia II is no longer a thing. Personally I really liked that system :/
In all fairness, even with those cons, the game is still really nice to play. Hostile AI, especially during combat, plays fairly well, and listening to some of the mobster's conversations with one another while you sneak about is hilarious, such as a couple of guys talking about how one guy's wife dragged him to the cinema to watch '2001: A Space Odyssy'
I'd give this game an 8/10

My thoughts so far:
Pros:
- The story is really good, but they did take alot of shortcuts.
- Combat is awesome, and really impactful.
- The Animations are really really good.
- The Realism: You can't just run past an army of enemies, most often you will die trying. Taking cover is also important for survival.
- The racism seems quite toned down, not as bad as i thought it would be. Cops barely bother you, and the white people on the street don't really say much if anything either. The black people keep talking about Martin Luther King, and starting a revolution. (Even had a woman say they should start a revolution, and 2 seconds after say that she was gonna call the cops on me. So i'm quessing she's not really that dedicated to that idea.) The only racism you'll really experience is from the cinematics, the store owners and the southern union.
- The open world: You will be marked for killing by enemy gangs, thus sending hitmen to kill you whilst you're roaming the city. Enemy gangs regurlarly respawn around the map, although fighting them outside of missions doesn't really feel that satisfying.
- The stealth gameplay is alright, but also way too easy. Guards can outright see you, and still just walk slowly up to you so you can stab them. They should react much faster and more hostile, whilst warning others that you're here, not walk up to you as if you're some rare unicorn they don't wanna frighten. And if hit squad is after you, and shoot at you or your allies whilst your hiding from the police, the police will automatically find you, even though neither enemies knew your location.
- Dividing territory between partners is a really cool addition to the game, and the personalities of your partners gives you lots of reasons to prioritize the one or the other. Also, lots of cool unlocks!
Cons:
- The Story: It sucks that the NPC dialog is so pointless, really just a filler most of the time. There were times when you would enter certain rackets expecting to hear or see some f**ked up s**t, but i was disappointed repeatedly. At one point one of your partners might turn on you for no reasonable reason, and it just annoyed me how pointless it was.
- The Realism: The driving SUUUUCKS. It makes sense for this point in time, but driving is absolutely horrendous, i truly hate it. If you wanna turn, you have to slow all the way down, or you will slide further in the direction you came from, instead of drifting towards the turn. Also the acceleration on most cars is so bad, you're better off running from the cops than grabbing a car. Atleast then you can hide in alleys, take cover, and shoot back.
- The game is the hardest in the beginning, and as you upgrade equipment throughout playing, it only gets easier, and easier. I personally feel like it should be the opposite.
- Unlocking doors and various other things: It's really just an annoying puzzle to delay your entry. Some might like this because it gives you the illussion that you're skillful when you click those two times when it goes green, i personally just find it annoying and a waste of my time and energy.
- The AI is disappointing, and i hate that enemies just pop up around the player. One minute im escaping the police, the next second there's a cop car that just appeared right infront of me. It's so ridiculously annoying.
- End Game: It pretty much doesn't exist... much like Mafia 2, all you can really do is rob stores and fight cops. The best i could find was 3 mobs standing around on a corner, 2 seconds after they were dead, and i was once again bored.
- Rather repetetive, i wish they would do more with the missions. They definitely need to be bigger and require more tactical gameplay.
Final thoughts on story: (no spoilers)
Killing Burke: Pretty good death scene
Killing Vito: Great death scene, i felt so bad afterwards.
Killing Cassandra: Next to nothing happens, which is so freaking disappointing.
Worth the money and I definitly can't wait for the update of Act 2 of the game later this year!

I'm also one of those weirdos that are really into Lovecraft for some reason. And this is pretty much just all of the Lovecraft and none of the racism. I mean it's a better adaptation than Dark Corners of the Earth in that it doesn't turn into a bad shooter two hours in.
It's also very much focused on the narrative, doing the whole Amnesia thing minus monsters and works more or less as a point and click adventure and... I'm ok with that. I've never been a fan of monster encounters in these games. It's an unpopular opinion but this genre works better without a heavy mechanical focus. There's only one bit where you have to run away from a thing in this one and it's predictably rubbish. But it's mercifully over in two minutes so it's fine, everything's fine.
That said, if you're not into walking around, looking at things and reading stuff as a core mechanical conceit, avoid like the plague. I liked it but I also like Lovecraft and appreciated the references, and I was also really into Gone Home so I guess what I'm trying to say is that Conarium would have been better with lesbians in it.
It's also really short and the voiceacting is more terrifying than the horror.
I guess it's a qualified recommendation from me. It's nothing ground-breaking but it's a decent Lovecraftean fan service and a cool little adventure thing with the occasional decent puzzle and a pretty great atmosphere.

I have the ultimate license, so that anyone can play in my games without having to pay a dime (they can use the beta version). It took me over a year to get the courage to try out the program, as it seemed very intimidating, but after I looked at tutorials online and tried it out for myself with some friends, I found that it is very easy and fun to use.
I have used this and Roll20, and I must say that Fantasy Grounds is far superior for a number of reasons. First is the price. With Roll20, the free version is okay if you're just a player, but as a DM, you need to upgrade. With Roll20, you don't buy the program and it's yours. Instead, you must "rent" it by the month or year with a subscription. With Fantasy Grounds, once you buy it (at once, or through monthly payments), it's yours to keep. One thing I will say about Roll20 is that as it uses Google Hangouts, you can see and hear each other in chat, where Fantasy Grounds does not have a chat function yet. My group uses Razer Comms, a free team voice chat program by the company who makes gaming peripherals. One of the many cool functions is the ability to speak in a racial tongue, and the words will be seem by others who speak the same language. Those who don't will only see strange glyphs which match the language. For example, Dwarvish and Elvish match the runes that were on the code wheel from the original SSI Gold Box game, Pool of Radiance(!). It's got a very nice combat system, where players can simply drop their attack die onto an enemy, and the program will automatically add modifiers, know if they hit, and even deal damage and conditions. It can even do the critical hits and fumbles for you.
Something else to keep in mind is that if you want to be the DM, you will have to have at least the $39 version of the game. With that one, you can play in games with others who have paid for the $39 version, as well. If you get the Ultimate license for $149, then you can play in anyone's games, and you can host the game for people with the free demo version. Also, you'll need to purchase the rulesets for the games you want. For example, You can get the D&D 5E basic rules for cheap (or maybe free), but you're better off getting the full core books to get all the races and classes. At about $40 - $50 apiece, it isn't cheap. Also, the official modules cost around $35 each. I will say, as I own all the offical books and modules, that it's worth it in the end. Sure, it's easy to make your own adventures with PDFs and understanding the format, but all the work is done for you with the purchases.
All-in-all, it may seem a little costly and intimidating at first, but me and my group who live thousands of miles away are having a blast every Monday night. Your best bet is to get the free trial, watch some of the videos online, and jump in someone's game as an observer. You'll be hooked. Just remember that it isn't a "video game" of D&D. It helps keep track of rules, and it's still just a tabletop for playing with friends. Definitely recommended, if you have the extra money.
