ADHD: Trackher is a single-player split-screen

classic-arcade style game. At first, it's fairly simple. Shoot enemies in a top-down vertical shooter on the left, collect resources and materials and avoid danger on the right.
At the time of writing, it appears most of the gameplay takes place on the right. The player can completely ignore the left side of the screen, though not destroying enemies will significantly increase the difficulty on the right, as the enemies can actually cross from the left screen to the right, and the right screen ship has no weapons or defense of its own! Each level, or "Tear" is increasingly difficult, but more rewarding. Additional enemies and hazards, as well as point bonuses, appear. Tear 3 is by far the most difficult but fun experience you will have in the entire game. You continue as usual, but your screens may flip upside down, your controls may reverse, or your screens may even swap sides!
Aside from a few balancing acts that could enhance the game, such as allowing the left screen ship to take damage, there is a lot of fun to be had with ADHD: Trackher. The graphics are pretty, and the sound design is fairly interesting, even if it needs a bit of pollish.
This game is still clearly in early-acces, as basic features and options are missing. The game runs smooth, but is locked into (presumably) 1080p resolution. This writer's display does not support 1080p, thus the UI is either cut off or rearranged and overlaps. The gameplay is completely unaffected, however.
Aside from a few balancing acts (only the right-screen ship's death results in a game-over), this game really is a lot of fun! Once you top the leaderboards, however, there is no incentive to keep playing. Starting any game will completely clear your current leaderboard position. The game does use this as a challenge fairly well, but if you lack the confidence to top your old high score, you're better off creating a new Steam account and purchasing the game again if you don't want to risk losing your bragging rights. Personally, I've never been one for leaderboard domination, so I have no problem starting fresh again each time to explore what the game has to offer.
Slight issues like this are to be expected from early-access titles, so there is absolutley no harm in givng this game a shot. ADHD: Trackher is very much worth the $8 price tag. Give it a try if you're a fan of classic arcade games or 2D shooters! I'll probably buy this game a second time when the Nintendo Switch port drops!

You've likely already heard a lot about Broken Age as it's been covered in a lot of media... Long story short, it's the adventure game that was publicly funded using Kickstarter, the man behind it is Tim Schaefer (of Full Throttle / Grim Fandango / Psychonauts fame), and was touted to be a revival of the adventure game genre.
Whether they've succeeded seems to be open to personal opinion, with the majority that don't agree disliking either the art style (which you can see in the trailer and screenshots, and I think is gorgeous), or that the puzzles are too easy. I'll come back to that point in a moment.
The game itself is charming and always interesting. There are two protagonists, you pick one at the start and begin to play through their story. They are in completely different worlds (one science fiction, the other fantasy), and you can swap between the worlds to experience the other's story at any time. This gives you the opportunity to take a break and return with fresh eyes, or just mix up the pacing. These two separate story-threads do start to show hints of coming together towards the conclusion of the games first act (whilst act two will release later this year as a free update).
One thing the game doesn't have is particularly tricky puzzles. It is worth baring in mind that as only the first act of two so far, the second act has been promised to have more difficult puzzles when it launches. I don't think the puzzles are SO simple to be insulting, but you certainly won't be stuck on any puzzles for longer than a couple of minutes. Most solutions are readily apparant with a little thought, and there's usually enough clues through the environment or the character's comments that you soon realise what needs to be done.
I fully recommend it for anyone who enjoys a good story. As an adventure puzzle game it's a little on the easy side, but the story-telling, dialogue and superb voice acting, setting and music all make for an interesting experience regardless. If the second act has harder / more complex puzzles that's a bonus, but I personally feel there's enough to enjoy here.
(Full disclosure, I backed this game on Kickstarter for $30 / £19)

- Gorgeous visuals: Great play of light and dark, some stunning idyllic mountain-ish background settings (see screenshots/videos)
- Interesting theme. City dude with writer's block going on vacation in remote town which is being taken over by an omnious dark presence controlling people and things; battle between dark and light; a lot of psychologial mindplay and questioning whether it is all actually happening or not; manuscript pages scattered around that describe the events before Wake has them happening to him and the townsfolk.
- Game is designed like an episodic TV thriller. Theme is packed into a damsel-in-distress story which is not totally chliché all over, but I don't know, is love the only thing that keeps heroes going on in fiction? There is more to life than that, there are other ambitions and there can be more reasoning. But I guess it serves as some kind of red thread.
- Gameplay has interesting ideas: Getting attacked by dark figures from multiple sides in small spaces, dodging their attacks (melee mostly), "burning" away the darkness that has captured them with a flashlight and shooting them, using other light sources for area-of-effect attacks or as defense barriers and seeking them as beacons of hope and restoration. Sometimes however it felt repetitive and (on my difficulty setting) too easy in it's execution. The game wants you to feel constantly haunted by the dark presence, there sure is enough action, but once you understand how to dodge and fight the enemies there is some lack of challenge, and with it the feel of being threatened boils down somewhat.
- Settings sometimes become rather repetitive too. Many levels play in rather dense forest and rural areas. Which makes sense gameplay- and (I assume) geographical-wise. Most enemies attack you with melee, they would pose no threat if they were engaging visibly from longer ranges, but sometimes it felt a bit tedious and I just wanted to get out of those forests. Or maybe that was (at least partly) the feeling the devs were intending to create?
- The game comes with some bonus "episodes" originally released as DLCs on the Xbox. They were very entertaining and refreshing, they advance the story further, add more interesting mindplay ideas and also bring in some refreshments gameplay-wise (you interact more with your surroundings, "summon" objects and light sources, not easy to explain but makes a lot of sense in the context of the story and mindplay.
Overall a nice-looking, thoughtfully crafted and well optimized (it was running like a charm on my computer) episodic story-driven action thriller with an appealing "hero", some interesting gameplay ideas and some noteable music too (rock band Poets of the Fall has provided some tracks with perfectly fitting lyrics, and those songs are cleverly put into the game as there is a "rock band" (two old geezers somewhat past beyond their time) in it too loosely resembling PotF.

+ Plot feels as though it has plenty of thought put into it, with many branches that play out based on your decisions & dialogue choices; consequences often feel as though they have some weight behind them
+ Solid voice-acting for the most part (not entirely)
+ Can form alliances with several factions & characters as the story progresses
+ Ample things to do in-between missions, such as preparing for major operations by securing intel, or purchasing better equipment, etc.
+ Many dialogue options boil down to decisions between the tone of, & implications behind, the tone of your reply; A refreshing change of pace from the standard formula
+ RPG elements are generally favorable in the way they were implemented
- Hit detection is often atrocious
- Aiming reticle is perhaps the worst I've yet seen implemented
- Shooter mechanics are generally lackluster at best, infuriatingly unpolished at worst
- Visuals & animations feel underwhelming even for the year of release, & have certainly not aged well
- Enemy AI is horrid across the board; boss fights manage to be an even more painful experience
- Terrible quality of animations

In my gameplay I almost romanced a mercenary, got great friends with another merc group's top agent and got pals with russian weapon traffickers and spared an arab terrorist who in turn helped me with info. There aren't evil in this game. Just money, power and connections, and you choose who you trust, like or kill as soon as you can, and it feels wonderful even after 7 years after release.
Bugs... oh right, the bugs. Nothing gamebreaking happened with me, but seen floaing men, palm trees without leaves, got shot through a wall by an enemy standing in a wall. Some animations, and the super-narrow sigh-cones should be reworked for stealth as it's a bit too easy, and the mouse acceleration is a pain until getting used to.
Even with it's weird controls, it was a treat to play.

When this game was originally released, it, like most of Obsidian's work, was riddled with bugs, and it didn't quite live up to the lofty expectations that the developers had heaped upon it. However, having been patched long ago, and without the specter of hype hanging over it, Alpha Protocol is an excellent little game.
The gameplay is fairly standard stealth fare, sneaking up on people, performing takedowns, shooting from the shadows, and so on. It all works quite well, and there are RPG mechanics that add further abilities to better refine your preferred method of sneaking. My main criticisms regarding the gameplay are twofold, but related. First, every weapon besides the pistol is useless if you take a stealthy approach to every mission (and given that this is a STEALTH GAME, one assumes that's what you're looking for), as only the pistol can be silenced. Second, if you decide to go on a shooting spree with your other weapons, you'll find that the game immediately becomes almost trivially easy outside of boss battles, where stealth isn't an option. That having been said, these facts do little to impact the core experience, outside of being mildly irksome from a design standpoint. The stealth itself is quite good, it's easy to intuit what areas enemies can see, and you're given a number of gadgets and abilities that help you avoid detection. Another criticism would be that gadgets are only particularly useful on higher difficulties, and outside of that, are mere curiosities.
The narrative is where Alpha Protocol shines. The main plot is a fairly standard espionage story, but you have a great deal of control over the fine details. Much like Telltale's The Walking Dead, you don't do much to affect the gameplay in any big way, you still play through all the same missions. However, the choices you make will affect the context of those missions, and can alter a large number of scenes, as well as determine some of the options available to you. Various "Perks", small bonuses for your character, are available based on your dialog choices, and your choices during missions can affect what equipment is available to purchase, available "Intel" (purchaseable bonuses that make upcoming missions easier in some way), and your relationship with NPCs (which can affect how the story plays out in significant ways). The many small variations based on every possible combination of choices give Alpha Protocol a great deal of replay value (a good thing, given it caps out at ten to fifteen hours per playthrough), and you may find yourself experimenting with the order in which you complete missions, just to see what new lines of dialog become available.
Of course, the reason you'll want to see every line of dialog is because the writing is impeccable, and easily the game's strongest point. Dialog is snappy, with characters trading witty banter like a more serious-minded variant of FX's Archer. The cast does a fantastic job of portraying their characters, with even minor characters proving quite endearing.
All in all, while it has its design flaws, Alpha Protocol is an well-made game, and provides an experience you won't find anywhere else. I recommend it wholeheartedly for any fans of stealth games or dialog-heavy games like Mass Effect and The Walking Dead.

This game was in my wishlist for a very long time. Alpha Protocol has some flaws like bad interface and incomplete tutorial, but there is one flaw that ruins it all.
The game has no "save when you want" feature, and it brings more problems than one would expect. Even in tutorial, when you learn everything for the first time, you expected to perform the tasks in one try or you will have to replay a whole sequence again, not just the task that needs training.
It's worse in dialogue: you can never slow down or pause conversation (without concealing subtitles), never ask to repeat a phrase. Game doesn't wait even for you: you have to choose the line with timer ticking. It could be tolerable, but in order to speed up the player they made you choose from paraphrases. As a result you never know what your character will say. How bad is it? Very bad.
I'll explain. When my agent had the first conversation with his colleague (a lady who specialises in weapons), selection of "Sarcastic" line means that protagonist will say "Don't worry, babe, my 'gun' is alright". That's not even a humor. To reload this you'd have to replay for a couple of minutes and repeat everything from the last checkpoint.
And another problem: when a new big mission starts, you receive a briefing: fast, long dialogue with multiple choices. If the players fails to hear something, missclicks, or chooses "Sarcasm" and wants to replay, they are screwed: after the dialog the game saves. It's a checkpoint, there is no way back! You can use one of manual saves (they are just your copies of autosaves, so there is seems to be no reason to bother and make them regularly). If you're anything like me and have no manual save, you need to start a new game. If you do have the save, the game will waste only a few minutes of your time for something as simple as reloading.

Are you someone who hasn't played the games and is curious about this installment? That was me two weeks ago.
The Political Machine 2016 is definitely a novelty for the politically inclined. In the game you have the option of living out a political fantasy to run for President or you want to see how your candidate fairs against opponents with you as ytheir mastermind, or you just like simple simulators. It is no doubt with the selection of candidates to choose from and create that you have a multitude of ways to play the game.
The game works by choosing your candidate and who they are matched up against. You have the option to randomize populations and issue importance as well as set the pace of the game and dictate starting funds. The beginning of the game starts wit ha rush to score endorsements then transistions to building up funds and political capital (which allows you to buy cronies that can affect yours and your opponents ratings in a state as well as cut advertising and gain awareness). Then you use a strategy of setting headquarters and making ads as you go across the US winning states favors.
To gain the support of the public you have to talk about the issues with the five starting issues being centered around the perceived importance (by the devs) from the state. To expand your talking points you have to lay down a headquarters in the state. You can run advertisements on if you favor/oppose or if your opponent favors/opposes the topic to sway opinion. The more you talk about an issue in the state, the more important it can become.
Typically, the candidate who has the most votes, wins the game.
So where are the games faults? For right now it would have to be a lack of features that could make it a truly interesting and engrossing sim.
Features that should be added:
Debates
Primary Season
Random Events that Dictate Public Opinion on Topics
A main issue thats available to a candidate for each state (Bernie Sanders - Income Inequality, Donald Trump - Immigration)
More varied questions during talk shows
Different types of talk shows
Steam Workshop
Overall, I think its a decent game worth the $10 you pay for it. It is a bit lacking in features but I have put 10+ hours into it and will probably play out my Bernie Sanders campaign fantasies until the election is over.

As a Lovecraft fan I loved this game, very beautifully made and a good story. Upon buying this game however I expected it to be your typical Amnesia-esque horror game, where you have to avoid monsters and solve puzzles etc etc. I'm quite a big fan of pretty much all the games Frictional Games have released (Amesia, Penumbra, Soma) and thought this game seemed it would be quite similar in atmosphere and mechanics.
However I was quite disappointed that it is more of a 'interactive first person movie' sort of game. There's a lot of walking, reading and listening, but not much action. The puzzles were okay, some of them stumped me but it was just because I hadn't looked around enough. It was easier for me to find the 'secrets' than actually progress in the game sometimes. It was actually pretty short too, I expected it to be longer but it only took me about 3 hours to complete, which was annoying, I really wish there was more to it, because it wasn't until I got to almost the very end I felt quite invested in it and that the story was starting to fully develop.
One of my main problems with the story however was that I felt like there was no goal, it was kind of just keep going forward until something happens. A lot of stuff was left unexplained and forgotten which kinda sucked too, I feel like they could have done much more. But that being said I know it's a small team and what they accomplished was actually pretty cool.
At some points things felt pretty creepy, and I did enjoy that it wasn't exactly the easiest game as well. The atmosphere was great and the game ran very well. Overall I would definitely reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys the works of Lovecraft.

A deliberate, and satisfying callback to the classic 90's adventure game. What I love about Broken Age is that it is exactly the game creative director Tim Schafer wanted to make when the idea sprung up in his enigmatic little head. In an industry insistent on pumping out the same pattern of homogenous, committee designed, focus tested, hormonal teenage boy marketed, soulless piles of cash-grab slog with each installment, we finally have a game of the modern day that is the blooming manifested wonder that its developer always wanted it to be.
Broken Age is unique and intriguing. It is charming and imaginative. It has character, heart, sincerity, and a level of unmatched artistic talent. The puzzles are challenging without being frustrating. Its two parallel stories run together with seemingly minor connections, but have similarities that pair together thematically, and the ability to switch between the two stories at any time ensures that boredom is impossible. I can recommend Broken Age for a lot of reasons. It really is a gem, and if you enjoy a good story, puzzles, and smiling, you'll enjoy this too.

Broken Age is a point 'n' click adventure game with lovingly created visuals that just pop on the screen.  Those that played the Lucas Arts and Sierra classics from the golden era will feel right at home with the interface.  This is part 1 of a 2 part game so there is more to come and after finishing the first part, I am slightly curious to know how the story will play out.  Reason I say slightly is because there are a few issues with gameplay and story.
I'm not sure whether it's because this was a first part of the game and the game wants to gently lead you into more complex puzzles, but the puzzles felt overly simplistic for an adventure game.  There were hardly any times where you're required to combine items or think too hard for that matter, and every item's use is practically hand fed to you in the form of dialogue clues.  The only struggle was making sure you collect all items within a scene.  I missed one item in a particular scene and it took a half hour of aimlessly trying all items on all characters and making sure I had exhausted all dialogue options before I discovered I had missed picking up that item.  Ironically, I felt just as frustrated as Shay (one of the main characters in the game) who was being coddled in the spaceship.  I hope part 2 will amp up the difficulty.
The second issue is that the story stays rather flat throughout the whole game.  For me, all the characters seem a bit dull and lack any charisma or personality.  It's definitely not akin to Monkey Island where the lead character although a goofball, would make me laugh at the idiotic things he'd say or do to overcome obstacles or be ridiculed by NPCs for the same reasons.  On that note, I found clicking through the dialogue in Broken Age was merely to progress the story further and didn't enhance the experience at all.
So would I say I'm looking forward to part 2?  Sort of.  I'm curious to find out how the story unfolds but that's about it.  Maybe I placed too many high hopes that this would be similar to Monkey Island or Grim Fandango but it's falling short so far..
It's not fair to giving a recommendation based on half a game so I'm just going leave it for now.

Score updated. It seems like woods area is poorly balanced. Game recovers itself from a disaster very fast after you get an advanced weapons like flares and flashbangs. Its amazes me how this game is faulty by design.
At the begining game feels great, combat is intence, but doable, and you have just enough ammo and resources to make progress. Graphics are good too. I was really interested to finish the game.
But later in the game(that's only a second chapter):
* You will be spammed by respawning hordes of enemies.
* You will have to save your ammo, but you really can't do that because of tougher enemies and respawning 3-4 at a time. Ordinary enemy takes 3 shots before he goes down, and tougher ones takes much more. Since you can't kill them all you have to avoid them and run.
* You can't sprint for a more than 5 meters before Alan burns all his stamina and starts to walk. Enemies catch up with you in a few seconds. You can use flashlight to make them keep the distance, but since they can throw their unlimited axes and knives that doesn't really helping. You have to use dodge mechanics.
* You can't use dodge mechanics reliably when multiple projectiles are incoming and while you dodging 1-2 axes at once enemies are closing in.
* Game suggests you to explore to find missing pages to unfold some plot, possible collectibles and ammo, but if you go explore you will be spammed by enemies you can't kill because you will run out of ammo.
* Enemies could spawn at point blank range behind a tree you stand by, behind a boulder, even behind your back. You turn around to see if there is enemies - no, but in an instant there they are ready to strike.
* Poorly ballanced ammo placements and sooo low max ammo cap is the last nail in game's coffin.
To sum up you can't fight back because of ammo, you can't outrun because of stamina, you can't explore because of respawns, you can't dodge reliably, you can't keep enemies at distance with constantly discharging flashlight.
I can't believe combat in this game is sooo broken and gameplay is so unrealistic.

Story is alright, I mean... I've never played a platformer with a memorable story. It does have some nice voice acted dialogues though.
The whole setting is grim, and don't expect too much from the graphics, they're good enough to pass the concept of the game... meaning if you play this - do it because you like puzzles and platformers, not for any other reason.
The price of $9 definitely sounds like they were building too much on this one when developed, so get it instead during a sale / bundle, as the content you get here is simply too short and not very polished (stuttering, repeating graphics, clunky movement).
Overall a decent game if you're into this kind of thing, 6.5/10 from me.

I find this game a little pretentious. It is like the sort of writing you would expect from a high school kid. Someone who thinks that adding long winded explanations and if you don't use a word over five sylibles in every sentence it will be ignored. Kind of juvanile really.
The combat isn't up my street either really. I find that by focusing the torch on something directly in front of you the game sends in enemies from the flanks on purpose because it is trying to force you to move. But the fact you need to degrade enemies shields with light before you can kill them means the entire thing just ends up feeling cheap. You have such a limited amount of vision at the sides that enemies which have ranged attacks or that I don't see more often than not end up sledge hammering me in the back of the skull, before I've even had a chance of dodging.
Also the ability to evade enemies and run in this game is downright broken. The game actually advises that you sometimes evade enemies and run for the safety of light but normally the enemies are faster than you and will just slaughter you the second your back is turned. That coupled with the fact that the combat in some areas feels so limited that you just want to run away, you end up trapped between a rock and a hard place.
The game is very linear, and the gameplay is quite tedious. You just know that in every chapters sooner or later you are going to go tumbling down a cliff or get knocked out and end up in the dark, running through the woods trying to get from point A to point B. Running into a constant stream of enemies that sping up when you cross a threshold. It does break up the gameplay with the odd tweak like some vehicle driving and the fact you have to search for light sources and often this involved starting up generators using a small quick time mini-game type thing.
But negatives asside the game is very good. It has a fantastic atmosphere and a very intriguing story. I am a science nerd by nature so anything that pulls and messes around with space-time and the fabric of reality and multi-verses is right up my street. I like the fact that it has a good amount of twists and turns and it does break up the action using well placed radios to listen to about local events and the TV shows which mess around with physics ideas and weird sub-plot.
Also this game is very good at making you low on ammo. For the most part anyway there are some annoying areas where they will place an obscene amount of ammo in a massive box right where there is a boss, so you basically have unlimited ammo if you can get to it. Kind of pointless really but when you are out in the wilderness you do want to concerve your ammo because if you aren't careful you will run out.
There are a variety of weapons and picking up different types of torches as you go along is a nice twist.
The game is based around Alan Wake, a writer who's wife gets locked away in some unknown place and there is a woman who captures Wake and forces him to write a story. A story which when finished will allow the woman to regain her life. Somehow though Wake manages to write his own escape into said story at the same time and it is this escape that you are playing out. As you go along you pick up manuscript pages which give insite into the world and is a kind of progressive narrative. You find them as you move along and some searching is often needed though I have not deviated massively from the path and I have found the majority of them.
There is also a rather stupid addition of finding coffee thermos flasks at random around the place. Which kind of make sense if you find them in a cafe or in someone's kitchen but when you find them out in the middle of the woods on a rock or just happened to have been left on the tracks of a piece of lumberjack equipment it kind of seems idiotic.
But overall this game IS very great. Though I don't worship the virtual ground it is made on, I do see how people can like it. If you are a gamer looking for a great story, this is for you. Don't expect a top-top end performance overall but it is still a great adventure. If you aren't sure waiting for a sale might be the best option.

Alpha Protocol is one of the most original games you'll find, and it's Sega's only good PC game. It was developed by Obsidian Entertainment of New Vegas fame, a team that definitely knows their way around an RPG. But how did they do with Alpha Protocol?
The game's presentation is decent. The graphics aren't the best you'll find from a game of this age, but they aren't bad and they aren't the main focus of the game. I will say that the faces all look realisitic and full of expression and they are very well animated. However, the rest of the animations are just horrible across the board, perhaps with a few exceptions. The worst of these is the sneaking animation, in which Mike bobs up and down in a weird, unnatural way. It will take time to get used to these stilted animations. The voice acting is of quite a high standard and all lines are delivered believably. The soundtrack is surprisingly good and gives an interesting movie vibe, and the whole game actually feels rather cinematic - an achievement for an RPG.
The story is nothing groundbreaking. Basically you're a guy named Mike Thorton who gets recruited by a completely deniable ultra-secret government agency called Alpha Protocol. After a typical RPG-style tutorial mission reminiscent of an Elder Scrolls "tutorial dungeon", you're sent to Saudi Arabia to investigate some terrorists. However, it quickly becomes apparent that the agency you're working for is serving some shady corporate interests that break more than a few laws, and you end up turning into Jason Bourne after the first three missions, after which you're tasked with stopping an arms manufacturer from starting world war 3 because of the Military Industrial Complex. It's not really original, but the excitement comes from the way it is told.
On that note, the gameplay. Firstly, I will say that this game is rather geared towards consoles and on my PC the keyboard controls were pretty much broken. Suffice to say that this is best played with a controller. Secondly, I don't understand what the fuss is with the gameplay. Apparently the idea of having to spend time aiming is foreign to some people, but the original Deus Ex used similar shooting mechanics and I found both games fine. Pistols and martial arts are the game's most overpowered weapons (unsurprisingly, it's a spy game after all) with most others being optional extras. The gameplay isn't the game's strong suit but the hacking, bypassing and lockpicking minigames are fantastic (if you play with a controller, otherwise you're screwed) and strike a good balance between luck and skill. But who plays an RPG for the gameplay? The dialogue mechanics are where the game shines and it's fantastic to judge the characters and carefully choose whether you want to be professional, flirtatious, witty or a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Another standout is the mission selection. You can choose what order to do your operations in and this has ramifications on the game's story, which was a nice touch.
Overall, Alpha Protocol may be a little rough round the edges but it's still worth your time and is my choice for 2009 game of the year.

This game is fun and humorous, but also pretty basic at the moment. Given that it's Early Access, I expect more features to be implemented. I know multiplayer is on the horizon, and it seems like it'd be a fun way to kill an hour or two with a friend, since it has a board game type of feel to it.
My wishlist for the full version:
1. Some sort of primary season. It's probably a lot of work to incorporate the full primaries, but I think having some sort of national debates that behave similarly to the way the game handles media interviews would add another layer of fun to it. Maybe break it down into "Early Primary States," "Super Tuesday" and "The rest of the primary season" as a way to avoid feeling dragged out. I just think it'd be fun to have to simulate a campaign against the other members of your party, then shift back to the center to win a general election. And really, the primaries are where candidates say the most outrageous things anyway.
2. Related to the above, debates. The debates are among the most attention-grabbing parts of Presidential campaigns, but they're omitted entirely from this game.
3. Slightly more interactive fundraisers. Right now, you just click "fundraise" and get some cash in your campaign. Something as simple as selecting "Exclusive VIP fundraiser," "grassroots fundraiser," etc. and then selecting the target demographic to make fundraising more dynamic than just "Go to California if you're a Democrat, go to Texas if you're a Republican, click the button and get money." At the moment it just feels more like a stamina bottleneck than a real mechanic.
4. The ability to raise issues from your platform. Right now, you can only give speeches and create ads about the issues that are important to the state you're in. You start out with access to just the state's top 5 issues, and then that gradually expands as you build awareness and campaign infrastructure. It makes sense, but it also doesn't allow much of an opportunity to introduce niche issues to the campaign. In real life, Donald Trump made immigration a major issue, Bernie Sanders made income inequality a major issue, etc. In the game, if your candidate has a more niche issue in their platform you'll probably never get to actually give a speech or make an ad about it. If I want to create a candidate with "fixing infrastructure" as their main issue, it should be an uphill battle to make people care about that issue while my opponent is talking about things like Obamacare and unemployment, but in the current framework of the game it's virtually impossible to even talk about the issue until the very late game when you're not going to be able to build your campaign on it. Some of the issues that never come up aren't even particularly niche - things like global warming, Planned Parenthood/abortion rights and fighting ISIS rarely come up, but they're major issues of this campaign season.
5. The ability to have your running mate do something. Right now, you just stash them in a state and they provide an awareness boost, basically making them just a beefed up consultant. Given that, choosing a running mate is pretty meaningless. In real life, running mates are used to balance the ticket - a more hardline candidate chooses a moderate running mate, a more moderate candidate chooses a hardline running mate, etc. A running mate should be a meaningful choice, and they should be able to bring some kind of boost to your campaign.

From a players perspective it's excellent and everything you could want/need/desire from a Table Top simulator.
From a GM perspective it's excellent and allows you to control everything you need to.
The interface could definitly use some work and polish, the learning curve can be staggering and initially a little overwhelming. But if you spend a few hours tinkering and watching the tutorials available you overcome it quickly. Also, as with everything nowadays, check youtube, and watch some of the content and how-tos there. They're an excellent step by step resource. Also the developers on Steam are quick to respond and really take the time to answer every question and lend a hand. Probably best support team for a game I've run across.
While I use it for playing Pathfinder it supports a variety of RPG's and allows for homebrew rules in all of them. I haven't decided if I like that the rulesets aren't binding. If a level 1 Fighter is only supposed to have 1D10 + con for hitpoints he can still write 50 in the block and the program allows for it. Really all that means is that the GM needs to look over every character to make sure there aren't any mistakes. Which is the same thing you have to do sitting around the table. Also, as far as I can tell there is no way for casters to memorize their spells. So they need to be tracked manually, which is a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for the GM, but also no different then if you were sitting around the table and started wondering why your level 5 wizard says he's going to cast his 4th fireball of the night.
Something I love from both a Player and GM standpoint is the language options. If you're characters speak Orc or Giant and they have to negotiate with these creatures the GM can set his language settings to the appropriate language and type in the game and it will come out in that language. The player(s) that speak that language will also see it in their program language (ie English, or French) finally making them useful. It adds a lot of depth to negoitations and allows the player to really feel the knowledge means something. It is interesting (and often amusing) to see how one player or another diseminates information to the rest of the party. OR in one case totally screws his companion, doing him a favour and haggling the price of a suit of amour from a Dwarven blacksmith my bard decided to pay back the fighter for a precieved slight buy not dropping the price as far as he could have.
Fantasy Grounds is an excellent resource for those looking for a virtual Table Top. Again, there is a very steep inital learning curve, but by watching the tutorials and (even more important) some of the youtube content and how-tos available you can overcome it fairly quickly. Once you get the feel for it everything really flows. I haven't found another program that does everything Fantasy Grounds does as well as it does. There are tons of things you can do once you figure out the nuances. Granted, that does take some time on the part of the user. But I don't know any GM's that do homebrew campaigns that aren't willing to put in the time.
Ultimately the the major drawback to Fantasy Grounds is the cost. While you can get your games created manually imputting everything this takes an exorbiant amount of time on the part of the GM. To have access to everything for your particular RPG it is very expensive. Granted it's not as expensive as buying the hardcopies, but it not cheap either. Especially when you consider that the content your given doesn't give you the same as what you'd see in the books. I don't see any reason why the program couldn't come with an assortment of tile sets already available in the program. There are ways around buying tilesets but like finding them and imputing them takes a lot of time.

Really great game. It follows a really cool 80's style with gory fast-paced gameplay, along with a decent storyline. The game is a lot of fun, and I've really done all you can do here, so I'll be a better guide for whether to buy this game or not.
First off, this game has some really fun gameplay. It focuses on a ranking system, where you unlock masks that give little bonuses and special weapons you can find spawn in missions. These masks give some replayablity since getting every single one gets hard to do and each has their own fun strategy. Other than that, it gives a really fast paced game where all you have to do is clear each room. It sounds simple, and it is, but it's all about learning the timing and the best way to kill each enemy, and becomes pretty easy to beat each level once you learn the idea of how to beat it. Now, I think that actually also adds replayability because the "hard" games like Dark Souls has it to where it's always hard, and it's less about getting the timing right and more about learning how to fight, which is just improved as you play the game, and no matter what any point in the game will be managable once you learn it, instead of constantly learning in the "hard" Hotline Miami and putting it into play later on a second playthrough. The story is pretty good, but there isn't much to say about it. After you start playing the game a second time, you start to search for all masks, and in the process, collecting all of the letters in the levels (collectables). The really cool thing about this is that when you complete the game a first time, you don't really know what happened and what's going on, and why it happened; when you collect all of these letters and find out a secret code you figure out the game's world and everything there is to know, and it's really satisfying.
This game is just made well, and you can see it. Everything feels really exciting and you actually sometimes can get scared, or amused, or angry, and it feels good. No matter what you experience, there is always a sense of acomplishment once you finish the fair levels, and it's really nice. It makes you want to play more until there is no more missions, and it doesn't stop there, like I said before. The replayability in this game is a good relief since the story can be beaten in like 8 hours, and beating it again takes like 6 hours if you go for completionist second playthough. I am really glad I have these hours and so are most people, and it's really an experience everyone should get to feel.

My comments are strictly from the perspective of a D&D 5e DM.
Prior to getting Fantasy Grounds, I reviewed other options primarily because FG is fairly expensive - or so it seemed.  As I started pricing it, it became obvious that the D&D components were priced the same as full priced retail manuals - since they come with the full text and in-game functional tables, this makes sense.
Once I saw it as a licensing issue and understood that this really was an electronically functional version of the game manuals, I was on-board - I wanted the real rules and the full text to be available to me.  Since none of my players had an FG license, I also elected to carry the burden and nabbed an ultimate license.
One thing that you will hear is that Fantasy Grounds has a learning curve.  This is true.  I was 12 hours in before I felt comfortable with it and it was another 12 hours before I realized that I could have done a better job on some things.  As time has gone on, I have realized that I want things structured a little differently to better facilitate online gaming - things that don't become clear until you are actually hosting a game.
To learn Fantasy Grounds, I recommend finding a PDF module that you want to use and then 'port' it as a module.  Create a campaign just for the module and start moving the text, creating encounters, and building parcels as needed.  There is a lot to learn, so use youtube and ask questions in forums when you get frustrated.
At the time of this writing, I've DMed a pair of 4 hour sessions via Fantasy Grounds and have had a blast.  My players are satisfied with the visual and rules assistance provided by FG and I am thrilled to be DMing my first campaign since 1989.  I anticipate putting over 1000 hours into this software and appreciate what it allows me to do.

The program claims to support Dungeons and Dragons 4th Edition games and on the very basic level it does.  Provided YOU have every single manual and every single source book, you can create a 4th edtion game and build 4th edition characters.  If you don't have these now out of print and difficult to find books, none of the DLC for Fantasy Grounds will help you.  All of the D&D material is for 5th edition, because that is the only edition for which they have a license.
Now, I would normally not be upset about this.  Wizards of the Coast is notorious for making their previous products obsolete to ensure their current ones are sold like hotcakes, just look at Magic the Gathering (5 months after a collection is completed a new one is released and a year after that neither are deemed "playable" by serious gamers), so I understand that the developers might not be able to get the license for a gaming system the creators want to fade into ancient history.
My problem is that NO WHERE on their Steam Store page or main website does it say that the DLC items are not compatible with older verson of the systems their program supports. I spent several hours searching and eventually found one after utilitizing Google Search and it was an archived post on their Forum Boards about others having a simliar issue with creating 3.5 games.  The Steam Store does, however,  celebrates the fact that the company received permission to create 5th Edition data packs, but does not clarify that the data packs are ONLY for 5th.
I bought the game to help run my 4th Edition D&D game.  I returned it when I realized it couldn't.

I think you can tell by my nickname that I like Lovecraft's stories. So if you think "he loves lovecraftian horror, of course he's gonna like this game", you'd be
correct. There are some issues, but I'm getting ahead of myself. Let's start out by saying what this game actually is.
Conarium is a first person adventure game with some elements taken from games like Amnesia our Outlast. The game is set after the events of story named "At the Mountains of Madness", but it's not a direct sequel, it's more of a spinoff. It has puzzles, the story is driven by finding notes and visions, there are few monsters you have to avoid, there's even short submarine scene where you have to find your way without taking too much damage and there are secrets on every corner.
1. This is a very story driven game. And for the most part Conarium actually does decent job building up the atmosphere of H.P. Lovecraft's stories and keeping it up to the end. Imagine this- you wake up from coma, not knowing how long you've been unconscious. But it must've been a long time, because the power in the entire base is dead. From the very start you can feel there's something seriously wrong with the place. It might seem like you're alone, but you can always feel presence of something else watching your every step. You were part of an expedition tasked with exploring a frozen temple/catacombs in the style of what is described in the novel. Eventually you'll find out, that you're not alone at all.
2. While this is an adventure game, there aren't really any moments, where you'd be stuck wondering what the hell are you supposed to do. So, while this game is tamer than adventure games in the past, this doesn't mean it's braindead. Far from it actually. There was one moment, where I got stuck for a little while, but that happened as a result of me missing a clickable spot. It has never happened with any of the puzzles.
3. The game screws with your head, besides those vision I've talked about, there are transitions between the Antarctic and an old mansion. And if the endings are anything to go by, you really don't know which part is real.
4. The voice acting (at least the main protagonist) is great. The other one- Dr Faust (really?) has a bit strange accent, but it generally works.
5. You can probably guess this one, being Lovecraft fan I enjoyed all the little references and easter eggs that are in this game. Lovecraft is hard to translate from book to other media (there were other games before, but from what I can see, most of them don't look very good) and this game has surpassed my expectations.
6. It'll take you about 8 hours to beat this game. Possibly 9 if you hunt for collectibles.
1. There's a lot of ideas here, but they're not really tied together. It's hard to explain without spoiling a lot, so I'll keep it brief. For instance there is a monster resembling anthropomorphic octopus, that is clearly malicious, but it's never explained what it is, where it came from and it's dropped from the story quickly.
2. This is a big one. Oh boy. While the mood is great, the conclusion of the story isn't. It's a lot of build up that is fun, but by the time you reach the end you'll be scratching your head wondering "that's it?". That's because it feels like there's part of the story missing. The end of the game feels like you're in the middle. It'll make you want more.
3. You've got exploration on top of a completely linear game. Once you've found every secret and collected every document and collectible, that's it. There are no branching points besides one at the very end. A little bit of non-linearity would be really welcome.
4. The submarine section was tedious. You basically have to follow lights and avoid obstacles in the way. The movement is a bit floaty and it doesn't feel like you're in full control.
5. I said you have to avoid monsters, but the AI is completely broken. Crouch and they will never figure out where you are, even if you're right in their line of sight (literally I was walking in front of it). This is absolutely hilarious, but it needs to be fixed.
1. One of the easter eggs is the novel At the Mountains of Madness.
2. The reptilian race from Nameless City is featured.
3. The Great Old Ones are key part of the story.
4. Harley Warren from The statemend of Randolph Carter is mentioned in one of the many documents you can find.
5. You get to meet Shoggots. Well, one of them. For about 10 seconds (I'd like to see more). But you get to hear their iconic "Tekeli-li!", I approve.
6. The device from the beggining of the game and experiments tied to it resemble the story Beyond the wall of sleep.
7. Elder sign
You'll get the most out of this game if you're Lovecraft fan, but you'll enjoy yourself even if you're not. While the endings leave a bit to be desired, the journey to get there is quite enjoyable.

So - How did it go?
As a GM I have been impacted by the learning curve somewhat, but not to the point of giving up. The issues I have had learning FG were similar in scope to the learning curve for the previous VTT.
I did not have the chance to test out combat before our session kicked off, so it was fairly slow to start. Again, the time taken for our first combat was comparable to our first combat in the old VTT.
There were a couple of hiccups at my end due to inexperience. At one point i selected monsters from the bestiary and dropped them on the map, but could not work out how to then get them to the combat tracker. Ended up deleting the tokens, adding the monsters to the combat tracker first, THEN dragging the icons from the combat tracker on to the map. This was for an encounter  I had not prepared earlier, so I am keen to see how the pre-loaded encounters I have input work in actual play.
Spells work very differently to our old VTT. In the old VTT we did not trust the spell system at all and most of the spell stuff was handled manually. What a pleasure it was to have FG manage all the heavy lifting for us with regards to the spells and associated effects.
Speaking of effects - I think i need more help here. Perhaps I was doing it wrong, but things like Barkskin (Copy pasted from the FG forums
) did not appear to affect the characters AC. Some of the included effects did appear to work as intended.
Maps worked well except for 3 issues:
1) Could not work out how to have FG measure player movement during combat (IE - manage how far characters are allowed to move each round). Not sure if there is a way to do this.
2) At one point the map zoomed right in to one area for the PLAYERS only and they could not zoom out. Tried to sync view, re-share etc. In the end I closed the map and re-opened it and that seemed to fix the issue.
3) Seemed that any player could move anyone else's tokens. Is there a way to restrict movement of tokens only to the player who 'owns' the character and the GM? (edit - apparently there is - according to the forums)
Libraries took a few minutes to sync (the first time), but hopefully this wont happen every session.
So - the bottom line:
(TL;DR)
My players LOVED IT. Absolutely no question we will be sticking with FG from now on. I took a big chance buying the ultimate licence, but after last night I have NO REGRETS.
Thankyou Smiteworks for this great product. Keep up the good work!

This is a game by Lovecraft fans, for Lovecraft fans. It hits a lot of the right notes when it comes to Lovecraftian horror and references. That being said, if you jump into this game, you have to go ahead and pre-forgive it for its heavy-handedness when it comes to Lovecraftian horror (it's what you are signing up for, after all). It is very pretty and runs very well. The atmosphere is great. The gameplay aspects are what you would normally expect of a game like this. There is no combat, there are a few failure states, and there is a lot of detective work going on to discover the backstory, exploration, and puzzle solving. When its over, will you understand everything? Nope, you are dabbling in unknowable cosmic horror, after all. Is it the best game in the world? Not really. It's more of an experience where you are trying to figure out what the hell is going on, reading journals, poking around in places you shouldn't be, and waiting for things to go very bad. Will you enjoy it if you are a Lovecraft fan? Absolutely.

Hi-Rez have a bit of a reputation of silently killing off their games. Tribes just got shot out back with no real explanation and a good chunk of Smite players have nothing but negative things to say with updates being very slow, especially compared to similar games like League and Heroes. Paladins is becoming that way because of an absolutely ludicrous decision to completely revamp the card system in OB64, making it basically pay to win.
In Paladins, you had card loadouts that had a 12 point limit, those points being levels you set for the cards so you can't have stupidly overpowered cards and you were forced to either make a balance or focus on only one card. Basically, you were able get cards by either buying them with gold (later essence which I'll get onto) or getting them with boxes. Gold was given out like candy so it was no problem getting the cards you want and nothing really felt too overpowered for the most part. Now what they've done is made every card available but they're all level 1 and you have to permanently level them up by getting dupes in loot boxes. Despite the backlash of Shadow of War and Battlefront 2, Hi Rez thought it would be a good idea to jump on this awful bandwagon of locking away beneficial items with boxes and someone that's either grinded for absolutely ages or paid for loot boxes has an advantage. While they're flimsily trying to balance these cards in competitive (a mode I could barely find anyone playing, personally), there is no limit in quick play. JazzyJeff209 will be better than you because you just jumped in the new patch, or heck, started playing Paladins to check it out and they bought hundreds of loot boxes and levelled up their cards on day one of the patch.
Despite the many complaints about this on message baords and their social media accounts, Hi Rez have barely done anything to even acknowledge the backlash, one member of Hi Rez even being toxic towards the criticism;
Here's a thread where people were complaining as early as the 29th of November with no acknowledgement of any criticism;
This was the breaking point for a lot of people, including myself, but there have been other problems such as having FOUR currencies at one point; gold (free currency that became less frequent after they messed with daily rewards and because of the prominence of the other currencies), crystals (paid currency, fine for a free to play), essence (introduced to replace gold in regards to cards which meant gold was less frequent and most rewards and dailies were replaced with this essence rubbish) and VIP (a second "prestigious" currency you buy with crystals that just wasn't needed. A lot of skins are locked behind VIP and it results in spending more money on crystals for VIP stuff). OB64 removed essence but because of how the new card system is, they've basically pulled a splinter out of the left foot and shot the right. They also keep messing up daily rewards and crystals have become even harder to get without paying. Your only chance now really is the infrequent events they have where crystals are given out for wins.
I hope this negative review is some sort of penance because I am severely disappointed in Hi Rez and in myself for ever spending a penny on this game.

TLDR (Analysis further down): In short, Broken Age Act 1 is a masterpiece, but it is very short. The short length could have meant ABSOLUTELY NOTHING and be absolutely doubly-fine... if not for cut-down tablet-style gameplay, where the most fun part of questing is absent.
This means: "poking around and performing a lot of available actions to achieve an initially non-obvious goal (to get closer to bigger goal)" VS. "clicking around to find a SINGLE next action that will nudge the game to reveal next single action".
So gameplay disappointed me a little. I was very surprised to see that I finished it in 3,5 hours, despite clicking on everything and trying to milk every line of dialogue and funny interaction.
==The long version:==
Any praises for this game could not be more spot on: the sophistication and delivery simply knocks out anyone who has ever seen an animated film, played a quest game or read a good story. In any aspect, this is an artistic triumph. Nevertheless, there are some nagging questions behind the excitement of discovery and heart-pounding plot realizations: namely, does Broken Age succeed as a game? Sadly, this is not so clear-cut.
Every location is a stunning gallery of quirky characters and beautiful backgrounds. But each time, there are only one to four active objects on-screen, and only one way to solve the one puzzle that game feeds you at the moment. The gameplay is, sadly, as straight as an arrow and as bare as a plank. Even if you think and fantasize about how the objects may interact and what it could mean for the characters and NPCs, it ultimately boils down to trial-and-error, simply because there are so few options. Meaning, you are better off sticking everything into everything, because it will take less time than figuring out the answer. No matter how good the story and setup, the actual gameplay is to exhaust dialogue options in any order without a chance of failure, then combine two objects, then repeat.
It may seem like a normal quest experience, but there are good reference points: content-wise, Broken Age Act 1 amounts to about 2 chapters of Curse of Monkey Island. Gameplay-wise, it is less than one (and one of the shortest at that). Curse of Monkey Island had six. Moreover, you can't perform various actions on objects or people, so every step is reduced to one try; one line to make a joke; one obstacle. Whereas classic LucasArts quests were, essentially, a search for a hidden action among the multitude of highly entertaining failures to act. You literally get less bang (trademark Schafer humor, which is still hilarious) for your buck.
So in the end, you fly through very rich and insanely beautiful locations with no time to appreciate or explore them and make mistakes - like you're watching a cool animated show. The locations are packed with possibilities - but the only ones available are the ones you MUST utilize to move the plot along.
The "length issue" is even more sad because of the 2nd part of Velle's quest. I say it this time from a perspective of a writer.
****SPOILERS****
The Meriloft section does nothing to the plot, and doesn't change the character in any way - it's just an interlude to get from Sugar Bunting to Shellmound. It's crazy good looking and ripe with plot possibilities (at the very least, the mystery of the cloud prophet/charlatan who (maybe?) duped these people into his religion). But inside Act 1, it doesn't mean anything at all. It's all the more obvious when you play both characters intermittently: I finished Shay's part (basically a single-part affair) while Velle was in Meriloft, and then he lay unconscious while Vella was getting through Merriloft and then got to actually move the plot in Shellmound. So it's 1 or 2-part vs 3-part (where the middle part is disposable). Again, Meriloft is rad - it's just sad that it doesn't matter much (maybe it will matter more in Act 2? still applies though).
****END****
Anyway, Broken Age still kicks♥♥♥♥♥and is gorgeous. I sincerely recommend it to EVERYONE, not only nostalgic quest players. This includes people who have kids. And maybe especially them. Kids will be super-grateful for this when they grow up. And for a reason.
